Thus degree-zero cocycles are chain maps and boundaries are chain homotopies. Appendix A.1 gives the exact injective functor \(G(F)=\prod_x(e_x)_*F_x\) and its natural monomorphism \(F\to G(F)\). Exactness of \(G\) can be tested even on sections: its maps are products of exact stalk sequences of vector spaces. Let \(C(F)\) be the cokernel of this monomorphism. The diagram of the two exact rows \(0\to F\to G(F)\to C(F)\to0\), applied to a short exact sequence of \(F\)'s, shows that \(C\) is exact: injectivity at the left follows by subtracting a lift from \(F\), surjectivity at the right by lifting in \(G(F)\), and the same subtraction proves equality of image and kernel in the middle. This is a stalkwise argument.

The functors \(G C^q\), for \(q\ge0\), therefore give an additive functorial injective resolution of every sheaf. For a complex \(E\) zero below degree \(a\), apply these resolutions to every \(E^p\). Totalize with the differential \(d_E+(-1)^p d_{\mathrm{res}}\) on the component \(G C^q(E^p)\). In total degree \(n\), only \(a\le p\le n\) occur, so every term is a finite sum of injectives. Denote this complex by \(I(E)\).

The map \(E\to I(E)\) is a quasi-isomorphism. In its augmented double complex, the resolution direction is exact. For a total cocycle, begin with its smallest original degree \(p\). Exactness in the resolution direction allows that component to be removed by a boundary. Proceed to the next \(p\). There are finitely many components on the diagonal; at the final augmented position injectivity of \(E^p\to G(E^p)\) makes the remaining component zero. This proves exactness of the augmented total complex. The construction sends a homogeneous map to its componentwise images under \(G C^q\); the vertical terms cancel in (B.1), so it respects differentials of Hom complexes and compositions.

Hom into a bounded-below injective complex sends acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes. Here is the required homotopy construction. For an acyclic \(N\) and a chain map \(f:N\to I\), start below the first nonzero degree of \(I\). Suppose the homotopy equations hold below \(n\). The map \(f^n-d_Ih^n\) vanishes on \(\ker d_N^n=\operatorname{im}d_N^{n-1}\), using the previous equation and \(d_If=fd_N\). It therefore defines a map on \(\operatorname{im}d_N^n\) by \(h^{n+1}(d_Nx)=f^n(x)-d_Ih^n(x)\). Injectivity of \(I^n\) extends it to \(N^{n+1}\), giving the next equation. Induction yields \(f=d_Ih+hd_N\). Apply this in every shift to see that the whole Hom complex is acyclic. Applying it to the acyclic cone of a quasi-isomorphism proves that Hom into \(I\) preserves that quasi-isomorphism. In particular an acyclic bounded-below injective complex is contractible, by applying that assertion to its identity. Hence a quasi-isomorphism between such complexes is a homotopy equivalence. Explicitly, in a contraction of its cone the lower-left block is a chain map back; the two diagonal equations say that both composites are homotopic to the identity. The homotopy category of these injective complexes realizes the localization of bounded-below complexes at quasi-isomorphisms: replace by \(I(E)\), which inverts those maps, and use the natural quasi-isomorphism \(E\to I(E)\). On injective complexes that natural map is already a homotopy equivalence. This proves the claimed universal localization property and gives the usual \(D^+(X)\).

For clarity about the triangle input, our cone is \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)^n=F^n\oplus E^{n+1}\), with \(d(y,x)=(d_Fy+fx,-d_Ex)\). Cone triangles use the inclusion of \(F\) and projection to \(E[1]\). Their triangle identities can be checked inside the homotopy category. The cone of an identity contracts by \((y,x)\mapsto(0,y)\). The cone of the inclusion \(F\to\operatorname{Cone}(f)\) projects to \(E[1]\) with a contractible identity summand; a section sends \(x\) to \((0,x,-fx)\), giving the rotated last map \(-f[1]\). A square with \(bf-f'a=dh\) induces the cone map \((y,x)\mapsto(by+hx,ax)\); this verifies the triangle-map axiom, including squares commuting only up to homotopy.

For the octahedron of \(E\xrightarrow fF\xrightarrow gH\), take

\[ \operatorname{Cone}(f)\xrightarrow{(y,x)\mapsto(gy,x)} \operatorname{Cone}(gf)\xrightarrow{(z,x)\mapsto(z,fx)} \operatorname{Cone}(g). \tag{B.2} \]

The cone of the first arrow has coordinates \((z,x,y,x')\). Its projection \((z,x,y,x')\mapsto(z,y+fx)\) onto \(\operatorname{Cone}(g)\) is a chain map with section \((z,y)\mapsto(z,0,y,0)\). In the coordinates \((z,y+fx,x,x')\), the remaining summand has differential \((x,x')\mapsto(-dx+x',dx')\) and contracts by \((x,x')\mapsto(0,x)\). The resulting last arrow is \((z,y)\mapsto(y,0)\) into \(\operatorname{Cone}(f)[1]\). Write the first two arrows of (B.2) as \(\alpha,\beta\), and write cone inclusions and projections as \(\iota,p\). The required squares are the identities \(\alpha\iota_f=\iota_{gf}g\), \(p_{gf}\alpha=p_f\), \(\beta\iota_{gf}=\iota_g\), and \(p_g\beta=f[1]p_{gf}\). The last arrow is \(\iota_f[1]p_g\). The composite \(\beta\alpha\) contracts by \((y,x)\mapsto(0,y)\): its homotopy differential is \((gy,fx)\). These are the octahedron identities and its cone triangle, proving the remaining triangle axiom. Shifts and cones preserve bounded-below injective complexes, so these verifications apply to \(D^+(X)\).

The ordinary t-structure also follows from complexes. The good lower cut uses a kernel in its final degree, and the good upper cut uses a cokernel in its first degree. Their cohomology is respectively the original cohomology below and above the cut, with zero cohomology on the other side; the cut triangle follows from the quotient complex and its direct kernel/image calculation. If one object has cohomology in degrees \(\le0\), represent it by its lower cut with zero terms above zero. Resolve the upper cut of an object in degrees \(\ge1\) by the construction above, with zero terms below one. There is no degree-zero chain map between these representatives. This proves orthogonality and all ordinary t-structure axioms used below.

For later use, these models also give long exact cohomology and section sequences. A short exact sequence of sheaves becomes a termwise short exact sequence under \(I\), since every \(G C^q\) is exact. Each resulting sequence of injectives splits on terms because its left term is injective; applying sections therefore leaves an exact sequence of complexes. The connecting map sends a quotient cocycle to the differential of any lift, regarded in the subcomplex. Changing the lift changes this by a boundary, and lifting or subtracting a coboundary proves exactness at each of the three kinds of term. The same argument on the termwise split sequence of any cone proves its long cohomology sequence. These arguments justify the cohomology sequences used in the body of the lesson.

B.2. The actual open-closed recollement

Let \(i:F\hookrightarrow X\) be closed and \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) its open complement. Ordinary inverse image \(i^*\), open restriction \(j^*\), closed pushforward \(i_*\) and open extension by zero \(j_!\) are exact: their stalks are the indicated original stalks or zero. Their adjunctions follow by restricting a morphism and gluing its forced zero values outside the relevant support. For closed pushforward, opens of \(F\) are intersections with opens of \(X\), which also proves \(i^*i_*=1\). For open direct image, sections on \(O\) are sections on \(O\cap U\), giving \(j^*\dashv j_*\) and \(j^*j_*=1\).

There is a stalkwise short exact sequence of sheaves

\[ 0\longrightarrow j_!j^*E\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow i_*i^*E\longrightarrow0. \tag{B.3} \]

It gives the first triangle in (B.5) below. More explicitly, for a monomorphism of complexes \(A\to B\), the cone projects quasi-isomorphically onto the quotient complex: the kernel is an identity cone on \(A\). Thus this use of a short exact sequence really gives a cone triangle, even if the sequence does not split on terms.

The exact left adjoints above show that \(j_*\) and \(i_*\) preserve injectives, and exact \(j_!\) shows that \(j^*\) preserves injectives. Consequently the chain adjunctions, applied to injective targets, give the derived adjunctions, including \(j^*\dashv Rj_*\). The identity \(j^*Rj_*=1\) follows on an injective resolution by restriction.

There is also an ordinary support right adjoint \(i^!_{\mathrm{sh}}\) to \(i_*\). Define \(i_*i^!_{\mathrm{sh}}E\) to be the kernel of \(E\to j_*j^*E\). A sheaf zero on \(U\) is identified with its closed pushforward by (B.3), so this defines a sheaf on \(F\). Any map from \(i_*A\) lands in that kernel, since \(\operatorname{Hom}(i_*A,j_*j^*E)=\operatorname{Hom}(j^*i_*A,j^*E)=0\). This proves the right adjunction. Since \(i_*\) is exact, \(i^!_{\mathrm{sh}}\) sends injectives to injectives.

An injective \(I\) is flabby by A.1. Its sections on \(O\cap U\) extend to \(O\), so

\[ 0\to i_*i^!_{\mathrm{sh}}I\to I\to j_*j^*I\to0 \tag{B.4} \]

is exact, even on sections. Resolve a complex by injectives and apply this sequence degreewise. Since \(j^*I\) is an injective resolution on \(U\), (B.4) gives the second triangle (B.6) below with \(i^!=Ri^!_{\mathrm{sh}}\), and its chain adjunction proves \(i_*\dashv i^!\). Restriction of an extension gives \(j^*j_!=j^*Rj_*=1\) and \(i^*i_*=1\). Resolving on \(F\) and pushing forward gives \(i^!i_*=1\), while disjoint support gives \(j^*i_*=i^*j_!=0\). On an injective open model \(J\), the map \(j_*J\to j_*j^*j_*J\) is the identity, so its support kernel is zero and \(i^!Rj_*=0\). These unit and counit identities prove full faithfulness of \(j_!,Rj_*\) and \(i_*\): the corresponding adjunction identifies maps between two extensions with the maps between their restrictions. All these operations preserve shifts and cone triangles on the models just constructed. This establishes recollement in \(D^+\), allowing complexes unbounded above.

Explicitly, the two triangles are

\[ j_!j^*K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow i_*i^*K \longrightarrow j_!j^*K[1], \tag{B.5} \] \[ i_*i^!K\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow Rj_*j^*K \longrightarrow i_*i^!K[1]. \tag{B.6} \]

B.3. Point support, local excision and the smooth-disc costalk

Write \(i_p:\{p\}\hookrightarrow X\) for a closed point and \(j:X\setminus\{p\}\hookrightarrow X\). Applying exact \(i_p^*\) to the support triangle gives the natural model

\[ i_p^!K\simeq\operatorname{Fib}\bigl(i_p^*K\longrightarrow i_p^*Rj_*j^*K\bigr). \tag{B.7} \]

Here the fiber of \(f:E\to F\) has terms \(E^n\oplus F^{n-1}\) and differential \(d(x,y)=(d_Ex,fx-d_Fy)\). Its projection to \(E\) and connecting map to \(F\) give the support triangle with the corresponding cone sign convention. Formula (B.7) determines the object and its restriction map, not just the dimensions of its groups.

It also computes cohomology supported at \(p\) on every open neighbourhood \(W\). For an injective sheaf \(I\), put \(\Gamma_p(W,I)=\ker(\Gamma(W,I)\to\Gamma(W\setminus\{p\},I))\). Flabbiness makes the latter restriction surjective. A section supported at \(p\) extends uniquely by zero from \(W\) to any larger neighbourhood, by gluing on \(W\) and the complement of \(p\). Thus \(\Gamma_p(W,I)=i_p^!{}_{\mathrm{sh}}I\), independently of \(W\). Restriction to \(W\) preserves injectives by A.1, so the degreewise exact section sequence on an injective resolution proves

\[ i_p^!K\simeq R\Gamma_p(W,K|_W) \simeq\operatorname{Fib}\bigl(R\Gamma(W,K)\longrightarrow R\Gamma(W\setminus\{p\},K)\bigr). \tag{B.8} \]

This is the sheaf-theoretic relative-section calculation and its excision statement. It has been proved from resolutions; no assertion of homotopy invariance of arbitrary sheaf cohomology is being inserted.

For a smooth complex disc and its centre, A.3 gives \(R\Gamma(D,\Lambda)=\Lambda[0]\), and A.4 gives \(R\Gamma(D^*,\Lambda)=[\Lambda\xrightarrow0\Lambda]\) in degrees zero and one. The restriction map sends a constant to the same constant in degree zero. Its fiber is

\[ \Lambda\xrightarrow{1}\Lambda\xrightarrow{0}\Lambda \quad\text{in degrees }0,1,2. \tag{B.9} \]

Cancel the identity pair: the costalk is \(\Lambda[-2]\). Formula (B.8) also proves that this is the costalk in any larger curve neighbourhood with the same local sheaf and disc chart. For \(j_!L\), the point stalk is zero and the boundary term is Proposition 1.1, so (B.7) gives its shift by \([-1]\). For \(Rj_*L\), the boundary restriction map is an identity, so the fiber is zero. These are all the classical assertions of Proposition 1.2.

B.4. Finitely many smooth branches

Let \(X_r\) be \(r\) open complex discs with their centres identified to a point \(p\), with the quotient topology, and let \(k_a:D_a\hookrightarrow X_r\) be the branch inclusions. Each branch is closed. Its complement is the union of the other punctured discs, which is open; conversely the quotient topology restricts to the usual disc topology. The map from the disjoint union of the discs separates the branches. Its pushforward of the constant sheaf is \(N=\bigoplus_{a=1}^r(k_a)_*\Lambda_{D_a}\), since sections on a disjoint union are products of sections on the components and here there are finitely many components.

The constant-sheaf restriction to all branches gives an exact sequence

\[ 0\to\Lambda_{X_r}\to N\xrightarrow{(s_a)\mapsto(s_2(p)-s_1(p),\ldots,s_r(p)-s_1(p))} i_{p*}\Lambda^{r-1}\to0. \tag{B.10} \]

The formula describes the last map on an open containing \(p\); elsewhere it is zero. It is a sheaf morphism, and exactness follows on stalks: away from \(p\) the first map is the identity on its branch, and at \(p\) it is the diagonal \(\Lambda\to\Lambda^r\). Each small neighbourhood of the centre is connected, so the constant-sheaf stalk is indeed \(\Lambda\). The difference map at that stalk is surjective with precisely the diagonal kernel.

Closed pushforward is exact and preserves injectives by B.2. Thus derived sections of each branch pushforward are derived sections of its disc; by A.3 they are \(\Lambda\) in degree zero. The point term is also acyclic. Applying derived sections to (B.10) therefore proves \(R\Gamma(X_r,\Lambda)=\Lambda[0]\), with its specified constant-section identification: the complex is the fiber of the surjective difference map \(\Lambda^r\to\Lambda^{r-1}\). The same argument works after decreasing the radius of each disc. It justifies the neighbourhood acyclicity used in the relative-section interpretation.

Alternatively compute the costalk directly from (B.7). The puncture is a disjoint union of punctured discs, so its boundary complex is \([\Lambda^r\xrightarrow0\Lambda^r]\). This identification is compatible with decreasing radii by A.4 and with the exact stalk colimit by A.1. For \(\Lambda_{X_r}\), the attaching map is diagonal in degree zero. Therefore

\[ i_p^!\Lambda_{X_r}\simeq \bigl[\Lambda\xrightarrow{\mathrm{diag}}\Lambda^r \xrightarrow0\Lambda^r\bigr] \quad\text{in degrees }0,1,2. \tag{B.11} \]

Its cohomology is \(\Lambda^{r-1}\) in degree one and \(\Lambda^r\) in degree two, with all other groups zero. For \(N\), the point stalk is \(\Lambda^r\) and the same attaching map is the identity on \(\Lambda^r\). Its fiber cancels that identity pair and leaves \(\Lambda^r[-2]\). This proves the normalization costalk in the branch model using exact sheaf operations alone. The case \(r=1\) is (B.9); \(r=2\) is Proposition 1.3.

For an ordinary complex node we use its analytic local model \(xy=0\); its two coordinate discs give exactly \(X_2\). For an ordinary multiple point with smooth branches and distinct tangent lines, the same topological model has \(r\) branches. Here is the local topological verification. Choose analytic disc coordinates on each smooth branch. Each branch parametrization is an embedding, and for two distinct tangent lines its two first-order tangent vectors are linearly independent over \(\mathbb C\). Thus the norm of the difference of their linear parts is bounded below by \(c(|s|+|t|)\) for some \(c>0\): restrict that injective linear map to the compact unit sphere. The higher-order remainders are bounded by a quantity smaller than \(c(|s|+|t|)/2\) after shrinking the parameters. The branches therefore meet only at the common centre. A finite union of smaller closed parameter discs maps continuously and bijectively to its image, and the inverse is continuous because the domain is compact and the ambient complex analytic space is Hausdorff: images of closed subsets are compact, hence closed. Restricting to the interiors gives the asserted local quotient topology. The disc charts used here are part of the smooth-branch hypothesis. L.3–L.5 prove that the algebraic normalization separates exactly these smooth branches and is a local analytic isomorphism on each; L.2–L.4 derive the two-branch model from the completed-local node criterion. The explicit cubic below also verifies its branch description directly.

B.5. The displayed cubic and its actual normalization

For \(X:\ y^2z=x^2(x+z)\subset\mathbb P^2_\mathbb C\), define

\[ \nu:\mathbb P^1\longrightarrow X,\qquad [u:v]\longmapsto[(u^2-v^2)v:u(u^2-v^2):v^3]. \tag{B.12} \]

The three coordinates never vanish together, and direct substitution verifies the cubic equation. On \(z\ne0\), write \(t=u/v\). The map is \(x=t^2-1\), \(y=t(t^2-1)\). It identifies the affine curve ring with the subring

\[ A=\mathbb C[t^2-1,t(t^2-1)]\subset\mathbb C[t]. \tag{B.13} \]

To check that there are no extra relations, divide by the monic polynomial \(y^2-x^2(x+1)\). A possible kernel element has the form \(P(x)+yQ(x)\). After substitution its first summand is even in \(t\), and its second is odd. Both must vanish; hence \(P=Q=0\). The function fields agree, because \(t=y/x\) where \(x\ne0\). The element \(t\) satisfies \(t^2=x+1\), so \(\mathbb C[t]\) is a finite \(A\)-module generated by \(1,t\).

The polynomial ring \(\mathbb C[t]\) is integrally closed in its fraction field. Indeed, write an integral rational function as \(p/q\) with coprime polynomials. Multiplying a monic integral equation by \(q^n\) shows that \(q\) divides \(p^n\). Polynomial division and the Bézout identity then force \(q\) to be a nonzero constant. Any element integral over \(A\) is also integral over \(\mathbb C[t]\), using the same monic equation; hence it is in \(\mathbb C[t]\). Conversely reduce a polynomial in \(t\) to \(a+bt\) with \(a,b\in\mathbb C[x]\subset A\). This element satisfies the monic equation \((Z-a)^2-b^2(x+1)=0\), so every element of \(\mathbb C[t]\) is integral over \(A\). Thus this is the actual normalization on the affine chart.

At infinity use the chart \(y\ne0\) and coordinates \(\xi=x/y\), \(\zeta=z/y\). Its equation is \(\zeta(1-\xi^2)=\xi^3\). The factor \(1-\xi^2\) is a unit: in this ring \((1-\xi^2)(1+\xi^2+\xi\zeta)=1\). The chart ring is therefore \(\mathbb C[\xi,(1-\xi^2)^{-1}]\), which is integrally closed by the same coprime-denominator argument with the inverted factors allowed. On its preimage, \(s=v/u\) is a coordinate, \(s^2\ne1\), and (B.12) gives \(\xi=s\), \(\zeta=s^3/(1-s^2)\). Thus \(\nu\) is an isomorphism on this chart. These two charts cover \(X\), proving that (B.12) is finite and is its normalization. In particular the normalization is the smooth rational curve \(\mathbb P^1\).

The two preimages of \(p=[0:0:1]\) are \(t=1,-1\). For \(|x|<1\), the convergent binomial series \(h(x)=(1+x)^{1/2}\), with \(h(0)=1\), has \(h(x)^2=1+x\): convergence follows from the ratio test and the identity by multiplying its power series. The two branches of the cubic are exactly \(y=xh(x)\) and \(y=-xh(x)\). They are graphs over the \(x\)-disc, have distinct tangent lines \(y=x\) and \(y=-x\), and meet only at zero after shrinking because \(h\) is nonzero there. The map in (B.12) restricts to their inverse parametrizations \(t=\pm h(x)\). This verifies the branch model and the two-dimensional normalization stalk for the concrete cubic used in Section 1 (the node calculation).

Finally, this cubic has no other singularities. On \(z=1\), the derivatives of \(y^2-x^3-x^2\) are \(2y\) and \(-3x^2-2x\); their simultaneous zeros on the curve give only \((0,0)\). At its sole point at infinity, \([0:1:0]\), the derivative with respect to \(z\) of the homogeneous equation is \(y^2-x^2\ne0\). Consequently the single-point sequence (1.2) is global for this cubic. On a curve with several nodes it instead holds locally at the chosen node; globally the quotient has a summand at each node, obtained from the same stalkwise difference maps.

Appendix C. Sheaf cohomology of the cone and local orientation groups

This appendix supplies the comparison needed in Section 1 (the cone calculation). Throughout it, coefficients are a field. The spaces considered below are locally compact, second countable and metrizable, and have a basis of contractible open neighbourhoods. The cone neighbourhood, its puncture, its link, and their open subsets satisfy these hypotheses by the explicit geometry in C.3. A deformation retraction is used only after the comparison with singular cochains has been proved.

C.1. The prism and small chains

For a homotopy \(H:Y\times[0,1]\to Z\), write \(v_i=(e_i,0)\) and \(w_i=(e_i,1)\) in the prism over a standard \(q\)-simplex. On a singular simplex \(\sigma\), define

\[ Q_H\sigma=\sum_{i=0}^q(-1)^i H\circ(\sigma\times1)\big|_{[v_0,\ldots,v_i,w_i,\ldots,w_q]}. \tag{C.1} \]

The notation for a bracket means the affine map from the standard simplex with that ordered list of vertices. Expanding the face boundary gives

\[ \partial Q_H+Q_H\partial=(H_1)_\#-(H_0)_\#. \tag{C.2} \]

Here is the cancellation. Deleting a vertex other than the duplicated index \(i\) gives a simplex in the prism over that face, with the negative of its coefficient in \(Q_H\partial\). Deleting either occurrence of the duplicated index gives an interior face shared with the adjacent prism simplex; its two coefficients are opposite. The two unpaired terms are the all-upper face with coefficient \(+1\) and the all-lower face with coefficient \(-1\). This proves (C.2) in every degree, including degree zero. It also proves the formula for pairs whenever the homotopy preserves the subspace. Dualizing gives the corresponding cochain homotopy. In particular, a contraction identifies cohomology with that of a point. The point's augmented chain complex is exact directly: it has one basis simplex in each degree, with boundary alternately zero and identity, and augmentation the identity in degree zero.

For any open cover \(\mathcal U\) of any space \(Y\), the inclusion of small chains

\[ C_\bullet^{\mathcal U}(Y)\longrightarrow C_\bullet(Y) \tag{C.3} \]

is a quasi-isomorphism. This follows from the actual operators (A.5)–(A.6), without convexity of \(Y\). A finite cycle \(z\) becomes small after enough subdivisions, and \(z-S^Nz=\partial P_Nz\), proving surjectivity on homology. If a small cycle bounds an arbitrary chain, \(z=\partial b\), choose \(N\) making \(S^Nb\) small. Then \(z=\partial(S^Nb+P_Nz)\), and both summands in this filling are small: the second preserves the images of the already small simplices of \(z\). This proves injectivity. The same proof works for augmented chains.

Dualizing (C.3) over a field remains a quasi-isomorphism. Indeed its cone is an exact complex of vector spaces. Choose complements to the cycle subspaces degree by degree; the differentials identify the complementary pieces with the next cycle subspaces. This gives a contraction of the cone. Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(-,V)\) to that contraction proves exactness of the dual cone for every coefficient vector space \(V\). Thus this step does not assume finite-dimensional chain groups.

C.2. The actual sheaf–singular comparison

Let \(Y\) have the hypotheses stated above. Every open \(O\subset Y\) admits a compact exhaustion \(E_m\subset\operatorname{int}E_{m+1}\). To construct one, choose a countable cover by relatively compact open sets \(B_m\). Such a cover exists because local compactness and the metric give a precompact neighbourhood inside any prescribed neighbourhood, and a second countable space reduces any open cover to a countable one: for each basic open set contained in a cover member, choose one such member. Inductively take a finite union of relatively compact open sets covering \(E_m\cup\overline B_{m+1}\), and let \(E_{m+1}\) be its compact closure. Beginning with \(E_0=\varnothing\) gives the asserted exhaustion of \(O\).

Put \(E_{-1}=E_0=\varnothing\). For any prescribed open cover of \(O\), cover each compact layer \(E_m\setminus\operatorname{int}E_{m-1}\) by finitely many neighbourhoods whose closures lie in a cover member and in \(\operatorname{int}E_{m+1}\setminus E_{m-2}\). The metric permits this shrinking. Those closures give a locally finite closed refinement: a neighbourhood inside \(\operatorname{int}E_M\) meets no layer chosen after \(M+2\). This proves the refinement property on every open subset, not just on \(Y\).

Sheafify the singular cochain presheaves as in A.2, writing \(\mathscr C_Y^q(V)\). The representative argument there now applies with this refinement: assign a simplex the first eligible local representative, and near a point exclude all the finitely many relevant closed sets not containing it. The remaining representatives agree after shrinking because they have the same germ. Every sheaf section is therefore represented by one cochain. Extending that cochain by zero on other basis simplices proves that \(\mathscr C_Y^q(V)\) is flabby.

On a contractible neighbourhood, (C.1)–(C.2) and the point complex show that augmented cochains are exact. Exact filtered colimits therefore prove stalkwise exactness of

\[ 0\to V_Y\to\mathscr C_Y^0(V)\to\mathscr C_Y^1(V)\to\cdots. \tag{C.4} \]

Its degree-zero kernel is the locally constant functions: a zero coboundary makes values equal along every path in a small contractible neighbourhood. Thus (C.4) is a flabby resolution of the constant sheaf, and A.1 shows that its sections compute derived sheaf sections.

The same representative and zero-germ arguments as in (A.4) identify those sections on every \(O\) with

\[ \Gamma(O,\mathscr C_Y^\bullet(V)) =\varinjlim_{\mathcal U} \operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(C_\bullet^{\mathcal U}(O),V). \tag{C.5} \]

By (C.3), the restriction map from all singular cochains to each complex on the right is a quasi-isomorphism. Refinements commute with those maps. Exactness of filtered colimits, proved in A.1, now gives the natural quasi-isomorphism

\[ C^\bullet(O;V)\longrightarrow \Gamma(O,\mathscr C_Y^\bullet(V))\simeq R\Gamma(O,V_O). \tag{C.6} \]

It commutes with restriction to smaller open sets. It also respects continuous pullback wherever both spaces have these hypotheses: composing a singular simplex with the map defines pullback on cochains and on their germs, and the latter agrees with the pullback of the constant sheaf. The injective comparison in A.1 identifies that map with the derived section map. Consequently the prism proves homotopy invariance for these constant-sheaf cohomology calculations. No such assertion is made for arbitrary sheaves.

For an open \(O'\subset O\), the restriction of singular cochains is surjective on terms because the simplices in \(O'\) form a subset of the basis simplices in \(O\). Its kernel is the relative cochain complex \(\operatorname{Hom}(C_\bullet(O)/C_\bullet(O'),V)\). The termwise exact sequence identifies this kernel with the fiber of the restriction map; the identity-cone argument in B.2 proves that identification. Taking the two natural quasi-isomorphisms (C.6) identifies this relative complex with the relative derived-section fiber. In particular, when \(O'=O\setminus\{p\}\), (B.8) proves the promised relative singular-cohomology interpretation of the costalk.

C.3. Radial geometry and the vertex complex

Give the tautological line bundle \(L=\mathcal O_C(-1)\subset C\times\mathbb C^3\) its induced Hermitian norm, and write \(E=\{(x,u)\in L:\|u\|=1\}\). The maps

\[ E\times(0,R)\longrightarrow B_R\setminus\{v\}, \quad ((x,u),r)\longmapsto ru, \qquad z\longmapsto(([z],z/\|z\|),\|z\|) \tag{C.7} \]

are continuous inverses, where \(B_R=X\cap\{\|z\|<R\}\). The line-bundle description itself is an explicit isomorphism away from zero: a nonzero cone vector spans its point of \(C\), and the tautological vector maps back to itself. In a projective coordinate chart these are the usual coordinate ratios, so they are continuous (and algebraic in the line-bundle statement).

The link of radius \(\epsilon\) is identified with \(E\) by \((x,u)\mapsto\epsilon u\). In a local holomorphic frame \(s(x)\), its coordinates are \((x,e^{i\theta})\mapsto e^{i\theta}s(x)/\|s(x)\|\). These show that it is a smooth three-manifold. Its orientation is the complex orientation of the base followed by the increasing angular coordinate. A change of frame adds a smooth angle locally; the coordinate Jacobian has positive base determinant and angular derivative \(1\), so the orientations agree. The link is compact because it is a closed subset of the compact sphere.

Collapsing \(E\times\{0\}\) in \(E\times[0,R)\) gives exactly \(B_R\) topologically. Only continuity of the inverse at the collapsed point needs checking. An open subset of the product containing \(E\times\{0\}\) contains \(E\times[0,\delta)\) for some \(\delta>0\): cover compact \(E\) by finitely many product neighbourhoods and take their minimum positive radius. These are precisely the small radial neighbourhoods of \(v\). The contraction \(z\mapsto(1-t)z\) proves contractibility of \(B_R\).

All spaces just used are metrizable and second countable as subspaces or local products of the displayed Euclidean charts. They are locally compact. Away from the vertex, those charts give contractible neighbourhood bases; at the vertex the sets \(B_\delta\) do. Thus C.2 applies. In particular \(R\Gamma(B_R,\Lambda)=\Lambda[0]\).

Let \(p_R:B_R\setminus\{v\}\to E\) be the projection in (C.7). It has section at radius \(R/2\); the homotopy \((u,r,t)\mapsto(u,(1-t)r+tR/2)\) stays in that puncture and contracts each fiber. Equations (C.2) and (C.6) prove that \(p_R^*\) is a quasi-isomorphism on cochains and computes derived sheaf sections. The projections agree under restriction to every smaller radius. Hence the exact stalk colimit on an injective resolution gives a compatible object identification

\[ i_v^*Rj_*\Lambda\simeq C^\bullet(E;\Lambda), \qquad i_v^!\Lambda_X\simeq \operatorname{Fib}\bigl(\Lambda[0]\longrightarrow C^\bullet(E;\Lambda)\bigr). \tag{C.8} \]

The first arrow sends a scalar to the constant zero-cochain. Indeed that is the restriction of a constant section on every \(B_R\); the comparisons respect those sections and the shrinking maps. Thus (C.8) identifies the attaching map as well as its source and target objects. The fiber's cohomology is

\[ H^k(i_v^!\Lambda_X)=\widetilde H^{k-1}(E;\Lambda), \tag{C.9} \]

with the usual augmented meaning of reduced cohomology. For connected \(E\), degree one vanishes. Equations (C.8)–(C.9) prove the vertex comparison used in Proposition 1.5. They still require the separate circle-bundle and curve-cohomology calculation of Proposition 1.4 for its numerical dimensions. Finally \(i_v^!Rj_*\Lambda=0\) is the already proved injective support-kernel calculation in B.2; it needs no additional homotopy assertion.

C.4. Spheres, local orientation and coordinate changes

The same constructions determine the local orientation groups in every real dimension. Cover \(S^d\), for \(d\ge1\), by the complements of its north and south poles. Stereographic projection identifies either open with \(\mathbb R^d\); the intersection is \(S^{d-1}\times(-1,1)\), by separating the last coordinate and normalizing the other coordinates. The two-open-cover exact sequence on injectives in (A.9), together with C.2, gives the reduced Mayer–Vietoris sequence. Both opens are contractible, so its connecting map is

\[ \widetilde H^{k-1}(S^{d-1};\Lambda) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\widetilde H^k(S^d;\Lambda). \tag{C.10} \]

For \(S^0\), the two points give reduced degree-zero cohomology \(\Lambda\) and zero otherwise. Induction proves that \(\widetilde H^k(S^d;\Lambda)\) is \(\Lambda\) for \(k=d\) and zero otherwise. This also proves finiteness here without a triangulation theorem.

The puncture of \(\mathbb R^m\) retracts radially onto \(S^{m-1}\). Its ambient space is contractible, so B.8 and C.2 give

\[ i_0^!\Lambda_{\mathbb R^m}\simeq\Lambda[-m] \qquad(m\ge1). \tag{C.11} \]

For \(m=0\) the point functor is the identity. A choice of ordered real coordinates fixes a generator in (C.11) by the connecting maps above. Reflecting one coordinate acts by \(-1\). In dimension one this is the swap of the two puncture components on \(\Lambda^2/\Lambda\). In higher dimensions, use that coordinate as the polar coordinate in the sphere cover. Reflection swaps the two opens, while its action on their intersection retracts to the identity on the equator. The cover differential is a difference of restrictions; swapping the order negates it, and hence negates the connecting generator. This proves the sign assertion in all dimensions.

Every invertible real linear map of positive determinant is joined to the identity through invertible maps. One explicit reduction is Gram–Schmidt: it writes the matrix as \(QR\), with positive diagonal in the upper triangular \(R\) and \(Q\in SO(m)\). The path from \(R\) to its diagonal obtained by decreasing the entries above it stays invertible, and its positive diagonal entries can then be moved to \(1\). Successive rotations in coordinate two-planes move the columns of \(Q\) to the standard columns, keeping the preceding columns fixed; the last column has positive sign because the determinant is one. These rotations give a path from \(Q\) to the identity. A negative-determinant map is a coordinate reflection times a positive-determinant one. The prism therefore shows that a linear coordinate change acts on (C.11) by the sign of its determinant.

For a differentiable change of coordinates fixing zero, write \(\phi(x)=Ax+r(x)\), with \(A\) invertible and \(\|r(x)\|/\|x\|\to0\). There is \(c>0\) with \(\|Ax\|\ge c\|x\|\), by compactness of the unit sphere. On a sufficiently small ball, all maps \(Ax+t r(x)\) avoid zero away from zero. They give a homotopy of pairs to the linear map. Relative comparison and (C.2) therefore prove the same determinant rule for the local cohomology generator. Its signs are locally constant on chart overlaps and multiply under composition; they define the orientation local system.

For a complex-linear coordinate change \(A\), its real determinant is \(\det_{\mathbb C}A\,\overline{\det_{\mathbb C}A}=|\det_{\mathbb C}A|^2>0\). To verify the formula, complexify the underlying real matrix: in the complex coordinates \((z,\bar z)\) it has the two diagonal blocks \(A,\bar A\); determinants are invariant under that change of basis. Holomorphic charts therefore give a consistent real orientation.

C.5. Compact support on an open ball

For a locally compact Hausdorff space and a sheaf \(F\), compactly supported sections are \(\Gamma_c(Y,F)=\varinjlim_K\Gamma_K(Y,F)\), over compact subsets \(K\). Apply this equality to an injective resolution. Filtered colimits of vector spaces are exact, and the resolution computes every derived support functor, so

\[ H_c^q(Y,F)=\varinjlim_K H_K^q(Y,F). \tag{C.12} \]

For a closed compact \(K\), flabbiness gives the termwise surjective restriction to \(Y\setminus K\). Its kernel is \(\Gamma_K\), so the fiber formula (B.8) holds with \(K\) in place of the point. If \(K\subset W\subset Y\) with \(W\) open, a section supported in \(K\) extends uniquely by zero; the injective restriction argument gives excision for these supported derived sections as well.

In \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), \(m\ge1\), the centered closed balls \(K_R\) are cofinal among compact subsets. Their complements are \(S^{m-1}\times(R,\infty)\). C.2 and C.10 identify the support fiber with \(\Lambda[-m]\). Increasing \(R\) leaves the sphere projection and constant-section map unchanged, so the induced maps on the sole nonzero group are identities in these coordinates. Equation (C.12) proves

\[ R\Gamma_c(\mathbb R^m,\Lambda)\simeq\Lambda[-m]. \tag{C.13} \]

The assertion for \(m=0\) is immediate. Transport across a chart proves the same statement for an open ball. In particular its linear dual has its unique nonzero cohomology in degree \(-m\). These are the compact-support and orientation calculations needed in Proposition 2.3. Appendix F constructs the global right adjoint and its compact-support pairing and identifies these local duals with its restriction; the compact ball calculation is one of that construction's proved inputs.

The freely available inputs are Sella's cochain-sheaf discussion and Hatcher's prism and subdivision arguments. The refinement, resolution, comparison, radial maps, support fibers and coordinate signs used here have all been included above.

Appendix D. Integral Thom classes and the circle-bundle sequence

This appendix proves the classical Gysin sequence used in Section 1 (the cone calculation) and Exercise 5. It works with an arbitrary abelian coefficient group \(G\), in particular \(\mathbb Z\) or the field \(\Lambda\). The vector bundles in the theorem have a finite trivializing open cover; a bundle on the compact curve in Section 1 (the cone calculation) has such a cover. No assertion about étale Gysin maps follows from this topological argument.

D.1. Integral small chains, pairs and covers

Write \(C_\bullet(Y)\) for the free abelian singular chain complex, and put \(C_\bullet(Y,A)=C_\bullet(Y)/C_\bullet(A)\). These relative groups are free: their basis consists of the simplices not wholly contained in \(A\). Cochains with values in \(G\) are \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb Z}(C_\bullet(-),G)\), with \((da)(c)=a(\partial c)\). The prism, subdivision and homotopy formulas (C.1)–(C.2) and (A.5)–(A.6) have integer coefficients. Their face cancellations and mesh estimates therefore hold over \(\mathbb Z\) without change.

To dualize the small-chain comparison with arbitrary coefficients, we need more than the field argument in C.1. For a fixed open cover \(\mathcal U\), construct a retraction \(\rho:C_\bullet(Y)\to C_\bullet^{\mathcal U}(Y)\) and an operator \(D:C_n(Y)\to C_{n+1}(Y)\) satisfying

\[ 1-\iota\rho=\partial D+D\partial,\qquad \rho\iota=1, \tag{D.1} \]

where \(\iota\) is inclusion. Induct over the dimension of each basis simplex \(\sigma\), starting with \(D=0\) in negative degrees. Suppose the construction is made on its faces. Set \(z=\sigma-D\partial\sigma\); the induction identity gives \(\partial z=\rho\partial\sigma\), which is small. Choose \(N\) so that \(S^Nz\) is small and define

\[ \rho\sigma=S^Nz+P_N(\rho\partial\sigma),\qquad D\sigma=P_Nz. \tag{D.2} \]

The second term in \(\rho\sigma\) is small because \(P_N\) preserves simplex images. The identity for \(P_N\) gives both \(\partial\rho\sigma=\rho\partial\sigma\) and \(\partial D\sigma=\sigma-D\partial\sigma-\rho\sigma\). If \(\sigma\) is already small, its faces have \(D=0\) by induction, and we choose \(N=0\). Thus \(\rho\sigma=\sigma\) and \(D\sigma=0\). Every term in (D.2) remains in the image of \(\sigma\), so these operators preserve chains in every subspace. They descend to relative chains. Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}(-,G)\) to (D.1) proves the absolute and relative small-cochain comparisons for every \(G\).

The pair sequence follows directly from the degreewise split chain sequence \(0\to C_\bullet(A)\to C_\bullet(Y)\to C_\bullet(Y,A)\to0\): restriction of cochains is onto by extending their values on basis simplices. Its connecting map sends a cocycle on \(A\) to the differential of any extension on \(Y\), regarded as a relative cocycle. Changing the extension changes this by a relative coboundary. This construction proves exactness: a class killed by the next map is represented, after subtracting a differential of a lift, by a cocycle in the preceding complex. The same lifting argument gives the homology long exact sequence.

For \(Y=U\cup V\), there is also a degreewise split exact sequence

\[ \begin{aligned} 0\longrightarrow& C_\bullet(U\cap V,A\cap U\cap V)\\ &\xrightarrow{c\mapsto(c,-c)} C_\bullet(U,A\cap U)\oplus C_\bullet(V,A\cap V)\\ &\xrightarrow{(c,d)\mapsto c+d} C_\bullet^{\{U,V\}}(Y,A)\longrightarrow0. \end{aligned} \tag{D.3} \]

To check this, examine one basis simplex at a time: a simplex in the overlap has two copies with their difference in the kernel; one outside the overlap has exactly one copy; simplices in \(A\) are zero. Dualizing and using (D.1) gives relative Mayer–Vietoris, with the cochain restriction difference \((a,b)\mapsto a-b\). The same argument proves the excision needed below: for a finite union of disjoint open discs about a finite subset \(Z\subset Y\), the cover consisting of those discs and \(Y\setminus Z\) identifies the relative small chains for \((Y,Y\setminus Z)\) with the direct sum of the disc-relative complexes.

The two-hemisphere argument of C.4 now applies to integral singular homology and cohomology, using (D.3) and the integral prism. Reduced homology of \(S^0\) is \(\mathbb Z\) in degree zero: the augmentation \(\mathbb Z^2\to\mathbb Z\) is the sum. The contractible hemispheres and their equatorial overlap consequently give, by induction, \(\widetilde H_k(S^m;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\) for \(k=m\) and zero otherwise. Radial retraction and the pair sequence then give

\[ H_k(\mathbb R^r,\mathbb R^r\setminus0;\mathbb Z) =\begin{cases}\mathbb Z&k=r,\\0&k\ne r,\end{cases} \qquad r>0. \tag{D.4} \]

Reflection acts by \(-1\) on the chosen orientation generator: it interchanges the two hemispheres, reversing their difference in (D.3). The positive-determinant path and the decomposition into a reflection and a positive-determinant map in C.4 therefore prove the determinant sign rule integrally as well. This fixes the fiber orientations used below.

D.2. The product maps and their homotopies

We give the product comparison needed for a trivial bundle. On chains the tensor differential is \(\partial(c\otimes d)=\partial c\otimes d+(-1)^{\deg c}c\otimes\partial d\). For \(\sigma:\Delta^n\to X\times Y\), define the front-back map

\[ A\sigma=\sum_{p+q=n} \sigma_X[0,\ldots,p]\otimes\sigma_Y[p,\ldots,n]. \tag{D.5} \]

For a \(p\)-simplex \(c\) and a \(q\)-simplex \(d\), define \(B(c\otimes d)\) as follows. Take all lattice paths \(w\) from \((0,0)\) to \((p,q)\) with horizontal and vertical unit steps. If their successive vertices are \((i_k,j_k)\), let \(\ell_w:\Delta^{p+q}\to\Delta^p\times\Delta^q\) send vertex \(k\) to \((e_{i_k},e_{j_k})\). Set

\[ \begin{aligned} B(c\otimes d)&=\sum_w(-1)^{\nu(w)}(c\times d)\ell_w,\\ \nu(w)&=\#\{(a,b):1\le a<b\le p+q,\ w_a=V,\ w_b=H\}. \end{aligned} \tag{D.6} \]

Here \(w_a\) records whether step \(a\) is vertical or horizontal. The exponent counts ordered pairs of step positions: the word \(VHH\) has two such pairs and therefore sign \(+1\). Interchanging adjacent unlike steps changes this count by exactly one; all pairs involving any other step keep their contribution.

Here are the boundary checks, including the signs. In \(\partial A\sigma\), deletion of a vertex before the split has its usual face sign and deletion after it has the tensor sign \((-1)^p\) followed by its sign in the back face. They match \(A\partial\sigma\). The remaining terms delete the shared vertex from one of the two factors; consecutive splits give identical tensors with opposite signs, and cancel. For \(\partial B\), an interior face obtained by deleting the corner between unlike steps occurs for both orders of those two steps. Their inversion numbers differ by one and their deleted-vertex index agrees, so they cancel. Deleting a vertex between two horizontal steps removes a vertex \(i\) of \(\Delta^p\). If \(j\) vertical steps precede it, the deleted index is \(i+j\), and deleting a horizontal step changes \(\nu\) by \(j\). The resulting sign is thus \((-1)^i\) times the smaller shuffle sign. For two vertical steps the change in \(\nu\) is \(p-i\), so the resulting sign is \((-1)^{p+j}\), as required for the second tensor factor. The initial and final faces obey the same calculation with \(i\) or \(j\) at an endpoint. Thus \(A\) and \(B\) are chain maps.

For completeness, their inverse homotopies can be constructed on universal simplices. Suppose the homotopy for \(1-BA\) is defined below degree \(n\). In \(C_n(\Delta^n\times\Delta^n)\), take the diagonal simplex \(\delta_n\) and the cycle

\[ z_n=(1-BA)\delta_n-H\partial\delta_n. \tag{D.7} \]

Its boundary is zero by the lower-degree homotopy identity. In degree zero it is zero; otherwise the cone to a fixed point in the convex space \(\Delta^n\times\Delta^n\) fills it. A cone on an augmented cycle has boundary that cycle by the cone formula in A.3. Choose this filling as the universal value, and push it forward under \(\sigma_X\times\sigma_Y\) to define \(H\sigma\). Face restrictions are pushforwards of their corresponding lower-dimensional universal simplices. Therefore the pushed version of (D.7) gives \(\partial H+H\partial=1-BA\) on every simplex. This construction is natural in \(X,Y\).

The other composition is handled on the universal tensor \(\operatorname{id}_{\Delta^p}\otimes\operatorname{id}_{\Delta^q}\). The augmented chain complex of each simplex contracts to one chosen vertex by coning: if \(K,L\) are the contractions, then \(\partial K+K\partial=1-i\epsilon\) and \(\partial L+L\partial=1-j\epsilon\) on the nonaugmented complexes. The tensor operator

\[ T(a\otimes b)=K a\otimes b+(-1)^{\deg a}i\epsilon(a)\otimes Lb \tag{D.8} \]

has \(\partial T+T\partial=1-(i\epsilon)\otimes(j\epsilon)\); expanding the tensor differential cancels the two mixed terms. Consequently every positive-degree cycle in this tensor complex bounds. Induct on \(p+q\), fill the cycle \((1-AB)(\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id})-H'\partial(\operatorname{id}\otimes\operatorname{id})\) with (D.8), and push the filling under \(c\otimes d\). In degree zero the cycle is zero. This proves \(\partial H'+H'\partial=1-AB\).

All these universal constructions stay inside the two simplex images. They preserve \(C_\bullet(X)\otimes C_\bullet(Y_0)\) and \(C_\bullet(X\times Y_0)\) for a subspace \(Y_0\subset Y\). We have therefore proved the relative chain homotopy equivalence

\[ C_\bullet(X)\otimes C_\bullet(Y,Y_0) \underset{A}{\stackrel{B}{\rightleftarrows}} C_\bullet(X\times Y,X\times Y_0). \tag{D.9} \]

The associated cup operation is equally explicit. For a \(G\)-valued \(p\)-cochain \(a\) and an integer-valued \(q\)-cochain \(b\), put \((a\smile b)(\sigma)=a(\sigma[0,\ldots,p])b(\sigma[p,\ldots,p+q])\). The front-back cancellation just checked gives \(d(a\smile b)=da\smile b+(-1)^pa\smile db\). Restrictions commute with this operation, and evaluating on three successive faces proves associativity. If \(b\) is relative, the product is relative. Right multiplication by a fixed closed \(b\) commutes with the differential without an extra sign. It thus commutes with the connecting homomorphisms of (D.3): extend a cochain, multiply by the restricted global cocycle \(b\), and then take its differential. These identities specify the convention for the Thom and Euler maps.

D.3. The Thom isomorphism on a trivial bundle

We first justify the integral chain splitting used here. A subgroup \(H\) of a free abelian group is free. Indeed, well-order a basis of the ambient group and let \(H_\alpha\) be its intersection with the span of the basis elements before \(\alpha\). At a successor step, projection onto the new coordinate identifies \(H_{\alpha+1}/H_\alpha\) with a subgroup of \(\mathbb Z\), hence either zero or \(n\mathbb Z\). Choose a lift of its generator; this splits the step as a direct sum. At a limit step take the union. Each element has finite support, so the resulting generators form a basis. In particular the cycles and boundaries of a free chain complex are free.

If such a complex \(F_\bullet\) has free homology, choose splittings of \(0\to Z_k\to F_k\to B_{k-1}\to0\) and \(0\to B_k\to Z_k\to H_k\to0\) by lifting bases. In these coordinates the complex is the direct sum of its homology with zero differential and two-term identity complexes on the boundary groups. Mapping each lower member of an identity pair to its upper member contracts those pairs. Apply this to \(F_\bullet=C_\bullet(\mathbb R^r,\mathbb R^r\setminus0)\), using (D.4). It contracts onto \(\mathbb Z\) in degree \(r\). The projection is represented by an integer cocycle \(u_r\), chosen to take value one on the oriented homology generator. It follows at once, by dualizing this contraction, that the relative cohomology of the fiber is \(G\) in degree \(r\) and zero otherwise, for every \(G\).

Tensor this contraction with \(C_\bullet(B)\). If \(h\) contracts the fiber summands, the tensor homotopy is \(c\otimes f\mapsto(-1)^{\deg c}c\otimes hf\); expansion of its boundary gives the claimed tensor contraction. Combine it with (D.9) and dualize with values in \(G\). The resulting cohomology isomorphism is specifically

\[ \Phi_B:H^j(B;G)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^{j+r}(B\times\mathbb R^r,B\times(\mathbb R^r\setminus0);G), \qquad a\longmapsto \pi_B^*a\smile\pi_{\mathbb R^r}^*u_r. \tag{D.10} \]

To verify the formula, the tensor projection sends a tensor of bidegree \((j,r)\) to the value of its second factor under \(u_r\), times the first factor; all other second degrees give zero. Pulling its dual through (D.5) evaluates exactly the displayed front-back cup cochain. This identifies the map, not just the abstract groups. Degrees below \(r\) vanish. In degree \(r\), the integral classes correspond to \(H^0(B;\mathbb Z)\), whose cocycles are the integer-valued functions on points constant along every path. Thus a class is uniquely determined by its restrictions to all fibers, and the class corresponding to the constant function one is their chosen generator.

D.4. Gluing the oriented class on a finite cover

Let \(E\to B\) be an oriented real vector bundle of rank \(r>0\), with a finite cover by oriented trivializations. Put \(E^\times=E\setminus s(B)\), where \(s\) is the zero section. We prove simultaneously the existence and uniqueness of a class

\[ u_E\in H^r(E,E^\times;\mathbb Z) \tag{D.11} \]

restricting to the positive generator on every fiber, the vanishing in degrees below \(r\), and the isomorphism \(\Phi(a)=\pi^*a\smile u_E\) for every \(G\). The one-chart case is D.3. Suppose the cover has \(N\) charts; let \(U\) be the union of the first \(N-1\), and \(V\) the last. The bundle on \(U\) satisfies the induction hypothesis, and the bundles on \(V\) and \(W=U\cap V\) are trivial. Their classes agree on \(W\): they have the same oriented fiber restrictions, which determine a class there by D.3. Orientation-preserving transition matrices act as \(+1\) by the integral determinant calculation in D.1. Mayer–Vietoris gives a lift to \(H^r(E,E^\times;\mathbb Z)\), unique because \(H^{r-1}(E_W,E_W^\times;\mathbb Z)=0\). The same exact sequence shows vanishing below \(r\).

Choose a global relative cocycle representing this lift. Cup on its right gives a map from the base Mayer–Vietoris sequence with coefficients \(G\) to the relative bundle sequence with degrees increased by \(r\). The squares commute by D.2, including the connecting squares. All vertical maps for \(U,V,W\) are isomorphisms. Here is the exact-sequence argument for the remaining one on \(B\). For surjectivity, restrict a target class to \(U,V\), lift those restrictions through the two isomorphisms, and use injectivity on \(W\) to see their difference is zero. They lift to a base class. The difference from the target then lies in the image of the bundle connecting map; lift its preimage through the isomorphism on \(W\) and add its base connecting image. For injectivity, a base class killed upstairs restricts to zero on \(U,V\), hence comes from a class on \(W\) by the connecting map. Its bundle image is killed by that connecting map, so comes from \(U,V\). Lift this pair back using their isomorphisms and subtract its restriction from the class on \(W\); injectivity on \(W\) makes the remainder zero. Its base connecting image was therefore zero. This proves the required isomorphism in every degree and completes the induction.

Uniqueness also proves naturality under pullback when both bundles have finite trivializing covers: the pulled-back class has the specified fiber generators. Reversing the fiber orientation replaces \(u_E\) by \(-u_E\). This proof uses the finite cover itself and needs no CW replacement or unproved passage to an infinite cover.

D.5. Euler class, Gysin sequence and the dual-line sign

Let \(J:H^r(E,E^\times;\mathbb Z)\to H^r(E;\mathbb Z)\) forget support and define \(e(E)=s^*J(u_E)\). Fiber scaling contracts \(E\) to its zero section, so \(\pi^*\) and \(s^*\) are inverse on cohomology by the prism. In particular \(J(u_E)=\pi^*e(E)\). Associativity and naturality of the cup operation give

\[ J\Phi(a)=\pi^*(a\smile e(E)). \tag{D.12} \]

Transport the long exact sequence of the pair \((E,E^\times)\) through \(\Phi\) and \(\pi^*\). If the bundle has a continuous fiber norm, its nonzero vectors retract to its unit-sphere bundle \(p:S(E)\to B\) via \(v\mapsto((1-t)+t/\|v\|)v\). We obtain the exact sequence

\[ \begin{aligned} \cdots\longrightarrow& H^{j-r}(B;G) \xrightarrow{\ a\mapsto a\smile e(E)\ }H^j(B;G) \xrightarrow{p^*}H^j(S(E);G)\\ &\xrightarrow{p_!}H^{j-r+1}(B;G) \xrightarrow{\ a\mapsto a\smile e(E)\ }H^{j+1}(B;G) \longrightarrow\cdots . \end{aligned} \tag{D.13} \]

The map \(p_!\) here means the pair connecting map followed by \(\Phi^{-1}\). This definition fixes all its signs; exactness follows from the proved pair sequence. A complex line has its real rank-two orientation because its transition maps have positive real determinant, as proved in C.4. The Hermitian norm on the tautological line in \(\mathbb C^3\) supplies the required norm in Section 1 (the cone calculation). Hence (D.13) proves its circle-bundle Gysin sequence over both \(\Lambda\) and \(\mathbb Z\).

For a Hermitian line bundle \(L\), take the convention that its metric \(h\) is linear in the first variable. The real bundle isomorphism \(L\to L^*,\ v\mapsto h(-,v)\) is conjugate-linear on each complex line. In an orthonormal coordinate it is complex conjugation, of real determinant \(-1\). Pullback therefore sends \(u_{L^*}\) to \(-u_L\), by their fiber restrictions and uniqueness in D.4. Pulling further along the zero section proves

\[ e(L^*)=-e(L). \tag{D.14} \]

Thus the minus sign for \(\mathcal O_C(-1)=\mathcal O_C(1)^*\) has a proof independent of the computation of the positive degree.

D.6. Local zeros and the Euler class

There is also a precise local form of the degree computation. Let \(B\) be an oriented surface and \(L\to B\) an oriented real plane bundle with a finite trivializing cover. Let \(t\) be a section with a finite set \(Z=\{x_1,\ldots,x_k\}\) of isolated zeros. It is a map of pairs \((B,B\setminus Z)\to(L,L^\times)\), so \(t^*u_L\) is a relative degree-two class. Its absolute image is \(e(L)\): as maps to \(L\), \(t\) and the zero section are homotopic by fiber scaling.

Take disjoint oriented coordinate discs \(D_i\) on which the bundle is orientedly trivial. The relative excision proved in D.1 gives

\[ H^2(B,B\setminus Z;\mathbb Z) \simeq\bigoplus_i H^2(D_i,D_i\setminus\{x_i\};\mathbb Z) \simeq\bigoplus_i\mathbb Z. \tag{D.15} \]

Write the section in the \(i\)-th trivialization as a map \(f_i:D_i\to\mathbb R^2\) with its sole zero at \(x_i\). Formula (D.10) identifies the \(i\)-th component of \(t^*u_L\) with \(f_i^*u_2\), an integer multiple \(m_i\) of the oriented local generator. This integer is the local degree. If \(\eta_i\in H^2(B;\mathbb Z)\) is the absolute image of that generator under the inverse of (D.15), we have proved

\[ e(L)=\sum_i m_i\eta_i. \tag{D.16} \]

For a complex coordinate expression \(f(z)=z^m a(z)\), \(m\ge1\), with \(a\) continuous and \(a(0)\ne0\), shrink the disc until \(|a(z)-a(0)|<|a(0)|\). The straight-line homotopy from \(a(z)\) to \(a(0)\) remains nonzero, so it does not change the local degree. Multiplication by \(a(0)\) preserves the real orientation. On a small boundary circle the remaining map is \(z\mapsto z^m\), of degree \(m\). Here is a chain check of that last integer. The loop \(\gamma(t)=\exp(2\pi i t)\) generates integral \(H_1(S^1)\): cutting it into its upper and lower arcs makes the connecting homomorphism for the two-arc cover the difference of its two overlap points, the generator used in D.1. Splitting any path at parameter \(a\) does not change its homology class relative to its endpoints, since the image of the affine triangle with parameter values \(0,a,1\) has boundary equal to the two subpaths minus the original path. Split \(\gamma(mt)\) at \(1/m,\ldots,(m-1)/m\); its pieces are each \(\gamma\). Its homology class is therefore \(m[\gamma]\). The relative connecting isomorphism for the disc identifies this circle degree with \(m_i\). This proves the multiplicity asserted in (D.16) whenever the displayed local factorization has been established.

Equations (D.14) and (D.16) explain the sign and the local contributions to the Euler class in Section 1 (the cone calculation). They do not themselves prove that all positive point classes on the compact curve agree, that a hyperplane section has total multiplicity \(n\), the surface cohomology groups, or the canonical-degree/genus identity. Appendix E supplies those geometric and global topological steps separately. The construction above supplies the classical Thom/Gysin prerequisite used there.

The permitted source input is Hatcher's freely available author text on singular products and the Thom/Gysin construction. The integral small-chain retraction, product homotopies, chain splitting, finite-cover gluing, maps and signs needed here are written out in this appendix.

Appendix E. The compact plane curve, its degree and its genus

We now supply the classical curve inputs in Section 1 (the cone calculation). Let \(F(x,y,z)\) be a nonzero homogeneous polynomial of degree \(n>0\), with no point of \(C=\{F=0\}\subset\mathbb P^2(\mathbb C)\) at which all its first partial derivatives vanish. We prove connectedness, construct a finite decomposition into oriented triangles, compute integral cohomology, identify the positive point class, and calculate the relevant line-bundle degrees. In this classical calculation genus has the topological normalization \(\chi(C)=2-2g\). The proof below gives \(2g=\operatorname{rank}H_1(C;\mathbb Z)=(n-1)(n-2)\), including its integrality. No comparison with coherent or étale cohomology is needed here.

E.1. The analytic and polynomial facts needed for projection

We use analytic functions in the concrete sense of locally convergent complex power series. Their sums, products and compositions are analytic on smaller discs: absolute convergence permits regrouping the series, and their differentiated series converge uniformly on every smaller closed disc. The identity principle follows directly. A series which is not identically zero has the form \(z^m a(z)\), with \(a(0)\ne0\), near a zero; such a zero is isolated. If a function vanishes on a nonempty open part of a connected domain, the set of points where it vanishes in a neighbourhood is open and closed. At a limit point all derivatives vanish by continuity, so its Taylor series is zero there. Thus the function vanishes throughout the domain.

We will need convergence in the implicit function theorem, so we include that step. After translating and scaling, write a convergent series with \(f(0,0)=0\) and \(f_w(0,0)\ne0\) as

\[ f(t,w)=w+at+R(t,w),\qquad R\text{ has only terms of total degree at least two}. \tag{E.1} \]

Let \(A_r\) be the space of series \(u(t)=\sum u_k t^k\) with norm \(\|u\|_r=\sum |u_k|r^k\). It is a complete normed algebra: multiplication obeys the product bound by the absolutely convergent double sum; a Cauchy sequence converges coefficientwise, and the Cauchy tail estimate, first for finite partial sums and then for their supremum, proves convergence in this norm. Take the closed ball \(u(0)=0,\ \|u\|_r\le s\). For sufficiently small \(s\), and then sufficiently small \(r\), the absolute coefficient sums of \(R\) give

\[ \|R(t,u)-R(t,v)\|_r\le\tfrac12\|u-v\|_r, \qquad \|at+R(t,0)\|_r\le s/2. \tag{E.2} \]

Indeed \(u^j-v^j=\sum_{a=0}^{j-1}u^a(u-v)v^{j-1-a}\), so the first bound follows from \(\sum j|R_{ij}|r^is^{j-1}\le1/2\). All its terms tend to zero since the linear \(w\)-term of \(R\) is absent. The second bound follows by decreasing \(r\). The map \(u\mapsto-at-R(t,u)\) preserves this ball. Its iterates have successive differences bounded by a geometric series and hence converge in \(A_r\) to a unique fixed point \(\phi\). The same estimates on the scalar disc \(|w|\le s\) show that for each \(|t|\le r\) this is the unique small solution. Thus the zero set of \(f\) near the point is the analytic graph \(w=\phi(t)\). Implicit differentiation gives \(\phi'=-f_t/f_w\). The same construction applied to \(h(w)-t\) gives an analytic local inverse whenever \(h'(0)\ne0\).

A nonconstant analytic map between discs has the local form \(t=\zeta^e\), after translating the two centres and changing the source coordinate, for an integer \(e\ge1\). To see this, write \(t(w)=w^e a(w)\), \(a(0)\ne0\). After choosing one \(e\)-th root of \(a(0)\), the binomial series gives an analytic \(e\)-th root of \(a(w)\) on a smaller disc. For precision, the series for \((1+u)^{1/e}\) converges for \(|u|<1\) by the ratio test; its coefficients give \((1+u)P'=P/e\) and \(P(0)=1\), whence \(P^e=1+u\) by comparing coefficients in that differential equation. Set \(\zeta=w a(w)^{1/e}\); its derivative at zero is nonzero, so the inverse just proved applies. In particular such a map is open, and its critical points are isolated unless it is locally constant.

We also need the following growth fact: an entire analytic function bounded by \(M(1+|t|)^k\) is a polynomial of degree at most \(k\). Here is the coefficient argument with its analytic justification. A convergent power series has a local primitive, obtained by integrating its coefficients. Consequently an integral around the boundary of a sufficiently small triangle vanishes. Subdivide a polygonal annulus into triangles small enough to lie in primitive neighbourhoods; internal edges cancel. Applying this to \(a(t)/t^{j+1}\) shows that its integrals over two concentric polygonal boundaries enclosing zero agree. Regular polygons approximate the circles, with both their parametrizations and piecewise derivatives converging, so the circle integrals agree as well. On a small circle, termwise integration of the series gives

\[ a_j=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{|t|=R}\frac{a(t)}{t^{j+1}}\,dt, \qquad |a_j|\le \frac{\max_{|t|=R}|a(t)|}{R^j}. \tag{E.3} \]

For the subdivision assertion it suffices to take concentric regular polygons, join corresponding vertices to form an annular strip of quadrilaterals, divide these into triangles, and repeatedly subdivide. Compactness supplies a Lebesgue number for the primitive neighbourhoods, exactly as in A.3. Thus no global Cauchy theorem has been assumed. Letting \(R\to\infty\) in (E.3) gives \(a_j=0\) for \(j>k\); the identity principle extends this polynomial equality from a neighbourhood of zero to the whole plane.

Finally every nonconstant complex polynomial has a root. Its modulus tends to infinity, so it attains a minimum. If the value at a minimum were \(c\ne0\), expansion there would give \(c+bw^m+O(w^{m+1})\), \(b\ne0\). Choose a ray with \(bw^m/c\) negative real. For sufficiently small \(|w|\), its negative term decreases the modulus, since the remainder is of smaller order, a contradiction. Factoring out one linear factor and repeating proves that a degree-\(n\) polynomial has \(n\) roots counted with multiplicity. It also proves that a nonzero homogeneous polynomial of positive degree in two variables vanishes at some point of \(\mathbb P^1\): use its value at \((t,1)\), and include \([1:0]\) if its degree in \(t\) drops.

E.2. A finite branched projection and connectedness

Projective space is compact: every complex line has a unit representative, so it is a continuous image of the compact unit sphere. It is Hausdorff; for example \(\ell\mapsto vv^*/\|v\|^2\) embeds its set of lines into the Hausdorff space of Hermitian matrices, continuously in each projective chart. The equation \(F=0\) defines a closed subset. At each of its points, a nonzero partial derivative in an affine chart and E.1 give a complex analytic coordinate on \(C\). Such a partial exists: Euler's identity \(xF_x+yF_y+zF_z=nF\), proved termwise on monomials, rules out the possibility that only the omitted homogeneous coordinate has nonzero derivative at a zero. Thus \(C\) is a compact smooth real surface, with the complex orientation justified in C.4.

Choose \(q\notin C\) and coordinates with \(q=[0:0:1]\). Scale \(F\) to have leading coefficient one as a polynomial in \(z\). Projection is then everywhere defined on \(C\):

\[ f:C\longrightarrow\mathbb P^1,\qquad [x:y:z]\longmapsto[x:y]. \tag{E.4} \]

For fixed \([x:y]\), its fiber consists of the roots of the monic degree-\(n\) polynomial \(F(x,y,z)\). Every fiber is finite and nonempty. In a local analytic coordinate, \(f\) cannot be constant on a neighbourhood, since that would put infinitely many points in one fiber. E.1 therefore gives the local expression \(t=\zeta^{e_p}\). Critical points are locally isolated, including in charts above infinity; their set is closed because the derivative is continuous. Compactness makes it finite. Let \(B\) be the finite set of critical values.

Off \(B\), the map is a finite covering. Indeed each point of a fiber has an inverse chart. Choose disjoint such charts, and shrink the target neighbourhood so that no further points appear: the complement of these charts is compact and its image omits the target point. This produces an evenly covered neighbourhood. Each regular fiber has \(n\) points. In the coordinates \((t,z)\), the kernel of \(df\) on the tangent line is nonzero exactly when \(F_z=0\); a regular fiber thus has simple roots, whose number is \(n\) by E.1. At any value, its local power charts show

\[ \sum_{p\in f^{-1}(b)}e_p=n. \tag{E.5} \]

This follows by counting a nearby regular fiber in the disjoint power charts; compactness again excludes other inverse images. In particular the branch multiplicities in this argument need not be simple.

We give connectedness its own proof. First a smooth homogeneous plane equation cannot factor as \(F=GH\) with both degrees positive. Suppose their degrees are \(d,e\). As \(G(q)H(q)\ne0\), scale their leading \(z\)-coefficients to make both monic. For each \((x,y)\), consider the square coefficient matrix of

\[ (u,v)\longmapsto uG+vH, \quad \deg_z u<e,\quad \deg_z v<d, \quad \deg_z(uG+vH)<d+e. \tag{E.6} \]

Its determinant \(R(x,y)\) vanishes precisely when the two monic polynomials have a common root. If there is a common factor, take \(u=H/D,\ v=-G/D\) to obtain a nonzero kernel vector. If there is none, factoring into linear factors shows that \(G\mid vH\) implies \(G\mid v\), impossible with \(\deg v<d\) unless \(v=0\); then \(u=0\). Every determinant term is homogeneous of degree \(de\). Explicitly, the entry in output row \(z^k\) and input column \(u_jz^j\) has degree \(d+j-k\), and the corresponding \(v_j\)-entry degree \(e+j-k\). Summing over all columns and subtracting \(\sum_{k=0}^{d+e-1}k\) gives \(de\). If \(R\) is identically zero, any nonzero \((x,y)\) supplies a common root. If it is not, E.1 supplies a projective zero since \(de>0\). At the resulting point \(G=H=0\), all derivatives of \(F=GH\) vanish. This contradicts smoothness and proves irreducibility without assuming a general intersection theorem.

Now suppose \(C=C_1\sqcup C_2\) is a decomposition into two nonempty closed and open subsets. Both are compact. The local power description makes the image of either open, while compactness makes it closed. Since \(\mathbb P^1\) is connected, both images are all of \(\mathbb P^1\). On the complement of \(B\), form the monic polynomial whose roots are the \(z/y\)-coordinates of the points belonging to \(C_1\), with \(t=x/y\). Its degree \(m\) is constant there, with \(0<m<n\); the punctured sphere is path connected because a polygonal path can be detoured around finitely many missing points. Its coefficients are single-valued analytic functions on \(\mathbb C\setminus B\): local inverse sheets are analytic, and continuation only permutes roots within the same closed-and-open subset.

These coefficients extend analytically across a branch value. In a power chart \(t-t_0=\zeta^e\), write the other coordinate as an analytic series \(z/y=h(\zeta)\). All \(e\) nearby roots from this chart belong to the same subset, since the chart is connected. The product \(\prod_{\omega^e=1}(Z-h(\omega\zeta))\) has coefficients given by convergent series invariant under \(\zeta\mapsto\omega\zeta\). Their coefficients with exponents not divisible by \(e\) vanish, so they are convergent power series in \(t-t_0\). Multiplying these local factors proves the extension.

Near infinity use \(s=y/x\) and \(w=z/x\). The monic polynomial \(F(1,s,w)\) has bounded coefficients for small \(s\), and its roots are bounded: if the coefficients after the leading term have modulus at most \(M\), no root has modulus greater than \(1+M\), by comparing its leading term with the geometric sum of the other terms. Since \(z/y=t w\), the coefficient of degree \(k\) in the polynomial for \(C_1\) grows at most as a constant times \((1+|t|)^k\). By (E.3) it is a polynomial of degree at most \(k\). Homogenizing these coefficients gives a homogeneous monic factor of degree \(m\) in \((x,y,z)\). The same reasoning for \(C_2\) gives a factor of degree \(n-m\); their product equals \(F\) on every regular fiber and hence as a polynomial. This contradicts (E.6). Thus \(C\) is connected. It is also path connected: path components of a surface are open by its coordinate discs, and their complements are open as unions of other path components.

E.3. A finite collection of triangles on the actual curve

The projection produces the finite topology model required for integral cohomology. Choose an affine target coordinate with all points of \(B\) finite. Inside that plane take a large triangle containing them. Its exterior in the sphere is a closed disc: radial coordinates from an interior point, followed by inversion of the radial variable, give such a parametrization, with infinity as the disc centre. Joining infinity to the three vertices divides this exterior into three triangles. Together with the inner triangle, this is a four-face decomposition of the sphere, with \(4\) vertices and \(6\) edges. Insert the points of \(B\) one at a time. A point inside a face is joined to its three vertices; a point on an edge splits that edge and the two adjacent faces. In either case \(V-E+T\) is unchanged. We obtain a finite decomposition with all branch values as vertices and \(V-E+T=2\). Near a finite vertex its edges are straight in the affine coordinate. Extra subdivisions may be made without changing this identity.

Over an open edge or open face there are \(n\) disjoint sheets, each mapped homeomorphically onto that cell. Here is the covering argument for the faces. Lift a path by subdividing its parameter interval into inverse-chart intervals; its initial lift determines each succeeding piece uniquely. Subdivide a path homotopy into a grid whose small rectangles map into evenly covered sets. Uniqueness on each rectangle proves that lifts of homotopic paths with the same endpoints have the same endpoint. A disc contracts its paths to radial paths, so lifting paths from its centre gives the disjoint global inverse sheets, continuous by the inverse charts. This establishes the claimed trivialization on the open face without assuming a covering-classification theorem.

The closure of each lifted face is a closed triangle. Along an edge its inverse extends by the inverse chart. At a branch vertex the target face occupies a sector, and the local expression \(t=\zeta^e\) has a single continuous inverse branch on that sector, extending to zero. If the edges are curved in a local parameter, their parametrized sector still has a continuous argument of width less than \(2\pi\), after shrinking; in the finite branch coordinate the edges here are straight. Different vertices of a base triangle remain different points in every lift. These extensions give a continuous bijection from the closed triangle to the lifted closure and hence a homeomorphism, because the domain is compact and \(C\) is Hausdorff. The resulting finite glued collection of triangles maps bijectively to \(C\), including its edges and vertices, and the same compactness argument proves it is the actual topology of \(C\). Fix an ordering of the base vertices and one parametrization of every edge. Choose each face parametrization with those boundary parametrizations: a change of boundary parametrization extends across a disc by the radial formula \(r\theta\mapsto r h(\theta)\). Lift these choices to \(C\). Adjacent singular face simplices then have literally the same edge maps, with the boundary signs dictated by the vertex order; multiplying each face by its orientation sign makes their common edge terms cancel.

Let \(v,e,t\) count its vertices, edges and faces, and put \(R=\sum_p(e_p-1)\). The faces and edges each have \(n\) lifts, and (E.5) counts the vertices above every base vertex. Consequently

\[ v-e+t=n(V-E+T)-R=2n-R. \tag{E.7} \]

The complex orientation orients every face. The two faces adjacent to an edge induce opposite directions on it, as follows by inspecting an oriented coordinate disc across the edge. The adjacency graph of faces is connected. Indeed the faces meeting a vertex are joined successively across edges in its disc neighbourhood. Therefore any union of face-adjacency components, including their edges and vertices, is open and closed in the surface. Connectedness of \(C\) leaves only one component. The graph consisting of its vertices and edges is connected as well: the boundary of every face is connected, so attaching these discs cannot join two different components of that graph.

E.4. Integral cohomology and the positive point class

We verify that the finite chain complex of these triangles computes singular homology; this also fixes its orientation generator. For \(K^0\subset K^1\subset K^2=C\), the relative groups \(H_i(K^j,K^{j-1};\mathbb Z)\) vanish for \(i\ne j\) and are free on the \(j\)-cells for \(i=j\). To prove this at the used dimensions, take an open collar of the boundary of every closed cell, together with \(K^{j-1}\). Pushing radially to the boundary retracts this neighbourhood onto \(K^{j-1}\); continuity follows on each of the finitely many characteristic discs and hence on their quotient. The pair sequence and this retraction replace \(K^{j-1}\) by its neighbourhood without changing relative homology. Cover the rest by slightly larger open cell interiors. Relative small chains from D.1 then split into the finite direct sum of the complexes for an open \(j\)-ball relative to its outer annulus. The ball contracts and the annulus retracts onto \(S^{j-1}\), so (D.4) and the pair sequence give exactly the asserted relative groups.

Their connecting maps give the complex

\[ 0\longrightarrow \mathbb Z^{t} \xrightarrow{\partial_2}\mathbb Z^{e} \xrightarrow{\partial_1}\mathbb Z^{v}\longrightarrow0. \tag{E.8} \]

The first boundary of an oriented edge is its final vertex minus its initial vertex. The boundary of an oriented triangle is its three edges with their induced signs: represent the relative generator by its oriented singular triangle, and use the singular boundary formula. Its boundary loop is the positive circle generator from D.6, so the relative generator agrees with the one used in the ball computation. For \(K^1\), its pair sequence gives \(H_1(K^1)=\ker\partial_1\), \(H_0(K^1)=\operatorname{coker}\partial_1\), and zero higher homology. The pair sequence for \((C,K^1)\) then gives \(H_2(C)=\ker\partial_2\), \(H_1(C)=\ker\partial_1/\operatorname{im}\partial_2\), and the same \(H_0\), with zero groups above degree two. This proves the singular comparison for (E.8).

Since the edge graph is connected, differences of vertices along paths generate the kernel of the sum map \(\mathbb Z^v\to\mathbb Z\), so \(H_0(C)=\mathbb Z\) and \(\partial_1\) has rank \(v-1\). A 2-chain is a cycle precisely when its coefficients on adjacent oriented faces agree: their coefficients at the common edge are their difference, up to the edge's chosen sign. The connected face graph therefore gives \(H_2(C)=\mathbb Z[C]\), where \([C]\) is the sum of all positively oriented faces.

There is no hidden integral torsion in \(H_1(C)\). Choose a spanning tree in the face-adjacency graph, and a root face. Projection of \(\partial_2\) onto the edge coordinates belonging to this tree, restricted to the free group on the nonroot faces, is an isomorphism onto \(\mathbb Z^{t-1}\). To see this, successively remove a leaf other than the root. Its tree edge involves that leaf with coefficient \(\pm1\) and its parent; it solves uniquely for the leaf coefficient, and induction solves all coefficients over the integers. The boundaries of the nonroot faces generate \(\operatorname{im}\partial_2\), since the sum of all face boundaries is zero. Thus projection is a left inverse on this image, which is a direct summand of \(\mathbb Z^e\). Its quotient is free, and \(H_1(C)\), a subgroup of that quotient, is free by D.3. Its rank is

\[ b=e-(v-1)-(t-1)=2-(v-e+t). \tag{E.9} \]

All singular homology groups are therefore free. The splitting of a free chain complex proved in D.3, now applied to \(C_\bullet(C;\mathbb Z)\), yields for every abelian group \(G\)

\[ H^j(C;G)= \begin{cases} G&j=0,2,\\ G^b&j=1,\\ 0&j\notin\{0,1,2\}. \end{cases} \tag{E.10} \]

In degree two the identification is evaluation on \([C]\), independent of the chosen splittings. If \(p\) lies in the interior of a face, the image of \([C]\) in \(H_2(C,C\setminus\{p\};\mathbb Z)\) is its positive local generator: all other face chains vanish relatively, and the remaining face is the oriented local ball class by the same excision. Thus the positive local cohomology class at \(p\) maps to the unique \(\eta\in H^2(C;\mathbb Z)\) with \(\langle\eta,[C]\rangle=1\).

This holds at edges and vertices too, and the needed invariance can be checked explicitly. In an oriented real coordinate disc, take a continuously differentiable cutoff \(\rho\) equal to one near a point and zero outside a smaller compact disc. Such a cutoff can be obtained by a polynomial transition with zero derivatives at both ends, applied to the squared radius. If its Lipschitz constant is \(L\), then \(F_s(x)=x+s v\rho(x)\), \(0\le s\le1\), is a homeomorphism for \(|v|L<1\). Injectivity follows from the Lipschitz inequality; for any target \(y\), iteration of \(x=y-sv\rho(x)\) converges geometrically to its unique inverse image, and the same inequality makes the inverse continuous. Its derivative differs from the identity by norm less than one, so its determinant remains positive along \(s\). Extend it by the identity outside the coordinate disc.
