It moves the chosen point to a nearby face interior, preserves its local orientation, and is homotopic to the identity on \(C\). Naturality of relative cohomology and of its absolute image shows that the positive class at the original point is also \(\eta\). We have proved equality of all positive point classes, and that this class is an integral generator, before using it to count zeros.

E.5. Hyperplane degree and the canonical line bundle

Recall that \(\mathcal O(-1)\) has fiber the line \(\ell\subset\mathbb C^{m+1}\) over \([\ell]\in\mathbb P^m\); \(\mathcal O(1)\) is its dual, and integral tensor powers define \(\mathcal O(k)\), using duals for negative \(k\). A homogeneous degree-\(k\) polynomial is a section of \(\mathcal O(k)\), since its restriction to \(\ell\) is a homogeneous functional of that degree. This identifies its local zero multiplicities with those of its affine coordinate expressions.

Take a regular value \([a:b]\) of (E.4). The linear section \(bx-ay\) of \(\mathcal O_C(1)\) has exactly \(n\) distinct zeros, one at each point of this fiber. Each zero is simple: its affine expression is a nonzero factor times the target coordinate of the projection minus its value, whose derivative is nonzero at that point. By the local zero formula (D.16) and E.4,

\[ e(\mathcal O_C(1))=n\eta,\qquad e(\mathcal O_C(-1))=-n\eta. \tag{E.11} \]

The same section raised to the \(k\)-th power has multiplicity \(k\) at each zero. For \(k>0\), (D.16) gives \(e(\mathcal O_C(k))=kn\eta\). A trivial line has Euler class zero: its nonvanishing section factors through the complement of the zero section, so its pullback of the relative Thom class is zero; it is homotopic to the zero section. For \(k<0\), use (D.14). Thus the formula holds for every integer \(k\), without needing an unproved tensor-additivity theorem.

We next construct adjunction at this exact scope. A nearby line to \(\ell\subset V=\mathbb C^{m+1}\) is the graph of a map from \(\ell\) to a chosen complement. Differentiating graph coordinates identifies the tangent bundle of \(\mathbb P^m\) with \(\operatorname{Hom}(\ell,V/\ell)\); changing the complement gives the same quotient map. Hence there is an exact sequence of complex vector bundles

\[ 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O \longrightarrow \mathcal O(1)\otimes V \longrightarrow T\mathbb P^m\longrightarrow0, \tag{E.12} \]

where the first map identifies \(\operatorname{Hom}(\ell,\ell)\) with scalar multiples of the inclusion. Taking determinants gives \(\det T\mathbb P^m\simeq\mathcal O(m+1)\), after fixing the standard basis of \(V\). The determinant rule used here follows by taking a basis of a subbundle and lifting a basis of its quotient: their wedge is unchanged by changing a lift by a subbundle vector, and changes by the product of the two basis determinants on overlaps.

The differential of the defining section \(F\) along its zero set is a well-defined map \(T\mathbb P^2|_C\to\mathcal O_C(n)\). If the expression of the section changes to \(uF\), its differential along \(C\) changes to \(u\,dF\), because \(F=0\) there; this is exactly the bundle transition. The map is onto by smoothness, and E.1 identifies its kernel with \(TC\). Therefore

\[ 0\longrightarrow TC\longrightarrow T\mathbb P^2|_C \xrightarrow{dF}\mathcal O_C(n)\longrightarrow0, \qquad K_C=(TC)^*\simeq\mathcal O_C(n-3). \tag{E.13} \]

Here \(K_C\), also denoted \(\omega_C\) in Section 1 (the cone calculation), is the complex line of holomorphic differentials; the coordinates and changes just used are analytic, so the isomorphism is one of holomorphic line bundles. Degree in this classical calculation is the integer \(\langle e(L),[C]\rangle\). Whenever a holomorphic section has isolated zeros, D.6 proves that this degree is the sum of their multiplicities. In particular (E.11)–(E.13) give \(\deg\mathcal O_C(k)=kn\) and \(\deg K_C=n(n-3)\).

E.6. Ramification, Euler characteristic and genus

The linear projection \(\mathbb C^3\to\mathbb C^2\), \((x,y,z)\mapsto(x,y)\), restricts on each tautological line over \(C\) to a nonzero map onto the tautological line over \(f(p)\). Its kernel line represents \(q\notin C\). These fiber maps give \(f^*\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(1)\simeq\mathcal O_C(1)\). Using (E.12) for \(m=1\), we have \(T\mathbb P^1\simeq\mathcal O(2)\). Consequently the actual derivative of the projection is a section of

\[ \operatorname{Hom}(TC,f^*T\mathbb P^1) \simeq K_C\otimes f^*\mathcal O(2) \simeq\mathcal O_C(n-1). \tag{E.14} \]

In the coordinates \(t=\zeta^{e_p}\) proved in E.1, this section is \(e_p\zeta^{e_p-1}\). Its zeros have multiplicities \(e_p-1\), including zero multiplicity at an unramified point. There are finitely many, and it is nowhere identically zero. The local zero formula, the positive point generator, and (E.11) now give

\[ R\eta=e(\mathcal O_C(n-1))=n(n-1)\eta, \qquad R=n(n-1). \tag{E.15} \]

This includes \(n=1\): the derivative then has no zeros and its bundle is trivial. Combine (E.7), (E.9) and (E.15). The chain computation identifies the alternating number of cells with the alternating rank of singular homology, so it is \(\chi(C)\). We obtain

\[ \begin{aligned} \chi(C)&=3n-n^2,\\ b&=2-\chi(C)=(n-1)(n-2),\\ g&=\frac{(n-1)(n-2)}2. \end{aligned} \tag{E.16} \]

The product of consecutive integers in (E.16) is even, and it is nonnegative for \(n\ge1\). Thus the topological genus normalization used here gives an integer and the middle rank in (E.10) is \(2g\). Equation (E.13) also proves, rather than assumes at this scope,

\[ \deg\omega_C=n(n-3)=2g-2. \tag{E.17} \]

In particular a line and a smooth conic have \(g=0\), while a smooth plane cubic has \(g=1\). The proofs give the integral inputs \(H^0(C;\mathbb Z)=H^2(C;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z\), \(H^1(C;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z^{2g}\), no higher cohomology, and the actual Euler class \(-n\eta\) for its tautological circle bundle. Together with Appendix D these discharge the classical numerical link calculation and the integral extension in Exercise 5. The comparison and vertex attaching complex were proved in Appendix C. Appendices F, H and J supply the general classical adjoint and Whitney-duality arguments. The étale-operation claims require their separate foundations.

The free sources consulted for this reconstruction are the MIT plane-curve notes for projection, resultants and the topological degree problem, Hatcher's author text for the cellular comparison, Lebl's free complex-analysis text for coefficient estimates, and McMullen's author notes for adjunction. Their cited results are not substituted for the explicit constructions above; in particular the convergence, connectedness, cellular, local-degree and ramification steps used in this calculation have been included.

Appendix F. The classical compact-support right adjoint

Here the coefficients are a field \(\Lambda\). Spaces are locally compact Hausdorff and metrizable; the varieties in the classical part have finite atlases by locally closed subsets of Euclidean spaces. We construct the right adjoint of \(R\Gamma_c\), including its local pairing, before using the smooth formula. General constructible biduality and Whitney local triviality are separate assertions. The sheaf resolutions, bounded-below injective comparison and open-closed operations of A.1 and B.1–B.2 are available throughout.

F.1. Compact extension and exact lifting

Write \(F(K)=\Gamma(K,F|_K)\) for a compact subset \(K\), where restriction means inverse image. Two elementary compactness facts will be used. First,

\[ F(K)=\varinjlim_{K\subset U\text{ open}}F(U). \tag{F.1} \]

To prove surjectivity, let \(\sigma\in F(K)\). Choose local representatives \(s_i\in F(V_i)\) of \(\sigma\), together with finitely many nonempty compact subsets \(K_i\subset K\cap V_i\) covering \(K\). To obtain these pieces, cover \(K\) by small metric balls whose compact closures lie in representing open sets, take a finite subcover, and intersect their closures with \(K\). For each pair \(i,j\), equality of the germs on \(K_i\cap K_j\) gives an open set \(W_{ij}\subset V_i\cap V_j\) containing that intersection on which \(s_i=s_j\).

Here is the simultaneous shrinking needed for gluing. Write \(N_\epsilon(A)=\{x:d(x,A)<\epsilon\}\). Compactness gives a positive \(\epsilon_i\) with \(N_{\epsilon_i}(K_i)\subset V_i\): otherwise points outside \(V_i\) approaching \(K_i\) would have a subsequence converging to a point of \(K_i\subset V_i\). Likewise, for each pair there is a positive \(\epsilon_{ij}\) such that

\[ N_{\epsilon_{ij}}(K_i)\cap N_{\epsilon_{ij}}(K_j) \subset W_{ij}. \]

Indeed, failure would give \(x_m\notin W_{ij}\) and points \(a_m\in K_i\), \(b_m\in K_j\) with \(d(x_m,a_m)<1/m\) and \(d(x_m,b_m)<1/m\). After a subsequence, compactness gives \(a_m\to a\in K_i\); then \(x_m,b_m\to a\), so \(a\in K_i\cap K_j\subset W_{ij}\), contradicting that \(W_{ij}\) is open. Choose \(\epsilon>0\) smaller than all these finitely many bounds. The restrictions of the \(s_i\) to \(N_\epsilon(K_i)\) now agree on every overlap, so they glue on an open neighborhood of \(K\). Their restriction is \(\sigma\), since the \(K_i\) cover \(K\). If two neighborhood representatives give the same element of \(F(K)\), their germs agree at every point of \(K\); the union of open neighborhoods on which they agree is itself a neighborhood of \(K\). This proves injectivity and hence (F.1). For \(K=\varnothing\), both sides are zero, since the empty open set is allowed in the colimit.

Second, sections on a finite closed cover of a compact set glue when they agree on intersections. Indeed, the space of germs of a sheaf is topologized by the images of its local sections; a section on a subspace is a continuous map to this space over the subspace. The finite closed-set pasting lemma proves continuity of the glued map. That lemma follows by taking inverse images of closed sets and their finite union.

A sheaf \(A\) is c-soft if \(A(X)\to A(K)\) is onto for every compact \(K\). An extension can be chosen with compact support inside any prescribed open neighborhood \(O\) of \(K\). Choose a compact neighborhood \(T\) with \(K\subset\operatorname{int}T\subset T\subset O\). Extend the section prescribed on \(K\) and zero on \(\partial T\), which are disjoint compact sets. The extension vanishes near \(\partial T\), and restriction to \(\operatorname{int}T\), followed by extension by zero, has the required support. Flabby sheaves are c-soft by (F.1). Restrictions of c-soft sheaves to open or closed subspaces are c-soft: compact data there are the same germs on a compact subset of the original space; for an open subspace use the prescribed-support extension just proved.

If \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) is open and \(A\) is c-soft on \(U\), then \(j_!A\) is c-soft on \(X\). To see this, take a section over a compact \(K\). Its nonzero germs have closed support \(S\) in \(K\), with \(S\subset U\); hence \(S\) is compact. Choose a compact neighborhood \(T\subset U\) of \(S\). On the compact subset \((K\cap T)\cup\partial T\) of \(U\), prescribe the given section on \(K\cap T\) and zero on \(\partial T\). They agree on their intersection, since that intersection avoids \(S\). Extend by c-softness and cut off across \(\partial T\). The resulting compactly supported section in \(U\), extended by zero to \(X\), gives exactly the original germs on \(K\). Closed direct image also preserves c-softness, since the intersection of a compact set with the closed subspace is compact.

Suppose \(0\to A\to B\to C\to0\) is exact and \(A\) is c-soft. A section of \(C\) on a compact \(K\) lifts to \(B(K)\). Choose local lifts on a finite compact cover \(K_1,\ldots,K_r\). Having glued a lift on the first pieces, compare it with the next lift on the compact intersection. Their difference is a section of \(A\) there. Extend that difference using c-softness and subtract it from the next lift. Finite closed gluing continues the induction. For a compactly supported section of \(C(X)\), perform this lifting on a compact neighborhood \(T\) of its support. Near \(\partial T\) the lift is a section of \(A\). Extend its boundary germs by c-softness, subtract, and extend the resulting lift by zero across \(\partial T\). Consequently

\[ 0\longrightarrow\Gamma_c(X,A)\longrightarrow\Gamma_c(X,B) \longrightarrow\Gamma_c(X,C)\longrightarrow0 \tag{F.2} \]

is exact. If \(B\) is also c-soft, lifting over a compact set and then extending in \(B\) shows that \(C\) is c-soft. Embed a c-soft sheaf into a Godement injective, iterate this quotient assertion, and apply (F.2). This proves that c-soft sheaves are \(\Gamma_c\)-acyclic, on every open subspace as well. The usual comparison with an injective resolution therefore computes \(R\Gamma_c\) on c-soft resolutions. For bounded-below complexes of acyclic sheaves the same assertion follows by resolving their terms and filtering the resulting double complex: each total degree has finitely many terms above its lower bounds, and the augmented acyclic rows give the comparison quasi-isomorphism.

Both \(j_!\) and closed direct image \(i_*\) are exact, preserve c-soft sheaves, and satisfy the equality of compact-section functors. It follows, by those resolutions, that

\[ R\Gamma_c(X,j_!G)=R\Gamma_c(U,G),\qquad R\Gamma_c(X,i_*H)=R\Gamma_c(Z,H). \tag{F.3} \]

This proves the derived compact-support identities rather than assuming a general proper-image theorem. It also gives a useful converse: if \(H_c^1(U,A)=0\) for every open \(U\), then \(A\) is c-soft. Apply the compact-support sequence to \(0\to j_!A|_{X\setminus K}\to A\to i_*A|_K\to0\) for a compact \(K\). By (F.3) the obstruction to extending \(A(K)\) by a compact section is the asserted zero group.

F.2. Filtered compact sections and a finite dimension bound

For a filtered system \(F_\alpha\), sections on a compact \(K\) commute with its sheaf colimit. A section in the colimit has local representatives at some indices; a finite compact cover chooses finitely many indices. On each compact pairwise intersection, equality in the colimit holds at a single later index after another finite subcover. A common upper index thus makes the representatives agree; finite closed gluing gives a section on \(K\). The same argument for zero germs proves injectivity. For compactly supported sections, choose a compact neighborhood \(T\) of the support, lift over \(T\), and pass to a later index where its boundary restriction is zero. Equation (F.1) and extension by zero then give

\[ \varinjlim_\alpha\Gamma_c(X,F_\alpha) \simeq\Gamma_c(X,\varinjlim_\alpha F_\alpha). \tag{F.4} \]

A filtered colimit of c-soft sheaves is c-soft: represent compact data at one index and extend at that index. Use the functorial Godement resolutions of the system. Their colimit is exact, since this is tested on stalks and filtered colimits of vector spaces are exact. Its terms are c-soft. Apply (F.4) termwise and the acyclicity proved above. This proves (F.4) also for every \(H_c^q\). In particular, arbitrary direct sums of c-soft sheaves are c-soft, and \(\Gamma_c\) commutes with arbitrary direct sums; alternatively, compact data in a direct sum use only finitely many summands, as follows from a finite subcover of local representatives.

For a decreasing filtered family of closed subsets \(Z_\alpha\) with intersection \(Z\), the natural map \(\varinjlim i_{\alpha*}F|_{Z_\alpha}\to i_*F|_Z\) is an isomorphism. At a point of \(Z\) all its stalks are \(F_x\); outside \(Z\) a later closed subset misses the point. The preceding result and (F.3) imply

\[ \varinjlim_\alpha H_c^q(Z_\alpha,F|_{Z_\alpha}) \simeq H_c^q(Z,F|_Z). \tag{F.5} \]

Say that \(X\) has compact cohomological dimension at most \(N\) if \(H_c^q(X,F)=0\) for every sheaf \(F\) and \(q>N\). Formula (F.3) makes this bound pass to open and closed subspaces. We prove

\[ \dim_c(X\times\mathbb R)\leq\dim_c X+1. \tag{F.6} \]

Let \(q>N+1\) and suppose \(\gamma\ne0\) in \(H_c^q(X\times\mathbb R,F)\). Among closed subsets \(A\subset\mathbb R\) on which the restriction of \(\gamma\) is nonzero, choose one minimal under inclusion. It exists by Zorn's lemma: the intersection of a decreasing chain still has nonzero restriction by (F.5), since a class in a filtered colimit is zero only if it becomes zero at some stage. Such an \(A\) is neither empty nor a singleton, since the corresponding fibers have dimension at most \(N\). Choose \(t\) strictly between two of its points and split it into the two proper closed subsets \(A_-\) and \(A_+\) on the two sides of \(t\). The exact sheaf sequence for this closed cover, checked by its diagonal and difference maps on stalks, gives

\[ H_c^{q-1}(X\times(A_-\cap A_+),F) \longrightarrow H_c^q(X\times A,F) \longrightarrow H_c^q(X\times A_-,F)\oplus H_c^q(X\times A_+,F). \]

The left group vanishes because the intersection is empty or one fiber, and the image of \(\gamma\) on the right vanishes by minimality. This contradicts its nonzero restriction to \(A\). Thus (F.6) holds. A point has dimension zero, so \(\dim_c\mathbb R^m\leq m\).

The bound is also local when it is uniform. For clarity, first prove local c-softness implies c-softness. Given compact data on \(K\), take a compact neighborhood \(T\) and finitely many compact pieces covering \(T\), each lying in an open set on which the sheaf is c-soft. Prescribe the data on \(K\) and zero on \(\partial T\). Extend successively over the pieces: their intersection with the already prescribed compact set is compact in the relevant open set, so c-softness there and finite closed gluing apply. The extension over \(T\) is zero near its boundary by (F.1); extending by zero finishes the proof.

Now suppose an open cover has dimension at most \(N\). For \(N\geq1\), truncate an injective resolution of any \(F\) into the exact sequence

\[ 0\to F\to I^0\to\cdots\to I^{N-1}\to Q\to0. \tag{F.7} \]

On every open subset of a covering set, dimension shifting gives \(H_c^1(Q)=H_c^{N+1}(F)=0\). The converse in F.1 shows that \(Q\) is locally c-soft, hence c-soft. Sequence (F.7) is a c-soft resolution of length \(N\), proving the global bound. For \(N=0\), the same converse applies directly to \(F\). Thus any space with a finite atlas of locally closed subsets of \(\mathbb R^m\), with bounded \(m\), has finite compact cohomological dimension. In particular, a chosen finite affine atlas of a complex algebraic variety, embedded in finite-dimensional complex affine spaces, supplies the required bound. No stratification or Whitney triviality theorem is used for this bound.

F.3. An exact functor with an explicit sheaf adjoint

Fix such a bound \(N\) and a c-soft sheaf \(M\). We first prove that \(F\otimes M\) is c-soft for every sheaf \(F\). There is a surjection onto \(F\) from the sum of the sheaves \(\Lambda_U=j_!\Lambda\), indexed by pairs consisting of an open set \(U\) and a section of \(F(U)\). The section supplies the map, and these maps are onto on stalks. Repeat for the successive kernels to obtain a left resolution. Tensoring is exact over a field, and every term after tensoring with \(M\) is a sum of \(j_!(M|_U)\), hence c-soft. If \(N\geq1\), take \(N\) consecutive terms of this resolution. On any open subset, their short exact sequences identify \(H_c^1(F\otimes M)\) with \(H_c^{N+1}\) of the leftmost kernel, which vanishes. If \(N=0\), every sheaf is already c-soft. The converse in F.1 proves the claim.

Consequently

\[ T_M(F)=\Gamma_c(X,F\otimes M) \tag{F.8} \]

is exact by (F.2), and preserves direct sums by (F.4). It therefore preserves cokernels and all colimits, since a colimit is the cokernel of the two maps between the sums indexed by the arrows and objects of its diagram. Its right adjoint on a vector space \(V\) has the explicit form

\[ \mathcal D_M(V)(U)=\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(\Gamma_c(U,M|_U),V). \tag{F.9} \]

Restrictions are precomposition with extension by zero. To check the sheaf condition, for an open cover of \(U\) use the exact presentation \(\bigoplus_{\alpha,\beta}\Lambda_{U_\alpha\cap U_\beta}\to \bigoplus_\alpha\Lambda_{U_\alpha}\to\Lambda_U\to0\). Its exactness is checked on stalks: all copies at a point are identified by their pairwise differences. Apply \(T_M\) and then \(\operatorname{Hom}(-,V)\); the resulting kernel diagram is precisely the sheaf gluing diagram for (F.9).

Moreover,

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_X(F,\mathcal D_M(V)) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(T_M(F),V). \tag{F.10} \]

For \(F=\Lambda_U\) this is (F.9), using the exact open adjunction. For a sum of such sheaves it follows by products. For general \(F\), take the surjection by sections above, and a similar surjection onto its kernel. Both sides of (F.10) are the same kernel for that two-term presentation. The identification is natural because its value on every map \(\Lambda_U\to F\) is the prescribed section map. This presentation also includes the linear relations between sections; a diagram containing only restrictions of individual sections would not suffice. Since \(T_M\) is exact and every vector space is injective, (F.10) shows that \(\mathcal D_M(V)\) is an injective sheaf.

F.4. Constructing the right adjoint, with its differential

Apply (F.7) to \(\Lambda_X\). It gives a c-soft resolution \(\Lambda_X\to L^\bullet\) supported in degrees \(0,\ldots,N\); for \(N=0\) use \(L^0=\Lambda_X\). All its terms are flat, since the coefficients form a field. For a bounded-below complex \(F^\bullet\), the augmentation \(F^\bullet\to F^\bullet\otimes L^\bullet\) is a quasi-isomorphism: on stalks the bounded exact augmented complex of vector spaces splits and contracts. Its total terms are finite sums of the c-soft sheaves of F.3. Hence

\[ R\Gamma_c(X,F^\bullet)\simeq \Gamma_c(X,F^\bullet\otimes L^\bullet). \tag{F.11} \]

For a bounded-below complex \(V^\bullet\) of vector spaces define

\[ (a^!V)^n=\bigoplus_{p=0}^N\mathcal D_{L^p}(V^{n+p}), \qquad (du)_p=d_Vu_p-(-1)^n u_{p+1}d_L. \tag{F.12} \]

Here the second term uses contravariance in \(L\), and out-of-range components are zero. Squaring the differential gives zero: the two mixed terms have opposite signs and the two square terms vanish. The complex is bounded below by the lower bound of \(V\) minus \(N\), and every term is injective by F.3. B.1 therefore makes it a valid derived-Hom target.

Currying (F.10) gives an isomorphism of mapping complexes

\[ \operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}_\Lambda \bigl(\Gamma_c(F^\bullet\otimes L^\bullet),V^\bullet\bigr) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}_X(F^\bullet,a^!V^\bullet). \tag{F.13} \]

To check its signs, let a homogeneous map have degree \(n\) and restrict to \(F^i\otimes L^p\). On both sides its differential has the three terms \(d_Vh_{i,p}-(-1)^n h_{i+1,p}d_F-(-1)^{n+i}h_{i,p+1}d_L\). Thus this is a complex isomorphism, not only a degreewise bijection. Products in a mapping complex cause no rearrangement issue: the \(p\)-index has only finitely many values. Complexes of vector spaces compute derived Hom, since every acyclic vector-space complex splits and contracts; the same bounded-below injective assertion on \(X\) was proved in B.1. Equations (F.11)–(F.13) therefore prove

\[ R\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(R\Gamma_c(X,F),V) \simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_X(F,a^!V). \tag{F.14} \]

Mapping complexes here are allowed to be unbounded; no bounded-below assertion about \(R\operatorname{Hom}\) is needed. Taking degree zero gives the desired adjunction on bounded-below derived categories. Formula (F.12) is functorial, and sends quasi-isomorphisms of \(V\) to isomorphisms in the derived category, either by (F.14) and Yoneda or directly by the injective comparison. Different choices of \(L\) give the unique compatible right adjoint by the same Hom characterization. This constructs \(a^!\), rather than assuming its existence.

F.5. Local pairing, orientation, and smooth local systems

Put \(\omega_X=a^!\Lambda\). Restriction of the construction to an open \(U\) uses the c-soft resolution \(L|_U\) and gives \(\omega_X|_U=\omega_U\). Since (F.12) consists of injectives, its sections over \(U\) calculate derived sections. Formula (F.9) consequently gives the actual local comparison

\[ R\Gamma(U,\omega_X) \simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(R\Gamma_c(U,\Lambda),\Lambda). \tag{F.15} \]

More generally, for a bounded complex \(F\), internal Hom into this injective complex and (F.14) on \(U\) give

\[ R\Gamma(U,R\mathcal Hom(F,\omega_X)) \simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(R\Gamma_c(U,F),\Lambda). \tag{F.16} \]

Here internal derived Hom can indeed be computed this way: restriction of an injective sheaf to an open set is injective, because its left adjoint \(j_!\) is exact. Thus sheaf Hom into an injective is exact in its first variable. Moreover \(\mathcal Hom(F^i,I)\) is injective when \(I\) is injective: its Hom functor is \(\operatorname{Hom}(-\otimes F^i,I)\), which is exact over a field. The bounded complex \(F\) therefore gives a bounded-below complex of injectives by finite totalization; its ordinary sections compute the required derived sections. The maps in (F.15)–(F.16) are compatible with shrinking \(U\), where their right sides use the dual of extension by zero. Evaluation followed by the adjunction counit \(R\Gamma_c(\omega_X)\to\Lambda\) is the compact-support pairing: under (F.14), that counit corresponds to the identity of \(\omega_X\), so (F.16) identifies this pairing, including its evaluation map, with the displayed derived linear dual.

On a real \(m\)-manifold, compute stalks of (F.15) on coordinate balls. By C.5 their only compact-support group is \(\Lambda\) in degree \(m\). Extension by zero from a smaller ball preserves its local oriented generator: represent it with support on a still smaller closed ball and use the support excision of C.5; the two representatives then have the same relative sphere generator. Hence the sole cohomology sheaf of \(\omega_X\) is in degree \(-m\), with transition signs the orientation signs of C.4. The dual sign is the same sign. If \(\mathrm{or}_X\) denotes this rank-one orientation sheaf, the truncation construction in B.1 gives

\[ \omega_X\simeq\mathrm{or}_X[m]. \tag{F.17} \]

Complex charts have positive real determinant by C.4, so their positive generators agree and \(\mathrm{or}_X=\Lambda_X\) canonically for a complex \(d\)-manifold. A finite-rank local system \(L\) is locally a finite sum of copies of \(\Lambda\). Sheaf Hom out of it is exact and is \(L^\vee\otimes-\), as follows on these trivializations, whose changes of basis act by inverse transpose. Therefore

\[ D_XL=L^\vee[2d],\qquad D_X(L[d])=L^\vee[d]. \tag{F.18} \]

Finite-dimensional evaluation gives biduality for these local systems and their shifts. This proves the classical assertion of Proposition 2.3. It does not yet prove biduality for all constructible complexes across singular strata.

F.6. Closed support and the costalk of a dual

Let \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\) be closed, with the same finite-dimensional hypotheses. B.2 constructs \(i^!\) as the derived right adjoint of the exact \(i_*\). By (F.3), \(R\Gamma_c(X,i_*H)=R\Gamma_c(Z,H)\). Applying the two adjunctions, for every bounded-below \(H\) we obtain \(R\operatorname{Hom}_Z(H,i^!\omega_X)=R\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(R\Gamma_c(Z,H),\Lambda)\). Yoneda and F.4 identify

\[ i^!\omega_X=\omega_Z. \tag{F.19} \]

This also proves the independence of a closed ambient embedding in the definition of the structural dualizing complex. Its counit is the composed counit, since both correspond to the identity under the composed adjunction.

For bounded \(K\), tensor-Hom adjunction and the stalkwise identity \(i_*H\otimes K=i_*(H\otimes i^*K)\) now give

\[ i^!D_XK\simeq D_Zi^*K. \tag{F.20} \]

Explicitly, mapping a bounded-below \(H\) into the left side gives the successive complexes \(R\operatorname{Hom}_X(i_*H,R\mathcal Hom(K,\omega_X))\), \(R\operatorname{Hom}_X(i_*H\otimes K,\omega_X)\), and \(R\operatorname{Hom}_Z(H\otimes i^*K,\omega_Z)\), which identify with maps into the right side. The tensor-Hom comparison follows by ordinary currying against the injective resolution used in F.4; tensoring over a field preserves acyclic complexes, as is checked on stalks. These identifications commute with evaluation, so Yoneda supplies the stated natural map and its inverse. For bounded \(H\), the same calculation on every open set gives \(D_Xi_*H=i_*D_ZH\). Likewise the open adjunction and \(j_!H\otimes K=j_!(H\otimes j^*K)\) give \(D_Xj_!H=Rj_*D_UH\).

For \(Z=\{x\}\), the structural adjoint is the identity on vector spaces. Equation (F.20) yields the second formula in (2.1), \(H^m(i_x^!D_XK)=H^{-m}(i_x^*K)^\vee\), without assuming constructible biduality. The first formula in (2.1) and constructible biduality are subsequently proved in Appendix J from the Whitney geometry of I and the finite-neighborhood criterion of G.1. Appendix H supplies the general classical operation identities, and K.8 proves their algebraic constructibility hypotheses.

The permitted source comparison was with the free author notes of Mathew and the free arXiv manuscript of Schnürer–Soergel. Their soft-resolution construction guided the choice of model. The compact lifting, finite-bound argument, explicit section presentation, total-complex signs, local pairing and closed-support arguments actually used here have been proved above; references to other works inside those sources do not supply omitted prerequisites.

Appendix G. Biduality from finite neighborhoods, and the actual cone models

We continue over a field on the finite-dimensional classical spaces of Appendix F. For a complex of vector spaces write \(P^\vee=R\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(P,\Lambda)\). A bounded complex with finite-dimensional cohomology is perfect: choose complements to its cycles and boundaries, split off the resulting contractible pairs, and retain its finite-dimensional cohomology complex. Its evaluation into \(P^{\vee\vee}\) is an isomorphism. For homogeneous \(v\in P^r\) it is the map \(\phi\mapsto(-1)^r\phi(v)\); this sign makes evaluation a chain map with our Hom differential.

G.1. A local biduality criterion with its actual comparison maps

Proposition. Let \(F\) be bounded. Suppose that a point \(x\) has a cofinal basis of open neighborhoods \(U\) for which \(R\Gamma(U,F)\) is perfect. Then the canonical evaluation \(F\to D_XD_XF\) is an isomorphism on the cohomology stalks at \(x\). If this holds at every point, it is an isomorphism of sheaf complexes.

First note that all duals in this assertion exist and are bounded. F.4 gives \(\omega_X\) as a bounded complex of injectives, in degrees \([-N,0]\). A bounded representative of \(F\), and the exact tensor–Hom argument in F.5, therefore computes its internal dual by a bounded complex of injectives. The same applies to the second dual.

Choose nested neighborhoods from the stated basis and compact neighborhoods with \(U_{n+1}\subset K_n\subset U_n\), all containing \(x\). They can be made cofinal by requiring \(U_n\) to lie inside the metric ball of radius \(1/n\). Put

\[ C(U,G)=R\Gamma_c(U,G),\qquad S(K,G)=R\Gamma_K(X,G). \]

Extension of supports gives natural maps

\[ C(U_{n+1},G)\longrightarrow S(K_n,G) \longrightarrow C(U_n,G). \tag{G.1} \]

Their composites are the original support-extension maps. These can be represented on the same injective resolution, using the actual inclusions of support-section complexes and the filtered unions over compact supports. After applying a contravariant functor and then taking filtered colimits of cohomology, the two resulting systems have the same colimit: the displayed interleaving supplies maps both ways, and their composites are transitions, hence identities in the colimit. This elementary argument does not assert that duality commutes with an inverse limit.

F.6 supplies, for the closed inclusion of a compact \(K\),

\[ S(K,D_XF)=R\Gamma(K,D_K(F|_K)) \simeq R\Gamma(K,F|_K)^\vee. \tag{G.2} \]

The second equality uses the compactness of \(K\), so that its ordinary and compact-support sections agree, and the structural adjunction F.14 on \(K\). Closed subsets inherit the required finite dimension by F.2.

On the other hand, ordinary restriction interleaves the systems \(R\Gamma(U_n,F)\) and \(R\Gamma(K_n,F|_{K_n})\): restrict first from \(U_n\) to \(K_n\), then to \(U_{n+1}\). The maps here are the derived restriction maps induced by the sheaf adjunction units. Their composites are the original restrictions. Interleaving still holds after applying the covariant double-dual functor. Apply F.16 to \(D_XF\), take stalks, then use (G.1), (G.2), and this ordinary interleaving. For every \(q\) the result is

\[ \begin{aligned} H^q((D_XD_XF)_x) &=\varinjlim_n H^q\bigl(C(U_n,D_XF)^\vee\bigr)\\ &\simeq\varinjlim_n H^q\bigl(R\Gamma(K_n,F|_{K_n})^{\vee\vee}\bigr)\\ &\simeq\varinjlim_n H^q\bigl(R\Gamma(U_n,F)^{\vee\vee}\bigr). \end{aligned} \tag{G.3} \]

We must check the morphism, not only the groups. The pairing giving the first line is evaluation followed by the counit of F.14. Under closed adjunction, restricting a section of \(F\) to \(K_n\) pairs it with the supported dual section in (G.2). Currying this pairing gives precisely the vector-complex evaluation \(v\mapsto(\phi\mapsto(-1)^{|v|}\phi(v))\). Thus the map from \(F_x\) in (G.3) is the filtered colimit of the evaluation maps for the ordinary section complexes. Each is an isomorphism by the assumed perfectness. Finally, on an injective resolution, exact filtered colimits give \(\varinjlim_n H^q(R\Gamma(U_n,F))=H^q(F_x)\). This proves the proposition, including its canonical evaluation map. No stabilization or finiteness of the intermediate compact-neighborhood groups was assumed. Those groups were handled by the actual interleaving maps.

G.2. Local coefficients and finite cohomology of the links used here

We record the local-coefficient extension of C.1–C.2 needed below. Let \(L\) be a local system on a locally compact metrizable manifold. Transport along paths and its invariance under endpoint-fixed homotopies were proved in Appendix A.4. A degree-\(n\) singular cochain assigns to a simplex \(\sigma\) an element of \(L_{\sigma(v_0)}\). Its differential on an \((n+1)\)-simplex is

\[ (du)(\sigma)=\tau_{10}u(\sigma|[v_1,\ldots,v_{n+1}]) +\sum_{r=1}^{n+1}(-1)^r u(\sigma|[v_0,\ldots,\widehat v_r,\ldots,v_{n+1}]), \tag{G.4} \]

where \(\tau_{10}\) is transport along the first edge from \(v_1\) to \(v_0\). Every codimension-two face in \(d^2\) occurs twice with opposite signs. The only apparently different transports are the direct edge from \(v_2\) to \(v_0\) and the two consecutive edges; they agree by the homotopy inside the simplex. Thus \(d^2=0\).

The small-chain, subdivision and prism constructions of C.1 extend to these cochains as follows. Pull the local system back to each simplex or prism, and trivialize it by transport from its first vertex. That domain is contractible, so transport is path independent there. Each subdivided simplex receives the transport of its first-vertex value along the straight edge in the original domain. On common faces these identifications agree, and the cancellations proving the subdivision and prism identities in C.1 are consequently unchanged. This proves both the small-cochain comparison and homotopy invariance, with the induced transport on coefficients.

We first justify the countability needed to apply C.2. Every connected component of a metrizable manifold has a countable basis. Here is a metric proof, allowing arbitrarily many components. A separable metric space has a countable basis, given by rational-radius balls about a countable dense set; its subspaces consequently have countable bases and are separable, by choosing a point in each nonempty basic open set. Let \(X_n\) consist of the points whose radius-\(1/n\) ball is separable. Coordinate charts show that the \(X_n\) cover the manifold. Starting with \(A_0=\{x_0\}\), define

\[ A_{k+1}=A_k\cup\bigcup_{n\geq1}\ \bigcup_{y\in A_k\cap X_n} B\bigl(y,1/(2n)\bigr),\qquad A=\bigcup_{k\geq0}A_k. \]

Each \(A_k\) is separable: replace each set of centers \(A_k\cap X_n\) by a countable dense subset, which gives exactly the same union of open balls of that fixed radius. Those balls are separable by definition of \(X_n\). A countable union of separable subspaces is separable, by taking the union of their countable dense sets. The set \(A\) is open because every point belongs to some \(A_k\cap X_n\). It is also closed. If \(x\in\overline A\), choose \(n\) with \(x\in X_n\) and \(y\in A\) with \(d(x,y)<1/(4n)\). Then \(B(y,1/(2n))\subset B(x,1/n)\) is separable, so \(y\in X_{2n}\). The construction includes \(B(y,1/(4n))\) in \(A\), and this ball contains \(x\). Thus the connected component of \(x_0\) lies in the separable set \(A\) and inherits a countable basis. Components are open, since coordinate balls are path connected. The same argument applies to every open submanifold. Consequently C.2's compact exhaustions and locally finite closed refinements can be chosen separately on its components; their union remains locally finite because the components are disjoint and open.

Sheafify the cochains. On a trivializing convex chart this is the exact augmented cochain resolution proved in A.2–A.3. Hence it resolves \(L\) on stalks. It is flabby by the representative argument of C.2, now with the componentwise refinements just justified: refine an open cover so that the representatives lie in trivializing charts, extend their values on the small simplices to the ambient space by zero, and sheafify. A simplex lies in one component, so the componentwise representatives give one cochain on the entire open set. Agreement is a local assertion on smaller simplices and is preserved by these extensions. Thus its ordinary sections compute sheaf cohomology. The refinement comparison of C.2 identifies them with (G.4); the subdivision identities just checked prove that comparison for these local coefficients. In particular, a product with an interval induces the ordinary-cohomology equivalence given by projection and a slice, with all interval restrictions compatible.

We also need this interval assertion for a bounded complex \(J\) whose cohomology sheaves are finite-rank local systems on \(M\times I\). Let \(p:M\times I\to M\). For a sufficiently small contractible chart \(V\subset M\), each cohomology sheaf of \(J\) is constant on \(V\times I\). The preceding cochain contraction computes its sections in degree zero. Apply the finitely many truncation triangles of B.1 to \(J\); they show that \(R\Gamma(V\times I,J)\) has the cohomology of its stalk and that restriction to a slice is an isomorphism on those groups. Since ordinary direct image preserves injectives, these computations on \(V\) identify the counit

\[ p^*Rp_*J\longrightarrow J \tag{G.5} \]

as a quasi-isomorphism on every stalk. Put \(J_0=Rp_*J\); it is bounded with finite-rank locally constant cohomology and is identified with every slice restriction. Derived composition of ordinary sections and direct image gives \(R\Gamma(M\times I,J)=R\Gamma(M,J_0)\). These identifications come from the counit, so restriction to a subinterval yields the same comparison, rather than an unrelated isomorphism of vector spaces.

For a circle, A.4 identifies the ordinary cohomology of a finite-rank local system with \([V\xrightarrow{T-1}V]\). Hence it is perfect, as is a finite disjoint union of circles. The same is true of every finite-rank local system on the circle bundle \(M\to C\) in Section 1 (the cone calculation). Here are the finite-cover details. The actual finite triangle decomposition of \(C\) was constructed in E.3. Subdivide it until each open vertex star lies in a trivializing chart for the tautological line bundle. This is possible: the compact realization has a Lebesgue number for the finite trivializing cover, subdivision decreases the simplex mesh by the factor at most \(2/3\), and a star has diameter at most twice that mesh. The homeomorphism from the compact triangle realization to \(C\) is uniformly continuous. The Lebesgue-number assertion itself follows by choosing, at every point, a metric ball contained in a covering set, taking a finite subcover by the half-radius balls, and taking the minimum of their radii.

If the original triangle decomposition has more than one cell with the same vertex set, first use its barycentric subdivision: vertices then label cells and simplices label chains of faces, giving an ordinary simplicial complex with the same realization. Every nonempty finite intersection of its open vertex stars is the open star of their spanned simplex. On this triangulated surface it is an open disc: a triangle has its interior, an edge has its two adjacent triangle halves, and a vertex has the cyclic fan of triangles given by the local disc model in E.3. Each lies in a line-bundle chart. The inverse image of such an intersection in \(M\) is therefore a product of an open disc with a circle. By (G.4) and interval or disc contraction, the cohomology of a finite-rank local system there is the finite two-term circle cohomology.

Finally use the derived two-open-set sequence proved by the sheaf resolution in A.4. Finite induction shows that a finite cover whose nonempty intersections have perfect section complexes has perfect global sections: separate the last set from the union of the preceding ones, apply the induction to their intersections, and take the fiber of the two-set difference map. Kernels, cokernels and extensions of finite-dimensional vector spaces remain finite-dimensional, and the finite number of these triangles keeps the degree range bounded. This proves perfectness on \(M\). Applying finitely many truncation triangles proves it for every bounded \(J_0\) with finite-rank locally constant cohomology on this link.

G.3. The attaching complex on an actual open cone

Let \(M\) be one of the compact links just considered, and let \(U_R=(M\times[0,R))/(M\times\{0\})\) be the open cone, with vertex \(v\). Write \(j:U_R\setminus\{v\}\hookrightarrow U_R\) and \(i:\{v\}\hookrightarrow U_R\). Suppose \(F\) is bounded, its vertex stalk \(A=i^*F\) is perfect, and its cohomology on the puncture consists of finite-rank local systems. Equation (G.5) writes \(j^*F=p^*J_0\). Put

\[ B=R\Gamma(M,J_0),\qquad a:A\longrightarrow B. \tag{G.6} \]

Here \(B\) is perfect by G.2. The identification \(i^*Rj_*j^*F=B\) uses the compatible subinterval restrictions in (G.5) and the injective stalk calculation of A.4. The map \(a\) is the actual restriction of the adjunction unit \(F\to Rj_*j^*F\).

For completeness, the reconstruction required here follows directly from B.2:

\[ F\simeq\operatorname{Fib}\bigl(Rj_*j^*F\oplus i_*A \xrightarrow{\mathrm{res}-i_*a}i_*B\bigr). \tag{G.7} \]

The units give maps from \(F\) to the two summands, whose compositions agree by naturality. Represent the units on complexes and choose the resulting commuting homotopy; the cone differential of B.1 then gives the map into the displayed fiber. On the puncture it is the identity of \(j^*F\). At the vertex the fiber is \(\operatorname{Fib}(B\oplus A\to B)\), and projection to \(A\) is a quasi-isomorphism, since the \(B\xrightarrow1B\) pair contracts. The map from \(F\) induces the identity under this projection. It is therefore a quasi-isomorphism on every stalk, proving (G.7). This also shows that the attaching map, rather than merely its effect on cohomology dimensions, is being retained.

Taking ordinary sections in (G.7) gives the same contractible pair and hence

\[ R\Gamma(U_R,F)=A, \qquad R\Gamma(M\times(r,R),F)=B\quad(0<r<R). \tag{G.8} \]

The restriction from the first complex to the second is \(a\). All smaller-radius comparisons use the original units and the product restrictions in (G.5), so (G.8) is compatible with those restrictions.

Let \(K_r\) be the closed subcone of radius \(r<R\), which is compact. The support fiber formula of C.5, now for \(F\), gives

\[ R\Gamma_{K_r}(U_R,F)=\operatorname{Fib}(A\xrightarrow a B). \tag{G.9} \]

Increasing \(r\) restricts the complementary annulus and induces the identity on \(B\) under (G.5); it induces the identity on \(A\) as well. These support groups consequently have identity transition maps in the displayed model. The sets \(K_r\), \(r\uparrow R\), are cofinal among compact subsets of \(U_R\). Taking their filtered union in an injective resolution, as in C.12, proves

\[ R\Gamma_c(U_R,F)=\operatorname{Fib}(A\xrightarrow a B)=i_v^!F. \tag{G.10} \]

The last equality is B.2's point-support fiber. Its comparison with (G.9) is the support-extension map: restriction from the puncture to an annulus gives the identity of \(B\). Thus extension from \(U_r\) to \(U_R\) also induces the identity on (G.10). We have proved the local stabilization with its actual maps; no general stratified homotopy theorem has been presumed.

Ordinary neighborhoods at the vertex have the perfect section complex \(A\). At every other point, a sufficiently small chart trivializes the finite local cohomology systems, and the truncation argument of G.2 gives perfect sections there. G.1 proves biduality for \(F\). F.16 and (G.10), with their compatible extension maps, give the other point exchange, and F.20 gives its companion:

\[ i_v^*D_XF\simeq\operatorname{Fib}(a)^\vee, \qquad i_v^!D_XF\simeq A^\vee. \tag{G.11} \]

Both are perfect. Away from the vertex, F.5 and the local truncation argument show that the dual still has finite-rank locally constant cohomology. Thus duality preserves these two-stratum constructible complexes, and G.1 applies to their duals too. In particular, F.6's identity \(D_Xj_!H=Rj_*D_UH\), followed by this actual biduality, gives the reverse identity \(D_XRj_*H=j_!D_UH\) for these models. This conclusion has been proved at their full bounded-complex scope, not only for constant sheaves.

G.4. Consequences for the curve and cone calculations

A punctured disc is a cone on a circle, and the model of finitely many discs with their centers identified is a cone on the finite disjoint union of those circles. The radial maps and quotient topology were proved in B.3–B.4. A finite-rank local system on each punctured branch has the two-term complex of A.4. Thus G.3 proves biduality and both stalk/costalk exchanges for every bounded complex constructible for these branch-and-vertex decompositions. In particular both classical punctured-line duality formulas in Section 2 now have proofs.

For the branch-normalization sheaf \(N\) of Section 1 (the node calculation), one also obtains \(D_XN=N[2]\) canonically. Locally \(N\) is the sum of the closed direct images of the constant sheaves on the separate smooth discs, by B.4. F.6 and F.5 dualize each such summand to the same summand shifted by two. The local degree \(-2\) generators are the positive complex orientation generators on the respective branches. They agree when a branch neighborhood is shrunk, by C.5, and are permuted when branch labels are permuted. They therefore identify the sole cohomology sheaf of \(D_XN\) with \(N\). The truncation isomorphism gives \(D_XN=N[2]\), also across overlaps with the smooth part of the curve. Dualizing the actual short exact sequence (1.2) now proves the triangle (2.2). This proves that classical dual object and its attaching maps at the branch model. L.2–L.4 supply the general algebraic node criterion and identify its actual normalization with these analytic branches, so the calculation applies to every complex algebraic node.

For the affine cone of Section 1 (the cone calculation), C.3 proves that the neighborhoods really are the cones \(U_R\) on its compact circle-bundle link. G.2 proves the needed link finiteness even with finite-rank local coefficients. Therefore G.3 proves both dual exchanges and biduality for every bounded complex constructible for its smooth puncture and vertex. For \(F=\Lambda_X\), \(A=\Lambda\), \(B=C^\bullet(M;\Lambda)\), and \(a\) is the constant-cochain map of C.3. Equations (1.3), (G.10) and (G.11) prove all the asserted classical dual stalk and costalk groups in Proposition 1.5, including their degree signs. For \(F=Rj_*\Lambda\), the map \(a\) is the identity of \(B\), so its costalk and the stalk of its dual vanish, as the reverse extension identity also shows.

G.1 isolates the exact finiteness input for general biduality, while G.2–G.4 verify it on the actual curve and cone spaces used in Sections 1–2. Appendices I–J subsequently construct the general normal neighborhoods and prove coefficient stabilization, compact-link finiteness and fixed-stratification duality. K.6 subsequently proves existence of finite algebraic Whitney refinements.

The free-source comparison for the local model is Goresky's author-hosted notes, §§9.1–9.4 and 12.4–12.8. The general finiteness and stratification assertions there are not imported as completed proofs. The finite cover, local-coefficient comparison, attaching fiber, support maps and evaluation argument required here have instead been written out using Appendices A–F.

Appendix H. Classical proper-support operations and their duality identities

Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a continuous map between locally compact Hausdorff metrizable spaces of the finite compact cohomological dimension proved in F.2. Coefficients are a field. All derived inputs are bounded below unless a stronger bound is stated. The same hypotheses are imposed on spaces in a base-change square; they hold for the classical algebraic fiber products in this course. This appendix proves the operation identities used in Sections 2–3. Preservation of algebraic constructibility requires the additional geometric arguments subsequently proved in K.6–K.8.

H.1. Proper supports and the fiber map

We call a map proper when the inverse image of every compact subset is compact. For maps between locally compact Hausdorff spaces this condition implies that the map is closed. Indeed, to test whether a point \(y\) lies in the image of a closed set, choose a compact neighborhood \(T\) of \(y\). Its inverse image is compact, and the image of its intersection with the closed set is compact, hence closed in \(T\). If \(y\) is a limit of the original image, this compact image contains \(y\). Properness is local on the target: a compact set has a finite closed shrinking of an open cover by relatively compact neighborhoods, and its inverse image is then a finite union of compact inverse images. It is preserved under base change: over a compact subset of the new target, the pullback is a closed subset of the product of that compact set and the compact inverse image of its image in the old target. Closed restrictions and finite unions of proper supports remain proper for the same reasons.

Define

\[ (f_!F)(V)=\{s\in\Gamma(f^{-1}V,F): f|_{\operatorname{supp}s}:\operatorname{supp}s\to V\text{ is proper}\}. \tag{H.1} \]

The preceding local property proves the sheaf axiom. Finite unions of supports prove closure under addition. The functor is left exact: a section in the kernel of a sheaf map lifts uniquely into its kernel sheaf, with exactly the same support. If \(f\) is proper then \(f_!=f_*\). For the structural map this is \(\Gamma_c\), and for open or closed inclusions it agrees with the functors of B.2.

The ordinary inverse image \(f^*\) is sheafification of the usual neighborhood-colimit presheaf. Its stalk at \(x\) is \(F_{f(x)}\), so it is exact. The section definition of \(f_*\) gives its adjunction with \(f^*\); hence \(f_*\) preserves injectives. Injective resolutions therefore give \(Rf_*\) and the derived ordinary adjunction, including composition of ordinary direct images. These assertions require no constructibility hypothesis.

We will use the following consequence of F.1. If \(M\) is c-soft and \(Z\subset X\) is closed, then every compactly supported section of \(M|_Z\) extends to a compactly supported section of \(M\) on \(X\). Choose a compact neighborhood \(T\) of its support. On \((Z\cap T)\cup\partial T\), prescribe the given section and zero, respectively. They agree on the intersection because the support lies in \(\operatorname{int}T\). The finite closed gluing and compact extension of F.1 extend these data; cutting off across \(\partial T\) gives the required section, and it agrees with the original section on all of \(Z\), including the zero germs outside \(T\).

For \(y\in Y\), let \(X_y=f^{-1}(y)\). Restricting a section with proper support defines

\[ (f_!F)_y\longrightarrow\Gamma_c(X_y,F|_{X_y}). \tag{H.2} \]

This map is injective. If a representative \(s\) restricts to zero on \(X_y\), the closed image of its proper support misses \(y\); on the complementary neighborhood its restriction is zero. If \(F\) is c-soft, (H.2) is also onto: \(X_y\) is closed, so the compact extension just proved extends a compact fiber section to one on \(X\). A compact support is proper over \(Y\). For arbitrary \(F\), take the beginning \(0\to F\to I^0\to I^1\) of the Godement resolution. Both \(I^0,I^1\) are c-soft. Both sides of (H.2) are left exact in \(F\), since restriction to the fiber is exact. The two isomorphisms for \(I^0,I^1\) identify their kernels, proving that (H.2) is an isomorphism for every sheaf.

H.2. Derived fibers, bounds, and arbitrary proper-support base change

An injective sheaf on \(X\) restricts to a c-soft sheaf on the closed fiber, by F.1. Restricting an injective resolution to the fiber is exact, and that restricted resolution therefore computes compact-support cohomology. Apply (H.2) termwise to get the canonical derived fiber formula

\[ (Rf_!F)_y\simeq R\Gamma_c(X_y,F|_{X_y}). \tag{H.3} \]

The same proof works for a bounded-below complex, using the acyclic-resolution comparison proved in F.1. In particular, a sheaf which is c-soft on each fiber is \(f_!\)-acyclic. Bounded-below complexes of such sheaves compute \(Rf_!\) termwise.

If \(\dim_cX\leq N\), its closed fibers have dimension at most \(N\) by F.2. Thus \(R^qf_!F=0\) for \(q>N\) for every sheaf \(F\). Finitely many truncation triangles now show that

\[ F\in D^{[a,b]}(X)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad Rf_!F\in D^{[a,b+N]}(Y). \tag{H.4} \]

This is a bound for sheaves without a finiteness assumption on their stalks. It does not imply that the resulting cohomology sheaves are constructible.

Consider the Cartesian square with \(f':X'=X\times_Y Y'\to Y'\), \(g:Y'\to Y\), and \(g':X'\to X\). Pullback of a proper support is proper by H.1. Pulling back sections consequently gives the natural morphism

\[ g^*f_!F\longrightarrow f'_!g'^*F. \tag{H.5} \]

It may equivalently be formed by the inverse/direct-image adjunction units; on a local representative it is precisely restriction to the pullback support. At \(y'\), (H.2) identifies this map with the identity on compact sections of the same fiber \(X_{g(y')}=X'_{y'}\), with its same restricted sheaf. It is therefore an isomorphism.

To derive it, choose an injective resolution \(I\) on \(X\). The restriction of \(g'^*I\) to every \(f'\)-fiber is the restriction of \(I\) to the corresponding \(f\)-fiber and is c-soft. Thus \(g'^*I\) is termwise \(f'_!\)-acyclic, while \(g^*\) is exact. Applying (H.5) termwise proves

\[ g^*Rf_!F\xrightarrow{\sim}Rf'_!g'^*F. \tag{H.6} \]

This proves the actual base-change map on bounded-below complexes. Pasting two squares gives the same map: both underived maps pull back the same local section to its iterated pullback support, and the acyclic comparisons used to derive them are natural. If \(f\) is proper, \(f_!=f_*\), so this includes classical proper base change for ordinary direct image.

H.3. Composition and c-soft images

Proper direct image preserves c-soft sheaves. Let \(M\) be c-soft on \(X\), and take a section of \(f_!M\) over a compact \(K\subset Y\). By F.1 it is represented on an open neighborhood \(V\) of \(K\), hence by a section \(s\) of \(M\) over \(f^{-1}V\) with support proper over \(V\). Choose a compact neighborhood \(T\) of \(K\) inside \(V\). The restriction to the closed set \(f^{-1}T\) has compact support. The compact closed-section extension in H.1 extends it to a compactly supported section \(t\) on \(X\). As a section of \(f_!M\), it agrees with the original section on \(\operatorname{int}T\), and thus extends its germs on \(K\). This proves c-softness of \(f_!M\).

For composable \(X\xrightarrow fY\xrightarrow gZ\), the ordinary identity \(g_*f_*=(gf)_*\) restricts to

\[ g_!f_!=(gf)_!. \tag{H.7} \]

Here is the support check in both directions. A section of \(F\) over \((gf)^{-1}V\) has a closed support \(S\). If \(S\to V\) is proper, then \(S\to g^{-1}V\) via \(f\) is proper: the inverse image of a compact \(T\subset g^{-1}V\) is a closed subset of the compact inverse image of \(g(T)\). Thus the section defines one of \(f_!F\). Its support is \(f(S)\), by the fiber isomorphism (H.2); this image is closed. Its inverse image over a compact subset of \(V\) is the image of the corresponding compact subset of \(S\), so it is proper over \(V\). Conversely, if \(S\to g^{-1}V\) is proper and \(f(S)\to V\) is proper, the inverse image in \(S\) of a compact subset of \(V\) is obtained by two successive compact inverse images. This proves (H.7).

An injective resolution on \(X\) has c-soft terms. Its image under \(f_!\) has c-soft terms by the first paragraph, hence is termwise \(g_!\)-acyclic by H.2. The bounded-below acyclic comparison therefore derives (H.7) to

\[ Rg_!Rf_!\simeq R(gf)_!. \tag{H.8} \]

Threefold composition and the identity map are compatible because the underived identifications preserve the same section and support, and the resolution comparisons are natural. This also proves \(R\Gamma_c(Y,Rf_!F)=R\Gamma_c(X,F)\).

H.4. Sums and the projection formula

Proper direct image commutes with filtered colimits. Indeed, after taking a stalk, this is (H.2) and the compact-section colimit theorem F.4 on the fiber; inverse image commutes with these colimits because it is computed on stalks. In particular \(f_!\) commutes with arbitrary direct sums.

Multiplying a section with proper support by a pulled-back section defines

\[ f_!F\otimes G\longrightarrow f_!(F\otimes f^*G). \tag{H.9} \]

Its support is contained in the original proper support. On a fiber over \(y\), the pulled-back sheaf \(G\) is the constant sheaf with value \(G_y\). The stalk of (H.9) is therefore \(\Gamma_c(X_y,F|_{X_y})\otimes G_y\to \Gamma_c(X_y,F|_{X_y}\otimes\underline{G_y})\). This is an isomorphism: choose a basis of \(G_y\), express the tensor sheaf as a sum of copies of \(F|_{X_y}\), and use the compact-section direct-sum statement in F.2. The resulting map is the original multiplication map, independent of the chosen basis. Hence (H.9) is an isomorphism of sheaves.

For complexes, replace \(F\) by a bounded-below injective resolution \(I\), and use a bounded-below representative of \(G\). Each term of \(I\otimes f^*G\), restricted to a fiber, is a finite sum of tensor products of a c-soft sheaf with a constant vector space. Such a tensor product is a direct sum of c-soft sheaves, hence c-soft. Thus this complex computes its proper-support image termwise. Over a field tensoring preserves quasi-isomorphisms: stalkwise an acyclic complex of vector spaces contracts, and its tensor product contracts by the same homotopy with the Koszul sign convention. Applying (H.9) termwise gives

\[ Rf_!(F\otimes^L f^*G)\simeq Rf_!F\otimes^L G. \tag{H.10} \]

This proves the projection formula for the stated bounded-below complexes, with arbitrary coefficient sheaves, rather than only for finite-rank local systems.

H.5. The general classical exceptional inverse image

Let \(M\) be c-soft on \(X\). F.3 proves that \(F\otimes M\) is c-soft for every sheaf \(F\). Thus \(T_{M,f}(F)=f_!(F\otimes M)\) is exact: apply the long exact sequence of \(Rf_!\) and the acyclicity of its kernel tensor term. It preserves direct sums by H.4, hence all colimits by the cokernel presentation of a colimit used in F.3.

Its right adjoint on a sheaf \(G\) on \(Y\) is the sheaf

\[ f^{\#}(M,G)(U)= \operatorname{Hom}_Y\bigl(f_!j_{U!}(M|_U),G\bigr). \tag{H.11} \]

The proof is the actual section presentation of F.3 with \(T_{M,f}\) in place of \(T_M\). For clarity, apply this exact, sum-preserving functor to the open-cover presentation of \(\Lambda_U\); taking Hom into \(G\) gives the equalizer which proves the sheaf axiom for (H.11). A presentation of arbitrary \(F\) by sums of \(\Lambda_U\), followed by such a presentation of its kernel, identifies both kernels and gives

\[ \operatorname{Hom}_X(F,f^{\#}(M,G)) =\operatorname{Hom}_Y(f_!(F\otimes M),G). \tag{H.12} \]

If \(G\) is injective, exactness of \(T_{M,f}\) implies injectivity of \(f^{\#}(M,G)\).

Choose the bounded c-soft resolution \(\Lambda_X\to L\) of F.4 in degrees \(0,\ldots,N\). Replace a bounded-below \(G\) on \(Y\) by an injective resolution \(J\). Define

\[ (f^!G)^n=\bigoplus_{p=0}^N f^{\#}(L^p,J^{n+p}), \qquad (du)_p=d_Ju_p-(-1)^n u_{p+1}d_L. \tag{H.13} \]

This is a bounded-below complex of injectives. The mixed terms in its square cancel exactly as in F.12. The augmentation \(F\to F\otimes L\) is a quasi-isomorphism, and its total terms are c-soft, so \(f_!(F\otimes L)\) computes \(Rf_!F\). Currying (H.12) identifies the two mapping complexes: on \(F^i\otimes L^p\), a degree-\(n\) map has differential \(d_Jh_{i,p}-(-1)^nh_{i+1,p}d_F-(-1)^{n+i}h_{i,p+1}d_L\) on both sides. Hence

\[ R\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_!F,G) \simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_X(F,f^!G). \tag{H.14} \]

As in F.4 the mapping complexes may be unbounded; the adjunction objects themselves lie in \(D^+\). Quasi-isomorphisms and different choices of resolution give the same right adjoint by this Hom characterization. Its counit \(Rf_!f^!G\to G\) is the trace associated to the identity of \(f^!G\). Equation (H.8) identifies the right adjoint of a composite with the composite of these right adjoints, and identifies its counit with the composed counit. In particular \(\omega_X=f^!\omega_Y\). For an open immersion this agrees with \(j^!=j^*\), and for a closed immersion with B.2's \(i^!\), by uniqueness of the respective right adjoints.

H.6. Duality identities before constructible biduality

For bounded \(A\) and bounded-below \(B\) on \(Y\), the constructed operations satisfy

\[ f^!R\mathcal Hom(A,B) \simeq R\mathcal Hom(f^*A,f^!B). \tag{H.15} \]

Map a bounded-below \(H\) on \(X\) into either side. The adjunction (H.14), tensor–Hom currying, and (H.10) give in order \(R\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_!H\otimes A,B)\), \(R\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_!(H\otimes f^*A),B)\), and \(R\operatorname{Hom}_X(H\otimes f^*A,f^!B)\). These are precisely the mapping complexes into the right side. All targets are bounded below because \(A\) is bounded; the injective Hom construction of F.5 justifies the internal derived Hom. Naturality and Yoneda prove (H.15), with the map obtained from evaluation and the adjunction counit.

For bounded \(K\) on \(X\) and bounded-below \(B\) on \(Y\), the same argument, now testing with \(H\) on \(Y\), gives

\[ Rf_*R\mathcal Hom(K,f^!B) \simeq R\mathcal Hom(Rf_!K,B). \tag{H.16} \]

Indeed, its mapping complexes are successively \(R\operatorname{Hom}_X(f^*H\otimes K,f^!B)\), \(R\operatorname{Hom}_Y(Rf_!(f^*H\otimes K),B)\), and \(R\operatorname{Hom}_Y(H\otimes Rf_!K,B)\). Bound (H.4) makes \(Rf_!K\) bounded, so this internal-Hom target again lies in \(D^+\). Taking the structural dualizing complexes in (H.15)–(H.16) proves

\[ D_Xf^*A\simeq f^!D_YA, \qquad D_YRf_!K\simeq Rf_*D_XK. \tag{H.17} \]

Neither identity uses constructible biduality. The model (F.12) for \(\omega_X=a_X^!\Lambda\) is a bounded complex of injectives: the coefficient complex has its sole term in degree zero and \(L\) has only finitely many degrees. Consequently \(D_XK\) is bounded for bounded \(K\), by the internal-Hom construction of F.5. Equation (H.4) then also bounds \(Rf_!D_XK\). If evaluation is additionally known to be an isomorphism for both \(K\) and \(Rf_!D_XK\), applying the second identity to \(D_XK\) and then dualizing gives \(D_YRf_*K\simeq Rf_!D_XK\). This proves the exact reduction for the reverse exchange. Appendix J proves the biduality hypothesis for every complex constructible on a given finite Whitney stratification. K.6–K.8 prove the required algebraic refinements and proper-support image constructibility, then establish the reversal for every classical algebraic image at the stated scope. Likewise (H.13) constructs \(f^!\) on \(D^+\), and K.8 proves its preservation of bounded algebraic constructibility using the pullback exchange and canonical biduality. No such preservation is inferred merely from the existence of the adjunction.

The freely accessible sources used for comparison are Mathew's author notes, §§2.3–2.6 and 4, and Schnürer–Soergel's arXiv manuscript, §§3–7. The proofs here include the compact closed-section extension, fiber-kernel argument, proper-support composition, acyclic base-change comparison, projection map and explicit adjoint needed at the classical field-coefficient scope. Their references to other works are not used in place of these proofs.

Appendix I. Control tubes and normal local triviality

This appendix proves the geometric local-triviality input for a given finite Whitney stratification. Work locally in a smooth real manifold, with smooth meaning \(C^\infty\), and let \(Z\) be a closed subset partitioned into finitely many smooth locally closed strata. The frontier of a stratum is a union of smaller strata. We write \(S<T\) when \(S\subset\overline T\setminus T\). The local assertions also apply to a locally finite stratification by restricting to a neighborhood meeting finitely many strata. Existence of a finite algebraic Whitney stratification and finite cohomology for constructible coefficients on its links are separate assertions; they are not consequences of the definition. Appendix J proves the latter coefficient assertion after the geometry constructed here; K.6 proves the algebraic refinement assertion.

I.1. The elementary smooth tools used below

We record the smooth constructions needed in the argument. They do not require a triangulation theorem. A second-countable smooth manifold has a compact exhaustion \(K_n\subset\operatorname{int}K_{n+1}\): cover it by countably many relatively compact coordinate balls and successively add finitely many such balls covering the preceding compact set. On each compact annulus \(K_n\setminus\operatorname{int}K_{n-1}\), choose finitely many smaller coordinate balls whose closures lie in prescribed covering sets and in \(\operatorname{int}K_{n+1}\setminus K_{n-2}\). The resulting family is locally finite. This proves the refinement and closed-shrinking properties used here.

The function \(b(t)=e^{-1/t}\) for \(t>0\), and zero for \(t\leq0\), is smooth. Its successive right derivatives are polynomials in \(1/t\) times \(e^{-1/t}\), and tend to zero: use \(e^s\geq s^m/m!\) with \(m\) larger than the polynomial degree. Translates and products give smooth bumps supported in the preceding coordinate balls and positive on the smaller balls. Divide them by their locally finite positive sum to get a partition of unity. In particular every positive continuous function has a positive smooth minorant: choose each bump's constant coefficient below the function on that bump's support, then sum using the partition. The same construction supplies a smooth metric and a proper smooth exhaustion function. For the latter, take smooth cutoffs \(\chi_n=1\) near \(K_n\), supported in \(\operatorname{int}K_{n+1}\), and sum \(1-\chi_n\). Near any point all but finitely many summands vanish; outside \(K_{m+1}\) the sum is at least \(m\).

The smooth metric also supplies a compatible distance by taking infima of lengths of piecewise smooth paths on each connected component. On a compact coordinate ball its quadratic form is bounded above and below by positive multiples of the Euclidean form. Straight segments give the upper local distance bound; every path exiting a larger coordinate ball must cross a shell of positive Euclidean width, giving the lower local bound. Thus this distance induces the manifold topology. Distinct components can be assigned a bounded positive separation after bounding the distance within each component.

The smooth inverse-function argument can be obtained directly by contraction. After translating and applying an invertible linear map, write a map as \(F(x)=x+R(x)\), with \(\|dR\|<1/2\) on a closed ball. For small \(y\), iteration of \(x\mapsto y-R(x)\) stays in that ball and converges, since successive differences decrease geometrically. It gives the unique inverse. Subtracting the equations for two values gives continuity and a Lipschitz bound; taking difference quotients gives derivative \((dF)^{-1}\). Repeated differentiation proves smoothness. The same estimates, uniform on a compact parameter set, give the parameter version. If \(dq\) is onto, complete its rows to an invertible coordinate differential and apply this result: \(q\) becomes a coordinate projection. If \(S\) is a submanifold and \(q|_S\) is onto, first choose coordinates on \(S\) with these first coordinates, extend them to a submanifold chart, and use \(q\) itself for the first coordinates. Thus simultaneously

\[ S=\{v=0\},\qquad q(u,v)=(u_1,\ldots,u_p). \tag{I.1} \]

We also need the elementary flow theorem. In a compact coordinate ball a smooth vector field \(V\) has bounds \(|V|\leq M\), \(\|dV\|\leq L\). For \(aM\) smaller than the available radius and \(aL<1\), the integral operator \(x(t)\mapsto x_0+\int_0^tV(x(s))\,ds\) is a contraction on the closed set of continuous paths staying in that ball, with the supremum norm. Its iterates converge geometrically to a differentiable solution; the integral equation gives its derivative. The same argument proves uniqueness and continuous dependence. More explicitly, iterating the inequality for two solutions bounds their difference by \(e^{L|t|}|x_0-y_0|\); the remainder after \(m\) iterations is bounded by a constant times \((L|t|)^m/m!\), which tends to zero. The differentiated integral equation for the initial-value derivative is a linear integral equation with the same contraction estimate. Higher differentiated equations have already constructed lower derivatives in their inhomogeneous terms, so induction proves smooth dependence of every order. Uniqueness gives the composition law and the inverse flow at negative time. Patching the coordinate solutions gives a maximal open time interval on a manifold. At a finite endpoint its trajectory leaves every compact subset of that manifold: otherwise a convergent subsequence in a compact set enters a coordinate ball with a uniform positive existence time and extends the trajectory. These are all the smooth-flow facts used below.

I.2. Whitney regularity and the tubular submersion

In Euclidean coordinates Whitney (b) for \(T,S\) says: if \(x_n\in T\), \(y_n\in S\) converge to \(p\in S\), their tangent planes converge to \(E\), and their secant lines converge to \(\ell\), then \(\ell\subset E\). It is invariant under smooth coordinate changes. Indeed, for a diffeomorphism \(h\), integration of its derivative on the short segment between the two points gives

\[ h(x_n)-h(y_n)=dh_p(x_n-y_n)+o(|x_n-y_n|). \tag{I.2} \]

The limiting tangent plane becomes \(dh_pE\), and the limiting secant becomes \(dh_p\ell\), since \(dh_p\) is invertible. Applying the inverse diffeomorphism proves both directions.

Condition (b) implies (a), namely \(T_pS\subset E\). For \(0\ne v\in T_pS\), choose a smooth curve \(c(t)=p+tv+o(t)\) in \(S\). With \(t_n=\sqrt{|x_n-p|}\), the secants from \(x_n\) to \(c(t_n)\), divided by \(t_n\), tend to \(-v\). Condition (b) puts \(v\) in \(E\). In coordinates flattening \(S\), the unit normal direction from \(x_n\) to its coordinate projection onto \(S\) also has a convergent subsequence. Condition (b) puts its limit in \(E\); it is nonzero and perpendicular to \(T_pS\). Consequently \(\dim T>\dim S\) for every incident distinct pair. The compactness used here is elementary: orthogonal projectors of fixed rank form a closed bounded subset of the finite-dimensional matrix space.

A tube of \(S\) is a diffeomorphism \(\phi\) from a neighborhood of the zero section in an inner-product vector bundle \(E\to S\) onto a neighborhood of \(S\), restricting to the identity on that section. Write

\[ \pi_S(\phi(v))=\operatorname{base}(v),\qquad \rho_S(\phi(v))=|v|^2. \tag{I.3} \]

In an orthonormal bundle chart these are coordinate projection and squared normal distance. Such a chart exists by applying Gram–Schmidt to a local frame; its divisions are by positive smooth norms. For a Whitney pair \(T,S\),

\[ (\pi_S,\rho_S)|_T:T\cap U_S\longrightarrow S\times(0,\infty) \quad\hbox{is a submersion after shrinking the tube.} \tag{I.4} \]

Here is the rank argument. Use the tube chart and put \(r=|v|>0\), \(u=v/r\). Rank failure of \((\pi_S,r)|_T\) gives \(a_n\in T_pS\cong\mathbb R^{\dim S}\), \(b_n\in\mathbb R\), with \(|a_n|^2+b_n^2=1\), such that \(a_n+b_nu_n\) annihilates \(T_{x_n}T\). If failing points approach \(p\in S\), pass to limits of these vectors, the unit normals, and the tangent planes. Conditions (a) and (b) put both the whole horizontal space and \(u\) in the limiting plane. Thus \(a+bu\) belongs to that plane and its orthogonal complement, although its norm is one. This contradiction proves (I.4); replacing \(r\) by \(r^2\) does not change rank away from \(S\). A positive smooth minorant of the pointwise permitted radii makes the shrinking global. There are only finitely many relevant pairs, so it can be done for all of them at once.

I.3. Relative construction and gluing of tubes

We prove the precise relative tube fact needed for compatible controls. Suppose \(q:M\to P\) is smooth and \(q|_S\) is a submersion. A tube is called \(q\)-compatible if \(q\pi_S=q\). If such a tube is prescribed on an open \(O\subset S\), and \(C\subset O\) is closed in \(S\), it extends to a \(q\)-compatible tube on all of \(S\), preserving the prescribed tube on some neighborhood of \(C\). We prove preservation of the full embedding germ: two tubes agree there when an inner-product bundle isomorphism \(\psi_0:E_0\to E_1\), over the identity on the base, satisfies \(\phi_1\psi_0=\phi_0\) near the zero section. This implies equality of \(\pi_S,\rho_S\) after shrinking.

The converse implication would be false. On \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(R_\theta\) be rotation through \(\theta\), and compare the tube embeddings of the point \(\phi_0(v)=v\) and \(\phi_1(v)=R_{|v|^2}v\). The latter is a smooth diffeomorphism, with inverse \(w\mapsto R_{-|w|^2}w\); it preserves the norm and has derivative the identity at zero. Both tubes therefore have the same projection and radius functions. If a linear isometry \(\psi_0\) identified their embedding germs, differentiation would force \(\psi_0=1\), whereas \(\phi_1(v)\ne v\) for sufficiently small nonzero \(v\). We retain the full tube when protecting a prescribed region, so this ambiguity does not enter the construction.

Local existence follows from (I.1), taking the trivial normal bundle and the product coordinates. We first show that two local \(q\)-compatible tubes can be made to agree near a compact subset of a common chart by a diffeomorphism supported in that chart, fixing \(S\) and preserving \(q\). Let their embeddings be \(\phi_0,\phi_1\), and let \(\alpha_i:E_i\to TM|_S/TS\) be their normal differentials. Put

\[ \beta=\alpha_1^{-1}\alpha_0,\qquad A=\beta^*\beta,\qquad \psi=\beta A^{-1/2}. \tag{I.5} \]

Then \(\psi\) is a bundle isometry and \(\beta^{-1}\psi=A^{-1/2}\) is positive self-adjoint. For completeness, a real symmetric operator has an orthonormal eigenbasis: maximize its quadratic form on the unit sphere, differentiate along that sphere to obtain an eigenvector, and induct on its invariant orthogonal complement. For a positive operator all eigenvalues are positive; this defines its unique positive square root. Smooth dependence of its inverse square root follows locally from the convergent binomial series for \(\alpha^{-1/2}(1-(1-A/\alpha))^{-1/2}\), choosing \(\alpha\) so that \(\|1-A/\alpha\|<1\). On a smaller neighborhood the series and each differentiated series converge uniformly. Thus (I.5) is smooth.

Use the simultaneous affine coordinates (I.1). On a small common domain define

\[ \Phi_t(v)=(1-t)\phi_0(v)+t\phi_1(\psi v), \qquad h_t=\Phi_t\phi_0^{-1},\quad 0\leq t\leq1. \tag{I.6} \]

Each map fixes \(S\) and preserves \(q\). Its normal differential is \(\alpha_0((1-t)1+tA^{-1/2})\), which is invertible. The parameter inverse-function argument gives a common neighborhood of the compact subset where every \(h_t\) is a diffeomorphism onto its image. Injectivity can be made uniform there: otherwise pairs of distinct points with equal images, approaching the compact zero section, have convergent subsequences and contradict the parameter local inverse at their common limit. Notice that \(h_0=1\), while \(h_1\phi_0=\phi_1\psi\). On a region where a full germ identification \(\phi_1\psi_0=\phi_0\) is already given, taking normal derivatives gives \(\alpha_1\psi_0=\alpha_0\). Thus \(\beta=\psi_0\), \(A=1\), and \(\psi=\psi_0\) there. Formula (I.6) is consequently constant in \(t\) on that region: \(\Phi_t=\phi_0\), so \(h_t=1\). Equality of projection and radius alone is not used to infer this identity.

To extend the germ to an ambient diffeomorphism, choose a smooth cutoff \(\chi\), equal to one near the compact set and supported in a small common image neighborhood. For \(s,t\) close define, in the affine chart and by the identity outside it,

\[ G_{s,t}(z)=z+\chi(z)\bigl(h_t h_s^{-1}(z)-z\bigr). \tag{I.7} \]

These preserve \(q\), fix \(S\), and equal the identity wherever the full embedding germs agree through the given bundle isometry. Uniformly on the compact support, \(G_{s,t}-1\) has derivative norm less than \(1/2\) when \(|s-t|\) is small. Extending the difference by zero to Euclidean space, the contraction equation \(z=w-(G_{s,t}(z)-z)\) proves global invertibility; the inverse is smooth by I.1. Choose an integer \(m\) with \(1/m\) below that bound and compose \(G_{(m-1)t/m,t}\cdots G_{0,t/m}\). Near the compact set all cutoff factors are one, so this telescopes to \(h_t\). At \(t=1\) it gives the required ambient diffeomorphism. The support can avoid any closed protected subset disjoint from that compact set. This proves the local gluing assertion, including preservation of a previously agreed germ.

Here are the global extension details. Replace \(M\) by \(M\setminus(\overline S\setminus S)\), so \(S\) is closed. Choose a locally finite relatively compact chart cover as in I.1, with compact smaller pieces whose interiors cover \(S\). Starting from the prescribed tube, attach one chart at a time. At a finite stage let \(D\subset S\) be the closed protected set, consisting of \(C\) and the preceding protected compact neighborhoods, and let \(B\subset S\) be an open neighborhood on which the old tube is defined. Choose a smooth function \(0\leq\theta\leq1\), equal to one near \(D\) and zero outside \(B\). Such a function follows from I.1's locally finite bumps and closed shrinking: choose \(D\subset B_0\subset\overline B_0\subset B\), take a partition subordinate to \(B\) and \(S\setminus\overline B_0\), and sum the terms supported in \(B\).

Let the next compact piece \(K\) lie in a relatively compact open base region \(W_0\), with \(\overline W_0\) inside one simultaneous \(q\)-chart \(W\). Retain the old tube over \(B_1=\{\theta>1/3\}\) and use the chart's product tube over \(A_1=W_0\cap\{\theta<2/3\}\). Their union contains \(D\cup K\). The closure of their overlap is contained in the compact set
