\[ Q=\overline W_0\cap\{1/3\leq\theta\leq2/3\} \subset B\cap W, \]

which avoids a neighborhood of \(D\). Apply (I.5)–(I.7) near \(Q\), with compact ambient support in \(W\) disjoint from \(D\), to send the old tube embedding to the product tube embedding through \(\psi\). Such support is possible because \(D\) is closed in \(M\) and \(Q\) is compact and disjoint from it. After shrinking the normal radii, the full embedding germs agree throughout the overlap \(A_1\cap B_1\). Glue their inner-product bundles by \(\psi\) there and glue their embeddings. There are only two pieces at this step; the transition and its inverse are the displayed bundle isometries. The new embedding remains \(q\)-compatible, and it is the prescribed old embedding near \(D\), where the ambient diffeomorphism is the identity. Choose an additional closed neighborhood of \(K\) inside \(A_1\cup B_1\) and protect it in all later stages.

Protect successively the earlier compact pieces and slightly larger closed neighborhoods of them. Their interiors exhaust \(S\). Hence every point has a neighborhood on which subsequent tube germs are unchanged. This produces a smooth bundle and embedding germ along the entire zero section, retaining the original germ near \(C\). A single positive radius makes that germ an embedding: take a proper exhaustion \(u\) of \(M\), shrink so that \(|u(\phi(v))-u(\operatorname{base}v)|<1\), and consider successive compact annuli of \(S\). Colliding images must have base exhaustion values differing by less than two. On each corresponding larger compact annulus, the compactness/inverse-function argument used above supplies a uniform injectivity radius. A positive smooth minorant below these locally finite bounds excludes every collision. Shrink once more to remain inside the domain of the germ. This establishes the claimed global relative tube, with no appeal to a tubular-neighborhood existence theorem.

I.4. Compatible control data

Suppose \(f:M\to P\) is smooth and its restriction to every stratum of \(Z\) is a submersion. We construct tubes for the given finite Whitney stratification satisfying

\[ \pi_S\pi_T=\pi_S,\qquad \rho_S\pi_T=\rho_S \quad(S<T),\qquad f\pi_S=f, \tag{I.8} \]

where the compositions are defined. The construction uses only I.1–I.3. We explain the shrinking choices as well as the induction. Two incomparable strata have disjoint closures after removing their frontiers; distance neighborhoods there separate them. Thus their tubes can be chosen disjoint. A tube of \(S\) can also avoid every other stratum not lying above \(S\): none of the closures of those finitely many strata meets \(S\). Radius minorants implement these separations. Further shrinkings retain equations already established.

We additionally shrink each tube of \(R\) so that \(d(m,\pi_Rm)<d(\pi_Rm,\partial R)/3\) when \(\partial R\ne\varnothing\). This follows from continuity along the zero section and a positive radius minorant on \(R\). The triangle inequality gives \(d(m,\pi_Rm)<d(m,\partial R)/2\). Consequently, as a point in that tube approaches \(s\in\partial R\), its projection also approaches \(s\). This ensures that shrinking a lower tube can make all the required higher projections lie in its original domain; it prevents an uncontrolled jump of a higher projection toward a distant base point. Finitely many pairs can be treated simultaneously.

Induct upward on stratum dimension. Assume the tubes of smaller strata have been constructed, with (I.4) for every larger stratum. For a new stratum \(T\), first construct its tube over the part of \(T\) meeting those smaller tubes. Proceed downwards through their dimensions. At one stage let \(O\subset T\) be the union of the already treated, larger-dimensional lower tubes intersected with \(T\), and suppose a tube on \(O\) preserves their projection and radius. Shrink its domain so that every point and its projection lie in at least one of those treated tubes. This is possible pointwise since they cover \(O\), followed by the radius-minorant construction.

Now consider a lower stratum \(S<T\) of the next dimension. On \(U_S\cap T\) the map \(q_S=(\pi_S,\rho_S)\) is a submersion by (I.4). On its overlap with the already constructed tube on \(O\), that tube is \(q_S\)-compatible after shrinking. Indeed choose a treated stratum \(R\) whose tube contains the point and its projection. When it also meets the \(S\)-tube, comparability and dimensions give \(S<R\). The existing equations give

\[ q_S\pi_T=q_S\pi_R\pi_T=q_S\pi_R=q_S. \tag{I.9} \]

All these compositions can be kept in their domains: near a base point each of the finitely many needed memberships is open; shrink the new tube there, then take a positive minorant. Choose a closed smaller region \(C_O\subset O\) retaining the intersections with sufficiently smaller treated tubes. Such a choice is possible because the complement of \(O\) in \(T\) cannot accumulate at a base point of a treated lower stratum: that stratum already has an ambient open tube. A compact-annulus shrinking in each treated tube gives closure inside \(O\), relative to \(T\).

Apply the relative extension of I.3 on \(U_S\cap T\), for \(q_S\), preserving the old tube near \(C_O\cap U_S\). Shrink the treated lower tubes to the retained smaller regions and glue. Distinct \(S\)'s at this stage have disjoint tubes, so these extensions do not interfere. This finishes the descending induction. There are finitely many strata and dimensions, so only finitely many such shrinkings occur.

The resulting tube near all lower strata is \(f\)-compatible: on a lower tube, \(f=f\pi_S\), and (I.9) gives \(f\pi_T=f\). Apply I.3 once more, now to \(f\), to extend it over all of \(T\), preserving a closed smaller neighborhood of the lower-tube intersections. Shrink those lower tubes accordingly. Finally apply I.4 to make the new tube's projection-radius map a submersion on every higher stratum. This completes the upward induction and proves (I.8).

For later compactness arguments, tubes may always be shrunk to closed-radius disk bundles with radius strictly below their original radius. Over a compact subset of \(S\), these disk bundles are compact: finitely many local bundle trivializations reduce this to closed bounded balls. Intersecting with the closed set \(Z\) retains compactness.

I.5. Controlled lifts and continuous stratified flows

A stratified vector field consists of a smooth field \(V_T\) on each stratum. It is controlled if, on a sufficiently small tube of every lower stratum \(S\),

\[ d\pi_S(V_T)=V_S\pi_S,\qquad d\rho_S(V_T)=0. \tag{I.10} \]

For every smooth field \(W\) on \(P\), there is a controlled lift with \(df(V_T)=Wf\). Construct it upwards by dimension. On a new stratum \(T\), choose smaller closed tubes \(E_S\) around each \(S<T\), inside the neighborhoods where the already defined fields satisfy (I.10). Arrange additionally that \(\pi_R(E_S\cap E_R)\) lies in the original control neighborhood of \(S\) whenever \(S<R<T\). To justify this shrinking, first give \(E_S\) closure inside its original neighborhood relative to \(M\setminus\partial S\). At a point \(r\in R\) outside that original neighborhood there is then a neighborhood disjoint from \(E_S\); shrink the \(R\)-tube there. Inside it continuity of \(\pi_R\) gives the required membership. Repeat for the finitely many pairs. Incomparable closed tubes are disjoint as before.

At \(x\in T\), the indices with \(x\in E_S\) form a chain. If nonempty, take its largest member \(R\). Solve \((d\pi_R,d\rho_R)V_T=(V_R\pi_R,0)\) locally, using the submersion (I.4). A smooth right inverse is explicit: for a surjective matrix \(B\), use \(B^*(BB^*)^{-1}\). Equations (I.8), together with the already proved control of \(V_R\), imply every required smaller-stratum equation and \(df(V_T)=Wf\). Indices inactive at \(x\) can be excluded from a neighborhood of \(x\), since \(E_S\cap T\) is closed. If the chain is empty, solve just \(df(V_T)=Wf\). These constructions give local fields satisfying all constraints at every point where they are required. A partition of unity on \(T\) glues them: the constraints are affine linear with the same right-hand side, and the weights sum to one. This completes the lift.

The stratumwise smooth flows supplied by I.1 combine into a continuous local flow on \(Z\). We prove the two points that do not follow from the separate smooth flows. First, a trajectory cannot have a finite maximal endpoint while visiting a compact subset of \(Z\). If it did, choose a sequence of times tending to that endpoint with images tending to \(y\in S\). If the trajectory's stratum is \(S\), the ordinary coordinate-flow argument extends it. Otherwise the frontier condition makes \(S\) a lower stratum. Choose a compact coordinate neighborhood in \(S\) on which the lower flow exists for a fixed time \(\delta>0\), and a small closed tube over its compact flow image lying inside the control neighborhood. For a sufficiently late time \(t_i\), the trajectory is in this tube, with \(\rho_S=c_i>0\), and the remaining time is less than \(\delta\). For as long as it is defined, (I.10) forces its projection to be the lower trajectory and its radius to remain \(c_i\). It cannot leave the control neighborhood: these two conditions confine it to a compact subset of that neighborhood, so a first exit would contradict continuity. All later points of the convergent subsequence therefore have radius \(c_i\), contradicting their limit \(y\), whose radius is zero. This proves escape from compact sets at every finite maximal endpoint.

Second, fix a stratumwise flow value \(\Phi(t,x)\), with \(x\in S\). Choose a compact neighborhood \(K\subset S\) of \(x\) and a time margin so the lower flow of \(K\) over the enlarged time interval is compact. Choose a sufficiently small closed disk tube over that compact image, inside the control neighborhood. For \(z\) near \(x\), the same equations give

\[ \rho_S(\Phi(s,z))=\rho_S(z),\qquad \pi_S(\Phi(s,z))=\Phi_S(s,\pi_Sz). \tag{I.11} \]

They hold first for short times, and then throughout the enlarged interval: a first exit is impossible and a finite maximal endpoint would contradict the compact-escape result just proved. Thus the domain of the combined flow is open near \((t,x)\). As \((s,z)\to(t,x)\), the right side of the second identity tends to \(\Phi_S(t,x)\), while the first tends to zero. Compactness of the disk tube implies that every convergent subsequence of the images has that same limit on its zero section; hence the images converge to it. This proves joint continuity. The group and inverse identities hold on each stratum, so the combined local maps are homeomorphisms preserving every stratum. No continuity of the ambient vector-field values across strata was assumed.

I.6. Proper stratified submersions and normal cones

If \(f|_Z:Z\to P\) is proper and a submersion on each stratum, then it is locally a product, by homeomorphisms preserving all strata. Choose a coordinate box in \(P\), centered at \(p\), and use I.4–I.5 to lift its coordinate fields. A trajectory lifting a coordinate segment in a compact smaller box stays in its compact inverse image. The compact-escape result proves existence for the entire segment. Compose these flows in the fixed order \(1,\ldots,d\) to define

\[ F_p\times B\longrightarrow f^{-1}(B),\qquad (z,t)\longmapsto\Phi_d(t_d,\ldots\Phi_1(t_1,z)\ldots), \quad F_p=f^{-1}(p). \tag{I.12} \]

Its inverse uses the negative flows in reverse order, together with the value of \(f\). Both are continuous by I.5 and preserve strata. The lifted fields need not commute; the specified inverse order is what proves the two composite maps are the identity. The same argument works over a whole coordinate box whenever the map is proper over that box, since each particular coordinate path is compact. This is the first isotopy lemma at the finite Whitney scope used here.

Now fix \(p\in S\subset Z\). Work in a neighborhood avoiding all strata not above \(S\), so \(S\) is closed there. Take its tube, a relatively compact coordinate box \(B\subset S\), and a constant \(\epsilon>0\) below the squared tube radius over \(\overline B\), small enough for (I.4) on every upper stratum. On the punctured tube,

\[ q=(\pi_S,\rho_S): Z\cap\{\pi_S\in B,\ 0<\rho_S<\epsilon\} \longrightarrow B\times(0,\epsilon) \tag{I.13} \]

is proper: the inverse image of a compact subset is closed in a compact disk bundle and has radius bounded away from zero and the outer boundary. It is a submersion on every stratum. Apply the proved isotopy lemma, using controls compatible with this \(q\), to obtain a product with the compact fiber \(L=q^{-1}(p,\epsilon/2)\). Adjoin the zero section and collapse \(L\times\{0\}\) to a vertex. The resulting map is a stratum-preserving homeomorphism

\[ Z\cap\{\pi_S\in B,\ \rho_S<\epsilon\} \simeq B\times c_{<\epsilon}L. \tag{I.14} \]

Here the cone parameter is squared normal distance. Continuity at the added vertex follows from compact disk-bundle compactness: if the base tends to \(s\) and the radius tends to zero, every cluster point is the unique zero-section point \(s\). The inverse is continuous there because a neighborhood of the vertex in a cone on a compact \(L\) contains all sufficiently small radii. The empty-link case gives just \(B\). Restricting \(B\) and the radius gives arbitrarily small such neighborhoods, since the tube is an actual ambient neighborhood and its compact fibers shrink to the zero section. This proves normal local triviality, including compatible shrinking in the displayed product.

The link inherits Whitney regularity. More generally, if a smooth map \(q\) is a submersion on every stratum, its level intersections have tangent spaces \(T_xT\cap\ker dq_x\). In a convergent pair of tangent planes the limit contains the tangent space of the lower stratum by (a), on which \(dq\) is onto. The kernels therefore have constant codimension and converge to the intersection of the limiting plane with \(\ker dq_p\); this follows by solving the surjective rows with \(B^*(BB^*)^{-1}\). Secants between points of the same level have limit in \(\ker dq_p\), by the derivative estimate (I.2) applied to \(q\). Original condition (b) then gives condition (b) for the intersections. For (I.13), the product identifies every nonempty upper piece with its whole link piece times the base box, so its original full frontier incidences restrict to full incidences on \(L\). The dimension of each link piece is \(\dim T-\dim S-1\), strictly below the dimension of \(T\).

These arguments supply the normal local-triviality theorem used in Sections 2 and 4 once a finite Whitney stratification is given. Appendix J next proves finite-dimensional link cohomology with constructible coefficients and the associated duality theorem. K.6–K.8 subsequently prove existence of algebraic Whitney refinements and preservation of algebraic constructibility by the classical operations. The geometric comparison source is Mather's freely accessible Notes on Topological Stability, §§1–2 and 6–10, with the first-isotopy statement in §11.1. The relative tube extension, its identity-starting local deformation, the smooth-flow construction, the compact-escape argument and the cone extension needed here have all been given above.

Appendix J. Constructible coefficients on Whitney neighborhoods

Let \(X\) be a locally closed subset of a finite-dimensional smooth real manifold, with a given finite Whitney stratification \(\mathcal S\). We retain the Hausdorff, metrizable and finite-dimensional hypotheses of Appendices F–I. A complex is \(\mathcal S\)-constructible here if it is bounded and its cohomology sheaves restrict to finite-rank local systems on every stratum. The coefficient ring is a field \(\Lambda\).

This appendix proves the coefficient comparison, finite cohomology on compact links, biduality and preservation of this fixed constructibility system. The order of proof matters:

\[ \begin{gathered} \text{proper interval comparison} \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{ordinary neighborhood stabilization}\\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{local evaluation is an isomorphism} \ \Longrightarrow\ \text{finite cohomology on compact spaces}\\ \Longrightarrow\ \text{finite normal support groups and constructible duals}. \end{gathered} \]

Thus finite link cohomology is proved after local evaluation, using G.1; it is not inserted as an assumption into that criterion. No existence theorem for algebraic Whitney refinements is used.

J.1. The coefficient comparison along an interval

Put \(I=[0,1]\). If \(E\) is a bounded complex on \(Y\times I\) and the cohomology sheaves of its restriction to each fiber \(\{y\}\times I\) are locally constant, then, for the projection \(p:Y\times I\to Y\), the counit is an isomorphism:

\[ p^*Rp_*E\xrightarrow{\sim}E. \tag{J.1} \]

Here \(Y\) has the classical hypotheses above; no local constancy in the \(Y\) direction is assumed. The map \(p\) is proper: its inverse image of a compact set is a product of two compact spaces. Proper base change (H.6) identifies the counit's stalk at \((y,t)\) with evaluation

\[ R\Gamma(I,E|_{\{y\}\times I})\longrightarrow E_{(y,t)}. \tag{J.2} \]

A local system on \(I\) is constant. Indeed Appendix A.4's transport identifies its fibers by the unique endpoint-fixed homotopy class of paths in \(I\); linear interpolation contracts any two such paths relative to their endpoints. The constant-sheaf singular resolution in A.2 and C.1–C.2 applies also to an interval with its endpoints: their neighborhood basis consists of intervals or half-intervals, with the same straight-line contraction. Its prism identity gives \(H^0(I,\underline V)=V\) and \(H^q(I,\underline V)=0\) for \(q>0\), and evaluation is the displayed isomorphism in degree zero. Apply the finitely many truncation triangles to the fiber complex. They show that (J.2) is an isomorphism in every degree. This proves (J.1). They also show that \(Rp_*E\) has the same cohomological bounds as \(E\), so every complex just used remains bounded.

There is a useful map-level consequence. Suppose \(H:Y\times I\to X\) is a continuous homotopy such that, for each \(y\), its track \(H(y,I)\) lies within one stratum of \(X\). For constructible \(F\), set \(E=H^*F\), and write \(h_t(y)=H(y,t)\). Exact inverse image identifies the fiber cohomology sheaves of \(E\) with the pulled-back local systems on that track. Restricting (J.1) to the two endpoints gives natural isomorphisms

\[ h_0^*F\ \xleftarrow{\sim}\ Rp_*H^*F\ \xrightarrow{\sim}\ h_1^*F. \tag{J.3} \]

These also compare the maps on derived ordinary sections. The adjunction map \(R\Gamma(X,F)\to R\Gamma(Y\times I,H^*F) =R\Gamma(Y,Rp_*H^*F)\), followed by either endpoint map, is the original pullback by \(h_0\) or \(h_1\). This follows directly from composition of the inverse/direct-image adjunction units in H.1. For a constant homotopy the comparison is the identity. Restricting \(Y\), or restricting the parameter to a subinterval, restricts the same evaluation maps. Thus this construction controls the actual restriction morphisms, not just their cohomology dimensions.

In particular, suppose \(V\subset U\) and a map \(r:U\to V\) is joined to the identity of \(U\) by such a homotopy, all of whose maps also carry \(V\) into \(V\). Then

\[ R\Gamma(U,F)\longrightarrow R\Gamma(V,F|_V) \tag{J.4} \]

is an isomorphism. To exhibit its inverse, pull back sections along \(r\), then use (J.3) to identify \(r^*(F|_V)\) with \(F\). The composite on \(U\) is the identity by the preceding compatibility with pullback. The composite on \(V\) is the identity by the restriction of the same homotopy to \(V\). This supplies both inverse identities.

We will also use a product form of this argument. Let \(B\) be a convex open box or an interval, fix \(b_0\in B\), and suppose \(E\) on \(Y\times B\) is constructible for strata \(T\times B\). The homotopy \((y,b,t)\mapsto(y,(1-t)b+tb_0)\) has its tracks in those strata. Formula (J.3) gives

\[ E\simeq \operatorname{pr}_Y^*E_0,\qquad R\Gamma(Y\times B,E)\simeq R\Gamma(Y,E_0), \qquad E_0=E|_{Y\times\{b_0\}}. \tag{J.5} \]

For the assertion on sections, projection and the slice are inverse up to this very homotopy; use its compatibility with their pullback maps as in (J.4). The same proof applies to \(\operatorname{pr}_Y^*G\) for any bounded \(G\), because its fiber restrictions are constant. Comparisons for different slices are the interval evaluation maps. In particular restrictions between subintervals, after transport to one fixed slice, are identities. This last assertion also follows by using a larger interval containing both slices and factoring all maps through its section complex.

J.2. Ordinary local cohomology and canonical biduality

At \(x\in S\), I.6 supplies one fixed stratum-preserving chart \(B\times C_R(L)\), taking \(x\) to \((0,v)\), with \(L\) compact. Here \(C_R(L)=(L\times[0,R))/(L\times\{0\})\), and \(v\) is its vertex; the cone coordinate is the squared normal radius of I.6. Smaller boxes and smaller positive radii give a cofinal basis of neighborhoods of \(x\).

For \(0<r<R\), take homothetic boxes and cones \(U_r=B_r\times C_r(L)\subset U_R=B_R\times C_R(L)\). The map

\[ (b,[z,s])\longmapsto (\lambda b,[z,\lambda s]),\qquad \lambda=r/R>0, \tag{J.6} \]

maps \(U_R\) into \(U_r\). Interpolate \(\lambda\) linearly from \(1\) to \(r/R\). Every track stays in the same stratum: a positive radial coordinate remains positive, its link point is fixed, and the vertex stays in the vertex stratum. The homotopy preserves \(U_r\) as well. Thus (J.4) proves that restriction between these neighborhood section complexes is an isomorphism. The case of an empty link is the same box contraction.

Exact filtered colimits on an injective resolution give \(\varinjlim_r H^q(R\Gamma(U_r,F))=H^q(F_x)\), as in G.1. Since all the restriction maps are isomorphisms, each original evaluation map is an isomorphism:

\[ R\Gamma(U_r,F)\xrightarrow{\sim}F_x. \tag{J.7} \]

The stalk complex is perfect, by boundedness and finite-dimensional cohomology. G.1 therefore applies at every point and proves the canonical map

\[ F\xrightarrow{\sim}D_XD_XF. \tag{J.8} \]

We have used neither finite link cohomology nor constructibility of \(D_XF\) here. Its boundedness, needed in G.1, comes from F.4–F.5: \(\omega_X\) has a bounded injective model, and internal Hom from a bounded complex into that model is again bounded. The same applies to the second dual. These are results for arbitrary coefficient sheaves over the field.

J.3. Compact constructible cohomology is finite

Suppose now that \(X\) is compact. The structural duality of F.14–F.16, applied twice, gives

\[ \begin{aligned} R\Gamma(X,D_XF)&\simeq R\Gamma(X,F)^\vee,\\ R\Gamma(X,D_XD_XF)&\simeq R\Gamma(X,F)^{\vee\vee}. \end{aligned} \tag{J.9} \]

Ordinary and compact supports agree on \(X\). Under (J.9), the sections of the map in (J.8) are the linear-complex evaluation map: both are obtained by currying evaluation followed by the structural counit. The sign is the degree sign checked in G.1. Thus \(R\Gamma(X,F)\) is canonically isomorphic to its algebraic double dual.

Here is the finite-dimensional conclusion, including the necessary linear algebra. For a vector space \(V\), its evaluation \(V\to V^{\vee\vee}\) is onto only if \(V\) is finite-dimensional. If \(V\) had an infinite basis \(\{e_i\}\), choose distinct \(e_{i_n}\), \(n\geq1\). In \(V^\vee\), let \(W\) be the span of all the coordinate functionals \(e_i^\vee\), and let \(a\) take value \(1\) on every \(e_{i_n}\) and \(0\) on the other basis vectors. Then \(a\notin W\). Define a functional on \(W+\Lambda a\) to be zero on \(W\) and one on \(a\), and extend it to \(V^\vee\) by extending a basis. This extension cannot be evaluation at any \(v\in V\): vanishing on all the coordinate functionals would force \(v=0\), while its value on \(a\) is one. This proves the assertion. The basis extension used here follows from the maximal-linearly-independent-set argument: a maximal independent extension must span, since otherwise one more vector could be added.

Linear dual is exact over a field by that same extension argument. Hence \(H^q(P^{\vee\vee})=H^q(P)^{\vee\vee}\), with the map induced by evaluation, for every complex \(P\). Apply this to \(P=R\Gamma(X,F)\) and (J.9). Its cohomology groups are finite-dimensional. They vanish outside a finite range by H.4, applied to the proper structural map. We have proved

\[ X\ \text{compact},\ F\in D^b_{\mathcal S}(X) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad R\Gamma(X,F)\ \text{perfect}. \tag{J.10} \]

In particular this holds on every link \(L\) from I.6: that link is compact, has the inherited finite Whitney stratification proved there, and is a closed subset of its smooth level manifold. No triangulation or unproved finite-type assertion about the individual open strata is required in this deduction.

J.4. The general normal attaching and support complexes

Consider the normal slice \(C_R(L)\) in I.6. Let \(F_0\) be a constructible complex on it. On the puncture, (J.5) gives \(j^*F_0=p_L^*J_0\), with \(J_0\) the restriction to one link slice. Set

\[ A=(F_0)_v,\qquad B=R\Gamma(L,J_0),\qquad a:A\longrightarrow B. \tag{J.11} \]

Both \(A\) and \(B\) are perfect, the latter by (J.10). The map \(a\) is the vertex restriction of the actual unit \(F_0\to Rj_*j^*F_0\). The interval comparisons of J.1 identify \(i^*Rj_*j^*F_0=B\), compatibly with decreasing the outer radius.

The same localization proof as (G.7) now applies to this arbitrary stratified link:

\[ F_0\simeq \operatorname{Fib}\bigl(Rj_*j^*F_0\oplus i_*A \xrightarrow{\mathrm{res}-i_*a}i_*B\bigr). \tag{J.12} \]

To check it, use the two units and their natural commuting homotopy to map into the displayed cone fiber. On the puncture the map is the identity. At the vertex its target is \(\operatorname{Fib}(B\oplus A\to B)\); the identity \(B\)-pair contracts, leaving \(A\), and the induced map on \(A\) is the identity. This proves the quasi-isomorphism on every stalk.

Ordinary sections of the cone are \(A\), either by (J.7) or by canceling this same pair in (J.12). Sections of any annulus \(L\times(r,R)\) are \(B\), by (J.5); the restriction map from the cone is \(a\). For the compact closed subcone \(K_r\), support localization therefore gives

\[ R\Gamma_{K_r}(C_R(L),F_0)=\operatorname{Fib}(A\xrightarrow a B). \tag{J.13} \]

Changing \(r\) restricts the complementary annulus, which is the identity on \(B\) under the interval comparison. Thus the support-extension maps in (J.13) are identities in this model. The \(K_r\), \(r\uparrow R\), are cofinal among compact subsets of the open cone. Taking their union on an injective resolution proves

\[ R\Gamma_c(C_R(L),F_0) \simeq i_v^!F_0 \simeq C_0:=\operatorname{Fib}(A\xrightarrow a B). \tag{J.14} \]

For the point costalk use the puncture rather than an annulus in the support fiber; the comparison from the puncture to each annulus is again the identity on \(B\). This identifies (J.14) with the actual support-extension morphism. Extension by zero between smaller and larger open cones also induces the identity on this model. In particular all the groups in (J.14) are finite-dimensional. Empty links give \(B=0\) and the same formulas.

J.5. Duality preserves the given Whitney stratification

Return to a fixed product neighborhood \(B_d\times C_R(L)\) of a point of a real \(d\)-dimensional stratum. Contracting only the box factor in (J.5) gives \(F=\operatorname{pr}_C^*F_0\) on this neighborhood. This is an isomorphism of complexes, so it includes the attaching data along all the link strata. Write \(C_0\) for (J.14).

For an oriented open box \(V\subset B_d\), let \(p:V\times C_r(L)\to C_r(L)\). Proper-support base change from \(V\to\{*\}\), followed by the projection formula H.10, gives

\[ Rp_!\Lambda=\Lambda[-d],\qquad Rp_!p^*(F_0|_{C_r(L)})=(F_0|_{C_r(L)})[-d]. \tag{J.15} \]

The first identification is C.5's compact-support calculation for the open box with its chosen orientation, transported by H.6. Composition H.8 and (J.14) now give

\[ R\Gamma_c(V\times C_r(L),F)\simeq C_0[-d]. \tag{J.16} \]

These comparisons have the required transition maps. For an inclusion of smaller oriented boxes, C.5 and F.5 identify extension by zero with preservation of the same local orientation generator. For smaller cone radii, it is the identity by (J.13)–(J.14). Base change, composition and the projection map are natural in these inclusions; hence the resulting maps in (J.16) are the identity under a fixed coordinate orientation.

The structural pairing (F.16) consequently yields

\[ R\Gamma(V\times C_r(L),D_XF)\simeq C_0^\vee[d], \tag{J.17} \]

with identity restriction maps for these boxes and radii. For points on \(B_d\times\{v\}\), such neighborhoods form a basis, with boxes allowed to be centered at each point of the fixed larger box. Taking stalks and their restriction identifications shows that each cohomology sheaf of \(D_XF\) restricts to a constant finite-dimensional sheaf there, with the groups of \(C_0^\vee[d]\). This is a sheaf identification: the maps arise from the same compact-support pairings and orientation class, so their restrictions agree on smaller boxes. Changing a coordinate orientation inserts its usual sign and still gives a local system.

Every stratum is covered by these boxes. Boundedness was established before (J.8). We have therefore proved

\[ D_X:D^b_{\mathcal S}(X)^{\mathrm{op}} \longrightarrow D^b_{\mathcal S}(X),\qquad D_X^2\simeq1, \tag{J.18} \]

with the canonical evaluation isomorphism. This proves the classical part of Proposition 2.4 for a given Whitney stratification.

F.20 applied to \(D_XF\), followed by (J.8), gives \(i_x^!F=(i_x^*D_XF)^\vee\). The latter stalk is perfect by (J.17). Dualizing and using its finite evaluation proves the other point exchange \(i_x^*D_XF=(i_x^!F)^\vee\). Together with F.20 this proves both identities in (2.1), including finiteness of the point costalks, at this classical scope.

J.6. Open and closed operations within the fixed stratification

Let \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\) be an open union of strata and \(K\in D^b_{\mathcal S|_U}(U)\). Extension by zero is constructible: it is \(K\) on the retained strata and zero on the others. The already proved identity \(D_Xj_!=Rj_*D_U\), applied to \(D_UK\), and (J.18) give

\[ Rj_*K\simeq D_Xj_!D_UK\in D^b_{\mathcal S}(X), \qquad D_XRj_*K\simeq j_!D_UK. \tag{J.19} \]

No independent boundary-image finiteness is assumed here. For a closed union of strata \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\), exact \(i_*\) and \(i^*\) preserve constructibility. Apply F.20 to \(D_XF\) and use (J.18) on \(X\) to obtain

\[ i^!F\simeq D_Zi^*D_XF\in D^b_{\mathcal S|_Z}(Z). \tag{J.20} \]

The inherited stratification on \(Z\) has the same Whitney and frontier properties, so J.18 applies there too. Locally closed unions are composites of such open and closed inclusions; the already proved composition identities give the corresponding assertions for them. Tensor products preserve constructibility on stalks and on stratum trivializations. Finally tensor–Hom currying against the bounded injective dualizing model and (J.18) identify

\[ R\mathcal Hom(F,G)\simeq D_X(F\otimes^L D_XG). \tag{J.21} \]

Both sides are bounded, and the right side is constructible by what was just proved. Thus internal Hom preserves the fixed constructibility system as well.

J.7. Proper images when compatible Whitney data are supplied

Here is the precise geometric image statement available without an algebraic refinement-existence theorem. Suppose \(f:X\to Y\) is proper, both spaces have given finite Whitney stratifications, and for every target stratum \(T\), the map \(f^{-1}T\to T\) has a smooth ambient extension and is a submersion on each of its source strata. The source strata in \(f^{-1}T\) form its inherited finite Whitney stratification. Then \(Rf_*F=Rf_!F\) is constructible on the given target stratification.

Indeed proper base change restricts this complex to the proper map over \(T\). By I.6 that map is locally a stratum-preserving product \(Z\times B\to B\), with \(Z\) a compact fiber. The kernel and secant argument of I.6 gives the induced Whitney stratification on \(Z\). Formula (J.5) identifies the restricted coefficient complex with the pullback of its fiber restriction \(F_Z\). Proper base change from \(Z\to\{*\}\) then identifies the image on \(B\) with the constant complex \(R\Gamma(Z,F_Z)\). It is perfect by (J.10); the uniform cohomological bound is H.4. This proves finite local constancy along every \(T\).

K.6–K.7 subsequently construct the compatible algebraic Whitney stratifications used in this statement. K.8 uses affine graph compactifications and finite open-cover descent to prove nonproper classical image constructibility without a global compactification theorem. The étale and normalized adic constructions have separate coefficient and geometric hypotheses.

For general homotopy invariance, see Haine–Porta–Teyssier, Theorem 0.4 and Section 5. At the bounded field-coefficient scope used here, J.1 gives a direct proof from proper base change and the interval calculation already established in this lesson. J.2–J.7 then give the local stabilization, compact finiteness, normal-support comparison and duality arguments themselves.

Appendix K. Algebraic Whitney refinements and classical images

In this appendix varieties are reduced separated schemes of finite type over \(\mathbb C\), considered also with their usual complex topology. Nilpotents do not change the classical sheaf spaces. We prove existence of finite algebraic Whitney refinements, compatible stratifications of algebraic maps, and the classical constructibility statements of Section 3. The proof is for field coefficients in its sheaf-theoretic part. It does not supply an étale comparison.

K.1. The elementary algebraic tools

We first give the algebra needed for the geometric construction. A monomial order below is degree followed by lexicographic order. It is a well-order and is preserved by multiplication. Every upward-closed subset of \(\mathbb N^n\) has finitely many minimal elements. Indeed any infinite sequence of nonnegative integers has an infinite nondecreasing subsequence: either some value repeats infinitely often or one successively chooses larger values. Applying this extraction to each coordinate proves that an infinite sequence in \(\mathbb N^n\) contains two terms comparable in their original order. Thus an infinite set of minimal elements is impossible. Every element lies above a minimal one, by descending the sum of coordinates.

For an ideal \(I\) in a polynomial ring over a field, choose polynomials whose leading monomials generate the upward-closed set of leading monomials of \(I\). Division by these finitely many polynomials terminates, since each subtraction decreases the leading monomial. The remainder of an element of \(I\) is still in \(I\), so a nonzero remainder would have a divisible leading monomial, a contradiction. This proves finite generation of every ideal and the monomial division criterion. Quotients and localizations are therefore Noetherian. In particular algebraic closed sets have finite irreducible decompositions: otherwise choose a minimal closed set without such a decomposition, using the descending-chain condition, and split it into two smaller closed sets. Both have finite decompositions, a contradiction.

Here is the normalization argument we need. If generators \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) of a nonzero finite-type algebra satisfy a nonzero polynomial relation, choose an integer \(e\) larger than every exponent in that relation and replace \(x_i\), for \(i<n\), by \(y_i=x_i-x_n^{e^i}\). The highest power of \(x_n\) in the transformed relation has a nonzero constant coefficient: its exponents are the distinct base-\(e\) encodings \(a_n+\sum_{i<n}a_i e^i\). Dividing by that coefficient makes \(x_n\) integral over the subalgebra generated by the \(y_i\). Its finitely many lower powers generate the original algebra as a module over that subalgebra. Induction on the number of generators, stopping at an algebraically independent set, produces

\[ B=\mathbb C[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\ \hookrightarrow A, \qquad A\ \text{finite as a }B\text{-module}. \tag{K.1} \]

For a domain \(A\), its fraction field is a finite extension of \(\mathbb C(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\). We use transcendence degree for \(d\). Its invariance under an algebraic field extension follows by exchange: clear denominators in an algebraic relation to solve for a parameter which occurs in it, replacing that parameter by the new transcendental element. Repeated exchanges compare two finite transcendence bases in both directions.

We recall and prove the required facts about integrality. If an algebra is generated by finitely many integral elements, the bounded powers in their monic equations generate it as a module. Conversely multiplication by an element on finitely many module generators gives a square matrix; multiplying \(tI-M\) by its adjugate gives its monic characteristic equation on that module. If the module contains \(1\), this is an equation for the element. These observations prove that integral elements form a ring and that integrality is transitive. Monic equations also show that integrality survives quotients and localization.

For an integral inclusion \(B\subset A\), every prime of \(B\) has a prime above it. Localize at that prime and choose a maximal ideal upstairs. Its contraction is maximal downstairs: a subring of a field over which that field is integral is a field, since a monic equation for the inverse of a nonzero element expresses that inverse in the subring. The local base has only one maximal ideal. This proves the assertion. Applying it after quotienting a prime proves going up. Two comparable primes above the same base prime are equal: quotient by the smaller and localize the base at its fraction field; the resulting integral domain algebraic over a field is a field. These are lying over, going up and incomparability in the form used here.

A field which is a finite-type \(\mathbb C\)-algebra is \(\mathbb C\). In (K.1) its polynomial subring must be a field by the preceding inverse argument, so \(d=0\); the field is then finite over \(\mathbb C\), and the fundamental theorem of algebra in E.1 applies. Hence maximal ideals of finite-type \(\mathbb C\)-algebras are their complex points. If \(f\) is not nilpotent in such an algebra, its localization at \(f\) is nonzero and is still of finite type; a maximal ideal there gives a complex point where \(f\ne0\). This proves the radical form of the Nullstellensatz as well. The prime-ideal and irreducible-closed-set descriptions consequently agree.

We will also use that polynomial rings over a field are unique-factorization domains and are integrally closed. Here is the algebra behind both assertions. For polynomials over a unique-factorization domain, factor out the greatest common divisor of the coefficients. The product of two primitive polynomials remains primitive: reduction modulo any prime factor of their contents would otherwise give a product of two nonzero polynomials equal to zero over a domain. Factorization over the fraction field, clearing denominators and using this content calculation, gives factorization and its uniqueness in the polynomial ring. Induct from the one-variable Euclidean algorithm. Finally, if a reduced fraction \(a/b\) satisfies a monic equation, every prime factor of \(b\) divides \(a\) after clearing denominators, a contradiction. Thus an integral fraction belongs to the ring.

If \(A\) is a domain finite over the polynomial ring \(B\) in (K.1), a nonzero \(g\in A\) has a monic minimal polynomial over \(\operatorname{Frac}B\) whose coefficients belong to \(B\). One way to see the coefficient assertion is to take the conjugate roots in a finite splitting field: they are integral over \(B\), so their symmetric expressions are integral, and those expressions lie in \(\operatorname{Frac}B\), where \(B\) is integrally closed. Its constant term is nonzero and belongs to \(gA\). Thus

\[ 0\ne h\in (gA)\cap B. \tag{K.2} \]

For a proper irreducible closed subset of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\), take \(g\) in its nonzero prime ideal. Its coordinate algebra is finite over a quotient of \(B/(h)\). The images of the \(d\) parameters now satisfy a nonzero polynomial relation, so its transcendence degree is less than \(d\). This proves the strict dimension decrease used in all the finite inductions below.

We record explicitly the Chinese remainder calculation. For pairwise comaximal ideals \(I_1,\ldots,I_r\) of a ring \(R\), choose \(a_{ij}\in I_j\) with \(a_{ij}\equiv1\pmod{I_i}\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Then \(e_i=\prod_{j\ne i}a_{ij}\) is one modulo \(I_i\) and zero modulo every other ideal. Given residues represented by \(c_i\in R\), the element \(\sum_i c_i e_i\) maps to those residues. The kernel of this surjection \(R\to\prod_i R/I_i\) is exactly \(\bigcap_i I_i\). For two comaximal ideals, write \(a+b=1\) with \(a\in I\), \(b\in J\); if \(x\in I\cap J\), then \(x=ax+bx\in IJ\). Thus \(I\cap J=IJ\). Their powers are also comaximal: every term in \((a+b)^{2n-1}=1\) belongs to \(I^n\) or \(J^n\). In particular \((I\cap J)^n=I^n\cap J^n\), which will be used for the two node branches in L.2.

Finite morphisms of affine complex varieties are closed and have finite fibers. For closedness, quotient by the closed-set ideal and use lying over to identify the image with the zero set of its contraction. A fiber has a finite-dimensional coordinate algebra \(H\) over \(\mathbb C\). Any \(r\) distinct maximal ideals are pairwise comaximal, and their residue fields are \(\mathbb C\) by the Nullstellensatz just proved. The preceding surjection \(H\to\mathbb C^r\) forces \(r\leq\dim_{\mathbb C}H\), so there are finitely many such ideals. For later analytic use these morphisms are also proper in the usual topology. Each affine coordinate satisfies a monic equation over the base. Over a compact base set all its coefficients are bounded; a root of \(z^m+\sum_{j<m}a_jz^j\) has modulus at most \(1+\max|a_j|\). Indeed, for \(|z|>1+M\), where \(M=\max|a_j|\), the geometric sum gives \(\sum_{j<m}|a_jz^j|\leq M(|z|^m-1)/(|z|-1)<|z|^m\), contradicting the equation. The inverse image is therefore closed and bounded in a finite product of coordinate discs over that compact set, hence compact.

Every irreducible complex variety has a nonempty smooth algebraic open set. On an affine chart use (K.1). In characteristic zero its finite fraction-field extension is separable: an irreducible polynomial has no common factor with its nonzero derivative. It has a primitive element \(z\) which can be chosen as a complex linear combination of algebra generators. To justify this choice, the distinct embeddings in a splitting field are obtained by choosing roots successively in a tower of simple extensions; there are as many as the degree. Avoid the finitely many linear equalities which would give two embeddings the same value on \(z\). Such a choice exists over the infinite field \(\mathbb C\), for instance by substituting \((1,c,\ldots,c^{n-1})\) and avoiding the finitely many roots of the resulting nonzero polynomials. The number of conjugate values then equals the extension degree, so \(z\) generates it.

Let \(P(t,z)\) be its monic minimal polynomial. The other generators are polynomials in \(z\) with rational functions of \(t\) as coefficients. After inverting one nonzero polynomial \(h(t)\), \(A_h=B_h[z]=B_h[Z]/(P)\). Invert also the nonzero discriminant, or equivalently the denominator-cleared resultant of \(P\) and \(P_Z\). Their coprimality follows from separability; the Euclidean algorithm supplies the nonzero denominator-cleared identity. The analytic implicit-function argument of E.1, with several parameter variables and the same absolutely convergent series norm, identifies this open set with sheets over an open subset of \(\mathbb C^d\). It is smooth of dimension \(d\). The implicit derivative formulas also show that its tangent spaces depend algebraically on the point, using the nonvanishing Jacobian minors. This proves the dense smooth charts and algebraic tangent maps needed below.

K.2. Going down and an algebraic curve through a prescribed point

We need going down for a finite extension of domains \(B\subset A\), where \(B\) is an integrally closed domain of characteristic zero. Write \(K=\operatorname{Frac}B\), put \(\operatorname{Frac}A\) in a finite normal splitting field \(L/K\), and let \(C\) be the integral closure of \(B\) in \(L\). It is a ring by K.1, contains \(A\), and is integral over both \(B\) and \(A\). Let \(G\) be the finite Galois group. The fixed field is \(K\): an element outside \(K\) has at least two distinct conjugates by separability, and embeddings extend along the root tower in the splitting field. Thus \(C^G=B\), by normality of \(B\).

The group acts transitively on the primes of \(C\) over a given prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(B\). Otherwise choose primes \(Q,P\) such that \(Q\) is none of the conjugates of \(P\). They are incomparable by K.1. Finite prime avoidance gives \(a\in Q\setminus\bigcup_{\sigma\in G}\sigma P\). Explicitly, for distinct incomparable primes \(P_i\), choose \(a_i\in Q\setminus P_i\) and \(b_i\in\bigcap_{j\ne i}P_j\setminus P_i\), the latter by multiplying elements of \(P_j\setminus P_i\); then \(\sum a_ib_i\) has the required property. But \(\prod_{\sigma\in G}\sigma a\) is in \(B\cap Q=\mathfrak p\), hence in \(P\), forcing some \(\sigma a\in P\), a contradiction.

Now let \(\mathfrak p_1\subset\mathfrak p_2\) in \(B\) and \(P_2\) in \(A\) lie over \(\mathfrak p_2\). Lift \(P_2\) to \(Q_2\) in \(C\) by lying over. First choose a prime of \(C\) above \(\mathfrak p_1\), then use going up to obtain \(Q'_1\subset Q'_2\) above the two base primes. A Galois automorphism carries \(Q'_2\) to \(Q_2\). Contracting its image of \(Q'_1\) to \(A\) gives

\[ P_1\subset P_2,\qquad P_1\cap B=\mathfrak p_1. \tag{K.3} \]

This proves going down without a finiteness assertion for \(C\).

Let \(Z\) be an irreducible affine variety, \(D\subsetneq Z\) closed, and \(p\in Z\). If \(p\in D\), there is an irreducible algebraic curve through \(p\) which is not contained in \(D\). Indeed choose (K.1) for its domain \(A\), a nonzero \(g\) vanishing on \(D\), and \(h\) as in (K.2). With \(a\) the image of \(p\) in \(\mathbb C^d\), choose a line through \(a\) on which \(h\) is not identically zero. Such a line exists by applying a nonzero homogeneous term of \(h(a+tv)\) to a direction \(v\). Here \(d\ge1\), since a zero-dimensional irreducible affine variety is a point by (K.1) and the Nullstellensatz.

Let \(\mathfrak q\) be the line ideal. Going down supplies \(P\subset\mathfrak m_p\) in \(A\) over \(\mathfrak q\). The domain \(A/P\) is finite over \(B/\mathfrak q\simeq\mathbb C[t]\); it defines a curve through \(p\). Since \(h\notin\mathfrak q\), (K.2) gives \(g\notin P\). Its intersection with \(D\) is finite: the zero set of \(g\) lies over the finitely many zeros of the nonzero polynomial \(h|_{\text{line}}\), and the finite morphism has finite fibers. For a point already outside \(D\), a constant arc will suffice in the next assertion.

K.3. The complex algebraic arc lemma

For the curve just obtained, there is a convergent analytic arc \(\gamma\) through \(p\) whose puncture lies outside \(D\). Here are the convergence and prescribed-endpoint details. Translate the finite coordinate \(t\) so that \(t(p)=0\). Choose a primitive element \(z\) of its function field as in K.1, additionally separating the finitely many points over \(t=0\). These add finitely many nonzero linear inequalities on its coefficients, so the same choice argument applies.

Its monic polynomial \(P(t,Z)\in\mathbb C[t,Z]\) is separable over \(\mathbb C(t)\). After inverting a polynomial \(h(t)\), every curve coordinate is a polynomial in \(z\) with coefficients in \(\mathbb C[t,h^{-1}]\). Choose a small punctured disc on which \(h\) and the discriminant have no zeros. The distinct roots of \(P\) form a finite analytic covering there, by E.1 and the monic root bound. Pulling back by \(t=u^m\), with \(m\) a multiple of the order of the permutation obtained by continuation around zero, makes each root single valued and analytic on the punctured \(u\)-disc. For clarity, the fundamental group used here is \(\mathbb Z\): lift a path's argument using finitely many short arcs; uniqueness gives its continuous lift to the logarithm half-plane. Loops lift with endpoint difference \(2\pi i n\), and two lifts with the same endpoints are homotopic by straight interpolation in that convex half-plane. Thus the power map kills precisely the needed finite monodromy.

A bounded analytic function on a punctured disc extends analytically across zero. This follows from the triangle-integral argument in E.1: apply it to \(f(\zeta)/(\zeta-u)\) on an annulus with a small circle around \(u\) removed. The circle around zero has integral tending to zero by boundedness; the circle around \(u\) tends to \(2\pi i f(u)\). The outer-circle formula for \(f(u)\) then expands into a power series by the uniformly convergent geometric series for \(1/(\zeta-u)\). This proves the asserted extension, not merely continuity.

All the root branches are bounded by their monic equation and hence extend. Every root of \(P(0,Z)\) is a limit of some branch. To verify that none is lost, take a sequence \(t_n\to0\), list all roots of each monic polynomial \(P(t_n,Z)\), and extract convergent subsequences using their common bound. Passing to the product of the linear factors gives \(P(0,Z)\), with multiplicities. There are only finitely many branches after the power pullback, so every such limit is one of their values at zero.

Choose a branch with \(z(0)=z(p)\). On its puncture the rational coordinate formulas give a point of the original curve. Each of these coordinates is itself integral over \(\mathbb C[t]\), so its monic equation bounds it too; each extends analytically. Their equations continue to hold at zero. The limit lies over \(t=0\) and has coordinate \(z(p)\), so it is \(p\), by the separating choice of \(z\). Shrink the disc to avoid the finite intersection with \(D\) away from \(p\). We have proved

\[ \gamma(0)=p,\qquad \gamma(u)\in Z\setminus D\quad(0<|u|<\epsilon). \tag{K.4} \]

For a reducible algebraic set and an open subset dense in every component, apply this proof to a component containing \(p\). Quasi-projective varieties reduce to an affine chart at \(p\). In particular a Zariski-dense open set in such a variety is dense in its usual topology as well. This is the only curve-selection statement used below.

K.4. Generic density in fibers

Let \(B\) be a finite-type complex domain and \(A=B[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I\) a finite-type \(B\)-algebra. There is a nonzero \(b\in B\) such that \(A_b\) is a free \(B_b\)-module, possibly of infinite rank. To prove this particular generic-freeness statement, pass to \(K=\operatorname{Frac}B\). Choose a finite monic leading-monomial basis for \(I_K\) by K.1. Clear the finitely many denominators in its coefficients and its expressions in the original finite generators of \(I\). After inverting their product \(b\), these polynomials belong to \(I_b\) and are monic. Division of every original generator has zero remainder over \(K\), so it also has zero remainder over \(B_b\). Thus they generate \(I_b\). Division expresses the quotient in the monomials not divisible by their leading monomials. Those monomials are independent over \(K\), hence over \(B_b\). They give the asserted basis.

Suppose now that \(E\to Y\) is a dominant morphism of irreducible varieties and \(V\subset E\) is a dense open subset. There is a nonempty open \(Y^0\subset Y\) such that

\[ V\cap E_y\ \text{is dense in }E_y \quad\text{for every }y\in Y^0. \tag{K.5} \]

Work first over an affine open \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}B\), and use a finite affine cover of \(E\). Each nonempty chart has domain \(A\), and dominance makes \(B\to A\) injective. Choose \(0\ne\delta\in A\) with \(D(\delta)\subset V\) on that chart. Apply the preceding argument to the finite-type algebra \(A/\delta A\). After inverting one base element it is free over the base. Consequently the exact sequence

\[ 0\longrightarrow A\xrightarrow{\delta}A \longrightarrow A/\delta A\longrightarrow0 \tag{K.6} \]

splits as a sequence of base modules: lift its free basis. Reducing modulo any base maximal ideal therefore preserves its left injection. Hence \(\delta\) is a non-zero-divisor in every resulting fiber algebra.

It cannot lie in a minimal prime of that fiber. Localize there; the maximal ideal of this Noetherian zero-dimensional local ring is its nilradical and is nilpotent. The latter assertion follows by taking finitely many nilpotent generators and a power larger than the sum of their nilpotence exponents. A non-zero-divisor cannot become nilpotent in a nonzero localization. Thus \(D(\delta)\) is dense in every fiber component. This proves (K.5) on the chart; multiply the finitely many base elements for the affine cover. We used here the elementary description of the nilradical as the intersection of primes: a nonnilpotent element can be avoided by a prime, by choosing an ideal maximal among those disjoint from its powers and checking the prime property.

The same freeness argument shows that a dominant morphism of irreducible varieties has image containing a nonempty open subset of its target. Choose an affine source chart dominating an affine target and make its coordinate algebra free over the target by localization. It is nonzero, so each fiber is a nonzero finite-type complex algebra and has a complex point by K.1.

K.5. Generic Whitney regularity

Let \(T,S\subset\mathbb C^n\) be disjoint smooth irreducible locally closed algebraic sets. There is a nonempty algebraic open \(S^0\subset S\) such that \((T,S)\) satisfies Whitney (b) at every point of \(S^0\) in the closure of \(T\). If \(S\) is not contained in that closure, first remove the proper closed intersection; otherwise use the following construction.

For \(d=\dim_{\mathbb C}T\), take the graph

\[ \Gamma=\{(x,y,[x-y],T_xT):x\in T,\ y\in S\} \subset\overline T\times S\times\mathbb P^{n-1} \times\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbb C}(d,n), \tag{K.7} \]

and let \(E\) be its reduced algebraic closure. The secant and tangent maps are algebraic; for the latter, solve the constant-rank Jacobian rows using a nonzero minor. The Grassmannian has finitely many algebraic matrix charts, obtained by putting a chosen invertible \(d\)-row minor equal to the identity. Their rational transition formulas give its algebraic structure; its Plücker coordinates are the minors. On a chart the usual quadratic Plücker equations solve every coordinate as one of these minors, so the decomposable locus is closed in projective space. In the usual topology it is compact, also seen from the closed bounded set of orthogonal projection matrices of rank \(d\).

The graph is open in \(E\): over \(T\times S\) its equations determine its two projective entries uniquely, and a graph of a regular map into a projective variety is closed there. The product \(T\times S\) is irreducible. For an algebraic verification on affine charts, if two nonzero functions in \(A\otimes_{\mathbb C}B\) had product zero, evaluation on each complex point of \(\operatorname{Spec}B\) would make one factor zero in the domain \(A\). Write each factor using linearly independent coefficients in \(A\); its zero-specialization locus is a proper closed subset of \(\operatorname{Spec}B\). Two such sets cannot cover an irreducible variety. Thus the tensor ring is a domain; the affine charts establish the assertion. It follows that \(E\) is irreducible and dominates \(S\).

Apply (K.5) to \(\Gamma\subset E\) and \(E\to S\), the second-coordinate projection. For \(p\in S^0\), every point of \(E_p\) is approachable by an analytic arc with puncture in \(\Gamma_p\), by (K.4). Now take any sequences \(x_i\in T\), \(y_i\in S\), tending to \(p\), with limiting secant line \(\ell\) and limiting tangent plane \(\tau\). Their graph points tend to \(q=(p,p,\ell,\tau)\in E_p\). Choose the just-proved arc through \(q\), whose second coordinate is identically \(p\). Its first coordinate has an expansion

\[ x(u)=p+u^m v+O(u^{m+1}),\qquad m\ge1,\quad v\ne0. \tag{K.8} \]

The puncture belongs to \(T\), so \(x'(u)\in T_{x(u)}T\). After multiplication by \(u^{1-m}/m\), these tangent vectors tend to \(v\). The tangent planes tend to \(\tau\), hence \(v\in\tau\). The secant lines along the same arc tend to \([v]=\ell\). Therefore \(\ell\subset\tau\), proving (b).

This is also real Whitney (b) for the underlying smooth strata. Their tangent planes are complex subspaces regarded as real subspaces; a real limiting secant vector spans a complex line contained in the limiting complex tangent plane, so the real vector lies in the underlying real plane. Whitney (a) and the strict frontier dimension inequality follow as in I.2.

The assertion is intrinsic to an algebraic variety, not to an affine embedding. Two local embeddings can be compared with their common graph in the product of the ambient spaces. The coordinates of either embedding extend to regular, hence smooth, functions on a neighborhood in the other ambient space. The graph is carried to the zero-section embedding by the smooth triangular change \((u,v)\mapsto(u,v-g(u))\). Adding zero coordinates does not change tangent or secant inclusion, and I.2 proves invariance under this smooth coordinate change.

K.6. Finite compatible Whitney refinements

Every complex variety admits a finite algebraic Whitney stratification compatible with any prescribed finite family of constructible subsets. Here constructible means a finite union of algebraically locally closed subsets. Replace the family by the finitely many closed sets whose membership determines it, using a locally closed subset as the difference of its closure and a closed boundary.

We give a finite construction. At a stage let \(Z\) be the closed part not yet stratified, and retain the finitely many strata already chosen outside it. For each irreducible component \(C\) of \(Z\), choose a dense smooth open in one affine chart, by K.1. Delete its intersections with the other components. For each prescribed closed set and each closure of a previously chosen stratum, either it contains \(C\), or delete its proper intersection with \(C\). Thus membership in every such set will be constant on the new piece.

For each previous stratum \(T\) whose closure contains \(C\), apply K.5 to \(T\) and the chosen smooth open of \(C\), in the chart containing that open. Intersect the finitely many resulting nonempty opens. The result \(S_C\) is a nonempty smooth algebraic open in \(C\), satisfies (b) with every relevant previous stratum, and has all the required constant membership decisions. The pieces \(S_C\) are disjoint. Remove their union from \(Z\); its complement is closed, and every remaining component has smaller dimension by (K.2). Repetition therefore terminates after finitely many dimension decreases.

The frontier condition holds because every later piece was made either wholly contained in, or disjoint from, the closure of each earlier piece. A later closure cannot acquire a point in an earlier open piece: the later pieces lie in the closed residual set from that earlier stage. Every incident pair is (b)-regular by its construction when the lower piece was chosen. The construction preserved all prescribed membership conditions. This proves the theorem, including finiteness and the frontier condition.

Two variants will be used. First, any finite collection of finite algebraic stratifications has a common Whitney refinement: prescribe all their strata. A local system remains a local system on a refined smooth piece by inverse image. Second, if a closed subset \(Z\subset X\) remains to be stratified and a finite algebraic Whitney stratification of \(X\setminus Z\) is already fixed, the same construction extends it over \(Z\), without altering those fixed strata. Include their closures among the membership decisions and their pairs among the applications of K.5; if a fixed stratum has several irreducible components, test those finitely many components separately without changing the stratum. The previously fixed pairs remain unchanged. All these constructions work across a finite affine atlas by the embedding independence in K.5.

K.7. Compatible stratifications of an algebraic map

We first prove the needed algebraic critical-value assertion. A dominant map \(f:M\to N\) of smooth irreducible complex varieties has surjective differential on a nonempty open of \(M\). Choose a transcendence basis \(t_1,\ldots,t_e\) of \(\mathbb C(N)\), and extend it by \(u_1,\ldots,u_r\) to one of \(\mathbb C(M)\). Both remaining field extensions are finite separable. The derivations \(\partial/\partial t_i\) on the rational function field extend across a separable algebraic generator \(z\): differentiating its minimal equation gives

\[ Dz=-\frac{(DP)(z)}{P'(z)}. \tag{K.9} \]

The nonzero denominator and the quotient polynomial rule verify both existence and uniqueness, and a tower gives the extension to the field. Thus the \(dt_i\) stay linearly independent in the source's rational differentials. Clear denominators in smooth coordinate charts from K.1. Some differential minor is nonzero, proving the assertion.

The critical locus in \(M\) is algebraically closed there, defined by the rank-drop minors in its finite smooth chart cover. No irreducible component \(R\) of it can dominate \(N\). Otherwise the dense smooth open of \(R\) would have generically surjective differential to \(N\) by the preceding argument, and its tangent vectors are tangent to \(M\); this contradicts criticality on \(M\). Thus the union of the closures of their images is a proper closed subset of \(N\). After deleting it and, if needed, the complement of the generic image supplied by K.4, the map is everywhere submersive and onto this target open. The same argument works simultaneously for finitely many smooth source pieces. Nondominant pieces are excluded by deleting their proper image closures.

Now let \(f:X\to Y\) be any algebraic morphism, with finite constructible markings in both spaces. We construct finite Whitney stratifications such that every source stratum maps onto a target stratum by a submersion. At a stage, let \(B\subset Y\) be the closed residual target and \(R=f^{-1}B\) the residual source; outside them keep the strata already fixed.

Extend the target stratification over \(B\) by K.6, respecting its markings, and choose its dense smooth pieces \(T_C\) on the irreducible components \(C\) of \(B\). Extend the source stratification over \(R\), respecting its markings and all \(f^{-1}T_C\). For each \(T_C\), apply the preceding critical-value argument to the finitely many source pieces mapping into it. Remove their critical-image closures and the image closures of nondominant pieces. For each dominant piece also restrict to the nonempty open contained in its image from K.4. Their intersection is a nonempty open \(T_C^0\subset T_C\). Its complement in \(C\) is closed and proper.

Retain the \(T_C^0\) and the source pieces above them. Every retained source piece is an open subset of a candidate Whitney stratum and is submersive and onto its target piece. These cuts are restrictions to the single open set \(Y\setminus B'\), and its inverse image, where \(B'=B\setminus\bigcup_C T_C^0\) is closed. Hence the retained pairs remain Whitney regular and keep the frontier incidences already constructed. Every component of \(B'\) has smaller dimension. Repeat the relative extension over \(B'\) and \(f^{-1}B'\). The process terminates with the asserted stratifications. Empty fibers cause no difficulty; they simply have no source stratum above them.

The smooth ambient extension required by J.7 is available locally. Extend the regular coordinate functions of \(f\) from an affine source embedding to its ambient open set. Near a target stratum, smooth submanifold coordinates from I.1 give a local retraction onto that stratum; compose with it. On the source part mapping to the stratum this equals \(f\). Thus J.7 applies to proper algebraic maps with the stratifications just constructed.

K.8. Constructibility of the classical operations

Let \(f:X\to Y\) be separated of finite type and \(F\) a bounded algebraically constructible complex of field sheaves. By K.6 its cohomology is constructible for a finite algebraic Whitney refinement. If \(f\) is proper in the classical topology, K.7 and J.7 show that \(Rf_*F=Rf_!F\) is bounded and algebraically constructible.

We include the ambient-space detail for a variety which has only local affine embeddings. Over a small coordinate box \(B\) in a target stratum, choose a slightly larger box with compact closure; the inverse image \(K\) of that closure is compact by properness. Cover \(K\) by finitely many source charts \(\psi_i\) which are locally closed algebraic embeddings in Euclidean spaces. Ambient smooth bumps, supported compactly inside these charts and positive on smaller sets covering \(K\), extend by zero and normalize to functions \(\chi_i\) with \(\sum\chi_i=1\) on a neighborhood of \(K\). Such bumps are those constructed in I.1. Regular changes of source coordinates extend locally to the ambient spaces, so these functions are smooth on every stratum and have compatible local ambient extensions.

The map \(z\mapsto(\chi_i(z),\chi_i(z)\psi_i(z))_i\), with zero entries off the respective supports, is an embedding near \(K\). Where \(\chi_i>0\), dividing its coordinate block by \(\chi_i\) recovers the original chart coordinates. This proves injectivity, a continuous local inverse and a smooth stratumwise immersion. In that chart, the remaining coordinates extend smoothly as functions of the recovered coordinates, so this is a graph embedding; the argument at the end of K.5 preserves Whitney regularity. Append the coordinate values of \(f\) to this embedding. Its image of \(K\) is compact, and its image of \(f^{-1}B\) is the intersection of that compact image with the ambient open set where the appended base coordinate lies in \(B\). It is closed in that ambient open set, and \(f\) is now the ambient coordinate projection. This reduces exactly to the ambient hypotheses of I.6 and J.7. The local topological properties used here follow from the finite affine atlas: local compactness and second countability hold in each chart, and separatedness makes the diagonal closed, hence makes the usual topology Hausdorff.

For proper supports of a general \(f\), work over an affine open \(V\subset Y\) and cover \(f^{-1}V\) by finitely many affine opens \(U_i\). Their finite intersections are affine: for two affine opens in a separated variety, the intersection is the inverse image of its closed diagonal in their affine product, hence is a closed affine subvariety of that product. Iterate. For any such intersection \(U\), embed it in \(\mathbb A^n\). The graph of \(f|_U\) is closed in \(V\times\mathbb A^n\); take its algebraic closure \(\overline U\) in \(V\times\mathbb P^n\). The original \(U\) is its open intersection with the affine chart, and

\[ U\xrightarrow{j}\overline U\xrightarrow{p}V,\qquad p\ \text{proper in the usual topology}. \tag{K.10} \]

The properness follows directly from compactness of \(\mathbb P^n(\mathbb C)\): over a compact subset of \(V\), the closed set \(\overline U\) lies in its compact product with projective space. The extension \(j_!(F|_U)\) is algebraically constructible, with zero stalks on the algebraic boundary. K.6 and the proper case therefore prove that \(R(f|_U)_!(F|_U)=Rp_*j_!(F|_U)\) is bounded constructible.

For completeness, these finitely many affine computations recover \(Rf_!F\). The alternating complex of extensions by zero from the nonempty intersections \(U_{i_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{i_q}\), augmented to \(F|_{f^{-1}V}\), is a resolution. At a point its stalk is the augmented simplex complex on the nonempty set of indices of opens containing that point, tensored with the stalk of \(F\). Inserting one fixed such index, with the alternating sign, contracts it. Totalize with a bounded representative of \(F\); the finite number of intersections keeps it bounded. Applying \(Rf_!\) and the composition isomorphism (H.8) expresses its result by finitely many triangles of the already treated pieces. Constructibility is closed under these triangles by Proposition 2.1 and common Whitney refinement K.6. Proper-support base change (H.6) identifies these computations with the restriction to \(V\). A finite affine cover of \(Y\), refined by its finite membership conditions, gives algebraic constructibility globally. The uniform degree bound is H.4.

Inverse image preserves bounded algebraic constructibility: refine the inverse images of a finite target stratification using K.6; on each resulting source stratum it pulls a local system back to a local system. Tensor and internal Hom preserve it by a common Whitney refinement and J.6. In particular \(D_XF\) is bounded algebraically constructible by (J.18). The just-proved proper-support assertion makes \(Rf_!D_XF\) constructible too, so both evaluation hypotheses in H.6 now hold. Its reversal gives

\[ D_YRf_*F\simeq Rf_!D_XF,\qquad Rf_*F\simeq D_YRf_!D_XF. \tag{K.11} \]

There is no hidden boundedness assumption on the original \(Rf_*F\) in this deduction. The pre-bidual identity of H.6 applied to \(D_XF\) already identifies \(D_YRf_!D_XF\) with \(Rf_*D_XD_XF=Rf_*F\); its left side is bounded. Evaluation then gives the first identity in (K.11).

Finally the pre-bidual pullback identity \(D_Xf^*=f^!D_Y\), applied to \(D_YG\), yields

\[ f^!G\simeq D_Xf^*D_YG \tag{K.12} \]

for bounded algebraically constructible \(G\). The right side is bounded constructible, as just proved. Thus all six classical operations and internal Hom have the bounded algebraic constructibility asserted in Section 3, with the adjunctions, base change, projection and duality maps already constructed in H. These arguments use affine graph compactifications and finite open-cover descent; no unproved global compactification theorem is needed at this classical scope.

Monomial division, finite characteristic-zero going down, convergent prescribed-point arcs and generic graph-fiber density are the inputs to this complex-algebraic proof. For normalization, the Nullstellensatz, generic freeness and going down, see the Stacks Project references below. For generic Whitney regularity and finite stratifications, see [Kaloshin]. Real transversality is not required.

Appendix L. Nodes, normalization and the actual branches

We now justify the algebraic and analytic branch identifications used in Section 1 (the node calculation) and Exercise 3. A curve here is reduced and of pure dimension one. The local node argument works over an algebraically closed field of any characteristic. The analytic assertions and the general finite-normalization construction in L.3 are over \(\mathbb C\). In particular no topological comparison is used to assert an étale purity theorem.

L.1. Finite modules, completion and smooth curve points

We give the completion facts used below. Nakayama's lemma in the needed form says that a finite module \(M\) over a local ring \((R,\mathfrak m)\) with \(M=\mathfrak mM\) is zero. Choose generators and express this equality as \(v=Cv\) with matrix entries in \(\mathfrak m\). The adjugate of \(I-C\) shows that \(\det(I-C)\) annihilates every generator. This determinant is a unit since it is \(1\) modulo \(\mathfrak m\). Applying this to a quotient also shows that lifts of generators of \(M/\mathfrak mM\) generate \(M\).

For a Noetherian ring \(R\), every submodule of a finite module is finite. For a free module this follows by induction on its rank, projecting a submodule onto the last coordinate ideal and lifting its finite generators; pass to a free presentation for a general finite module. The polynomial ring \(R[T]\) is Noetherian as well. For an ideal, the ideals of possible leading coefficients in degrees at most \(d\) form an increasing sequence which stabilizes. Choose finitely many polynomials realizing generators up to a stabilization degree. Their multiples subtract the leading term of every sufficiently large-degree member of the ideal. The remaining bounded-degree part is a submodule of a finite free \(R\)-module, hence is finite. This proves the assertion, and induction handles finitely many variables.

Fix a Noetherian ring \(R\), an ideal \(I\), and finite modules \(N\subset M\). Put all ideal powers into the graded ring \(\mathcal R=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}I^nt^n\) and module \(\mathcal M=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}I^nMt^n\). Generators of \(I\), multiplied by \(t\), generate \(\mathcal R\) as an \(R\)-algebra; the polynomial-ring argument above makes it Noetherian. Generators of \(M\) in degree zero generate \(\mathcal M\). Thus its graded submodule \(\bigoplus_{n\geq0}(N\cap I^nM)t^n\) is finite. Replacing a finite generating family by its homogeneous components gives generators of degrees \(d_j\leq c\), for some \(c\). For \(n\geq c\), their degree-\(n\) multiples lie in \(I^{n-c}(N\cap I^cM)\), because \(I^{n-d_j}=I^{n-c}I^{c-d_j}\). The opposite inclusion follows by multiplication. We have proved Artin–Rees:

\[ N\cap I^nM=I^{n-c}(N\cap I^cM)\quad(n\ge c). \tag{L.1} \]

In particular \(I^nN\subseteq N\cap I^nM\subseteq I^{n-c}N\). These inclusions give canonical inverse maps between the limits for the two filtrations on \(N\): a coordinate modulo one filtration is obtained by projecting from a sufficiently fine coordinate of the other. Choosing a common finer index proves independence of the choice, compatibility and that the maps compose to the identity.

Write \(\widehat M=\varprojlim_{n\geq1}M/I^nM\). The finite-level sequence

\[ 0\longrightarrow N/(N\cap I^nM)\longrightarrow M/I^nM \longrightarrow (M/N)/I^n(M/N)\longrightarrow0 \]

is exact. Its kernel transition maps are surjective, since each kernel is a quotient of the same \(N\). This gives exactness on limits without assuming a general exactness theorem for inverse limits. For a compatible element in the right-hand limit, choose its lift at stage one. Having chosen a lift at stage \(n\), lift its prescribed right-hand value at stage \(n+1\) arbitrarily. The discrepancy at stage \(n\) lies in the kernel; lift that discrepancy through the surjective kernel transition and subtract it. The corrected lift is compatible. Induction proves surjectivity on limits. Injectivity and equality with the kernel are checked coordinate by coordinate. The cofinal-filtration comparison now identifies the left-hand limit with \(\widehat N\). Hence completion is exact on finite modules.

A finite free presentation \(R^a\to R^b\to M\to0\) yields the same cokernel after completion and after tensoring with \(\widehat R\): both maps of finite free \(\widehat R\)-modules have the original matrix entries. Right exactness of tensor follows directly from its balanced-map universal property, which imposes precisely these relations. Thus the natural tensor map is an isomorphism. Applying exactness to \(I^n\subset R\) gives the second identity below: the quotient \(R/I^n\) is already complete, and a finite set of generators of \(I^n\) shows that the image of its completion is \(I^n\widehat R\).

\[ \widehat M=M\otimes_R\widehat R, \qquad \widehat R/I^n\widehat R=R/I^n. \tag{L.2} \]

The same argument applied to \(I^nM\subset M\), using the surjection from a finite direct sum of copies of \(M\) defined by generators of \(I^n\), gives \(\widehat M/I^n\widehat M=M/I^nM\). These identifications commute with the quotient transition maps. Consequently \(\widehat M\) is complete and separated for its own ideal-power topology, not just for an unspecified limit topology.

For separation before completion, put \(N=\bigcap_n I^nM\). It is a finite submodule. Formula (L.1) at \(n=c+1\) gives \(N=IN\). The determinant proof of Nakayama gives an annihilator of \(N\) in \(1+I\). If \(R\) is local and \(I\) is contained in its maximal ideal, this annihilator is a unit, so \(N=0\). Thus \(M\to\widehat M\) is injective for every such ideal, and \(\widehat M=0\) implies \(M=0\). Applied to a quotient, the same assertion says that every submodule of a finite module is closed for this ideal-power topology. In particular it applies to the ideal \(\mathfrak mB\subset\mathfrak n\) in U.2, which need not equal \(\mathfrak n\). The complete filtration proof is also given in Noetherian and Artinian rings, Sections 5–6; compare [Stacks, finite-module completion].

We record two further properties of the completed ring used with formal local equations. If \(I=\mathfrak m\) is maximal, an element of \(\widehat R\) with nonzero residue in \(R/\mathfrak m\) is a unit: its coordinates are units in every \(R/\mathfrak m^n\), and their inverses are compatible. The projection to \(R/\mathfrak m\) is surjective by successive lifting, so \(\widehat R\) is local with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\widehat R\), by (L.2).

For any ideal \(I\), the ring \(\widehat R\) is Noetherian. Set \(J=I\widehat R\). The consecutive quotient identities in (L.2) identify \(\operatorname{gr}_J\widehat R\) with \(\operatorname{gr}_I R\), a quotient of a polynomial ring over \(R/I\) on finitely many degree-one generators. This graded ring is therefore Noetherian. For an ideal \(Q\subset\widehat R\), its initial classes form a homogeneous ideal in this graded ring. Choose finitely many homogeneous generators and lift them to \(q_1,\ldots,q_s\in Q\), of orders \(d_i\). Starting with \(q\in Q\), cancel the degree-\(n\) initial class of the current residual by a sum \(\sum_i a_{i,n}q_i\), where \(a_{i,n}\in J^{n-d_i}\), using zero when \(d_i>n\). The residual then lies in \(Q\cap J^{n+1}\). Each coefficient sum \(a_i=\sum_n a_{i,n}\) converges by completeness, since the orders tend to infinity. Separatedness makes the limiting residual zero, so \(q=\sum_i a_iq_i\). Thus \(Q\) is finitely generated. No prior closedness assumption on \(Q\) entered this argument. These completion statements are also proved in Completion, Sections 1–3.

For a local finite-type \(k\)-algebra at a \(k\)-rational point, translate the point to the origin in a polynomial presentation. Modulo the \(n\)-th power of its maximal ideal, every polynomial inverted in forming the local ring is already a unit: its constant term is nonzero, and a finite geometric series in its nilpotent remaining part gives an inverse. Hence the completed ambient polynomial local ring is \(k[[z_1,\ldots,z_r]]\), coefficient by coefficient. Exactness of completion and a finite generating family for the equation ideal give its quotient by those same equations. Finally a power-series coordinate map with invertible linear part has a unique inverse: after degrees below \(d\) have been determined, cancel the degree-\(d\) error by that invertible linear matrix. Induction gives compatible inverse maps at every order, hence inverse power-series maps. Consequently \(r-1\) equations with independent linear terms have completed local ring \(k[[z]]\), where \(z\) is any complementary linear coordinate.

We will need two elementary valuation facts. Suppose a Noetherian local ring has maximal ideal \((z)\), with \(z\) a non-zero-divisor and not a unit. The intersection \(J=\bigcap_n z^nR\) satisfies \(J=zJ\): divide an element by \(z\) and cancel \(z\) in every higher divisibility statement. Nakayama gives \(J=0\).
