Every nonzero element is therefore uniquely \(z^e u\), with \(e\ge0\) and \(u\) a unit. Products add exponents, so the ring is a domain. Fractions of negative exponent cannot satisfy a monic equation, whose lowest exponent would occur only in its leading power. Thus this is a discrete valuation ring and is integrally closed.

Conversely a Noetherian normal local domain \(R\) of dimension one is such a ring. Choose \(0\ne a\in\mathfrak m\). Every nonzero prime is maximal, so \(\sqrt{(a)}=\mathfrak m\), and finite generation gives \(\mathfrak m^n\subset(a)\) for some least \(n\ge1\). Choose \(b\in\mathfrak m^{n-1}\setminus(a)\) and set \(w=b/a\). Then \(w\notin R\) but \(w\mathfrak m\subset R\). If \(w\mathfrak m\subset\mathfrak m\), the adjugate argument on generators of the faithful module \(\mathfrak m\) makes \(w\) integral, a contradiction. Hence \(wc\) is a unit for some \(c\in\mathfrak m\). Rescale so that \(wc=1\). Every \(d\in\mathfrak m\) equals \(c(wd)\), proving \(\mathfrak m=(c)\).

A one-dimensional finite-type local \(k\)-algebra with residue field \(k\) and maximal ideal generated by a non-zero-divisor is a smooth curve point. Here is the required presentation argument. Its tangent space has dimension one. In an affine embedding, choose \(n-1\) equations with independent linear terms and let \(S\) be their local quotient. Its completed ring is \(k[[z]]\) by the formal inverse construction, and \(S\) injects into it by (L.2). Its maximal ideal is \((z)\) by Nakayama, so it is a discrete valuation ring by the preceding argument. The given local ring is \(S/J\) and has dimension one. Any nonzero ideal of this discrete valuation ring contains a power of \(z\) and has zero-dimensional quotient. Thus \(J=0\). The chosen Jacobian minor stays invertible on an algebraic neighborhood. This supplies the local smooth presentation. Over \(\mathbb C\), E.1's convergent implicit-function argument makes it an actual analytic disc, with \(z\) an analytic coordinate. No formal-to-convergent approximation theorem is being assumed.

L.2. The node criterion and its finite normalization

Let \(A=\mathcal O_{X,p}\) for a reduced curve over an algebraically closed field \(k\), with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\) and residue field \(k\). The following two conditions are equivalent:

  1. \(\widehat A\simeq k[[u,v]]/(uv)\).
  2. \(\dim_k\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2=2\), and the kernel of \(\operatorname{Sym}^2_k(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2)\to\mathfrak m^2/\mathfrak m^3\) contains a product of two distinct linear forms.

The implication from 1 to 2 follows from (L.2) and the degree-two relation \(uv\). We prove the converse while constructing the normalization.

Choose a basis \(x,y\) of \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\), lifted to \(A\), such that the coefficient of \(y^2\) in the given quadratic relation is nonzero and \(x\) is a non-zero-divisor. These requirements can be met simultaneously. A reduced Noetherian ring embeds in the product of the fraction fields of its finitely many minimal-prime quotients: their intersection is its zero nilradical. Avoiding every minimal prime therefore makes an element a non-zero-divisor. In our one-dimensional local curve none of these primes is maximal. Since lifts of a tangent basis generate \(\mathfrak m\), the linear combinations lying in any such prime form a proper linear subspace of the coefficient space. The two forbidden tangent directions impose two further proper subspaces. A finite union of proper linear subspaces cannot cover a vector space over the infinite field \(k\): choose a polynomial line avoiding their finitely many nonzero linear equations. This gives \(x\) and then a complementary \(y\).

Scale the quadratic relation to obtain \(y^2-a_0xy-b_0x^2\in\mathfrak m^3\), where \(T^2-a_0T-b_0\) has two distinct roots in \(k\). Since \(\mathfrak m=(x,y)\), the relation gives \(\mathfrak m^2=x\mathfrak m+\mathfrak m^3\). Nakayama on \(\mathfrak m^2/x\mathfrak m\) gives \(\mathfrak m^2=x\mathfrak m\). Now \(\mathfrak m^3=x^2\mathfrak m\), so the error can be absorbed into the coefficient of \(x^2\) without changing its residue. Thus for some \(a,b\in A\), reducing to \(a_0,b_0\),

\[ y^2=axy+bx^2,\qquad t=y/x,\qquad B=A[t]\subset A[1/x],\qquad t^2-at-b=0. \tag{L.3} \]

The ring \(B=A+At\) is finite over \(A\), is reduced, and is birational: after inverting \(x\) it is \(A[1/x]\). Moreover \(\mathfrak mB=xB\) and \(\mathfrak m B\subset A\), because \(xt=y\) and \(yt=ay+bx\).

There is a surjection \(k[T]/(T^2-a_0T-b_0)\twoheadrightarrow B/\mathfrak mB\). Its target is nonzero by lying over, proved in K.1 using only integrality. It cannot have dimension one. If it did, the constants from \(A\) would surject onto it, so \(B=A+\mathfrak mB\); Nakayama on the finite module \(B/A\) would imply \(B=A\). Then \(t\in A\) and \(y=xt\), making \(\mathfrak m=(x)\), contrary to its tangent dimension two. Therefore the surjection is an isomorphism, and

\[ B/\mathfrak mB\simeq k\times k. \tag{L.4} \]

The two maximal ideals \(\mathfrak n_1,\mathfrak n_2\) of \(B\) above \(\mathfrak m\) are all its maximal ideals, since \(B\) is integral over the local ring \(A\). Each localization has maximal ideal generated by \(x\), which remains a non-zero-divisor. L.1 makes each a discrete valuation ring. Hence \(B\) is normal in its total quotient ring: an integral fraction belongs to every maximal localization, and a fraction belonging to all of them belongs to \(B\). For the latter assertion, its denominator ideal \(\{c\in B:cq\in B\}\) would otherwise be a proper ideal contained in a maximal ideal where the fraction did not belong. Thus \(B\) is the integral closure of \(A\). Indeed anything integral over \(A\) is integral over \(B\) by the same monic equation, while every element of \(B\) is integral over \(A\).

The residue difference in (L.4) gives an exact sequence of finite \(A\)-modules

\[ 0\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow B \xrightarrow{\mathrm{res}_1-\mathrm{res}_2}k\longrightarrow0. \tag{L.5} \]

To check its kernel, \(\mathfrak m\) kills \(B/A\), which is generated by the class of \(t\). That class is nonzero, so \(B/A\) has dimension one. Its two residues differ by the nonzero difference of the two roots of the quadratic. This proves exactness, including the specified last map.

Complete (L.5) using L.1. Since \(\mathfrak mB=xB=\mathfrak n_1\cap\mathfrak n_2\) and the two maximal ideals are comaximal, the Chinese remainder calculation in K.1 applies at every power and gives \(B/x^nB=B/\mathfrak n_1^n\times B/\mathfrak n_2^n\). Localization at \(\mathfrak n_i\) does not change its quotient: every element outside that ideal is invertible modulo its power by a finite geometric series. In its discrete valuation ring, successive subtraction of residue constants gives unique expansions modulo \(x^n\). Thus

\[ \widehat B=k[[x]]\times k[[x]],\qquad \widehat A=\{(f,g):f(0)=g(0)\} \simeq k[[u,v]]/(uv). \tag{L.6} \]

The last isomorphism sends \(u\) to \((x,0)\) and \(v\) to \((0,x)\). Every pair with equal constant terms has a unique constant plus a positive-power series in each variable. This proves the node criterion, its two actual normalization points, their regular local rings and the completed comparison. The argument also covers characteristic two: the only needed quadratic condition is two distinct linear factors.

This is a criterion on the algebraic local ring, not a definition requiring a prior plane presentation. In particular a reduced plane curve with a nonzero quadratic term which is a product of distinct lines is nodal. Its tangent space has dimension two, and that quadratic term gives condition 2. Conversely a completed node has exactly that tangent relation. A finite presentation of (L.3) spreads the local normalization to a finite map on an algebraic neighborhood of \(p\): clear its finitely many denominators outside \(\mathfrak m\). The smooth presentations of the two local rings from L.1 hold on neighborhoods of both inverse-image points. Their complement has closed image under the finite map by K.1; remove that image from the base. On the resulting neighborhood the finite ring is normal and birational, and hence is its normalization by the same integral-closure argument.

L.3. Finite normalization of a complex curve

For the multiple-branch comparison we also need existence of the algebraic normalization beyond nodes. We prove it at the complex curve scope. Let \(A\) be the coordinate domain of an affine irreducible complex curve. K.1 supplies a finite inclusion \(R=\mathbb C[s]\subset A\). Its fraction field \(L\) is finite separable over \(K=\mathbb C(s)\). Choose the primitive element \(z\in A\) as in K.1; \(e_i=z^i\), \(0\le i<d=[L:K]\), form a \(K\)-basis.

Here is the trace calculation, including its nondegeneracy. In a splitting field let \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_d\) be the distinct embeddings of \(L\), constructed by the root choices in K.1, and put \(V_{ri}=\sigma_r(z)^i\). Its determinant is the Vandermonde product: it vanishes when two row parameters coincide, has the total degree of the product of their pairwise differences, and the coefficient of the diagonal monomial fixes the remaining constant as one. The conjugate values of \(z\) are distinct, so \(V\) is invertible. If \(M(c)\) is the matrix of multiplication by \(c\in L\) in the basis \(e_i\), evaluating each column gives

\[ V M(c)=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1(c),\ldots,\sigma_d(c))V, \qquad \operatorname{Tr}_{L/K}(c)=\sum_{r=1}^d\sigma_r(c). \]

The second identity follows by conjugation and \(\operatorname{tr}(UV)=\operatorname{tr}(VU)\), obtained by interchanging the two finite summation indices. Consequently the trace pairing matrix \(G_{ij}=\operatorname{Tr}_{L/K}(e_ie_j)\) equals \(V^{\mathsf T}V\), and its determinant \(\Delta\) is the square of the nonzero Vandermonde product. Its entries lie in \(K\), as traces of matrices over \(K\). Each \(\sigma_r(z)\) is integral over \(R\), because it satisfies the same monic equation as \(z\). The trace sum and K.1's closure of integral elements under sums and products show that every entry of \(G\) is integral over \(R\). Since \(R\) is integrally closed, \(G_{ij}\in R\) and \(0\ne\Delta\in R\).

Let \(C\) be the integral closure of \(A\) in \(L\). Its elements are integral over \(R\) by transitivity. For \(c=\sum c_i e_i\in C\), every trace \(\operatorname{Tr}(ce_j)\) is likewise integral over \(R\) and belongs to \(R\). Solving the trace matrix equation gives \(c_i\in\Delta^{-1}R\). Hence

\[ C\subset\bigoplus_i\Delta^{-1}R e_i. \tag{L.7} \]

It is an \(R\)-submodule of this finite module, so is finite. The same generators make it finite over \(A\). It is normal: an element integral over \(C\) is integral over \(A\) by transitivity and therefore lies in \(C\).

For a reduced affine curve, apply this to its finitely many irreducible component domains. The product of their normalizations is a finite algebra over \(A\): each component quotient is a cyclic \(A\)-module, and each normalization is finite over that quotient. It is integral, embeds in the product of the component fraction fields and contains every element of that product integral over \(A\), by the domain case. This is precisely the integral closure in the total quotient ring. To see that this total quotient ring is the indicated product, choose an element in every other minimal prime but outside one specified minimal prime, using finite prime avoidance as in K.2. Sums of these elements have nonzero image in every component and can be inverted; their ratios give the component idempotents. Each component's nonzero denominator can then be included in such a sum, giving its full fraction field.

Integral closure commutes with localization here. If a fraction is integral after localizing, one denominator from the multiplicative set clears all coefficients of its monic equation. A sufficiently large power of that denominator times the fraction then satisfies a monic equation over the original ring. This proves both inclusions. The affine constructions consequently glue to a finite normalization \(\nu:\widetilde X\to X\). A finite morphism is closed algebraically by K.1 and is proper in the usual topology by the same monic root bounds used there.

The normal local rings of \(\widetilde X\) at its closed points are one-dimensional: their component rings are finite over \(\mathbb C[s]\), and lying over, going up and incomparability give this dimension. L.1 makes them discrete valuation rings and then actual smooth analytic curve points. Thus \(\widetilde X\) is a smooth complex curve. On each affine chart finitely many generators of its normalization are fractions on the original components. A common denominator nonzero on every component gives \(A_d=C_d\). Its zero set on a curve is finite, by the strict dimension decrease in K.1. Therefore \(\nu\) is an isomorphism away from finitely many points locally on \(X\). At a smooth point the local ring is already a discrete valuation ring, so the normalization is an isomorphism there as well.

L.4. The convergent branches of an algebraic node

Return to a complex node \(p\). In (L.3), \(x\) is a uniformizer at each of the two points \(q_i\) above \(p\). By L.1 it is an analytic coordinate on a disc at \(q_i\), and the regular function \(t\) has a convergent expression \(t_i(x)\) there. Their constant terms are the two distinct roots \(\lambda_i\) in (L.4). Hence the normalization maps these discs to

\[ y=x t_1(x),\qquad y=x t_2(x). \tag{L.8} \]

To interpret these as full ambient branches, choose an affine embedding of \(X\) near \(p\). Tangent dimension two gives \(n-2\) equations with independent linear terms. Keep \(x,y\) as the complementary coordinates; these regular functions extend to an ambient neighborhood. Let \(S\) be the local ring cut out by those equations and write \(A=S/J\). The formal inverse construction gives \(\widehat S=k[[x,y]]\). Its surjection to the completed node has principal kernel: lift the two node parameters to \(\widehat S\); their independent linear terms make them formal coordinates, and in those coordinates the kernel is their product. Exact completion and reduction modulo the maximal ideal now give \(\dim_k J/\mathfrak m_SJ=1\). Nakayama supplies a single generator \(f\) of \(J\), whose initial term is the nondegenerate quadratic relation. These local equation equalities hold on a sufficiently small algebraic neighborhood after clearing the finitely many denominators.

The convergent implicit-function argument of E.1 eliminates the other coordinates, so the analytic curve is cut out in that surface by the convergent function \(f(x,y)\). Its restriction to each graph in (L.8) is zero. Division by \(y-x t_1(x)\) is convergent: the identity \(f(x,y)-f(x,g(x))=(y-g(x))\int_0^1\partial_y f(x,g(x)+s(y-g(x)))\,ds\) gives a convergent analytic quotient on a smaller polydisc. On the other graph the quotient vanishes for \(x\ne0\), hence also at zero by continuity. A second division therefore gives \(f=(y-x t_1(x))(y-x t_2(x))h\), with \(h(0)\ne0\) by the quadratic initial term. Thus the following coordinate change identifies the analytic equation itself, as well as its underlying set.

There are no additional points of \(X\) near \(p\) outside these images. The normalization is surjective by lying over. Its fiber at \(p\) consists of \(q_1,q_2\), and properness allows the neighborhood to be shrunk so that its full inverse image lies inside the two chosen discs. Explicitly, the complement of their union is closed and has closed image under a proper map; that image avoids \(p\). Proper maps here are closed in the usual topology: a convergent sequence in such an image lies in a compact base set together with its limit, and properness provides a convergent subsequence of inverse-image points. Thus the two graphs in (L.8) describe exactly the local set.

The analytic coordinate change

\[ u=y-x t_1(x),\qquad v=y-x t_2(x) \tag{L.9} \]

has nonzero Jacobian determinant \(\lambda_2-\lambda_1\) at zero. Its inverse is convergent by E.1. It sends the local curve to \(uv=0\), and its two normalization discs to the two coordinate branches. In particular this proves the asserted analytic local model from the completed-local-ring criterion, without replacing an algebraic normalization by a merely formal one. Each branch has its usual disc topology; their union has the quotient topology proved in B.4. At a node the normalization pushforward is therefore the sheaf on those two separated discs used in Proposition 1.3.

L.5. Several smooth branches and the normalization sheaf

Suppose a reduced complex algebraic curve has, near a point \(p\), exactly \(r\) smooth analytic branches meeting only at \(p\). Distinct tangent lines, as in Exercise 3, imply that last property after shrinking by B.4. The finite normalization of L.3 separates exactly these \(r\) branches and is locally an isomorphism from a disc onto each of them.

Here are the comparison details. The inverse-image set of \(p\) is finite. Each of its points has a smooth disc neighborhood by L.1, and these neighborhoods can be chosen disjoint. Remove the finitely many other exceptional image points from a small neighborhood of \(p\); there the normalization is an isomorphism off \(p\). Properness, as in L.4, then keeps the full inverse image inside the chosen discs. Each sufficiently small punctured disc is connected and maps into one of the disjoint punctured branches. In that branch's analytic parameter its map is a nonconstant holomorphic function vanishing only at the centre, with expression \(h(z)=z^e a(z)\), where \(a(0)\ne0\).

The function \(a(z)\) has a convergent \(e\)-th root near zero: divide by its constant term, choose a root of that constant, and apply the binomial series near \(1\). Its convergence follows from the ratio test and its identity from multiplication of power series. Thus a local coordinate change puts \(h\) in the form \(w\mapsto w^e\). Since the normalization is one-to-one off \(p\), \(e=1\). So the disc maps isomorphically onto a neighborhood in its smooth branch. Two different inverse-image discs cannot map to the same branch, again by injectivity off \(p\). Every branch is reached, by surjectivity and properness. This proves the required bijection and the local isomorphisms.

Consequently, with \(i_p:\{p\}\hookrightarrow X\), the actual algebraic normalization gives the local exact sequence of classical sheaves

\[ 0\longrightarrow\Lambda_X\longrightarrow \nu_*\Lambda_{\widetilde X}\longrightarrow i_{p*}(\Lambda^r/\operatorname{diag}\Lambda) \longrightarrow0. \tag{L.10} \]

Away from \(p\) it is the identity sequence, and at \(p\) it is the diagonal inclusion, so exactness is stalkwise. For \(r=2\), choosing an order of the branches identifies its final map with their difference; exchanging them changes this identification by a sign. For several singular points the global quotient is the sum of these local quotients. The branch labels carry no preferred global order. B.4 now applies to the actual normalization in Exercise 3, and G.4 applies to the actual nodal normalization in Section 1 (the node calculation), with their previously proved support complexes and duality maps.

There is also a purely algebraic comparison under the étale smooth-branch hypothesis in Exercise 3. If the branches in the chosen neighborhood have prime ideals \(P_1,\ldots,P_r\), their local ring product \(\prod_i A/P_i\) is finite over \(A\), since each quotient is cyclic. Its factors are the regular local rings of the given smooth curves, hence are discrete valuation rings by L.1. It embeds in the total quotient ring of \(A\), which is the product of the component fraction fields as proved in L.3 by prime avoidance; that argument works over any field. The product is normal and integral over \(A\), so it is exactly the local normalization. It separates the \(r\) branch points. This verifies the normalization assertion under the stated smooth-branch hypothesis, without asserting that every singularity has such branches.

At a geometric node over an algebraically closed field of positive characteristic, L.2 supplies the finite normalization with its two smooth algebraic branch points and the module comparison (L.5) directly, without a prior split-branch presentation. Thus the local branch geometry for the étale nodal computation does not require a classical analytic model. The sheaf computation and its descent from geometric branch neighborhoods still use the separately identified finite-map étale base change and smooth purity arguments in Section 3. Over a finite field branch labels may be exchanged by Frobenius; the displayed two copies in geometric stalk and costalk groups do not assert that each summand is arithmetically fixed. Singular finite-coefficient duality and the normalized adic passage are treated in M and BV–BX.

The freely accessible Stacks Project node, completion, Artin–Rees and discrete-valuation statements provide comparison sources. The finite ring \(A[y/x]\), its two residue maps, the completion sequence and the convergent branch identification have all been proved here; no normalization-completion compatibility theorem is imported without proof.

Appendix M. Ordinary étale finiteness and singular biduality over a field

We prove the field case needed here, including the steps which a reference to a general finiteness theorem would leave unwritten. Throughout this appendix, schemes are separated and of finite type over a field \(k\), \(n\) is invertible in \(k\), and \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\). Constructibility means finite locally constant values on a finite locally closed partition; it does not require the pieces to be smooth over an imperfect field. The ordinary direct-image assertion also holds for any finite coefficient ring whose order is invertible in \(k\), by forgetting to a \(\mathbf Z/n\)-module. The duality assertion below uses the self-injectivity of \(\mathbf Z/n\), not a claim that every finite ring is self-injective.

The proofs use the finite-coefficient proper-support finiteness and smooth trace of Propositions 3.2–3.3. Their earlier-programme inputs are the actual proper and smooth base-change theorems identified in Section 3; the finite presentations and Noetherian subobject argument in Constructible sheaves and extension by zero, §§4–7; and the cohomological-dimension and continuity arguments in Cohomological dimension and the Künneth formula, §§1–8. Proposition 3.3 constructs the exceptional adjoint by proving representability through presheaves and exact sheafification, with exact programme locators for compact representability and unbounded resolutions. Its internal-Hom adjunction and local description are used as written in Poincaré duality for smooth varieties, §§8–10. These arguments use those geometric and categorical hypotheses at the stated coefficient scope.

The mathematical comparison source is the freely accessible author edition of SGA \(4\frac12\), Théorèmes de finitude, §§2.1–2.8 and 4.1–4.7. We give a field-only dimension argument below; no generic base-change theorem over an arbitrary parameter scheme is assumed.

M.1. Preparations: fields, smooth open subsets and bounds

First, ordinary higher images have a finite bound before their constructibility is known. On an affine target and an affine source of dimension at most \(d\), the support estimate of the cohomological-dimension companion, Theorem 6.2, gives \(R^qf_*F=0\) for \(q>d\), for every torsion sheaf \(F\). Cover a general separated source by \(r\) affine opens. All multiple intersections are affine, of dimension at most \(d\). The finite Čech-to-derived-image spectral sequence therefore gives the sufficient bound \(d+r-1\). Finite affine covering of the target gives a uniform bound. This is a bound on the relative functor, so it does not assume that \(k\) has finite Galois cohomological dimension. The same companion proves filtered-colimit continuity and, over a separably closed field, absolute torsion cohomological dimension at most \(2d\). Every spectral sequence below consequently has a finite contributing range when the input is bounded.

One detail in that affine-bound proof is useful here. Its boundary calculation, Theorem 5.1, Interlude A, uses a local domain \(R\) containing a separably closed field \(L\), and \(0\ne f\in\mathfrak m_R\). The element \(f\) is transcendental over \(L\): a nonzero algebraic element has its inverse in \(L[f]\), contradicting membership in the maximal ideal. Moreover \(R[1/f]\) contains the whole rational function field \(L(f)\). For every nonzero polynomial write \(P(T)=T^r(c+TQ(T))\), with \(c\ne0\). Then \(c+fQ(f)\) is a unit in the local ring, and \(P(f)\) becomes a unit after inverting \(f\). This supplies every denominator of \(L(f)\). The strict-local finite models have fraction fields of the dimension stated there, so the smaller-dimensional affine induction applies to their finitely generated \(L(f)\)-subalgebras. The support-drop proof in Theorem 6.2 then uses those affine bounds and continuity, not ordinary geometric-fibre cohomology for a nonproper map.

Let \(k_s\) be a separable closure of \(k\). The morphism \(\operatorname{Spec}k_s\to\operatorname{Spec}k\) is an affine inverse limit of finite étale morphisms. Étale localization and the continuity argument AL.4 identify pullback of \(Rf_*F\) with the corresponding direct image over \(k_s\). The extension from \(k_s\) to an algebraic closure is purely inseparable; étale topological invariance identifies the two sites and their direct-image functors. These pullbacks are conservative. Constructibility descends along this surjective quasi-compact change of base by the finite-presentation detection lemma in the extension-by-zero companion. Thus it suffices to prove ordinary finiteness over algebraically closed fields, simultaneously in all characteristics prime to \(n\).

We record the geometry needed to choose a smooth dense open, including positive characteristic. If \(L/k\) is a finitely generated field extension of transcendence degree \(d\), with \(k\) perfect of characteristic \(p>0\), choose any transcendence basis \(t_1,\ldots,t_d\) and put \(e=[L:k(t_1,\ldots,t_d)]\). Frobenius is an isomorphism of the extensions \(L/k(t)\) and \(L^p/k(t^p)\). Comparing degrees over \(k(t^p)\) gives

\[ [L:L^p]=p^d. \tag{M.1} \]

Choose successively \(z_i\) outside \(L^p(z_1,\ldots,z_{i-1})\) until that field is \(L\). Each step has degree \(p\), so there are exactly \(d\) steps and the monomials \(z_1^{a_1}\cdots z_d^{a_d}\), \(0\leq a_i<p\), are a basis over \(L^p\). The \(z_i\)'s are algebraically independent over \(k\). Indeed, regroup a polynomial relation of least positive total degree according to the exponents modulo \(p\). Perfection of \(k\) writes it as \(\sum_a z^a P_a(z)^p=0\). Independence of those monomials makes every \(P_a(z)\) zero, whereas each nonzero polynomial \(P_a\) has smaller degree, a contradiction.

The finite extension \(L/k(z)\) is separable. To see this without a differential criterion, let \(E\) be its maximal separable subextension. There is one \(r\) with \(L^{p^r}\subset E\): for each of finitely many algebraic generators, its minimal polynomial is a separable polynomial in some \(p\)-power of the variable. But \(L=L^p k(z)\), hence by iteration \(L=L^{p^r}k(z)\subset E\). In characteristic zero any transcendence basis is separating. A primitive element for this finite separable extension, after clearing its monic polynomial's coefficients and inverting its discriminant, gives a finite étale algebra over an open of \(\mathbf A^d_k\). The given integral affine variety and this algebra have the same fraction field; expressing their finite lists of generators as fractions and inverting the denominators identifies nonempty open subsets of the two. Hence every reduced variety over a perfect field has a smooth dense open. For several components first remove their intersections. Intersect this open with the generic locally constant loci of a constructible sheaf. The result is smooth, the sheaf is lisse there, and the complement has smaller dimension.

The dimension statements used here follow from the monic-elimination proof of Noether normalization in K.1: that proof does not use characteristic zero. It makes the dimension of an integral affine algebra equal to the transcendence degree of its fraction field. In particular, on every component on which a regular function \(t\) is nonconstant, the generic fibre over \(k(t)\) has dimension one less. A component on which \(t\) is constant has empty generic fibre. Algebraic field extension preserves these dimensions, as is also seen by base changing the finite normalization map to affine space.

M.2. A finite-support lemma for an initially arbitrary sheaf

Assume \(k\) algebraically closed. Let \(Y\) be affine, embedded as a closed subscheme of \(\mathbf A^a_k\), with coordinate functions \(t_i\). Write \(Y_{\bar\eta_i}\) for the fibre over an algebraic closure of \(k(t_i)\). Suppose a \(\Lambda\)-sheaf \(E\), not yet assumed constructible, has constructible restriction to each \(Y_{\bar\eta_i}\). Then there is a constructible subsheaf \(G\subset E\) such that \(E/G\) is supported on closed points.

Here are the finite-presentation details. On a Noetherian scheme every sheaf of finite-ring modules is the filtered union of constructible subsheaves: take the images of finite sums of the étale generators \(u_!\Lambda\); each image is constructible by the Noetherian subobject and quotient lemma. Pullback is exact and commutes with this union. The constructible sheaf \(E|Y_{\bar\eta_i}\) is finitely presented, hence compact for filtered colimits. Its identity therefore factors through one member of the pulled-back union. Since that member is a subsheaf, it equals the whole restriction. Choose one such subsheaf for every \(i\), and let \(G\) be their finite sum. The quotient has zero restriction to every coordinate geometric generic fibre.

If \(y\in Y\) is not closed, then \(\kappa(y)\) has positive transcendence degree over \(k\). Some \(t_i(y)\) is transcendental: these coordinates generate the residue field as a field. The point lies over that coordinate's generic point. After extending its geometric field to contain the chosen algebraic closure of \(k(t_i)\), its stalk is a stalk of the zero generic restriction. Thus \((E/G)_{\bar y}=0\).

This argument works on finitely many affine opens of a general \(Y\). If \(G_i\subset E|_{U_i}\) are the resulting subsheaves and \(v_i:U_i\to Y\), take the sum of the images of \(v_{i!}G_i\to E\). These images are constructible, and the resulting quotient is supported on closed points on each open, hence on \(Y\). Closed points here are the points with residue field algebraic over \(k\), so closedness agrees on the affine charts.

A sheaf \(Q\) supported on closed points is the filtered union of constructible sheaves with finite support. A constructible subset containing only closed points is finite: each of its finitely many locally closed pieces has dimension zero, since a positive-dimensional piece contains a nonclosed generic point. Such a finite-support sheaf is the finite sum of its point sheaves, by the closed-open stalk criterion. A closed point over \(k\) has a trivial étale topos, so its section functor is exact. Filtered cohomological continuity gives

\[ Q=\bigoplus_{y\in Y(k)}i_{y*}Q_{\bar y},\qquad H^{b}(Y,Q)=0\ (b>0),\qquad \Gamma(Y,Q)=\bigoplus_y Q_{\bar y}. \tag{M.2} \]

The direct sum description can equally be checked on stalks of the filtered finite-support subsheaves. It does not assume that an arbitrary sheaf has finite stalks. In particular, if \(\Gamma(Y,Q)\) is finite, then \(Q\) is constructible and has finite support.

M.3. Recovering finiteness on a proper scheme

Let \(Y/k\) be proper and \(C\in D^b(Y,\Lambda)\). Suppose \(R\Gamma(Y,C)\) has finite cohomology and that, on each affine coordinate chart, every \(\mathcal H^qC\) has constructible restrictions to the coordinate geometric generic fibres. Then \(C\in D^b_c(Y,\Lambda)\).

Apply M.2 in each of the finitely many nonzero degrees. We obtain

\[ 0\longrightarrow G_q\longrightarrow \mathcal H^qC \longrightarrow Q_q\longrightarrow0, \tag{M.3} \]

with \(G_q\) constructible and \(Q_q\) supported on closed points. Proper finiteness from Proposition 3.2 and (M.2) show that \(H^b(Y,\mathcal H^qC)\) is finite for every \(b>0\). In the bounded hypercohomology spectral sequence

\[ E_2^{b,q}=H^b(Y,\mathcal H^qC) \ \Longrightarrow\ H^{b+q}(Y,C), \tag{M.4} \]

all entries with \(b>0\) are therefore finite. No differential enters column zero. Every differential leaving it has finite image, since its target is a subquotient of a finite entry with positive first index. Only finitely many differentials can occur. The final column-zero term is a subquotient of the assumed finite abutment. Working backwards through these finitely many kernels proves that \(H^0(Y,\mathcal H^qC)\) is finite. The exact sequence of (M.3) then puts \(H^0(Y,Q_q)\) between a quotient of this finite group and a subgroup of the finite group \(H^1(Y,G_q)\). It is finite. By (M.2), \(Q_q\), and therefore \(\mathcal H^qC\), is constructible. This proves the assertion.

M.4. The ordinary direct-image theorem

Theorem. For every separated finite-type morphism \(f:X\to Y\) over a field, \(Rf_*\) takes \(D^b_c(X,\Lambda)\) to \(D^b_c(Y,\Lambda)\).

By M.1, we may work over algebraically closed fields, and boundedness is already known. It is enough to treat a constructible sheaf, then use its cohomology triangles. Induct on \(\dim X\), over all algebraically closed fields simultaneously. Dimension zero follows from exact finite direct image: a zero-dimensional finite-type source is finite over the field, and its morphism to the separated target is finite, by its closed graph. Reduction and nilpotent thickenings do not change the étale site.

At dimension \(d>0\), first let \(j:V\to W\) be an open immersion, with \(V\) smooth and \(L\) finite lisse on \(V\). Discard the part of \(W\) outside the closure of \(V\), using exact closed direct image. Localize \(W\) to an affine open. Its projective closure \(\bar W\) has the same dimension; \(V\) remains open in it. It suffices to prove constructibility of \(Rj_*L\) on this proper closure.

Cover \(\bar W\) by affine coordinate charts. Over each coordinate geometric generic point the source has dimension at most \(d-1\), by M.1. The base change from the coordinate line to \(k(t_i)^{\mathrm{sep}}\) is an affine inverse limit of étale changes of base: finite separable extensions spread to finite étale covers after removing finitely many points. Étale localization and AL.4, followed by purely inseparable topological invariance, identify

\[ (Rj_*L)|_{\bar W_{\bar\eta_i}} =Rj_{\bar\eta_i*}(L|_{V_{\bar\eta_i}}). \tag{M.5} \]

Induction makes the right side bounded constructible. Its source need not be smooth over the new field; the induction statement covers all sources.

The other hypothesis of M.3 is global finiteness. Write \(V\) as the finite disjoint union of its smooth pure-dimensional components. On a component of dimension \(e\), Proposition 3.3 and the internal-Hom adjunction give

\[ R\Gamma(V,L) =R\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda} \bigl(R\Gamma_c(V,L^\vee(e)[2e]),\Lambda\bigr). \tag{M.6} \]

Indeed the dual of the lisse sheaf \(L^\vee(e)[2e]\) is \(L\). The finite-module argument at the start of M.6 proves self-injectivity and evaluation independently of any geometry; the finite-free resolution calculation in M.5 sheafifies it with the actual pairing. This step does not assume that \(L\) is free or has finite projective dimension, and does not use singular biduality. Compact-support finiteness proves finiteness of the right side. Also \(R\Gamma(\bar W,Rj_*L)=R\Gamma(V,L)\). Apply M.3 with (M.5). This proves the open-immersion assertion for smooth lisse source in dimension \(d\).

Next let \(f:V\to Y\) have smooth source and lisse coefficient sheaf. On an affine target cover \(V\) by finitely many affine opens. Their intersections are affine. For each such affine source, a closed embedding into affine space over the affine target and projective closure of its graph factor the map as

\[ V\xrightarrow{j}\bar V\xrightarrow{p}Y, \qquad j\text{ open},\quad p\text{ projective},\quad \dim\bar V=\dim V. \tag{M.7} \]

The open case just proved makes \(Rj_*L\) constructible; Proposition 3.2 makes \(Rp_*Rj_*L\) constructible. The finite Čech-to-derived-image sequence for the affine cover proves the assertion for the whole smooth source. This sequence is for ordinary images of the intersections; it does not replace them by extensions by zero.

Finally take any reduced \(X\) of dimension \(d\) and constructible \(F\). Choose the smooth dense open \(v:V\to X\) from M.1, with \(F|_V\) lisse, and let \(i:T\to X\) be its lower-dimensional complement. The cone

\[ F\longrightarrow Rv_*(F|_V)\longrightarrow C\longrightarrow F[1] \tag{M.8} \]

is bounded constructible by the smooth-open case already proved at this same dimension. Its restriction to \(V\) is zero. The localization triangle identifies \(C=i_*i^*C\); it is a bounded constructible complex on the smaller-dimensional \(T\). Induction makes \(Rf_*C\) constructible. The smooth-source case makes \(R(fv)_*(F|_V)\) constructible. Apply \(Rf_*\) to (M.8) to obtain the assertion for \(F\). This ordering is essential: constructibility of the cone is established before induction is applied to it. Field descent from M.1 completes the theorem. \(\square\)

M.5. Constructible duals before biduality

Put \(\omega_X=a_X^!\Lambda\) and \(D_XF=R\mathcal Hom(F,\omega_X)\). BF–BJ construct the operations and the specified smooth trace. We prove the restriction comparisons before using biduality.

Finite resolutions and restriction. A constructible sheaf \(F\) has a resolution \(P^\bullet\to F\), in degrees at most zero, whose terms are finite sums of \(u_!\Lambda\) with \(u\) affine étale of finite presentation. Indeed, the finite presentation in the constructible-sheaf companion gives a finite generating surjection. Its kernel is constructible by that companion's Noetherian subobject proof, so the same construction applies to the kernel. Repetition gives the asserted exact resolution; it need not have finite length.

For a bounded-below complex \(B\),

\[ R\mathcal Hom(u_!\Lambda,B)=Ru_*u^*B. \tag{M.9} \]

This is an equality of the canonical adjunction maps. On an étale test object, extension by zero, tensor-Hom adjunction and \(u_!\dashv u^*\) give the same Hom functor. To compute it, choose a bounded-below injective resolution of \(B\). Restriction to any étale object preserves injectives, since its left adjoint, extension by zero, is exact. Thus the sheaf Hom calculation on those test objects is the derived one, and its right side is the stated ordinary direct image.

The same observation computes \(R\mathcal Hom(F,B)\) by the total Hom complex from \(P^\bullet\) into a bounded-below injective resolution of \(B\). To justify replacing \(F\), restrict to any étale object. Hom into each injective is exact, and the augmented resolution is exact. If the target resolution starts in degree \(b\), its Hom double complex has indices \(r=-\deg P\geq0\) and \(s\geq b\), with total degree \(r+s\). Every diagonal is finite. The augmented exact rows therefore give the required quasi-isomorphism. Equivalently, finite truncations stabilize in each degree; no infinite product must commute with a pullback.

Let \(q\) be induced by an étale change of a parameter base, or an affine inverse limit of such changes. Pullback takes the displayed resolution to a resolution of \(q^*F\), with terms \(u'_!\Lambda\). For each term, AL.4's ordinary-image comparison gives \(q^*Ru_*u^*B\simeq Ru'_*u'^*q^*B\). These termwise comparisons are compatible with the resolution differential, since they are adjunction mates. Their resolution spectral sequences have terms \(R^su_*u^*B\) in bidegrees \((r,s)\) with \(r\geq0\), \(s\geq b\). They are bounded below and have only finitely many terms in each total degree. Exact pullback preserves the filtration and its associated cohomology sequences. Comparing its successive finite pieces, degree by degree, proves

\[ q^*R\mathcal Hom(F,B) \xrightarrow{\sim}R\mathcal Hom(q^*F,q^*B). \tag{M.10} \]

The map here is the transpose of pulled-back evaluation, under the tensor comparison of BH. It is the map just computed on (M.9), not a separately selected isomorphism. Cohomology triangles extend the result to bounded constructible \(F\). An equivalence of étale topoi from a purely inseparable change of field gives the same comparison directly. We retain the bounded-below condition on \(B\); finite generation alone would not justify the infinite resolution against an arbitrary target.

The dualizing complex. Locally embed \(X\) as a closed subscheme \(b:X\to\mathbf A^N_k\). Transitivity and the smooth trace of BJ give

\[ \omega_X=b^!\Lambda(N)[2N]. \tag{M.11} \]

If \(u\) is the complementary open immersion, \(b_*b^!C\) is the fibre of \(C\to Ru_*u^*C\). This is the closed-support localization triangle, with its adjunction unit and counit. Define its closed-support comparison by pulling back the counit \(b_*b^!C\to C\), applying exact closed-image base change, and transposing through \(b'_*\dashv b'^!\). Naturality gives a map of the localization triangles. AL.4 identifies the pullback of the open direct-image term with its counterpart upstairs, and the middle term is exact pullback of \(C\). The cohomology sequences therefore prove that the closed-support comparison is an isomorphism. This construction specifies its counit; it does not choose functorial cones in an abstract triangulated category.

The lower bound of (M.11) follows from this fibre construction. Its upper bound follows from the relative bound on \(Ru_*\) in M.1. Both are local bounds, and a finite affine cover gives bounds on \(\omega_X\) itself. This establishes boundedness before constructibility of \(\omega_X\) or its duals is asserted.

A separable algebraic field extension is an affine inverse limit of finite étale field extensions. The preceding closed-support comparison and (M.11) therefore identify its pullback of \(\omega_X\) with the structural dualizing complex upstairs: the ambient dimension and Tate orientation are unchanged, by BJ. Purely inseparable algebraic extension is an equivalence of the relevant étale topoi and gives the same identification. Combining with (M.10), duals commute with extension to an algebraic closure. Since (M.10) is induced by evaluation and the closed-support map preserves the counit, these comparisons also preserve the dual evaluation maps. A general separable field extension would additionally use full smooth base change; it is not needed for this reduction.

Lisse coefficients without a projective-dimension assumption. The coefficient argument at the start of M.6 proves that \(\Lambda\) is injective as a module over itself and that finite-module evaluation is biduality. If \(M\) is a finite \(\Lambda\)-module, choose a resolution by finite free modules in nonpositive degrees: kernels are finite, so finitely many generators suffice at every step. On a trivializing étale open, its constant-sheaf version is exact on stalks. The same finite-diagonal calculation as above computes internal derived Hom into \(\Lambda\) by the sheafified module Hom complex. Its positive cohomology vanishes by self-injectivity, and its degree zero is the constant sheaf \(M^\vee\). Evaluation is the sheafification of module evaluation, because the comparison uses the Hom evaluation pairing throughout. Thus for a finite lisse \(L\) on a smooth pure \(e\)-dimensional scheme, \(D_VL=L^\vee(e)[2e]\), with its canonical pairing. The resolution may be infinite; no finite Tor dimension has been assumed.

We can now establish bounded constructibility of \(D_XF\). Work over an algebraically closed field, then descend by the comparison just proved and constructibility detection in M.1. Induct on dimension, choosing a smooth dense open \(v:V\to X\), with \(F|_V\) lisse, and complementary closed immersion \(i:T\to X\). Tensor-Hom adjunction, the projection formula and transitivity give

\[ D_Xv_!L=Rv_*D_VL,\qquad D_Xi_*A=i_*D_TA. \tag{M.12} \]

For example, testing the first identity against \(E\) replaces \(E\otimes^Lv_!L\) by \(v_!(v^*E\otimes^LL)\); transpose its map to \(\omega_X\) through \(v_!\dashv v^*\). The result is Hom from \(E\) to \(Rv_*R\mathcal Hom(L,v^*\omega_X)\), and \(v^*\omega_X=\omega_V\). For the second, use the exact proper image \(i_*\), its projection formula and \(i^!\omega_X=\omega_T\). These are the evaluation-and-counit isomorphisms. No double dual is used in their construction.

The lisse calculation and Theorem M.4 make the open term of (M.12) bounded constructible. Induction handles the smaller-dimensional closed term. Apply \(D_X\) to the triangle \(v_!F|_V\to F\to i_*i^*F\), and then use the finite cohomology filtration for a bounded constructible complex. This proves preservation of \(D^b_c\) before asserting biduality. The use of M.4 is not circular: its smooth-source step needs only the independent finite-module calculation and the smooth trace, not singular biduality.

Generic restriction and evaluation. On an affine \(X\subset\mathbf A^N_k\), let \(t\) be an ambient coordinate and let \(q:X_{\bar\eta}\to X\) be its geometric generic fibre. A finite separable extension of \(k(t)\) spreads to a finite étale cover of a nonempty open of the coordinate line: clear coefficients of a separable defining polynomial and invert its discriminant. These charts form the required affine inverse system. Purely inseparable extension then gives the algebraic closure. Thus the comparisons above apply to this \(q\).

The new ambient scheme is \(\mathbf A^{N-1}_{\overline{k(t)}}\). Pull back (M.11) using the closed-support comparison. Its twist is still \((N)[2N]\), whereas structural duality over the new field uses \((N-1)[2N-2]\). The invertible-twist comparison (BH.21) therefore gives exactly

\[ q^*\omega_X=\omega_{X_{\bar\eta}}(1)[2],\qquad q^*D_XF=D_{\bar\eta}(q^*F)(1)[2]. \tag{M.13} \]

To track double evaluation, write \(T=\Lambda(1)[2]\) on the fibre. Internal Hom sends tensor with this invertible object in its first argument to tensor with \(T^{-1}\). Consequently two applications of (M.13) identify the pulled-back double dual with \(D_{\bar\eta}D_{\bar\eta}(q^*F)\otimes T^{-1}\otimes T\), followed by the evaluation \(T^{-1}\otimes T\to\Lambda\). Under this identification the pulled-back map \(F\to D_XD_XF\) is canonical double evaluation on the fibre. Indeed the first comparison is adjoint to evaluation; apply that identity twice and the tensor-Hom triangle identities cancel the two inverse-line maps. The shift in \(T\) is even, so moving these line factors creates no extra sign. This checks the actual map needed in the dimension induction, not merely its source and target objects.

M.6. Singular constructible biduality

We first supply the coefficient calculation, including its extension step. Put \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\). Suppose \(A\subset B\) are \(\Lambda\)-modules and \(h:A\to\Lambda\) is linear. For \(b\in B\), the scalars \(r\) with \(rb\in A\) form an ideal \(I=d\Lambda\), with \(d\mid n\). Indeed the inverse image of \(I\) in \(\mathbf Z\) is an ideal containing \(n\mathbf Z\); division by its least positive element gives this description. Write \(a=h(db)\). The relation \((n/d)db=0\) implies \((n/d)a=0\), so \(a=dc\) in \(\Lambda\) for some \(c\). Define \[ \widetilde h(x+rb)=h(x)+rc\qquad(x\in A,\ r\in\Lambda). \] This is well defined: if \(tb\in A\), write \(t=ds\); then \(h(tb)=sa=tc\). Thus every partial extension extends across one more generator. Order partial extensions by inclusion; their union along a chain is a partial extension. The maximality principle therefore gives an extension to all of \(B\). This proves that \(\Lambda\) is injective and that \(M\mapsto M^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(M,\Lambda)\) is exact.

For a finite module, duality also preserves cardinality and separates points. A cyclic subgroup \(C\) of order \(d\mid n\) has exactly \(d\) homomorphisms to \(\Lambda\), since the image of its generator is an element annihilated by \(d\). Sending that generator to \(n/d\) embeds \(C\) in \(\Lambda\); the extension just proved supplies a functional on the entire module which is nonzero at any specified nonzero element of \(C\). For \(0\ne C\subset M\), exactness gives \[ 0\longrightarrow(M/C)^\vee\longrightarrow M^\vee \longrightarrow C^\vee\longrightarrow0. \] Induction on \(|M|\) yields \(|M^\vee|=|M|\), including the zero module as the starting case. Evaluation \(M\to M^{\vee\vee}\) is injective by separation and surjective by this equality applied twice.

Exactness of duality applied to the cycle and boundary sequences of any complex gives \[ H^i\!\left(R\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(A,\Lambda)\right) =\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(H^{-i}(A),\Lambda). \] Here ordinary Hom into the injective module computes derived Hom: it sends acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes by those same sequences. Therefore canonical double evaluation is an isomorphism for every complex with finite cohomology modules. In particular it applies to a bounded complex with finite cohomology; neither a free resolution of finite length nor a classification of finite abelian groups is needed.

Theorem. For every \(K\in D^b_c(X,\mathbf Z/n)\), the canonical evaluation

\[ K\longrightarrow D_XD_XK \tag{M.14} \]

is an isomorphism, without a finite-Tor-dimension assumption on \(K\).

Over an algebraically closed field, first consider proper \(X\). The internal-Hom adjunction and its trace identify

\[ R\Gamma(X,D_XK) =R\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(R\Gamma(X,K),\Lambda). \tag{M.15} \]

We specify both this isomorphism and its evaluation compatibility. For any \(V\in D(\Lambda)\), tensor-Hom adjunction, \(Ra_{X!}\dashv a_X^!\) and the projection formula identify \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}(V,R\Gamma D_XK) &=\operatorname{Hom}(a_X^*V\otimes^LK,a_X^!\Lambda)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(V\otimes^LR\Gamma_c K,\Lambda). \end{aligned} \tag{M.15a} \] Yoneda gives (M.15), because compact and ordinary supports agree on this proper scheme. Write its map as \(\Phi_K:T(D_XK)\to(TK)^\vee\), where \(T=R\Gamma(X,-)\) and \(V^\vee=R\operatorname{Hom}_\Lambda(V,\Lambda)\). Its pairing is cup product, evaluation into \(\omega_X\), and the trace \(T\omega_X\to\Lambda\), in that order.

Let \(\eta\) denote canonical double evaluation. Then \(\Phi_{D_XK}\,T(\eta_K)=\Phi_K^\vee\,\eta_{TK}\). To check this equality, transpose both sides to pairings with \(T(D_XK)\). The defining identity for \(\eta_K\) says that evaluation of \(D_XK\) against \(\eta_K(K)\) is evaluation of \(K\) against \(D_XK\), after the tensor symmetry. Naturality and symmetry of cup product give the same identity after \(T\); composing with the same trace preserves it. The module evaluation on the right uses that same tensor symmetry, so the Koszul sign agrees. This proves equality of the maps in the derived category.

Proper finiteness makes \(TK\) bounded with finite cohomology. The coefficient calculation above makes \(\eta_{TK}\) an isomorphism, and both \(\Phi\)'s are the adjunction isomorphisms just proved. Therefore \(T(\eta_K)\) is an isomorphism. Thus the cone \(\Delta_K\) of (M.14) satisfies

\[ R\Gamma(X,\Delta_K)=0. \tag{M.16} \]

Induct on \(\dim X\), simultaneously over all algebraically closed fields. Dimension zero is finite-module biduality on finitely many points. Suppose the assertion proved below dimension \(d\). On every affine coordinate chart of a proper \(d\)-dimensional \(X\), the coordinate geometric generic fibres have dimension at most \(d-1\). By (M.13) and induction, \(\Delta_K\) restricts to zero on each such fibre. M.5 has already proved that its cohomology sheaves are bounded constructible. The coordinate argument of M.2 shows that they are supported on closed points, and constructibility makes that support finite. Formula (M.2) now identifies

\[ H^r(X,\Delta_K)=\Gamma(X,\mathcal H^r\Delta_K). \tag{M.17} \]

Each finite-support sheaf is detected by its global sections. Equations (M.16)–(M.17) force every \(\mathcal H^r\Delta_K\) to be zero. This proves biduality on all proper schemes of dimension \(d\).

For a general \(X\), the assertion is local on affine opens: restriction commutes with duality by (M.10)–(M.11). Embed an affine open into its projective closure of the same dimension and extend \(K\) by zero. That extension is bounded constructible; the proper case just proved applies to it. Restrict its evaluation isomorphism back to the open. This proves the induction step for every \(X\). Finally the field-extension comparisons of M.5 and conservativity descend the canonical isomorphism to arbitrary \(k\). \(\square\)

The finite-support step is why vanishing of global sections suffices here. It would be false to infer an arbitrary constructible complex is zero merely from vanishing of its global cohomology.

M.7. Exchanges, coefficients and the remaining foundations

The internal-Hom adjunction and transitivity give, before biduality,

\[ D_YRf_!K=Rf_*D_XK,\qquad D_Xf^*A=f^!D_YA. \tag{M.18} \]

Here are the two tests, which also specify the maps. Test the first identity against \(E\in D(Y,\Lambda)\). Tensor-Hom adjunction turns its left side into \(\operatorname{Hom}(E\otimes^LRf_!K,\omega_Y)\). The projection formula and the exceptional adjunction turn this into \(\operatorname{Hom}(f^*E\otimes^LK,f^!\omega_Y)\). Transitivity identifies \(f^!\omega_Y=\omega_X\); tensor-Hom and \(f^*\dashv Rf_*\) give \(\operatorname{Hom}(E,Rf_*D_XK)\). For the second identity, test against \(E\in D(X,\Lambda)\) and use \(\operatorname{Hom}(E,f^!D_YA)=\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!E\otimes^LA,\omega_Y)=\operatorname{Hom}(E,D_Xf^*A)\). Every equality is natural in the test object, so Yoneda proves (M.18). Each chain transposes evaluation through the projection formula and the composed counit. It consequently identifies the same double-evaluation maps used in M.6, rather than only producing isomorphic objects. M.4–M.6 and Proposition 3.2 show that all the objects needed to apply biduality are bounded constructible. Replace \(K\) by \(D_XK\) in the first identity, then dualize, to obtain

\[ D_YRf_*K=Rf_!D_XK, \qquad f^!A=D_Xf^*D_YA. \tag{M.19} \]

In particular \(f^!\) preserves bounded constructibility. For a closed geometric point over an algebraically closed field, the closed-immersion form of (M.18)–(M.19) proves both point exchanges in (2.1), with finite-module dual over \(\mathbf Z/n\). Over an arbitrary field they are the corresponding geometric closed-point statements, by separable extension and topological invariance. These untwisted point formulas concern closed points; generic restriction instead has the dimension correction explicitly displayed in (M.13).

The same arguments prove M.5–M.6 over every finite coefficient field: finite-dimensional linear duality replaces the self-injective \(\mathbf Z/n\)-module calculation; all geometric finiteness and comparison inputs hold for its underlying finite torsion sheaves. With these coefficients, tensor and internal Hom also preserve bounded constructibility. For tensor, use exact tensor on stalks and a common constructible partition; bounded complexes have a finite cohomology filtration. For internal Hom use the adjunction identity

\[ R\mathcal Hom(K,L)=D_X(K\otimes^L D_XL), \tag{M.20} \]

proved by tensor-Hom adjunction and (M.14). The tensor on the right is now bounded constructible, so its dual is too. Over \(\mathbf Z/\ell^r\) with \(r>1\), this bounded tensor/internal-Hom conclusion requires a finite-Tor-dimension hypothesis on the first argument. It is not needed for (M.14): a finite module can have infinite projective dimension while its dual against the self-injective ring is exact. This distinguishes the two coefficient claims.

Thus ordinary finite-coefficient direct-image finiteness, preservation by structural duality, singular biduality and the dual exchanges over fields have written arguments here. They do not establish the normalized adic operations or their rationalization comparisons. The inputs of Propositions 3.2–3.3 include compactification and curve completion, curve finiteness and duality, étale cohomological continuity and dimension bounds, and the categorical exceptional adjoint. This field argument does not imply generic local acyclicity over a trait or absolute purity for arbitrary regular schemes.

Appendix N. Finite monodromy, compatible lattices and congruence covers

The arithmetic arguments use two different kinds of finiteness. A finite local system is trivialized by one finite étale cover. A lisse adic system generally is not: each finite reduction has such a cover, but the covers may grow with the reduction level. We construct the relevant monodromy equivalences and then obtain the single congruence cover needed to remove wild prime-to-\(\ell\) monodromy.

Throughout this appendix \(X\) is connected and Noetherian, with a geometric point \(\bar x\). In its application to this lesson, \(X\) is a connected stratum of a finite-type scheme over a field. All finite covers below are étale. We use the elementary affine description of such covers as finite locally free algebras with vanishing relative differentials. The effective descent and fundamental-group equivalence used below are proved here, rather than imported as citations to the corresponding general theorems.

N.1. Descend a finite algebra before naming its monodromy

First we give the affine descent calculation. Let \(A\to B\) be faithfully flat and let \(M\) be a \(B\)-module with a descent isomorphism \[ \theta:M\otimes_A B\longrightarrow B\otimes_A M \tag{N.1} \] over \(B\otimes_A B\), satisfying the cocycle identity over three factors. Put \(\delta(m)=\theta(m\otimes1)\). If \(\delta(m)=\sum b_i\otimes m_i\), the cocycle and diagonal identities say \[ \sum b_i\otimes\delta(m_i)=\sum b_i\otimes1\otimes m_i, \qquad \sum b_i m_i=m. \tag{N.2} \] Indeed the two sides of the first identity apply the overlap isomorphism twice or once to \(m\otimes1\otimes1\); pulling the cocycle to the diagonal makes its invertible restriction idempotent, hence the identity. Also \(\delta(bm)=(b\otimes1)\delta(m)\).

Let \(N=\{m\in M:\delta(m)=1\otimes m\}\). Flatness identifies \(B\otimes_A N\) with the equalizer of the two maps from \(B\otimes_A M\) to \(B\otimes_A B\otimes_A M\) in (N.2). Thus \(\delta\) takes values in \(B\otimes_A N\). It is inverse to multiplication \[ B\otimes_A N\longrightarrow M,\qquad b\otimes n\longmapsto bn. \tag{N.3} \] One composition is the second identity of (N.2); the other uses \(\delta(bn)=b\otimes n\). A map respecting descent data preserves these equalizers, so the construction also descends every compatible module map, uniquely.

For completeness, starting with an \(A\)-module \(Q\) recovers exactly \(Q\) from \(B\otimes_A Q\). The equalizer sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow B\otimes_A Q \rightrightarrows B\otimes_A B\otimes_A Q \tag{N.4} \] is exact: after tensoring with \(B\), multiplication of the added factor with the first displayed factor contracts the augmented alternating complex. Inserting a unit in the first position gives the identity; all other insertions cancel in adjacent pairs. Flat tensor preserves its cohomology, and faithful flatness detects zero cohomology. This proves (N.4), including injectivity, before descent is used.

If \(M\) is a \(B\)-algebra and \(\theta\) respects its multiplication and unit, then \(N\) is an \(A\)-algebra and (N.3) is an algebra isomorphism. Suppose \(A\) is Noetherian and \(M\) is finite locally free over \(B\). Express a finite set of \(B\)-generators through (N.3). The finitely many elements of \(N\) occurring in those expressions generate \(N\): their cokernel vanishes after the faithfully flat base change. Thus \(N\) is finite and finitely presented over \(A\). It is flat, since injectivity after tensoring any injection with \(N\) can be tested after \(B\), where it is flatness of \(M\). It is therefore locally free. Explicitly, over a local ring choose lifts of a residue-field basis of \(N\). Nakayama gives a surjection from a finite free module; flatness makes its kernel zero modulo the maximal ideal, and finite generation plus Nakayama makes the kernel zero. This also proves the asserted local freeness.

If \(M\) is finite étale, then \(\Omega_{N/A}\otimes_A B=\Omega_{M/B}=0\); the equality follows from the universal property of differentials. Faithfulness gives \(\Omega_{N/A}=0\), so the descended finite locally free algebra is étale. The construction commutes with localizations, since flat localization preserves the defining equalizer. It therefore glues over affine opens, and its uniqueness makes the overlap identifications and all cocycles agree.

Now let \(\mathcal F\) be a finite locally constant set sheaf on \(X_{\mathrm{ét}}\). On an affine base open choose finitely many affine members of a trivializing étale cover; this is possible because étale maps are open and the base is quasi-compact. Their disjoint union is a faithfully flat affine cover. The finite constant sheaves there are represented by disjoint unions of copies of the cover. Their transition identifications give descent data on the finite product algebras, and the calculation above descends those algebras and their maps. Gluing the affine answers proves that \(\mathcal F\) is represented by a finite étale \(X\)-scheme. Conversely, the ordering cover of a finite étale scheme trivializes its represented sheaf, as constructed next. The same calculation on maps proves an equivalence, not merely existence of a representative.

N.2. Pointed ordering covers supply the finite quotients

Let \(Y\to X\) be a nonempty finite étale cover, of constant degree \(d\). Inside \(Y^d_X\), remove every pairwise diagonal. Each diagonal is open because the map is étale, and closed because it is finite and separated. The resulting ordering cover \(P\to X\) is finite étale; its geometric fibres are the orderings of a \(d\)-element set. Its tautological sections split \(Y_P\) into \(d\) copies of \(P\). A morphism between finite étale covers which is bijective on all geometric fibres is an isomorphism: on affine bases this is the map between finite locally free modules, checked after each residue field and then by the local basis criterion.

Choose an ordering above \(\bar x\), and take its connected component \(P_0\). Noetherianity makes the finitely many connected components open and closed. Each component of a nonempty finite étale cover maps onto the connected base: its image is both open and closed. The permutation group on \(d\) letters acts simply transitively on every fibre of \(P\). The stabilizer of \(P_0\) therefore acts simply transitively on every geometric fibre of \(P_0\). Indeed, the unique permutation carrying two fibre points to each other carries their connected components to each other. It follows that \[ \coprod_{a\in G_P}P_0\longrightarrow P_0\times_X P_0, \qquad z\longmapsto(z,a(z)) \tag{N.5} \] is an isomorphism, where \(G_P=\operatorname{Aut}_X(P_0)\). There are no additional automorphisms: two maps from a connected cover to an étale separated cover agreeing at one geometric point agree everywhere. Their equalizer is open and closed. Thus an automorphism is determined by its value at the chosen point.

Call a connected pointed cover with (N.5) a pointed Galois cover. Every pointed finite cover is dominated by one: use its ordering cover, with the specified point in the first position. Two pointed Galois covers have a common such refinement by taking the component containing the chosen pair in their fibre product. The product of their deck groups acts on that product; the stabilizer of the component is again simply transitive on its fibres, proving (N.5) for the refinement. Pointed maps are unique by the equalizer argument.

For a pointed map \(r:Q\to P\), every \(b\in G_Q\) determines a unique \(a\in G_P\) with \(rb=ar\): choose \(a\) to give the same value at the distinguished point, and then use the same equalizer argument. This defines a surjective group homomorphism \(G_Q\to G_P\). Surjectivity follows because \(r\) is a nonempty finite étale map to a connected cover, so is onto on every geometric fibre, and \(G_Q\) acts transitively there.

Define the profinite group \[ \Pi=\varprojlim_{(P,\bar p)}G_P. \tag{N.6} \] Every projection to \(G_P\) is onto. To lift a prescribed element, any finite collection of compatibility conditions can be solved in a common dominating cover, using the surjective homomorphisms just proved. The corresponding closed subsets of the product of the finite groups have the finite-intersection property, so compactness gives a compatible family. The same argument gives compactness of the inverse limit. Kernels of these projections form a neighbourhood basis at the identity; common refinements account for finite intersections.

N.3. The fibre functor and all of its morphisms

If \(P\) trivializes \(Y\), evaluation at its distinguished point gives a bijection \[ \operatorname{Hom}_X(P,Y)\longrightarrow Y_{\bar x}. \tag{N.7} \] A map is a section of \(Y_P\), and on connected \(P\) such a section chooses exactly one of its constant sheets. Give the left side the left \(G_P\)-action \(a\cdot h=h\circ a^{-1}\). The inverse is essential: it makes \(a\cdot(b\cdot h)=(ab)\cdot h\). Refinements respect this action, because \(rb=ar\). Equation (N.7) thus gives a well-defined continuous \(\Pi\)-action on every finite fibre, natural in \(Y\).

Conversely, a finite continuous \(\Pi\)-set \(S\) factors through some \(G_P\). The kernel of its finite permutation action is open and therefore contains one projection kernel; surjectivity of the projection makes the factorization well-defined. On \(P\times S\), let a deck transformation act by \[ a(z,s)=(a(z),a\cdot s). \tag{N.8} \] The torsor identity (N.5) turns this action into a descent datum on the disjoint union of copies of \(P\). N.1 descends it to a finite étale \(X\)-scheme. At the distinguished point, its fibre is \(S\), with the prescribed action: the section labelled \(s\), evaluated at \(a^{-1}\bar p\), is identified by (N.8) with the label \(a\cdot s\) at \(\bar p\).

Two covers are split by a common pointed Galois cover. A map of their fibres is \(\Pi\)-equivariant exactly when it is equivariant for that finite deck group. Such a map between the constant sheets respects their descent data, so N.1 gives a unique map of covers. We have proved full faithfulness and essential surjectivity of the fibre functor.

Finally \(\Pi\) is the automorphism group of that functor, not merely a group producing an equivalent category. A natural automorphism of the forgetful functor on finite \(\Pi\)-sets is determined on every regular quotient \(G_P\). It commutes with the equivariant right translations, so is left translation by a unique element of \(G_P\). Naturality for quotient maps makes these elements compatible. Conversely, their compatible family acts naturally on every finite set. The topology also agrees, since finite fibres define both neighbourhood bases. Thus \(\Pi=\pi_1(X,\bar x)\).

Finite products are preserved by fibre evaluation. Consequently group laws, module operations over a finite ring and all their identities descend through this equivalence. This proves the finite locally constant module/continuous finite-module correspondence, including morphisms, tensor products and quotient modules. Pullback is compatible as well: pulling back finite covers commutes with their geometric fibres and hence induces the corresponding continuous homomorphism of fibre-automorphism groups.

N.4. Recover the integral module from every finite level

Let \(\mathcal O\) be a complete discrete valuation ring with uniformizer \(\varpi\) and finite residue field \(\kappa\). This includes the ring of integers of every finite extension of \(\mathbb Q_\ell\), as well as complete discrete valuation rings of equal characteristic. Each quotient \(\mathcal O/\varpi^n\) is finite: its power filtration has \(n\) successive quotients isomorphic to \(\kappa\), via multiplication by \(\varpi^i\) in the \(i\)-th layer. A strict lisse \(\mathcal O\)-system consists of finite locally constant \(\mathcal O/\varpi^n\)-module sheaves \(\mathcal F_n\) whose transition maps identify the quotient of level \(n+1\) by \(\varpi^n\) with level \(n\). Set \(M_n=(\mathcal F_n)_{\bar x}\).

The transition maps are onto. In \(M=\varprojlim M_n\), projection to each \(M_n\) is onto by successive lifts. Its kernel equals \(\varpi^nM\). For the nontrivial inclusion, a compatible element vanishing at level \(n\) is divisible by \(\varpi^n\) at every later level. The finite sets of possible divisors have compatible choices: any finite collection of conditions is solved by choosing a divisor at the largest index and reducing. Compactness of these finite sets gives a compatible divisor. Therefore \[ M/\varpi^nM=M_n. \tag{N.9} \] Lift a finite generating set of \(M_1\) to \(M\). Successively approximate an arbitrary element modulo \(\varpi\), divide the error and repeat. Completeness makes the resulting coefficients converge in \(\mathcal O\), so the lifts generate \(M\). Alternatively their span is dense and is the compact, hence closed, image of a finite power of \(\mathcal O\). Thus \(M\) is finite, and (N.9) identifies its adic and inverse-limit topologies.

Here are the module facts needed for the converse. Every submodule \(A\subset\mathcal O^r\) is finite free. Induct on \(r\), starting with zero. Project onto the first coordinate. If its image is zero, apply induction inside \(\mathcal O^{r-1}\). Otherwise that image contains an element of least valuation \(a\), so it is \(\varpi^a\mathcal O\). Choose \(v\in A\) whose first coordinate is \(\varpi^a\), multiplying by a unit if necessary. Subtracting the appropriate multiple of \(v\) from any element gives \[ A=\mathcal O v\oplus\bigl(A\cap(0\oplus\mathcal O^{r-1})\bigr). \] Induction proves the assertion. A finite torsion-free module embeds in its finite-dimensional fraction space: a vector killed by localization is annihilated by a nonzero scalar. Choose a basis of that space and clear the denominators of finitely many module generators. This embeds the module in a finite free module, so the same argument proves it free.

Every finite \(\mathcal O\)-module \(T\), including one with torsion, is complete and separated. To see this without assuming freeness of \(T\), present it as \(\mathcal O^r/A\). The submodule calculation just proved gives finitely many generators of \(A\). Thus \(A\) is the image of a continuous map from some \(\mathcal O^s\). Since \(\mathcal O\) is complete with finite residue field, it is the compact Hausdorff inverse limit of its finite quotients. Consequently \(A\) is compact and closed, and \(T\) is compact Hausdorff. The images \(\varpi^nT\) are exactly a neighbourhood basis of zero for this quotient topology. Their intersection is zero, and any compatible family of cosets has a common point by compactness. Hence \(T\to\varprojlim T/\varpi^nT\) is an isomorphism of topological modules.

N.3 gives compatible continuous group actions on all \(M_n\); they define a continuous action on \(M\). Conversely a continuous action on a finite \(\mathcal O\)-module gives actions on its finite quotients, and N.3 constructs a strict lisse system. The preceding completeness argument recovers the original module. Every \(\mathcal O\)-linear map of finite modules is continuous, since it preserves their \(\varpi\)-adic filtrations. It is equivariant exactly when all its reductions are. Full faithfulness at every finite level and (N.9) prove that these constructions are inverse on objects and morphisms. In particular, systems whose inverse-limit stalk is torsion free correspond to finite free \(\mathcal O\)-modules.

N.5. Rational coefficients and the one congruence cover

Let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional continuous \(E\)-representation of the profinite group \(\pi_1(X,\bar x)\). Its image is compact. Choose a lattice \(L_0\subset V\). The matrix entries of a compact set are bounded, so all translates of \(L_0\) lie in \(\varpi^{-c}L_0\) for one integer \(c\). Their \(\mathcal O\)-span \(L\) contains \(L_0\), lies in that finite free module, and is invariant under the group. The coordinate submodule calculation in N.4 proves that \(L\) is finite free; since it contains \(L_0\), it spans \(V\). It is therefore a stable lattice, and N.4 constructs its strict lisse system.

Any two lattices in \(V\) lie between bounded powers of each other: write either basis in the other basis and bound the finitely many denominators. Likewise any equivariant \(E\)-linear map becomes an equivariant integral map after multiplication by a sufficiently large power of \(\varpi\). It follows that rationalization is fully faithful and independent of the lattice: \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{lisse},E}(L_E,L'_E) =\operatorname{Hom}_{\pi_1,\mathcal O}(L,L')\otimes_{\mathcal O}E. \tag{N.10} \] Consequently strict lisse systems, after inverting \(\varpi\), classify exactly finite-dimensional continuous \(E\)-representations. Kernels and cokernels of their maps are continuous representations, and their invariant subspaces have stable lattices by the same argument. This is the global-lattice coefficient category. A \(\overline{\mathbb Q}_\ell\)-object here is obtained by scalar extension from some finite \(E\), as in Section 3; no assertion about arbitrary representations over an infinite coefficient extension is needed.

Reduce the stable lattice representation modulo \(\varpi\). Its kernel is an open normal subgroup of the fundamental group and hence corresponds, by N.3, to a connected finite étale cover \(p:Y\to X\). More explicitly the finite image gives the regular transitive quotient set, whose descended cover is connected; a decomposition of a finite cover would be an invariant partition into the fibres of its open and closed components.

The diagonal section of the pulled-back cover shows that \(\pi_1(Y)\) fixes the chosen point of this regular finite quotient. Its stabilizer is the reduction kernel, so the reduced representation on \(Y\) is trivial. Thus on \(Y\) the image lies in \(1+\varpi M_r(\mathcal O)\). This is a pro-\(\ell\) group. Its successive congruence quotients inject into the additive group \(M_r(\mathcal O/\varpi)\), since \[ (1+\varpi^n A)(1+\varpi^n B) \equiv1+\varpi^n(A+B)\pmod{\varpi^{n+1}} \quad(n\ge1). \tag{N.11} \] Each quotient is therefore an \(\ell\)-group, and completeness recovers the congruence group as their inverse limit. A continuous homomorphism from a pro-\(p\) group with \(p\ne\ell\) into it is trivial: its image in every finite congruence quotient is both a \(p\)-group and an \(\ell\)-group. In particular, whenever a boundary's wild inertia has been proved to be pro-\(p\), this one finite cover makes its action trivial. That ramification theorem is a separate geometric prerequisite. The conclusion is not that the entire lisse system becomes constant on the cover; its remaining pro-\(\ell\) image can be infinite.

The construction supplies finite monodromy and strict lisse coefficient foundations. It does not identify the strict rational category with all locally free rational sheaves on the pro-étale site of a singular scheme: the latter may admit lattices only locally. Nor does it prove that arbitrary constructible derived operations preserve the required integral models, commute with normalization, or have the asserted rationalization comparisons. The distinction between strict lisse lattices, constructible integral models and derived rational sheaves is treated in BW–BX. The arguments here use finite étale algebra descent, module descent and geometric-stalk comparison as specified in N.1–N.4.

Appendix O. Complete the generic smooth curve and extend its finite diagram

We prove the precise geometric assertion needed in (3.3). Let \(S\) be a finite-type scheme over a field and \(X\to S\) a smooth affine morphism of relative dimension one. For each generic point \(\eta\) of \(S\), there are an open neighbourhood \(U\), a finite surjective radicial map \(V\to U\), and \[ X_V=\coprod_iY_i\ \subset\ \coprod_iC_i, \qquad C_i\longrightarrow T_i\longrightarrow V, \tag{O.1} \] where \(T_i\to V\) is finite étale, each \(C_i\to T_i\) is smooth proper with geometrically connected one-dimensional fibres, and the complement of \(X_V\) in \(\coprod_iC_i\) is finite over \(V\). Consequently \(Y_i\) is dense in every fibre of \(C_i\to T_i\). An empty generic fibre becomes an empty family after shrinking by the direct localization calculation in AH.3.

AG.1–AG.3 prove finite normalization over every field, including inseparable extensions, with the polynomial normalization of Y.5 and the trace calculation of L.3. L.1 supplies the general normal-local-ring-to-DVR proof; AG.4 proves smoothness at a regular curve point with finite separable residue field. For finite diagrams we use the object, map, equality, open-set and finiteness proofs in Limits of schemes and Noetherian approximation, §§1–4. AH.4 verifies their finite-presentation hypotheses for these particular systems and identifies the exact proofs of the opens, sections, affineness, diagrams and finiteness assertions. O.2 supplies the required smoothness descent by finite standard-smooth charts.

O.1. A proper smooth completion after a finite purely inseparable extension

First let \(K\) be a field and \(X/K\) a smooth affine curve. Choose a closed embedding in affine space and its reduced closure \(Z\) in projective space. AH.2 checks that every component of the closure is a curve and that its boundary is finite. Its intersection with the original affine chart is exactly \(X\), and \(X\) meets every irreducible component densely. AE.2 proves that this closed projective scheme is proper by the graded closed-image calculation.

In characteristic \(p>0\), let \(F=K^{\mathrm{perf}}\), the union in an algebraic closure of all finite purely inseparable extensions of \(K\); in characteristic zero set \(F=K\). The field \(F\) is perfect: in positive characteristic the \(p\)-th root of any of its elements lies in another finite purely inseparable extension of \(K\). AH.1 identifies the underlying space of \(Z_F\) with that of \(Z\), preserving the density of \(X_F\) in every component. Normalize \((Z_F)_{\mathrm{red}}\). AG.1–AG.3 construct this normalization and prove that the resulting map \(C_F\to Z_F\) is finite. AF.1 makes that map proper, so \(C_F\) is proper. Above \(X_F\) it is an isomorphism: Y.6 makes the smooth curve regular, L.1 makes its one-dimensional local rings normal DVRs, and its generic local rings are fields. The localization of integral closure proved in AG.3 therefore leaves this normal open unchanged.

AG.3 makes the normal local rings at closed points of \(C_F\) one-dimensional, and L.1 makes them DVRs. Their residue fields are finite by Y.5 and separable because \(F\) is perfect. AG.4 constructs a smooth chart at each of these points by the split residue-field derivation calculation and the local Jacobian presentation. Its final closed-point argument shows that these charts cover \(C_F\). Thus \(C_F\) is a smooth proper curve containing \(X_F\).

All this data descends to a finite purely inseparable \(K'/K\). Here are the properties that must descend, including smoothness.
