Here are the three checks in every degree. If a middle cycle maps to a boundary on the right, subtract the differential of a lift of that boundary's primitive; the result is a cycle from the left. If \(\delta[c]=0\), write \(a=da_0\); then \(b-a_0\) is a middle cycle lifting \(c\). If a left cycle becomes a middle boundary \(db\), the projection of \(b\) is a right cycle and its connecting class is that left class. Conversely the same formulas show that successive maps have zero composite. The first three terms are ordinary left exactness of sections from T.1. This proves (T.13) without an assumed long exact sequence theorem.

For completeness, compatible comparisons can be chosen for any map between two original short exact sequences. At the initial stage choose extensions on \(I_F^0\) and \(I_H^0\) into the corresponding target injectives \(J_F^0,J_H^0\). The required middle map has block form

\[ \begin{pmatrix}f&t\\0&h\end{pmatrix}: I_F^0\oplus I_H^0\longrightarrow J_F^0\oplus J_H^0. \tag{T.14} \]

On \(G\), the discrepancy between the prescribed first coordinate and \(fu\) vanishes on \(F\); it therefore factors through \(H\). Extend that map from \(H\subset I_H^0\) into the injective \(J_F^0\) to obtain \(t\). The second coordinate already agrees by the chosen extension on \(H\). Thus (T.14) gives a commuting diagram, which induces a map of the quotient sequences (T.10). Repeat at each stage. The resulting comparison is a map of the entire diagram (T.11). Applying it to a lift in (T.12) proves naturality. T.3 shows that all its component maps induce the unique cohomology maps; applying this to the identity original sequence also proves independence of all resolution and extension choices. Restrictions of sections commute with the construction by the same lift formula.

Together, T.1–T.4 and the exact slice adjoint proved in S.2 provide the abelian-sheaf foundations for S.3 and for the long exact divisor sequence used in R.5. They do not establish the additional geometric, unbounded or normalized adic results required elsewhere in the lesson.

Appendix U. Finite cohomology models and divisors in families

Retain the fixed smooth connected projective curve \(C/k\) of Appendix Q, with \(k\) algebraically closed. We prove the two algebraic assertions used there: the two-term cohomology model survives every change of parameter ring, and finite divisors and fibrewise nonzero sections give relative Cartier divisors over arbitrary parameter schemes.

U.1. Exact tensoring and a finite replacement

We first record an elementary tensor argument. If

\[ 0\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow D\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow0 \tag{U.1} \]

is exact and \(Q\) is flat over a ring \(A\), the sequence remains exact after tensoring with any module \(M\). Here is the assertion at its only nonautomatic position. Choose a free presentation \(V\to F\to M\to0\), where \(V\) is the kernel in the free module \(F\). Lift an element of \(E\otimes M\) that dies in \(D\otimes M\) to \(e\in E\otimes F\). Its image comes from some \(v\in D\otimes V\). The image of \(v\) in \(Q\otimes V\) dies in \(Q\otimes F\), hence is zero by flatness. Right exactness lifts \(v\) from \(E\otimes V\). Subtract this lift from \(e\); the difference dies in \(D\otimes F\), and is zero since \(F\) is free. Thus the original element is zero. If \(D\) is flat too, then \(E\) is flat: for an injection \(M\to M'\), embed \(E\otimes M\) in \(D\otimes M\) and use the injection into \(D\otimes M'\).

Now let \(A\) be Noetherian and let

\[ C^0\xrightarrow{d}C^1 \tag{U.2} \]

be a complex of flat modules with finite \(H^0\) and \(H^1\). The terms need not be finite. Choose a finite free module \(P\) surjecting onto \(H^1\), and lift its basis to a map \(g:P\to C^1\). The map \((d,-g):C^0\oplus P\to C^1\) is surjective. Put

\[ E=\ker(d,-g),\qquad K=[E\xrightarrow{\operatorname{pr}_P}P]. \tag{U.3} \]

The preceding argument makes \(E\) flat and makes its defining sequence universally exact. Projection to \(P\) also gives

\[ 0\longrightarrow H^0(C)\longrightarrow E \longrightarrow\ker(P\longrightarrow H^1(C))\longrightarrow0. \tag{U.4} \]

The right module is finite because \(A\) is Noetherian, so \(E\) is finite. It is locally finite free. Explicitly, over a localization of \(A\) at a prime, lift a basis of its residue-vector-space quotient. Nakayama gives a surjection from a finite free module onto \(E\). Its kernel is finite, and flatness of \(E\) makes reduction of that sequence exact at the left. The reduced map is an isomorphism, so Nakayama kills the kernel. The resulting basis spreads to an open neighbourhood: clear its denominators, then kill the finite kernel and cokernel by elements outside the prime. For this use of Nakayama, if a finite module \(N\) satisfies \(N=IN\), express a generating column as \(B\) times that column with entries of \(B\) in \(I\). The adjugate identity shows that \(\det(1-B)\in1+I\) annihilates \(N\). It is a unit when \(I\) lies in the maximal ideal.

The maps \(E\to C^0\) and \(g:P\to C^1\) define a comparison \(K\to C\). For every \(A\)-module \(M\), universal exactness identifies \(E\otimes M\) with the kernel of

\[ (C^0\otimes M)\oplus(P\otimes M) \xrightarrow{(d,-g)} C^1\otimes M. \tag{U.5} \]

The kernel of its projection to \(P\otimes M\) is exactly \(\ker(d\otimes M)\). Its projection image is exactly the kernel of the surjection \(P\otimes M\to\operatorname{coker}(d\otimes M)\). Consequently \(K\otimes M\to C\otimes M\) induces isomorphisms in both degrees. This proves the finite replacement and its arbitrary-tensor compatibility directly. It is the two-term instance of Base change and the Grothendieck complex, Lemma 3.1.

Apply this construction to Q.3's two-affine Čech complex over a finitely generated parameter algebra. Its flat terms and finite cohomology were established there. After localizing the parameter algebra, \(E\) and \(P\) are finite free. The comparison just proved can then be tensored first to the original parameter ring and subsequently to any algebra over it. This proves precisely (Q.8), including nonflat changes of base.

U.2. A nonzerodivisor on the closed fibre

Let \((A,\mathfrak m)\to(B,\mathfrak n)\) be a flat local map of Noetherian local rings. Suppose that multiplication by \(f\in B\) is injective on \(B/\mathfrak mB\). Then

\[ f:B\longrightarrow B\text{ is injective},\qquad B/fB\text{ is flat over }A. \tag{U.6} \]

Flatness identifies each layer of the \(\mathfrak m\)-adic filtration with

\[ \mathfrak m^rB/\mathfrak m^{r+1}B \simeq(\mathfrak m^r/\mathfrak m^{r+1}) \otimes_{A/\mathfrak m}(B/\mathfrak mB). \tag{U.7} \]

It is a direct sum of copies of \(B/\mathfrak mB\), on which \(f\) is injective. If \(fz=0\), induction through these layers puts \(z\) in every \(\mathfrak m^rB\). Their intersection is zero by L.1: apply its local separation theorem to the finite \(B\)-module \(B\) and the ideal \(I=\mathfrak mB\subset\mathfrak n\). That theorem explicitly permits any ideal inside the maximal ideal. Its Artin–Rees and determinant proof is given there, so no equality \(\mathfrak mB=\mathfrak n\) is required.

For any proper ideal \(J\subset A\), the map \(A/J\to B/JB\) is again flat, local and Noetherian, with the same closed fibre. The preceding argument therefore makes \(f\) injective on \(B/JB\). Equivalently,

\[ JB\cap fB=fJB. \tag{U.8} \]

Since \(B\) is \(A\)-flat, \(J\otimes_A B=JB\). Right exactness identifies \(J\otimes_A(B/fB)\) with \(JB/fJB\). Equation (U.8) says that its map into \(B/fB\) is injective. The ideal criterion now proves flatness. Its proof is Tor and flat modules, Theorem 2.1: induction on the rank of a free module extends the ideal injection test to its submodules; a tensor uses finitely many coordinates, so this extends to arbitrary free modules; presenting any inclusion as quotients of two nested submodules of a free module proves preservation of every injection. This argument uses the ideal criterion directly, without a derived replacement theorem.

Thus (U.6) has been proved from the stated Noetherian and tensor facts. It is the local algebra assertion of [Stacks, Tag 00MF]; the next two parts give the fixed-curve applications of [Stacks, Tag 062Y] with their descent steps specified.

U.3. A finite flat family has an invertible ideal

First suppose that the parameter algebra \(A\) is Noetherian and \(D\subset C_A\) is finite locally free over \(A\). At a point of \(C_A\), localize both the base and the curve, writing the quotient sequence as

\[ 0\longrightarrow I\longrightarrow B\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow0. \tag{U.9} \]

Both \(B\) and \(Q\) are flat over the local base: the curve is smooth, and localizing the finite flat family preserves base flatness. U.1 makes \(I\) flat too, and identifies its reduction with the ideal of the fibre subscheme. X.1 proves the discrete valuation description at a closed point from the specified smooth regularity input, over arbitrary fields; the generic local ring is a field. An ideal cutting out a finite subscheme is therefore generated by a nonzerodivisor, including the unit ideal away from the subscheme. Lift such a generator to \(f\in I\). The finite \(B\)-module \(I/Bf\) has zero reduction modulo the base maximal ideal, so Nakayama makes it zero. The resulting surjection \(B\to I\) has finite kernel. Since \(I\) is flat over the base, U.1 makes its reduction exact; the fibre map is an isomorphism onto the fibre ideal. The kernel consequently has zero reduction, and Nakayama kills it as well. Thus \(I=Bf\simeq B\), with \(f\) a nonzerodivisor. This proves the Cartier assertion at every point.

Here is the descent needed when \(A\) is arbitrary. Work locally on \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) so that the finite algebra of \(D\) is free of rank \(d\) and the support of \(D\) lies in a fixed affine open \(U\subset C\). Such opens cover the base: choose \(d+1\) distinct points of \(C(k)\), use Q.1's affine complements, and note that a fibre of length \(d\) misses at least one of those points. The locus where the family misses that point is open, since its intersection with the point's section is closed in the base.

Write \(\mathcal O(U)=k[z_1,\ldots,z_m]/(r_1,\ldots,r_s)\). The quotient to the free algebra of \(D\) is specified by commuting multiplication matrices \(Z_i\), a vector \(v\) for the unit, and finitely many polynomials \(b_j\) such that \(b_j(Z)v\) are the chosen free basis. The equations \(r_a(Z)=0\), commutativity, and these basis identities are finite. Put their coefficients into a finitely generated \(k\)-subalgebra \(A_0\subset A\). Over \(A_0\) they define a cyclic module \(Q_0=A_0^d\) over \(\mathcal O(U)\otimes_k A_0\), with cyclic vector \(v\). The kernel of evaluation at \(v\) is an ideal: if an element kills \(v\), commutativity and cyclicity make it kill the whole module. Thus \(Q_0\) is a quotient algebra, free over \(A_0\), and its base change recovers \(D\).

The Noetherian argument makes the ideal of this quotient invertible and generated locally by a nonzerodivisor. Its quotient is \(A_0\)-flat, so U.1 preserves the ideal sequence after tensoring to \(A\). Invertibility is preserved by base change, and the injection remains an injection. We obtain a relative effective Cartier divisor over \(A\). This proves Q.2's assertion for arbitrary parameter schemes, since both invertibility and the displayed local equations can be checked on affine base opens.

U.4. A fibrewise nonzero section cuts out a flat divisor

Let \(L\) be a line bundle on \(C_A\), with \(A\) any \(k\)-algebra, and let \(s\) restrict to a nonzero section on every geometric curve fibre. We prove that its zero scheme is a relative effective Cartier divisor, finite locally free over the base. Its degree on a fibre is \(\deg L_t\).

Descend \(L\) and \(s\) to a finitely generated \(k\)-subalgebra \(A_0\subset A\). Q.3 explains the finite presentations, inverse trivializations and gluing identities for the bundle. Include the finitely many coefficients of the section on a finite trivializing affine cover and its overlap identities. This gives the section as well. It remains to arrange that the descended section is nonzero on every fibre near the image of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\); that assertion cannot be inferred merely from the existence of a descended bundle.

Use U.1's finite model locally on \(\operatorname{Spec}A_0\). The descended section is a cycle \(v\in K^0\), and the same is true after every change of base. Since \(H^0(K)=\ker(K^0\to K^1)\) embeds in \(K^0\), its fibre section is zero exactly when all coordinates of \(v\) vanish in the residue field. Nonvanishing therefore defines an open subset of the base. This open contains the image of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\): extension of residue fields is faithful on vector spaces. Replace the descended base by this open and work on its affine cover.

On the Noetherian descended curve, trivialize \(L\) at a point and write \(s=f\). Each fibre is geometrically integral, so a nonzero section of a line bundle is a nonzerodivisor in every fibre local ring. U.2 shows that \(f\) is a nonzerodivisor on the curve and that its quotient is flat over the base. The zero scheme \(D_0\) is thus a relative effective Cartier divisor. U.1 shows that its defining sequence remains exact after every base change. In particular its pullback to \(A\) is exactly the zero scheme of \(s\), with invertible ideal and flat quotient.

For completeness, finiteness can be checked without an extra compactification argument. At any point of the descended base, the finite zero divisor on the fibre misses some \(q\in C(k)\); there are infinitely many such points by Q.1. Restrict to the open base locus where the section does not vanish at \(q\). Then \(D_0\) lies in \((C\setminus\{q\})\times\operatorname{Spec}A_0\), an affine scheme by Q.1, and is closed there. Its coordinate algebra is finite over \(A_0\): it is the global sections of the coherent quotient \(\mathcal O_{D_0}\) on the projective curve, so W.4's projective cohomology finiteness applies. Hence \(D_0\) is finite. A finite flat module over the Noetherian base is locally free by U.1's basis argument. These statements survive the arbitrary base change to \(A\). Finally the local discrete valuation lengths identify its fibre length with the degree of the zero divisor of \(s_t\), which equals \(\deg L_t\) by (Q.2).

This also justifies the sum of graph divisors in Q.2. A graph is a closed finite locally free family of degree one, so U.3 makes its ideal invertible. The product of the \(d\) graph ideals is the image of a section of their inverse tensor product. On each curve fibre its equation is a product of parameters, with repetitions allowed, and is nonzero. The argument above makes its zero scheme finite locally free of degree \(d\). In Q.4 apply the same result to the evaluation section of \(L\otimes f^*(f_*L)^{-1}\). Its fibre is the unique nonzero section up to scalar, and its degree is \(g\). Thus the divisor construction and its inverse in (Q.10) hold over all parameter schemes and commute with arbitrary base change.

Appendix V. Coordinates on the finite-divisor scheme

Let \(C/k\) and \(H_d\) be as in Q.2. We construct étale charts \(H_d\supset V\to\mathbf A^d_k\) around every closed point. This proves smoothness directly and also identifies the completed local rings in (Q.7).

V.1. One coordinate at all support points

Write a nonempty divisor as \(D=\sum_{i=1}^r d_i x_i\), with distinct \(x_i\in C(k)\). Q.1 supplies an affine open \(U_0\) containing the support: remove a different rational point of \(C\). Let \(B=\mathcal O(U_0)\) and let \(\mathfrak m_i\) be the maximal ideal of \(x_i\). Choose \(u_i\in\mathfrak m_i\) nonzero in \(\mathfrak m_i/\mathfrak m_i^2\), which is one-dimensional because \(C\) is smooth of dimension one. Choose distinct \(a_i\in k\). The Chinese remainder theorem gives \(t\in B\) satisfying

\[ t\equiv a_i+u_i\pmod{\mathfrak m_i^2}\quad(1\le i\le r). \tag{V.1} \]

The ideals \(\mathfrak m_i^2\) are pairwise comaximal. For example, if \(a+b=1\) with \(a\in\mathfrak m_i\), \(b\in\mathfrak m_j\), expanding \((a+b)^3\) puts \(1\) in their sum of squares. For two comaximal ideals \(I,J\), a decomposition \(1=e+f\), \(e\in I,f\in J\), makes \(fy+ez\) a simultaneous representative of the residues \(y\bmod I,z\bmod J\); induction proves the finite version used in (V.1).

Shrink to an affine neighbourhood \(U\) of all \(x_i\) where \(dt\) is a basis of \(\Omega_{C/k}\). To obtain one affine neighbourhood, the complement of this locus in \(U_0\) is closed and misses all \(x_i\). Its ideal contains an element equal to one at each \(x_i\), again by the Chinese remainder calculation. Invert that element. The map

\[ t:U\longrightarrow\mathbf A^1_k \tag{V.2} \]

is étale. Here is a lifting proof that also fixes the precise coordinate criterion. Work on a smooth affine chart of \(U\), with \(dt\) a differential basis. Given a square-zero extension \(A'\twoheadrightarrow A\), ideal \(J\), and a compatible map to the chart over \(k[T]\), first lift it as a \(k\)-map using smoothness. If \(b\in A'\) is the prescribed image of \(T\), its discrepancy \(e=\widetilde t-b\) lies in \(J\). The universal property of differentials gives a unique derivation into \(J\) sending \(dt\) to \(e\). Subtract it from the lift. Because \(J^2=0\), the product rule says that the corrected map is a ring map, now with \(t\mapsto b\). Two such maps differ by a derivation vanishing on \(dt\), hence are equal. This proves formal étaleness on these charts. The lifts agree on overlaps by uniqueness, so the assertion holds for (V.2). Finite presentation over \(k[T]\) follows by adjoining the single equation identifying \(T\) with the chosen polynomial representative of \(t\).

The algebraic prerequisites for this argument have explicit proofs in Formally smooth, unramified and étale ring maps, Sections 1–5: square-zero differences are derivations; a smooth presentation has a split conormal sequence; choosing independent rows gives standard smooth neighbourhoods; and an invertible Jacobian solves the lifting equations. The differential universal property, quotient and localization formulas are proved in Kähler differentials, Sections 1–3 and 5. The rank-one assertion for a smooth curve is the standard-chart calculation in Smooth morphisms, Proposition 1.1.

V.2. A divisor recorded by one monic polynomial

The image of \(t-a_i\) is a uniformizer at \(x_i\). In the quotient of its discrete valuation ring by \((t-a_i)^{d_i}\), the powers from zero to \(d_i-1\) are a basis over \(k\): reduce the constant coefficient modulo the maximal ideal and iterate through its successive principal powers. Independence follows by taking the least nonzero coefficient and its valuation. Since the \(a_i\) are distinct, Chinese remainders now give

\[ \mathcal O_D\simeq k[T]/(F_0(T)),\qquad F_0(T)=\prod_i(T-a_i)^{d_i}. \tag{V.3} \]

In particular \(1,t,\ldots,t^{d-1}\) form a basis of the length-\(d\) algebra.

Inside the open scheme \(H_d(U)\subset H_d(C)\), let \(V_t\) be the locus where these powers form a basis of the universal finite algebra. It is open: in any local basis the condition is the invertibility of a determinant. It contains \(D\). The unique relation expressing \(t^d\) in that basis has the form

\[ F(T)=T^d+c_1T^{d-1}+\cdots+c_d. \tag{V.4} \]

Its coefficients are regular functions on \(V_t\), since the inverse basis matrix is regular where its determinant is invertible. They define

\[ \Phi_t:V_t\longrightarrow\mathbf A^d_k. \tag{V.5} \]

For any parameter ring \(A\), the algebra of a divisor in this chart is canonically \(A[T]/(F)\), with \(T\) acting as \(t\). Monic division makes the source free on the same \(d\) powers, and the map to the divisor algebra carries that basis to a basis, proving the assertion over arbitrary \(A\). Thus a chart point consists of its monic polynomial together with its embedded map into \(U\) over the coordinate line.

The construction of \(H_d(U)\) used here is the finite commuting-matrix construction in Q.2, with full proof in Hilbert and Quot schemes, Proposition 5.1. The openness of \(H_d(U)\) follows because a finite family is contained in \(U\) exactly off the closed image of its intersection with \(C\setminus U\). No projectivity theorem for a general Hilbert functor enters this chart.

V.3. Unique lifting proves that the chart is étale

Take any square-zero extension \(A'\twoheadrightarrow A\), a divisor \(Z\) in \(V_t(A)\), and a lift \(F'\in A'[T]\) of its polynomial (V.4), with the same monic leading coefficient. Set

\[ Q'=A'[T]/(F'),\qquad Z'=\operatorname{Spec}Q'. \tag{V.6} \]

It is free of rank \(d\) over \(A'\), and its reduction is canonically \(Z\). The map \(Z\to U\) is over \(\mathbf A^1\). Formal étaleness of (V.2) lifts it uniquely to \(Z'\to U\). The lift respects \(A'\), so gives \(Z'\to U_{A'}\). Local lifting and uniqueness glue on \(Z'\); only a square-zero ideal is being tested.

This map is a closed immersion. On rings its map \(\mathcal O(U)\otimes_k A'\to Q'\) sends the coordinate \(t\) to the class of \(T\). That class together with \(A'\) generates the whole quotient algebra, so the map is surjective. The powers of \(t\) still form the monic basis, making this a point of \(V_t(A')\). Every candidate lift has the algebra (V.6) by V.2, and its map to \(U\) is the unique étale lift just constructed. Thus it is unique. We have proved every square-zero lifting test for \(\Phi_t\).

The map \(\Phi_t\) is locally of finite presentation: its source is locally of finite type over the Noetherian field \(k\), and an affine presentation over \(k[c_1,\ldots,c_d]\) adds finitely many equations for these coefficient functions. Finite presentation and the proved formal lifting property make it étale. Equivalently, the local algebra criterion is the definition and standard-form theorem in the ring-map lesson linked in V.1. On an affine open of \(V_t\), the lift lands in that same open because square-zero thickenings preserve the underlying points.

It follows that \(V_t\) is smooth over \(k\): lift the \(d\) coefficients freely, then use the unique lift over them. Moreover its differentials over \(k\) are freely generated by \(dc_1,\ldots,dc_d\). To see this without just using a rank formula, the unique-lift test with split square-zero rings says that every derivation on the polynomial coefficient ring into any module extends uniquely to the chart ring. The representing property of differentials makes their natural map an isomorphism. Y.5–Y.6 prove polynomial local regularity and the standard smooth presentation calculation. Applied here, (Y.16) gives regular closed local rings of dimension \(d\); thus the chart is smooth of dimension \(d\).

Every closed point of \(H_d\) has the chart just constructed, since \(k\) is algebraically closed. These opens cover \(H_d\): their closed complement in a finite-type \(k\)-scheme, if nonempty, would contain a closed point by the weak Nullstellensatz. For \(d=0\), \(H_0=\operatorname{Spec}k\) already has the required property. Thus \(H_d\) is smooth of dimension \(d\) in every characteristic.

V.4. Completed coefficients and separate support clusters

Let \(D\) correspond to coefficients \(b_1,\ldots,b_d\in k\) in (V.4). Put \(A=\mathcal O_{H_d,D}\). The chart gives a continuous map

\[ \alpha:k[[X_1,\ldots,X_d]]\longrightarrow\widehat A, \qquad X_j\longmapsto c_j-b_j. \tag{V.7} \]

We construct its inverse explicitly. Over each Artinian ring \(R_n=k[X_1,\ldots,X_d]/(X_1,\ldots,X_d)^n\), the coefficient tuple \((b_j+X_j)_j\) has a unique lift to \(V_t\) reducing to \(D\). Apply V.3 successively to the square-zero kernels of \(R_{n+1}\to R_n\). Uniqueness makes the resulting maps \(A\to R_n\) compatible. They give a local map \(A\to k[[X_1,\ldots,X_d]]\), continuous for the maximal-ideal topologies, and hence an extension \(\beta:\widehat A\to k[[X_1,\ldots,X_d]]\). Indeed its map to \(R_n\) kills \(\mathfrak m_A^n\), so it factors through that quotient and is defined on the inverse limit.

The composite \(\beta\alpha\) fixes every \(X_j\), hence every power series by continuity. For \(\alpha\beta\), reduce to each \(A/\mathfrak m_A^n\). Its induced map from \(A\) and the canonical quotient map have the same coefficient tuple and the same closed point. V.3's uniqueness, iterated through the nilpotent maximal ideal, makes them equal. Equality in every quotient makes \(\alpha\beta=1\). Thus (V.7) is an isomorphism; no comparison of dimension before and after completion is needed for this conclusion.

To obtain exactly the separate coefficients in (Q.6)–(Q.7), let \(R\) be any local Artinian \(k\)-algebra with residue field \(k\). A deformation of \(D\) has a finite free algebra whose special fibre is the product of the support clusters. The idempotents lift uniquely. For a square-zero ideal this follows by correcting a lift \(a\) of an idempotent by

\[ a\longmapsto a-(2a-1)^{-1}(a^2-a). \tag{V.8} \]

Here \((2a-1)^2=1+4(a^2-a)\) is a unit. Two corrected idempotents differ by an element killed by their sum minus one, which is a unit, proving uniqueness. Iterate through the powers of the nilpotent maximal ideal. Orthogonality and summing to one persist by uniqueness. This gives the individual free rank-\(d_i\) algebras.

The coordinate \(t-a_i\) identifies the completed curve ring at \(x_i\) with \(k[[t-a_i]]\), by the same étale lifting argument as (V.7), now for (V.2). Any other formal parameter \(u_i\) has nonzero linear term in this coordinate; coefficient-by-coefficient inversion gives the inverse power series. In an Artinian deformation the coordinate is nilpotent, so those series evaluate by finite sums. The powers \(1,u_i,\ldots,u_i^{d_i-1}\) reduce to a basis, hence are a basis of the free cluster algebra: Nakayama gives a surjection between free modules of the same rank, and its determinant is a unit. The unique monic relation is precisely (Q.6), with every \(a_{i,j}\in\mathfrak m_R\).

Conversely, any such coefficient list gives a free monic quotient. If \(\mathfrak m_R^N=0\), its relation implies \(u_i^{d_iN}=0\). Therefore it defines a map from the completed curve ring, and thus a map to a neighbourhood of \(x_i\). It is a closed embedded cluster: the actual coordinate \(t-a_i\) and \(u_i\) are inverse polynomial expressions on this nilpotent quotient. Distinct clusters combine to a closed divisor; the polynomials in \(t\) supported at the distinct residues \(a_i\) are comaximal, so their quotient factors separate the clusters. These constructions are inverse and commute with all Artinian base changes.

The independent coefficient lists consequently describe the completed local ring. More explicitly, lift the universal lists over the quotients of \(k[[a_{i,j}]]\) by powers of its maximal ideal to obtain a map from \(A\); in the other direction, apply the coefficient construction to every \(A/\mathfrak m_A^n\). Their inverse-limit maps are inverse because the two constructions are inverse on each Artinian quotient, exactly as above. This proves (Q.7), including repeated points and all characteristics, with the specific coefficient coordinates asserted there.

Appendix W. The coherent cohomology used by the Picard construction

Q.1 and Q.3 need a specific chain of cohomology statements: affine vanishing, a finite ordered Čech model, and finiteness on a projective scheme over a Noetherian ring. We give that chain here. Throughout this appendix cohomology is ordinary Zariski sheaf cohomology, with the abelian-sheaf resolutions of T.1–T.4. No assertion about unbounded or adic complexes is involved.

W.1. Modules, affine sections and the principal-cover contraction

For an \(A\)-module \(M\), localization is exact. A fraction vanishes exactly when an allowed denominator kills its numerator; this criterion proves injectivity and exactness in the middle, and lifting a numerator proves surjectivity. The maps \((a/s)\otimes m\mapsto am/s\) and \(m/s\mapsto (1/s)\otimes m\) identify localization with tensoring by the localized ring.

Every cover of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) has a finite refinement by principal opens. Indeed, principal opens form its defining basis. If their defining elements generate a proper ideal, a maximal ideal containing it gives a point outside the cover. Otherwise a finite expression for \(1\) supplies the finite refinement. The same reasoning in \(A_f\) applies to \(D(f)\). Thus these basis objects are quasi-compact and their finite intersections are again basis objects.

Take a finite principal cover \(D(f_1),\ldots,D(f_r)\). The augmented ordered complex is

\[ 0\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow \prod_i M_{f_i} \longrightarrow \prod_{i<j}M_{f_if_j}\longrightarrow\cdots \longrightarrow M_{f_1\cdots f_r}\longrightarrow0. \tag{W.1} \]

To prove exactness, localize at one \(f_j\). That member of the cover is now the whole space. Extend an ordered cochain to alternating tuples, with zero on repetitions, and define \((hc)_{i_0\ldots i_{p-1}}=c_{j,i_0,\ldots,i_{p-1}}\); the degree-zero map is evaluation at \(j\) into the augmentation. The alternating differential satisfies \(dh+hd=1\): deleting the inserted index supplies the original term, and all other terms cancel in pairs. The full Čech complex with all tuples, as used in S.2, has the same contraction without the alternating extension. Localization commutes with the finite products in each degree and with cohomology. Hence every cohomology module of either augmented complex becomes zero after inverting each \(f_j\). Such a module is zero: for any element choose a common power \(f_j^a\) killing it for all \(j\); those powers still generate the unit ideal. This proves the assertion before localization.

The equalizer part of (W.1) constructs \(\widetilde M\) on the principal basis, with sections \(M_f\) and stalk \(M_{\mathfrak p}\). Finite refinements give its sheaf property on all covers. We also need the converse: if \(F\) is quasi-coherent on this affine scheme, then

\[ F=\widetilde{\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}A,F)},\qquad \Gamma(D(f),F)=\Gamma(\operatorname{Spec}A,F)_f. \tag{W.2} \]

Here are the gluing details. Restriction of an associated module sheaf from \(\operatorname{Spec}B\) to an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}C\) is associated to \(C\otimes_B M\): the natural map is an isomorphism on stalks, since the local rings of an open subscheme are the same. Consequently quasi-coherence supplies a finite principal cover of \(\operatorname{Spec}A\) on which \(F\) is associated to modules \(N_i\). The sheaf equalizer expresses its global sections as the kernel of the difference map from \(\prod_i N_i\) to the product of overlap sections. Localize this finite equalizer at \(f\). Exactness of localization identifies it with the equalizer for the induced cover of \(D(f)\), proving (W.2). The map from the associated global-section module to \(F\) sends \(m/f^a\) to \(f^{-a}m\) on that open; (W.2) proves it is an isomorphism. Association is exact on stalks, so its inverse, affine sections on quasi-coherent sheaves, is exact too. Tensor products and pullbacks on affines correspond to module tensor products by the same stalk calculation. These arguments also prove that kernels of quasi-coherent maps remain quasi-coherent. Compare the complete affine construction in Quasi-coherent sheaves, Section 1.

W.2. From those contractions to derived cohomology

Apply the proof of S.3 on the Zariski principal basis just checked in W.1. Its hypotheses hold: intersections remain in the basis, covers have finite refinements, and the full Čech complexes of \(\widetilde M\) are acyclic in positive degrees on every finite basis cover. T.1–T.4 construct the required injective resolutions on this site. More explicitly, a positive-degree resolution cycle becomes a boundary on a finite cover. S.2 identifies the total Čech-resolution complex with global resolution sections. Induction on the degree then removes the positive vertical components on the intersections, until only a Čech cycle of \(F\) remains; W.1 makes that cycle a boundary. This proves

\[ H^q(\operatorname{Spec}A,\widetilde M)=0\quad(q>0) \tag{W.3} \]

for any ring and module. The steps are precisely S.2–S.3's signed, finite-diagonal elimination, so the passage uses derived cohomology rather than merely exactness of affine sections within the quasi-coherent subcategory. See also Affine cohomology, Sections 2–3 and [Stacks, coherent cohomology prerequisites].

For use of an ordered finite cover, its augmented free sheaf chain complex is exact as well. At any stalk choose a covering index containing that point; insert it, with the sign of its position in the ordered tuple. The resulting simplex contraction is the identity up to the boundary. Applying \(\operatorname{Hom}(-,I)\) to this exact complex for an injective sheaf \(I\) gives exact augmented ordered Čech rows. Thus S.2's row elimination applies to the ordered double complex as well.

Let \(U_1,\ldots,U_r\) cover a separated scheme by affines. Each intersection is affine: for two such opens, their intersection is the inverse image of the closed diagonal in the affine product, hence a closed subscheme of an affine scheme; repeat for more opens. Apply an injective resolution of \(F\), with double differential \(d_h+(-1)^p d_v\) in column \(p\). Row elimination gives global cohomology. By (W.3), every column has cohomology only in vertical degree zero, where it is the corresponding section module of \(F\). To verify the other comparison explicitly, start with a total cycle and its lowest nonzero column having positive vertical degree. That component is a vertical cycle; choose a primitive, with sign \((-1)^p\), and subtract its total differential. This removes it and changes only the next column. Continue until the representative has vertical degree zero. For injectivity, apply the same procedure to a primitive whose total differential lies in that bottom row; positive vertical components of the primitive can successively be removed without changing its differential. Both procedures terminate on the finite diagonal. Hence the ordered section complex computes \(H^q(X,F)\), and

\[ H^q(X,F)=0\quad(q\geq r). \tag{W.4} \]

All maps are restriction maps and module maps over the base ring. In particular Q.1's two affine opens compute cohomology in degrees zero and one, also after any change of parameter ring: the base-changed opens and their intersection are still affine, and their associated modules tensor by (W.2).

W.3. Polynomial weights calculate every projective twist

Write \(P=\mathbf P_A^N\), with homogeneous coordinates \(T_0,\ldots,T_N\). On its standard charts the frame for \(\mathcal O_P(m)\) is \(T_i^m\). On the intersection indexed by a nonempty subset \(I\), its section module is the degree-\(m\) part of \(A[T_0,\ldots,T_N,T_i^{-1}:i\in I]\). These formulas follow directly by identifying the frames through the coordinate ratios. They also give the affine intersections needed in W.2.

Assume first \(N>0\). Decompose the ordered complex by Laurent monomial exponents \(e=(e_0,\ldots,e_N)\) with \(\sum e_i=m\). A monomial occurs at \(I\) exactly when \(I\) contains its negative support \(S(e)=\{i:e_i<0\}\). For that weight every occurring component is one copy of \(A\), and its differential is the signed identity to the larger allowed subsets. There are three cases. If the negative support is empty, this is the simplex cochain complex: augment it by \(A\) and insert any vertex to contract it, leaving just \(A\) in degree zero. If the negative support is a nonempty proper subset, insert a vertex outside it; the same cancellation contracts the complex without augmentation. In degree zero the potentially extra constant term is zero because the singleton at the inserted vertex is not allowed. If every exponent is negative, only the full subset occurs, giving \(A\) in degree \(N\).

Each Laurent polynomial has finite support; there are only finitely many subsets in each degree. The whole complex is therefore the direct sum of these weight complexes, and kernels and images in a direct sum are computed componentwise. We have proved

\[ H^q(P,\mathcal O_P(m))= \begin{cases} \displaystyle\bigoplus_{\substack{e_i\geq0\\\sum e_i=m}} A,&q=0,\\ \displaystyle\bigoplus_{\substack{e_i<0\\\sum e_i=m}} A,&q=N,\\ 0,&q\ne0,N. \end{cases} \tag{W.5} \]

For fixed \(m\) each displayed sum is finite, including when it is empty. Thus every group is finite free, and positive-degree groups vanish for \(m\geq0\). If \(N=0\), there is one chart, every twist is the trivial line, and the answer instead is \(A\) in degree zero for every \(m\), zero in higher degrees. The decomposition and contractions involve only signed identity maps, so these particular cohomology calculations commute with any ring change. This assertion is about twists, not arbitrary coherent sheaves. It is the calculation in Cohomology of projective space, Sections 1–3; see also [Stacks, coherent cohomology prerequisites] for the coefficient-wise contraction.

W.4. Finite generation, descending induction and the fixed curve

Now suppose \(A\) is Noetherian. Polynomial rings over \(A\) are Noetherian: in one variable, choose finitely many polynomials in an ideal whose leading coefficients generate the ideal of all leading coefficients. Above the maximum of their degrees, subtract multiples to lower the degree. The remaining elements of smaller degree form a submodule of a finite free \(A\)-module, hence have finitely many generators. Those elements and the chosen polynomials generate the ideal. Repeat one variable at a time. Here finite free modules are Noetherian by induction on rank, and their finite quotients are Noetherian. Localizations and quotients of Noetherian rings remain Noetherian by contracting and extending ideals. In particular the standard charts of \(P\) are Noetherian, and kernels of maps of coherent sheaves are coherent by W.1.

We next construct a finite quotient by twists, rather than assuming one. Fix a section \(u\) of a coherent sheaf \(F\) on \(U_i=D_+(T_i)\). On each standard chart \(U_j\), the intersection with \(U_i\) is principal. By (W.2), \(u\) is a fraction in that chart's module. Clearing the finitely many denominators gives local sections of \(F(a)\) whose quotients by \(T_i^a\) equal \(u\) on \(U_i\). On each affine overlap the difference of these lifts vanishes after inverting \(T_i\); a power of its local equation therefore kills that difference. Choose a common power for the finitely many overlaps and multiply all lifts by it. They now glue to a section of a larger twist. The same argument kills any global twisted section that restricts to zero after this inversion. In particular every chosen local generator extends after a power, without requiring \(T_i\) to be regular on \(F\).

Choose finitely many generators on each \(U_i\) and extend them in this way. Raise their twist degrees to one common nonnegative integer \(a\), using further powers of the coordinate for their original chart. Their restrictions in that chart's frame still give the original generators. Together the resulting global sections give an exact sequence

\[ 0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow0, \qquad E=\mathcal O_P(-a)^{\oplus b}, \tag{W.6} \]

with \(b\) finite and \(K\) coherent. For \(n\geq a\), the degree-\((n-a)\) monomials generate \(E(n)\), so their images generate \(F(n)\).

W.2 bounds cohomology by \(N\) on this cover. Descend in \(q\), proving finiteness simultaneously for all coherent sheaves. The induction starts above \(N\). The long exact sequence constructed in T.4 contains

\[ H^q(P,E)\longrightarrow H^q(P,F) \longrightarrow H^{q+1}(P,K). \tag{W.7} \]

Its left term is finite by W.3 and its right term by induction. The middle term is an extension of a quotient of the left term by a submodule of the right term. Both are finite over the Noetherian base, hence so is the middle term. This includes degree zero. For \(q>0\), apply the same descending induction to (W.6) tensored by \(\mathcal O(n)\). W.3 kills the left cohomology group for large \(n\), and induction kills the right one. Thus \(H^q(P,F(n))=0\) for large \(n\); taking the largest threshold over \(1\leq q\leq N\) proves simultaneous eventual vanishing. No finite resolution by line bundles has been assumed. These are the proofs used in Coherent sheaves on projective schemes, Sections 1–2.

If \(i:X\hookrightarrow P\) is a closed subscheme, a coherent sheaf on \(X\) gives a coherent sheaf \(i_*F\) on \(P\). On each chart this is simply its finite module viewed over a Noetherian ring mapping onto the coordinate ring of the closed subscheme. The common affine cover and W.2 give identical ordered complexes on both spaces. Their cohomology is therefore identical, proving finite coherent cohomology for every such projective \(X\).

Apply this to \(C_{A_i}\) in Q.3. The curve's fixed projective embedding remains a closed embedding after base change, so the cohomology of the descended line bundle is finite. The fixed two-affine cover remains a two-affine cover over \(A_i\). On any of its intersections the coordinate ring is \(B\otimes_k A_i\), which is \(A_i\)-flat because a \(k\)-basis of \(B\) exhibits it as a free \(A_i\)-module. An invertible module there is flat over that ring: locally its tensor operation is the identity, and exactness can be checked after localizing at all prime ideals. Composition of these exact tensor operations makes it \(A_i\)-flat. This establishes both inputs of U.1's finite replacement of the two-term complex. Q.3's finite-presentation descent followed by that replacement handles arbitrary \(A\); we make no general nonflat cohomology-base-change claim. The same projective finiteness proves that the affine zero scheme in U.4 has a finite coordinate module. AF.1 extends this finite-cohomology calculation to the finite-over-projective family in O.3; AF.2–AF.4 then supply its constant-field and connected-fibre argument after shrinking the base.

Appendix X. Valuations, rational functions and divisor degree

We supply the divisor calculations used in P.2, Q.1 and U.3. They apply after any field extension \(K/k\), where \(k\) and \(C\) are as in Q. In particular \(K\) is infinite but need not be perfect. Multiplicities below use residue-field degrees and include inseparable maps.

X.1. The local parameter and the constant field

Y.4 proves that regular local rings are domains and that independent parameter quotients are regular, using the length-growth calculation of Y.1–Y.3 and separation in L.1. Y.5 proves polynomial local regularity. Y.6 derives a standard smooth presentation directly from infinitesimal lifting and applies those results to prove smooth local regularity after every field extension. In particular the closed local rings of a smooth curve are one-dimensional regular domains. No assumption that a closed point has separable residue field is made.

On a smooth curve the local ring at a closed point has dimension one, so its maximal ideal is generated by one element \(\pi\). Indeed regularity says its cotangent space has dimension one, and Nakayama, with the determinant proof in U.1, lifts a basis to a generator of the maximal ideal. At a generic point the local ring is a field. Components of a smooth curve are disjoint: two meeting components would give two minimal primes in a local ring, contradicting the domain assertion. There are finitely many components; being disjoint closed subsets, they are also open. Thus a connected smooth curve is integral.

Here is the valuation argument for a Noetherian local domain \(R\) with nonzero maximal ideal \((\pi)\). A nonzero \(a\) cannot belong to every \(\pi^nR\). Otherwise the elements \(b_n=a/\pi^n\) lie in \(R\), and the ascending sequence of ideals \((b_n)\) stabilizes. At a stable step \(b_{n+1}=c b_n\), while \(b_n=\pi b_{n+1}\). Cancellation in the domain gives \(1=c\pi\), impossible for a nonunit \(\pi\). Choose the largest exponent \(n\) for which \(a\in\pi^nR\). The quotient \(a/\pi^n\) lies outside the maximal ideal and hence is a unit. The exponent is unique, since two different exponents would make a positive power of \(\pi\) a unit. Set \(v(a)=n\), \(v(a/b)=v(a)-v(b)\) and \(v(0)=+\infty\). Then

\[ \begin{gathered} v(ab)=v(a)+v(b),\qquad v(a+b)\geq\min\{v(a),v(b)\},\\ R=\{0\}\cup\{a:v(a)\geq0\}. \end{gathered} \tag{X.1} \]

Every nonzero ideal is \(\pi^nR\): take the least valuation of a nonzero element in it. Its quotients have the explicit length calculation

\[ \operatorname{length}_R(R/\pi^nR)=n, \tag{X.2} \]

because the successive powers have one-dimensional residue-field quotients. This proves the DVR assertion and its ideal and length statements directly from the local input. Compare Discrete valuation rings, Section 1 and [Stacks, curve divisor foundations].

The global constants and geometric integrality needed in Q can also be checked now. The integral projective curve \(C\) has a finite-dimensional \(k\)-algebra \(H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)\) by W.4. It embeds in its function field, so is a domain. Multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space, hence surjective; the algebra is a field. As \(k\) is algebraically closed it equals \(k\). W.2's finite affine-cover complex, tensored with a field extension, gives

\[ H^0(C_K,\mathcal O_{C_K})=K. \tag{X.3} \]

A nontrivial open-and-closed decomposition would give a nontrivial idempotent in this field. Thus \(C_K\) is connected. Smoothness survives field extension by base change of its standard smooth presentations; the regularity input above then makes its components disjoint and its local rings domains. Hence \(C_K\) is integral. This works for every extension \(K/k\) and proves geometric integrality as used here.

X.2. Every line bundle has a finite divisor representative

Write \(F=K(C_K)\). A rational function in \(F^\times\) has only finitely many nonzero orders. To see this, use a finite affine cover and write the function on each chart as a quotient of two nonzero elements of its coordinate domain. Their zero sets are proper closed subsets of a Noetherian integral curve, hence zero-dimensional and finite: each has finitely many irreducible components, and each component of dimension zero consists of its single closed generic point.

For a finite divisor \(D=\sum_x m_x[x]\), define \(\mathcal O(D)\) as the subsheaf of the rational-function sheaf with sections satisfying \(v_x(f)+m_x\geq0\). Near a point \(x\), choose a rational representative of a uniformizer \(\pi_x\), and discard its other finitely many zeros and poles and the other points of \(D\). On this neighbourhood the module is generated by \(\pi_x^{-m_x}\). The valuation criterion in (X.1) identifies its stalks with these free rank-one modules; equality of sheaves is checked on stalks. Thus \(\mathcal O(D)\) is invertible, including when some coefficients are negative. A rational function regular in every local ring of an open set is a section there: its local representatives agree in \(F\) and glue. This justifies the section description, not only its stalk version.

Now choose a nonzero vector \(s\) in the generic fibre of a line bundle \(L\). In each local frame write \(s=f_i e_i\). Units relating the frames have valuation zero, so the orders of the \(f_i\) agree on overlaps. The finite-cover argument above shows that they define a finite divisor \(D(s)\). Multiplication by \(s\) gives an isomorphism

\[ \mathcal O(D(s))\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }L: \quad f\longmapsto fs. \tag{X.4} \]

At \(x\), the frame \(\pi_x^{-v_x(f_i)}\) maps to a unit times \(e_i\), verifying the assertion. Replacing \(s\) by \(as\) adds \(\operatorname{div}(a)\). Conversely a trivialization of \(\mathcal O(D)\subset F\) is multiplication by a rational generator whose orders are \(-m_x\), so \(D\) is principal. We obtain, with the indicated sign convention,

\[ \operatorname{Pic}(C_K) =\operatorname{Div}(C_K)/\operatorname{div}(F^\times), \qquad D\longmapsto[\mathcal O(D)]. \tag{X.5} \]

These are the constructions of The multiplicative group on a curve, Proposition 5.1, here retaining arbitrary residue fields. Tensoring the local sequence \(0\to(\pi_x)\to R\to\kappa(x)\to0\) by a line bundle proves the point sequence (Q.1). Its last term has no positive Zariski cohomology: it is quasi-coherent, and on any finite affine cover the opens containing \(x\) give a simplex complex with coefficient \(L|_x\), contracted by any such index. W.2 gives the derived assertion. Its degree-zero dimension over \(K\) is \([\kappa(x):K]\).

X.3. A nonconstant rational function gives a finite map

For \(a\in F^\times\), (X.1) says that either \(a\) or \(a^{-1}\) is regular at each point. Each condition holds on a neighbourhood of that point. The corresponding affine-coordinate maps glue to a morphism \(f_a:C_K\to\mathbf P^1_K\), because on their overlap the coordinates are reciprocal. If \(a\notin K\), this morphism is nonconstant. In fact, an element of \(F\) algebraic over \(K\) has valuation zero at every closed point when nonzero: a negative valuation contradicts its monic equation by the uniquely lowest-order leading term; apply the same argument to its inverse to exclude positive valuation. It is therefore a global regular function, and (X.3) puts it in \(K\). Thus \(a\notin K\) is transcendental and the generic point maps to the generic point of \(\mathbf P^1\).

We prove finiteness in a form also useful for degrees. Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a nonconstant morphism of integral projective curves over the infinite field \(K\), with \(Y\) separated. It is dominant: if the image of the generic point of \(X\) were a closed point, continuity would put the entire image in that point. Every closed fibre is a proper closed subset of \(X\), hence has finite support. Fix a closed point \(y\in Y\), and embed \(X\) in \(\mathbf P^N_K\). A hyperplane can be chosen to miss the fibre and not contain \(X\): for each of its finitely many closed points, vanishing is a proper linear condition on the coefficients over \(K\); include one additional closed point of \(X\) if the fibre is empty. A finite union of proper linear subspaces does not exhaust a vector space over an infinite field. For example, choose a nonzero linear form annihilating each subspace; their product is a nonzero polynomial, which cannot vanish on all \(K^{N+1}\), by induction on the number of variables.

The intersection \(Z=X\cap H\) with that hyperplane is finite, and its image in \(Y\) is a finite closed set avoiding \(y\). Images of these closed points are closed: their residue fields are finite over \(K\), so the image residue field is also algebraic and finite over \(K\). Choose an affine neighbourhood \(V\) of \(y\) disjoint from this image. The graph of \(f\) is closed in \(X\times_KY\), since \(Y\) is separated. Hence it is closed in \(\mathbf P^N_K\times_KY\), and over \(V\) it lies in

\[ (\mathbf P^N_K\setminus H)\times_K V\simeq\mathbf A^N_V. \tag{X.6} \]

Its restriction is closed in this affine scheme, so \(f^{-1}V\) is affine. It is simultaneously a closed subscheme of \(\mathbf P^N_V\). W.4 therefore makes its coordinate module finite over the Noetherian coordinate ring of \(V\). This says precisely that \(f^{-1}V\to V\) is finite. Such neighbourhoods cover the closed points and the generic point of \(Y\), so \(f\) is finite. This proof uses projective coherent finiteness, and needs no general theorem about proper quasi-finite morphisms or formal functions. The comparison statement is [Stacks, curve divisor foundations].

X.4. Weighted fibre lengths and principal degree zero

Let \(f:X\to Y\) now be a nonconstant morphism between smooth integral projective curves over \(K\). X.3 makes it finite. At a closed point \(y\), put \(A=\mathcal O_{Y,y}\), with uniformizer \(\pi_y\). The finite semilocal algebra \(B=(f_*\mathcal O_X)_y\) is contained in \(K(X)\), and is torsion free over \(A\). Its generic fibre is the field \(K(X)\) over \(K(Y)\): inverting the nonzero elements of a target affine coordinate ring gives a finite-dimensional domain over its fraction field, hence a field with fraction field \(K(X)\). Denote its dimension by \(d\).

A finite torsion-free module \(M\) over this DVR is free. Lift a basis of \(M/\pi_yM\); Nakayama gives a surjection \(A^r\to M\). If a nonzero relation among these lifts existed, divide all its coefficients by their largest common power of \(\pi_y\). Torsion freeness ensures the divided vector is still a relation. At least one coefficient is now a unit, contradicting linear independence after reduction. Thus the lifts are a basis. Applied to \(B\), its rank is \(d\), and

\[ \dim_{\kappa(y)} B/\pi_yB=d. \tag{X.7} \]

This finite-dimensional algebra is the product of its local factors at the points above \(y\). One can see the decomposition directly: there are only finitely many maximal ideals, since the Chinese remainder surjections to products of their residue fields bound their number by the vector-space dimension. All primes are maximal. The nilradical is nilpotent, since it is finitely generated by nilpotent elements. The product of the distinct maximal ideals equals their intersection; a sufficiently high power is therefore zero. The Chinese remainder theorem for those powers gives the claimed local factors. In the factor at \(x\), the pullback of \(\pi_y\) is a unit times \(\pi_x^{e_x}\). The filtration by powers of \(\pi_x\) and (X.2) give

\[ \sum_{x\mid y} e_x[\kappa(x):\kappa(y)]=d, \qquad f^*[y]=\sum_{x\mid y}e_x[x]. \tag{X.8} \]

Here \(e_x\) is positive. In particular every fibre is nonempty, since \(B\) is free of positive rank; its nonzero finite-dimensional quotient has a maximal ideal. The generic fibre is nonempty too, so \(f\) is surjective. Formula (X.8) also shows

\[ \deg(f^*D)=d\deg D, \qquad \deg D=\sum_y m_y[\kappa(y):K], \tag{X.9} \]

first for points and then for any divisor. Pullback of the local frames in X.2 identifies \(f^*\mathcal O(D)\) with \(\mathcal O(f^*D)\), so it is also the line-bundle degree formula once degree is shown well-defined. These are the local multiplicity arguments of The multiplicative group on a curve, Proposition 8.1, with residue-field factors included.

Apply this to \(f_a\). Its fibres at zero and infinity have the same weighted degree \(d\); their difference is \(\operatorname{div}(a)\), by (X.1). Constants have zero divisor. Thus every principal divisor has degree zero. Formula (X.5) now makes degree an intrinsic function of the line bundle, and (X.9) applies to every line bundle, including negative degree. No separability of the extension \(K(X)/K(Y)\) was used.

Finally these arguments give the affine complement used in Q.1. The point exact sequences, W.4 finiteness and X.2 yield (Q.2) by adding or removing finitely many points. For \(m\geq g+1\), that formula gives a nonconstant section of \(\mathcal O_C(mp)\). Viewed as a rational function, it has no pole except possibly \(p\), and it must have that pole because the global regular functions are \(k\). X.3–X.4 give a finite surjective map to \(\mathbf P^1_k\). The inverse image of \(\mathbf A^1_k\) is exactly \(C\setminus\{p\}\), hence is affine by finiteness. Fibres over the infinitely many points of \(\mathbf P^1(k)\) also show that \(C(k)\) is infinite. The degree argument precedes this affine-complement deduction, so the latter has not been assumed in proving (Q.2).

Appendix Y. From local growth to smooth curve parameters

The curve arguments need regular local rings to be domains, polynomial local rings to be regular, and a precise dimension count after independent equations are imposed. The common-zero argument in R.1 also needs a height bound. We prove these statements together. All rings in a local dimension assertion are nonzero and Noetherian. Polynomial rings are Noetherian by the leading-coefficient argument in W.4; finite-module Artin–Rees and local separation are proved in L.1; we use the determinant form of Nakayama proved in U.1.

Y.1. Counting the layers of a finite module

Let \((R,\mathfrak m,\kappa)\) be local and let \(I\) have radical \(\mathfrak m\). Since \(\mathfrak m\) has finitely many generators, powers of those generators lie in \(I\), and a sufficiently large power of \(\mathfrak m\) lies in \(I\). A finite module killed by a power of \(\mathfrak m\) has a finite filtration whose successive quotients are finite-dimensional \(\kappa\)-spaces. It therefore has finite length. We use length with its usual additivity: a composition series in a submodule, followed by lifts of a composition series in the quotient, is a composition series in the middle module. Independence of its length is proved by the maximal-submodule induction in Noetherian and Artinian rings, Theorems 3.2–3.3.

For a finite module \(M\), put

\[ H_{I,M}(n)=\ell_R(M/I^nM) =\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\ell_R(I^jM/I^{j+1}M). \tag{Y.1} \]

If \(I\) is generated by \(r\) elements, its graded ring is a quotient of \((R/I)[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\), with each variable of degree one. The graded module \(\bigoplus I^jM/I^{j+1}M\) is finite over that polynomial ring: generators of \(M/IM\), multiplied by monomials in the generators of \(I\), generate every layer.

Here is the graded calculation needed for (Y.1). For any finite graded module \(G\) over \(A[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\), where \(A\) has finite length over \(R\), set \(F_G(t)=\sum_j\ell_R(G_j)t^j\). The grading is bounded below and every component has finite length. Write \(L=\operatorname{ann}_G(T_r)\) and \(C=G/T_rG\). The degreewise kernel and cokernel sequence of multiplication by \(T_r\) gives

\[ (1-t)F_G(t)=F_C(t)-tF_L(t). \tag{Y.2} \]

Both \(L\) and \(C\) are finite graded modules over the polynomial ring in \(r-1\) variables: finiteness of \(L\) follows from Noetherianness, and \(T_r\) kills both. For \(r=0\) only finitely many homogeneous degrees occur. Induction in (Y.2) proves that \(F_G(t)\) is a Laurent polynomial divided by \((1-t)^r\). For \(r>0\), the coefficient of \(t^n\) in \((1-t)^{-r}\) is \({n+r-1\choose r-1}\): it counts the ways to distribute \(n\) among \(r\) nonnegative exponents, or follows by multiplying geometric series. Summing coefficients adds one factor \((1-t)^{-1}\). Consequently (Y.1) agrees, for all sufficiently large \(n\), with a polynomial of degree at most \(r\). If \(r=0\), then \(I=0\), and the same assertion means a constant function.

For \(M\ne0\), Nakayama gives \(M/IM\ne0\). Thus the eventual polynomial is nonzero with positive leading coefficient. Denote its degree by \(d(M)\), and put \(d(0)=-\infty\). This degree is independent of \(I\): if \(I,J\) both have radical \(\mathfrak m\), choose positive \(a,b\) with \(I^a\subset J\) and \(J^b\subset I\). Then

\[ H_{J,M}(n)\le H_{I,M}(an),\qquad H_{I,M}(n)\le H_{J,M}(bn). \tag{Y.3} \]

Positive leading coefficients force equal degrees. Finally \(d(M)=0\) precisely when \(M\) has finite length. An eventually constant (Y.1) gives \(I^nM=I^{n+1}M\), hence \(I^nM=0\) by Nakayama. Conversely a composition series of length \(l\) over the local ring has all factors \(\kappa\), so \(\mathfrak m^lM=0\), making (Y.1) eventually constant.

Y.2. Exact sequences and a strict decrease

In a short exact sequence \(0\to N\to M\to Q\to0\), identify \(N\) with its image. L.1 gives, for a fixed \(c\) and \(n\ge c\),

\[ I^nN\subset N\cap I^nM\subset I^{n-c}N. \]

The kernel of \(M/I^nM\to Q/I^nQ\) is \(N/(N\cap I^nM)\). Taking lengths therefore gives

\[ H_{I,N}(n-c)+H_{I,Q}(n) \le H_{I,M}(n) \le H_{I,N}(n)+H_{I,Q}(n). \tag{Y.4} \]

The two bounding eventual polynomials have the same degree and the same leading coefficient. It follows that \(d(M)=\max(d(N),d(Q))\); in that largest degree their leading coefficients add. This also covers zero modules and degree zero. We only assert additivity of the largest-degree coefficient, not of the entire polynomial.

Suppose now that multiplication by \(x\in\mathfrak m\) is injective on nonzero \(M\). The quotient \(M/xM\) is nonzero by Nakayama. Apply (Y.4) to \(0\to M\xrightarrow{x}M\to M/xM\to0\). If the quotient had degree \(d(M)\), its positive leading coefficient would have to add to that of \(M\) without changing it, which is impossible. Hence

\[ d(M/xM)<d(M). \tag{Y.5} \]

Y.3. Prime chains, parameters and height

Write \(\delta(R)\) for the least number of generators of an ideal with radical \(\mathfrak m\). We prove

\[ \dim R=d(R)=\delta(R). \tag{Y.6} \]

First \(\dim R\le d(R)\), by induction on \(d(R)\). If this degree is zero, Y.1 gives \(\mathfrak m^n=0\) for some \(n\), so \(\mathfrak m\) is the only prime. For a chain \(\mathfrak p_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\mathfrak p_l\), there is nothing to prove if \(l=0\). Otherwise choose \(x\in\mathfrak p_1\setminus\mathfrak p_0\). In the local domain \(B=R/\mathfrak p_0\), multiplication by \(x\) is injective, and the positive-length chain ensures that \(x\) is a nonunit. Y.2 gives \(d(B/xB)<d(B)\le d(R)\). Lengths and growth degrees for these quotient rings are the same as for their underlying \(R\)-modules, since their simple factor is still \(\kappa\). The remaining chain has length \(l-1\) in \(B/xB\). Induction gives \(l-1\le d(B/xB)\le d(R)-1\), as required. This also proves that the local dimension is finite.

For clarity, the minimal-prime facts used next need no dimension theorem. Ascending chains of ideals make descending chains of closed subsets of \(\operatorname{Spec}R\) stabilize. A closed subset without a finite decomposition into irreducible closed subsets would have a minimal such counterexample; splitting it into two proper closed subsets gives a contradiction. Irreducible closed subsets are exactly \(V(\mathfrak p)\) for primes, so there are finitely many minimal primes and every prime contains one. Here the radical of an ideal is the intersection of primes containing it: if an element is not in the radical, localize at its powers and take a maximal ideal in the resulting nonzero quotient. This also proves the stated correspondence with irreducible closed subsets.

Induct on \(D=\dim R\) to prove \(\delta(R)\le D\). If \(D=0\), the only prime is \(\mathfrak m\), so the zero ideal already has radical \(\mathfrak m\). If \(D>0\), no minimal prime is \(\mathfrak m\). Choose \(x\in\mathfrak m\) outside their union. The finite avoidance argument is explicit: for incomparable primes \(\mathfrak p_i\), choose \(a_i\in\mathfrak m\setminus\mathfrak p_i\) and, for each \(j\ne i\), choose \(b_{ij}\in\mathfrak p_j\setminus\mathfrak p_i\). The sum \(\sum_i a_i\prod_{j\ne i}b_{ij}\) is outside each \(\mathfrak p_i\). A single prime uses the empty product. Every prime chain in \(R/xR\) lifts to a chain in \(R\) whose bottom contains a strictly smaller minimal prime, because that minimal prime does not contain \(x\). Therefore \(\dim(R/xR)\le D-1\). Induction produces at most \(D-1\) elements generating an ideal of definition in this quotient. Their lifts together with \(x\) give \(\delta(R)\le D\). Finally Y.1 bounds \(d(R)\) by the number of generators of any ideal of definition. These three inequalities prove (Y.6).

If \(\mathfrak p\) is minimal over an ideal generated by \(r\) elements in a Noetherian ring, localize at \(\mathfrak p\). The extended ideal has radical the maximal ideal: a smaller prime containing it would contradict minimality. Its \(r\) generators and (Y.6) give

\[ \operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=\dim R_{\mathfrak p}\le r. \tag{Y.7} \]

For \(x\in\mathfrak m\), lift a minimal system of parameters of \(R/xR\) and adjoin \(x\). Equation (Y.6) gives \(\dim(R/xR)\ge\dim R-1\). If \(x\) avoids all minimal primes, the chain-prepending argument gives the reverse inequality. A nonzerodivisor does avoid them: in \(R_{\mathfrak p}\) for a minimal prime \(\mathfrak p\), the maximal ideal is the nilradical, so any element of it is nilpotent. Multiplication by a nonzerodivisor remains injective after localization; a nilpotent element cannot act injectively on this nonzero ring. We have proved

\[ \dim(R/xR)=\dim R-1 \quad\text{if }x\in\mathfrak m\text{ is a nonzerodivisor}. \tag{Y.8} \]

This proof does not need the theory of associated primes.

Y.4. Regular parameters and their initial forms

Nakayama identifies \(e=\dim_\kappa\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\) with the least number of generators of \(\mathfrak m\). Thus (Y.6) gives \(\dim R\le e\). Suppose equality holds, and set \(D=e=\dim R\); this is the definition of a regular local ring. Choose minimal generators \(x_1,\ldots,x_D\). They give a graded surjection

\[ \kappa[T_1,\ldots,T_D]\longrightarrow \operatorname{gr}_{\mathfrak m}R, \qquad T_i\longmapsto\operatorname{in}(x_i). \tag{Y.9} \]

For \(D=0\), Nakayama gives \(\mathfrak m=0\), so \(R=\kappa\). For \(D>0\), a nonzero homogeneous relation \(F\) of degree \(a>0\) in (Y.9) would bound \(H_{\mathfrak m,R}(n)\) by the number of monomials of degree less than \(n\) in the quotient by \(F\). Multiplication by \(F\) is injective in the polynomial ring over the field. For \(n\ge a\), that number is

\[ {n+D-1\choose D}-{n-a+D-1\choose D}, \tag{Y.10} \]

which has degree at most \(D-1\). This contradicts (Y.6). Hence (Y.9) is an isomorphism.

L.1 separation shows that every nonzero element of \(R\) has a finite \(\mathfrak m\)-adic order. Its initial form is nonzero in the polynomial domain (Y.9). Products of nonzero initial forms remain nonzero, so orders add and products of nonzero elements do not vanish. Thus \(R\) is a domain. In particular \(x_1\) is a nonzerodivisor, and the order calculation gives

\[ (x_1)\cap\mathfrak m^n=x_1\mathfrak m^{n-1}\qquad(n\ge1). \tag{Y.11} \]

Indeed, if \(x_1b\in\mathfrak m^n\) with \(b\ne0\), additivity of order forces \(b\in\mathfrak m^{n-1}\). To compute the graded ring of \(R/x_1R\), a kernel class in degree \(n\) is represented by \(u=x_1b+v\), with \(u\in\mathfrak m^n\) and \(v\in\mathfrak m^{n+1}\). Equation (Y.11) identifies its initial form as a multiple of \(T_1\), and every such multiple occurs. Consequently

\[ \operatorname{gr}(R/x_1R)=\kappa[T_2,\ldots,T_D]. \tag{Y.12} \]

Its length-growth degree is \(D-1\), hence so is its dimension by (Y.6); its embedding dimension is also \(D-1\). The quotient is therefore regular. Repeating proves that the entire list is a regular sequence and that quotienting by its first \(c\) terms gives a regular local domain of dimension \(D-c\). Any independent list of classes in \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\) extends to a basis, so the same conclusion applies to any such chosen list of elements.

We will also use the converse lifting step. If \(x\in\mathfrak m\) is a nonzerodivisor and \(R/xR\) is regular of dimension \(e\), then (Y.8) gives \(\dim R=e+1\). Lifts of its \(e\) maximal-ideal generators, together with \(x\), generate \(\mathfrak m\). Thus the embedding dimension is at most \(e+1\), and the general reverse bound proves regularity of \(R\). Apply this step repeatedly when the quotient is by a regular sequence.

Y.5. Polynomial local rings over any field

Let \(A\) be a Noetherian ring whose prime localizations are regular. For a prime \(\mathfrak q\) of \(A[t]\), put \(\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap A\), \(R=A_{\mathfrak p}\) and \(B=A[t]_{\mathfrak q}\). Choose a regular system of parameters \(a_1,\ldots,a_d\) of \(R\), whose regular-sequence property was just proved. The map \(R\to B\) is flat: polynomial extension is free, localization is exact, and tensoring these operations preserves exact sequences. Hence multiplication by each \(a_i\) stays injective after the preceding ones are killed in \(B\). The quotients are nonzero, since the \(a_i\) belong to the maximal ideal of \(B\).

The last quotient is a local ring of \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)[t]\), either its fraction field or its localization at one monic irreducible polynomial \(h\). Euclidean division proves the description of the prime ideals of this one-variable ring. These two local rings are regular of dimensions \(\varepsilon=0\) and \(\varepsilon=1\), respectively: in the latter case the maximal ideal is generated by \(h\), and the only prime chain is \((0)\subsetneq(h)\). Repeated use of (Y.8) gives \(\dim B=d+\varepsilon\); the lifting step in Y.4 gives regularity of \(B\). Induction starting with a field proves regularity of all polynomial local rings, without a homological global-dimension theorem or a flat-local dimension formula.

The same induction calculates their dimensions. In the fraction-field case the residue field is \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)(t)\), adding one transcendence degree; in the irreducible-polynomial case it is finite algebraic over \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)\), adding none. Thus for any field \(K\) and any prime \(\mathfrak q\subset K[t_1,\ldots,t_N]\),

\[ \dim K[t_1,\ldots,t_N]_{\mathfrak q} =N-\operatorname{trdeg}_K\kappa(\mathfrak q). \tag{Y.13} \]

We also need the residue-field statement at closed points. The normalization construction of K.1 works over every field: a sufficiently separated choice of integer weights makes a selected highest weighted monomial unique, and division by its nonzero coefficient makes the resulting relation monic in the last variable. Neither step uses characteristic zero or an infinite field. Successively eliminating dependent generators makes any finite-type domain finite integral over a polynomial subring on algebraically independent elements. If the domain is itself a field, that polynomial subring must be a field: an integral equation for the inverse of a nonzero base element, multiplied by the appropriate power of that element, puts its inverse back in the base. A polynomial ring in a positive number of variables is not a field. Thus a field of finite type over \(K\) is finite algebraic over \(K\). Applied to a maximal quotient, this proves the assertion for closed points, including over imperfect fields. Over an algebraically closed \(K\), the residue field is \(K\). If an element \(f\) in a finite-type algebra is not nilpotent, its localization at \(f\) is nonzero and still of finite type; a maximal quotient there gives a closed \(K\)-point where \(f\ne0\). This is the strong Nullstellensatz used in R.1.

Y.6. Smooth presentations and the dimension used above

We finish by verifying the direction of the smoothness criterion actually needed in V and X. Suppose \(S\) is a finitely presented, formally smooth algebra over a field \(K\), and write \(S=P/I\), where \(P=K[t_1,\ldots,t_N]\). Formal smoothness applied to \(P/I^2\to S\) lifts the identity to a \(K\)-algebra section \(\sigma:S\to P/I^2\). The function

\[ \delta:P\longrightarrow I/I^2,\qquad \delta(p)=p-\sigma(\overline p)\pmod{I^2} \tag{Y.14} \]

is a \(K\)-derivation, with values in the \(S\)-module \(I/I^2\), and sends \(f\in I\) to its class. Indeed multiplication of two differences vanishes modulo \(I^2\), giving the Leibniz rule. A derivation on a polynomial ring is determined by its values on the variables: induction on monomials gives \(\delta(p)=\sum_i (\partial p/\partial t_i)\delta(t_i)\). Therefore the map

\[ I/I^2\longrightarrow S^N,\qquad f\longmapsto(\partial f/\partial t_i)_i \tag{Y.15} \]

has a left inverse supplied by \(\delta\). In particular it is a split injection. Its cokernel represents derivations of \(S\), because precisely the derivatives of the relations must vanish; this is the differential module \(\Omega_{S/K}\). Both \(I/I^2\) and that cokernel are finite projective, as direct summands of \(S^N\). Finite projective modules are locally free by the finite-flat local argument in U.1.

At a prime of \(S\) choose \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I\) whose classes are a basis of \((I/I^2)\) at that local ring. The split injection (Y.15) makes their gradient rows independent over the residue field; choose a nonzero \(c\)-column minor. At the polynomial prime \(\mathfrak Q\) above this point, Nakayama applied to the finite module \(I_{\mathfrak Q}/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\) gives \(I_{\mathfrak Q}=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\): its equality with \(I_{\mathfrak Q}\) times itself follows from the basis assertion modulo \(I^2\), and \(I_{\mathfrak Q}\) is inside the maximal ideal. Finite generation lets one invert a single element outside \(\mathfrak Q\) so that these generators and the nonzero minor work on a neighborhood. This supplies the required standard smooth presentation locally.

Now Y.5 makes \(P_{\mathfrak Q}\) regular. The classes of the \(f_i\) in its maximal ideal modulo its square are independent: their images under the differential map are the independent gradient rows, and the differential of a product of two maximal-ideal elements vanishes over the residue field. Y.4 therefore makes their quotient a regular local domain and gives

\[ \dim S_{\mathfrak q} =N-c-\operatorname{trdeg}_K\kappa(\mathfrak q). \tag{Y.16} \]

On this neighborhood the invertible minor identifies the differential module with a free module of rank \(N-c\), by solving the \(c\) independent linear relations. At a closed point, Y.5 makes the transcendence degree zero. Hence its local dimension is exactly that differential rank. Formal smoothness is preserved by field extension: restrict a lifting problem for \(S\otimes_K K'\) to \(S\), lift it there, and combine the lift with the given structural map from \(K'\). Finite presentation is also preserved. The entire argument consequently applies after any field extension, with no assumption on residue-field separability.

In V.3 the differential rank of the coefficient chart is \(d\), so every closed local ring on that chart is regular of dimension \(d\). This also gives dimension \(d\) of the chart: every prime chain extends to a maximal ideal, and a closed local ring has dimension \(d\). In X.1 the smooth curve has differential rank one after every field extension, so its closed local rings are one-dimensional regular domains. These are exactly the local inputs for the valuation and divisor calculations. Finally the strong Nullstellensatz in Y.5 and the height bound (Y.7) give the common-nonzero-zero assertion in R.1. Each application uses a proof given here, in addition to the previously established finite-module and normalization arguments.

Appendix Z. Splitting algebras and killing scalar two-cocycles

We prove the algebra and descent statements needed for (R.4). The fields to which R applies contain the algebraically closed field \(k\), and are therefore infinite. This lets us construct a separable splitting field by choosing one element with distinct eigenvalues. The final step turns a scalar two-cocycle into semilinear matrices and exhibits its coboundary after splitting the associated algebra.

Z.1. The finite simple-algebra calculation

Let \(A\) be a finite-dimensional simple algebra over a field \(F\). A nonzero left ideal of least positive dimension is a simple left module. The sum of all simple left ideals is a nonzero two-sided ideal: right multiplication maps any simple left ideal either to zero or isomorphically onto another simple left ideal. Simplicity makes that sum all of \(A\). Choose a direct sum of simple left ideals of maximal dimension. Every other simple left ideal either meets it trivially, so could be added, or is contained in it. Maximality thus makes the direct sum equal to \(A\).

All its simple summands have one isomorphism type \(S\). To see this, group a chosen decomposition by type. A homomorphism between nonisomorphic simple modules is zero, since any nonzero homomorphism is injective and surjective. Projections therefore show that any simple submodule of a given type lies in that type's group of summands. Right multiplication preserves each such group. Each is consequently a two-sided ideal, and simplicity permits only one. Write \({}_AA\simeq S^r\), and set \(E=\operatorname{End}_A(S)\). The same kernel-and-image argument makes \(E\) a division algebra. Matrices of endomorphisms give

\[ A^{\mathrm{op}}=\operatorname{End}_A({}_AA)\simeq M_r(E), \qquad A\simeq M_r(D),\quad D=E^{\mathrm{op}}. \tag{Z.1} \]

The first equality sends an endomorphism to its value at \(1\): the endomorphism is right multiplication by that value, which reverses multiplication. Transposition identifies the opposite matrix algebra with matrices over the opposite division algebra. The center of \(M_r(D)\) is the scalar matrices over \(Z(D)\), as is checked by commuting with the matrix units and then the diagonal entries. Thus, if \(A\) is central over \(F\), so is \(D\). This proves the part of the finite Wedderburn theorem used below.

Central simplicity survives every extension \(K/F\). Here is the tensor argument, including infinite extensions. In a nonzero two-sided ideal of \(A\otimes_F K\), choose a nonzero element \(x=\sum_{i=1}^t a_i\otimes b_i\) of least tensor length, with the \(b_i\) linearly independent over \(F\) and \(a_1\ne0\). Since the ideal \(Aa_1A\) is all of \(A\), choose \(u_j,v_j\) with \(\sum_j u_ja_1v_j=1\). Then \(y=\sum_j(u_j\otimes1)x(v_j\otimes1)\) has first coefficient \(1\), so is nonzero. Its commutator with \(a\otimes1\) has at most \(t-1\) terms and must vanish by minimality. Independence of the \(b_i\) makes all remaining coefficients central in \(A\), hence scalar. Thus \(y=1\otimes b\) for nonzero \(b\in K\). It is a unit, proving simplicity. For any central element, the same coefficientwise commutator argument puts it in \(1\otimes K\), proving centrality.

Over an algebraic closure \(\overline F\), a finite-dimensional division algebra has only scalar elements. An element satisfies a polynomial relation; factor that polynomial into linear factors over \(\overline F\). Evaluation at this one element respects their product, and a division algebra has no zero divisors, so one factor vanishes. Applying (Z.1) after scalar extension gives

\[ A\otimes_F\overline F\simeq M_n(\overline F), \qquad \dim_F A=n^2. \tag{Z.2} \]

We also need only the matrix case of inner automorphisms. For an automorphism of \(M_n(K)\), let \(f_{ij}\) be the images of its matrix units. Choose nonzero \(v\) with \(f_{11}v=v\), and put \(v_i=f_{i1}v\). The identities \(f_{ij}v_l=\delta_{jl}v_i\) show that the \(n\) vectors \(v_i\) are linearly independent, by applying \(f_{1j}\) to a proposed relation. They are a basis, and in that basis the \(f_{ij}\) are the ordinary matrix units. Thus the automorphism is conjugation by a change-of-basis matrix. A matrix commuting with all matrix units is scalar.

Z.2. A separable splitting field and the norm form

Assume \(F\) infinite and let \(D\) be central division, with \(\dim_F D=n^2\). Fix (Z.2) and an \(F\)-basis \(a_1,\ldots,a_{n^2}\). Its images \(B_i\) form an \(\overline F\)-basis of \(M_n(\overline F)\). For scalar coordinates \(z\), set \(B(z)=\sum_i z_iB_i\) and consider the polynomial

\[ \Delta(z)=\det\bigl(\operatorname{tr}(B(z)^{i+j})\bigr)_{0\le i,j<n}. \tag{Z.3} \]

If the eigenvalues of \(B(z)\), counted with multiplicity, are \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n\), this determinant is \(\prod_{i<j}(\lambda_j-\lambda_i)^2\). Indeed a matrix over an algebraically closed field can be made upper triangular by choosing an eigenvector and continuing on the quotient. Its power traces are \(\sum_l\lambda_l^{i+j}\); the displayed matrix is the product of the Vandermonde matrix with its transpose. The Vandermonde determinant is the indicated product: it vanishes whenever two variables coincide, has the same total degree as that product, and comparison of the leading monomial gives coefficient one. In particular (Z.3) is not the zero polynomial, since the \(B_i\) span a diagonal matrix with distinct entries. This works in every characteristic.

A nonzero polynomial over \(\overline F\) cannot vanish on every tuple from infinite \(F\).
