Induct on the number of variables, using the one-variable root bound and then a nonzero coefficient polynomial. Choose \(z\in F^{n^2}\) with \(\Delta(z)\ne0\), and let \(a=\sum_i z_i a_i\in D\). Its matrix has \(n\) distinct eigenvalues, so its minimal polynomial over \(\overline F\) is the product of the \(n\) distinct linear factors. The least degree of a relation among \(1,a,a^2,\ldots\) does not change under a field extension: ranks of matrices with entries in \(F\) do not change, as their nonzero minors and zero minors do not change. A linear system with coefficients in \(F\) that is soluble over \(\overline F\) is soluble over \(F\), by row reduction. Thus the unique monic minimal polynomial of \(a\) over \(F\) has degree \(n\) and those same distinct roots.

The commutative finite-dimensional algebra \(L=F[a]\) is a domain inside \(D\), hence a field: multiplication by a nonzero element is injective and therefore surjective as a linear map. We have proved that \(L/F\) is separable of degree \(n\). Regard \(D\) as a right \(L\)-space, of dimension \(n\). The map

\[ D\otimes_F L\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_L(D), \qquad u\otimes l\longmapsto(x\longmapsto uxl) \tag{Z.4} \]

is multiplicative because \(L\) is commutative. Its domain is simple by Z.1, and it preserves the identity, so is injective. Both sides have \(L\)-dimension \(n^2\), making it an isomorphism. A finite Galois extension \(E/F\) containing \(L\) therefore splits \(D\). Such an extension is obtained by adjoining all roots of its separable minimal polynomial. The elementary Galois facts used here and below are detailed in Z.3.

Choose a splitting \(\phi:D\otimes_F E\to M_n(E)\). For the same basis of \(D\), write \(C_i=\phi(a_i)\). The polynomial

\[ N(z)=\det\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n^2}z_iC_i\right) \tag{Z.5} \]

is homogeneous of degree \(n\), and all its coefficients belong to \(F\). For \(g\in\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)\), transport \(1\otimes g\) across \(\phi\). Composing that semilinear automorphism with inverse entrywise \(g\) gives an \(E\)-algebra automorphism of matrices. Z.1 makes it inner, so \(g(C_i)\) are simultaneously conjugate to \(C_i\). Taking determinants gives \(g(N)=N\) coefficientwise. The fixed-field assertion in Z.3 puts those coefficients in \(F\).

The value of (Z.5) at an element of \(D\) is zero precisely when that element is not invertible. One direction follows by extending an inverse. Conversely, if the matrix is invertible, left multiplication by the element on \(D\) becomes invertible after extension to \(E\). Its determinant over \(F\) is consequently nonzero, so there is already a right inverse in \(D\). Injectivity of that left multiplication turns a right inverse into a two-sided inverse. This argument also works for a general finite algebra once a matrix splitting is given.

For an infinite \(C_1\)-field \(F\), (Z.5) rules out \(n>1\): it would be a degree-\(n\) homogeneous form in \(n^2>n\) variables, with a nonzero zero, contrary to division. Hence every central division algebra over \(F\) is \(F\), and (Z.1) makes every finite central simple algebra a matrix algebra. In particular its Brauer group is zero. R.1 proves the required \(C_1\) property for every field algebraic over the function field under consideration, so this conclusion holds for all those fields.

Z.3. Finite field automorphisms and semilinear descent

We record the field facts used in this calculation over infinite \(F\). An embedding of a field into an algebraically closed field extends over a finite algebraic extension by adjoining generators in succession and choosing a root of each transported minimal polynomial. If the extension is separable, the number of embeddings is its degree: at each step the distinct roots count the degree, and the counts multiply. For two separable generators \(a,b\), only finitely many \(c\in F\) make two distinct embeddings take the same value on \(a+cb\). Choose \(c\) outside that set. The element \(a+cb\) then has as many distinct conjugates as the degree of \(F(a,b)/F\), so it generates this extension. Induction gives the primitive-element assertion for every finite separable extension over infinite \(F\).

For a finite splitting field \(E/F\) of separable polynomials, every embedding permutes their roots and thus maps \(E\) onto itself. There are \([E:F]\) such automorphisms. Their fixed field is \(F\): if \(x\in E\setminus F\), its separable minimal polynomial has another root, and the corresponding embedding of \(F(x)\) extends to an automorphism of \(E\) moving \(x\). More generally, if \(H\) is any subgroup of this finite automorphism group and \(K=E^H\), a primitive generator \(a\) for the separable extension \(E/K\) satisfies \(\prod_{h\in H}(T-h(a))\in K[T]\). Thus \([E:K]\le |H|\), while its \(|H|\) distinct automorphisms give the reverse inequality. Hence \(\operatorname{Gal}(E/E^H)=H\) and \([E:E^H]=|H|\). Normal subgroups give normal fixed-field extensions by the same conjugation action. These arguments give the finite fixed-field statements needed for Galois splitting and finite quotient cochains.

Distinct automorphisms \(g:E\to E\) are linearly independent as functions with coefficients in \(E\). If a relation of least positive length existed, all its coefficients would be nonzero. Choose an element \(b\) on which its first automorphism and another differ. Subtract the first automorphism's value at \(b\) times the relation at \(x\) from the relation at \(bx\). One term disappears and another remains, giving a shorter nonzero relation. A one-term relation is impossible. This proves independence.

Let \(Q=\operatorname{Gal}(E/F)\), and let \(V\) be a finite-dimensional \(E\)-space with a genuine semilinear \(Q\)-action \(T_g\). Its fixed vectors span \(V\) over \(E\). Otherwise choose a nonzero \(E\)-linear functional \(\lambda\) annihilating their span. For every \(v\in V\) and \(b\in E\), the vector \(\sum_g g(b)T_g(v)\) is fixed, by reindexing after applying any \(T_h\). Hence

\[ \sum_{g\in Q}g(b)\lambda(T_g(v))=0\qquad(b\in E). \tag{Z.6} \]

Independence of automorphisms forces each coefficient to vanish; the coefficient for the identity gives \(\lambda(v)=0\) for every \(v\), a contradiction. Choose an \(E\)-basis consisting of fixed vectors. A vector in that basis is fixed exactly when each coefficient lies in \(E^Q=F\). Consequently multiplication gives an isomorphism

\[ E\otimes_F V^Q\xrightarrow{\sim}V. \tag{Z.7} \]

When \(V\) is an algebra and the action is by semilinear algebra automorphisms, this map is also multiplicative and unital, so it is algebra descent. This finite-dimensional proof needs neither a trace-dual basis nor a normal-basis theorem.

The same independence proves scalar Hilbert 90 in the convention used for cochains. For \(b_{gh}=b_g g(b_h)\), choose \(x\in E\) such that \(u=\sum_g b_g^{-1}g(x)\ne0\), possible by independence. Applying \(h\), the cocycle identity and a change of index give \(h(u)=b_hu\). Thus \(b_h=h(u)/u\). Continuous cocycles on an absolute Galois group reduce to this finite calculation by the finite-quotient comparison in R.3.

Z.4. A scalar two-cocycle becomes a coboundary

Let \(F\) be one of the fields in R.1, and fix a continuous scalar two-cocycle on \(G_F\). By the continuous-cochain finite-quotient comparison (AA.4), it is represented over some finite Galois \(E/F\) by \(c:Q\times Q\to E^\times\), where

\[ c(g,h)c(gh,t)=g(c(h,t))c(g,ht). \tag{Z.8} \]

We can arrange \(c(1,g)=c(g,1)=1\). In fact (Z.8) gives \(c(1,g)=a\) independent of \(g\), and \(c(g,1)=g(a)\). Multiplying by the coboundary of the constant one-cochain \(a^{-1}\) gives those normalizations.

On the \(E\)-space \(W\) with basis \((e_h)_{h\in Q}\), define invertible semilinear maps

\[ T_g(be_h)=g(b)c(g,h)e_{gh}. \tag{Z.9} \]

Substitution in (Z.8) gives \(T_gT_h=c(g,h)T_{gh}\), and \(T_1=1\). Thus conjugation by \(T_g\) is a genuine semilinear group action on \(\operatorname{End}_E(W)\), since its scalar multiplier cancels. Let

\[ A=\operatorname{End}_E(W)^Q. \tag{Z.10} \]

Z.3 gives \(E\otimes_F A=\operatorname{End}_E(W)\). The algebra \(A\) is central simple over \(F\). A nonzero proper two-sided ideal would stay nonzero and proper after extending scalars, by vector-space dimensions, contradicting simplicity of a matrix algebra. For completeness, that simplicity follows by multiplying any nonzero matrix entry in an ideal by matrix units and its scalar inverse to obtain every matrix unit. A central element of \(A\) commutes after extension with every endomorphism of \(W\), since \(A\) spans them over \(E\); it is scalar. Invariance then puts that scalar in \(F\).

By Z.2 and R.1, \(A\simeq M_m(F)\), with \(m=|Q|\) by dimensions. Choose its matrix units inside \(\operatorname{End}_E(W)\). The basis construction in Z.1 puts these units into their usual form. In this basis each \(T_g\) fixes them under conjugation. Write \(T_g=B_g g\), with \(g\) acting entrywise on coordinates. The matrix units have entries in \(F\), so \(B_g\) commutes with all of them and is scalar, say \(B_g=b_g I\). Comparing multipliers gives

\[ c(g,h)=b_g g(b_h)b_{gh}^{-1}. \tag{Z.11} \]

Thus \(c\) is a coboundary at this same finite stage. Inflating proves \(H^2(G_F,(F^s)^\times)=0\); the identical argument applies to every field algebraic over \(F\). Along with Z.2, this gives both vanishings in (R.4). The full Brauer–cohomology isomorphism remains the theorem in R.2's programme reference; the vanishing used in R.3 follows already from the explicit scalar identity (Z.11).

Appendix AA. Continuous cochains and the Sylow reduction

We supply the group-theoretic steps used in R.3–R.4. In particular the Sylow subgroup can have infinite index in the profinite group. The transfer calculation below is performed in a finite quotient containing both a cocycle and a primitive for its restriction.

AA.1. Compact finite limits and fixed fields

A product of finite discrete spaces is compact. Here is the form of the proof we need. Extend a family of closed sets with the finite intersection property to an ultrafilter, using Zorn's lemma. Exactly one cell of each finite coordinate partition lies in that ultrafilter: two disjoint cells cannot both belong, and if none belonged their complements would have empty intersection. These selected coordinates define a point. Every basic neighborhood of that point lies in the ultrafilter, so the point lies in every original closed set, by closedness. Compatibility equations in a product of finite sets are closed conditions. If every finite collection of such equations can be satisfied, their whole system therefore has a solution. This also proves that a directed inverse system of nonempty finite sets with surjective transition maps has a nonempty limit, and that each limit projection is surjective, by imposing one prescribed coordinate value.

We use a profinite group in its inverse-limit topology. It is compact and Hausdorff, and the open normal subgroups form an identity-neighborhood basis. Each has finite index. A continuous map from a finite product of profinite groups to a discrete set has finite image and factors through one finite quotient in each coordinate: choose finitely many basic open rectangles on which it is constant and intersect their open normal coordinate subgroups. If finitely many values belong to a discrete continuous module, the subgroup can be shrunk further to fix them all. For a closed subgroup \(H\subset G\), its topology is induced from \(G\), so the subgroups \(H\cap U\), for open normal \(U\subset G\), give the corresponding basis in \(H\).

For clarity, the Galois group assertions needed in R.3 are Profinite groups and infinite Galois theory, Section 3, with the finite algebra proved in Section 0 and also in Z.3. Every finite subset of a separable closure lies in a finite Galois extension. Compatible automorphisms of those finite fields define an automorphism of their union, giving the inverse-limit description. Restrictions to finite Galois fields are surjective: the successive-root extension of an embedding extends through an algebraic closure by a maximal-extension argument, and normality makes it preserve the separable closure. The image of that extended embedding is algebraically closed and contains the base field, so contains all elements algebraic over that base; thus it is an automorphism. This is the extension argument written out in the cited section.

Here is the closed-subgroup consequence in the exact form we use. For closed \(H\subset G_F\), put \(L=(F^s)^H\). If \(g\notin H\), compactness and the open normal basis give a finite quotient in which its image lies outside the image of \(H\). Finite Galois correspondence supplies an element of the latter image's fixed field moved by \(g\). That element belongs to \(L\), so the subgroup fixing \(L\) is exactly \(H\). The field \(F^s\) is algebraic separable over \(L\): the minimal polynomial over \(L\) of any of its elements divides its separable polynomial over \(F\). It is already separably closed, hence is a separable closure of \(L\). Its Krull topology over \(L\) is the induced topology, since both have the finite-element stabilizers as a basis. Consequently \(G_L=H\) as a topological group.

AA.2. Why these continuous cochains compute cohomology

For a discrete continuous \(G\)-module \(M\), use equivariant homogeneous cochains

\[ \begin{aligned} C_h^n(G,M)=\{f:G^{n+1}\to M\text{ continuous}:{}&\\ f(gg_0,\ldots,gg_n)&=g f(g_0,\ldots,g_n)\}, \end{aligned} \tag{AA.1} \]

with the alternating omission differential. The two orders of omitting a pair of entries have opposite signs, so \(d^2=0\). An equivariant cochain is determined by the arbitrary continuous function \(f(1,x_1,\ldots,x_n)\); its recovery formula is \(f(g_0,\ldots,g_n)=g_0 f(1,g_0^{-1}g_1,\ldots,g_0^{-1}g_n)\). Thus a surjection of discrete modules induces a surjection of cochain groups: lift the finitely many values of that arbitrary function, using its clopen fibres. A short exact sequence of modules gives a short exact sequence of cochain complexes. The cycle-lifting argument in T.4 gives its natural long exact sequence. Degree-zero cohomology is \(M^G\).

For an abelian group \(A\), put

\[ I_G(A)=\operatorname{Maps}_{\mathrm{cont}}(G,A), \qquad (g b)(t)=b(tg). \tag{AA.2} \]

This is discrete, by finite-quotient factorization. The functor is exact, since a function's finitely many values can be lifted through any surjection. Evaluation at \(1\) identifies \(G\)-maps \(M\to I_G(A)\) with abelian-group maps \(M\to A\); the inverse sends \(\psi\) to \(m\mapsto[t\mapsto\psi(tm)]\). These are inverse by equivariance, and the displayed functions are continuous because the orbit of \(m\) is finite. Thus \(I_G\) is right adjoint to the exact forgetful functor and preserves injectives. The map \(m\mapsto[t\mapsto tm]\) embeds \(M\) equivariantly in \(I_G(M)\).

There are enough injective abelian groups. One direct construction embeds any \(A\) in a divisible group. At one stage adjoin a symbol \(e_{a,n}\) for every \(a\in A\), \(n>0\), with relation \(n e_{a,n}=a\). The map from \(A\) into this quotient is injective: a finite sum of these relations with zero symbol coordinates has every coefficient zero. Repeat for all elements of the new group and take the union over countably many stages. Every element then has a root of every positive order, so the union is divisible. A divisible group \(D\) is injective: extend a map from a subgroup maximally by Zorn. To adjoin an omitted element \(x\), if no positive multiple of \(x\) lies in the current subgroup, choose its image arbitrarily. Otherwise choose the least positive \(n\) with \(nx\) in that subgroup and solve \(ny=f(nx)\) in \(D\). The formula \(f(b+mx)=f(b)+my\) is well-defined, since every relation has \(m\) a multiple of \(n\). Either choice contradicts maximality unless the domain is the whole group. Embedding the underlying group of \(M\) in such a \(D\) and using \(M\to I_G(D)\) proves enough injectives for discrete \(G\)-modules.

Positive-degree cochain cohomology of \(I_G(A)\) is zero. Evaluation at \(1\) takes an equivariant cochain with these coefficients to an arbitrary continuous function \(h:G^{n+1}\to A\). Its inverse is \(f(g_0,\ldots,g_n)(t)=h(tg_0,\ldots,tg_n)\). These formulas are continuous also as maps into the discrete function group: a finite quotient through which \(h\) factors works uniformly for the argument tuples. The differential becomes ordinary omission on \(h\). Inserting \(1\) as the first argument contracts the augmented omission complex; expansion gives \(ds+sd=1\). Therefore

\[ H^q(C_h^\bullet(G,I_G(A)))=0\qquad(q>0). \tag{AA.3} \]

For an injective \(G\)-module \(J\), the embedding \(J\to I_G(J)\) splits equivariantly. Its positive cochain cohomology is a direct summand of zero, so is zero. This proves that the cochain groups compute the right derived functors of invariants. More explicitly, embed \(M\) in an injective \(J\) with quotient \(N\). Both the cochain and injective-resolution long exact sequences identify degree one with \(\operatorname{coker}(J^G\to N^G)\), and identify degree \(q>1\) with degree \(q-1\) for \(N\). Iterating gives the comparison in every degree; compatible choices for maps are constructed as in T.4, and T.3's resolution homotopies give independence of choices. We can henceforth write these cohomology groups as \(H^q(G,M)\).

The finite-factorization observation in AA.1, applied to the arbitrary inhomogeneous coordinates of a cochain, gives

\[ H^q(G,M)=\underset{U\trianglelefteq_{\rm open}G}{\operatorname{colim}} H^q(G/U,M^U). \tag{AA.4} \]

Indeed every cochain and every equality of cochains occurs at a common finite quotient after shrinking \(U\) to fix their values. Transition maps are inflation with inclusion of coefficient invariants. Kernels and images commute with this filtered union: a cycle equation or a boundary equation involves finitely many elements and holds at one stage. The same finite-value argument shows that cochain cohomology commutes with filtered colimits of coefficient modules. Lift finitely many values to a common stage; any equality between two such lifts holds at a later common stage. These arguments prove both assertions at the level of complexes before passing to cohomology.

AA.3. Constructing compatible Sylow subgroups

Let a finite group \(Q\) have order \(\ell^a m\), with \(\ell\nmid m\). The number of subsets of \(Q\) with \(\ell^a\) elements is not divisible by \(\ell\). In fact the coefficient of \(T^{\ell^a}\) in

\[ (1+T)^{\ell^a m}\equiv(1+T^{\ell^a})^m\pmod\ell \tag{AA.5} \]

is \(m\) modulo \(\ell\). The congruence follows by iterating \((u+v)^\ell=u^\ell+v^\ell\) over \(\mathbf F_\ell\). Left translation acts on these subsets. Some orbit has cardinality prime to \(\ell\), since otherwise their total cardinality would be divisible by \(\ell\). Its stabilizer \(S\) has order divisible by \(\ell^a\), by the orbit-stabilizer coset count. On the selected subset, left translation by \(S\) is free, so \(|S|\) divides its cardinality \(\ell^a\). Hence \(|S|=\ell^a\), proving existence of a Sylow subgroup.

Any \(\ell\)-subgroup \(P\) of \(Q\) acts on the \(m\) cosets \(Q/S\). Its orbits have \(\ell\)-power size. Because \(m\) is prime to \(\ell\), a fixed coset exists, and it gives \(P\subset qSq^{-1}\). Thus every \(\ell\)-subgroup is contained in a Sylow subgroup and all Sylow subgroups are conjugate. If \(N\) is normal in \(Q\), then \(S\cap N\) is Sylow in \(N\): a Sylow subgroup of \(N\) is contained in a conjugate of \(S\), and normality brings that conjugate subgroup back into \(S\cap N\). Counting orders now shows that the image of \(S\) is Sylow in \(Q/N\). Every Sylow subgroup of \(Q/N\) is obtained this way, by conjugacy and lifting its conjugating element.

For profinite \(G\), the finite sets of Sylow subgroups of \(G/U\) therefore form an inverse system under quotient images. Any finite collection of compatibility conditions is satisfied by taking a Sylow subgroup in a common finer quotient. AA.1 compactness supplies compatible choices \(P_U\). Put

\[ P=\{g\in G:gU\in P_U\text{ for every open normal }U\}. \tag{AA.6} \]

The chosen quotient maps on \(P_U\) are surjective. The prescribed-coordinate form of compactness shows that \(P\) maps onto every \(P_U\). It is closed and is their inverse limit, so is pro-\(\ell\). This is the Sylow pro-\(\ell\) subgroup used in R.3.

AA.4. Restriction detected by a finite transfer

First let \(Q\) be finite and \(S\subset Q\). Choose one representative in each orbit of left multiplication by \(S\) on \(Q\), including \(1\) for the orbit \(S\). Define \(r:Q\to S\) by \(r(st)=s\) in this choice. It is \(S\)-equivariant and restricts to the identity on \(S\).

Suppose a homogeneous \(Q\)-cocycle \(c\) of degree \(n>0\) restricts to \(db\) on \(S\). We first construct a primitive on all tuples from \(Q\), equivariant only for \(S\). Regard \(u=r\) as a map \(Q\to Q\). For a degree-\(n\) cochain \(f\) on \(Q\), set

\[ \begin{aligned} (Hf)(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}) &=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(-1)^j\\ &\qquad\cdot f(ux_0,\ldots,ux_j,x_j,\ldots,x_{n-1}). \end{aligned} \tag{AA.7} \]

The omission expansion gives \(dH+Hd=1-u^*\). Terms deleting an entry before or after the place where the two lists meet cancel with the same deletion in the neighboring sum; the two end terms are \(f(x_0,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(-f(ux_0,\ldots,ux_n)\). This also verifies the sign in degree zero, where \(Hd f(x)=f(x)-f(ux)\). Both maps are \(S\)-equivariant. Therefore

\[ B=r^*b+Hc\quad\text{satisfies}\quad dB=c. \tag{AA.8} \]

Average this primitive over the cosets \(tS\in Q/S\):

\[ \begin{aligned} (\operatorname{Tr}B)(x_0,\ldots,x_{n-1}) &=\sum_{tS\in Q/S}t B(t^{-1}x_0,\ldots,t^{-1}x_{n-1}). \end{aligned} \tag{AA.9} \]

Replacing \(t\) by \(ts\) leaves the summand unchanged by \(S\)-equivariance. Translating all arguments by an element of \(Q\) and reindexing the cosets proves \(Q\)-equivariance. This sum commutes with omission, and every summand applied to the \(Q\)-equivariant cocycle \(c\) is \(c\). Thus \(d\operatorname{Tr}B=[Q:S]c\). If \(M\) is \(\ell\)-primary and \([Q:S]\) is prime to \(\ell\), multiplication by that index is an automorphism of \(M\), its cochains and its cohomology. Its inverse on an element killed by \(\ell^r\) is multiplication by the inverse residue modulo \(\ell^r\), independent of a larger choice of exponent. Restriction to \(S\) is consequently injective on cohomology with these coefficients.

Now let \(P\) be (AA.6) inside profinite \(G\), and let a continuous cocycle \(c\) restrict to a boundary on \(P\). Formula (AA.4) places \(c\) at a finite quotient. The primitive on \(P\) also has finitely many values and factors through a finite quotient of \(P\). Shrink the open normal subgroup \(U\subset G\) so that \(P\cap U\) suffices for that factorization and \(U\) fixes both finite sets of values. This is possible using the induced topology described in AA.1. Both the cocycle and its restricted primitive now lie over \(G/U\), with coefficients in \(M^U\). The image \(P_U\) is Sylow there, so the finite calculation kills the class already at that stage. Degree zero is the inclusion of invariant groups. We have proved

\[ \begin{gathered} H^n(G,M)\longrightarrow H^n(P,M)\text{ is injective}\\ \text{for every }n\ge0\text{ and every discrete }\ell\text{-primary }M. \end{gathered} \tag{AA.10} \]

No transfer of an infinite index was used.

AA.5. From one coefficient to all higher degrees

Suppose \(P\) is pro-\(\ell\) and \(H^2(P,\mathbf F_\ell)=0\), with trivial action. For any finite nonzero \(\ell\)-primary \(P\)-module \(M\), its subgroup \(M[\ell]\) is nonzero. Its action factors through a finite \(\ell\)-group. All nonsingleton orbits have cardinality divisible by \(\ell\), while \(|M[\ell]|\) is divisible by \(\ell\); the fixed set contains zero and therefore has at least \(\ell\) elements. A nonzero fixed element spans a trivial \(\mathbf F_\ell\)-line. Repeat on the smaller quotient. This gives a finite filtration by trivial lines, and the long exact cochain sequences give \(H^2(P,M)=0\).

Every discrete \(\ell\)-primary module is the union of its finite \(P\)-stable submodules. Each element has finite orbit, by its open stabilizer and compactness; the subgroup generated by finitely many such orbits is finite, since its finitely many generators have bounded \(\ell\)-power order. Formula (AA.4)'s coefficient-colimit assertion extends the degree-two vanishing to every such module.

Embed \(M\) in \(I_P(M)\). Both that module and its quotient are \(\ell\)-primary: each continuous function has finite image, hence is killed by one power of \(\ell\). Acyclicity (AA.3) and the long exact sequence give \(H^{r+1}(P,M)=H^r(P,I_P(M)/M)\) for \(r\ge1\). Repeat on the quotient to reduce any degree greater than two to the proved degree-two case. Thus all degrees greater than one vanish. Combining this result with (AA.10), and then taking finite sums and filtered unions of primary parts, proves the torsion assertion (R.9).

For the rational coefficient step in R.4, a finite group \(Q\) has the homogeneous cochain operator \(sf=\sum_{u\in Q}f(u,-)\). Reindexing proves equivariance, and the insertion expansion gives \(ds+sd=|Q|\) in positive degrees. Thus \(|Q|\) kills positive finite-group cohomology. By (AA.4), every positive profinite cohomology class is torsion. For a rational vector space of coefficients the cochain groups and their cohomology are rational vector spaces, so these torsion groups are zero. This proves exactly the rationalization input in (R.10)–(R.11).

Appendix AB. From field cohomology to the divisor sequence

The calculation in R passes from continuous Galois modules to sheaves on a field, and then from rational units to units on a curve. We give the exact field, slice and valuation arguments for those passages. Throughout the curve calculation, the ground field is the algebraically closed field \(k\) of R; the field calculation also applies to any field \(F\).

AB.1. The field objects of the étale site

An étale affine chart has a finitely presented formally étale coordinate algebra. Recall that formal étaleness means existence and uniqueness of a lift across a square-zero ideal. It implies formal smoothness and vanishing of the differential module: two lifts differ by a derivation, and the square-zero algebra \(B\oplus N\) tests all derivations into every \(B\)-module \(N\). Conversely a standard square presentation with invertible Jacobian has that unique lifting property, by correcting the tentative variables with the inverse Jacobian. These are the presentations obtained by the argument in Y.6 when its differential rank is zero.

Let \(B\) be such an algebra over \(F\), and put \(C=B\otimes_F\overline F\). Formal étaleness and finite presentation survive field extension: restrict a lifting problem to \(B\), solve it, and combine its lift with the given map from \(\overline F\); uniqueness is preserved as well. At each maximal ideal of \(C\), Y.6 gives a regular local ring of dimension zero, because the differential module is zero. That local ring is \(\overline F\): its maximal ideal has no generators and is zero by Nakayama, and its residue field is \(\overline F\) by Y.5.

Every prime of \(C\) is maximal. Otherwise a strict prime inclusion ending in a maximal ideal would remain strict in that localization, contradicting dimension zero. There are finitely many such primes, since a Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal primes. The ring is reduced: a nilpotent maps to zero in every maximal localization, hence is zero. Indeed, a nonzero element has a proper annihilator contained in a maximal ideal, and cannot vanish in that localization. The distinct maximal ideals are comaximal and their intersection is the nilradical, so the Chinese remainder map gives

\[ C\simeq\overline F^{r} \quad\text{for some finite }r\ge0. \tag{AB.1} \]

The Chinese remainder assertion follows for two comaximal ideals from \(1=a+b\), with one term in each ideal, and then by induction. Extension of scalars preserves linear independence over a field, so (AB.1) makes \(B\) finite-dimensional over \(F\). It is reduced by its injection into \(C\). In a finite-dimensional algebra every prime quotient is a field: multiplication by a nonzero element in that domain is an injective linear map and therefore surjective. The same finite-prime and Chinese remainder argument writes \(B\) as a finite product of finite fields \(E_i/F\).

Each \(E_i/F\) is separable. If some element had an inseparable minimal polynomial, its subalgebra tensored with \(\overline F\) would contain a nonzero nilpotent. Tensoring its injection into \(E_i\) preserves injectivity, contradicting (AB.1). Conversely a finite separable extension is generated by one element, by the finite Galois algebra in Z.3 and Profinite groups and infinite Galois theory, Section 0. For its separable minimal polynomial \(p\), the derivative at the generator is invertible. The correction \(t\mapsto t-p(t)/p'(t)\) lifts a root uniquely across a square-zero ideal. Thus the extension is étale; finite products and arbitrary disjoint unions are étale locally on their components.

Every point of an étale scheme over \(F\) therefore has an open neighbourhood equal to the spectrum of a finite separable field. The scheme is a disjoint union of these open one-point schemes. It is quasi-compact precisely when the union is finite. This proves the field-fibre description in (R.12), including the empty fibre, after base change to the generic point.

AB.2. Descent on a finite Galois cover

Put \(G=G_F\). The preceding field description and AA.1 identify finite étale schemes \(V/F\) with finite continuous \(G\)-sets \(S_V=\operatorname{Hom}_F(\operatorname{Spec}F^s,V)\). For a connected object \(\operatorname{Spec}L\), choosing an embedding in \(F^s\) identifies this set with \(G/G_L\). An equivariant map of such orbits is a coset whose stabilizer contains the source stabilizer, and hence is exactly an embedding of the corresponding fixed fields in the opposite direction. Extension of embeddings and the closed fixed-field statement are proved in AA.1. This verifies full faithfulness, not just the correspondence on objects.

Products and covers become products and jointly surjective maps of these sets. To check this explicitly, place the finitely many field extensions in one finite Galois extension \(E/F\). A separable polynomial splits there with distinct roots; its Chinese remainder decomposition makes every finite étale algebra a product of copies of \(E\). Maps and products are then maps and products of finite indexing sets. A map between connected field objects is surjective, and is surjective on their embedding orbits by extension of embeddings. This also checks the assertion for covering families, component by component.

For a sheaf \(\mathscr F\) on this site define

\[ M=\operatorname*{colim}_{E/F\text{ finite Galois in }F^s} \mathscr F(\operatorname{Spec}E). \tag{AB.2} \]

Restrictions between field objects are injective: the field extension is a cover, and the sheaf separatedness axiom detects equality. Field automorphisms act compatibly on this colimit. Every representative at \(E\) is fixed by \(G_E\), so the resulting action on \(M\) is continuous.

For a finite separable \(L\subset F^s\), restriction identifies

\[ \mathscr F(\operatorname{Spec}L)=M^{G_L}. \tag{AB.3} \]

Injectivity follows from the same covering argument. To prove surjectivity, represent a fixed element at a finite Galois \(E/F\) containing \(L\). Its section \(t\) is fixed by \(\operatorname{Gal}(E/L)\): equality in the colimit implies equality at \(E\), since its map into the colimit is injective. The two restrictions of \(t\) to \(E\otimes_L E\) therefore agree. In fact

\[ E\otimes_L E\longrightarrow \prod_{\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(E/L)}E, \qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto(a\sigma(b))_\sigma \tag{AB.4} \]

is the Chinese remainder isomorphism for a primitive element's distinct roots. The sheaf axiom for \(\operatorname{Spec}E\to\operatorname{Spec}L\) descends \(t\) uniquely, proving (AB.3).

Conversely a continuous discrete \(G\)-set \(M\) gives a sheaf by \(V\mapsto\operatorname{Hom}_G(S_V,M)\): functions descend along a surjection precisely when they agree on its fibre product. Its colimit (AB.2) recovers \(M\), because each element has an open stabilizer containing some open normal \(G_E\). Formula (AB.3), and products over field components, show that the constructions are naturally inverse. This is the field-topos equivalence of Galois cohomology and the étale cohomology of a field, Theorem 1.1, expressed directly with finite Galois covers.

The constructions preserve abelian group operations, so give an equivalence of abelian categories. An equivalence preserves kernels, cokernels and injectives, by their universal properties and the extension definition of injectivity. Sections at \(F\) are invariants. Their injective-resolution complexes therefore agree. For the units sheaf, (AB.2) is exactly \((F^s)^\times\), since every element and its inverse occur in a finite Galois extension. Thus

\[ H^q(\operatorname{Spec}F,\mathbf G_m) =H^q(G_F,(F^s)^\times). \tag{AB.5} \]

The same reasoning gives the additive group, roots of unity and constant coefficients with their actual actions. For algebraically closed \(F\), the group is trivial and the sheaf category is the category of sets; its abelian section functor is exact.

AB.3. Exact inverse images and the slice calculation

We spell out the site operations used in R.5. Étale presentations are stable under base change and composition by their finite presentation and unique square-zero lifting property. Their diagonals are open immersions. In affine coordinates, the kernel \(I\) of \(B\otimes_A B\to B\) is finitely generated, and \(I/I^2=\Omega_{B/A}=0\). The latter equality sends \(b\otimes1-1\otimes b\) to \(db\); the product rule gives its universal derivation property. A finitely generated ideal with \(I=I^2\) is generated by an idempotent. Indeed, write a finite generator column \(x\) as \(Tx\) with entries of \(T\) in \(I\). The adjugate identity gives \(\det(1-T)I=0\). Write \(\det(1-T)=1-e\), where \(e\in I\). Then \((1-e)e=0\) and \(x=ex\), so \(e^2=e\) and \(I=(e)\). The quotient is the localization at \(1-e\), hence defines an open immersion. These affine diagonal charts cover the diagonal. A section of an étale map is a base change of its open diagonal, hence is open; factoring a morphism between étale schemes into its graph and a projection now shows that this morphism is étale too.

For any scheme map \(f:Y\to X\), write \(Y_V=Y\times_XV\). Base change preserves covering families, so \((f_*\mathscr F)(V)=\mathscr F(Y_V)\) is a sheaf. Its left adjoint is the sheafification of

\[ U\longmapsto \operatorname*{colim}_{(V,\ a:U\to Y_V)}\mathscr A(V). \tag{AB.6} \]

The indexing uses restriction toward a refinement \(V'\to V\). It is filtered: \(X\) gives an object, a fibre product gives a common refinement, and the open equalizer of two maps gives a refinement equalizing them. The latter is open by the diagonal calculation just proved; the map from \(U\) factors through its base change by the required equality. Filtered colimits of sets and groups preserve finite limits, as is checked by placing finitely many representatives and their equalities at one common stage. Sheafification preserves finite limits by T.1. Formula (AB.6) is therefore left exact. The universal properties of its colimit and sheafification give the adjunction with \(f_*\); hence it also preserves cokernels and is exact on abelian sheaves. Consequently \(f_*\) preserves injectives.

For an object \(V\) of a site, restriction to its slice has the exact left adjoint which sheafifies

\[ W\longmapsto\bigoplus_{a:W\to V}\mathscr E(W,a). \tag{AB.7} \]

Adjunction follows by specifying the map on each summand. Injectivity is sectionwise injectivity in each summand. An epimorphism lifts a finite sum locally by choosing a common refinement for the finitely many local lifts; T.1 sheafification gives exactness. Slice restriction itself is exact, since local lifts are taken over that same slice object. It therefore carries an injective resolution to an injective resolution on the slice.

Apply this to an injective resolution \(\mathscr F\to I^\bullet\) on \(Y_{\rm ét}\). On the slice over \(Y_V\), its section complex is \(I^\bullet(Y_V)\). Exact sheafification commutes with kernels and images, so

\[ R^qf_*\mathscr F =a\bigl[V\longmapsto H^q(Y_V,\mathscr F|_{Y_V})\bigr]. \tag{AB.8} \]

Here \(a\) denotes associated sheaf. This is the direct resolution calculation in Pushforward, pullback and finite morphisms, Lemma 2.1; its proof uses neither higher-cohomology continuity nor a strict-local limit. For an étale object \(Y_V\), its small étale site is the slice: composition and the graph argument above identify the objects and maps, and the covers are the same.

AB.4. Uniformizers on étale curve neighbourhoods

Let \(U\to X\) be an étale chart of finite presentation over the smooth curve of R.5. It is smooth over \(k\): lift a map from \(X\) first, then use formal étaleness to lift the map from \(U\). Moreover

\[ \Omega_{U/k}\simeq\Omega_{X/k}\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}\mathcal O_U. \tag{AB.9} \]

For completeness, a derivation from the base algebra into any module on the chart extends uniquely to the chart algebra. Apply the unique lifting property to its split square-zero algebra with structural map \(a\mapsto(a,da)\). This proves (AB.9) by the representing property of differentials. Its rank is one. By Y.6 the local rings are regular, and the closed local rings have dimension one. Distinct irreducible components cannot meet, since their meeting would give a local ring with two minimal primes instead of a domain. There are finitely many components on a quasi-compact chart. Each is an integral smooth curve; X.1 makes its closed local rings discrete valuation rings.

A closed point \(y\in U\) has residue field \(k\), and its image \(x\in X\) is closed: the induced quotient of an affine coordinate ring into \(k\) has image \(k\). Let \(\pi\) be a parameter at \(x\). Its differential is a basis of the cotangent space at \(x\). To see the identification, a \(k\)-derivation from its local ring to \(k\) is the same as a linear form on \(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2\): subtract the residue scalar, use the linear form, and the product rule follows because products of two maximal-ideal elements vanish there. Formula (AB.9) carries this basis to the cotangent space at \(y\). Nakayama therefore gives

\[ \mathfrak m_y=\pi\mathcal O_{U,y}. \tag{AB.10} \]

In particular each component maps nonconstantly to \(X\). If it mapped to a closed point, that point's parameter would pull back to zero, contradicting (AB.10) and dimension one. Its generic field is a finite separable extension of \(K=k(X)\), by AB.1 applied to the generic fibre. Every local map between these curve neighbourhoods has ramification index one: a parameter remains a parameter, a unit remains a unit, and \(u\pi^m\) keeps the same valuation. This proves compatibility of valuation with étale restriction.

It also proves the strict-local ring assertion mentioned in R.5. In the filtered system of pointed local étale neighbourhoods at \(x\), every ring is a discrete valuation ring with the same \(\pi\). The local transition maps are injective, since they take a nonzero \(u\pi^m\) to a nonzero element of that form. Their colimit is a domain, each nonzero element is still \(u\pi^m\), and each nonzero ideal is generated by an element of least valuation. Thus this colimit is a discrete valuation ring, including Noetherianity. Its fraction field is the colimit of the finite separable generic fields and is algebraic separable over \(K\). This degree-zero statement does not assert a higher-cohomology limit theorem.

AB.5. Local lifts of every divisor section

For a quasi-compact chart \(U\), its generic fibre consists of the generic fields of its components. Hence \(j_*\mathbf G_{m,K}(U)\) is the product of their multiplicative groups. A nonzero rational function on a component has finite divisor support: on a finite affine cover, numerator and denominator have zero-dimensional closed zero sets, which are finite in a Noetherian one-dimensional scheme. Its valuations give a section of the divisor sheaf, using the exact section description (S.2). AB.4 shows that these maps commute with restriction.

The kernel consists precisely of regular units. Valuation zero at every closed point puts both the function and its inverse in all the closed local rings. Their local representatives glue on the integral component to a regular function and its regular inverse; the generic point is already included. Thus the kernel agrees with \(\mathbf G_m\) on every chart.

To prove surjectivity as a sheaf map, let \(D=\sum_y n_y[y]\) be a section of (S.2), with finite support. At each support point choose a rational representative of a uniformizer \(\pi_y\). Shrink an open neighbourhood \(W_y\) to remove the other support points and all the other zeros and poles of \(\pi_y\). Then

\[ \operatorname{ord}(\pi_y^{n_y})|_{W_y}=D|_{W_y}. \tag{AB.11} \]

On the complement of the support, the function \(1\) is a lift. These opens cover \(U\), and open immersions are étale. The local epimorphism criterion of T.1 proves surjectivity, establishing (R.14) directly. This construction does not require the divisor to be globally principal.

Finally, for a closed \(k\)-point \(x\), the sheaf \(i_{x*}A\) has sections \(A^{U_x}\), because AB.1 identifies the fibre as a discrete union of copies of \(\operatorname{Spec}k\). A short exact sequence of groups stays exact under this product: coordinates in a surjection can be lifted separately. Thus \(i_{x*}\) is exact. It preserves injectives by AB.3, and AB.2 makes sections over \(k\) exact. Applying it to an injective resolution gives \(H^q(X,i_{x*}A)=0\) for \(q>0\). Appendix S supplies the additional argument for the infinite point sum; exactness and acyclicity of its individual summands alone would not suffice.

Appendix AC. Why the curve site admits finite covers

Appendix S uses finite covering families on a basis stable under fibre products. The geometric input is that the covering maps are open. We prove the Noetherian finite-type image theorem and the flat prime-lifting argument, then verify flatness for the étale curve maps in question directly from their local parameters. This supplies the basis properties used in the divisor-sheaf calculation.

AC.1. A dominant image contains an open subset

Let \(A\subset B\) be an inclusion of domains, with \(B\) a finite-type \(A\)-algebra, and write \(K=\operatorname{Frac}A\). The normalization argument of K.1, extended to every field in Y.5, gives algebraically independent elements \(t_1,\ldots,t_d\) in \(B\otimes_AK\) such that this algebra is finite over \(K[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\). Invert a nonzero \(a\in A\) to put all the \(t_i\) in \(B_a\). Each member of a finite algebra generating set for \(B\) satisfies a monic equation over that polynomial ring. Invert one further product of denominators so that all coefficients belong to \(A_a[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\). Thus

\[ A_a[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\hookrightarrow B_a \quad\text{is finite and integral}. \tag{AC.1} \]

Injection follows from algebraic independence over \(K\); the bounded powers in the monic equations give the finite generating module. The equations already hold in \(B_a\), since the domain \(B_a\) injects into \(B\otimes_AK\).

Lying over for integral inclusions is proved in K.1 by localizing at a prime and choosing a maximal ideal upstairs. Its contraction is maximal in the local base: a subring over which a field is integral is a field, as a monic equation for an inverse expresses that inverse in the subring. Applying it to (AC.1), and then taking the prime \(\mathfrak p A_a[t]+(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\) over each prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(A_a\), gives

\[ D(a)\subset\operatorname{im}(\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A). \tag{AC.2} \]

Consequently any dominant finite-type map between integral Noetherian schemes has an image containing a nonempty open subset of its target. Choose an affine target open and a nonempty affine source open over it. The restriction is still dominant, since it contains the source generic point; apply (AC.2). Open restrictions remain of finite type here because every open of a Noetherian scheme is quasi-compact.

AC.2. Constructible images and the topological criterion

In a Noetherian scheme a constructible set is a finite union of locally closed subsets. Such sets are closed under finite unions, intersections and complements: write a locally closed set as the intersection of an open and a closed set, and distribute finite Boolean operations. Every open is quasi-compact. For example, if an open cover had no finite subcover, its finite unions would have no maximal member, contradicting the ascending-chain condition on opens. Every closed set has finitely many irreducible components: a minimal closed counterexample could be split into two proper closed subsets, each already having a finite decomposition. These are the topological forms of Noetherianity used below.

For a finite-type map \(f:Y\to Z\) between Noetherian schemes, the image of each closed subset of \(Y\) is constructible. Suppose otherwise and take a minimal closed counterexample \(T\). If \(T\) were reducible, its finitely many proper irreducible components would contradict minimality. Give \(T\) and the closure \(Z'\) of its image their reduced structures. The induced map is dominant between integral schemes. AC.1 supplies a nonempty open \(W\subset Z'\) contained in \(f(T)\). Its inverse image is nonempty open in \(T\), so

\[ f(T)=W\ \cup\ f\bigl(T\setminus f^{-1}(W)\bigr) \tag{AC.3} \]

is constructible: \(W\) is locally closed in \(Z\), and the second set is the image of a proper closed subset of \(T\). This contradicts minimality. The empty set causes no exception. A locally closed subset of \(Y\) has a reduced locally closed subscheme structure of finite type over \(Y\); its open part is quasi-compact. Applying the full-image assertion to these schemes and taking finite unions proves constructibility of the image of every constructible subset. In particular the image of each quasi-compact open under \(f\) is constructible. This is the Noetherian form of Quasi-finite morphisms and Chevalley's theorem, Theorem 4.2.

A constructible subset of a Noetherian scheme which is stable under specialization is closed. To see this, take an irreducible component of its closure and remove the other components. The constructible subset is dense on the remaining nonempty open part. A finite locally closed decomposition of this dense subset has a member dense in that component, hence containing a nonempty open of the component and its generic point. Specialization stability then includes the whole component. Doing this for the finitely many components includes the entire closure. Applying this to the complement proves:

\[ \text{constructible and stable under generization} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{open}. \tag{AC.4} \]

AC.3. Flat local maps lift prime chains

Let \((A,\mathfrak m)\to(B,\mathfrak n)\) be a flat local map. Tensoring with \(B\) detects every nonzero \(A\)-module. Indeed, a nonzero element of a module \(N\) generates a submodule \(A/I\) with \(I\subset\mathfrak m\). Its tensor product is \(B/IB\ne0\), since \(IB\subset\mathfrak n\); flatness embeds this nonzero group in \(N\otimes_AB\). Thus the map is faithfully flat. This is the direct detection proof of Faithful flatness and the local criterion for flatness, Theorems 1.1 and 2.1.

For each prime \(\mathfrak p\subset A\), the ring \(B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) is therefore nonzero and has a prime ideal. Its inverse image in \(B\) contracts to \(\mathfrak p\): all elements outside \(\mathfrak p\) have been inverted, and the field \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) injects into the nonzero prime quotient. Hence the spectrum map is surjective.

Now let \(f:Y\to Z\) be flat, let \(y\) map to \(z\), and let \(z'\) be a generization of \(z\). In affine neighbourhoods write the corresponding primes as \(\mathfrak q\) over \(\mathfrak p\). The local map \(A_{\mathfrak p}\to B_{\mathfrak q}\) is flat and local. The prime for \(z'\) lifts to a prime of \(B_{\mathfrak q}\) by the preceding argument. Viewed in \(B\), it is contained in \(\mathfrak q\), so defines a generization \(y'\) of \(y\) mapping to \(z'\). Every open neighbourhood of \(y\) contains \(y'\). The image of every source open is consequently stable under generization.

If \(Y,Z\) are Noetherian and \(f\) is locally of finite type, cover a source open by affine opens mapping into affine target opens. Their maps are of finite type. AC.2 makes their images constructible, and (AC.4) makes them open. Their union is open. We have proved the flat-openness theorem in the Noetherian setting used here, with its prime-lifting prerequisite. The general theorem is Flat morphisms, Theorem 3.2; its broader non-Noetherian statement is not required for this basis calculation.

AC.4. Applying openness to every curve chart

Let \(X\) be the smooth separated curve of R.5. AB.4 shows that an étale chart of finite presentation over \(X\) is a finite disjoint union of smooth integral curves, and that the local maps at closed points send a parameter to a parameter. Such a local map \(A\to B\) of discrete valuation rings is injective and makes \(B\) torsion free over \(A\): every nonzero element of \(A\) is a unit times a power of the parameter, which remains nonzero in \(B\).

A torsion-free module over a discrete valuation ring is flat, even if it is not finite. It is the filtered union of its finite submodules. Each is free by the basis-and-division proof in X.4: lift a residue basis using Nakayama, and divide a putative relation by the largest common parameter power to contradict its residue independence. Tensor product commutes with this union, and filtered colimits of modules preserve injections because every element and every equality occurs at a finite stage. Thus tensoring the whole module preserves injections. At generic points the map is a field extension and is flat as a map of vector spaces. Closed and generic points exhaust these curves; each component dominates its image curve by AB.4. This proves flatness of their étale maps at every point. AC.3 now makes them open. The same argument applies to maps between two such charts, which are étale by AB.3.

Let \(\mathcal B\) consist of the quasi-compact separated étale \(X\)-schemes of finite presentation. These schemes are Noetherian, by the Hilbert basis argument in W.4. Every étale \(X\)-scheme is covered by affine étale presentation charts over affine opens of \(X\). Each chart is separated over \(X\) and belongs to \(\mathcal B\). Its map to the affine target is affine, hence separated: multiplication of coordinate rings makes its diagonal a closed immersion. The affine target open in \(X\) is separated as well. Thus \(\mathcal B\) is a basis.

For \(V,W,U\in\mathcal B\) and maps \(V,W\to U\), the fibre product \(V\times_UW\) belongs to \(\mathcal B\). It is the inverse image of the closed diagonal of \(U\to X\) in \(V\times_XW\), hence is a closed subscheme of that Noetherian quasi-compact scheme. It is separated over \(X\). Its map to \(X\) is étale by base change, composition and cancellation from AB.3. Finite presentation follows locally from these étale maps, and globally from the finite affine cover: over Noetherian rings finite-type affine algebras have finitely generated relation ideals. The same reasoning applies to repeated fibre products.

Finally, start with any étale covering family of \(U\in\mathcal B\). Refine its members by the affine charts just described. Their maps to \(U\) are étale and open by the preceding local flatness argument. Their images form an open cover of quasi-compact \(U\), so finitely many images suffice. The corresponding finite family is a cover refining the original one. After base change to another basis object, the selected fibre products stay in \(\mathcal B\) and form a finite cover. Therefore finite covering families generate the topology on this basis, with exactly the base-change property required in S.1–S.3. T.1 then identifies its sheaves and cohomology with those on the full small étale site.

Appendix AD. Descent and degree-one multiplicative cohomology

The Picard calculation has two separate inputs: a line bundle can be recovered from faithfully flat local data, and degree-one derived cohomology records the units comparing local frames. We prove these inputs with the arbitrary parameter schemes of Q.4 in view. Throughout this appendix all schemes are over the field \(k\) used there.

AD.1. Rank one descends without a Noetherian hypothesis

Let \(A\to B\) be faithfully flat. N.1 constructs an equivalence between \(A\)-modules and \(B\)-modules with a descent datum, including their maps. Its equalizer and coaction proof does not assume \(A\) Noetherian. We extend its finiteness check to arbitrary \(A\).

If \(B\otimes_A N\) is finitely generated, finitely many tensor expressions for generators involve finitely many elements of \(N\). They generate \(N\): the quotient by their span becomes zero after faithfully flat tensoring. If \(B\otimes_A N\) is finitely presented, choose a surjection \(A^r\to N\) with kernel \(K\). The module \(B\otimes_A K\) is finitely generated. Indeed, for two finite free surjections \(E\to M\) and \(F\to M\), their pullback \(E\times_M F\) has split projections and consequently

\[ \ker(E\to M)\oplus F\simeq\ker(F\to M)\oplus E. \tag{AD.1} \]

Taking one surjection from a finite presentation shows that the kernel of the other is finitely generated. Apply the already proved generator descent to \(K\). This makes \(N\) finitely presented.

Flatness also descends. Tensor an injection of \(A\)-modules with \(N\), and then with \(B\). Flatness of \(B\) and of \(B\otimes_A N\) makes the resulting map injective. Flatness of \(B\) identifies its kernel with the tensor product of the original kernel, and faithfulness makes that original kernel zero.

For completeness, a finitely presented flat module over a local ring is finite free. Lift a basis of its residue-field fibre to generators, using Nakayama's determinant argument from L.1. The kernel of the resulting finite free surjection is finitely generated by (AD.1). Flatness makes tensoring this kernel sequence with the residue field left exact; the chosen basis makes the tensorized kernel zero. Nakayama kills the kernel. Over a general ring this local isomorphism extends to a neighbourhood: choose representatives of the local basis, kill the finitely generated cokernel on a principal neighbourhood, and then kill the finitely generated kernel there. Thus a finitely presented flat module is finite locally free.

Every prime of \(A\) has a prime of \(B\) over it: the fibre algebra is nonzero by faithfulness and hence has a prime. Comparing fibres at such a pair shows that rank is unchanged by descent. In particular, if \(B\otimes_A N\) is locally free of rank one, so is \(N\). These arguments give the full arbitrary-ring version of Faithfully flat descent, Proposition 3.1.

AD.2. Effective descent over every parameter scheme

We first justify the finite affine refinements needed for an fppf cover over a possibly non-Noetherian \(k\)-scheme. A finitely presented \(A\)-algebra has the form \(B=A[x_1,\ldots,x_r]/(f_1,\ldots,f_s)\). Put all coefficients of the \(f_i\) into a finitely generated \(k\)-subalgebra \(A_0\subset A\), and let \(B_0\) have the same presentation over \(A_0\). The Noetherian theorem AC.1–AC.2 makes the image of \(\operatorname{Spec}B_0\to\operatorname{Spec}A_0\) constructible. The image for \(B\) is exactly its inverse image: for \(\mathfrak p\subset A\) over \(\mathfrak p_0\subset A_0\),

\[ B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p) =\bigl(B_0\otimes_{A_0}\kappa(\mathfrak p_0)\bigr) \otimes_{\kappa(\mathfrak p_0)}\kappa(\mathfrak p). \tag{AD.2} \]

A field extension detects nonzero vector spaces. Thus the two relevant fibres are simultaneously nonempty. A constructible subset of the Noetherian affine stage is a finite Boolean combination of principal opens, so its inverse image is constructible in the same finite Boolean sense over \(A\). This is the affine approximation argument in Quasi-finite morphisms and Chevalley, Section 5.

Here is the topological step for this larger base. Give a spectrum the topology generated by the clopen sets \(D(a)\) and \(V(a)\). It is compact: an ultrafilter determines the prime \(\{a:V(a)\text{ belongs to the ultrafilter}\}\). The equations for sums and products of vanishing sets prove primality, and membership of the basic clopen neighbourhoods proves convergence. Distinct primes are separated by \(D(a)\) and \(V(a)\), so this topology is Hausdorff. A finite Boolean combination of these sets is compact. If such a compact set \(Z\) is stable under specialization and \(\mathfrak p\) lies in its Zariski closure, all the sets \(Z\cap D(a)\), \(a\notin\mathfrak p\), have the finite intersection property. Compactness gives \(\mathfrak q\in Z\) contained in \(\mathfrak p\); specialization stability puts \(\mathfrak p\) in \(Z\). Hence \(Z\) is closed. Taking complements shows that a constructible generization-stable subset is open.

The flat prime-lifting argument of AC.3 works over arbitrary rings: the localized flat local map is faithful by the cyclic-submodule proof, and its nonzero fibre has a prime. Thus the image of a flat finitely presented affine map is generization-stable and, by (AD.2), constructible. It is open. Applying this to affine charts inside any open of the source proves that a flat morphism locally of finite presentation is open. Base change retains both hypotheses and therefore openness. This supplies the version of Flat morphisms, Theorem 3.2 needed here.

Now take a jointly surjective fppf family \(\{U_i\to S\}\). Above an affine open \(W\subset S\), affine charts of the \(U_i\) have open images covering \(W\). Quasi-compactness selects finitely many charts. Their disjoint union is affine and gives a flat surjection \(\operatorname{Spec}B\to\operatorname{Spec}A=W\). Its ring map is faithful: for a nonzero module choose a nonzero cyclic submodule \(A/I\), a maximal ideal containing \(I\), and a point above that ideal. Then \(B/IB\ne0\), and flatness preserves the cyclic submodule inclusion. The same construction applies after base change. This also proves directly that every fppf family is an fpqc family in the finite affine refinement convention.

Suppose line bundles on the \(U_i\) have overlap isomorphisms satisfying the triple cocycle. Restrict to one such finite refinement above \(W\). N.1 descends its module and AD.1 makes the result a line bundle on \(W\). For an affine open \(V\subset U_i\) mapping into \(W\), the affine faithfully flat cover \(V\times_W\operatorname{Spec}B\to V\) compares the descended bundle with the prescribed bundle on \(V\). The original triple cocycle says precisely that this comparison respects descent data. N.1 descends the comparison and its inverse. Uniqueness makes these isomorphisms agree on affine opens in their overlaps, and hence on all of \(U_i\).

Repeat on affine opens \(W\) of \(S\). On an affine open in the intersection of two such opens, pull the two constructions back to their common faithfully flat refinement. They become the same original datum. Full faithfulness in N.1 therefore gives a unique comparison downstairs. These comparisons satisfy the cocycle by the same uniqueness. Ordinary open gluing constructs the global bundle: its sections are compatible tuples of local sections, with module operations defined componentwise. The projection to each local bundle is an isomorphism locally, and so the result is locally free of rank one. Compatible morphisms descend by the same argument. This is the line-bundle case of Faithfully flat descent, Theorem 5.1, with no separation or Noetherian assumption on \(S\).

AD.3. The degree-one comparison and its group law

On the small étale site of \(C\), let \(F\) be any abelian sheaf. T.2 gives an injection \(F\to I\) with \(I\) injective; put \(Q=I/F\). T.3 gives

\[ H^1(C,F)=Q(C)/\operatorname{im}\bigl(I(C)\to Q(C)\bigr). \tag{AD.3} \]

For \(q\in Q(C)\), local surjectivity gives a cover and lifts \(b_i\in I(U_i)\). AC.4 lets us choose a finite cover from its basis. The differences \(a_{ij}=b_j-b_i\) belong to \(F(U_i\times_C U_j)\) and satisfy

\[ a_{jk}-a_{ik}+a_{ij}=0. \]

Changing lifts changes this cocycle by a coboundary; adding a global section of \(I\) to \(q\) leaves its class unchanged.

Conversely, an \(F\)-valued cocycle on such a cover is an \(I\)-valued cocycle. The injective Čech acyclicity proved in S.2 supplies \(b_i\) with \(a_{ij}=b_j-b_i\). Their images in \(Q\) match, so glue to \(q\in Q(C)\). A second choice of primitives differs by a matching family in \(I\), hence a global section. If the original cocycle changes by the coboundary of an \(F\)-valued zero-cochain, its primitives can change by that zero-cochain and its \(Q\)-section is unchanged. These constructions commute with restriction to a common refinement and are inverse. They also add, proving

\[ \mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_{\mathcal U}\check H^1(\mathcal U,F) \simeq H^1(C,F). \tag{AD.4} \]

The colimit can be read as cocycles identified when their restrictions to a common refinement are cohomologous. It does not depend on the choice of maps defining a refinement: the two resulting local lifts represent the same \(q\), so their differences are an \(F\)-coboundary. The construction agrees with the connecting map in (AD.3), thus with derived degree-one cohomology. This is the degree-one calculation of Cohomology on sites, Theorem 6.2, here obtained directly from the local resolutions and injective Čech proof.

Apply it to \(F=\mathbf G_m\), written multiplicatively. The unit sheaf property follows from N.4 and affine descent: coefficients and inverses descend, and their product remains one. A cocycle \(g_{ij}g_{jk}=g_{ik}\) glues trivial line bundles by the rule \(e_j=e_i g_{ij}\). AD.2 makes this a line bundle on \(C\). Conversely, Zariski local frames of a line bundle give such a cocycle. Changing frames to \(e_i b_i\) changes the units to \(b_i^{-1}g_{ij}b_j\). Bundle isomorphisms give exactly these changes after a common trivializing refinement. These constructions are inverse by full faithfulness of descent. Products of cocycles are the transition units of tensor products. Therefore

\[ H^1(C,\mathbf G_m)\simeq\operatorname{Pic}(C) \tag{AD.5} \]

as groups, naturally under pullback wherever the same constructions are made. In particular, the first equality of (P.5) is independent of the function-field vanishing argument used for its higher degrees.

AD.4. Rigidification and the Kummer epimorphism

Let \(f:C_T\to T\) and let \(p_T:T\to C_T\) be the chosen section. W.1 and X.1 show \(f_*\mathcal O_{C_T}=\mathcal O_T\): on an affine open \(\operatorname{Spec}A\subset T\), compute sections using a finite affine cover of \(C\) and its overlaps, then tensor its degree-zero kernel with the flat \(k\)-module \(A\). The result is \(k\otimes_k A=A\). These identifications restrict and glue.

Consequently an automorphism of any line bundle is multiplication by a unique unit from \(T\). For a bundle \(L\), set

\[ L^{\mathrm{rig}}=L\otimes f^*(p_T^*L)^{-1}. \tag{AD.6} \]

Evaluation gives its canonical trivialization along \(p_T\). A rigidified automorphism is the identity. Tensoring \(L\) by a bundle pulled back from \(T\) leaves (AD.6) canonically unchanged. Conversely, isomorphic normalizations mean that the original bundles differ by such a pullback. Thus normalization identifies \(\operatorname{Pic}(C_T)/f^*\operatorname{Pic}(T)\) with rigidified isomorphism classes. An isomorphism between two rigidified objects, when it exists, is unique. Compatible classes on an fppf cover therefore have unique overlap isomorphisms satisfying the cocycle. AD.2 descends both the bundle and its trivialization along the section. This proves that the quotient presheaf is already an fppf sheaf here and establishes the assertion used in Q.4 on every \(T\).

Finally let \(n\) be invertible in \(k\). For a unit \(u\in A^\times\) on an affine étale chart, put \(B=A[t]/(t^n-u)\). It is free of rank \(n\) over \(A\), its fibres are nonzero, and \(t\) is a unit. It is étale: across a square-zero extension, any lift of a root is uniquely corrected by subtracting its equation error divided by \(nt^{n-1}\); this derivative is a unit. Thus the finitely presented algebra is formally étale. The resulting étale cover supplies an \(n\)-th root of \(u\). Together with the definition of \(\mu_n\), this proves exactness of

\[ 1\longrightarrow\mu_n\longrightarrow\mathbf G_m \xrightarrow{(\cdot)^n}\mathbf G_m\longrightarrow1 \tag{AD.7} \]

on the small étale site. T.3 now gives its long exact sequence, AD.5 identifies its degree-one terms, and Appendix R supplies the higher vanishing used in P.2.

Appendix AE. Flat charts and proper geometrically integral parameter spaces

This appendix proves the geometric permanence statements used in P.1 and Q.2–Q.5. It connects the infinitesimal calculations to open images, proves properness of the projective spaces used here directly from their graded charts, and checks geometric integrality of the powers of the curve.

AE.1. Smooth local equations give flatness

Let \(A\) be Noetherian and let \(S=A[x_1,\ldots,x_N]/I\) be finitely presented and formally smooth over \(A\). The splitting argument (Y.14)–(Y.15) works with \(A\) in place of the field: lift the identity of \(S\) to \(A[x]/I^2\), subtract this lift from the quotient map, and differentiate polynomials over \(A\). It gives a split injection

\[ I/I^2\longrightarrow S^N. \tag{AE.1} \]

At a chosen prime \(\mathfrak q\) of \(S\), this finite projective module is free. Choose \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I\) giving a basis there. Their gradient rows are independent over \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)\), so a \(c\)-column minor is nonzero. If \(\mathfrak Q\) is the corresponding prime of \(A[x]\), the basis assertion gives

\[ I_{\mathfrak Q}=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)_{\mathfrak Q}+I_{\mathfrak Q}^2. \tag{AE.2} \]

Nakayama applied to the finite \(A[x]_{\mathfrak Q}\)-module \(I_{\mathfrak Q}/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\) makes it zero. Clearing the finitely many denominators in its generators supplies a neighbourhood where the \(f_i\) generate the ideal and the minor is invertible. Thus the local presentation is exactly the one established in Formally smooth, unramified and étale ring maps, Theorem 5.1.

Put \(\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap A\) and \(B=A[x]_{\mathfrak Q}\). The local map \(A_{\mathfrak p}\to B\) is flat, because polynomial algebras are free and localization preserves flatness. Its closed fibre is a localization of the polynomial algebra over \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)\), hence is regular by Y.5. The images of the \(f_i\) have independent classes in the cotangent space of this local fibre ring: differentiating a product of two maximal-ideal elements gives zero over the residue field, whereas the selected gradient minor is invertible. Y.4 makes these classes part of a regular system of parameters. In particular, the \(f_i\) form a regular sequence in the closed fibre.

Apply U.2 successively. At each step the next equation is a nonzerodivisor on the closed fibre of the preceding flat local quotient. U.2 proves flatness of that quotient by the next equation. We obtain

\[ S_{\mathfrak q}=B/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)B \quad\text{flat over }A_{\mathfrak p}. \tag{AE.3} \]

This implies flatness of \(S\) over \(A\). Indeed, the kernel obtained by tensoring any injection of \(A\)-modules with \(S\) is an \(S\)-module. Its localization at every \(\mathfrak q\) vanishes by (AE.3). Such a module is zero: a nonzero element generates \(S/J\), which remains nonzero at a maximal ideal containing the proper ideal \(J\). Thus every tensorized injection is injective.

We have proved that every smooth morphism with Noetherian base is flat on its affine charts. Étale morphisms are formally smooth and locally finitely presented, so the same conclusion applies. Combining this with AD.2 proves that they are open in the situation of P.1. The polynomial-fibre and successive-quotient proof is also given in Smooth algebras over a field and the Jacobian criterion, Theorem 5.1; here its flatness input is the explicit U.2 argument.

AE.2. Projective space is universally closed

Let \(A\) be any ring, let \(S=A[X_0,\ldots,X_r]\) with its usual grading, and let \(Z\) be a closed subset of \(\mathbf P^r_A\). By the topology of \(\operatorname{Proj}\), write \(Z=V_+(I)\) for a homogeneous ideal \(I\). Put \(M=S/I\). If \(\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}A\) is outside the image of \(Z\), then

\[ \operatorname{Proj}\bigl(M\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)\bigr)=\varnothing. \tag{AE.4} \]

Each standard affine chart therefore has zero coordinate ring. In the localization at \(X_i\), the equality \(1=0\) means that some positive power of \(X_i\) vanishes in the graded quotient over \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)\). If these powers are \(e_i\), every monomial of degree greater than \(\sum_i(e_i-1)\) vanishes. Choose such a degree \(m\). The finite \(A\)-module \(M_m\) has zero fibre at \(\mathfrak p\). Nakayama gives \((M_m)_{\mathfrak p}=0\), and finitely many generators then give an element \(a\notin\mathfrak p\) for which \((M_m)_a=0\). Since the graded algebra is generated in degree one, all its pieces of degree at least \(m\) vanish after this localization. Every projective fibre over \(D(a)\) is empty. Thus the complement of the image of \(Z\) is open.

The projection \(\mathbf P^r_A\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) is closed. The argument applies to every ring, and therefore to every affine chart of every changed base. It proves universal closedness. The finitely many standard charts give finite type. The equations

\[ X_iY_j-X_jY_i=0\qquad(0\leq i,j\leq r) \tag{AE.5} \]

cut out the diagonal in \(\mathbf P^r_A\times_A\mathbf P^r_A\). On the chart where \(X_i=Y_j=1\), one equation is \(X_jY_i=1\). Both factors are therefore units, and the other equations identify every coordinate ratio in the two projective points. This identifies the closed subscheme with the diagonal on each chart. Hence projective space is separated. These three properties prove properness, without a restriction on the base ring.

A closed subscheme of projective space is proper too. A closed immersion is of finite type, separated and universally closed; each property is preserved by composition and base change. For universal closedness this says that the composition of two closed maps is closed after every base change. For finite type it follows from composing finite algebra-generator lists and finite affine covers. For separation, the relative diagonal of a composite factors as its first relative diagonal followed by the pullback of the second closed diagonal. Thus products of proper schemes over a field are proper: the product projection is a base change, followed by the other structure map. In particular the projective curve \(C\), all its powers, and all their base changes have the properness used in Q.2. Compare Proper morphisms and the valuative criterion of properness, Theorem 2.1; the graded argument above supplies the projective case directly.

AE.3. The curve powers remain integral over every field extension

For every \(T/k\), AD.4 proves

\[ (C_T\longrightarrow T)_*\mathcal O_{C_T}=\mathcal O_T. \tag{AE.6} \]

Successive projections, starting with \(T=\operatorname{Spec}K\), therefore give

\[ \Gamma((C_K)^d,\mathcal O)=K \qquad(K/k\text{ any field extension},\ d\geq0). \tag{AE.7} \]

The schemes \((C_K)^d\) are smooth over \(K\). Base change preserves the lifting property and finite presentation. Products preserve them as well: a map to a product is a pair of maps, lift the two components on a common open refinement, and use the combined finite presentations. Y.6 consequently makes all their local rings regular local domains, including when \(K\) is imperfect.

They are Noetherian and have finitely many irreducible components. Distinct components cannot meet: components through a point give distinct minimal primes in its local ring, which is a domain. Thus each component is open and closed. Two or more components would give a nonconstant idempotent global function, by gluing zero on one component and one on the others. This contradicts (AE.7). Each power is therefore irreducible. Its local rings are reduced, so the scheme is reduced as well, and hence integral. This proves geometric integrality of \(C^d\), including \(d=0\).

The universally surjective map \(C^d\to H_d\) in Q.2 now gives geometric irreducibility of \(H_d\). Its smooth charts give geometric reducedness by Y.6. Thus \(H_d\) is geometrically integral. The Abel surjection \(H_g\to P^g\) in Q.5 similarly gives geometric irreducibility of the Picard piece; smoothness gives geometric reducedness. The properness argument there pulls back closed subsets along this universally surjective map and uses AE.2, so it works over arbitrary changed bases. Translation by \(\mathcal O_C(dp)\) gives the same properties of every degree piece. In particular \(P^0\) is the proper geometrically connected group required by (P.1).

Appendix AF. Constants and connected fibres on the generic curve neighbourhood

In O.3 the smooth curve family comes with a finite map to a projective scheme over an integral Noetherian base. We use that map to prove the cohomological statements needed in O.4, including base change to every geometric fibre after one further shrinking. All cohomology below is ordinary Zariski cohomology, as constructed in T and computed in W.

AF.1. Finite maps and the projective cohomology calculation

First, finite morphisms are proper. Here is the algebraic closed-image argument in the finite case. For a finite algebra \(R\to D\) and an ideal \(J\subset D\), put \(R'=R/(J\cap R)\) and \(D'=D/J\). The induced map \(R'\to D'\) is injective and finite. At any prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(R'\), its localization is still injective, so \(D'_{\mathfrak p}\ne0\). If its residue algebra were zero, Nakayama would make this finite module zero. Thus the residue algebra is nonzero and has a maximal ideal. Its inverse image is a prime of \(D'\) over \(\mathfrak p\). This proves

\[ \operatorname{image}(V(J)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}R) =V(J\cap R). \tag{AF.1} \]

Tensoring a finite list of module generators proves that every base change remains finite, so the same argument proves universal closedness. The multiplication map \(D\otimes_R D\to D\) is surjective, giving a closed diagonal on affine charts. Module generators also generate the algebra, proving finite type. Hence the morphism is proper. Composition of finite maps is finite, by taking products of module generators. This is the finite-case argument in Affine, integral and finite morphisms, Sections 4–5, with the needed lying-over assertion proved above by Nakayama.

Let \(B\) be Noetherian and suppose

\[ q:C\longrightarrow\mathbf P^N_B \quad\text{is finite}. \tag{AF.2} \]

For a coherent sheaf \(F\) on \(C\), the sheaf \(q_*F\) is coherent. On a standard affine chart with coordinate ring \(R\), its inverse image is \(\operatorname{Spec}D\), where \(D\) is finite over \(R\). A finite \(D\)-module is finite over \(R\), by multiplying the two finite generating lists. Restriction to a principal open localizes that module, by W.1, so these descriptions give a coherent sheaf on the projective space. This also proves the pushforward description directly, without a higher-direct-image theorem.

The standard affine cover of \(\mathbf P^N_B\) and its inverse-image cover of \(C\) have identical ordered section complexes for \(q_*F\) and \(F\). All intersections in both covers are affine. W.2 therefore gives

\[ H^i(C,F)=H^i(\mathbf P^N_B,q_*F). \tag{AF.3} \]

W.4 makes these modules finite over \(B\), and W.2 makes them zero for \(i>N\). The finite map of O.3, composed with the closed projective embedding of its target, has form (AF.2). Thus (AF.3) proves precisely the coherent finiteness needed for that family.

AF.2. A bounded flat complex after shrinking an integral base

Let \(B\) now be a domain, with fraction field \(K\). Every finite \(B\)-module \(M\) becomes finite free after inverting one nonzero element. Choose elements of \(M\) whose images form a \(K\)-basis of \(M\otimes_B K\); clearing denominators of a chosen basis supplies such elements. The resulting map \(B^r\to M\) is injective, since its kernel becomes zero over \(K\) and \(B^r\) is torsion-free. Its finite cokernel becomes zero over \(K\). Each member of a finite generating list for that cokernel is killed by a nonzero element of \(B\). Inverting their product kills the cokernel. This includes rank zero. For finitely many modules, multiply their finitely many choices of denominator.

We will also use the following tensor calculation. Suppose \(D^\bullet\) is a bounded complex of flat modules over a ring \(A\), and every \(H^i(D)\) is flat. Write \(Z^i\) for its cycles and \(B^i_D\) for its boundaries. If \(b\) is its last degree, \(Z^b=D^b\) is flat. The two sequences

\[ \begin{aligned} 0\longrightarrow B^i_D\longrightarrow Z^i \longrightarrow H^i(D)\longrightarrow0,\\ 0\longrightarrow Z^{i-1}\longrightarrow D^{i-1} \longrightarrow B^i_D\longrightarrow0. \end{aligned} \tag{AF.4} \]

and U.1 show successively that \(B^b_D,Z^{b-1},B^{b-1}_D,\ldots\) are flat and that all these sequences remain exact under every tensor product. The differential factors through its boundary module. The tensorized sequences identify its kernel and image with \(Z^i\otimes_A M\) and \(B^i_D\otimes_A M\). Consequently

\[ H^i(D^\bullet\otimes_A M)=H^i(D^\bullet)\otimes_A M \quad\text{for every }A\text{-module }M. \tag{AF.5} \]

This argument uses boundedness and flatness of the cohomology as well as flatness of the terms. It is the cycle calculation underlying Base change and the Grothendieck complex, Lemma 3.1; no assertion that arbitrary cohomology always commutes with tensoring is being made.

Apply it to the inverse-image affine cover in AF.1 with \(F=\mathcal O_C\), for the smooth family over the integral Noetherian ring \(B\) in O.3. AE.1 makes each affine coordinate module flat over \(B\). The ordered complex is bounded, its cohomology modules are finite by (AF.3), and only finitely many degrees occur. Localize \(B\) once so that every one of those modules is free, using the preceding denominator argument. Localization commutes with the complex and its cohomology by W.1.

After this localization, every \(B\)-algebra \(A\) gives the base-changed affine cover with section complex \(D^\bullet\otimes_B A\), by W.1. W.2 and (AF.5) prove

\[ H^i(C,\mathcal O_C)\otimes_B A \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } H^i(C_A,\mathcal O_{C_A}) \qquad\text{for every }B\text{-algebra }A. \tag{AF.6} \]

The comparison sends a section or cocycle to its scalar extension, so the degree-zero isomorphism is an isomorphism of algebras. Further localizations preserve it. The affine-cover comparison is also described in [Stacks, curve constants]; here W.1–W.2 supply its cohomology proof and (AF.4) supplies the additional arbitrary-tensor step on this open neighbourhood.

AF.3. The finite algebra separates exactly the geometric components
