Its comparison cone has \(F\)-acyclic terms and is acyclic; the argument just given proves that applying \(F\) to the comparison remains a quasi-isomorphism. This proves the computation statement.

There is also an actual cohomological window: \[ RF(D^{\geq a})\subset D^{\geq a}, \qquad RF(D^{\leq b})\subset D^{\leq b+N}. \tag{BG.7} \] For the first inclusion, replace a lower truncation by its bounded-below injective resolution; the construction is T.4 and the homotopy argument is B.1. For the second take a termwise injective K-injective resolution \(I\) of an object with no cohomology above \(b\). If \(i>b+N\), the cycle sequences in the exact tail give \[ H^i(FI)=R^1F(Z^{i-1}) \simeq R^{N+1}F(Z^{i-N-1})=0. \tag{BG.8} \] The last surjection used is \(I^b\to Z^{b+1}\) when \(i=b+N+1\), which is surjective because \(H^{b+1}(I)=0\). For \(N=0\), the functor is exact and the assertion follows directly. The truncation triangles and (BG.7) show that \(H^i(RFE)\) depends only on \(\tau_{\geq i-N}\tau_{\leq i}E\): the omitted upper part has no image cohomology through degree \(i\), and the omitted lower part has none from degree \(i\) onward. This argument neither assumes left completeness of a derived category nor exchanges cohomology with an infinite product.

BG.4. Unbounded proper comparison and coproducts

Let \(p:T\to S\) be proper, and consider any change of base with projections \(a:T'\to T\), \(g:S'\to S\) and proper map \(p':T'\to S'\). For \(E\in D(T,\Lambda)\), choose a termwise injective K-injective resolution \(I\). The proper comparison theorem BE.7, applied to each individual term, gives \[ R^qp'_*a^{-1}I^m=0\quad(q>0), \qquad g^{-1}p_*I^m\xrightarrow{\sim}p'_*a^{-1}I^m. \tag{BG.9} \] All those sheaves are torsion because \(\Lambda\) is killed by an integer. The local finite bound (BG.3) and BG.3 make the unbounded complex \(a^{-1}I\) compute its derived direct image. Thus the termwise maps in (BG.9) give the canonical isomorphism \[ g^{-1}Rp_*E\xrightarrow{\sim}Rp'_*a^{-1}E \tag{BG.10} \] for arbitrary \(E\). They are the usual adjunction base-change maps: after comparing with a K-injective target resolution, the termwise direct-image adjunction defines the same morphism. Naturality of that adjunction proves compatibility with successive base changes and with compositions of proper maps. This identifies the comparison morphism itself, not only its source and target.

The same finite bound proves preservation of coproducts. Choose resolutions \(I_t\) for a family \(E_t\). BA's higher-direct-image continuity on quasi-compact, quasi-separated schemes, together with BB.3, implies that each term \(\bigoplus_t I_t^m\) is \(p_*\)-acyclic: a sum is the filtered colimit of its finite subsums, whose positive derived images vanish. Direct image also commutes with these sums in degree zero. BG.3 therefore computes both sides of \[ \bigoplus_t Rp_*E_t\longrightarrow Rp_*\left(\bigoplus_tE_t\right) \tag{BG.11} \] by the identical termwise image complex. BF.3 identifies the termwise sums with the derived coproducts. This proves (BG.11), without asserting that a sum of injective or K-injective objects is injective. Both statements are local on the base; a single global finite bound is unnecessary when the base is not quasi-compact.

BG.5. Compactification at the required field scope

For a separated finite-type map of finite-type schemes over a field, the needed existence theorem is The right adjoint of derived pushforward, Appendix N, Theorem N.E.1. Its N.A–N.E prove Nagata compactification for Noetherian schemes, preserving nilpotents and the entire open source. This hypothesis holds here. The theorem gives \[ X\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\xrightarrow{p}Y, \qquad j\text{ open},\quad p\text{ proper}. \tag{BG.12} \]

We specify the complete geometric inputs for that proof in the present use. AU.1 gives the finite affine equalizer, its localization and flat-base-change identities, and properness of maps from proper schemes to separated schemes. AU.2 gives scheme-theoretic closure and the Noetherian Chow modification. For a nonaffine Noetherian base the needed Chow statement is Projective morphisms and Chow's lemma, Theorem 4.1: its finite affine-cover construction and gluing retain the base and the schematically dense source. The relative immersion of each affine piece used there is constructed explicitly in N.E.1: finitely many distinguished opens over affine base charts supply algebra generators; their numerators and denominators are global coordinates, and on the corresponding target opens the coordinate-ring maps are surjective. This proves the relative immersion even when the base is not affine. The valuation domination and specialization witnesses are proved in Valuation rings and separatedness, Theorems 2.1 and 4.1; AW.1 identifies their algebraic use. Proper morphisms and valuative criteria, Sections 1–4 gives the all-valuation properness criterion and properness of projective space. Its quasi-compact image criterion is the elementary localization argument in Finiteness of morphisms, Theorem 1.2, and its graph and projective-chart inputs are The diagonal and separated morphisms, Sections 1–2 and 4–6.

There is a useful direct replacement for the auxiliary quasi-affineness assertion N.A.4. AW.5 factors every separated quasi-finite finite-type map occurring there as an open immersion into a finite scheme over the target. That finite scheme is affine over the target, so the original map is quasi-affine. This proves the required assertion directly from AW.1–AW.5, with their conductor, regular-local and slicing arguments.

The rest of Appendix N consists of its written blowup-chart and strict-transform calculations, the protected elimination construction N.B.1, the three assembly lemmas N.C.1–N.C.3, and the two-open construction N.D.1. The blowup charts embed in localizations, so their protected opens stay schematically dense. The elimination construction uses finitely generated conductor ideals to extend rational coordinate maps and then separates the protected boundary. The two-open construction keeps a closed gluing graph, checks all valuation limits from a dense open and applies the proved Chow modification. Finally N.E.1 compactifies the finite affine cover. These arguments establish (BG.12) with the original possibly singular and nonreduced schemes; smoothness or quasi-projectivity of \(X\) is not added.

BG.6. Construction, independence and the right adjoint

Define, using (BG.12), \[ Rf_!E=Rp_*j_!E. \tag{BG.13} \] Open extension by zero is exact and preserves coproducts, by its stalk description in Constructible sheaves and extension by zero. BF.4 constructs \(Rp_*\) as an exact functor of derived categories, and (BG.11) proves that it preserves coproducts. Therefore (BG.13) is exact and coproduct-preserving on all of \(D(X,\Lambda)\).

The definition is canonical. Here is the comparison mechanism, with its full earlier proof locator. In a commuting square with open horizontal maps \(j:U\to T\), \(i:V\to S\) and proper vertical maps \(p':U\to V\), \(p:T\to S\), the induced open map \(U\to T\times_SV\) is proper, by the closed graph and proper projection argument. It is consequently clopen. Restriction to \(V\) thus identifies \(Rp_*j_!E\) with \(Rp'_*E\), and the open adjunction defines \[ i_!Rp'_*E\longrightarrow Rp_*j_!E. \tag{BG.14} \] It is an isomorphism over \(V\). On its complement the right side is zero by (BG.10), because the pulled-back support open is empty. The left side is zero by definition. Geometric stalks detect the resulting isomorphism. The square need not be cartesian.

A refinement \(h:\overline X_1\to\overline X_2\) gives (BG.14) in the form \(j_{2,!}\simeq Rh_*j_{1,!}\), hence an isomorphism between the two definitions (BG.13). Common refinements exist by taking the scheme-theoretic closure of the diagonal \(X\) in the product of two compactifications. Above the open \(X\) in either factor its graph is already closed, so the same copy of \(X\) is open in that closure. Parallel refinement maps are equalized by their closed equalizer, which still contains that open. The quasi-coherent closure ideal is the kernel of restriction; AU.1's finite affine equalizer gives its localization, also over a non-Noetherian base. These facts prove the cofiltered refinement assertion used here.

The identities and coherence of these particular maps are proved in Cohomology with compact support, Lemma 6.1 and Theorems 7.1–9.1. The inputs to those proofs are now (BG.10), exact open extension, proper composition from BF.4 and the preceding refinement construction. For precision, their pasting argument restricts an exchange to its source open, where it is the clopen pushforward identity; the open adjunction determines the entire map from that restriction. Stacking squares consequently agrees with composing the adjunction units. A common refinement then makes comparisons between any choices identical and proves their cocycle rule. For three composable maps, successive compactifications give a single array of opens and proper maps, and the two parenthesizations are the two pastings of that same array. Arbitrary base change pulls back (BG.12), and (BG.10) with exact open base change gives its comparison; the same pasting argument proves compatibility with refinements and composition. Thus these are canonical and associative functor isomorphisms, not choices of unrelated isomorphisms.

Finally apply BF.6 to (BG.13). This supplies an exact right adjoint \(f^!\) on arbitrary ordinary \(\Lambda\)-complexes, with the adjunction unit and counit. It completes the existence and coproduct-preservation prerequisite in Proposition 3.3. The smooth trace normalization, the ensuing Gysin comparisons, enhanced operation compatibilities and passage to normalized adic coefficients retain their own arguments; none follows solely from the existence of this right adjoint.

Appendix BH. Tensor products and the proper-support projection formula

Fix a constant commutative coefficient ring \(\Lambda\). Sections BH.1–BH.4 work on the small étale site of a scheme, with a small basis fixed as in BF.5. Sections BH.5–BH.7 use a ring killed by an integer and the proper-support scope of BG. Every complex below may be unbounded; tensor totalization uses direct sums.

BH.1. Flat resolutions on the étale site

For a basis object \(u:U\to X\), put \(B_U=u_!\Lambda_U\). The explicit construction and adjunction in Constructible sheaves and extension by zero, Proposition 1.1 give \[ \operatorname{Hom}(B_U,F)=F(U),\qquad (B_U)_{\bar x}=\bigoplus_{\bar u\mapsto\bar x}\Lambda. \tag{BH.1} \] In particular these stalks are free. Tensor sheaves have stalks equal to the tensors of their stalks: each tensor and each relation expressing its vanishing involve finitely many factors and balancing relations, which can all be represented on one pointed étale refinement. Sheafification leaves these germs unchanged. Exactness is detected on geometric stalks, so every \(B_U\) is flat. The sum \[ L(F)=\bigoplus_{U}\ \bigoplus_{s\in F(U)}B_U\longrightarrow F \tag{BH.2} \] is an epimorphism: its summand indexed by \(s\) represents that section, and every germ has such a representative. All indices form a set. Direct sums and filtered colimits of flat sheaves are flat, by their stalk tensor functors and exactness of these operations on modules.

A complex \(P\) is K-flat if \(A\otimes P\) is acyclic for every acyclic complex \(A\). A flat sheaf in one degree is K-flat: tensor its exact cycle sequences with that sheaf. Sums and filtered colimits of K-flat complexes are K-flat, since tensor commutes with them and filtered colimits are exact. A degreewise split extension of two K-flat complexes is K-flat: after tensoring, it remains degreewise split, and its long exact cohomology sequence applies. In particular a bounded complex of flats is K-flat by finite induction; a bounded-above complex of flats is the filtered union of its bounded brutal lower truncations and is K-flat as well. None of these assertions says that an arbitrary complex of flat terms is K-flat.

Here is a resolution for an arbitrary \(G\). Let \(D_n(F)\) have \(F\) in degrees \(n,n+1\) and identity differential. Start with \[ P_0=\bigoplus_nD_n(L(G^n))\longrightarrow G. \tag{BH.3} \] The lower term maps by (BH.2), and the upper term by its composite with \(d_G\). This is a termwise epimorphism. Each disk is contractible; tensoring its contraction \(h\) with an element of degree \(a\) uses the sign \((-1)^a h\). Thus \(P_0\) is K-flat and has flat terms.

Given a termwise epimorphism \(P_s\to G\), take its kernel \(K_s\). For every \(z\in Z^q(K_s)(U)\), attach one \(B_U\) in degree \(q-1\), with differential equal to the map represented by \(z\), and with zero image in \(G\). Explicitly, writing \(V_s\) for the graded sum of the added terms, set \[ P_{s+1}=P_s\oplus V_s,\qquad d(p,v)=(d p+\alpha(v),0). \tag{BH.4} \] Here \(d\alpha=0\) and the composite of \(\alpha\) with \(P_s\to G\) is zero. Therefore (BH.4) is a complex over \(G\). Its quotient by \(P_s\) is a sum of shifts of flat sheaves, with zero differential. The degreewise splitting proves K-flatness by induction and preserves flat terms.

Set \(P(G)=\varinjlim_sP_s\). Filtered-colimit exactness gives \[ H^q(\ker(P(G)\to G)) =\varinjlim_sH^q(K_s)=0. \tag{BH.5} \] For the last equality, a germ of a kernel class is represented on some \(U\) by a cycle at stage \(s\); the cell attached at stage \(s+1\) kills it. Hence every transition map on these cohomology sheaves is zero. The long exact sequence of the termwise epimorphism proves that \(P(G)\to G\) is a quasi-isomorphism. This proves the resolution theorem on the actual étale site. It is the disk-and-cycle construction of Sheaves of modules and their derived categories, Sections 8–9, with (BH.1) supplying the required étale generators in place of topological open sets.

The construction can be made functorial on chain maps: send a generator indexed by a section to the generator indexed by its image, and do the same for each kernel cycle at each stage. These maps commute with the differentials in (BH.4), with identities and with composition. The resolution functor need not be additive; the derived functor constructed next will be additive.

BH.2. Derived tensor, morphisms and coherence

Use the total differential \[ d(a\otimes b)=d a\otimes b+(-1)^{|a|}a\otimes d b. \tag{BH.6} \] Tensoring a quasi-isomorphism with a K-flat complex preserves quasi-isomorphisms: tensor its acyclic cone, and distribute the two cone summands, using (BH.6). If \(P\to P'\) is a quasi-isomorphism between K-flat complexes, tensoring it with any \(G\) also preserves quasi-isomorphisms. Indeed, resolve \(G\) by \(Q\). In the square with rows \(Q\otimes P\to Q\otimes P'\) and \(G\otimes P\to G\otimes P'\), both vertical maps and the top map are quasi-isomorphisms by K-flatness. The induced cohomology square makes the bottom map one too.

Consequently the functor on pairs of complexes \[ (E,F)\longmapsto P(E)\otimes P(F) \tag{BH.7} \] inverts quasi-isomorphisms in each variable. BF.2's localization property, including its property for natural transformations, lets (BH.7) descend in the two variables successively. This constructs \(E\otimes^LF\) as a bifunctor on the actual derived categories. For fixed \(F\), the natural quasi-isomorphism \(P(E)\otimes P(F)\to E\otimes P(F)\) identifies it with tensoring by \(P(F)\). The latter respects homotopies, addition, shifts and cones, by the formula (BH.6). Thus the derived functor is additive and exact in each variable despite the resolution functor's possible nonadditivity.

For completeness, two termwise-surjective K-flat resolutions of \(F\) have a common comparison: resolve their ordinary fibre product over \(F\). Each projection is a surjective quasi-isomorphism, with kernel the acyclic kernel of the other resolution. The resulting maps between K-flat complexes remain quasi-isomorphisms after tensoring with any \(G\). Resolving a triple fibre product proves the cocycle rule. Resolving the fibre product of two comparison resolutions proves independence of that choice. An arbitrary K-flat resolution becomes surjective by adding the contractible disk complex (BH.3). This establishes the same comparison for arbitrary choices, without assuming a direct map between them.

Tensor products of K-flat complexes are K-flat, because tensoring an acyclic complex first with one factor and then the other remains acyclic. The usual chain maps \[ (a\otimes b)\otimes c\longmapsto a\otimes(b\otimes c), \qquad a\otimes b\longmapsto(-1)^{|a||b|}b\otimes a \tag{BH.8} \] therefore give associativity and symmetry on simultaneous K-flat models. The three differential signs for associativity are \(1,(-1)^{|a|},(-1)^{|a|+|b|}\) on both sides. Every route through four-factor associativity gives the same ordered tensor. Moving a degree \(a\) past degrees \(b,c\) gives \((-1)^{a(b+c)}=(-1)^{ab}(-1)^{ac}\), proving symmetry coherence. Multiplication by the degree-zero flat unit \(\Lambda\) proves the unit identities. These calculations survive the canonical model comparisons. Tensoring preserves arbitrary coproducts: use the sum of the K-flat models and distribute the direct-sum totalization. Exactness of sums makes that sum a resolution of the corresponding derived coproduct.

BH.3. Stalks and inverse image preserve K-flat models

For constant \(\Lambda\), a complex \(P\) is K-flat if and only if every \(P_{\bar x}\) is K-flat over \(\Lambda\). First assume sheafwise K-flatness and let \(N\) be any acyclic complex of \(\Lambda\)-modules and take its constant sheaf complex \(\underline N\). Its stalks are \(N\), so it is acyclic. Hence \(\underline N\otimes P\) is acyclic, and its stalk is \(N\otimes P_{\bar x}\). This is the defining test for \(P_{\bar x}\). In the other direction all stalk tests make \(A\otimes P\) acyclic for every acyclic sheaf complex \(A\).

For a scheme map \(g:Y\to X\), exact inverse image has stalk \((g^{-1}P)_{\bar y}=P_{g\bar y}\). The preceding test shows that \(g^{-1}P\) is K-flat whenever \(P\) is. Inverse image also preserves tensor sheaves and sums: this follows on stalks from the finite tensor presentation used in BH.1, and from the inverse-image stalk formula. We obtain the natural isomorphism \[ g^{-1}(E\otimes^LF) \simeq g^{-1}E\otimes^Lg^{-1}F. \tag{BH.9} \] On K-flat models it is the ordinary inverse-image tensor map. Its compatibility with (BH.8), units and successive inverse images follows by applying the same maps to elementary tensors. Exact inverse image of a complex of flat terms alone would not have established this assertion; K-flatness itself has now been checked.

BH.4. The derived tensor–Hom adjunction on the same site

For sheaf complexes write \[ \mathcal H^r(B,I)=\prod_{a\in\mathbb Z} \mathcal Hom(B^a,I^{a+r}),\qquad d h=d_Ih-(-1)^r h d_B. \tag{BH.10} \] The internal sheaf Hom is characterized on an étale object \(U\) by morphisms between the restrictions to \(U\); the usual sheaf gluing of module morphisms proves this description. In (BH.10) the products are products of sheaves. No exactness of products is assumed. The two middle terms cancel in \(d^2\), and the other two contain a squared differential.

A K-injective \(I\) remains K-injective after restriction to any étale \(u:U\to X\). Indeed, the exact left adjoint \(u_!\) in (BH.1) sends acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes, and \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{K(U)}(A,u^{-1}I[r]) =\operatorname{Hom}_{K(X)}(u_!A,I[r])=0 \tag{BH.11} \] for every acyclic \(A\) and integer \(r\). If \(B\) is acyclic, sections on every \(U\) of \(\mathcal H(B,I)\) consequently form an acyclic complex. Sheafification of these cohomology presheaves proves acyclicity of \(\mathcal H(B,I)\). Thus a quasi-isomorphism in the first variable induces a quasi-isomorphism of these internal Hom complexes. A quasi-isomorphism between K-injective second variables is a homotopy equivalence by BF.1, and internal Hom preserves that equivalence. We may therefore define \[ R\mathcal Hom(B,C)=\mathcal H(B,I_C) \tag{BH.12} \] independently of choices, with natural maps in both variables.

Take a K-flat \(P\to B\) and K-injective \(C\to I\). Currying sends \(\alpha(a)(p)\) to the same expression viewed as a function of \(a\otimes p\). For a degree-\(r\) homogeneous \(\alpha\), the differential on either side is \[ \begin{aligned} d_I\bigl(\alpha(a)(p)\bigr) &-(-1)^r\alpha(d_Aa)(p)\\ &-(-1)^{r+|a|}\alpha(a)(d_Pp). \end{aligned} \tag{BH.13} \] Hom out of direct sums and into products proves that this is a bijection of all components, even when unbounded. It is a natural chain isomorphism. For acyclic \(A\), the complex \(A\otimes P\) is acyclic, so this adjunction makes \(\mathcal H(P,I)\) K-injective. It computes (BH.12), by the first-variable invariance. BF.1 now gives \[ \operatorname{Hom}_D(A,R\mathcal Hom(B,C)) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_D(A\otimes^LB,C). \tag{BH.14} \] This is the unbounded tensor–Hom adjunction actually used here. The same calculation on the localized étale site gives the étale restriction isomorphism for (BH.12), since the chosen K-injective remains K-injective there and internal Hom restricts by its just-given description. It does not claim an internal-Hom isomorphism for arbitrary inverse image. Evaluation is the transpose of the identity under (BH.14); composition is the transpose of two successive evaluations. Their associativity and unit identities follow by evaluating on a third factor and using the unique transpose. The corresponding topological computations are also given in Supporting verifications for open prerequisites, DF-A–DF-F; (BH.1) and (BH.11) establish the étale-site inputs here.

BH.5. A coefficient complex can be tested using free modules

Let \(T\) be qcqs with finite cohomological dimension for \(\Lambda\)-modules. For \(E\in D(T,\Lambda)\) and \(M\in D(\Lambda)\), there is a natural comparison \[ R\Gamma(T,E)\otimes^LM \longrightarrow R\Gamma(T,E\otimes^L\underline M). \tag{BH.15} \] It is adjoint to evaluation from the constant complex \(\underline{R\Gamma(T,E)}\) to \(E\), tensored with \(\underline M\). BF.4 supplies that derived adjunction. Both sides are exact functors of \(M\) and preserve sums: for tensor this is BH.2; for global sections use BA's filtered-cohomology continuity and the finite-bound acyclic-complex argument of BG.3–BG.4. The map is the unit identification when \(M=\Lambda\), and likewise for shifts and sums of that object.

Here is the complete generation argument. For a sequence of complexes \(M_0\to M_1\to\cdots\), the map \(1-s\) on \(\bigoplus_iM_i\), where \(s\) moves each summand along its transition to the next, is termwise injective. A vector in its kernel has finite support; its zeroth component is zero, then its first component is zero, and induction kills them all. Its cokernel is the termwise colimit, by the defining relations of a direct limit. Hence \[ \operatorname{Cone}(1-s)\simeq\varinjlim_iM_i. \tag{BH.16} \] The quasi-isomorphism is the projection from the target sum to its cokernel; the long exact sequence of the termwise short exact sequence proves it.

Every module has a free resolution in nonpositive degrees: successively take the free module on the underlying elements and the kernel of its surjection. Every bounded brutal truncation of this resolution is obtained by finitely many cones from sums of shifts of \(\Lambda\). Its longer lower truncations have union the resolution, so (BH.16) and preservation of sums and cones prove (BH.15) for a module. A bounded-above complex is similarly the union of its bounded brutal lower truncations, now assembled from modules. Finally an arbitrary complex is the union of its good upper truncations \(\tau_{\leq b}M\) as \(b\) increases: at any fixed degree its terms and differential eventually agree with those of \(M\). Each truncation is bounded above. Applying (BH.16) a final time proves (BH.15) for every \(M\). This argument uses neither a finite free resolution nor finite Tor dimension.

BH.6. Proper projection and its actual comparison map

For proper \(p:T\to S\), define \[ \gamma_{p,E,M}:Rp_*E\otimes^LM \longrightarrow Rp_*(E\otimes^Lp^{-1}M) \tag{BH.17} \] by transposing the counit \(p^{-1}Rp_*E\to E\) tensored with \(p^{-1}M\), using (BH.9) and BF.4. Take a geometric stalk \(\bar s\). By (BH.9) and unbounded proper comparison BG.4, (BH.17) becomes (BH.15) on the proper geometric fibre \(T_{\bar s}\). This identification respects the map: both are adjoint to the pulled-back direct-image counit. The fibre has finite dimension, and BG.2 gives the required finite cohomological bound. Thus every stalk map is an isomorphism; geometric points detect quasi-isomorphisms, so (BH.17) is an isomorphism for arbitrary \(E,M\) over the torsion ring.

The maps retain composition and tensor coherence. For composable proper maps \(p,q\), the projection map for \(qp\) is the composite of the one for \(q\), with coefficient \(M\), and \(Rq_*\) of the one for \(p\), with coefficient \(q^{-1}M\). Transpose both maps through \((qp)^{-1}\dashv R(qp)_*\): each is the tensor of \(p^{-1}\) of the \(q\)-counit followed by the \(p\)-counit. Uniqueness of transpose proves equality. Applying this twice proves the three-map identity. With two coefficient factors, both orders of projection transpose to the same counit tensored with both factors, so (BH.8) proves compatibility with their associator and unit. Arbitrary base-change compatibility follows in the same way from BG.4's compatibility of the actual base-change map with counits and from (BH.9). These verifications identify the canonical maps, rather than just their isomorphism classes.

BH.7. Proper supports and invertible twists

For an open \(j:U\hookrightarrow T\), extending a K-flat complex by zero preserves K-flatness: its stalk is the old K-flat stalk on \(U\) and zero elsewhere. The stalkwise tensor construction gives \[ j_!E\otimes^LN\simeq j_!(E\otimes^Lj^{-1}N). \tag{BH.18} \] Combine this with (BH.17) for a compactification \(f=pj\). We obtain \[ Rf_!E\otimes^LM \xrightarrow{\sim}Rf_!(E\otimes^Lf^{-1}M). \tag{BH.19} \] It is independent of compactification. Indeed, a refinement comparison is BG.6's proper–open exchange. After restriction to its support open, compatibility with (BH.18) and (BH.17) is the identity on the open tensor factors and the naturality of the proper counit. Its source is an extension by zero, so the open adjunction determines the whole map from that restriction. This proves compatibility with a single refinement; a common refinement proves independence. The same square argument and the proper composition calculation in BH.6 prove composition compatibility. Pulling back the squares proves compatibility with arbitrary base change. These are the exact comparisons used in Cohomology with compact support, Section 10, now with the tensor and étale-site prerequisites proved.

Transposing (BH.19) followed by the counit produces a canonical map \[ f^!A\otimes^Lf^{-1}M\longrightarrow f^!(A\otimes^LM). \tag{BH.20} \] For an invertible locally constant rank-one sheaf \(L\), it is an isomorphism. Its inverse tensor is \(L^\vee\); the evaluation isomorphisms hold on trivializing étale covers and therefore globally. For every \(T\), the following natural chain of adjunctions proves the assertion: \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}(T,f^!A\otimes f^{-1}L) &=\operatorname{Hom}(T\otimes f^{-1}L^\vee,f^!A)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!(T\otimes f^{-1}L^\vee),A)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!T\otimes L^\vee,A)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(Rf_!T,A\otimes L)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(T,f^!(A\otimes L)). \end{aligned} \tag{BH.21} \] The tensor functors here are exact because these lines and their inverses are locally free. Evaluating the chain on the identity gives precisely the counit-and-projection transpose (BH.20); evaluation with the inverse line gives its inverse. Shift compatibility follows from exactness of the functors. This establishes the invertible Tate-line cancellation used in Proposition 3.3. It makes no invertibility claim for (BH.20) with arbitrary \(M\), and does not by itself prove the smooth orientation or any adic comparison.

Appendix BI. The affine-line trace and its local comparison

Fix a field \(k\), an integer \(n\geq2\) invertible in \(k\), and \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\). The schemes in this appendix are separated of finite type over \(k\), unless a selected strict localization is specified. We use the ordinary unbounded derived categories constructed in BF, proper support from BG, and tensor and internal Hom from BH.

BI.1. The local adjunction and its actual maps

Let \(f:X\to S\) be separated of finite type and let \(j:U\to X\) be a separated affine étale neighbourhood. The adjunctions of BG.6 and BH.1 give, for every complex \(A\) and integer \(r\), \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}_S(R(fj)_!\Lambda,A[r]) &=\operatorname{Hom}_X(j_!\Lambda,f^!A[r])\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}_U(\Lambda,j^{-1}f^!A[r]). \end{aligned} \tag{BI.1} \] These are adjunction bijections, so their transitions under a refinement are the étale counits on the left and restrictions on the right. To identify the last group, take a K-injective representative \(I\) of \(f^!A\). Its restriction is K-injective by (BH.11); the group is \(H^r(\Gamma(U,I))\). Exact filtered colimits over pointed étale neighbourhoods commute with kernels and images in the section complexes. Their termwise colimit is the stalk complex \(I_{\bar x}\). Consequently \[ \mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_{(U,\bar u)} \operatorname{Hom}_S(R(fj)_!\Lambda,A[r]) =H^r(f^!A)_{\bar x}. \tag{BI.2} \] This proves the local test for unbounded \(A\).

There is also the internal adjunction \[ Rf_*R\mathcal Hom(E,f^!A) \simeq R\mathcal Hom(Rf_!E,A). \tag{BI.3} \] Indeed Hom from any complex \(M\) into its left side is successively \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}_X(f^{-1}M\otimes^LE,f^!A) &=\operatorname{Hom}_S(Rf_!(f^{-1}M\otimes^LE),A)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}_S(M\otimes^LRf_!E,A). \end{aligned} \tag{BI.4} \] The first derived adjunction uses exact inverse image and BF.4. BH.4 supplies the tensor–Hom bijections, and BH.7 supplies the middle projection isomorphism. The last group is Hom into the right side of (BI.3). Naturality and the representing property prove (BI.3). Its map is evaluation followed by the counit: transposing that composite through these same bijections returns the identity. Thus this comparison includes its normalization and its compatibility with composition.

BI.2. The projective-line splitting specifies the trace

Write \(p:\mathbf P^1_S\to S\), \(q:\mathbf A^1_S\to S\), and let \(i\) be the infinity section. The unit and the Kummer class \(c=c_1^{(n)}(\mathcal O(1))\) define \[ \alpha:\Lambda\oplus\Lambda(-1)[-2] \longrightarrow Rp_*\Lambda. \tag{BI.5} \] For the second summand this means the adjoint of the class viewed as a morphism \(p^{-1}\Lambda(-1)[-2]\to\Lambda\). This uses the invertible twist, not a choice of a primitive root on \(S\).

Here is the full geometric-fibre check. Over an algebraically closed field \(\Omega\), the divisor presentation from AD.3 identifies \(\operatorname{Pic}(\mathbf P^1_\Omega)\) with \(\mathbf Z\) by degree. Every finite closed point is \(a\in\Omega\), and \(\operatorname{div}(t-a)=[a]-[\infty]\), so each divisor is equivalent to its degree times \([\infty]\). A rational function has divisor of degree zero: write it as a quotient of split polynomials and include its order at infinity. These observations prove both surjectivity and injectivity of the degree presentation. Global units are \(\Omega^\times\), on which the \(n\)-th power map is onto. Kummer therefore makes \(H^1(\mathbf P^1,\mu_n)=0\). The Kummer calculation (P.7), using the rational-unit vanishing (P.5), and the curve bounds of AL identify \(H^2(\mathbf P^1,\mu_n)=\Lambda\), with \(c\) mapping to \(1\), and give zero in higher degrees. The connected projective line has constant sections \(\Lambda\). Thus (BI.5) is a quasi-isomorphism on every geometric fibre. Proper comparison in BG.4 identifies these with its geometric stalks, which detect isomorphisms.

Under \(\alpha\), restriction \(Rp_*\Lambda\to\Lambda\) along \(i\) is projection onto the first summand. Its composite with the unit is the identity. Its composite with the other summand is zero because \(i^*\mathcal O(1)\) is the trivial line bundle and its Kummer class is zero. Apply proper pushforward to the open–closed triangle for \(\mathbf A^1_S\subset\mathbf P^1_S\). The map \[ Rq_!\Lambda\longrightarrow Rp_*\Lambda \xrightarrow{\alpha^{-1}}\Lambda\oplus\Lambda(-1)[-2] \longrightarrow\Lambda(-1)[-2] \tag{BI.6} \] is an isomorphism, as its long cohomology sequence shows. Formula (BI.6) specifies the map itself. Tensor with the Tate line and shift to obtain \(\operatorname{Tr}_q:Rq_!\Lambda(1)[2]\to\Lambda\). Proper-support base change, the unit, open extension and Kummer classes all commute with inverse image. Applying their maps to (BI.6) proves base-change compatibility of this trace. On each fibre it is the degree-normalized compact curve trace.

BI.3. Étale transfer is transpose to restriction

For a separated étale map \(u:V\to U\) of smooth curves over an algebraically closed field, its transfer on compact cohomology is induced by the counit \(u_!u^{-1}\Lambda\to\Lambda\). Its stalk formula sums the values at the finitely many lifts, as proved in BH.1's extension-by-zero provider. This transfer preserves the degree-normalized curve trace.

To check the last assertion at the needed generality, complete the target to a smooth projective curve. For each component of \(V\), its nonconstant map gives a finite separable extension of the target function field. Normalize the completion in that extension. AG.1–AG.4 and X.4 give a smooth projective curve finite over the target completion, and the original \(V\) is an open in it: the birational map between smooth curves extends through their discrete valuation rings, and its inverse does so wherever both curves are defined. On this open the finite-map trace restricts to the étale summation counit. More explicitly, over the dense unramified locus both maps sum the same sheets; maps from \(u_!\Lambda\) into the constant sheaf are determined by adjunction on \(V\), where they are the constant value \(1\) on each sheet. Thus they agree everywhere. The norm and divisor argument in Poincaré duality for curves, Proposition 2.1 makes the finite trace preserve degree; its open-completion argument makes extension by zero preserve compact trace. Their composite proves the assertion for \(u\).

For classes \(a\in H^r_c(V,\Lambda(1))\) and \(b\in H^{2-r}(U,\Lambda)\), the projection formula and the counit give \[ \operatorname{Tr}_U\bigl(u_!a\mathbin\cup b\bigr) =\operatorname{Tr}_V\bigl(a\mathbin\cup u^{-1}b\bigr). \tag{BI.7} \] This is an equality of the actual pairings. To verify it, apply BH.7's projection map to \(u_!(\Lambda(1))\otimes^L\Lambda\), then evaluation. Its transpose under \(u_!\dashv u^{-1}\) is the identity coefficient pairing on \(V\). Composing with compact pushforward and the trace identity just proved gives (BI.7). The compact class remains first, so no interchange sign is introduced.

The finite and mutually perfect curve pairings are proved by the full argument in Sections 4–11 of that companion: AJ.1–AJ.3 supply the ramified-coefficient calculation, and AJ.4 supplies the finite counting and effacement inputs without a Jacobian pairing assumption. AK and AL supply their cohomological finiteness and degree bounds. Formula (BI.7) proves that compact transitions in AI.3 are exactly the duals of ordinary restrictions. It also proves the same assertion after passing from a separably closed geometric field to its algebraic closure, using the topological invariance in BE.4. This step concerns these curve pairings, without assuming the higher-dimensional smooth duality being proved.

BI.4. Finite chains of triangles suffice

The trace arrows form an inverse system of arrows. A cone for each arrow need not come with a chosen functor on all arrows. We now state the precise finite construction used in AI.3–AI.4.

On a fixed base, write a trace triangle as \[ K_i\xrightarrow{t_i}T_i\longrightarrow C_i\longrightarrow K_i[1], \qquad K_i\in D^{[0,2]},\quad T_i\in D^{[2,2]}, \tag{BI.8} \] and suppose \(H^2(t_i)\) is surjective. In the relative-curve case, \(T_i=\Lambda(-1)[-2]\). After extension along a base neighbourhood it is its exact étale extension by zero; the same degree statements hold. The long exact sequence gives canonical identifications \[ \begin{aligned} H^{-1}(C_i)&=H^0(K_i),\\ H^0(C_i)&=H^1(K_i),\\ H^1(C_i)&=\ker\bigl(H^2(K_i)\to H^2(T_i)\bigr), \end{aligned} \tag{BI.9} \] and all other cohomology is zero. For every commuting square between trace arrows, the triangle-map axiom gives a map between chosen cones. Its induced maps in (BI.9) are forced by the square, regardless of the chosen completion. The explicit cone formula in B.1 proves that axiom in the complexes used by BF; here no functorial choice of completions is needed. The terminology agrees with Stacks, Tag 05QK.

Suppose a refinement kills the three maps in (BI.9). Every completion of its square is then a ghost. For completeness, let a finite chain of ghosts have all its objects in \(D^{[a,b]}\). After \(m\) steps its composite factors through the truncation \(\tau_{\leq b-m}\) of its target. This is an induction. Given the factorization after \(m\) steps, compose its last truncation with the next ghost \(v\). Its composite with \(\tau_{\geq b-m}\) of the new target is zero: by t-structure orthogonality the map into that truncation is determined by the map on \(H^{b-m}\), which \(v\) kills. The truncation triangle therefore factors it through \(\tau_{\leq b-m-1}\). For \(m=b-a+1\) this target truncation is zero, proving the assertion. Four steps suffice in the interval \([-1,2]\) used in AI.3; (BI.9) even permits the smaller interval \([-1,1]\).

For any fixed trace arrow, perform the constructible compactness refinement of AI.3, then repeat it three more times, descending the finitely many schemes and zero sheaf maps as in AI.4. At that finite stage, shrink the base to a pointed affine open in the intersection of the images of its finitely many smooth curve maps. Each image is open and contains the selected point, so this is an allowed refinement and makes every fibre nonempty. The top trace maps are then surjective on that actual base, so (BI.9) applies there. On that one final base neighbourhood, choose triangle completions for these four consecutive squares. Their composite is zero by the ghost argument. It is still a morphism of triangles, over the composite of the prescribed trace-arrow squares. Exact étale extension by zero carries it to a zero cone map on the original base. Thus every target trace triangle admits a later trace triangle and a morphism to it whose cone component is zero. This finite assertion is all that is required; no globally coherent cone system has been assumed.

BI.5. Direct proof of the filtered Hom comparison

Let \(K_i\to T_i\) be the actual inverse system of trace arrows on \(S\). Assume the finite zero-cone assertion just proved. For any complex \(A\), composition gives \[ \mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_i\operatorname{Hom}(T_i,A[r]) \longrightarrow \mathop{\mathrm{colim}}_i\operatorname{Hom}(K_i,A[r]). \tag{BI.10} \] Here the two Hom systems are defined by the actual transitions of \(K\) and \(T\), so their colimits need no choice of cone transitions.

To prove surjectivity, represent a class by \(a:K_i\to A[r]\). Choose a later triangle mapping to the triangle at \(i\) with zero cone map \(C_j\to C_i\). The obstruction to extending \(a\) from \(K_i\) to \(T_i\) is its composite with the boundary \(C_i[-1]\to K_i\). At stage \(j\) this obstruction factors through the zero map \(C_j[-1]\to C_i[-1]\). Exactness of Hom applied to the triangle at \(j\) therefore extends the restricted \(a\) to \(T_j\).

For injectivity, represent a class by \(b:T_i\to A[r]\) whose restriction becomes zero in the right colimit. At a later stage it restricts to zero on \(K\). Replace \(i\) by that stage. Exactness of Hom now factors \(b\) through \(T_i\to C_i\). Choose a further triangle with zero cone map into this one. The restriction of \(b\) to its \(T_j\) factors through that zero map and is zero. This proves injectivity and hence (BI.10) for every integer \(r\), with no boundedness imposed on \(A\).

For \(q:\mathbf A^1_S\to S\), take the pointed pairs \((U,V)\) and selected strict base maps of AT.4. Put \[ K_{U,V}=R(qj_U)_!\Lambda, \qquad T_{U,V}=j_{V,!}\Lambda(-1)[-2]. \tag{BI.11} \] We may restrict to pairs whose smooth map \(U\to V\) is surjective: its open image contains the selected base point, and shrinking \(V\) to a pointed affine open in that image is a cofinal refinement. Define the trace arrow by (BI.6), the étale counit for \(U\to\mathbf A^1_V\), and extension along \(j_V\). Transitivity of those counits makes its refinement squares commute. BI.3 identifies its fibre pairings and transitions. AT.4 supplies the ordinary fibre colimit; finiteness kills the unwanted compact cohomology and the top trace kernel. Nonempty fibres make the top trace surjective. Constructible compactness and finite descent in AI.3–AI.4 give exactly the hypothesis of BI.4, so (BI.10) applies.

The projection from pointed pairs to either their source or base neighbourhoods is cofinal: a prescribed finite list is refined by fibre products and then a pointed affine chart, and parallel maps agree after a pointed étale refinement. The selected base map is retained throughout, as in (AT.9). The left colimit in (BI.10) is therefore \(H^{r+2}(A(1))_{\bar s}\), by the exact étale adjunction and the same K-injective stalk calculation as BI.1. The right colimit is \(H^r(q^!A)_{\bar x}\) by (BI.2). Consequently \[ H^{r+2}(A(1))_{\bar s} \xrightarrow{\sim}H^r(q^!A)_{\bar x}. \tag{BI.12} \] Finally this is the stalk map of the specified comparison \(q^{-1}A(1)[2]\to q^!A\). Define that comparison by transposing the projection formula followed by \(A\otimes\operatorname{Tr}_q\). Test it by \(j_{U,!}\Lambda[-r]\) in (BI.1). Adjunction, BH.7's counit compatibility, and the definition of the neighbourhood trace turn that test into precomposition by \(K_{U,V}\to T_{U,V}\), which is precisely (BI.10). This proves the assertion about the map, including its orientation. Since exact geometric stalks detect quasi-isomorphisms, it proves the arbitrary-complex affine-line formula used in Proposition 3.3.

Appendix BJ. Coordinate independence and the smooth trace

Let \(f:X\to S\) be separated and smooth of constant relative dimension \(d\), between finite-type schemes over a field \(k\). Fix \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/n\), with \(n\geq2\) invertible in \(k\). The trace will first be constructed as a map of cohomology sheaves. This lets us compare coordinates on geometric fibres before transposing the trace to an exceptional inverse image. BF–BI supply the ordinary unbounded operations and the affine-line comparison used below.

BJ.1. Top cohomology and descent on the source

For a separated finite-type map \(h:Y\to S\) with fibres of dimension at most \(e\), \[ R^rh_!F=0\quad(r>2e) \tag{BJ.1} \] for every \(\Lambda\)-sheaf \(F\). To see the precise dimension used here, compactify \(h\) and apply the geometric-fibre formula of BG. At a geometric fibre let \(Z\) be the reduced closure of \(Y_{\bar s}\) in that proper fibre. Its dimension is at most \(e\): its finitely many components meet the dense open \(Y_{\bar s}\), and a finite-type integral scheme over a field and a dense open have the same function field and dimension. The extended coefficient sheaf is zero off \(Z\), so it is the exact closed direct image of its restriction to \(Z\), as the stalk formula verifies. BG.2's proper bound on \(Z\) gives (BJ.1). Thus a compactification with larger boundary fibres causes no change to the bound.

It follows that \(Q_h=R^{2e}h_!\) is right exact on sheaves. In the long exact sequence of a short exact sequence, the obstruction to surjectivity is \(R^{2e+1}h_!\), which is zero. It also preserves finite direct sums. For a finite jointly surjective family of separated étale maps \(u_i:U_i\to Y\), the sequence \[ \bigoplus_{i,j}u_{ij,!}u_{ij}^{-1}F \longrightarrow\bigoplus_i u_{i,!}u_i^{-1}F \longrightarrow F\longrightarrow0, \qquad U_{ij}=U_i\times_YU_j, \tag{BJ.2} \] is exact. The first map is the difference of the projection counits. At a geometric stalk the middle term is the direct sum of copies of \(F_{\bar y}\) indexed by all lifts, and the first map imposes all relations \(e_a m-e_b m\). The set of lifts is nonempty, so summation identifies the quotient with \(F_{\bar y}\). Exact stalks prove (BJ.2). Applying \(Q_h\) gives the corresponding right exact sequence of top compact direct images. A map out of \(Q_h(F)\) is therefore determined by compatible maps on the cover.

For maps \(g:Z\to Y\), \(h:Y\to S\) of fibre dimensions at most \(b,a\), respectively, truncation gives the natural isomorphism \[ R^{2(a+b)}(hg)_!F \simeq R^{2a}h_!R^{2b}g_!F. \tag{BJ.3} \] Indeed \(Rg_!F\) has cohomology in \([0,2b]\). Apply \(Rh_!\) to its triangle with top quotient \(R^{2b}g_!F[-2b]\). The remaining term has finitely many cohomology sheaves in degrees at most \(2b-1\); successive good-truncation triangles and (BJ.1) place its image in degrees at most \(2(a+b)-1\). Taking the next degree proves (BJ.3). This argument uses only a finite interval, even though the operation itself is defined on unbounded complexes.

We compose top trace maps by (BJ.3) and the invertible-twist projection formula. This composition is associative: for three maps, the two orders are the two routes through the naturality square of the middle truncation map after truncating the innermost complex. Applying the outer direct image and taking top cohomology identifies the routes. The same square permits coefficient maps at each stage. Exact pullback commutes with these truncations; BG's base-change and composition comparisons therefore make (BJ.3) compatible with base change.

BJ.2. Coordinate maps and a change in one coordinate

The local presentation from AE.1 writes a smooth affine algebra, after shrinking, as \[ B=\bigl(A[x_1,\ldots,x_m]/(F_1,\ldots,F_c)\bigr)_h \tag{BJ.4} \] with an invertible \(c\)-column Jacobian minor. Its differential module has rank \(m-c=d\), and the remaining \(d\) variables define an étale map to \(\mathbf A^d_A\). The square-zero lifting check solves the \(c\) error equations uniquely using that minor; AE.1 supplies flatness of the presentation. This is the coordinate construction also described in Stacks, Tag 054L.

More generally, if functions \(z_1,\ldots,z_d\) have differential classes forming a basis at a point of a smooth \(A\)-scheme, they are étale coordinates near that point. Lift them to the localized polynomial ring in (BJ.4) and adjoin the equations \(z_i-Z_i\) over \(A[Z_1,\ldots,Z_d]\). Their rows, together with the rows of the \(F_j\), form an invertible square Jacobian precisely when the \(dz_i\) give the stated basis modulo the original relations. Clearing the finitely many denominators and inverting that determinant gives the unique square-zero correction and the flat presentation just used. This proves the criterion without treating a tangent-space calculation alone as étaleness.

Over an algebraically closed field \(\Omega\), two coordinate maps \(u,v:W\to\mathbf A^d_\Omega\) can be joined locally by a finite sequence in which only one coordinate changes at each step. At a closed point, their differential bases differ by a matrix in \(\mathrm{GL}_d(\Omega)\). Gaussian elimination expresses it by row additions and nonzero row scalings: choose a nonzero pivot, move it to the diagonal, scale it, eliminate its column and continue on the smaller square matrix. A row interchange itself is a sequence of single-row changes, \[ (a,b)\mapsto(a+b,b)\mapsto(a+b,-a) \mapsto(b,-a)\mapsto(b,a). \tag{BJ.5} \] Each intermediate basis is invertible, including in characteristic two. Apply these operations to the functions \(u_i\). The resulting tuple \(z\) has \(dz_i=dv_i\) at the chosen point. Replacing its functions successively by the \(v_i\) keeps a differential basis there. The preceding criterion makes every intermediate tuple étale on one common open neighbourhood. These opens cover \(W\): a nonempty closed complement in a finite-type \(\Omega\)-scheme would have a closed point, by Y.5. Quasi-compactness gives a finite subcover.

BJ.3. Relative curves and products of affine lines

For a relative affine line use exactly the trace of (BI.6). For a smooth relative curve \(h:C\to S\), cover the source by finitely many coordinate opens \(u_i:C_i\to\mathbf A^1_S\). Compose the étale counit with the affine-line trace to obtain \[ t_i:R^2(hu_i')_!\Lambda(1)\longrightarrow\Lambda, \tag{BJ.6} \] where \(u_i':C_i\hookrightarrow C\) denotes the open inclusion. At each geometric base point this is the degree-normalized trace of the smooth fibre curve, by BI.3. On each overlap the two maps therefore agree as sheaf maps, since their geometric stalks agree. Sequence (BJ.2), after applying top direct image, glues them uniquely to \(t_h:R^2h_!\Lambda(1)\to\Lambda\). Its fibre description proves independence of the cover and compatibility with arbitrary étale refinement. Base change follows by pulling back (BJ.2), using exact inverse image and BG's compact-support comparison; every coordinate trace pulls back to the same coordinate trace. None of this construction uses a higher-dimensional orientation.

For \(p_{d,S}:\mathbf A^d_S\to S\), compose \(d\) copies of the affine-line trace using (BJ.3). Denote the result by \(t_{d,S}\). It commutes with base change and is unaffected by grouping consecutive coordinates. It is also invariant under coordinate permutations. Here are the product and sign checks. For structural maps \(a:V\to S\), \(b:W\to S\), first push the external tensor product along \(V\times_SW\to V\). Proper-support base change and the projection formula identify that pushforward with \(F\otimes^La^{-1}Rb_!G\); the outer projection formula then gives \[ R(a\pi_V)_!(F\boxtimes G) \simeq Ra_!F\otimes^LRb_!G. \tag{BJ.7} \] The external product comparison is induced by the two counits and tensor evaluation, so reversing the factors reverses those two counits and applies the graded tensor symmetry of (BH.8). Equivalently, compactify the two maps: extension by zero commutes with external tensor on stalks, and the proper comparison is the transpose of the tensor of the two proper counits. This identifies (BJ.7) and its symmetry with the specified maps, rather than an arbitrary isomorphism.

On each geometric fibre, the tensor of the \(d\) positive degree-two affine-line classes generates \(H_c^{2d}(\mathbf A^d,\Lambda(d))\), by (BJ.7) and BI.2. Its iterated trace is \(1\). An adjacent permutation exchanges two degree-two factors and hence multiplies by \((-1)^4=1\). It fixes that generator and the trace. All permutations are products of adjacent ones; geometric stalks now prove invariance of \(t_{d,S}\). The dimension-zero case is the étale summation counit and satisfies the same composition rule directly by summing lifts.

BJ.4. Independence of coordinates

For an étale chart \(u:X\to\mathbf A^d_S\), let \[ t(f,u)=t_{d,S}\circ R^{2d}p_{d,S!}\bigl(\varepsilon_u(d)\bigr). \tag{BJ.8} \] Composition of lower shrieks identifies its source with \(R^{2d}f_!\Lambda(d)\). For an étale refinement \(v:V\to X\), the composite counit is summation over successive lifts, and is the counit for \(uv\). Thus restricting (BJ.8) by transfer from \(V\) gives \(t(fv,uv)\).

Compare two charts of the same \(f\). Their candidate maps are sheaf maps and commute with base change, so it suffices to compare them over algebraically closed geometric fields. BJ.2 and the source-cover descent (BJ.2) reduce the problem to charts differing in one coordinate on a common open. By permutation invariance, place that coordinate last. Their first \(d-1\) functions give the same smooth relative curve map \[ h:W\longrightarrow\mathbf A^{d-1}_\Omega. \tag{BJ.9} \] Both last coordinates are étale maps from that relative curve to its relative affine line. BJ.3 says their inner traces are the same map \(t_h\). Composing with \(t_{d-1,\Omega}\), using the associativity proved after (BJ.3), makes the two maps (BJ.8) equal. For \(d=1\) this is already the curve comparison; for \(d=0\) it is summation. Thus (BJ.8) is independent of coordinates in every dimension.

For a general \(f\), choose a finite coordinate cover, locally on \(S\) if necessary. On overlaps its traces now agree, so the right exact sequence from (BJ.2) gives a unique \[ t_f:R^{2d}f_!\Lambda(d)\longrightarrow\Lambda_S. \tag{BJ.10} \] Refining two covers to their intersections proves independence of the cover. It also proves compatibility with étale localization on the source. These are equalities of actual morphisms of sheaves, not an inference from dimensions of cohomology groups. Over overlapping base opens the same construction agrees, so ordinary sheaf descent defines (BJ.10) on all of \(S\).

BJ.5. From the trace to the unbounded smooth adjunction

The bound (BJ.1) puts \(Rf_!\Lambda(d)[2d]\) in \(D^{\leq0}\). For \(K\in D^{\leq0}\) and a degree-zero sheaf \(B\), the truncation triangle gives \[ \operatorname{Hom}_D(K,B)=\operatorname{Hom}(H^0K,B). \tag{BJ.11} \] Both adjoining Hom groups vanish by t-structure orthogonality: they have source \(\tau_{\leq-1}K\) or its shift by \(1\), and target in \(D^{\geq0}\). Therefore (BJ.10) specifies a unique derived trace \(T_f:Rf_!\Lambda(d)[2d]\to\Lambda\). Transpose, for every complex \(A\), the map \[ Rf_!\bigl(f^{-1}A(d)[2d]\bigr) \simeq A\otimes^LRf_!\Lambda(d)[2d] \xrightarrow{1\otimes T_f}A \tag{BJ.12} \] to obtain \(\theta_{f,A}:f^{-1}A(d)[2d]\to f^!A\). BH.7 proves the arbitrary-complex projection formula and its counit compatibility, so this is defined without a finite Tor-dimension assumption.

On a coordinate open it is the composite of the affine-line isomorphisms (BI.12) and exact étale inverse image. Indeed its transposed counit is the composed coordinate trace by (BJ.8) and (BJ.11). Uniqueness of the adjunction transpose identifies the maps. Exact étale restriction and BI.1's local adjunction therefore show that \(\theta_{f,A}\) is an isomorphism on every source neighbourhood and hence on every geometric stalk. It is an isomorphism in the unbounded derived category. This proves (3.7) with the coordinate-independent orientation just constructed.

BJ.6. Composition, base change and the parameter section

There is one interchange needed for composition. For étale \(u:X\to A\), form \(u':\mathbf A^e_X\to\mathbf A^e_A\), with vertical projections \(q,r\). Under the canonical composition comparison, the two maps \[ \varepsilon_u\circ u_!t_{e,X} \quad\text{and}\quad t_{e,A}\circ R^{2e}r_!\bigl(\varepsilon_{u'}(e)\bigr) \tag{BJ.13} \] agree. At a geometric point of \(A\), each sends a finite family of top affine-space classes indexed by the lifts in \(X\) to the sum of their traces. BG's fibre and composition comparisons and the étale stalk formula identify these as the stalks of the displayed maps. Stalks detect equality, proving (BJ.13).

For smooth maps \(g:Y\to X\) and \(f:X\to S\) of dimensions \(e,d\), choose successive coordinate opens. Their concatenation is an étale chart into \(\mathbf A^{d+e}_S\). Formula (BJ.13) moves the intermediate étale counit past the affine-space trace; associativity after (BJ.3) then identifies its trace with \(t_f\) composed with \(t_g\). Sequence (BJ.2) extends this equality from the source cover to the entire map. Equation (BJ.11) makes it the equality of derived traces. Applying the projection formula and transposing (BJ.12) proves the corresponding composition of the \(\theta_{f,A}\). All orientation shifts are even, so no additional sign occurs.

Base change pulls a coordinate cover to a coordinate cover, preserves the right exact sequence (BJ.2), and preserves each coordinate trace by BI.2, (BJ.3) and (BJ.7). It therefore preserves (BJ.10) and (BJ.12). In a cartesian square with base map \(b:S'\to S\) and source map \(b_X\), the usual exceptional comparison is the transpose of \[ Rf'_!b_X^{-1}f^!A \simeq b^{-1}Rf_!f^!A\longrightarrow b^{-1}A. \tag{BJ.14} \] Under the two smooth isomorphisms, both sides of its transpose identify with \(f'^{-1}b^{-1}A(d)[2d]\), and trace compatibility makes the map the identity. Thus it is the canonical base-change isomorphism, including its counit. These assertions apply to the changes of base in the stated field scope; the same coordinate traces and top-degree comparisons pull back along arbitrary base maps for which the compact-support construction is used.

In particular take the parameter-line projection \(q:\mathbf A^1_S\to S\). The base-change isomorphism just proved gives (3.8). If \(s:S\to\mathbf A^1_S\) is a parameter section, transitivity for \(qs=\mathrm{id}\) and the affine-line formula give, for every \(B\), \[ s^!q^{-1}B=B(-1)[-2]. \tag{BJ.15} \] This follows by canceling the pulled-back invertible Tate line in \(s^!q^!B=B\), using (BH.21). Its coefficient orientation is the positive point class. The two-open Kummer calculation of AI.2 applies to the standard charts of \(\mathbf P^1_S\): it uses their transition function and the exact coefficient sequences, and gives the image of \(-\lambda\kappa(t-t_0)\) as \(c_1^{(n)}(\mathcal O(s))\). The section divisor has line bundle \(\mathcal O(1)\), so (BI.6) sends this class to \(1\). Transitivity says that the composite section counit followed by the affine-line trace is the identity. Hence its generator is precisely that negative boundary, fixing the sign in (BJ.15) without a closed-base-change assumption for a general exceptional inverse image.

Finally, if \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\) is a closed immersion of smooth \(S\)-schemes of relative dimensions \(d-c,d\), write \(g=fi\). Transitivity gives \(i^!f^!A=g^!A\). Substituting the proved smooth formulas and canceling the invertible twist gives \[ i^!f^{-1}A\simeq g^{-1}A(-c)[-2c]. \tag{BJ.16} \] For \(A=\Lambda\) this is the smooth-pair purity identification in (3.9). Its counit defines the corresponding Gysin map; composition of such maps is composition of adjunction counits, by the triangle identities. This conclusion concerns these smooth pairs. It introduces no assertion of absolute purity for arbitrary regular schemes or a normalized adic comparison.

Classical and arithmetic scope

The arithmetic constructions distinguish finite coefficients, complete integral coefficients and rational coefficients. Their geometric and categorical hypotheses enter at different stages. Appendix M gives the ordinary-image finiteness and singular biduality arguments over fields. M.5 proves the bounded-below internal-Hom restriction, closed-support comparison, nonfree lisse calculation and dimension-corrected generic evaluation; M.6 identifies double evaluation after proper global sections, and M.7 specifies the dual exchanges by their adjunction tests. These arguments retain their exact prerequisite and coefficient hypotheses. Propositions 3.2–3.3 prove the stated finite-coefficient proper finiteness and smooth trace/duality/smooth-pair purity from their identified programme foundations. The geometric ingredients are organized as follows. AU.1–AU.6 prove the locally Noetherian proper geometry, coherent finiteness and formal-functions chain. AV.1–AV.6 prove the arbitrary-base approximation, Chow modification and Stein factorization. AW.1–AW.6 prove the arbitrary-base separated quasi-finite factorization and finite-cover refinement. AX.1–AX.7 prove henselian-pair idempotent lifting, arbitrary-sheaf degree-zero restriction, arbitrary-base finite direct image and full faithfulness for finite étale covers. AY.1–AY.6 complete arbitrary-sheaf proper degree-zero comparison, including faithfully flat section descent and the exact geometric-fibre identification. AZ.1–AZ.6 prove compactness, finite-stage descent and the finite-direct-image embedding for constructible coefficients over arbitrary qcqs schemes. BA.1–BA.7 prove affine closed-subscheme effacement for torsion sheaves and arbitrary-base higher continuity. BB.1–BB.4 prove henselization along arbitrary ideals, affine henselian comparison and restricted-injective vanishing, with module cohomology justified. BC.1–BC.6 prove coherent algebraization and proper finite-torsor lifting over complete Noetherian pairs, and projective-line comparison over complete Noetherian local rings. BD.1–BD.6 prove finite-cover descent and pointed approximation on local integer models, then finite-cover and torsor lifting for proper schemes over arbitrary henselian local rings and projective-line comparison there. BE.1–BE.8 prove general higher proper comparison for arbitrary torsion sheaves, bounded-below complexes with torsion cohomology, and arbitrary changes of base, with the actual geometric-fibre map. BF.1–BF.6 construct the unbounded ordinary derived categories, their triangles and coproducts, derived adjunction, and sheaf representability. BG.1–BG.6 prove finite relative cohomological bounds, unbounded proper comparison and coproduct preservation, and construct compactification-independent proper support and its right adjoint at the stated field scope. BH.1–BH.7 construct étale K-flat models, the unbounded derived tensor–Hom adjunction, arbitrary-complex projection formulas and the canonical invertible-twist comparison. BI.1–BI.5 give the local and internal adjunctions, the specified affine-line trace, its transfer pairings and the arbitrary-complex stalk comparison using finite chains of triangles. BJ.1–BJ.6 construct the coordinate-independent top trace by single-coordinate changes and curve traces, and prove the unbounded smooth adjunction, composition, base change and smooth-pair Gysin counit. Specialization comparisons and enhanced operation compatibilities require their specified geometric inputs. The field-scope argument does not assert general absolute purity. The algebraic and completed-local node criterion, the two actual normalization points and their analytic comparison are proved in L.1–L.4. L.3–L.5 also prove finite normalization of complex curves and the smooth-branch comparison used in Exercise 3.

Appendices A–E prove the classical resolutions, localization, puncture, branch, cone, orientation, Thom–Gysin and plane-curve calculations. Appendices F–H construct the structural and general classical proper-support operations, their bounds, pairings, adjoints and the identities before biduality. Appendices I–J prove normal local triviality, coefficient comparison, canonical biduality, compact-link finiteness, both point dual exchanges and fixed-stratification duality. Appendix K proves algebraic Whitney refinements and compatible map stratifications, followed by constructibility of all six classical operations and internal Hom. Its algebraic and analytic curve-selection prerequisites are proved in K.1–K.4. Appendix L gives the node and smooth-branch normalization arguments, including completion and discrete-valuation algebra.

The classical topological link calculations apply over the complex numbers. The finite-coefficient singular étale argument is given separately in Appendix M. Appendix N supplies finite-cover monodromy, effective descent, compatible lisse systems, stable lattices and the congruence-cover construction. AJ.1–AJ.3 prove the wild-inertia and ramified-coefficient calculations at strict smooth curve points. Smooth-pair Gysin comparisons use the positive trace and negative Kummer-boundary convention of BI–BJ. BK–BX treat completion, integral operations and rationalization. These étale constructions do not identify a positive-characteristic neighbourhood with a classical topological link.

Appendix BK. Derived reductions and completed comparison maps

Let \(O\) be a complete discrete valuation ring, with uniformizer \(\pi\) and residue characteristic \(\ell\), and put \(O_n=O/\pi^n\). Work with the constant coefficient ring \(\underline O\) on a pro-étale site. The completed constant sheaf \(\widehat O=\varprojlim\underline{O_n}\) need not be \(\underline O\). Completion below is a construction on complexes of \(\underline O\)-modules; restricting scalars also lets us apply it to complexes already carrying a \(\widehat O\)-action. We do not identify these two coefficient sheaves.

BK.1. The site properties used in the limit

The pro-étale site and ℓ-adic complexes, §1 proves two covering constructions over arbitrary rings. Theorem 1.1d refines a weakly étale affine object by a faithfully flat ind-étale cover whose composite to the base is ind-étale. Theorem 1.1f gives covers by w-contractible affines. Its proof first constructs w-local rings with strictly henselian maximal local rings, then replaces the profinite component space by an extremally disconnected cover. The retraction argument uses the local rigidity proof in Lemma 1.1a and the component-space constructions in Lemmas 1.1b–1.1e. These are the covering results used here; weakly étale does not mean ind-étale without refinement.

Evaluation on a w-contractible affine \(W\) takes sheaf epimorphisms to surjections: a lift exists on a finite affine cover, its disjoint union has a retraction to \(W\), and pulling the lift along that section gives a lift on \(W\). Successively lifting over such a cover proves repleteness, the assertion that the limit of a tower of epimorphisms surjects onto its first term locally. It also proves exactness of countable products of abelian sheaves. Given sections in the targets of countably many epimorphisms, the sheaves of lifts of the first \(r\) sections form a tower of epimorphisms; a compatible limit supplies all lifts at once. Kernels and finite products already commute with products, so the product functor is exact.

For a tower of complexes with actual transition maps, its homotopy limit is consequently \[ \operatorname{holim}_n A_n =\operatorname{Cone}\left(\prod_n A_n \xrightarrow{1-s}\prod_n A_n\right)[-1], \qquad s(a)_n=u_n(a_{n+1}). \tag{BK.1} \] This computes the derived inverse limit, including for unbounded complexes. Here is a resolution description. At level \(n\), embed a sheaf tower into \(B_n=\prod_{j\leq n}A_j\) by its maps to earlier levels. The quotient map takes successive differences \(x_j-u_jx_{j+1}\), and has target \(C_n=\prod_{j<n}A_j\). It is surjective by finite backward substitution. Both new towers are products of towers that are zero before a specified index and constant afterwards. The latter are the exact right adjoints to evaluation at that index. Injective resolutions and exact countable products show that \(B,C\) are limit-acyclic and give the two-term limit resolution (BK.1). On complexes this same finite resolution gives the displayed cone. Products preserve quasi-isomorphisms because they preserve cycle, boundary and cohomology sequences, so the formula also applies to unbounded complexes. All tower maps below will be specified; no inverse limit of mere isomorphism classes is taken.

BK.2. Classical coefficients on the enlarged site

Write \(\nu:X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}\to X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\). We give the particular comparison needed for reductions. On an affine ind-étale object \(U=\varprojlim U_i\) over an affine part of \(X\), define the pullback of an étale sheaf \(F\) by \[ (\nu^*F)(U)=\varinjlim_i F(U_i). \tag{BK.2} \] This description is independent of the presentation: maps between finite-presentation étale objects and their equalities descend to a common stage. It is a sheaf on the ind-étale basis. Indeed a finite family of ind-étale maps covering \(U\) can first be expressed through finite families of finitely presented étale maps over \(U\); each such family covers, since its images contain those of the limiting cover. These are finite families, not assertions that the individual morphisms are finite. A finite-presentation family and its covering property then descend to a stage of \(U\). The sheaf equalizer there passes to the filtered colimit, which commutes with the finite products and equalizer. Affine refinement from BK.1 makes this a basis for the whole site. The definitions agree on overlapping affine parts of \(X\), so they glue.

On an étale object (BK.2) is \(F(U)\). Conversely, sections of a pro-étale sheaf on the finite stages restrict to its sections on \(U\). These maps give the adjunction counit; on represented sections both triangle identities are identities. Thus the construction is \(\nu^*\) and satisfies \(\nu_*\nu^*F=F\). It preserves finite limits by the filtered-colimit formula, and preserves cokernels by its left adjunction. It is therefore exact on module sheaves.

If \(I\) is an injective étale module sheaf, the positive Čech cohomology of \(\nu^*I\) for any finite basis cover vanishes. Express the cover and its finite fibre products by the two stage systems just used. Each degree of its Čech complex is a filtered colimit of the corresponding degree on an étale cover of an étale object. Those augmented complexes are acyclic: the augmented free-sheaf Čech resolution is locally contracted by a section of the cover, and Hom into the restricted injective is exact. Exact filtered colimits preserve this acyclicity.

This Čech assertion implies derived acyclicity on every basis object. Embed a sheaf with those vanishings into an injective. A quotient section lifts on a cover; the differences of its lifts form a Čech 1-cocycle, whose coboundary expression corrects the lifts so that they glue. The quotient map is therefore surjective on sections of each basis object. Its quotient has the same positive Čech vanishings by the short exact sequences of Čech complexes. Iterating gives all higher derived vanishings. Applying this argument to \(\nu^*I\), and then to a bounded-below injective resolution, proves \[ L\simeq R\nu_*\nu^*L\qquad(L\in D^+(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)). \tag{BK.3} \] Restriction of injectives to an étale object is justified by its exact extension-by-zero left adjoint, as in M.5. Thus the calculation is local on the base and applies to module sheaves, not just sets.

For a qcqs map \(f:X\to Y\), evaluate on an affine ind-étale \(V=\varprojlim V_i\) over \(Y\). The cohomology of the left side below is computed on \(X\times_YV\). Formula (BK.3) and qcqs étale cohomological continuity identify it with the colimit of the cohomologies on \(X\times_YV_i\). Sheafifying and using the bounded-below cohomology spectral sequence gives \[ Rf_{\mathrm{pro\acute et},*}\nu_X^*L \simeq\nu_Y^*Rf_{\mathrm{\acute et},*}L. \tag{BK.4} \] The continuity and finite-stage descent here are the actual statements proved in AH, AK and BA, and in §§1–3 of the cited pro-étale lesson. The maps in (BK.2) are restriction maps, so (BK.4) identifies the adjunction comparison itself. Pullback commutes with \(\nu^*\) on those same represented sections. This will identify the finite-level base-change arrows, not merely their objects.

BK.3. The reduction complexes and their arrows

Put \[ P_n=[\underline O\xrightarrow{\pi^n}\underline O], \qquad \deg P_n=(-1,0). \tag{BK.5} \] The augmentation \(P_n\to\underline{O_n}\) is a quasi-isomorphism, since multiplication by \(\pi^n\) is injective on \(O\). Both terms are free, so \(P_n\otimes K\) computes \(K_n=K\otimes_O^LO_n\) for every complex \(K\), without a boundedness or flatness assumption on \(K\). The finite cone of free tensor functors preserves quasi-isomorphisms.

For \(m\geq n\), use the chain map \(P_m\to P_n\) whose degree-zero component is the identity and whose degree-minus-one component is \(\pi^{m-n}\). Its two composites with the differentials are both \(\pi^m\). The maps compose exactly. They induce the quotient maps \(O_m\to O_n\), and give an actual tower of reductions, with the commuting triangles \[ K\xrightarrow{\pi^n}K\longrightarrow K_n, \qquad (K\to K)\text{ transitions }(\pi,1). \tag{BK.6} \] Multiplication by \(\pi^n\) on \(P_n\) is null-homotopic: the degree-zero to degree-minus-one component of the homotopy is the identity. Tensoring this homotopy with \(K\), with the usual tensor differential, gives the same assertion on \(K_n\).

BK.4. Completion and unchanged derived reductions

Define \[ C(K)=\operatorname{holim}_n K_n, \qquad L_\pi(K)=\operatorname{holim}(\cdots\xrightarrow{\pi}K). \tag{BK.7} \] The telescope resolution of \(\underline{O[1/\pi]}\) is the two-term complex of countable free sums with differential \(1-\pi s\). Its cokernel is the localization and its kernel is zero: a finite-support element in the kernel has zero first coordinate, and induction kills every coordinate. Internal Hom from those free sums is an exact countable product. This finite resolution therefore identifies \(L_\pi(K)\) with \(R\mathcal Hom(\underline{O[1/\pi]},K)\), even for unbounded \(K\).

Take the homotopy limits of the actual cone triangles (BK.6). Finite cones commute with the products in (BK.1), including their differentials. The limit of the middle constant tower is \(K\): \(1-s\) has kernel the diagonal copy of \(K\), and a chain-level right inverse obtained by the recursion \(x_1=0\), \(x_{n+1}=x_n-b_n\). We obtain the natural triangle \[ L_\pi(K)\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow C(K). \tag{BK.8} \] Multiplication by \(\pi\) is invertible on \(L_\pi(K)\), since precomposition by that invertible map of \(O[1/\pi]\) induces its multiplication map.

Call \(E\) derived complete when \(L_\pi(E)=0\). Each \(K_n\) is complete. In its \(\pi\)-tower, the shift operator \(\pi s\) has its \(n\)-th power null-homotopic by BK.3; hence \(1-\pi s\) has inverse \(1+\pi s+\cdots+(\pi s)^{n-1}\) in the derived category. Derived internal Hom from \(O[1/\pi]\) preserves products and fibres, being right adjoint to tensor with that flat localization. Complete objects are consequently closed under homotopy limits and fibres. Thus \(C(K)\) is complete, and (BK.8) proves that \(K\) is complete precisely when \(K\to C(K)\) is an isomorphism.

There are no maps in any degree from a complex on which \(\pi\) is invertible to a complete complex. To verify this, such a source \(A\) satisfies \(O[1/\pi]\otimes_O^LA\simeq A\): localization is exact, and its action on cohomology inverts an already invertible map. Tensor-Hom adjunction then identifies its derived Hom into \(E\) with Hom from \(A\) into \(L_\pi(E)=0\). Applying this to (BK.8) proves that \(C\) is left adjoint to inclusion of the complete objects, with the displayed unit.

Most importantly, tensoring (BK.8) with \(P_n\) kills its first term, since \(\pi^n\) is invertible there. Hence the unit gives the canonical isomorphism \[ K\otimes_O^LO_n\xrightarrow{\sim}C(K)\otimes_O^LO_n. \tag{BK.9} \] Thus completion does not alter a derived reduction. A map between complete complexes is an isomorphism if all its derived reductions are isomorphisms: its complete cone has zero reductions, so its expression (BK.7) is zero. This detection statement needs neither finite generation nor a uniform cohomological bound.

BK.5. Direct image preserves this completion

For the map of pro-étale topoi induced by \(f\), exact inverse image on constant \(O\)-modules has derived right adjoint \(Rf_*\). The injective and K-injective construction of BF applies to this sheaf category as well: it is a Grothendieck category, with exact sheafification, exact filtered colimits and a set of site generators. A right adjoint preserves derived products and homotopy limits. Its \(O\)-linearity and exactness also give \[ Rf_*(K\otimes_O^LO_n)\simeq (Rf_*K)\otimes_O^LO_n, \qquad Rf_*C(K)\simeq C(Rf_*K). \tag{BK.10} \] For the first map, apply \(Rf_*\) to the two-term free complex (BK.5), or to its cone triangle. A finite cone of K-injectives is K-injective, so the computation uses the same multiplication and transition maps as BK.3. The second map follows by taking their homotopy limits. This verifies the maps and their compatibility with the unit in (BK.8). It is a perfect-coefficient calculation, and does not require a general projection formula for arbitrary \(O\)-complexes. In particular direct image takes complete complexes to complete complexes.

BK.6. The completed base-change arrow

For any Cartesian square as in Proposition 3.1, write \(g^*_{\mathrm{comp}}=Cg^*\). Start with the ordinary adjunction comparison \(\beta_K:g^*Rf_*K\to Rf'_*g'^*K\). Apply \(C\), and use (BK.10) on the target. This defines its completed comparison. If \(K\) is complete, the two objects identify canonically with \[ \operatorname{holim}_n g^*Rf_*K_n, \qquad \operatorname{holim}_n Rf'_*g'^*K_n. \tag{BK.11} \] Indeed exact pullback commutes with (BK.5), (BK.9) identifies the reductions after completion, and (BK.10) moves direct image past those reductions and limits. Under these identifications the completed arrow is \(\operatorname{holim}_n\beta_{K_n}\). The adjunction unit and counit are \(O\)-linear and commute with the two free terms and their multiplication maps; they therefore give exactly these compatible finite-level arrows. This also proves compatibility with composition of base changes.

Suppose each \(K_n\) comes from a bounded-below étale \(O_n\)-complex. Formula (BK.4) and its pullback compatibility identify \(\beta_{K_n}\) with the pullback of the bounded-below torsion comparison on the étale site. A power of \(\ell\) kills \(O_n\), because \(\ell\in(\pi)\); thus its coefficient condition is satisfied wherever \(\ell\) is invertible. When those torsion comparisons are isomorphisms, (BK.11) proves that the completed arrow is an isomorphism. The lower bound may depend on \(n\): comparison is applied separately at each level, and a derived limit preserves isomorphisms. A uniform bound or a constructibility theorem would be an additional input for a finiteness assertion.

For smooth changes of base, including the affine inverse limits in Proposition 3.1, AS.1–AS.7 now prove the required torsion comparison over arbitrary bases, with the qcqs direct-image hypothesis and each invertible modulus. The general geometric proof uses AM–AN, AR and arithmetic normalization AG.5. Applying it at every finite reduction in (BK.11) proves the completed comparison with those hypotheses. This geometric input and the formal completion argument have different roles: neither their conjunction nor a derived limit asserts constructibility or supplies the remaining normalized adic operations.

BK.7. A torsion example of the transition maps

Take \(K=\underline{O/\pi}\) in degree zero. Then \[ K\otimes_O^LO_n=[K\xrightarrow{0}K] \quad\text{in degrees }-1,0. \tag{BK.12} \] The transition from level \(n+1\) to \(n\) is zero in degree \(-1\), and the identity in degree zero, by BK.3. The first tower has zero homotopy limit: its shift is zero, so \(1-s\) is the identity. The second tower has limit \(K\). Thus \(C(K)=K\), while every derived reduction still has the additional degree-minus-one term. Ordinary quotients alone would discard it.

These arguments establish completion, its unit and reduction maps, and the passage of the specified torsion comparison to completed direct image. BL constructs the completed tensor, its internal Hom and the inverse-image adjunction, including composition and finite-reduction maps. Normalized \(f_!\), \(f^!\), adic duality, rationalization and equivalence with the relevant strict systems retain their separate coherence, coefficient and finiteness requirements.

Appendix BL. Tensor, internal Hom and inverse image after completion
