Keep the coefficient ring and the pro-étale sites of BK. Write \(D_X=D(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},\underline O)\), and let \(D_X^c\) be its full subcategory of derived-complete objects. The superscript here means complete, not constructible. All complexes in this appendix may be unbounded. Put \(Q=O[1/\pi]\). We construct the operations in \(D_X^c\) and their comparison maps before imposing constructibility.

BL.1. Tensor models on the enlarged site

The tensor constructions of BH extend to this site without a claim that ordinary étale geometric points detect every pro-étale sheaf. Here is the replacement for that use of stalks. For an object \(U\) of a site presenting the topos, let \(B_U\) be the sheafification of the free \(\underline O\)-module presheaf on its represented sheaf. For a sheaf \(M\), \(B_U\otimes M\) is the sheafification of the presheaf whose sections over \(V\) are finite sums of elements of \(M(V)\), labelled by sections of \(U\) over \(V\).

This tensor functor is exact. A section in its target has locally a finite-sum representative. An epimorphism of sheaves lifts each of its finitely many coefficients after a covering refinement. For a kernel, a finite-sum representative mapping to zero becomes zero in the presheaf after another refinement, by the definition of sheafification. Collecting equal labels expresses this as finitely many zero coefficient sums. Exactness of the original sequence on sections at its first two terms lifts those sums to the kernel. This proves exactness locally and hence for the sheaf. Thus \(B_U\) is flat. The sums indexed by sections in (BH.2) still surject onto every sheaf: every local section is one of their generators.

Apply the disk-and-cycle construction (BH.3)–(BH.5) to these generators. Each stage is a degreewise split extension by shifts of flat sheaves. Every local kernel cycle is killed at the next stage; exact filtered colimits therefore make the final kernel acyclic. The same tensor tests prove K-flatness at each stage and at the limit. This gives K-flat resolutions on the pro-étale site, with the functorial model comparisons, signs and coherence of BH.2.

A topos inverse image is exact, preserves colimits and preserves the free-module construction on a sheaf of sets. It therefore takes these particular filtered cell resolutions to K-flat resolutions: their flat generators remain flat by the same finite-sum argument. This proves the derived tensor comparison for inverse image using the chosen models. It does not assume that an arbitrary complex with flat terms is K-flat.

For internal Hom, use a K-flat resolution in the first variable and a K-injective resolution in the second, as in BH.4. The local verification there applies too. Indeed restriction to a slice topos has an exact extension-by-zero left adjoint: its finite-sum description has the same lifting and kernel argument as above. Restriction consequently preserves K-injectives, by adjunction on complexes, and preserves the chosen K-flat cell models. The tensor–Hom identity on each slice then proves both local independence of models and the derived internal adjunction. In particular \(D_X\) is a closed symmetric monoidal derived category, with the associativity and Koszul symmetry maps already checked in (BH.8).

BL.2. Which changes disappear under completion

Call \(T\in D_X\) localized if multiplication by \(\pi\) on \(T\) is an isomorphism. Localization of modules is exact, so this is equivalent to \(\underline Q\otimes_O^LT\simeq T\). Equation (BK.8) says that the cone of the completion unit \(\eta_A:A\to C_XA\) is localized. Conversely, if \(C_XT=0\), (BK.8) identifies \(T\) with \(L_\pi(T)\), which is localized. Hence \[ C_XT=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad T\text{ is localized}. \tag{BL.1} \] Completion is exact: its expression in (BK.7) uses exact finite coefficient cones and a derived limit, which preserves triangles by the product-and-cone formula (BK.1).

Localized objects form a tensor ideal. If \(\pi:T\to T\) has an inverse, tensoring that inverse with the identity of \(A\) inverts multiplication by \(\pi\) on \(T\otimes_O^LA\). They are also preserved by inverse image, which carries that inverse to an inverse. Tensoring a completion unit with any object, or taking its inverse image, therefore gives a map with localized cone. Completing such a map makes it an isomorphism. In particular the unit supplies natural isomorphisms \[ C_X(A\otimes_O^LB)\xrightarrow{\sim} C_X(C_XA\otimes_O^LB),\qquad C_Xf^*A\xrightarrow{\sim}C_Xf^*C_YA. \tag{BL.2} \] The second formula is for \(f:X\to Y\). The same assertions apply to the other tensor factor. These are maps induced by \(\eta\), not choices of isomorphisms between objects.

BL.3. The completed tensor and its unit

For \(A,B\in D_X^c\), set \[ A\widehat\otimes_OB=C_X(A\otimes_O^LB),\qquad \mathbf1_X=C_X\underline O. \tag{BL.3} \] The unit is the completed coefficient sheaf \(\widehat O\) in degree zero. Indeed \(\underline O\otimes_O^LO_n=\underline{O_n}\), and the transition maps are epimorphisms. Their derived limit has no positive cohomology: for a section \((b_n)\) of the product, the equations \(a_n-u_na_{n+1}=b_n\) can be solved for each finite initial segment by successive lifting; their sheaves of solutions have epimorphic transitions. Repleteness in BK.1 supplies a local compatible infinite solution. Thus \(1-s\) on the product is surjective, its kernel is the ordinary limit, and (BK.1) gives the assertion. This need not identify \(\widehat O\) with \(\underline O\).

Both iterated tensors in the associativity constraint identify by (BL.2) with \[ C_X(A\otimes_O^LB\otimes_O^LD). \tag{BL.4} \] Transport the associativity map of BL.1 through these unit-induced identifications. Similarly transport its signed interchange for symmetry. The unit constraints come from \(\underline O\otimes_O^LA\simeq A\), (BL.2), and \(C_XA\simeq A\).

These constraints satisfy their coherence identities. For example every map from the raw four-factor tensor to a complete target has a unique factorization through its completion, by BK.4. Precomposing either route in the completed pentagon with the raw tensor and its units gives the same ordinary reassociation map. The bijection on Hom sets makes the two completed routes equal. The triangle and symmetry hexagon follow in the same way from the ordinary unit and signed-interchange calculations of BH.2. This also identifies the multiplication of \(\mathbf1_X=\widehat O\) with its usual pointwise multiplication: both maps restrict to multiplication on \(\underline O\), and the tensor-unit comparison in (BL.2) gives the same uniqueness.

This argument uses the universal property of completion to compare maps. Reduction modulo every \(\pi^n\) detects isomorphisms between complete objects by BK.4; it is not being asserted to be faithful on all morphisms.

BL.4. Internal Hom is already complete in its target

Let \(E\in D_X^c\) and \(A\in D_X\). The ordinary derived internal Hom \(H=R\mathcal Hom_O(A,E)\) is complete. Tensor–Hom adjunction and the symmetry from BL.1 give \[ R\mathcal Hom_O(\underline Q,H) \simeq R\mathcal Hom_O(A,R\mathcal Hom_O(\underline Q,E))=0. \tag{BL.5} \] For clarity, the isomorphism is checked by applying Hom from any \(T\): the two sides both represent maps from \(T\otimes_O^LA\otimes_O^L\underline Q\) to \(E\), with the specified reassociation and interchange. Yoneda therefore proves the internal identity and its naturality. The last equality is the definition of completeness in BK.4.

For complete \(A,B,E\), the two adjunctions now give \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{D_X^c}(A\widehat\otimes_OB,E) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D_X}(A\otimes_O^LB,E) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D_X^c}(A,R\mathcal Hom_O(B,E)). \tag{BL.6} \] Thus (BL.3) is a closed symmetric monoidal structure. Its evaluation is the unique extension to the completed tensor of the ordinary evaluation map; its adjunction unit is defined by the corresponding identity. Their triangle identities hold because the displayed bijections are natural inverses.

BL.5. Finite reductions of these operations

Write \(A_n=A\otimes_O^LO_n\). The units and the coefficient extension maps give \[ (A\widehat\otimes_OB)_n\simeq A_n\otimes_{O_n}^LB_n, \qquad (\mathbf1_X)_n\simeq\underline{O_n}. \tag{BL.7} \] The first comparison first uses (BK.9), then ordinary scalar extension of a tensor. On the cell models \(P_A,P_B\) of BL.1, its latter step is the equality \((P_A\otimes_OP_B)\otimes_OO_n=(P_A\otimes_OO_n)\otimes_{O_n}(P_B\otimes_OO_n)\). The reduced models are K-flat over \(O_n\): tensoring an acyclic \(O_n\)-complex with one is the same as tensoring its restricted \(O\)-complex with the original K-flat model. This proves the formula for unbounded complexes too.

There is also the canonical internal-Hom comparison \[ R\mathcal Hom_O(A,E)\otimes_O^LO_n \xrightarrow{\sim}R\mathcal Hom_{O_n}(A_n,E_n). \tag{BL.8} \] It is the adjoint of the reduced evaluation map. To prove it, restrict the target to \(O\)-modules. Derived extension/restriction adjunction identifies it with \(R\mathcal Hom_O(A,E_n)\). For this adjunction, resolve the source by a K-flat model and the target by a K-injective \(O_n\)-model. A quasi-isomorphism between the K-flat source models stays a quasi-isomorphism after coefficient extension, and Hom into the latter injective model preserves it. The ordinary scalar-extension adjunction therefore descends to the derived categories. Applying the same construction on each slice gives the internal adjunction. This uses no flatness of \(O_n\) over \(O\) and makes no assertion that restriction of an arbitrary K-injective \(O_n\)-complex is K-injective over \(O\).

Now \(E_n\) is the cone of \(\pi^n:E\to E\). The exact \(O\)-linear functor \(R\mathcal Hom_O(A,-)\) takes this to the cone of multiplication by \(\pi^n\) on \(R\mathcal Hom_O(A,E)\), which is the left side of (BL.8). The natural map just computed is its evaluation-defined comparison, since this holds on the two free terms of (BK.5). Restriction of scalars detects quasi-isomorphisms, proving (BL.8) as an \(O_n\)-comparison. These formulas commute with successive coefficient reduction: the tensor maps are scalar-extension maps, and the Hom maps are their evaluation adjoints. The transition maps are those of (BK.5), including their degree-minus-one factors.

BL.6. Inverse image, its adjunction and composition

Define \[ f_c^*=C_Xf^*:D_Y^c\longrightarrow D_X^c. \tag{BL.9} \] BK.5 proves that \(Rf_*\) takes complete objects to complete objects. For complete \(A,E\), completion and the ordinary derived adjunction give \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{D_X^c}(f_c^*A,E) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D_X}(f^*A,E) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D_Y^c}(A,Rf_*E). \tag{BL.10} \] Its counit is the unique map \(C_Xf^*Rf_*E\to E\) extending the ordinary counit. Its unit is the ordinary unit \(A\to Rf_*f^*A\) followed by \(Rf_*\eta_{f^*A}\). These descriptions are the maps corresponding to the identity under (BL.10), so they satisfy both triangle identities.

For composable maps \(X\xrightarrow fY\xrightarrow gZ\), (BL.2) and ordinary inverse-image composition give \[ f_c^*g_c^*\simeq(gf)_c^*. \tag{BL.11} \] All parenthesizations are coherent: after inserting the raw inverse-image object, each comparison is uniquely determined by its ordinary composition map and the completion unit. Applying the same argument to tensor and its unit gives \[ f_c^*(A\widehat\otimes_OB)\simeq f_c^*A\widehat\otimes_Of_c^*B, \qquad f_c^*\mathbf1_Y\simeq\mathbf1_X. \tag{BL.12} \] The associativity, symmetry and unit diagrams reduce by the bijections of BK.4 to the corresponding ordinary diagrams in BL.1. Thus completed inverse image is a strong symmetric monoidal functor, with the stated right adjoint.

Finally \((f_c^*A)_n\simeq f^*A_n\), by (BK.9) and the inverse-image models of BL.1. Together with (BK.10) this identifies the reductions of its unit and counit with the ordinary coefficient-level adjunction maps. In a Cartesian square, the mate made from these units and counits is exactly the completed comparison of BK.6: precomposition with the raw pullback gives the ordinary base-change map followed by completion, and the same uniqueness determines its extension. This verifies the operation map, in addition to its objectwise finite-level formula.

The free general comparisons for the last construction are derived-complete inverse image, Tag 099K and constant Noetherian coefficients, Tag 099N. Here the proof uses the explicit one-parameter completion and its unit from BK. BM uses these categorical operations to construct completed proper support, with its reduction-defined constructibility and comparisons. BP–BS supply the strict-system and derived-diagram comparisons; BV constructs exceptional inverse image and proves adic biduality. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization. BX proves the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves. General heart realization remains a distinct requirement.

Appendix BM. Proper support for completed coefficients

Let \(k\) be a field of characteristic different from \(\ell\), and initially let all schemes be separated and of finite type over \(k\). Keep \(O,\pi,O_n\) and \(C_X\) from BK. For the constructibility assertions below assume that the residue field of \(O\) is finite; in particular they apply to the valuation ring of every finite extension of \(\mathbf Q_\ell\).

Write \(\mathscr A_X\) for the full subcategory of complete pro-étale \(O\)-complexes \(K\) such that every \(K_n=K\otimes_O^LO_n\) is the pullback of a bounded-below étale \(O_n\)-complex. The bound may depend on \(n\). The categories and coefficient actions are specified: “comes from étale” refers to \(\nu_X^*:D^+(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)\to D^+(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},O_n)\). BK.2 proves this functor fully faithful, by its derived unit. Its image is closed under triangles, since maps lift uniquely and its exact functor takes their cones to the corresponding cones. Thus \(\mathscr A_X\) is triangulated. We will construct proper support on this category, then prove a constructible subcategory is preserved.

BM.1. Complete extension by zero

For a quasi-compact open immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\), restriction \(j^*\) is exact and is right adjoint to exact extension by zero \(j_!\). Exactness here can be checked directly from the open-subtopos construction: sections of an extension by zero are locally sections on the specified open, with zero extension wherever the support is absent; lifting and kernel equations are checked on those local representatives. This is the same finite local lifting argument as BL.1. The termwise adjunction therefore descends to derived categories.

As a right adjoint, \(j^*\) preserves products. Exactness makes it preserve the product-and-cone homotopy limits in BK.1. It commutes with the two free terms of \(P_n\), and hence with completion. In particular it preserves complete objects and \(j_c^*=j^*\). Define \[ j_{!,c}K=C_Xj_!K. \tag{BM.1} \] The completion adjunction proves \(j_{!,c}\dashv j^*\) on complete categories. Its unit and counit are obtained from the ordinary open adjunction and the completion unit, as in BL.6. Since \(j_!\) is exact and \(O\)-linear, it preserves localized complexes. Therefore inserting or deleting an intermediate completion inside \(C_Xj_!\) gives an isomorphism by (BL.1). This proves the composition law for complete extension by zero along two opens, with its ordinary composition map.

We will use \[ (j_{!,c}K)_n\simeq j_!K_n, \qquad j_{\mathrm{pro\acute et},!}\nu_U^*L \simeq\nu_X^*j_{\mathrm{\acute et},!}L. \tag{BM.2} \] The first follows from (BK.9) and the two-term coefficient cone. For the second, restriction and \(\nu_*\) commute on étale objects, because both are evaluation on those same objects. The two proposed functors are consequently left adjoint to the same functor, by the open and site adjunctions. Their identification is the one given by extension of the same local sections by zero. All these functors are exact, so the assertion applies to complexes and to their actual maps. It follows that \(j_{!,c}\) takes \(\mathscr A_U\) into \(\mathscr A_X\).

BM.2. A compactification and its finite reductions

For \(f:X\to Y\), choose the compactification established in BG.5, \(X\xrightarrow j\overline X\xrightarrow pY\), with \(j\) open and \(p\) proper. Define \[ F_{p,j}(K)=Rp_*j_{!,c}K \simeq C_YRp_*j_!K. \tag{BM.3} \] The isomorphism is (BK.10). The first expression is complete. Its canonical reductions are \[ F_{p,j}(K)_n\simeq Rp_*j_!K_n \simeq\nu_Y^*R p_{\mathrm{\acute et},*} j_{\mathrm{\acute et},!}L_n, \quad K_n\simeq\nu_X^*L_n. \tag{BM.4} \] Indeed \(Rp_*\) commutes with the finite free coefficient cone, (BM.2) handles extension by zero, and (BK.4) identifies the proper direct image. The étale complex on the right is bounded below. Thus (BM.3) takes \(\mathscr A_X\) into \(\mathscr A_Y\). It is exact, since each of its functors is exact on the derived categories.

The construction has a specified inverse-limit description: \[ F_{p,j}(K)\simeq \operatorname{holim}_n Rp_*j_!K_n. \tag{BM.5} \] These are the reductions of the single functor (BM.3), with the transitions of \(P_n\). Formula (BM.5) is not a choice of an inverse limit of isomorphism classes of étale complexes. This distinction retains the comparison maps when we change compactification.

BM.3. The completed proper–open exchange

Consider a commuting square \((U,T;V,S)\) with opens \(j:U\to T\), \(i:V\to S\) and proper maps \(p':U\to V\), \(p:T\to S\). It need not be cartesian. The induced map \(a:U\to T_V=T\times_SV\) is an open-and-closed immersion: it is open, and is proper by the closed graph into a separated \(V\)-scheme followed by proper projection. Thus \(a_!=a_*\) is exact, and preserves completion by the decomposition into the two open-and-closed topoi.

Restriction of a derived direct image to an open is its direct image on that open. One can check this without a proper base-change theorem: restriction preserves K-injectives because its extension-by-zero left adjoint is exact, and the section formula for direct image already has that equality. Hence \[ i^*Rp_*j_{!,c}E\simeq Rp'_*E. \tag{BM.6} \] The inverse of this identification and the complete open adjunction define a particular map \[ \epsilon_c:i_{!,c}Rp'_*E\longrightarrow Rp_*j_{!,c}E. \tag{BM.7} \] If \(E\in\mathscr A_U\), this map is an isomorphism. Reduce it modulo \(\pi^n\). The reduction rules in BK and (BM.2) identify its adjunction construction with the étale proper–open exchange (BG.14) on \(E_n\). That exchange is an isomorphism by its earlier proof: over \(V\) it is the clopen identity, and on the complement proper base change gives zero because the support open has empty fibre. The coefficients are torsion and bounded below, as required. Both sides of (BM.7) are complete. The complete cone has zero reductions, so it is zero by BK.4.

The maps (BM.7) obey pasting before any appeal to reduction. Restrict a vertically stacked exchange to its bottom open. The two candidates are the same proper pushforward of the same clopen-supported complex, with the composite direct-image adjunction unit. The identity for that composite unit makes the restrictions equal. The bijection for \(i_{!,c}\dashv i^*\) makes the maps themselves equal. Horizontal pasting uses the composition law of complete open extension from BM.1 and the same argument on the smallest open. Exchanges in separate positions commute by naturality. The argument is the explicit one in Cohomology with compact support, Lemma 6.1, now with the complete adjunction. Reduction was used to prove invertibility, not faithfulness on morphisms.

BM.4. Independence and associative composition

A refinement \(h:\overline X_1\to\overline X_2\) of compactifications is proper and restricts to the identity on \(X\). Apply (BM.7) with \(p'=\mathrm{id}_X\). It gives \[ j_{2,!,c}K\xrightarrow{\sim}Rh_*j_{1,!,c}K, \tag{BM.8} \] and hence a comparison from the second functor (BM.3) to the first. The comparison for two refinements is their composite by vertical pasting; the identity refinement gives the identity.

BG.6 supplies the necessary common refinements without deleting any part of \(X\): take its schematic closure in the product of two compactifications. Its graph is closed over either copy of the open \(X\), so the same \(X\) remains open in the closure. Parallel maps are equalized by their closed equalizer containing that open. To compare arbitrary compactifications, map each to a common refinement using (BM.8). A further common refinement makes comparisons through two different choices equal, by pasting and cancellation of isomorphisms. A common refinement of three choices proves the cocycle identity. Thus (BM.3) defines a canonical functor \[ Rf_{!,c}:\mathscr A_X\longrightarrow\mathscr A_Y. \tag{BM.9} \] For a proper map it is \(Rf_*\), and for an open immersion it is (BM.1), by choosing the identity part of the compactification.

Here is the composition map explicitly. For \(X\xrightarrow fY\xrightarrow gZ\), compactify \(g\) as \(Y\xrightarrow iD\xrightarrow qZ\), then compactify \(if\) as \(X\hookrightarrow T\xrightarrow pD\). Put \(V=p^{-1}Y\), with \(j:X\hookrightarrow V\), \(a:V\hookrightarrow T\) and \(h:V\to Y\). The proper–open exchange gives \[ Rq_*i_{!,c}Rh_*j_{!,c} \xrightarrow{Rq_*\epsilon_cj_{!,c}} Rq_*Rp_*a_{!,c}j_{!,c} \simeq R(qp)_*(aj)_{!,c}. \tag{BM.10} \] It is \(Rg_{!,c}Rf_{!,c}\simeq R(gf)_{!,c}\).

For completeness, compatible systems of this kind have common refinements too. First refine their compactifications \(D_1,D_2\) of \(Y\). In the product of their \(T_i\) with that refinement impose the closed equations equating the maps to \(D_1,D_2\), and take the closure of the diagonal \(X\). Properness and the closed-graph argument retain the required open and give a refinement at every vertex. Comparing (BM.10) in this diagram gives a grid of exchanges. Adjacent exchanges paste to the outer exchange by BM.3, and exchanges in disjoint positions commute. Thus its composition map is independent of choices. For three maps, successive compactifications give a single triangular grid; its two parenthesizations perform the same exchanges. The same two pasting rules make them equal. Identity maps use identity exchanges. This proves associative, unital composition, including its actual maps.

BM.5. Base change and the coefficient comparison

Given any change of base \(g:Y'\to Y\), pull back the chosen compactification to obtain \(X'\xrightarrow{j'}\overline X'\xrightarrow{p'}Y'\); write \(g_X,g_{\overline X}\) for the other projections. Use the completed proper comparison of BK.6 and complete open base change to form \[ g_c^*Rp_*j_{!,c}K \longrightarrow Rp'_*g_{\overline X,c}^*j_{!,c}K \xrightarrow{\sim}Rp'_*j'_{!,c}g_{X,c}^*K. \tag{BM.11} \] The open comparison follows from exact ordinary open base change and the localized-cone rule (BL.2); \(j_!\) also preserves localized cones by its exact \(O\)-linearity. For the proper comparison, each reduction of \(j_{!,c}K\) is a bounded-below classical torsion complex by (BM.2). BE.1–BE.8 prove its arbitrary-base proper comparison, and BK.6 identifies the completed map with the corresponding limit. Thus (BM.11) is an isomorphism. This construction and proof also work for the pulled-back compactifiable map even when \(Y'\) is not of finite type over \(k\); properness and quasi-compactness of the open are preserved by base change, and the comparison statements used above are local on \(Y'\).

This map commutes with refinement and composition. Indeed (BM.7) is defined by its restriction to the source open. After base change its two candidate restrictions are the same composition-compatible proper comparison and the same clopen identity. The complete open adjunction proves their equality. Expanding a refinement or composition comparison into its exchanges, as in (BM.8)–(BM.10), now gives a commuting grid. Consecutive base changes likewise paste, by BK.6 and exact open base change. Consequently (BM.11) is the canonical isomorphism \[ g_c^*Rf_{!,c}K\simeq Rf'_{!,c}g_{X,c}^*K \tag{BM.12} \] for the choice-independent functor. Its coefficient-level maps are the ordinary proper-support base-change maps, by (BM.4) and the definitions of the completed units and counits.

BM.6. Constructibility and bounds from the first reduction

Define \(\mathscr C_X\) to consist of complete \(K\) whose first derived reduction comes from a bounded constructible étale \(O_1\)-complex. This is a definition by derived reduction; the comparison with strict adic systems and their hearts is a further assertion, not part of this definition.

Every such \(K\) belongs to \(\mathscr A_X\). Suppose \(K_1\) has cohomology in \([a,b]\). Tensor the exact coefficient sequence \(0\to O_{n-1}\xrightarrow{\pi}O_n\to O_1\to0\) with \(K\). It gives a triangle \[ K_{n-1}\longrightarrow K_n\longrightarrow K_1. \tag{BM.13} \] View its outer terms as \(O_n\)-complexes by restriction along the quotient maps. The fully faithful image of bounded-below étale complexes is triangulated, as observed at the start. Induction therefore proves that \(K_n\) is classical as an \(O_n\)-complex. Its long cohomology sequence gives the same bound \([a,b]\) for every \(n\). Finite local constancy on a common refinement is closed under kernels and cokernels: after trivialization, the map is locally a fixed map of finite modules. It is also closed under extensions. In \(0\to A\to B\to D\to0\), trivialize finite \(A,D\), then lift every element of \(D\) on one étale refinement. Differences between sums of these lifts and the chosen lift of their sum lie in \(A\), as do the differences for scalar multiplication. There are finitely many such differences, because \(O_n,A,D\) are finite. Refine again until they are constant. They define one finite module extension, whose constant sheaf maps to \(B\); every section is locally a chosen lift plus an element of \(A\), and its kernel is zero. This is the required local trivialization. The same induction therefore proves constructibility at each level. No uniform stratification for all levels is asserted here.

If the fibres of \(f\) have dimension at most \(d\), Proposition 3.2 and (BM.4) show that every reduction of \(Rf_{!,c}K\) is constructible with cohomology in \([a,b+2d]\). In particular its first reduction is bounded constructible, so \[ Rf_{!,c}(\mathscr C_X)\subset\mathscr C_Y. \tag{BM.14} \] The complete complex itself also has cohomology in this range. Here are the inverse-limit details, which apply to \(K\) with \([a,b]\) as well. Exact products and (BK.1) give \[ \begin{aligned} 0&\to\operatorname{coker}(1-s:\prod H^{q-1}B_n\to\prod H^{q-1}B_n)\\ &\to H^q(\operatorname{holim}B_n)\\ &\to\ker(1-s:\prod H^qB_n\to\prod H^qB_n)\to0. \end{aligned} \tag{BM.15} \] Take \(B_n=Rp_*j_!K_n\), all in \([a,t]\), with \(t=b+2d\). Only a possible degree \(t+1\) remains outside that range. The coefficient sequence \(0\to O_1\xrightarrow{\pi^n}O_{n+1}\to O_n\to0\), followed by the exact functor \(Rp_*j_!\), gives \(B_1\to B_{n+1}\to B_n\). Since \(H^{t+1}(B_1)=0\), the transitions on \(H^t(B_n)\) are epimorphisms. Repleteness solves the successive lifting equations for their product, exactly as in BL.3, so the cokernel in degree \(t+1\) is zero. This proves the claimed bound. The indices and maps in this argument are the quotient transitions, not ordinary quotients substituted for derived reductions.

The construction has proved proper support, its composition and arbitrary base change on \(\mathscr A\), and bounded constructibility in the precise reduction-defined sense of (BM.14). BV constructs the exceptional right adjoint and proves biduality on this complete bounded constructible category. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX proves the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves and the ordinary operations. The strict-system comparison and its lisse subcategory are proved in BP; BQ proves constructible cohomology and identifies the heart of the restricted standard t-structure. BR constructs the derived-cartesian pro-étale diagram comparison, with its actual adjunction and higher morphisms; BS proves its étale-site presentation with the same coefficient transitions. BT proves finite-coefficient realization and constructs the adic heart realization functor. BU proves its equivalence in dimension zero over finite or algebraically closed fields; the general positive-dimensional effacement condition stated precisely in BT.5 remains required.

Free comparisons for the exchange and compactification construction are Tag 0F7A and Tag 0F7H. The completed maps above are derived from BK–BL and the stated finite-coefficient proofs, with the open adjunction supplying their coherence.

Appendix BN. Uniform coefficient bounds and completed projection

Keep the field, schemes and complete discrete valuation ring of BM, including its finite residue field. Write \(\kappa=O_1\). We use the category \(\mathscr C_X\) defined in BM.6 by complete complexes with bounded constructible first derived reduction. The tensor and inverse image in this appendix are the completed operations of BL. The result will identify the projection map itself and its compatibility with the proper-support comparisons of BM.

BN.1. Tor bounds at every finite coefficient level

Let \(K\in\mathscr C_X\), with \(K_1\) having cohomology in \([a,b]\). Every sheaf of modules over the constant field \(\kappa\) is flat, on either of the sites used here. Indeed sheaf tensor is obtained by sheafifying the sectionwise tensor over \(\kappa\): the additional relations over the constant ring sheaf are already locally relations over \(\kappa\), since each of the finitely many coefficients in a relation becomes constant on a cover. A monomorphism of sheaves is injective on sections. Tensoring an injective map of \(\kappa\)-vector spaces is injective: write a putative kernel element using a basis of the finite-dimensional span of its second factors; the coefficient of each basis vector must vanish. Sheafification preserves the resulting exact sequence. This proves the assertion without using ordinary étale points to detect arbitrary pro-étale sheaves.

Good truncation therefore represents \(K_1\) by a bounded complex of flat \(\kappa\)-sheaves in degrees \([a,b]\). Such a complex is K-flat: a single flat sheaf preserves exact complexes, and induction on the number of terms, using its termwise split truncation triangles, proves the claim. Consequently \(K_1\) has Tor amplitude in \([a,b]\), meaning that its derived tensor with any sheaf placed in degree zero has cohomology only in that interval.

In fact the same interval is a Tor bound for \(K_n\) over \(O_n\), for every \(n\). If \(M\) is an \(O_n\)-sheaf killed by \(\pi\), scalar-extension associativity gives \[ K_n\otimes_{O_n}^LM \simeq K\otimes_O^LM \simeq K_1\otimes_\kappa^LM. \tag{BN.1} \] These are derived identities: take a K-flat \(O\)-model of \(K\); its reduction is K-flat over each quotient by the tensor test in BL.5. For arbitrary \(M\), the finite filtration \(M\supset\pi M\supset\cdots\supset\pi^nM=0\) has layers killed by \(\pi\). Apply the exact derived tensor functor to each of its short exact sequences. The long cohomology sequences and (BN.1), by induction on the layers, give the same interval \([a,b]\). The argument applies to arbitrary sheaves \(M\), not just constructible ones.

BM.6 already proves that \(K_n\) is classical and bounded constructible. Its étale model also has this Tor bound. To see the descent of the bound, tensor that model with any étale \(O_n\)-sheaf and pull back by \(\nu_X^*\). The tensor comparison of BL.1 identifies the result with the tensor just bounded. Exact \(\nu_X^*\) detects zero étale sheaves by the unit comparison in BK.2, so the étale tensor has the same vanishing. This is an assertion about Tor amplitude, not a claim that every cohomology sheaf is flat. For example the complete torsion object \(\underline\kappa\) has derived reductions in degrees \(-1,0\), as BK.7 computes; ordinary quotients alone do not satisfy this calculation.

BN.2. Tensor and inverse image preserve the constructible category

Take \(K,A\in\mathscr C_X\), with first-reduction bounds \([a,b]\), \([c,e]\). The specified comparison (BL.7) reads \[ (K\widehat\otimes_OA)_1 \simeq K_1\otimes_\kappa^LA_1. \tag{BN.2} \] This is a classical complex: choose the bounded flat representatives from BN.1 on the étale site and apply exact inverse image. Its cohomology lies in \([a+c,b+e]\). It is constructible too, without assuming that a complex with locally constant cohomology has already been trivialized as a constant complex. Apply the finite cohomology truncation triangles to the two factors. They reduce the assertion to tensor products of two constructible \(\kappa\)-sheaves and to finite extensions of their cohomology sheaves. On a common finite locally closed partition the two sheaves are finite locally constant; their tensor is so as well, by tensoring their finite trivializations. Closure under kernels, cokernels and extensions was proved in BM.6. Induction through the triangles gives the assertion.

Thus \(K\widehat\otimes_OA\in\mathscr C_X\), and the completed object itself has cohomology in \([a+c,b+e]\) by the inverse-limit proof (BM.15). BN.1 gives this same Tor interval for all its reductions. The tensor unit belongs to \(\mathscr C_X\), since its first reduction is \(\underline\kappa\). The associativity, unit and symmetry constraints of BL therefore restrict to this category.

For \(f:X\to Y\) and \(A\in\mathscr C_Y\), the formula \[ (f_c^*A)_1\simeq f^*A_1 \tag{BN.3} \] shows that \(f_c^*A\in\mathscr C_X\). Exact inverse image preserves the cohomological interval. Inverse images of the finitely many locally closed strata form a finite partition, and pulling back their trivializing étale covers proves constructibility on that partition. BL.6 supplies the strong symmetric monoidal comparison and its actual maps. Together with BM.6, we now have all the objects needed in the completed projection formula inside \(\mathscr C\).

BN.3. The proper projection map

For a proper map \(p:T\to S\), \(E\in\mathscr C_T\) and \(A\in\mathscr C_S\), use the strong monoidal inverse image and its counit to form \[ \begin{aligned} p_c^*(Rp_*E\widehat\otimes_OA) &\simeq p_c^*Rp_*E\widehat\otimes_Op_c^*A\\ &\longrightarrow E\widehat\otimes_Op_c^*A. \end{aligned} \tag{BN.4} \] Transpose under \(p_c^*\dashv Rp_*\). This defines a canonical map \[ \gamma^c_{p,E,A}:Rp_*E\widehat\otimes_OA \longrightarrow Rp_*(E\widehat\otimes_Op_c^*A). \tag{BN.5} \] Both objects belong to \(\mathscr C_S\), by BM.6 and BN.2.

Reduce this particular map modulo \(\pi^n\). BK.5, BL.5 and BL.6 identify its transpose with the ordinary finite-coefficient counit tensored with \(p^*A_n\). BK.2 identifies the classical direct images and the adjunction maps with those on the étale site. Thus its reduction is exactly \[ Rp_*E_n\otimes_{O_n}^LA_n \longrightarrow Rp_*(E_n\otimes_{O_n}^Lp^*A_n), \tag{BN.6} \] the map proved invertible in BH.6. In particular the reduction for \(n=1\) is an isomorphism. Its complete cone is zero: the coefficient triangles (BM.13) give zero at all levels from zero at level one, and BK.4 then gives zero for the complete cone itself. This proves that (BN.5) is an isomorphism. The argument uses the actual counit-defined arrow, not an isomorphism selected from a comparison of objects.

The proper maps compose compatibly with (BN.5). For \(T\xrightarrow pS\xrightarrow qZ\), transpose the two proposed projection maps under \((qp)_c^*\dashv R(qp)_*\). Both are the \(q\)-counit pulled back by \(p_c^*\), followed by the \(p\)-counit, tensored with \((qp)_c^*A\). The composite-adjunction identity in BL.6 makes them equal. With two coefficient factors, their two orders similarly transpose to the same counit tensored with those factors; BL.3's associativity proves the tensor compatibility, and its unit constraint proves the unit compatibility. In a cartesian proper square the base-change map is the mate of the same units and counits by BK.6. Substituting (BN.4) on both sides therefore gives the same pulled-back counit and the same tensor reassociation. This proves base-change compatibility of the maps, not merely of their reductions.

BN.4. Extension by zero and projection

For an open immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow T\), the ordinary sheaf identity is \[ j_!M\otimes_ON\simeq j_!(M\otimes_Oj^*N). \tag{BN.7} \] One can verify it on the local representatives in BM.1: a section supported on the open is tensored with the restriction of the second section; wherever its first factor is extended by zero the tensor is zero. Finite sums and the bilinear relations give mutually inverse maps after sheafification. This proof works on the pro-étale site and does not use ordinary geometric stalks there.

The identity descends to derived tensors. If \(P\) is a K-flat complex on \(U\), then \(j_!P\) is K-flat: for any acyclic complex \(N\), the termwise identity (BN.7) identifies its tensor with \(j_!(P\otimes_Oj^*N)\), which is acyclic since \(j^*\) and \(j_!\) are exact. Direct sums in the total tensor commute with \(j_!\), by its left adjunction. Choose these resolutions for the first factor to obtain the derived form of (BN.7).

For complete \(E,A\), apply completion and the unit comparisons (BL.2) to this derived identity. Exact \(O\)-linear \(j_!\) preserves localized cones, as BM.1 proves, so an intermediate completion inside \(C_Tj_!\) may also be removed. Since \(j^*\) preserves completeness, the result is \[ j_{!,c}E\widehat\otimes_OA \xrightarrow{\sim}j_{!,c}(E\widehat\otimes_Oj^*A). \tag{BN.8} \] It restricts to the identity on the open tensor. This description fixes its compatibility with successive open immersions, tensor associativity and base change: the ordinary section maps have these properties, and completion factors them uniquely through the units. Equivalently the complete open adjunction determines each resulting map from that restriction.

BN.5. Proper support, refinements and composition

Let \(f:X\to Y\), \(K\in\mathscr C_X\) and \(A\in\mathscr C_Y\). Choose \(f=pj\) as in BM.2. Apply (BN.5) followed by (BN.8) and inverse-image composition: \[ \begin{aligned} Rf_{!,c}K\widehat\otimes_OA &\longrightarrow Rp_*(j_{!,c}K\widehat\otimes_Op_c^*A)\\ &\xrightarrow{\sim}Rf_{!,c}(K\widehat\otimes_Of_c^*A). \end{aligned} \tag{BN.9} \] Both arrows are isomorphisms. This proves the completed proper-support projection formula at the full field and finite-type scope of BM, for every pair of objects in its reduction-defined constructible categories.

We verify independence of the compactification. In the proper–open square of BM.3, compare projection before and after the exchange (BM.7). By (BN.8) its common source can be written as a complete extension from the bottom open \(V\). Maps from this source are determined by their restrictions to \(V\), using \(i_{!,c}\dashv i^*\). On \(V\), (BM.6) identifies the exchange with the clopen identity and the direct image by \(p'\). The two projection routes are now (BN.5) for \(p'\): transposition gives the same proper counit tensored with the restricted coefficient. Their equality follows from the ordinary direct-image restriction identity and the counit description (BN.4). The complete open adjunction proves equality before restriction. This establishes tensor compatibility with a single proper–open exchange.

A refinement (BM.8) is such an exchange; hence it commutes with (BN.9). Passing to a common refinement proves independence. The composition map (BM.10) is a proper–open exchange between composites of proper and open functors. Its compatibility follows from the exchange calculation just given, proper composition in BN.3 and open composition in BN.4. For three morphisms the common grid in BM.4 gives the same equality under either parenthesization. The tensor associativity and unit identities follow from the corresponding proper and open identities. Thus (BN.9) is a coherent natural comparison for the functor constructed in BM, not only for a chosen compactification.

Finally pull back that compactification in a cartesian square. The base-change comparison (BM.11) is a proper comparison followed by open base change. These commute with projection by BN.3 and BN.4. The resulting square for (BN.9) commutes; common refinements and BM.5 make it the comparison for the choice-independent functor. This argument also applies to arbitrary changes of base using BM.5's pulled-back compactification and bounded classical finite reductions. Every reduction of (BN.9) is the finite-coefficient projection map (BH.19), and its transition compatibility is inherited from the reduction maps in BL.5–BL.6.

We have proved tensor and inverse-image closure, uniform finite-level Tor bounds and completed proper-support projection with its operation maps. None of these proofs uses a simultaneous local trivialization of all coefficient complexes. BO proves that local trivialization, including its finite-coefficient theorem and actual compatible lifting map. BP identifies the strict coefficient systems in degree zero, and BQ proves constructible cohomology and standard truncations. BR supplies the derived-cartesian coefficient-diagram comparison. BV constructs the exceptional right adjoint and proves singular adic biduality. BW constructs the completed-ring equivalence and central rationalization. BX proves the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves. General bounded-derived realization of the strict heart remains a separate requirement. The free comparison for the uniform bound is Tag 09C2; BN.1 supplies the coefficient-filtration and étale-descent details used here. The finite projection comparison and its prerequisites are the proved BH.5–BH.7, also explained in Cohomology with compact support, Section 10.

Appendix BO. Local finite-free models and their compatible adic limit

Retain \(O,\pi,O_n\) from BM–BN, with finite residue field \(\kappa\). We prove the local model assertion needed for the adic coefficient comparison. If \(X\) is connected and \(K\in\mathscr C_X\) has locally constant first-reduction cohomology, there is one bounded finite free \(O\)-complex \(P\) such that, on a pro-étale covering, \(K\) is isomorphic to the completed constant complex associated to \(P\). The differential matrices of this model are constant matrices over \(O\). The proof will construct a morphism of complete objects; it will not take a homotopy limit of an unspecified family of morphism classes.

BO.1. A finite-coefficient complex can be made finite free locally

Put \(R=O_n\). Let \(L\) be an étale complex with finite locally constant cohomology and Tor amplitude \([a,b]\). We claim that étale locally it is represented by a constant complex of finite free \(R\)-modules in exactly that degree interval.

We first record the top-degree tensor calculation. A sheaf has a flat resolution in nonpositive degrees by repeatedly taking the epimorphism (BH.2) and its kernel. BH.1 proves such a bounded-above flat complex K-flat. Thus, for sheaves \(F,M\), \(F\otimes_R^LM\) has no positive cohomology and has degree-zero cohomology \(F\otimes_RM\). Applying the finite cohomology truncation triangles to a bounded complex \(B\) gives \[ H^b(B\otimes_R^LM)=H^b(B)\otimes_RM \quad\text{if }H^{>b}(B)=0. \tag{BO.1} \] Indeed the tensor of \(\tau_{\leq b-1}B\) has no cohomology above \(b-1\), by induction through its finitely many cohomology sheaves; the top truncation triangle then gives the equality. This also proves the asserted naturality of (BO.1).

Proceed by induction on \(b-a\). If \(a=b\), write \(L=F[-a]\). Trivialize \(F\) as a constant finite module \(M\). The Tor condition gives \(\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,\kappa)=0\), by testing the constant coefficient sheaf and a geometric stalk. Lift a basis of \(M/\pi M\) to obtain \(R^r\to M\). Its cokernel \(Q\) satisfies \(Q=\pi Q\), hence \(Q=\pi^nQ=0\). For its kernel \(J\), the Tor sequence gives an injection \(J/\pi J\to\kappa^r\), whose image is the kernel of the chosen basis isomorphism to \(M/\pi M\). It is zero. Therefore \(J=\pi^nJ=0\) too. We have proved \(M\simeq R^r\), including the algebra needed at the bottom of the induction.

Suppose \(a<b\). Trivialize \(H^b(L)\) and choose finitely many module generators. For any complex representing \(L\), its cycle sheaf surjects onto its cohomology sheaf. After an étale refinement the chosen generators lift to actual cycles. These define a map \(\underline{R^r}[-b]\to L\). Complete it to a triangle \[ \underline{R^r}[-b]\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow B \longrightarrow\underline{R^r}[-b+1]. \tag{BO.2} \] Its tensor with any sheaf \(M\) has zero cohomology outside \([a,b-1]\): below \(a\) this follows from the outer bounds and \(b-1\geq a\); in degree \(b\), (BO.1) makes the first map surjective. Hence \(B\) has Tor amplitude \([a,b-1]\). Its cohomology is still finite locally constant. The only new piece is an extension of \(H^{b-1}(L)\) by the kernel of \(\underline{R^r}\to H^b(L)\); the finite-module kernel and extension arguments are those proved in BM.6.

By induction, after another refinement \(B\) has a constant finite free model \(P^a\to\cdots\to P^{b-1}\). The last arrow in (BO.2) is determined by a sheaf map \(H^{b-1}(B)\to\underline{R^r}\): the lower truncation has cohomology at most \(b-2\), so the derived truncation orthogonality and its shift give this factorization and its uniqueness. Compose with the quotient from \(\underline{P^{b-1}}\). This is a map of finite free constant sheaves, so its finitely many matrix entries become constant after a common étale refinement. It kills the preceding differential. Append that matrix as the last differential of the model, with the cone sign convention of Appendix B. Rotating its cone triangle gives (BO.2), and the induced map of triangles is an isomorphism on the other two objects, hence on \(L\). This proves the claim. In particular no local-structure theorem has been substituted for a proof.

BO.2. One coefficient type on a connected scheme

If \(X\) is connected, all the coefficient complexes in these local models have the same isomorphism class in \(D(R)\). Where two covering opens have intersecting images, choose a geometric point in their fibre product. The two stalk complexes there are both the stalk of \(L\); hence their coefficient complexes are isomorphic. The union of the images carrying a fixed isomorphism class is open, because étale maps are open. Distinct such unions are disjoint and cover \(X\). Connectedness leaves one nonempty union. This gives one finite free coefficient complex \(M_n\), which may require many local trivializations. It does not give a global trivialization of \(L\).

Apply this to the classical models of \(K_n\). Their uniform Tor bounds are BN.1. If \(K_1\) has finite locally constant cohomology, the coefficient triangles (BM.13) and the local extension argument in BM.6 prove the same property for every \(K_n\), on this same scheme. Thus BO.1 applies at every level. Fix a geometric point of \(X\). Taking the stalks of the classical models and their transition maps selects the coefficient objects \(M_n\) and maps with \[ M_{n+1}\otimes_{O_{n+1}}^LO_n\simeq M_n. \tag{BO.3} \] The classical models and maps here can be obtained using the derived site adjunction of BK.2; its unit identifies them with the given reductions, and exact stalks commute with derived scalar extension. Consequently these are the reductions of the specified maps, not arbitrary maps between equal isomorphism classes.

BO.3. Compatible matrices over the complete ring

We give the coefficient lifting argument in this setting. In a bounded finite free complex over \(O_n\), a unit entry of a differential can be made into an isolated \(1\) by row and column operations. The equation \(d^2=0\) makes the neighbouring maps zero on that summand. It is the contractible direct summand \(O_n\xrightarrow{1}O_n\). Removing such summands terminates, and leaves a minimal complex: every differential entry is in \((\pi)\).

A bounded projective complex computes its derived maps by its ordinary Hom complex. Indeed Hom from a projective module preserves exact sequences, and finite truncation of the source shows that Hom from the complex takes acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes. The same observation shows that a quasi-isomorphism between bounded projective complexes is a homotopy equivalence. More explicitly, its bounded acyclic projective cone contracts by successively splitting the surjection onto its last nonzero term and removing the resulting two-term identity summand.

A homotopy equivalence between minimal complexes is an actual complex isomorphism. After reduction modulo \(\pi\), both differentials vanish, so the inverse homotopies say that its degree maps are mutually inverse. Lift their matrix inverses; the error matrices lie in the nilpotent ideal \((\pi)\), and the finite geometric series in that error corrects each to an inverse over \(O_n\).

Choose a minimal representative \(P_1\). Inductively choose a minimal representative at level \(n+1\). Its reduction is minimal, and (BO.3) gives a homotopy equivalence to \(P_n\), hence an actual isomorphism by the preceding paragraph. Change bases at level \(n+1\) to lift this isomorphism. Such a lift is invertible by the same nilpotent-ideal argument. Its reduced differential matrices are now exactly those of \(P_n\). At every level the term ranks are the dimensions of \(H^i(M_1)\), because minimal differentials reduce to zero. They vanish outside \([a,b]\). Taking inverse limits of these fixed-size matrices gives a bounded finite free \(O\)-complex \(P\) with \[ P/\pi^nP=P_n,\qquad P_n\simeq M_n. \tag{BO.4} \] Completeness identifies each matrix entry with its compatible residue sequence. The square of the limiting differential has zero image in every quotient and is zero since \(\bigcap_n\pi^nO=0\). The coefficient transitions in (BO.4) are the prescribed derived transitions. This matrix argument, also given in ℓ-adic sheaves and their cohomology, Theorem 6.1, uses the uniformizer \(\pi\); it includes ramified coefficient rings.

BO.4. A uniform stabilization argument on a contractible cover

Choose the weakly contractible affine pro-étale cover from BK.1 and work on one member \(W\). Restriction to this site object is the slice functor of BL.1. Its exact left adjoint makes restriction preserve products and homotopy limits, so it preserves completion as well. Write \(K_W\) for the resulting complete object. Let \[ \mathcal P=C_W\underline P, \qquad H=R\mathcal Hom_O(\mathcal P,K_W). \tag{BO.5} \] BL.4 proves \(H\) complete, and BL.5 identifies its actual reductions and their maps as \[ H_n=R\mathcal Hom_{O_n}(\underline{P_n},K_n|_W). \tag{BO.6} \] Here \(\mathcal P_n=\underline{P_n}\) by the completion unit. Since \(P_n\) is bounded finite free, the internal Hom in (BO.6) is computed by its finite Hom complex, or equivalently by its finite dual tensored with \(K_n|_W\).

For each \(n\) there is an isomorphism \(K_n|_W\simeq\underline{P_n}|_W\). To justify a global isomorphism on \(W\) at this single level, pull the étale trivializing cover of BO.2 back to \(W\). The weakly contractible covering property in BK.1 splits a finite affine refinement of that cover. Pulling its local isomorphism along the section gives the stated isomorphism. These choices need not commute as \(n\) varies.

Nevertheless the groups \[ A_n=H^0(W,H_n) =\operatorname{Hom}_{D(W,O_n)}(\underline{P_n},K_n|_W) \tag{BO.7} \] form a Mittag–Leffler tower, as follows. Put \(E_n=\operatorname{Hom}_{O_n}^{\bullet}(P_n,P_n)\). The groups \(G_n=H^0(E_n)\) are finite: \(O_n\) is finite, by its length-\(n\) filtration with finite residue-field layers, and every term of \(E_n\) is finite. For fixed \(n\), the descending images of \(G_m\to G_n\) consequently stabilize at some \(N(n)\).

For any finite segment \(q\geq m\geq n\), choose the single isomorphism \(K_q|_W\simeq\underline{P_q}\) at its highest level and reduce it to the other two levels. Derived reduction and the finite-free Hom calculation identify the whole segment \(H_q\to H_m\to H_n\) with \(\underline{E_q}\to\underline{E_m}\to\underline{E_n}\). The cohomology sheaves of this constant complex are the constant groups \(G_i\), because the constant-sheaf functor is exact. Thus, if \(q\geq m\geq N(n)\), the images from both higher levels into \(H^0(H_n)\) agree: under this one identification they are the equal coefficient-group images. This proves uniform stabilization as sheaves. Evaluation on \(W\) is exact by BK.1, so it preserves these images and identifies sheaf cohomology sections with \(H^0(W,H_i)\). The images in \(A_n\) therefore stabilize too. The section groups \(A_n\) themselves were not assumed finite, and no simultaneous choice of the preceding isomorphisms was used.

BO.5. Producing one actual isomorphism of complete objects

Let \(I_n\subset A_n\) be the eventual image. Its transition \(I_{n+1}\to I_n\) is surjective. Given an element of \(I_n\), choose a level beyond both stabilization indices, lift it from that level, and then map to level \(n+1\); the resulting element lies in \(I_{n+1}\). Moreover \(I_1\) contains an isomorphism \(\underline{P_1}\to K_1|_W\): take any single-level isomorphism at a level beyond \(N(1)\), and reduce it. Starting with this element and successively using the surjections gives \[ (\varphi_n)_n\in\varprojlim A_n, \qquad \varphi_1\text{ an isomorphism}. \tag{BO.8} \]

We now lift this compatible family of classes to a morphism. Because \(H\) in (BO.5) is complete, BK.4 identifies it with the homotopy limit of its actual reductions (BO.6). Apply derived sections on \(W\) to the product-and-cone formula (BK.1). Sections commute with products and are exact on this object by BK.1. The cohomology sequence therefore gives a surjection \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}_{D(W,O)}(\mathcal P,K_W) &=H^0(W,H)\\ &\longrightarrow\varprojlim_n H^0(W,H_n) \longrightarrow0. \end{aligned} \tag{BO.9} \] Explicitly the last group is the kernel of \(1-s\) on \(\prod_nH^0(W,H_n)\); the product-cone long exact sequence maps onto precisely this kernel. A possible preceding cokernel from degree \(-1\) affects uniqueness, not this surjectivity.

Choose a preimage \(\Phi:\mathcal P\to K_W\) of (BO.8). BL.5's evaluation-defined Hom comparison ensures that its reduction is the specified class \(\varphi_n\) at every level. In particular its first reduction is an isomorphism. Its cone is complete; the coefficient triangles give zero at all finite levels from zero at level one, and BK.4 then makes the cone zero. Thus \(\Phi\) is the required isomorphism. This construction supplies an actual map through the internal-Hom limit and its cohomology sequence. It does not assume that compatible classes automatically specify compatible chain representatives.

BO.6. The resulting local description and its scope

We have proved that on a connected scheme where the cohomology of \(K_1\) is finite locally constant, a single bounded finite free coefficient complex \(P\) gives the pro-étale local model of \(K\). The object \(C\underline P\) is the finite complex of completed constant finite free modules with the constant differential matrices of \(P\): completion is exact and the finite sums and successive cones constructing this complex are preserved by it. Its reductions are the actual complexes \(P_n\) of (BO.4).

For a Noetherian \(X\) in BM, choose the finite locally closed partition making the finitely many cohomology sheaves of \(K_1\) locally constant. Each piece has finitely many connected components, which are open and closed: its finitely many irreducible components group into finitely many connected intersection classes. Refining by those components and applying the theorem to the completed restriction to each piece gives a finite stratification on which \(K\) has the local description just proved. Completed restriction has the indicated first reduction by BL.6, so this use of the theorem meets its hypotheses.

This proves the forward local-model assertion for every object of \(\mathscr C_X\). It does not identify a category of unspecified inverse systems with the derived category, or assert that all pro-étale local models descend to a prescribed strict-system heart. BP proves the precise degree-zero equivalence and its sheaf morphisms. BQ proves standard truncation closure and identifies the strict-system heart. BR supplies a precise derived diagram category and proves its equivalence with complete objects, including all higher morphisms; BS proves the étale-diagram comparison. BT constructs realization from the bounded derived category of the strict heart and proves its low-degree Ext comparisons; the general higher-effacement condition remains to establish equivalence. BV constructs exceptional right adjoints and proves adic biduality at this bounded constructible scope. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX supplies the full rational-sheaf comparison, including its integral models and higher morphisms. The free comparisons are finite-coefficient local structure, Tag 09BI, stabilization, Tag 09C5, and adic local structure, Tag 09C6. The proof above uses finite Tor induction, finite coefficient groups and the internal-Hom product-cone map to establish the assertions at the stated complete-DVR scope.

Appendix BP. Strict systems and complete sheaves in degree zero

Keep the Noetherian schemes and the complete discrete valuation ring \(O\) with finite residue field from BM. A strict constructible system is a sequence \(F_n\) of constructible étale \(O_n\)-sheaves whose specified transitions induce \(F_{n+1}/\pi^nF_{n+1}\simeq F_n\). A morphism is a compatible sequence of sheaf maps. Quotients in this definition are ordinary quotients. We prove an equivalence between this category and the full subcategory of \(\mathscr C_X\) consisting of objects concentrated in degree zero. No derived equivalence is included in the statement.

BP.1. One stratification and a uniform torsion exponent

A constructible finite étale sheaf of sets on a Noetherian scheme satisfies the ascending chain condition on subsheaves. To prove it, restrict to a finite locally closed stratification on which it is finite locally constant. By N.1 its restriction is represented by a finite étale scheme \(Y\), which is Noetherian. A subsheaf of the represented sheaf is represented by an open subset of \(Y\). Indeed take the union of the images of all étale local sections belonging to the subsheaf. These images are open. A section factoring through this union belongs locally to the subsheaf, and hence belongs to it by the sheaf axiom; the reverse inclusion follows from the definition of the union. Increasing chains of such opens stabilize on Noetherian \(Y\). The finitely many strata give one stabilization index, and equality on their geometric stalks gives equality on the original scheme.

For a strict system form \[ D_j=\pi^jF_m/\pi^{j+1}F_m\quad(m>j). \tag{BP.1} \] Strictness identifies this independently of \(m\): first quotient \(F_m\) by \(\pi^{j+1}\), then take the indicated image. Lifting a section of \(F_1\) and multiplying by \(\pi^j\) defines a surjection \(F_1\to D_j\), independent of its lift. Multiplication by \(\pi\) gives compatible surjections \(D_j\to D_{j+1}\). Their kernels in \(F_1\) therefore form an increasing chain, which stabilizes by the preceding paragraph. All \(D_j\) after some index are the same quotient of \(F_1\).

The finitely many earlier \(D_j\) are constructible, being images and quotients of constructible finite-coefficient sheaves. Choose one finite partition making these and the stable quotient locally constant. The power filtration of every \(F_m\) has these locally constant graded pieces. The finite extension proof in BM.6 then makes every \(F_m\) locally constant on this same partition. Refine into finitely many connected pieces as in BO.6. On each piece N.4, with its complete discrete valuation ring and finite residue-field hypotheses, identifies the strict lisse system with the quotients of one finite \(O\)-module \(M\).

Such a module is \(O^r\oplus T\), where \(T\) is killed by some \(\pi^c\). Here is the needed algebra: N.4's submodule argument makes the torsion submodule finite; its finitely many generators have a common annihilating power. The quotient is finite torsion-free, hence free by that same argument, and lifting a basis splits the quotient map. Take the maximum exponent over the finitely many pieces. This gives one \(c\) valid on all of \(X\). The stratification concerns the whole system, rather than a separate choice at each level.

BP.2. Limits, quotients and the torsion kernel

We use the following consequence of BK.1. A sheaf tower with stabilizing images at every target index has zero degree-one derived limit on the pro-étale site. Let \(I_n\) be its eventual images. Their transitions are epimorphisms: lift an element from an index beyond the two stabilization indices and then project to the next level. The quotient tower has eventually zero transitions into each fixed index. On its product, the inverse of \(1-s\) is the sum \(1+s+s^2+\cdots\), which is finite in each coordinate. For the tower \(I_n\), repleteness solves the successive lifting equations, so \(1-s\) is surjective. Exact products applied to the short exact sequence of towers now make \(1-s\) surjective for the original tower. The product-cone formula proves the assertion. The same argument for an epimorphic tower gives its derived limit in degree zero.

Put \[ F=\varprojlim_n\nu_X^*F_n. \tag{BP.2} \] The transitions are epimorphisms. Thus this is also the derived limit and is a sheaf in degree zero. Each term is killed by a power of \(\pi\), hence complete by BK.4; closure under derived limits makes \(F\) complete.

Fix \(n\). For \(m\geq n\), the exact sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow\pi^nF_m\longrightarrow F_m \longrightarrow F_n\longrightarrow0 \tag{BP.3} \] has epimorphic transitions in its first terms. After exact pullback and passage to limits, it identifies the kernel of \(F\to\nu_X^*F_n\) with \(\varprojlim_m\nu_X^*(\pi^nF_m)\). To identify that limit as \(\pi^nF\), consider the kernels \(B_m=F_m[\pi^n]\). They have uniformly stabilizing images into each fixed level. On each piece of BP.1, for \(m\geq\max(n,c)\), their module is \[ \bigl(\pi^{m-n}O^r/\pi^mO^r\bigr)\oplus T[\pi^n]. \tag{BP.4} \] Its free-part image in level \(a\) is zero for \(m\geq a+n\), and its torsion-part image is constant for \(m\geq c\). The common \(c\) gives a uniform stabilization index. Equality of these finite constructible image sheaves is detected on étale geometric stalks. Exact \(\nu_X^*\) preserves the images. The preceding tower argument and the exact sequence with terms \(B_m,F_m,\pi^nF_m\) prove surjectivity of \(F\xrightarrow{\pi^n}\varprojlim_m\nu_X^*(\pi^nF_m)\). Consequently the canonical maps give \[ F/\pi^nF\simeq\nu_X^*F_n. \tag{BP.5} \]

There is also finite control of \(F[\pi^n]\). Limits preserve kernels, so this sheaf is the limit of the \(B_m\). Replace that tower by its eventual image sheaves. At every level \(a\geq c\), their geometric stalks are \(T[\pi^n]\), by (BP.4), and their subsequent transition maps are isomorphisms. Thus the eventual-image tower is eventually a constant tower of constructible étale sheaves. Its limit, pulled back by \(\nu_X^*\), is \(F[\pi^n]\). In particular this kernel is classical and constructible and is killed by \(\pi^c\), with the same \(c\) for all \(n\).

The two-term coefficient resolution therefore gives \[ \begin{aligned} H^{-1}(F\otimes_O^LO_n)&=F[\pi^n],\\ H^0(F\otimes_O^LO_n)&=\nu_X^*F_n, \end{aligned} \tag{BP.6} \] with no other cohomology. Both sheaves are bounded constructible classical coefficients. BK.2's fully faithful triangulated image, applied to the truncation triangle between these two sheaves, makes the complex classical too. Hence \(F\in\mathscr C_X\). This proves the forward functor, including the torsion information omitted by ordinary quotients.

BP.3. Recovering every morphism

An \(O\)-linear sheaf map \(F\to G\) preserves every power of \(\pi\), so (BP.5) gives maps between their finite quotient sheaves. Full faithfulness of \(\nu_X^*\) on étale sheaves in BK.2 recovers unique maps \(F_n\to G_n\). They commute with the transitions because the original quotient maps do. Conversely a compatible system of such maps has a limit map (BP.2). Taking its quotients returns the original maps, and taking the limit of the quotients of a map returns that map. Thus \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{strict}}((F_n),(G_n)) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{O,X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}}(F,G). \tag{BP.7} \] For objects concentrated in degree zero, this is also the Hom set in the derived category, by its ordinary truncation embedding. It is a statement about these Hom sets, not about all higher Ext groups or a derived equivalence.

BP.4. Every degree-zero constructible complete object is recovered

Now let \(F\in\mathscr C_X\) be concentrated in degree zero. BM.6 makes every derived reduction classical and bounded constructible. Its degree-zero cohomology is the ordinary quotient \(F/\pi^nF\). Let \(F_n\) be the corresponding étale sheaf. Ordinary successive quotient identities, exact pullback and its full faithfulness show that these form a strict constructible system. BP.2 constructs \(G=\varprojlim_n\nu_X^*F_n\in\mathscr C_X\) and a natural map \(u:F\to G\), whose ordinary quotient maps are all identities under (BP.5).

We prove that \(u\) is an isomorphism; derived completeness alone should not be silently replaced by ordinary completeness. Let \(C\) be its cone. Both objects are complete and in \(\mathscr C_X\), so the same is true of \(C\). The first reductions of \(F\) and \(G\) have cohomology only in \([-1,0]\), and their degree-zero map is an isomorphism. Hence \(C_1\) has cohomology in \([-2,-1]\). The actual complete-object bound proved in BM.6 makes \(C\) have cohomology in that interval. But the cone of a map of sheaves has cohomology only in \([-1,0]\). Its degree-zero cohomology is therefore zero: \(u\) is surjective. Its kernel \(T=C[-1]\) is a sheaf in \(\mathscr C_X\).

Tensor the resulting short exact sequence \(0\to T\to F\to G\to0\) with the specified two-term resolution of \(O_n\). Since the ordinary quotient map from \(F\) to \(G\) is an isomorphism, the cohomology sequence gives a surjection \[ G[\pi^n]\longrightarrow T/\pi^nT. \tag{BP.8} \] For \(m\geq n\), naturality in the resolution (BK.5) makes the transition on its left multiplication by \(\pi^{m-n}\), and the transition on its right the ordinary quotient map. BP.2 gives one \(c\) killing all \(G[\pi^m]\). Taking \(m\geq n+c\) makes the left transition zero. Surjectivity in (BP.8) makes the right transition zero as well. It is also a surjective quotient map. Thus \(T/\pi^nT=0\) for every \(n\).

In particular the first derived reduction of \(T\) has cohomology only in degree \(-1\). Since \(T\in\mathscr C_X\), BM.6 forces \(T\) itself into degree \(-1\). It is already a degree-zero sheaf, so it is zero. This proves \(F\simeq G\), establishing essential surjectivity together with the explicit inverse functor. The degree-zero comparison, on both objects and morphisms, is proved.

BP.5. Lisse objects, torsion and the next categorical distinction

The lisse subcategory in N.4 has the following compatible description. On a connected scheme, let a strict lisse system correspond to a finite \(O\)-module \(M\) with continuous fundamental-group action. On each affine open, take the tower of finite étale covers given by the kernels of its actions on \(M/\pi^nM\). Refinement and the tautological points make the trivializations compatible. The affine inverse limit is an ind-étale faithfully flat cover: its algebra is a filtered colimit of flat algebras, and each geometric fibre is the nonempty inverse limit of finite surjective fibres. On that cover (BP.2) becomes \[ \widehat{\underline M} =\varprojlim_n\underline{M/\pi^nM} \simeq\widehat O^{\,r}\oplus\underline T \quad(M\simeq O^r\oplus T). \tag{BP.9} \] The last identification follows from the module decomposition in BP.1; the finite torsion system is eventually constant. This is also \(C\underline M\), by exact completion, BL.3 and completeness of torsion objects. It is locally free precisely when the finite module is torsion-free.

Conversely, suppose a sheaf in the degree-zero category of BP.4 is pro-étale locally a completed constant finite module. Its quotients (BP.5) are then locally constant finite module sheaves in that topology. They are finite locally constant étale sheaves as well. Here is the finite descent step. On an affine base refine a trivializing cover to a faithfully flat affine ind-étale cover using BK.1. Each finite quotient there is represented by a finite disjoint union of copies of that cover. Its overlap maps are maps of represented sheaves, hence maps of their finite étale algebras, by the sheaf Yoneda property. The faithfully flat finite-algebra descent calculation N.1 descends them to a finite étale scheme over the base, along with their module operations. Its sheaf is the quotient by the same descent equalizer. This proves the assertion and gives the strict lisse system. BP.7 identifies all of its maps; N.4 then identifies its finite-module representation.

For example, the strict constant system \(F_n=\kappa\) has limit \(\underline\kappa\). Its ordinary quotients are still \(\underline\kappa\), whereas its first derived reduction is \([\underline\kappa\xrightarrow0\underline\kappa]\) in degrees \(-1,0\). For the torsion-free constant system \(F_n=O_n\), multiplication by \(\pi\) on its limit \(\widehat O\) is injective even though every finite-level kernel is nonzero: those kernels have zero transition maps. These examples identify exactly why neither levelwise kernels nor ordinary quotients can replace the required derived coefficient data.

This appendix proves the comparison for sheaves in degree zero, and its lisse subcategory. BQ proves that its cohomology sheaves and truncations stay constructible, and thus identifies this subcategory as the heart of the restricted standard t-structure on all of \(\mathscr C_X\). To identify a bounded derived category of strict systems with the full constructible derived category, one must additionally prove the higher-morphism and realization assertions. BR proves the higher-morphism comparison for the specified cartesian derived diagrams, and BS proves its étale presentation. BT constructs bounded-derived realization from this strict heart, proves the degree-one comparison and degree-two injection, and identifies the exact higher-effacement condition still needed for equivalence. The exceptional, duality and rationalization comparisons also remain separate from (BP.7). The free strict-system comparison material is ℓ-adic sheaves and their cohomology, Sections 1–3, the pro-étale lesson, Proposition 4.2, and Tags 03UN and 03UP. The common-stratification, division and complete-sheaf recovery proofs needed here have been given above.

Appendix BQ. Normalized cohomology and the constructible heart

Keep the complete discrete valuation ring \(O\), uniformizer \(\pi\), finite residue field and Noetherian scheme of BM–BP. For \(K\in\mathscr C_X\), we prove that every ordinary cohomology sheaf \(H^i(K)\) belongs to \(\mathscr C_X\). This will give the restricted standard t-structure and identify its heart with strict constructible coefficient systems. The finite-level cohomology sheaves themselves generally do not form a strict system; the proof identifies exactly which images do.

BQ.1. The coefficient calculation and its transition maps

Let \(P\) be a bounded finite free \(O\)-complex, and put \(M^i=H^i(P)\). These are finite modules: kernels and images of maps of finite modules over the Noetherian ring \(O\) are finite. Choose \(c\geq0\) which kills the torsion of every \(M^i\). There are only finitely many nonzero modules, and BP.1 supplies such an exponent for each.

The termwise exact sequence of complexes \(0\to P\xrightarrow{\pi^n}P\to P/\pi^nP\to0\) gives \[ 0\longrightarrow M^i/\pi^nM^i \longrightarrow H^i(P/\pi^nP) \longrightarrow M^{i+1}[\pi^n] \longrightarrow0. \tag{BQ.1} \] For \(m\geq n\), compare this sequence at the two indices using multiplication by \(\pi^{m-n}\) on its first copy of \(P\), the identity on its second copy, and the quotient on its last complex. The square of the first arrows commutes because \(\pi^n\pi^{m-n}=\pi^m\). The resulting map on the left of (BQ.1) is the ordinary quotient; on the right it is multiplication by \(\pi^{m-n}\).

Consequently, for \(m\geq n+c\), the image of \(H^i(P/\pi^mP)\to H^i(P/\pi^nP)\) is precisely the embedded module \(M^i/\pi^nM^i\). Indeed its image in the right term is zero, while the quotient map on the left terms is surjective. This proves both inclusions, with one exponent valid for every degree. It also proves that the maps between these stabilized images are the quotient maps of the modules \(M^i\). No choice of a splitting of (BQ.1) has entered the calculation.

BQ.2. Uniform stabilization on the scheme

Write \(A_n^i\) for the constructible étale sheaf whose pullback is \(H^i(K_n)\). These sheaves and their transition maps exist by BM.6 and the exact, fully faithful classical comparison in BK.2. Choose the finite connected stratification of BO.6. On a piece \(S\), the completed restriction \(K_S=C_Si^*K\) has the actual compatible local model \(C_S\underline{P_S}\) of BO.5. BL.6 identifies its finite reductions, with their maps, with \(i^*K_n\). Thus on a pro-étale cover of \(S\) the entire cohomology tower is that of the reductions of one bounded finite free complex \(P_S\).

Take the maximum of the exponents of BQ.1 for the finitely many \(P_S\). Call it \(c\). Exact inverse image commutes with the finite images and quotients under consideration. On the indicated cover of each stratum, BQ.1 therefore proves equality of the image sheaves from any two indices \(m,q\geq n+c\) into \(A_n^i\). Equality can be checked on a covering after the faithful classical pullback, and then on the étale geometric stalks of all the strata. Hence it holds on \(X\).

Define the constructible étale sheaf \[ I_n^i=\operatorname{im}(A_{n+c}^i\longrightarrow A_n^i). \tag{BQ.2} \] It is the image from every sufficiently late level, so the definition is independent of any larger choice of \(c\). The transitions take \(I_{n+1}^i\) onto \(I_n^i\), and the induced map \[ I_{n+1}^i/\pi^nI_{n+1}^i \xrightarrow{\sim} I_n^i \tag{BQ.3} \] is an isomorphism. To verify this, restrict the map to a stratum and the cover just used. Under the compatible local model, its source and target are respectively \((M_S^i/\pi^{n+1}M_S^i)/\pi^n\) and \(M_S^i/\pi^nM_S^i\), and the map is their quotient isomorphism. The kernel and cokernel of the global finite constructible map are therefore zero on every geometric stalk. This proves (BQ.3), including its actual transition map.

This argument used restrictions only at finite coefficient levels. It did not commute an arbitrary inverse image with an infinite limit, or assume that restricting \(H^i(K)\) agrees with taking cohomology after completed restriction. Those assertions are unnecessary for the construction of \(I_n^i\).

BQ.3. Recovering the cohomology sheaf

All the towers \(A_n^i\) have stabilizing images by BQ.2. The Mittag–Leffler argument of BP.2 makes the degree-one derived limit of \(\nu_X^*A_n^i\) vanish. Completeness of \(K\) and the exact-product cohomology sequence (BM.15) now give the natural identification \[ H^i(K)\simeq\varprojlim_n\nu_X^*A_n^i \simeq\varprojlim_n\nu_X^*I_n^i. \tag{BQ.4} \] For the second identification, the quotient tower \(A_n^i/I_n^i\) has zero transitions from index \(n+c\) to \(n\). Its product operator \(1-s\) is invertible by the coordinatewise finite geometric sum in BP.2, so its derived limit is zero. The short exact sequence of towers, followed by exact products and their cones, identifies the derived limits of \(I_n^i\) and \(A_n^i\). Both are ordinary limits, because their image towers stabilize.

Equations (BQ.2)–(BQ.3) make \((I_n^i)_n\) a strict constructible system. BP.2 therefore proves that its limit is a degree-zero object of \(\mathscr C_X\), and identifies its ordinary quotients. Thus \[ H^i(K)\in\mathscr C_X,\qquad H^i(K)/\pi^nH^i(K)\simeq\nu_X^*I_n^i. \tag{BQ.5} \] These isomorphisms are natural in \(K\). A map of complexes induces maps on all finite cohomology towers; taking a common stabilization index for source and target makes these preserve the images in (BQ.2). The maps are independent of that index, and (BM.15) and the quotient maps in BP.2 are natural.

There is a useful intrinsic check on the inclusion of these images. The actual coefficient cone triangle for \(K\) gives \[ 0\longrightarrow H^i(K)/\pi^nH^i(K) \longrightarrow H^i(K_n) \longrightarrow H^{i+1}(K)[\pi^n] \longrightarrow0. \tag{BQ.6} \] The first map is the map from (BQ.4) to its level \(n\), factored through the ordinary quotient. Under (BQ.5) it is exactly the image inclusion from (BQ.2). The transition on the last term is multiplication by \(\pi^{m-n}\), by the same comparison of coefficient cones as in BQ.1. BP.2, applied to each \(H^{i+1}(K)\), also proves directly that its torsion kernels have a common annihilating power. Thus the disappearance of the last term agrees with the finite-model calculation; it is not a claim that it is zero at every level.

BQ.4. Truncations, the heart and its kernels

BM.6 proves that \(K\) has cohomology in a finite interval. The subcategory \(\mathscr C_X\) is triangulated: complete objects are closed under shifts and cones by BK.4, and taking a first derived reduction is exact; the classical bounded constructible category is triangulated by BK.2 and the finite constructible kernel, cokernel and extension argument in BM.6.

Starting at the lowest nonzero cohomology degree, apply the ordinary truncation triangles \[ \tau_{\leq q-1}K\longrightarrow\tau_{\leq q}K \longrightarrow H^q(K)[-q]. \tag{BQ.7} \] The initial lower truncation is zero. Equation (BQ.5), induction and triangulated closure prove that every \(\tau_{\leq q}K\) lies in \(\mathscr C_X\). Its complementary truncation \(\tau_{\geq q+1}K\) lies there by the triangle with \(K\). Therefore intersection with the ambient standard subcategories \(D^{\leq0}\) and \(D^{\geq0}\) gives a bounded t-structure on \(\mathscr C_X\). Shift closure and orthogonality are inherited from the ambient derived category; (BQ.7) supplies its truncation triangles, and BM.6 supplies boundedness.

Its heart is precisely the degree-zero category compared with strict constructible systems in BP. Consequently BP.2–BP.4 give an equivalence of that heart with the category of strict systems and their compatible sheaf maps. This category is abelian. More concretely, if \(u:F\to G\) is a map of heart objects, its ordinary sheaf kernel and cokernel are \(H^{-1}(\operatorname{Cone}u)\) and \(H^0(\operatorname{Cone}u)\). They belong to the heart by (BQ.5). Images and coimages are obtained by applying the same assertion again. Their canonical comparison is the ordinary sheaf isomorphism, which lies in this full subcategory; finite sums also remain there. This proves the abelian assertions without assuming that termwise kernels are strict.
