The cokernel strict system is the termwise cokernel system, because \((\operatorname{coker}u)/\pi^n\) is the cokernel of \(F/\pi^nF\to G/\pi^nG\). For the kernel, first take \(\ker u\), then its ordinary quotients as in BP.4. Taking the termwise kernels instead can give a different tower. For example, multiplication by \(\pi\) on \(\widehat O\) has zero kernel, while the kernels of \(O_n\xrightarrow{\pi}O_n\) are nonzero. Their transitions are zero. The cohomology normalization (BQ.2) is applied to the derived reductions of the cone when recovering this kernel; it is not an assertion that arbitrary termwise kernel towers are strict.

BQ.5. Exactness of the completed inverse image and open extension

Let \(f:Y\to X\) be a morphism in the Noetherian scope above. BN proves \(f_c^*K\in\mathscr C_Y\), and BL.6 identifies its reductions with \(f^*K_n\). Ordinary inverse image on the finite coefficient sheaves is exact. It therefore commutes with their cohomology sheaves, the images (BQ.2) and the quotient maps (BQ.3). The same exponent \(c\) proves stabilization after pullback, and the normalized cohomology system is exactly \[ \bigl(f_{\acute et}^*I_n^i\bigr)_n. \tag{BQ.8} \] To apply this also to a heart object \(F\), use (BQ.5): its normalized systems vanish outside degree zero and in degree zero are \(F/\pi^nF\). Equation (BQ.8) implies that \(f_c^*F\) is a heart object with the pulled-back strict system. Applied first to \(K\) and then to \(H^i(K)\), this proves natural isomorphisms \[ H^i(f_c^*K)\simeq f_c^*H^i(K). \tag{BQ.9} \] Hence completed inverse image is t-exact and commutes with standard truncations. Explicitly, apply it to a truncation triangle: its two outer objects have the required cohomological bounds by (BQ.9), so truncation uniqueness identifies the resulting triangle. This statement concerns completed inverse image, with its specified coefficient comparisons.

For an open immersion \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\), the same argument uses BM.1's reduction comparison for \(j_{!,c}\). At each finite level, extension by zero is exact and sends a constructible sheaf to a constructible sheaf: extend its finite strata on \(U\) by the closed complement, on which the sheaf is zero. It preserves the image and quotient diagrams. Thus the normalized cohomology system of \(j_{!,c}K\) is \((j_!I_n^i)_n\). Membership in \(\mathscr C_X\) follows either from BM.14 or directly from its first reduction. As before, \[ H^i(j_{!,c}K)\simeq j_{!,c}H^i(K), \tag{BQ.10} \] and \(j_{!,c}\) is t-exact. This includes the exact extension functor on the strict-system heart, with the finite-level extension-by-zero maps.

The proof establishes normalized cohomology, bounded standard truncations, the strict-system heart and these two exact functors. BR proves a full comparison with the specified cartesian derived diagrams and a limit formula for their higher morphisms; BS proves the same comparison on the étale diagram site. BT proves the finite-coefficient heart realization, constructs the strict adic heart realization functor and gives its low-degree Ext comparison. Its general higher-effacement condition remains a separate obligation. BV supplies the exceptional right adjoints and adic biduality with their specified comparisons. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX completes its comparison with constructible rational sheaves and their operations. The free coefficient calculation is also explained in ℓ-adic sheaves and their cohomology, Theorem 7.3; Tag 09C5 provides a general stabilization comparison. BQ.1–BQ.3 prove the uniform complete-DVR estimate and the sheaf normalization actually used here.

Appendix BR. Derived coefficient systems and all their morphisms

Keep the complete discrete valuation ring \(O\), its uniformizer \(\pi\), and \(O_n=O/\pi^n\). We now specify a category of coefficient diagrams and prove its equivalence with complete complexes on the pro-étale site. Its morphisms are derived morphisms of whole diagrams. A family of morphism classes at the individual levels carries less information; BR.5 gives the exact difference.

BR.1. The category in which a coefficient diagram lives

Let \(\mathcal T=X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}\), presented by the site used in BK. Form the site whose objects are pairs \((U,n)\), with a map \((U,n)\to(V,m)\) when \(n\leq m\) and a site map \(U\to V\). Coverings at fixed index are the original coverings. A sheaf on this site is exactly an inverse system of sheaves on \(\mathcal T\): the maps of pairs give its transitions, and the covering condition is the sheaf condition at each index.

There are two ring sheaves on this diagram site. Write \(B\) for the constant system \(\underline O\), and \(A\) for the system \((\underline{O_n})_n\) with quotient transitions. An \(A\)-module is an actual system \((M_n,u_n)\), where \(M_n\) is an \(O_n\)-sheaf and \(u_n:M_{n+1}\to M_n\) is linear over \(O_{n+1}\). Kernels, cokernels and exactness are evaluated at each index. Colimits are computed at each index, using sheafification, so filtered colimits are exact.

These module categories are Grothendieck categories. To check the generator condition explicitly, for each \((U,n)\) use the free module on its represented sheaf. At index \(j\leq n\) its value is the free \(A_j\)-module on the sheaf represented by \(U\), and at larger indices it is zero. A map from it to \(M\) is a section of \(M_n\) on \(U\). The sum over this set of objects is therefore a generator. For \(B\) use the same construction with \(O\) at every level. Thus BF.1–BF.4 apply, including the general Grothendieck-category resolution proved in Sheaves of modules and their derived categories, Theorem 7.2. We obtain the locally small derived categories \(D(A)\) and \(D(B)\), by inverting the quasi-isomorphisms of actual diagram complexes.

There are also simultaneous K-flat resolutions. The displayed free generators are flat at each index by BL.1's finite-label sheafification argument. Tensor of diagram modules is evaluated at each index, so they are flat as diagram modules. Apply the disk-and-cycle construction of BL.1 to this set of generators. Its degreewise split attachments and exact filtered union give a quasi-isomorphism from a K-flat diagram complex; at each index the same filtration proves K-flatness and flatness of its individual terms. In particular, coefficient extension at a chosen index is computed by the same resolution of the whole diagram. Chain maps, cones and the comparisons of different resolutions retain the diagram maps throughout.

Call \(M\in D(A)\) derived cartesian if every transition induces an isomorphism \[ O_n\otimes_{O_{n+1}}^L M_{n+1}\xrightarrow{\sim}M_n. \tag{BR.1} \] Evaluation is exact, so \(M_n\) is unambiguously an object of \(D(\mathcal T,O_n)\). The map in (BR.1) is the adjoint of the specified transition. By composition and derived tensor associativity it is an isomorphism for any pair of indices \(m\geq n\). Let \(D_{\mathrm{cart}}(A)\) be the full subcategory with this property. It is triangulated, since derived extension is exact and the cone comparison at each index is an isomorphism whenever the first two comparisons are. This definition includes the morphisms in \(D(A)\), rather than replacing them by a termwise limit of Hom sets.

BR.2. Reduction and limit form a derived adjunction

First keep the constant coefficient ring \(O\). The constant-system functor \(c\) is exact and left adjoint to ordinary inverse limit on \(B\)-modules. Consequently its derived right adjoint is computed by taking a K-injective resolution \(J\) in the diagram category and then \(\varprojlim J_n\). Indeed inverse limit sends K-injectives to K-injectives: the Hom-complex adjunction tests it against the exact functor \(c\). Applying BF.6 proves the derived adjunction on all shifts and all morphisms.

Here this derived limit is the product-cone limit of BK.1. Choose \(J\) with injective terms, as supplied by the stated resolution theorem. For an injective \(B\)-diagram \(E\), the maps \(E_{n+1}(U)\to E_n(U)\) are surjective. To see this, the inclusion of the free diagram generated at \((U,n)\) into the one generated at \((U,n+1)\) is monic; extension of maps into \(E\) gives the asserted surjection on sections. The recursion for \(1-s\) can therefore be solved on sections. It follows that \[ 0\longrightarrow\varprojlim J_n \longrightarrow\prod_nJ_n\xrightarrow{1-s}\prod_nJ_n \longrightarrow0 \tag{BR.2} \] is an exact sequence of complexes. Countable products of \(O\)-sheaves on \(\mathcal T\) are exact by BK.1, so they preserve quasi-isomorphisms of arbitrary complexes. Hence the product-cone complex in (BR.2) computes the same functor on any representative of the original diagram. This proves the formula and its naturality as a functor of actual diagrams, without selecting nonfunctorial cones of morphism classes.

Factor coefficient reduction through the ring map \(B\to A\). Derived extension of scalars on the diagram site is left adjoint to exact restriction of scalars. The construction and verification are the scalar-extension argument of BL.5 on this site: use a K-flat diagram resolution in the source and a K-injective \(A\)-resolution in the target, and apply the ordinary tensor–Hom adjunction on complexes. If a K-flat source complex is acyclic, its extension is acyclic, so Hom into the latter K-injective resolution is acyclic. Replacing the middle object of a quasi-isomorphism roof by a K-flat resolution reduces the comparison to cones of quasi-isomorphisms between K-flat complexes. The preceding acyclicity makes precomposition by each such comparison an isomorphism on Hom groups in every degree. Thus the ordinary adjunction computes the localized Hom groups and descends through BF.2. This does not require restriction of that target resolution to be K-injective over \(B\).

Compose this adjunction with the constant-system adjunction. The result is \[ F:D(\mathcal T,O)\rightleftarrows D(A):G, \qquad F(K)_n=K\otimes_O^LO_n,\quad G(M)=\operatorname{holim}_n M_n. \tag{BR.3} \] For the displayed formula for \(F\), choose a K-flat \(O\)-resolution \(P\) of \(K\). Its constant diagram is K-flat over \(B\), since every tensor test is evaluated at an index. Extension gives the actual diagram \((P\otimes_OO_n)_n\). For \(G\), first forget the coefficient structures to a \(B\)-diagram and then apply (BR.2). Both formulas therefore describe the composed adjunction, including its unit and counit. The triangle identities follow from those of the two adjunctions.

Derived scalar associativity shows \(F(K)\) is cartesian. Every term \(M_n\), viewed as an \(O\)-complex, is complete: multiplication by \(\pi^n\) is zero, so the finite geometric inverse to its multiplication-tower operator is the one in BK.4. Complete objects are closed under homotopy limits. Thus \(G(M)\) is complete, even without assuming that \(M\) is cartesian. Finally, \[ GF(K)=C(K), \tag{BR.4} \] with the actual completion unit of BK.4. This follows on the displayed K-flat representative from exactly its reduction tower. In particular the adjunction unit is an isomorphism whenever \(K\) is complete.

BR.3. A cartesian diagram with zero limit is zero

We prove that \(G\) detects zero objects on \(D_{\mathrm{cart}}(A)\). Fix \(n\), and represent \(M\) by the simultaneous K-flat diagram \(P\) of BR.1. For \(m>n\), tensor the short exact coefficient sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow O_{m-n}\xrightarrow{\pi^n}O_m \longrightarrow O_n\longrightarrow0 \tag{BR.5} \] with \(P_m\) over \(O_m\). Its terms are flat, so we obtain an actual short exact sequence of complexes, hence the natural cone triangle. These sequences commute as \(m\) varies: both outer coefficient maps are quotient maps and the middle one is the quotient transition, and the two multiplication squares commute.

The left complexes \(P_m\otimes_{O_m}O_{m-n}\) map to \(P_{m-n}\), and the right complexes \(P_m\otimes_{O_m}O_n\) map to \(P_n\). These are actual chain maps induced by the transitions of \(P\). They are quasi-isomorphisms by (BR.1) and the levelwise K-flat property. The right maps form a map to the constant diagram \(P_n\); the left maps form a map to the shifted-index diagram \((P_{m-n})_{m>n}\). Thus the coherent triangle of diagrams has the form \[ (M_{m-n})_{m>n}\longrightarrow(M_m)_{m>n} \longrightarrow(M_n)_{m>n}. \tag{BR.6} \] This notation denotes the triangle just constructed from complexes and quasi-isomorphisms, not independently chosen triangle isomorphisms at each level.

Taking its product-cone limit is exact: finite cones commute with the products in (BR.2). Removing finitely many initial terms does not change that limit. For completeness, the forgotten initial coordinates form a finite complex of coordinate equations in \(1-s\); solving these successively eliminates them and gives a quasi-isomorphism with the tail product-cone complex. The left limit in (BR.6) is also \(G(M)\), by reindexing, and the right limit is \(M_n\): the diagonal and the successive-difference recursion identify the limit of a constant diagram, as in BK.4.

If \(G(M)=0\), the first two limits are therefore zero, so the triangle makes \(M_n=0\). This holds for every \(n\). A diagram complex is acyclic exactly when all its evaluations are acyclic, proving \(M=0\) in \(D(A)\). This argument uses the exact sequence (BR.5), available for the uniformizer in a discrete valuation ring; it asserts no such short exact sequence for arbitrary ideals in arbitrary rings.

BR.4. Equivalence, coefficients and the constructible restriction

Restrict (BR.3) to complete objects on the left and cartesian objects on the right. The unit is an isomorphism by (BR.4). For a cartesian \(M\), let \(\varepsilon_M:FG(M)\to M\) be the adjunction counit. Both objects are cartesian, so its cone is cartesian. The triangle identity says \(G(\varepsilon_M)\eta_{G(M)}=1\). Since \(G(M)\) is complete, \(\eta_{G(M)}\) is an isomorphism; hence \(G(\varepsilon_M)\) is an isomorphism. BR.3 makes its cartesian cone zero. Therefore \(\varepsilon_M\) is an isomorphism. We have proved inverse equivalences \[ D_X^c\simeq D_{\mathrm{cart}}(A). \tag{BR.7} \] In particular, evaluating this actual counit gives \[ G(M)\otimes_O^LO_n\xrightarrow{\sim}M_n \tag{BR.8} \] as \(O_n\)-complexes, with their coefficient transition maps. Using the counit proves its module structure and naturality; an isomorphism merely after forgetting the coefficient structure would not supply those assertions.

Let \(D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A)\) be the full subcategory for which \(M_1\) is the pullback of a bounded constructible étale \(O_1\)-complex. By (BR.8) and the definition in BM.6, (BR.7) restricts to \[ \mathscr C_X\simeq D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A). \tag{BR.9} \] Every finite reduction on the right is consequently classical and bounded constructible, with the common bounds of BM.6. Its inverse-limit object has normalized cohomology and the bounded standard t-structure proved in BQ. The transported heart is BP's strict constructible coefficient category.

The last sentence does not place a strict system into \(D(A)\) simply as a degree-zero diagram. For a strict system \((F_n)\), form its complete sheaf \(\mathcal F=\varprojlim\nu_X^*F_n\) and then its derived diagram \(F(\mathcal F)\) using the reduction functor in (BR.3). Its terms have the torsion correction (BP.6). For example, the strict constant system \(F_n=\kappa\) has limit \(\underline\kappa\); its derived reductions are represented by \([O_n\xrightarrow{\pi}O_n]\) in degrees \(-1,0\). In this model the transition is the quotient map in both terms. Its induced map on degree-minus-one cohomology is zero: the generator \(\pi^n\) of the kernel at level \(n+1\) becomes zero at level \(n\). This agrees with the multiplication-by-\(\pi\) transition on \(\kappa[\pi^n]\) obtained from the coefficient resolution in BK.3. The underived constant diagram \((\kappa)_n\) is not cartesian: already \(\kappa\otimes_{O_2}^L\kappa\) has nonzero negative cohomology. Indeed the free resolution over \(O_2\) with every differential multiplication by \(\pi\) is exact away from its last term, because kernel and image are both \(\pi O_2\); tensoring with \(\kappa\) makes all those differentials zero. This explains the required distinction between the strict heart and its derived coefficient diagram.

BR.5. The higher-morphism formula and its degree-one-limit term

For \(K,L\in D_X^c\), let \[ E_n=R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal T,O_n}(K_n,L_n) \quad\text{in }D(\mathbf{Ab}). \tag{BR.10} \] One explicit way to retain this diagram is to resolve the fixed-\(O\) target tower by a K-injective \(B\)-diagram \(J\). Each \(J_n\) is K-injective over \(O\): evaluation at \(n\) has the exact left adjoint which repeats an \(O\)-sheaf at indices at most \(n\) and is zero afterwards. The Hom-complex adjunction therefore tests K-injectivity after evaluation. The actual complexes \(\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}_{\mathcal T,O}(K,J_n)\) now retain every transition.

The coefficient extension adjunction identifies \(E_n\) with \(R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal T,O}(K,L_n)\). Use this identification to specify the transition maps: they are induced by \(L_{n+1}\to L_n\). Equivalently they reduce both source and target at once; associativity and the adjunction unit verify that description. Thus \((E_n)\) is the actual derived diagram obtained from the target reduction diagram by the fixed-source derived Hom functor.

Derived Hom in its second argument commutes with the products and the cones defining a homotopy limit. One can check the product assertion with K-injectives: a product of them is K-injective, since its Hom complex from any acyclic object is a product of acyclic complexes of abelian groups, and those products are exact. Ordinary Hom into the product is the product of the Hom complexes. The cone assertion follows from the two-summand cone formula. Since \(L\) is complete, this proves the natural isomorphism \[ R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal T,O}(K,L) \simeq\operatorname{holim}_n E_n. \tag{BR.11} \] These are derived Hom complexes of abelian groups, rather than sheaf Hom followed by an unproved interchange of ordinary sections and limits.

Taking cohomology of the product-cone complex gives, for every integer \(r\), \[ \begin{aligned} 0&\longrightarrow \varprojlim{}^{1}_n \operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal T,O_n)}(K_n,L_n[r-1])\\ &\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{D_X^c}(K,L[r])\\ &\longrightarrow\varprojlim_n \operatorname{Hom}_{D(\mathcal T,O_n)}(K_n,L_n[r]) \longrightarrow0. \end{aligned} \tag{BR.12} \] Here \(\varprojlim{}^1\) means the cokernel of \(1-s\) on the product of the indicated groups. The kernel is the ordinary limit. Exactness of products of abelian groups gives precisely these two terms in the cone's long cohomology sequence; no finite-level Mittag–Leffler assertion has been assumed.

The right arrow takes a morphism to its actual reductions. Thus every compatible family of these morphism classes lifts, but its possible nonuniqueness is the left term. Replacing the middle group by the right group without proving that term zero would lose morphisms. When the preceding Hom groups are finite, their descending images stabilize, and the eventual-image and finite-geometric-sum proof of BP.2 for abelian groups makes this cokernel zero. As an elementary coefficient example, for two bounded finite free \(O\)-complexes the finite-level Hom complexes have finite terms, so this finiteness condition holds in each degree. No analogous global finiteness claim on an arbitrary base is needed for (BR.12).

The adjunction in BR.2 gives the same morphisms in the diagram category under (BR.7), for all shifts. Its unit and counit make the identification compatible with identities and composition. The transition maps in (BR.10) are evaluation adjoints as in BL.5, so (BR.11) uses the same coefficient maps. This establishes the full derived-diagram comparison, not just a bijection on isomorphism classes of objects.

BT constructs the realization functor from the bounded derived category of the strict-system heart to \(\mathscr C_X\), proves its degree-one comparison and degree-two injection, and reduces equivalence to the specified higher-effacement condition. Neither (BR.9) nor (BR.12) establishes that condition: its extension classes are computed inside the heart. BS proves the presentation on the étale diagram site, including its comparison functors and all transition maps. BV supplies exceptional right adjoints and adic biduality. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX completes the full rational-sheaf comparison. Free comparisons for the constructions above are derived limits, Tag 0940, ringed-site adjunction, Tag 03D5, and derived coefficient systems, Tag 0GZG; the uniformizer-sequence and counit proof above establishes the precise pro-étale complete-DVR statement used here.

Appendix BS. Étale coefficient diagrams and their comparison maps

The coefficient diagrams of BR can also be formed on the étale site. We prove the comparison in the derived category of whole diagrams, including its arrows. Continue to write \(O_n=O/\pi^n\). Put \(A_{\mathrm e}=(\underline{O_n})_n\) on the diagram site of \(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}}\), and \(A_{\mathrm p}=(\underline{O_n})_n\) on the diagram site of \(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}\). Thus \(A_{\mathrm p}\) is BR's \(A\). The generators, exact filtered colimits and resolutions of BR.1 work on either site.

BS.1. Evaluation and its derived left adjoint

Let \(e_n\) denote evaluation at index \(n\). This is exact. Its ordinary left adjoint sends an \(O_n\)-sheaf \(H\) to the diagram \[ (e_{n,!}H)_j= \begin{cases} O_j\otimes_{O_n}H,&j\leq n,\\ 0,&j>n. \end{cases} \tag{BS.1} \] The transitions are the quotient maps on coefficients. A map from this diagram to \(M\) is determined by its component \(H\to M_n\); its other components are precisely the composites with the transitions of \(M\). This proves the adjunction. The functor in (BS.1) need not be exact: already \(O_1\) need not be flat over \(O_2\). Consequently evaluation of an injective coefficient diagram cannot be treated as injective by an exact-left-adjoint argument.

Resolve \(H\) by the K-flat cell complex of BL.1. Applying (BS.1) gives a derived functor with components \[ (Le_{n,!}H)_j= \begin{cases} O_j\otimes_{O_n}^LH,&j\leq n,\\ 0,&j>n. \end{cases} \qquad Le_{n,!}\dashv e_n. \tag{BS.2} \] Here is a verification of the last assertion that also explains its unbounded meaning. Formula (BS.1) sends a free sheaf generator \(O_n[U]\) to the free diagram generator at \((U,n)\). It therefore sends the chosen cell filtration to a diagram cell filtration. An acyclic K-flat source complex is sent to an acyclic diagram, since every component is a tensor of that complex. Choose a K-injective target diagram \(I\). The ordinary complex adjunction identifies \(\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(e_{n,!}P,I)\) with \(\operatorname{Hom}^{\bullet}(P,I_n)\). For an acyclic K-flat \(P\) the first complex is acyclic. To calculate a derived morphism to \(I_n\), replace the source and the middle object of each quasi-isomorphism roof by K-flat resolutions. The cone of the resulting quasi-isomorphism between K-flat complexes is acyclic and K-flat, so the preceding acyclicity makes precomposition an isomorphism on these Hom groups. The ordinary adjunction therefore descends to the localized Hom groups, exactly as in BR.2. Since \(I_n\) represents evaluation of the target, this proves (BS.2) without assuming it is K-injective.

The exact functor \(\nu^*\) of BK.2 acts on all components and transitions. Denote this diagram functor by \(\nu_{\mathrm s}^*\). Its right adjoint \(\nu_{\mathrm s,*}\) is ordinary componentwise \(\nu_*\): the component adjunction bijections take a commuting transition square to its adjoint commuting square. Exactness of \(\nu_{\mathrm s}^*\) makes \(\nu_{\mathrm s,*}\) preserve K-injectives, by the Hom-complex test. Thus \[ \nu_{\mathrm s}^*:D(A_{\mathrm e}) \rightleftarrows D(A_{\mathrm p}):R\nu_{\mathrm s,*} \tag{BS.3} \] is a derived adjunction.

Pullback commutes with coefficient extension and the prefixes (BS.2). Indeed inverse image preserves tensor products by their free-module and relation presentation. It pulls each flat free-sheaf cell to a flat free-sheaf cell; the degreewise split filtration therefore remains K-flat. Applying this to a chosen resolution gives the natural isomorphism \[ \nu_{\mathrm s}^*Le_{n,!}^{\mathrm e} \simeq Le_{n,!}^{\mathrm p}\nu_n^*. \tag{BS.4} \] The same argument gives the coefficient-extension comparison at any two indices. These are comparisons of the chosen complexes and their quotient maps, so associativity agrees for three or more indices.

BS.2. Deriving direct image retains every transition

For \(E\in D(A_{\mathrm p})\), (BS.2)–(BS.4) give, naturally in every \(H\in D(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)\), \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}(H,e_nR\nu_{\mathrm s,*}E) &=\operatorname{Hom}(Le_{n,!}^{\mathrm e}H,R\nu_{\mathrm s,*}E)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(\nu_{\mathrm s}^*Le_{n,!}^{\mathrm e}H,E)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(Le_{n,!}^{\mathrm p}\nu_n^*H,E)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(\nu_n^*H,E_n)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(H,R\nu_{n,*}E_n). \end{aligned} \tag{BS.5} \] Yoneda consequently identifies \[ e_nR\nu_{\mathrm s,*}E\simeq R\nu_{n,*}E_n. \tag{BS.6} \] The notation on the right means derived direct image of \(O_n\)-modules. In particular (BS.6) has been proved, rather than inferred by evaluating a diagram resolution and declaring it a resolution at each index.

We check transition compatibility. For an \(O_{n+1}\)-complex \(H\), there is a natural map \[ Le_{n,!}(O_n\otimes_{O_{n+1}}^LH) \longrightarrow Le_{n+1,!}H. \tag{BS.7} \] At indices at most \(n\) this is the tensor-associativity identification; at \(n+1\) it is the map from zero, and above that both sides are zero. Choose one K-flat resolution of \(H\) to construct all these components. Under the two evaluation adjunctions, precomposition with (BS.7) is exactly the transition from component \(n+1\) to component \(n\), with restriction of coefficients understood. Pullback respects (BS.7). Every bijection in (BS.5) therefore respects this precomposition, which proves compatibility of (BS.6) with the transitions. The same argument with the adjunction identity maps shows that the unit and counit of (BS.3), evaluated at \(n\), are the ordinary derived \(\nu_n\) unit and counit. There is no independent choice of an isomorphism at each level.

BS.3. Bounded-below descent and the constructible restriction

We recall the exact finite-coefficient input and its essential-image argument. By (BK.3), \(\nu_n^*\) is fully faithful on \(D^+(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)\). Call an \(O_n\)-sheaf on the enlarged site classical if it is a pullback from the étale site. A bounded complex whose cohomology sheaves are classical is in the image: induct on its finite cohomology interval. Its truncation triangle is glued from the previous truncation and a shifted classical sheaf. Full faithfulness lifts the connecting morphism, and its cone gives the required étale object.

For a bounded-below complex \(E\) with classical cohomology, apply this argument to \(\tau^{\leq r}E\). The functor \(R\nu_{n,*}\) preserves lower bounds. To verify this, represent any complex in degrees at least \(a\) by a bounded-below injective resolution starting in degree \(a\); ordinary direct image does not introduce lower terms. Hence \(R\nu_{n,*}(\tau^{>r}E)\) has cohomology only above \(r\). Exactness of \(\nu_n^*\) has the same property. Naturality of the counit triangle now identifies the counit for \(E\), through degree \(r\), with that for \(\tau^{\leq r}E\), which is an isomorphism. Letting \(r\) vary proves \(\nu_n^*R\nu_{n,*}E\simeq E\). This proves the bounded-below essential-image assertion using finite truncations; it assumes no preservation of arbitrary inverse limits by étale inverse image.

For \(L\in D^+(A_{\mathrm e})\), (BS.6) identifies every component of its unit with (BK.3), so the unit is an isomorphism. Evaluations detect acyclicity of diagram complexes. It follows that \(\nu_{\mathrm s}^*\) is fully faithful on \(D^+(A_{\mathrm e})\).

Conversely let \(E\in D^+(A_{\mathrm p})\) have classical cohomology at every index. Apply (BS.6) and the preceding finite-coefficient argument to its counit: every component is an isomorphism, hence so is the diagram counit. Its preimage is bounded below as a diagram. In fact \(R\nu_{\mathrm s,*}\), being a right derived functor of a left exact functor, preserves the common lower bound by the same bounded-below injective-resolution argument. We have proved an equivalence between bounded-below étale diagrams and bounded-below pro-étale diagrams with componentwise classical cohomology. It includes all derived morphisms, because it is the restriction of (BS.3).

Define \(D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A_{\mathrm e})\) to be the full subcategory of \(D(A_{\mathrm e})\) satisfying the cartesian transition condition (BR.1) and having bounded constructible first component. No separate bound on all components is imposed in this definition. Applying \(\nu_{\mathrm s}^*\) gives an object of \(D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A_{\mathrm p})\), by the tensor comparison proved in BS.1. BR.4 and BM.6 show that all its components have classical constructible cohomology with one common finite interval of degrees. The original étale components have those same bounds: exact \(\nu_n^*\) is conservative, since \(\nu_{n,*}\nu_n^*\) is the identity on sheaves by BK.2. Thus the étale diagram itself is bounded.

In the other direction a pro-étale cartesian constructible diagram is bounded with classical components by BR.4, so it descends by the bounded-below equivalence just proved. Its descended transitions are cartesian: their derived scalar-extension maps become isomorphisms after \(\nu_n^*\), by BS.1–BS.2, and conservativity makes them isomorphisms already on the étale site. Its first component is bounded constructible by the finite-level comparison and the definition in BR.4. Consequently \[ D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A_{\mathrm e}) \xrightarrow[\ \nu_{\mathrm s}^*\ ]{\ \sim\ } D_{\mathrm{cart,cons}}(A_{\mathrm p}) \simeq\mathscr C_X. \tag{BS.8} \] The inverse to the first arrow is \(R\nu_{\mathrm s,*}\). The inverse from \(\mathscr C_X\) to the left is \(R\nu_{\mathrm s,*}F\), with BR's reduction functor \(F\). All components, transitions, units and counits are those established above.

BS.4. Higher morphisms on the étale site

For \(K,L\in\mathscr C_X\), denote the components of their étale diagrams in (BS.8) by \(K_n^{\mathrm e},L_n^{\mathrm e}\). Their pullbacks are their actual derived reductions \(K_n,L_n\), with the transitions of BR. Thus full faithfulness of the bounded-below finite-level comparison identifies the groups and the transition maps in (BR.12). We obtain, for every integer \(r\), \[ \begin{aligned} 0&\longrightarrow\varprojlim{}^1_n \operatorname{Hom}_{D(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)} (K_n^{\mathrm e},L_n^{\mathrm e}[r-1])\\ &\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(K,L[r])\\ &\longrightarrow\varprojlim_n \operatorname{Hom}_{D(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n)} (K_n^{\mathrm e},L_n^{\mathrm e}[r]) \longrightarrow0. \end{aligned} \tag{BS.9} \] The transition maps reduce both arguments along the specified cartesian arrows, or equivalently use BR.5's fixed-source adjunction. Their agreement follows from the tensor and transition compatibilities in BS.1–BS.2. The middle term is equally the Hom group of the two actual étale diagrams under (BS.8). Identities and composition agree by the adjunction triangle identities. No finiteness hypothesis has been added to discard the degree-one-limit term.

The standard t-structure on \(\mathscr C_X\) transports through (BS.8). Its heart is BP's strict constructible systems, represented by the derived reductions of their complete sheaves. It is not identified by declaring their underived systems to be cartesian: BR.4's constant torsion example still has its negative-degree correction. BT constructs the realization functor from the bounded derived category of this heart, proves its low-degree extension comparisons and gives the exact remaining effacement condition for equivalence. That condition is not deduced from the existence of a bounded t-structure. BV supplies exceptional right adjoints and adic biduality on these categories. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX supplies the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves, all higher morphisms and the ordinary operations.

The free finite-level comparison is discussed in the Stacks Project, Section 61.19, especially Lemmas 61.19.4, 61.19.5 and 61.19.8. BK.2 proves the acyclicity and unit used here; BS.1–BS.3 supply the derived-prefix, transition and whole-diagram arguments needed to pass from that input to (BS.8).

Appendix BT. Finite-coefficient realization and the adic extension problem

The equivalence in BS concerns derived categories of coefficient diagrams. A different functor starts with bounded complexes in the abelian category of constructible sheaves. We construct this functor, prove the finite-coefficient equivalence, and state and prove the exact additional condition needed for its adic counterpart. Throughout, \(X\) has the arithmetic hypotheses of this lesson and \(R=O_n\) for a fixed \(n\geq1\).

BT.1. Constructible subsheaves and finite generation

Write \(\mathcal A_R=\operatorname{Mod}(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},R)\), and let \(\mathcal B_R\) be its full subcategory of constructible sheaves. Kernels, cokernels and extensions of its objects are constructible by the finite-module argument in BM.6. We need the stronger assertion that every ambient subsheaf of a constructible sheaf is constructible and that these sheaves are Noetherian objects of \(\mathcal A_R\).

Here is a local description of an arbitrary subsheaf \(Q\subset\underline M\), where \(M\) is a finite \(R\)-module on a Noetherian scheme \(V\). For \(m\in M\), the points where the constant germ \(m\) belongs to \(Q\) form an open subset \(V_m\). A germ belonging to \(Q\) lifts on an étale neighbourhood; equality of its image with the constant section holds after shrinking that neighbourhood. Its image in \(V\) is open. On overlaps the lifts agree, because \(Q\to\underline M\) is monic, so they descend to a section on this image. Taking their union proves both openness and the existence of the section \(m\in Q(V_m)\). Thus \(Q\) is determined by the finitely many membership opens \(V_m\). A partition refining these opens and their complements makes its stalk submodules constant, and hence makes \(Q\) locally constant on each part.

Apply this description on étale trivializing neighbourhoods of each stratum of a constructible sheaf \(F\). For clarity, constructibility descends here without assuming a stratification has already descended. On an irreducible stratum choose a trivializing étale neighbourhood of its generic point. Choose an irreducible component containing a point over that generic point, and remove the other components; this gives a nonempty irreducible open still mapping onto an open containing the generic point. In this irreducible neighbourhood, intersect the finitely many nonempty membership opens. The resulting nonempty open has \(Q\) constant; its open image contains the generic point, and \(Q\) is locally constant there by this étale cover. Separate the finitely many generic points first and repeat on the remaining closed subset. Noetherian induction gives a finite constructible partition. This proves that \(Q\subset F\) is constructible. A quotient of \(F\) is then constructible by the cokernel assertion already proved.

For an ascending sequence of subsheaves of \(F\), use one finite collection of quasi-compact étale neighbourhoods trivializing \(F\) on its finitely many strata. Each membership open is now an ascending sequence of opens in a Noetherian scheme, so it stabilizes. There are finitely many neighbourhoods and finitely many elements of their finite modules. One index therefore works for all of them. Equality on these neighbourhoods implies equality on all geometric stalks, hence equality of sheaves. Thus \(F\) is Noetherian even with respect to arbitrary ambient subsheaves.

The category \(\mathcal A_R\) is generated by such objects. Take affine étale maps \(u:U\to X\) of finite presentation, with image in an affine open of \(X\). The free sheaf \(R[U]\) represents sections on \(U\). It is also \(u_!\underline R_U\): by the exact étale adjunction of M.5, maps from either sheaf to \(H\) are \(H(U)\). Proposition 3.2 makes this sheaf constructible. The maps from these generators indexed by all local sections surject onto any \(H\in\mathcal A_R\), as is checked on stalks. Images of their finite sums are constructible quotients. Consequently \[ H=\bigcup_{H'\subset H,\ H'\in\mathcal B_R}H'. \tag{BT.1} \] The union is directed by sums. In particular, an epimorphism \(H\twoheadrightarrow F\) with constructible target has a constructible subobject of \(H\) still surjecting onto \(F\). Indeed the images in \(F\) form a directed union of subobjects; the ascending chain condition makes that union attained. If it were not attained, repeatedly choosing an image not contained in the previous one and taking sums would give a strictly ascending sequence.

BT.2. Extension classes as actual derived morphisms

For an abelian category \(\mathcal A\), write \(D^b(\mathcal A)\) for the localization of bounded complexes up to chain homotopy at quasi-isomorphisms. The construction by roofs, including common refinements, cancellation and composition, is proved in Complexes, cones and localization, §4. Its fraction squares and cancellation witnesses use finite sums, shifts and cones, so bounded inputs give bounded witnesses. This construction does not require injectives in \(\mathcal A\). We retain the shift \(K[r]^n=K^{n+r}\), with differential \((-1)^r d_K\), and the cone triangle with positive projection fixed in B.1.

The bounded-roof lemma proves that this localization embeds fully faithfully into the localization of all complexes, with essential image the objects of bounded cohomology. The actual comparison is useful here. For a roof \(F\leftarrow Q\to G\) with bounded ends, choose \(a<b\) strictly outside their term supports and put \(U=\tau_{\le b}Q\), \(L=\tau_{\ge a}U\). The upper cut uses \(\ker d_Q^b\); the lower cut uses \(U^a/\operatorname{im}d_U^{a-1}\). Both arrows \(Q\leftarrow U\to L\) are quasi-isomorphisms. The maps to \(F,G\) restrict to \(U\) and factor through \(L\), by their chain-map equations. A specified homotopy into a bounded target also descends after taking \(a\) below that target's support: its degree-\(a\) target is zero, and its equation descends along the termwise epimorphism \(U\to L\). Thus a common refinement or a nullhomotopy witnessing equality of bounded roofs has a bounded witness. This supplies both fullness and faithfulness; the same two cuts give the essential-image assertion. These arguments apply to the constructible and strict adic hearts below, independently of the ambient injective resolutions.

We will use the following elementary description in an abelian category \(\mathcal A\). For \(F,G\in\mathcal A\) and \(r>0\), an \(r\)-extension is an exact sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow E_{r-1}\longrightarrow\cdots \longrightarrow E_0\longrightarrow F\longrightarrow0. \tag{BT.2} \] Two such sequences represent the same Yoneda class if they are joined by a finite zigzag of maps of exact sequences that are the identity on \(F,G\). The Baer operation uses direct sum followed by pullback along the diagonal of \(F\) and pushout along addition on \(G\).

Let \(Q_E=[G\to E_{r-1}\to\cdots\to E_0]\) in degrees \(-r,\ldots,0\), with the differentials displayed in (BT.2). Its augmentation \(s_E:Q_E\to F\) is a quasi-isomorphism. Write \(p_E:Q_E\to G[r]\) for the projection that is the identity in degree \(-r\). Set \[ \varepsilon_r=(-1)^{r(r-1)/2},\qquad \Theta_r(E)=(\varepsilon_r p_E)s_E^{-1}. \tag{BT.3a} \] For \(r=0\), \(\Theta_0\) is the ordinary inclusion of morphisms. The scalar in (BT.3a) makes extension splicing agree with shifted composition, as verified below. For \(r>0\) this construction gives the natural map \[ \operatorname{Ext}^r_{\mathcal A}(F,G) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{D^b(\mathcal A)}(F,G[r]). \tag{BT.3} \] It is a bijection, as the following inverse construction shows. Represent a morphism by \(F\xleftarrow{\sim}Q\to G[r]\). Good truncation above zero, and then quotient truncation below \(-r\), preserve both arrows and the quasi-isomorphism to \(F\). We may therefore take \(Q\) in degrees \([-r,0]\), exact in all negative degrees. Its first differential \(Q^{-r}\to Q^{-r+1}\) is monic. If \(f:Q\to G[r]\) is the numerator, push this monomorphism out along \(\varepsilon_r f^{-r}:Q^{-r}\to G\). Appending \(Q^{-r+2},\ldots,Q^0,F\) gives (BT.2). For \(r=1\) the pushout is simply an extension of \(F\) by \(G\).

A common refinement of roofs gives maps between the pushed-out sequences. For the homotopy check, suppose two numerators satisfy \(f-g=hd_Q\) in degree \(-r\), where \(h:Q^{-r+1}\to G\). Write the pushout for \(f\) as the quotient of \(Q^{-r+1}\oplus G\) by the image of \(x\mapsto(d_Qx,-\varepsilon_r f x)\). The map \((e,y)\mapsto(e,y+\varepsilon_r h e)\) carries this relation to the relation for \(g\), so it gives an isomorphism of extensions fixing both endpoints. Its inverse uses the negative of the same added term. The augmentation to \(F[0]\) cannot change under a homotopy once the middle complex has been cut above zero: every possibly contributing homotopy term has zero source or target. Thus common refinements and their homotopies give a finite zigzag of actual extension maps.

Conversely the pushed-out extension receives a map from \(Q\), whose degree-\(-r\) component is \(\varepsilon_r f^{-r}\). Its normalized roof numerator is therefore \(\varepsilon_r^2 f=f\). Starting from an extension, the inverse construction pushes out along \(\varepsilon_r^2 1_G=1_G\), so it returns that extension. This proves the bijection and the zigzag criterion. Direct sums, diagonal pullbacks and addition pushouts give precisely addition of roofs; the same constructions show naturality in both endpoints.

Here is the sign computation for splicing. Let \(E\) be a \(p\)-extension of \(F\) by \(K\), let \(D\) be a \(q\)-extension of \(K\) by \(G\), and write \(C=Q_{D\#E}\) for their ordinary splice complex. There is a quasi-isomorphism \(v:C\to Q_E\): it is the identity in degrees greater than \(-p\), the augmentation \(D_0\to K\) in degree \(-p\), and zero below. It commutes with augmentation to \(F\). Define \(a:C\to Q_D[p]\) to be zero above \(-p\) and multiplication by \((-1)^{pj}\) in degree \(-p-j\), for \(0\le j\le q\). The successive factors satisfy \((-1)^p(-1)^{pj}=(-1)^{p(j-1)}\), exactly the chain-map equation for the shifted differential. At the joining degree both outgoing composites are zero. Moreover \(s_D[p]a=p_Ev\), whereas \(p_D[p]a=(-1)^{pq}p_{D\#E}\). These maps give the square for the unsigned roofs; replacing \(a\) by \(\varepsilon_p a\) gives the square for the normalized first numerator. Consequently \[ \begin{aligned} \Theta_q(D)[p]\,\Theta_p(E) &=\varepsilon_q\varepsilon_p(-1)^{pq} p_{D\#E}s_{D\#E}^{-1}\\ &=\Theta_{p+q}(D\#E),\\ \varepsilon_{p+q}&=(-1)^{pq}\varepsilon_p\varepsilon_q. \end{aligned} \tag{BT.3b} \] For \(p=q=1\), the map \(a\) is the identity on \(D_0\) and minus the identity on \(G\); the unsigned roof composite is therefore the negative of the splice projection. In degree one, \(\varepsilon_1=1\) and \(Q_E\) is the cone of \(G\to E_0\), so \(\Theta_1\) is exactly the connecting morphism with B.1's positive cone projection. Formula (BT.3b) therefore proves the compatibility with connecting morphisms used in BT.4–BT.5. No injective objects in the heart are needed.

BT.3. Finite subextensions give every higher comparison

Consider an \(r\)-extension (BT.2) in \(\mathcal A_R\), with \(F,G\in\mathcal B_R\). Choose a constructible \(E'_0\subset E_0\) surjecting onto \(F\), using (BT.1). Its kernel \(K_1\) is constructible. The inverse image of \(K_1\) in \(E_1\) surjects onto \(K_1\), so choose a constructible \(E'_1\) in that inverse image still surjecting onto \(K_1\). Continue towards \(G\). At the last step include the entire given \(G\) in \(E'_{r-1}\). The latter remains constructible, because finite sums and images are constructible. Its kernel is now exactly \(G\). This gives a subextension all of whose terms belong to \(\mathcal B_R\), with the original endpoints.

There is a useful relative version. Suppose finitely many constructible subcomplexes in the middle terms have already been specified. At degree zero include their sum when choosing \(E'_0\). At each next step their degree-\(i\) sum already maps into the chosen kernel, because they are subcomplexes. Include that sum in the chosen preimage and add the finitely many further generators needed to cover the kernel. This constructs a subextension containing every specified subcomplex.

It follows that all ambient extension classes lift to \(\mathcal B_R\). They have the same equivalence relation there. To prove this last point, take a finite zigzag relating two extensions already in \(\mathcal B_R\). Regard its nodes as extensions and orient each edge by its actual map. A finite path with these orientations has no directed cycles. Process the nodes in an order consistent with the arrows. At each nonfixed node choose a constructible subextension containing the images of all previously chosen incoming extensions, using the relative version. The two original endpoints are kept in their entirety. An arrow into such a fixed endpoint automatically lands in it. Every arrow now restricts to the chosen subextensions. This is a zigzag wholly inside \(\mathcal B_R\) with the same fixed ends.

Using (BT.3), we have proved for every \(r\geq0\) \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{D^b(\mathcal B_R)}(F,G[r]) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}_{D(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},R)}(F,G[r]). \tag{BT.4} \] For \(r=0\), a roof into \(G[0]\) can first be cut above zero; its numerator factors through its degree-zero cohomology, identified with \(F\) by the denominator. This identifies the derived Hom group with ordinary \(\operatorname{Hom}(F,G)\), in either category. For \(r<0\), the same upper cut has no term in the positive degree supporting \(G[r]\), so the group is zero. The bounded-comparison proof in BT.2 embeds the ambient bounded localization fully in the unbounded derived category constructed in BF. Thus (BT.3) computes exactly the groups in (BT.4).

Exact inclusion defines a functor on bounded complexes and takes acyclic complexes to acyclic complexes. Its derived functor lands in complexes with constructible cohomology. It is fully faithful on all bounded complexes: first fix a shifted heart object as source and induct on the target's finite cohomology interval, using its truncation triangle and the long exact Hom sequences; then induct on the source interval in the same way. At each step the five-term exact-sequence argument uses the already known outer comparisons and proves the middle one. For essential surjectivity, truncate a bounded constructible ambient complex. Inductively realize its lower truncation and its top cohomology sheaf; full faithfulness lifts the connecting map, and its cone realizes the original complex. We have proved \[ D^b(\mathcal B_{O_n})\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } D^b_c(X_{\mathrm{\acute et}},O_n). \tag{BT.5} \] This is an assertion for the category allowing all finite constructible stratifications. It does not assert realization for an arbitrarily prescribed fixed stratification or for the lisse subcategory alone. The construction in BT.1 may refine the stratification when it takes a subsheaf.

BT.4. The realization functor for the strict adic heart

Let \(\mathcal H_X=\mathscr C_X\cap D^{[0,0]}(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},O)\). BQ proves that this is an abelian category with exact inclusion into ambient \(O\)-sheaves, and BP identifies it with strict constructible systems. It is closed under ambient extensions: a short exact sequence with endpoints in \(\mathcal H_X\) gives a triangle in which the middle sheaf is complete and has constructible first derived reduction. Thus it belongs to \(\mathscr C_X\) and is in degree zero.

Applying exact inclusion to a bounded complex in \(\mathcal H_X\) gives an object of \(\mathscr C_X\). This follows also by its finite sequence of brutal-truncation triangles, whose individual terms are shifts of heart objects. Acyclic complexes remain acyclic. Localization therefore gives the specified functor \[ \operatorname{real}_X:D^b(\mathcal H_X)\longrightarrow\mathscr C_X. \tag{BT.6} \] It preserves standard cohomology, since inclusion preserves kernels, images and cokernels. Through BP this is also a realization functor from the strict-system heart. It is not the functor sending an underived strict tower directly to the cartesian diagram category; its image is first a complex of complete sheaves, whose diagram is then given by BR–BS.

For \(F,G\in\mathcal H_X\), write \[ \theta_r:\operatorname{Ext}^r_{\mathcal H_X}(F,G) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(F,G[r]). \tag{BT.7} \] The map \(\theta_0\) is an isomorphism. So is \(\theta_1\): (BT.3) identifies the ambient morphisms with short exact extensions, and their middle sheaves belong to \(\mathcal H_X\) by extension closure. Maps and equivalences of these extensions are maps in the same full subcategory.

The map \(\theta_2\) is injective. Represent a two-extension as the splice of \(0\to K\to E_0\to F\to0\) with a one-extension of \(K\) by \(G\), whose class is \(\beta\). If its ambient class is zero, the exact Hom sequence of the first triangle says that the ambient class of \(\beta\) is the restriction of a morphism \(E_0\to G[1]\). By \(\theta_1\), this morphism is a heart one-extension. Injectivity of \(\theta_1\) makes its restriction equal to \(\beta\) already in the heart. The connecting homomorphism inside \(D^b(\mathcal H_X)\) kills that restriction, so the original two-extension is zero. This argument proves injectivity; it does not supply surjectivity in degree two.

BT.5. The precise remaining effacement condition

For this specified functor, the following condition is necessary and sufficient for equivalence:

For every \(F,G\in\mathcal H_X\), every integer \(r>0\), and every \(\alpha:F\to G[r]\) in \(\mathscr C_X\), there exists an epimorphism \(E\twoheadrightarrow F\) in \(\mathcal H_X\) such that the composite \(E\to F\xrightarrow\alpha G[r]\) is zero. \[ \text{This condition will be denoted }(\mathrm E_X). \tag{BT.8} \] Only the given morphism is required to be killed; a single epimorphism killing all positive morphisms is not asserted.

Suppose \((\mathrm E_X)\) holds. We prove all \(\theta_r\) are isomorphisms by induction. Degrees zero and one are established above. Given an ambient class \(\alpha\) in degree \(r>1\), choose the indicated epimorphism and let \(K\) be its heart kernel. Exactness of Hom for \(K\to E\to F\) lifts \(\alpha\) to a morphism \(K\to G[r-1]\). Induction realizes that morphism by a heart extension. Splicing it with \(0\to K\to E\to F\to0\) proves surjectivity of \(\theta_r\).

For injectivity, represent a heart \(r\)-extension as the same kind of splice, with an \((r-1)\)-extension class \(\beta\) on \(K\). If its ambient image is zero, the ambient exact sequence expresses the image of \(\beta\) as the restriction of a morphism \(E\to G[r-1]\). Surjectivity in degree \(r-1\) lifts that morphism to a heart class; injectivity in degree \(r-1\) identifies its restriction with \(\beta\). The heart connecting homomorphism therefore kills \(\beta\), proving the original class zero. The finite-truncation argument of BT.3 now proves full faithfulness and essential surjectivity of (BT.6), since BQ supplies the bounded t-structure on \(\mathscr C_X\).

Conversely, if (BT.6) is an equivalence, any \(\alpha\) comes from a Yoneda extension by (BT.3). Take its final epimorphism \(E_0\twoheadrightarrow F\). Pullback along this epimorphism splits the last short exact sequence, so it kills the spliced extension, and therefore kills \(\alpha\). This proves \((\mathrm E_X)\).

The finite-coefficient result (BT.5) proves the corresponding condition separately at each fixed \(O_n\). It does not produce a compatible family of heart epimorphisms as \(n\) varies. Moreover, derived reduction of an adic heart object may have degree-minus-one cohomology, as BR.4 explicitly calculates for torsion. Ordinary quotient maps cannot simply replace these derived reductions in the effacement problem. Thus (BT.6), the degree-zero and degree-one isomorphisms, the degree-two injection and criterion (BT.8) are proved. BU establishes this condition and full equivalence in dimension zero over finite or algebraically closed fields. BY proves full integral and rational realization for curves over those fields, and proves the formal implication from a specified higher-dimensional projection theorem. The higher-dimensional projection and realization arguments are treated separately in BZ–CB. BV supplies exceptional right adjoints and adic biduality. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization; BX proves the full rational-sheaf comparison with integral models and operations.

Free comparisons are constructible sheaves on Noetherian schemes, Tag 03RY, constructible closure, Tag 03RZ, derived subcategories, Tag 06UP, and Yoneda extensions, Stacks Project §13.27. The sign distinction between ordinary splicing and unsigned roof composition is also discussed by Volkov and Witherspoon, Graded Lie Structure on Cohomology of Some Exact Monoidal Categories, §2, pp.82–83, free author-hosted copy. The membership-open, finite-subextension, roof and effacement arguments above give the particular realization statements used here, with the shift signs explicitly computed in (BT.3a)–(BT.3b).

Appendix BU. Adic realization in dimension zero

We prove the full realization assertion of BT over a finite field, over an algebraically closed field, and over every zero-dimensional scheme of finite type over either field. We retain the coefficient ring \(O\), its uniformizer \(\pi\), and \(O_n=O/\pi^n\). The residue characteristic of \(O\) is invertible on the scheme. Write \(\mathcal H_X\) for the strict adic heart of BP–BQ and \(\mathscr C_X\) for the complete constructible category.

BU.1. A natural two-term complex for finite-field coefficients

Let \(s=\operatorname{Spec}\mathbf F_q\), choose an algebraic closure, and put \(G=\operatorname{Gal}(\overline{\mathbf F}_q/\mathbf F_q)\). Here \(\phi(a)=a^q\) is arithmetic Frobenius. The field and sheaf arguments in Galois cohomology and the étale cohomology of a field, Sections 1–3 and 6 prove the following facts with their actual maps. The group \(G\) is \(\widehat{\mathbf Z}\), generated topologically by \(\phi\); discrete continuous \(G\)-modules are equivalent to étale module sheaves; and derived sections are computed by the continuous inhomogeneous cochain complex \(C^\bullet(G,N)\). The finite-étale field classification and exact sheaf equivalence required by those arguments are also proved in AB.1–AB.2; AA.1–AA.2 supply their compactness, continuous-cochain and injective-comparison prerequisites.

For a finite \(O_n\)-module \(N\), write \(T\) for the action of \(\phi\). Define \[ B_\phi(N)=[N\xrightarrow{T-1}N] \quad\text{in degrees }0,1. \tag{BU.1} \] There is a natural chain map \[ C^\bullet(G,N)\longrightarrow B_\phi(N) \tag{BU.2} \] which is the identity in degree zero, sends a degree-one cochain \(c\) to \(c(\phi)\), and is zero in higher degrees. The only nonzero differential to check is degree zero: \((dm)(\phi)=Tm-m\). Thus it is a chain map on all cochains, not merely a correspondence between cocycles.

It is a quasi-isomorphism. Here is the precise finite-quotient calculation supplying this conclusion. Section 6 of the cited lesson proves the cyclic resolution with alternating maps \(t-1\) and \(1+t+\cdots+t^{d-1}\). For inflation from the cyclic quotient of order \(d\) to the one of order \(ed\), its comparison map multiplies degree-\(r\) cochain representatives by \(e^{\lfloor r/2\rfloor}\). Its proof checks the chain equations and the resolution comparison homotopy. Once \(e\) kills \(N\), all classes in degree at least two die under this inflation. In degree one the map on representatives is the identity, and the norm condition becomes zero after this enlargement. Passing to the continuous cochains, which are the filtered union of these finite-quotient cochains by AA.1–AA.2, gives \[ \begin{aligned} H^0(G,N)&=\ker(T-1),\\ H^1(G,N)&=\operatorname{coker}(T-1),\\ H^{r}(G,N)&=0\qquad(r\geq2). \end{aligned} \tag{BU.3} \] The degree-one identification is evaluation at \(\phi\): a crossed homomorphism on a cyclic quotient is determined by its value at the generator, and its relation is exactly the norm condition. Hence (BU.2) induces these identifications. Every map in (BU.2) commutes with coefficient homomorphisms. In particular it compares an entire quotient tower of coefficients.

BU.2. Completed sections of a heart object

At \(s\), every constructible finite sheaf is lisse. BP and N.4 therefore identify \(\mathcal H_s\) with the abelian category of finite \(O\)-modules \(M\) with continuous \(G\)-action. Such an action is equivalent to an automorphism \(T\) of \(M\). Indeed \(T\) acts on each finite quotient \(M/\pi^nM\) with finite order, so the homomorphism from \(\mathbf Z\) extends to \(\widehat{\mathbf Z}\) on that quotient. Uniqueness makes these extensions compatible, and N.4 recovers a continuous action on \(M\). Conversely continuity and density determine the action from \(T\). An intertwining \(O\)-linear map is automatically continuous by preservation of the \(\pi\)-adic filtration. This proves the assertion also on morphisms.

Let \(H\) be the complete sheaf corresponding to \((M,T)\), and let \(H_n\) be its ordinary quotient sheaf. BP.2–BP.4 give the actual identification \[ H=\operatorname{holim}_n\nu_s^*H_n,\qquad (H_n)_{\bar s}=M/\pi^nM. \tag{BU.4} \] These are ordinary quotients of a heart object; their limit is justified by BP. This does not replace the derived reductions in BR–BS.

Derived sections commute with this homotopy limit. One can check the assertion on the product-and-cone model: use the diagram injective replacements of BR.5, apply sections to the products, and retain the actual \(1-s\) map. The finite-coefficient comparison BK.2 and the natural maps (BU.2) consequently give \[ R\Gamma(s_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},H) \simeq\operatorname{holim}_n B_\phi(M/\pi^nM) \simeq [M\xrightarrow{T-1}M]. \tag{BU.5} \] For the second isomorphism, both terms of the tower in (BU.1) have surjective quotient transitions. On their products the equations \(a_n-u_na_{n+1}=b_n\) are solved successively: choose \(a_1\), then lift \(a_n-b_n\) to choose \(a_{n+1}\). Thus \(1-s\) is surjective in each degree and its kernel is the degreewise inverse limit. The short exact sequence of complexes identifies the homotopy limit with that kernel. N.4 identifies its two terms with \(M\). This also proves naturality of (BU.5), including for modules with torsion.

For a geometric point \(\bar s=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\), with \(\Omega\) algebraically closed, the étale site has the one-point module category: every finite separable field extension is \(\Omega\). The same sheaf reconstruction proves exactness of sections. The corresponding argument yields \[ \mathcal H_{\bar s}\simeq\operatorname{Mod}_{\mathrm{fin}}(O), \qquad R\Gamma(\bar s_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},H)\simeq M[0]. \tag{BU.6} \]

BU.3. Derived Hom with a free source

Suppose \(F,G\in\mathcal H_s\), and the module \(M_F\) is finite free over \(O\). Its ordinary dual with action \[ (T_F^\vee\lambda)(x)=\lambda(T_F^{-1}x) \tag{BU.7} \] defines another heart object \(F^\vee\). Evaluation and the dual-basis coevaluation descend, since these actions make them equivariant. They exhibit \(F^\vee\) as the dual of \(F\) for the completed tensor of BL.3. Indeed BP.5 supplies a pro-étale cover on which the finite free module and its dual are powers of \(\widehat O\); there the two duality identities are the finite-basis identities. Equality of sheaf maps descends from that cover. The completed tensor and internal-Hom adjunction of BL.4 then give \[ R\mathcal Hom_O(F,G)\simeq F^\vee\widehat\otimes_O G. \tag{BU.8} \] The right side is a heart object. On the same cover tensoring by a finite power of the completed unit is a finite direct sum, hence has no additional cohomology. Its quotient modules descend to those of \[ P=\operatorname{Hom}_O(M_F,M_G),\qquad S(h)=T_GhT_F^{-1}. \tag{BU.9} \] Equivalently, this follows by reduction and BP's full faithfulness; freeness of \(M_F\) makes formation of this Hom module commute with the ordinary quotients. Applying (BU.5) proves \[ R\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_s}(F,G) \simeq[P\xrightarrow{S-1}P]. \tag{BU.10} \] Here the left side is the ambient derived Hom complex between these objects. In particular \(\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_s}(F,G[r])=0\) for \(r\geq2\). At a geometric point, (BU.6) makes this Hom complex \(P[0]\), so it vanishes in every positive degree. Freeness is imposed on the source only; \(G\) may have torsion.

BU.4. Free covers and comparison in every degree

Every \((M,T)\) admits an exact sequence in the heart \[ 0\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0, \qquad N,L\text{ finite free over }O. \tag{BU.11} \] To construct it, choose lifts \(m_1,\ldots,m_a\) of a basis of \(M/\pi M\). These generate \(M\), by the successive approximation argument of N.4. Express each \(T(m_j)\) in these generators, giving a matrix \(A\) on \(L=O^a\). Modulo \(\pi\) it is the invertible matrix induced by \(T\), so its determinant is a unit and \(A\) is invertible. With \(A\) as its automorphism, \(L\to M\) intertwines the actions. The kernel \(N\) is finite free by the submodule proof in N.4. It is stable under \(A\) and \(A^{-1}\), since the surjection intertwines both inverse automorphisms as well. BU.2 makes all these actions continuous. The equivalence of abelian categories there transports (BU.11) to the claimed heart sequence. The zero module permits \(a=0\). At a geometric point the same construction omits the automorphisms.

Let \(\theta_r\) be the realization comparison (BT.7). If its source \(L\) is finite free, (BU.10) and injectivity of \(\theta_2\) give \(\operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal H_s}(L,G)=0\) for every \(G\). Every longer Yoneda extension starting at \(L\) factors through a two-extension starting at \(L\): take the last two middle terms and their left kernel, then splice the remaining extension. The two-extension vanishes, so \[ \operatorname{Ext}^r_{\mathcal H_s}(L,G)=0 \quad(r\geq2). \tag{BU.12} \] Together with BT.4 this proves all comparison maps for a free source.

For arbitrary \(F,G\), use (BU.11) with \(M=F\), and apply Hom into \(G\) both in \(D^b(\mathcal H_s)\) and in \(\mathscr C_s\). The realization functor gives a map between the long exact sequences. The two adjacent degree-one comparisons for \(L,N\) are isomorphisms, and the degree-two groups with source \(L\) vanish on both sides. Thus both degree-two groups with source \(F\) are the corresponding cokernel: \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Ext}^2_{\mathcal H_s}(F,G) &=\operatorname{coker}\bigl( \operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal H_s}(L,G)\to \operatorname{Ext}^1_{\mathcal H_s}(N,G)\bigr),\\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_s}(F,G[2]) &=\operatorname{coker}\bigl( \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_s}(L,G[1])\to \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_s}(N,G[1])\bigr). \end{aligned} \tag{BU.13} \] The natural map is an isomorphism. For \(r\geq3\), the same sequences and the free-source vanishing make both groups zero. Degrees zero and one are BT.4, and negative degrees vanish by the t-structure. The finite truncation and connecting-map induction of BT.3 therefore proves \[ \operatorname{real}_s:D^b(\mathcal H_s)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathscr C_s. \tag{BU.14} \] At a geometric point the same proof applies, with the stronger free-source vanishing from BU.3. In that case the groups with arbitrary heart source vanish for \(r\geq2\). In particular (BU.14) also holds for \(\bar s\). By BT.5 these equivalences prove the required heart-epimorphism effacement at both kinds of point.

BU.5. Nilpotents and finite unions of points

The assertion extends to a zero-dimensional finite-type scheme \(X\) over \(\mathbf F_q\) or an algebraically closed field. We give the algebra and site reductions, including nilpotents.

A zero-dimensional Noetherian affine scheme has finitely many points: its primes are all maximal and minimal, and there are finitely many minimal primes. Its nilradical is nilpotent, since it is generated by finitely many nilpotent elements. Chinese remainders for sufficiently high powers of its distinct maximal ideals express its ring as a finite product of local rings with nilpotent maximal ideals. A finite affine cover gives the same conclusion for \(X\): every point is open, so its singleton neighbourhood is affine, and \(X\) is the finite disjoint union of these local spectra.

Their residue fields are finite extensions of the base. For completeness, the finite-type field argument works over either base field. Choose a maximal algebraically independent sublist of algebra generators of such a field \(K\). Clearing the finitely many denominators in their remaining algebraic equations makes \(K\) integral over \(k[t_1,\ldots,t_d,1/f]\). A subring over which a field is integral is itself a field: apply a monic equation for the inverse of a nonzero element and multiply by the appropriate power of that element. If \(d>0\), choose an irreducible polynomial in \(k[t_1]\) not dividing \(f\); there are infinitely many by the usual product-plus-one argument, whereas \(f\) has only finitely many such divisors. That polynomial remains a nonunit after inverting \(f\), a contradiction. Hence \(d=0\) and \(K/k\) is finite. The nilpotent maximal-ideal filtration has finite-dimensional residue-field quotients, since each ideal power is finitely generated. The local rings in question are consequently Artinian and finite over \(k\).

For an Artinian local ring \(A\) with residue field \(k'\), BC.4 proves that finite étale algebras over \(A\) and \(k'\) are equivalent, including every morphism. These objects form a basis of both small étale sites. To check this on the \(A\)-side, an affine étale algebra \(B\) of finite presentation has finite-dimensional reduction \(B/\mathfrak m_AB\), by the field-fibre description. Lift a finite module-generating list of this reduction to \(B\), and denote its \(A\)-span by \(V\). Then \(B/V=\mathfrak m_A(B/V)\); nilpotence implies \(B=V\), proving finiteness without a prior finite-module assumption. Covers are preserved and reflected, because nilpotent reduction changes no points and finite étale surjectivity is checked on residue-field fibres. Thus the equivalent bases, with their coverings, give equivalent sheaf categories.

This equivalence preserves the constant coefficient rings \(O_n\), their quotient maps and all module operations. Applying it to the diagram categories of BS preserves derived tensor, evaluation and cartesianness. It preserves constructibility and the coefficient bounds, since each local spectrum has one point. BS and BP therefore transport both \(\mathscr C_X\) and its heart to their counterparts on \(X_{\mathrm{red}}\), compatibly with realization. Finally sheaves and all these categories on a finite disjoint union are finite products of the categories on its parts. Kernels, complexes, quasi-isomorphisms and truncations are componentwise. Applying (BU.14) in each factor proves \[ \operatorname{real}_X:D^b(\mathcal H_X)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\mathscr C_X \quad(\dim X=0) \tag{BU.15} \] under the stated finite-type and base-field hypotheses.

BU.6. Frobenius conventions and the remaining geometric step

If the same representation is described using geometric Frobenius, its operator is \(T^{-1}\). The complexes \([M\xrightarrow{T-1}M]\) and \([M\xrightarrow{T^{-1}-1}M]\) are naturally isomorphic by the identity in degree zero and \(-T^{-1}\) in degree one. Indeed \(-T^{-1}(T-1)=T^{-1}-1\). Thus the convention change is explicit in (BU.5) and (BU.10).

The zero-dimensional theorem proves all higher extension comparisons for the strict adic heart, with no freeness assumption on its objects. Its proof does not supply an effacing heart epimorphism on a positive-dimensional scheme. In particular, neither separate finite-level covers nor a geometric stalk calculation establishes \((\mathrm E_X)\) for such a scheme. BV supplies exceptional right adjoints and adic biduality. BW proves completed-ring comparison and central rationalization. BX proves the full comparison with constructible rational sheaves. BY proves the curve case by constructible effacement; its general higher-dimensional projection input remains an additional assertion.

Free comparisons for the finite-field calculation and convention are Milne's freely available lecture notes, Section 14, pp. 98–99, and Frobenii, Definition 64.3.10. The earlier programme proof cited in BU.1 supplies the finite-group resolutions and continuous-cochain comparison; the completed passage and the realization argument are proved above.

Appendix BV. Exceptional inverse image and duality for complete coefficients

Let \(f:X\to Y\) be a separated morphism of finite-type schemes over a field \(k\), and let \(\ell\) be invertible in \(k\). Keep the complete discrete valuation ring \(O\) with finite residue field of characteristic \(\ell\), its uniformizer \(\pi\), the rings \(O_n=O/\pi^n\), and the category \(\mathcal C_X\) of BM–BS. Thus an object of \(\mathcal C_X\) is derived complete on the pro-étale site and has bounded constructible classical first derived reduction. This is the already constructed category, without assuming its realization from the derived category of its heart.

We construct a right adjoint \(f_c^!\) to the proper-support functor of BM and prove singular biduality in \(\mathcal C_X\). The construction uses the derived category of whole coefficient diagrams. In particular its adjunction retains the higher morphisms and the degree-one inverse-limit term of BR–BS.

BV.1. Coefficient change for ordinary and proper images

First use a finite commutative coefficient ring \(R\), killed by an integer invertible in \(k\). The bounds of M.1 and BG.2 apply to arbitrary \(R\)-module sheaves. Their comparison with underlying torsion-sheaf cohomology follows from the argument in AS.1 and BB.3: use free \(R\)-module sheaves on the hypercover terms; the local augmented contraction is \(R\)-linear, and Hom into an \(R\)-module injective makes the augmented complex exact. This proves the section-cohomology comparison on every étale test object. The finite cohomological windows of BG.3 extend the comparison to unbounded complexes. It also proves compatibility with exact restriction of coefficient rings.

Ordinary direct image \(Rf_*\) preserves coproducts at this scope. On individual sheaves, higher continuity from BA and M.1 identifies the image of a sum with the sum of its images: a sum is the filtered colimit of its finite subsums. A sum of injective resolutions consequently has direct-image-acyclic terms. The proof of BG.3, applied with M.1's ordinary-image bound, shows that this complex computes its unbounded derived image. The resulting comparison is the termwise coproduct comparison. This repeats BG.4's argument with the ordinary-image bound; it does not use a nonproper geometric-fibre formula. Proper support preserves coproducts by BG.4–BG.6.

Let \(P\in D(R)\) be a complex of coefficient modules, regarded as a constant complex on the schemes. For either \(T=Rf_*\) or \(T=Rf_!\), the projection map gives \[ P\otimes_R^L T(K)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ T(P\otimes_R^L K). \tag{BV.1} \] Here the copy of \(P\) on the source is its inverse image. Fix \(K\). Both sides are exact functors of \(P\) preserving coproducts, by the preceding paragraph and BH. The map is an isomorphism for \(P=R\), hence for its shifts, sums and cones. These objects generate \(D(R)\): the free-module cell resolution of BH.1 expresses any complex by successive additions of shifted free modules, and its union is the cone of \(1-s\) on the sum of the stages. Exactness of filtered module colimits identifies that cone with the union. The same cone argument proves that the class on which (BV.1) is invertible contains this union. This proves (BV.1) even when \(P\) has infinite projective dimension.

For a homomorphism \(R\to R'\) of such rings, extension of coefficients is \(T_R^{R'}=R'\otimes_R^L-\). Forgetting the \(R'\)-action is exact and conservative. The underlying-cohomology comparison above and (BV.1) therefore give the actual scalar-extension comparisons \[ T_R^{R'}Rf_{*,R}\simeq Rf_{*,R'}T_R^{R'}, \qquad T_R^{R'}Rf_{!,R}\simeq Rf_{!,R'}T_R^{R'}. \tag{BV.2} \] These are projection maps, rather than isomorphisms selected from the equality of cohomology groups. On K-flat coefficient resolutions their composites for \(R\to R'\to R''\) are the same tensor-associativity map followed by the same projection map. Thus successive coefficient changes, geometric compositions and the adjunction units agree.

For \(K\in\mathcal C_X\), BK.5 already shows that the pro-étale \(Rf_*K\) is complete and that \[ (Rf_*K)_n\simeq Rf_{*,O_n}(K_n). \tag{BV.3} \] The comparison with the classical étale image is the bounded-below comparison in BK.2 and BK.5. M.4 makes the right side bounded constructible at \(n=1\), so \(Rf_*K\in\mathcal C_Y\). Consequently the adjunction \(f_c^*\dashv Rf_*\) of BL.6 restricts to these constructible categories. The common cohomological bound from M.1 also bounds all finite reductions together.

BV.2. Finite-coefficient exceptional adjoints and their bounds

BF.1–BF.6 apply to sheaves of \(R\)-modules: their presheaf generators, exact sheafification and representability proof do not require \(R\) to be a field or self-injective. Since \(Rf_{!,R}\) preserves coproducts, they construct its right adjoint \(f_R^!\), with its specified counit. Composition of proper supports gives composition of these right adjoints.

The smooth formula of Proposition 3.3 holds with these \(R\)-coefficients too. We justify this coefficient extension without assuming the desired formula. Choose \(\Lambda=\mathbf Z/m\) mapping to \(R\), with \(m\) invertible in \(k\). Write \(T=R\otimes_\Lambda^L-\) and \(U\) for coefficient restriction. Equation (BV.2) and the two adjunctions give, for \(E\in D(X,\Lambda)\) and \(B\in D(Y,R)\), \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}(E,Uf_R^!B) &=\operatorname{Hom}(TE,f_R^!B)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(T Rf_{!,\Lambda}E,B)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(E,f_\Lambda^!UB). \end{aligned} \tag{BV.4} \] Thus \(Uf_R^!B=f_\Lambda^!UB\), naturally with respect to the coefficient action and the counit. No preservation of injectives by \(U\) was used.

For a smooth \(p\) of relative dimension \(d\), extend the trace of Proposition 3.3 from \(\Lambda\) to \(R\) using (BV.2). The resulting \(R\)-linear trace and projection map define \(p^*B(d)[2d]\to p_R^!B\). Under (BV.4), its underlying map is exactly Proposition 3.3 applied to \(UB\): reassociating \(UB\otimes_\Lambda^L Rp_!\Lambda(d)[2d]\) gives its trace pairing. Hence the map is an isomorphism, since \(U\) is conservative. In particular \[ p_R^!B\simeq p^*B(d)[2d]. \tag{BV.5} \] Its orientation is the positive Kummer orientation already fixed in BI–BJ. Extending that trace twice is extending it once through the composite ring map, so (BV.5) respects further coefficient change.

For a closed immersion \(i:Z\hookrightarrow W\), with complementary open immersion \(j\), the closed-support triangle is \[ i_*i_R^!B\longrightarrow B\longrightarrow Rj_*j^*B \longrightarrow i_*i_R^!B[1]. \tag{BV.6} \] It is the counit triangle of M.5, with the same proof over \(R\). Formula (BV.1) for \(j\) shows that its scalar extension is the corresponding triangle over \(R'\). Exact closed image commutes with coefficient extension, as can be checked on its zero and unchanged geometric stalks. Thus scalar extension commutes with \(i^!\). This is the map obtained by extending the counit and transposing, not a choice of a cone isomorphism.

More generally that construction defines \[ R'\otimes_R^L f_R^!B \longrightarrow f_{R'}^!(R'\otimes_R^L B). \tag{BV.7} \] To define it, apply \(Rf_{!,R'}\) to its proposed source, use (BV.2), extend the \(R\)-counit, and transpose. It is an isomorphism. The assertion is local on the source and target. Indeed restriction of \(f^!B\) to an open source is the right adjoint for the restricted map, because open extension by zero composes with \(f_!\). For an open target, the same Hom calculation with its inverse-image open proves the target restriction formula. Both identifications preserve the counit.

On affine pieces of source and target, write \[ X_0\xrightarrow{i}\mathbf A^N_{Y_0}\xrightarrow{p}Y_0 \tag{BV.8} \] with \(i\) closed and \(p\) the projection: finitely many algebra generators give the closed embedding. Here \(f_R^!=i_R^!p_R^!\). The smooth and closed calculations prove (BV.7) on this piece. These pieces cover \(X\), so their conservative restrictions prove it globally. The defining counit computation also proves that the comparison for a composite is the composite comparison: transpose either map and cancel the same successive adjunction units. This proves coherence for every sequence of coefficient changes.

This argument gives bounds independent of \(R\). If the input has cohomology in \([a,b]\), the smooth step has cohomology in \([a-2N,b-2N]\). If \(Rj_*\) has cohomological dimension at most \(c\), (BV.6) places its closed-support fibre in \([a-2N,b-2N+c+1]\). This deliberately sufficient bound follows from the long exact sequence. Finitely many choices of (BV.8) give one finite interval for \(f_R^!B\), depending on the geometry and \([a,b]\), not the coefficient modulus. M.4 over finite rings, exact pullback, (BV.5) and (BV.6) also prove that \(f_R^!\) preserves bounded constructibility. Neither assertion uses singular biduality or a finite projective resolution of \(R'\) over \(R\).

BV.3. The adjoint on whole coefficient diagrams

Let \(\mathcal A_X\) be the abelian category of étale sheaves of modules over the diagram \((O_n)_n\), as in BS. Fix one compactification \(X\xrightarrow{j}\overline X\xrightarrow{p}Y\), supplied by BG.5, and define \[ F_f=Rp_{\mathrm s,*}j_{\mathrm s,!}: D(\mathcal A_X)\longrightarrow D(\mathcal A_Y). \tag{BV.9} \] The subscript denotes the functor on entire diagrams. Extension by zero is componentwise exact. Direct image is right adjoint to componentwise exact inverse image. The proof of BS.2 applies with \(p\) in place of \(\nu\): inverse image commutes with the derived prefixes \(Le_{n,!}\), so their adjunction gives \[ e_nF_fK\simeq Rf_{!,O_n}K_n. \tag{BV.10} \] Precomposition with (BS.7) proves compatibility with transitions. This does not assume that evaluation of an injective diagram is injective.

Evaluations jointly detect zero objects and isomorphisms. The common proper-image bound of BG.2 and preservation of coproducts at every level therefore show that \(F_f\) is exact and preserves coproducts.
