The compactification comparisons of BG.6 give comparisons of (BV.9): use the same proper-image and open-extension adjunction maps on diagrams. Their evaluated maps are the finite-coefficient comparisons, so they are isomorphisms. Their composition identities are the adjunction identities before evaluation. Thus (BV.9) is independent of compactification with the specified composition maps.

We spell out why BF's representability proof applies to this diagram category. A presheaf diagram has a free generator at each pair \((U,n)\); Hom from it is \(M_n(U)\). Those functors are exact on presheaves and preserve sums, so the generators and their shifts are compact projective generators in the derived presheaf category, by BF.5. Their sheafifications generate the sheaf category. Sheafification is exact componentwise and preserves the coefficient action and transitions. The inclusion of sheaves has the fully faithful derived right adjoint of (BF.11). Hence the representability argument of BF.6 applies word for word to this explicit set of generators and this exact sheafification. The Grothendieck resolution hypotheses are those verified in BR.1. It follows that \(F_f\) has a right adjoint \(\Psi_f\) on \(D(\mathcal A)\).

Its components are the desired exceptional images. By (BV.2), proper support commutes with the derived prefixes: \[ F_fLe_{n,!}\simeq Le_{n,!}Rf_{!,O_n}. \tag{BV.11} \] At an index \(m\leq n\), this is precisely coefficient extension from \(O_n\) to \(O_m\) followed by proper support; above \(n\) both objects are zero. The projection maps of BV.1 respect all prefix transitions. For every test complex \(H\) at index \(n\), adjunction now gives \[ \begin{aligned} \operatorname{Hom}(H,e_n\Psi_fG) &=\operatorname{Hom}(Le_{n,!}H,\Psi_fG)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(Le_{n,!}Rf_{!,O_n}H,G)\\ &=\operatorname{Hom}(H,f_{O_n}^!G_n). \end{aligned} \tag{BV.12} \] These natural bijections identify \(e_n\Psi_fG=f_{O_n}^!G_n\).

To identify the transitions, precompose (BV.12) with the map (BS.7) between prefixes. Equation (BV.11) takes that map to its proper-support counterpart. Transposing then gives the exceptional coefficient-change map (BV.7), followed by \(f_{O_n}^!\) of the transition of \(G\). In particular, if \(G\) is derived cartesian, then \[ O_n\otimes_{O_{n+1}}^L(\Psi_fG)_{n+1} \simeq f_{O_n}^!(O_n\otimes_{O_{n+1}}^LG_{n+1}) \simeq(\Psi_fG)_n. \tag{BV.13} \] All these maps belong to the one object \(\Psi_fG\) in the derived category of diagrams. The construction does not replace such an object by a sequence of objects in separately formed derived categories.

BV.4. The complete exceptional inverse image

If \(G\) belongs to the cartesian constructible subcategory of BS.3, its components have one common bounded interval. BV.2 proves bounded constructibility of \((\Psi_fG)_n\), with one bound for all \(n\), and (BV.13) proves that this diagram is cartesian. Thus \(\Psi_f\) preserves exactly the subcategory corresponding to \(\mathcal C_Y\) and \(\mathcal C_X\).

Transport this restricted functor through BR–BS and call it \(f_c^!\). The identification of the restricted \(F_f\) with BM's \(Rf_!^c\) comes from actual diagram maps: extension by zero commutes with \(\nu^*\) by (BM.2), and the proper-image comparison is the diagram adjunction map of BS.2. Its evaluated maps are BK's proper comparisons, so it is an isomorphism. Applying BR's inverse equivalence, namely the derived limit, gives exactly (BM.5), with the reductions of the single functor (BM.3). Thus the identification preserves the whole diagram, rather than just its component isomorphism classes. The diagram adjunction consequently gives the full adjunction \[ Rf_!^c:\mathcal C_X\rightleftarrows\mathcal C_Y:f_c^!, \qquad (f_c^!G)_n\simeq f_{O_n}^!G_n. \tag{BV.14} \] Its unit and counit are the transported diagram unit and counit. They satisfy both triangle identities before restriction. The adjunction holds for every shift and every morphism in these categories; it was not obtained by replacing a derived inverse limit of Hom complexes with an ordinary inverse limit of Hom groups.

Composition of right adjoints, with the counits specified by (BV.14), gives \((gf)_c^!\simeq f_c^!g_c^!\). The identities for three composable maps follow by transposing to the same composite counit. Smooth orientation and closed supports likewise pass from the diagram maps to give \[ p_c^!G\simeq p_c^*G(d)[2d], \qquad i_*i_c^!G\longrightarrow G\longrightarrow Rj_*j_c^*G \longrightarrow i_*i_c^!G[1]. \tag{BV.15} \] The first formula is for smooth relative dimension \(d\), and the second for a closed immersion with open complement. The Tate object here is the compatible completed rank-one system; BN supplies its invertible completed tensor. The positive trace and its composition are inherited from the coefficient-compatible maps of BV.2.

BV.5. Finite internal Hom across the two sites

One comparison is needed before reducing duality. For bounded constructible étale \(O_1\)-complexes \(A,B\), the evaluation-defined map is \[ \nu^*R\mathcal Hom_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(A,B) \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ } R\mathcal Hom_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}}(\nu^*A,\nu^*B). \tag{BV.16} \] Here and below the internal Hom has coefficients \(O_1\).

To prove it, first let \(A\) be a constructible sheaf. BT.1 and M.5 give a resolution of \(A\) in nonpositive degrees by finite sums of \(u_!O_1\), for affine étale maps \(u\) of finite presentation. Pullback by \(\nu\) preserves the resolution and these extension-by-zero sheaves. On either site, internal derived Hom from \(u_!O_1\) is \(Ru_*u^*B\), by the local adjunction of M.5 and BL.1. The bounded-below comparison of BK.2 and BK.5 identifies these terms across \(\nu\). All have the same lower bound as \(B\).

Resolve the target in bounded-below injectives. If its lower bound is \(b\), the Hom resolution has bidegrees \((r,s)\) with \(r\geq0\), \(s\geq b\), and total degree \(r+s\). Every diagonal is finite. Thus the termwise comparisons and exact pullback compare the resulting filtration degree by degree and prove (BV.16). They compare the evaluation map itself, because each generator comparison is its adjunction map. The finite cohomology filtration of a bounded \(A\) extends the assertion to complexes. This is not an assertion that a topos inverse image preserves internal Hom for arbitrary unbounded objects.

Since \(O_1\) is a finite field, M.7 proves that its bounded constructible category is closed under tensor and internal Hom. Thus the right side of (BV.16) is again bounded constructible classical. For any \(K,L\in\mathcal C_X\), BL.4 proves completeness of \(R\mathcal Hom_O(K,L)\), while BL.5 identifies its first reduction with \(R\mathcal Hom_{O_1}(K_1,L_1)\). Equation (BV.16) and M.7 make that reduction bounded constructible classical. Therefore \[ R\mathcal Hom_O(K,L)\in\mathcal C_X. \tag{BV.17} \] Together with BN, this gives a closed completed tensor structure on the bounded constructible category itself.

BV.6. Singular biduality with the canonical evaluation

For \(a_X:X\to\operatorname{Spec}k\), put \[ \Omega_X=a_{X,c}^!\mathbf1_k,\qquad \mathbb D_XK=R\mathcal Hom_O(K,\Omega_X). \tag{BV.18} \] BV.4 puts \(\Omega_X\) in \(\mathcal C_X\), and BV.5 puts \(\mathbb D_XK\) there. The exceptional coefficient comparison identifies \((\Omega_X)_1=a_{X,O_1}^!O_1\), the structural finite-field dualizing complex used in M.5–M.7.

The evaluation of the closed completed tensor category defines \[ \eta_K:K\longrightarrow\mathbb D_X\mathbb D_XK. \tag{BV.19} \] Explicitly, it is adjoint to the evaluation of \(K\) against its dual after tensor symmetry. This fixes the Koszul signs. By BL.5, both reductions of internal Hom are adjoints of reduced evaluation. Equation (BV.16) also preserves evaluation. Consequently reduction of (BV.19) modulo \(\pi\) is the canonical finite-field biduality map of M.6, not just a map between objects abstractly isomorphic to its domain and codomain. M.6–M.7 prove that map invertible on every bounded constructible complex, including singular and nonreduced schemes.

Both objects in (BV.19) are complete. Its cone is therefore complete; its first derived reduction vanishes. BK.4's complete-object conservativity makes the cone zero. This proves that (BV.19) is an isomorphism. Naturality follows from evaluation, and the two evaluation triangle identities identify \(\mathbb D_X\eta_K\) with the inverse of \(\eta_{\mathbb D_XK}\). Hence \(\mathbb D_X\) is an involutive contravariant equivalence of \(\mathcal C_X\).

This proof includes torsion \(O\)-coefficients. Their first derived reduction can have two adjacent cohomology degrees; the argument applies M.6 to that whole complex. It never replaces derived reduction by the ordinary quotient of cohomology or assumes a torsion sheaf is \(O\)-flat.

BV.7. The dual exchanges and coefficient comparisons

Transitivity gives \(f_c^!\Omega_Y=\Omega_X\). Tensor–Hom adjunction, BN's proper-support projection formula and (BV.14) now give \[ \mathbb D_YRf_!^cK\simeq Rf_*\mathbb D_XK, \qquad \mathbb D_Xf_c^*G\simeq f_c^!\mathbb D_YG. \tag{BV.20} \] Here are the representing Hom calculations. Testing the first object against \(E\in\mathcal C_Y\) gives maps from \(E\widehat\otimes Rf_!^cK\) to \(\Omega_Y\). Projection and exceptional adjunction turn these into maps from \(f_c^*E\widehat\otimes K\) to \(\Omega_X\). Internal Hom and \(f_c^*\dashv Rf_*\) identify these with maps from \(E\) to the first right-hand side. For the second identity, test \(f_c^!\mathbb D_YG\) against \(E\in\mathcal C_X\). Successively applying exceptional adjunction, internal Hom and projection gives maps from \(E\widehat\otimes f_c^*G\) to \(\Omega_X\). This represents the second left-hand side. Every object in these calculations belongs to the stated constructible category by BV.1, BV.4, BV.5 and BN.

Both calculations transpose evaluation through the specified counit. Their naturality therefore makes (BV.20) compatible with double evaluation. Applying (BV.19) gives \[ \mathbb D_YRf_*K\simeq Rf_!^c\mathbb D_XK, \qquad f_c^!G\simeq\mathbb D_Xf_c^*\mathbb D_YG. \tag{BV.21} \] The same test, with an arbitrary \(G\) in place of \(\Omega_Y\), gives the internal exceptional adjunction \[ Rf_*R\mathcal Hom_O(K,f_c^!G) \simeq R\mathcal Hom_O(Rf_!^cK,G). \tag{BV.22} \] Indeed maps from \(E\) to either side become maps from \(Rf_!^c(f_c^*E\widehat\otimes K)\) to \(G\). This proves the comparison with its pairing and counit.

Thus ordinary image, exceptional inverse image, the structural dualizing complex and singular biduality are established in the complete bounded constructible category over the stated field. The construction supplies the duality prerequisite for the positive-dimensional realization problem. BY proves realization on curves and the precise remaining geometric reduction in higher dimension; realization is not a consequence of biduality alone. BW–BX prove the rational coefficient passage with its lattice and higher-morphism comparisons. The complete finite-coefficient arguments used above are M, BF–BJ and BK–BS, with their precise earlier-programme prerequisites. The free comparison text [Laszlo–Olsson, II], §§4 and 7–9, treats adic internal Hom, duality and these operations.

Appendix BW. The coefficient ring and central rationalization

The complete category constructed in BK–BV lives initially in the derived category of sheaves over the constant ring \(\underline O\). Its tensor unit is the different sheaf \(\widehat O=\varprojlim_n\underline{O_n}\). We now construct the comparison with actual complexes of \(\widehat O\)-modules. This must be an equivalence on derived morphisms, not just an identification of quotient sheaves. We then invert the uniformizer in the resulting constructible category, keeping track of its heart, torsion kernel and operations.

Use the hypotheses and notation of BV. Write \[ \begin{gathered} A_X=\underline O,\qquad R_X=\widehat O,\qquad E_X=R_X[1/\pi],\\ D_A=D(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},A_X),\qquad D_R=D(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},R_X). \end{gathered} \tag{BW.1} \] The map \(A_X\to R_X\) is the completion unit with its ring multiplication. Subscripts \(A,R\) on completion distinguish the two module categories. A superscript \(c\) means derived complete; \(\mathcal C_X\subset D_A^c\) is the bounded constructible category of BM–BV.

BW.1. Derived completion for the completed ring itself

BP.2, applied to the strict constant system \(O_n\), gives \[ R_X/\pi^nR_X=\underline{O_n},\qquad R_X[\pi]=0. \tag{BW.2} \] The second equality also follows directly: in the tower of kernels of multiplication by \(\pi\) on \(O_n\), every transition is zero. Thus \([R_X\xrightarrow{\pi^n}R_X]\), in degrees \(-1,0\), is a free resolution of \(\underline{O_n}\) as an \(R_X\)-module. Its transition from \(n+1\) to \(n\) is \((\pi,1)\), exactly as in BK.3.

The module categories over \(A_X\) and over \(R_X\) have exact countable products. Products and kernels are computed in the underlying sheaves of abelian groups, where BK.1 proves exactness; their compatible coefficient actions are defined componentwise. The cell and injective constructions of BL.1 work for either sheaf of rings: replace its free module on each represented sheaf by the corresponding free \(R_X\)-module. The finite-sum lifting proof of flatness, the filtered cell construction and the slice adjunction remain the same.

Consequently the proof of BK.3–BK.4 applies to \(R_X\) with the free complexes just specified. Explicitly put \[ C_R P=\operatorname{holim}_n (P\otimes_{R_X}^L\underline{O_n}),\qquad L_{\pi,R}P=\operatorname{holim}(\cdots\xrightarrow{\pi}P). \tag{BW.3} \] The free telescope of \(R_X[1/\pi]\) identifies the second expression with \(R\mathcal Hom_{R_X}(R_X[1/\pi],P)\). Taking the product-cone limits of the coefficient triangles gives \[ L_{\pi,R}P\longrightarrow P\longrightarrow C_RP. \tag{BW.4} \] Multiplication by \(\pi\) is invertible on the first term. Each finite reduction is complete: in its \(\pi\)-tower the \(n\)-th power of the shift is null-homotopic, and the finite geometric series in that shift inverts \(1-s\). Complete objects are closed under products and fibres, so \(C_RP\) is complete. Tensoring (BW.4) with the finite free coefficient complex kills its first term. The completion unit therefore induces the identity comparison on every derived reduction.

If \(Q\) is complete, maps in every degree from a \(\pi\)-invertible object to \(Q\) vanish by tensor–Hom adjunction with \(R_X[1/\pi]\). Equation (BW.4) then proves that \(C_R\) is left adjoint to the inclusion of complete objects. It also proves detection of isomorphisms by all derived reductions. A zero first reduction suffices: its cone says that multiplication by \(\pi\) is invertible, while a complete object with that property is zero by (BW.4). These arguments use the actual \((\pi,1)\) transitions and apply to unbounded complexes.

BW.2. Extension and restriction of the coefficient ring

Let \(U:D_R\to D_A\) forget the \(R_X\)-action, and let \(S=R_X\otimes_{A_X}^L-\) be its derived left adjoint. The adjunction follows on the cell and injective models of BL.1, also on every slice; it does not require that \(R_X\) be a finite \(O\)-module. Restriction is exact and conservative and preserves products and the finite coefficient cones. Hence \[ UC_RP=C_AUP,\qquad P\in D_R^c\ \Longleftrightarrow\ UP\in D_A^c. \tag{BW.5} \] These identifications preserve completion units and all transition maps.

For later use \(R_X\) is flat over \(A_X\). Here is the local algebra check. For each site object, the \(O\)-module of sections of \(R_X\) is torsion-free, by (BW.2). A torsion-free \(O\)-module is flat: each finitely generated submodule is free by the DVR submodule argument in N.4, it is the filtered union of those submodules, and tensor and exactness pass to filtered unions. This sectionwise argument gives the sheaf assertion by the finite-relation criterion. A finite list of coefficients from the constant sheaf is constant after a covering refinement; a relation in a tensor sheaf has a finite local representative. The preceding flat-module calculation resolves that relation on this refinement, and sheafification is exact. In particular \(S\) is also represented by the exact ordinary extension functor, though the derived notation will retain the coefficient comparisons. Its exactness implies that \(U\) takes K-injectives to K-injectives: Hom from an acyclic \(A_X\)-complex is Hom from its acyclic scalar extension.

Define \[ T:D_A^c\longrightarrow D_R^c,\qquad T(K)=C_R(SK). \tag{BW.6} \] Completion and scalar adjunction give \(T\dashv U\) on the complete categories. On the source side of this adjunction \(U\) means its restriction in (BW.5).

We verify its unit, rather than deducing full faithfulness from a list of matching objects. Equations (BW.2) and the two free resolutions give, naturally in \(K\), \[ U(TK)\otimes_{A_X}^L\underline{O_n} \simeq U\bigl(TK\otimes_{R_X}^L\underline{O_n}\bigr) \simeq K\otimes_{A_X}^L\underline{O_n}. \tag{BW.7} \] For the second comparison first discard \(C_R\) using its unit, then use associativity of scalar extension and \(R_X\otimes_{A_X}^L\underline{O_n}=\underline{O_n}\). The latter equality is the two-term multiplication complex with (BW.2); no underived quotient of \(K\) is used. Under (BW.7) the unit \(K\to UTK\) is the identity of the displayed reduction: both are induced by \(A_X\to R_X\) and the same augmentation to \(O_n\). Its cone is complete with zero first reduction. Thus the unit is an isomorphism.

For complete \(P\in D_R\), the triangle identity is \[ U(\epsilon_P)\circ\eta_{UP}=1_{UP}. \] Since \(\eta_{UP}\) is invertible, \(U(\epsilon_P)\) is its inverse. Conservativity of restriction makes the counit invertible as well. We have proved \[ D_A^c\ \simeq\ D_R^c \tag{BW.8} \] by a specified adjunction. In particular the comparison includes every higher morphism. Equality of maps has been obtained from the adjunction identities, not from an assertion that reduction is faithful on maps.

BW.3. Constructibility, strict systems and the standard heart

Let \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\) consist of the complete \(R_X\)-complexes whose first derived reduction is a bounded constructible classical \(\kappa\)-complex. Equations (BW.5)–(BW.7) restrict (BW.8) to \[ T:\mathcal C_X\xrightarrow{\sim}\widehat{\mathcal C}_X, \qquad U\text{ its inverse}. \tag{BW.9} \] The boundedness assertions of BM and BQ carry over because restriction is exact. In particular \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\) is closed under standard truncations, and (BW.9) is t-exact for these bounded t-structures.

In degree zero this is especially concrete. The strict system \((F_n)\) of BP has limit \(F=\varprojlim_n\nu^*F_n\), and \(R_X=\varprojlim_n\underline{O_n}\) acts on it component by component. Its underlying \(A_X\)-sheaf is exactly BP.2's limit. Equation (BW.9) identifies that module sheaf with \(TF\). Every \(A_X\)-linear map between two such complete sheaves is therefore \(R_X\)-linear, by full faithfulness of \(U\); BP.3 identifies it with the compatible maps on the ordinary quotients.

The same equivalence for complexes cannot be constructed by arbitrarily adding coefficient actions to their cohomology sheaves. It is supplied by the actual complex \(C_R(SK)\) and its counit. Reduction of this complex produces the specified whole diagram of BR–BS: its augmentation maps and the coefficient transitions in (BW.7) are the same \((\pi,1)\) maps. Thus their diagram adjunctions and the degree-one inverse-limit term in BR.5 remain in force. Neither replacing derived reductions by ordinary quotients nor deleting that term is part of the comparison.

BW.4. Tensor, internal Hom and evaluation

Equip \(D_R^c\) with completed tensor \[ P\widehat\otimes_{R_X}Q=C_R(P\otimes_{R_X}^LQ). \tag{BW.10} \] Its unit is \(R_X\): the epimorphic tower \(O_n\) has derived limit equal to its ordinary limit by BK.1, so \(R_X\) is complete.

The equivalence \(T\) is symmetric monoidal for these completed tensors. To prove this with the specified maps, scalar extension has its ordinary associative isomorphism \[ S(K\otimes_{A_X}^LL) \simeq SK\otimes_{R_X}^LSL. \] The cone of each completion unit is \(\pi\)-invertible, by (BW.4) or BK.4. Scalar extension and tensor carry such a cone to another \(\pi\)-invertible cone. Completing therefore identifies both sides, with any of their factors first completed, and gives \[ T(K\widehat\otimes_OL) \simeq TK\widehat\otimes_{R_X}TL. \tag{BW.11} \] The unit comparison \(T(\mathbf1_X)\simeq R_X\) is the counit of (BW.8) at \(R_X\). Associativity, symmetry and the unit identities follow by precomposing with the uncompleted scalar-extension maps: maps into a complete object factor uniquely through completion, and the ordinary tensor identities already agree before that factorization. This is the coherence argument of BL.3 applied to the present scalar adjunction.

If \(Q\) is complete, \(R\mathcal Hom_{R_X}(P,Q)\) is complete. Indeed internal Hom carries the \(\pi\)-tower of \(Q\) and its product-cone limit to the \(\pi\)-tower of this internal Hom; tensor–Hom adjunction makes its localization Hom vanish just as in BL.4. Restriction of coefficients gives the natural comparison \[ U R\mathcal Hom_{R_X}(P,Q) \xrightarrow{\sim} R\mathcal Hom_{A_X}(UP,UQ) \qquad(P,Q\in D_R^c). \tag{BW.12} \] Here is also a check of this arrow. On every slice, scalar adjunction identifies the right side with the internal Hom from \(S(UP)\) into \(Q\). Replacing \(S(UP)\) by its completion changes no maps into the complete \(Q\). The counit \(TUP\to P\) then identifies this with the left side. Slice restriction preserves products and completion, by its exact extension-by-zero left adjoint in BL.1, so this is a sheafwise derived comparison. It is precisely the restriction map on evaluation and is compatible with (BW.11).

Consequently the evaluation maps, dualizing object and double-evaluation isomorphism of BV transport to \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\). Constructibility of internal Hom and completed tensor is preserved by (BW.9). These assertions concern completed tensor. BX.3 proves that ordinary tensor over \(R_X\) already agrees with it on the bounded constructible category.

BW.5. Geometric operations with their coefficient maps

For \(f:X\to Y\), the quotient-ring maps define a natural ring map \(f^{-1}R_Y\to R_X\). Set \[ \widehat f^{\,*}P =R_X\otimes_{f^{-1}R_Y}^Lf^{-1}P,\qquad \widehat f_c^{\,*}P=C_{R_X}\widehat f^{\,*}P. \tag{BW.13} \] The tensor associativity map before completion gives \(\widehat f^{\,*}S_YK=S_Xf^{-1}K\). Completing and using the \(\pi\)-invertible cones of the units as in BW.4 proves \[ \widehat f_c^{\,*}T_YK\simeq T_X f_c^*K. \tag{BW.14} \] The formula uses scalar extension along the displayed ring map. It makes no assumption that a general naive inverse image already preserves the completed coefficient ring.

Ordinary derived image for these ringed topoi satisfies \[ U_YR\widehat f_*P=Rf_*U_XP. \tag{BW.15} \] Resolve \(P\) by a K-injective \(R_X\)-complex. BW.2 makes its restriction K-injective over \(A_X\); both sides of (BW.15) are its same sectionwise image with the same underlying \(O\)-action. BK.5 and BV.1 now show that \(R\widehat f_*\) preserves completeness and constructibility. Scalar and geometric adjunction identify it as the right adjoint of (BW.13) on complete objects. Formulas (BW.14)–(BW.15) preserve the actual units and counits.

For an open immersion \(j\), restriction is a slice functor and \(j^{-1}R_X=R_U\). Extension by zero has the same underlying \(O\)-sheaf extension by zero, with its unique extended ring action. Applying completion gives the transported functor of BM.1, by (BW.5). A compactification \(f=pj\) therefore transports BM's \(Rp_*j_{c,!}\), together with its refinement comparisons, to \(\widehat{\mathcal C}\). BV's exceptional right adjoint transports through (BW.9), since the adjunction is a natural bijection on all morphisms in these categories. The completed projection formula, base change, composition, duality and their exchange maps transport through the same units and counits. Thus the change of coefficient-ring presentation preserves these operations. Equivalence with the bounded derived category of the heart is the separate realization assertion of BT, BU and BY–CB.

BW.6. Inverting the uniformizer as a triangulated localization

Define \(\mathcal C_X[1/\pi]\) to have the objects of \(\mathcal C_X\) and morphisms \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C_X[1/\pi]}(K,L) =\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal C_X}(K,L)\otimes_O O[1/\pi]. \tag{BW.16} \] Composition multiplies fractions. The same construction for \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\) is identified with it by (BW.9). A fraction \(u/\pi^a\) vanishes exactly when some \(\pi^b u\) vanishes in the original Hom module.

Declare a triangle distinguished if it is isomorphic to the image of a distinguished triangle in \(\mathcal C_X\). We verify that this is a triangulated structure. Shifts commute with fractions. Every morphism \(u/\pi^a\) has a cone triangle: use the original triangle of \(u\) and rescale its source by the invertible \(\pi^a\). Identity and rotation axioms follow immediately. Hom sequences of these triangles are exact because localization of \(O\)-modules is exact: an element or equality involves only finitely many denominators, which can be cleared.

For the morphism-of-triangles axiom, first replace the two given triangles by images of original triangles. Multiply both vertical maps of a commuting square by a common denominator. Their commutativity defect is zero after localization, so another common power of \(\pi\) kills it in the original Hom module. The original axiom supplies a third vertical map for this now commuting square. Divide all three vertical maps by the common power used. This gives exactly the requested map of triangles.

For the octahedron, write the two composable maps as \(a/\pi^r\) and \(b/\pi^s\). The diagram of the original maps \(a,b\) is isomorphic after localization to this diagram: the maps on its three objects are respectively \(\pi^{r+s},\pi^s,1\), and the two squares commute. Apply the original octahedral axiom to \(a,b\) and transport the result. Any prescribed cone triangles can be substituted: the preceding morphism-of-triangles axiom supplies their comparison, and exact localized Hom sequences show that a map of triangles invertible on two objects is invertible on the third. This proves the remaining axiom.

The functor to (BW.16) is exact and universal among \(O\)-linear exact functors making \(\pi\) invertible: its value on \(u/\pi^a\) must be the value on \(u\) followed by the inverse of multiplication by \(\pi^a\). This prescription is well defined by the zero-fraction criterion, respects composition and is unique.

Its zero objects are exactly those \(K\) for which \(\pi^N1_K=0\) for some \(N\). They are also exactly the objects all of whose cohomology sheaves are killed by some power of \(\pi\). One direction follows by applying cohomology. For the converse only finitely many cohomology sheaves occur, by BM.6 and BQ. In a triangle \(A\to B\to C\), if \(\pi^a1_A=0\) and \(\pi^b1_C=0\), exactness of \(\operatorname{Hom}(B,-)\) makes \(\pi^b1_B\) factor through \(A\). Multiplication by \(\pi^a\) kills that factorization. Induction through the finite truncation tower kills \(K\) by the product of the powers killing its cohomology. This also proves directly that the zero objects form a thick triangulated subcategory.

BW.7. The rational heart, adjunctions and duality

The images of the standard nonpositive and nonnegative subcategories, closed under isomorphism, define a bounded t-structure on (BW.16). Orthogonality follows by localizing its zero Hom groups; every original truncation triangle gives the required triangle after localization. The shift inclusions and boundedness persist. Uniqueness of the truncation triangle follows from the same orthogonality argument as before localization, so these really are the induced truncation functors.

Its heart is the localization of the strict constructible heart in BP–BQ. Indeed this heart embeds fully faithfully by (BW.16). If an object of the localized category lies in the heart, its cohomology in every other degree is zero in that category. Each such cohomology sheaf is therefore killed by a power of \(\pi\). The finite-truncation argument in BW.6 makes both outer truncations zero, identifying the object with its degree-zero cohomology. For a morphism between heart objects, choose a numerator; its kernel and cokernel are the localized kernel and cokernel of that numerator, since multiplication by its denominator is an isomorphism. The explicit BP quotient and torsion constructions therefore also describe this rational heart.

Every operation constructed in BL, BM, BN and BV is \(O\)-linear, including the internal Hom contravariantly in its first variable. They consequently descend to this localization. Their adjunctions continue to hold: tensor each of their natural \(O\)-linear Hom bijections with \(O[1/\pi]\). For example \[ \operatorname{Hom}(f_!K,L) \simeq\operatorname{Hom}(K,f_c^!L) \tag{BW.17} \] in the localized categories is exactly the localization of BV's bijection. The completed tensor and its internal Hom remain adjoint for the same reason. All units, counits, projection and base-change maps, positive Tate orientations and the canonical biduality map are the images of those already constructed. Their identities and invertibility are preserved by the exact localization functor. In particular this gives the rational six-operation formalism on the localized complete category.

This statement is independent of whether the general realization functor of BT is an equivalence. No higher Ext comparison for that heart has been inferred just from constructing its localization.

BW.8. The canonical comparison with actual rational sheaves

There is a canonical exact functor \[ \Phi_X:\widehat{\mathcal C}_X[1/\pi] \longrightarrow D(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},E_X),\qquad P\longmapsto E_X\otimes_{R_X}^LP. \tag{BW.18} \] Localization of module sheaves is exact: it is the filtered colimit of the multiplication-by-\(\pi\) sequence. Thus the formula is also \(P[1/\pi]\), and multiplication by \(\pi\) is invertible on its target. BW.6 gives the displayed factorization on all fractions.

This functor is conservative. To check its kernel on objects, suppose \(P[1/\pi]=0\). Each cohomology sheaf \(F\) of \(UP\) then consists locally of sections killed by powers of \(\pi\). BP.1–BP.2 give a single exponent \(c_F\) killing all its torsion kernels \(F[\pi^n]\), simultaneously for every \(n\). Their filtered union is \(F\), so \(\pi^{c_F}F=0\). Only finitely many \(F\) occur, and BW.6 now makes \(P\) zero in the localized category. Conversely any zero object there plainly has zero image. Applying this to cones proves detection of isomorphisms.

BX proves full faithfulness on every higher Hom and constructs integral models for every bounded complex with constructible \(E_X\)-cohomology. It also identifies the ordinary tensor and geometric operations. These assertions require more than the conservativity just proved. A global lisse integral lattice can fail on a singular scheme, as the pro-étale lesson, Proposition 7.2 proves by its nodal example; BX.6 constructs the appropriate constructible integral models without assuming a global lisse lattice.

The coefficient categories and these rational comparisons are discussed in the freely accessible Bhatt–Scholze, §§6.5 and 6.8, version 2. The adjunction, localization and conservativity above are completed by the full comparison (BX.20). Heart realization is a separate assertion, treated in BT, BU and BY–CB.

Appendix BX. Strata, integral models and the rational sheaf category

Keep the finite-type schemes, complete DVR \(O\), finite residue field, uniformizer \(\pi\), and coefficient sheaves \(R_X=\widehat O\) and \(E_X=R_X[1/\pi]\) of BW. Write \(E=O[1/\pi]\). A constructible \(E_X\)-sheaf means one which is locally finite free in the pro-étale topology on each member of a finite algebraic stratification. Let \(D_{\mathrm{cons}}(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},E_X)\) be the full subcategory of complexes with bounded constructible cohomology. We will prove that (BW.18) is an equivalence with this category, including all higher morphisms. The proof also identifies the ordinary tensor and geometric operations. It does not assume the separate realization theorem for the derived category of the constructible heart.

BX.1. Lifting a closed-stratum neighbourhood

We first give the site calculation needed for restriction to a stratum. Let \(A\) be a ring, \(I\) an ideal, and \(B_0\) an ind-étale \(A/I\)-algebra. Consider all factorizations \(A\to C\to B_0\) with \(C\) étale over \(A\), and put \[ H_A(B_0)=\varinjlim_{(C\to B_0)}C. \tag{BX.1} \] This indexing category is filtered. Tensor products give common successors. To equalize two parallel maps \(C\rightrightarrows D\), take their equality locus in \(\operatorname{Spec}D\). The diagonal of the affine étale \(A\)-scheme \(\operatorname{Spec}C\) is both open and closed, so this locus is a clopen affine subscheme, still étale over \(A\). The map \(\operatorname{Spec}B_0\to\operatorname{Spec}D\) factors through it. Its coordinate algebra gives the required equalizer in the indexing category.

We use the following elementary lifting fact at its arbitrary-ideal scope. An étale \(A/I\)-algebra has a presentation by a square system with invertible Jacobian. Lift the coefficients to \(A\) and invert the lifted Jacobian determinant. The resulting algebra is étale over \(A\) and reduces to the given algebra. The square presentation and its determinant-trick proof are in Infinitesimal lifting, Lemma 6.1; the lifting calculation is Étale neighbourhoods, Lemma 5.4. In particular this assertion does not require \(I\) to be nilpotent.

The natural map \[ H_A(B_0)/IH_A(B_0)\longrightarrow B_0 \tag{BX.2} \] is an isomorphism. It is surjective because every element of \(B_0\) occurs at a finitely presented étale \(A/I\)-stage, and that stage has the preceding lift. For injectivity, represent an element in its kernel by \(c\in C\). The map \(C/IC\to B_0\) is ind-étale. To see the assertion about this map, descend the finitely presented algebra \(C/IC\) and its map to a stage of an étale presentation of \(B_0\). A map between two étale algebras over the same base is étale: its scheme map factors as its open graph into the fibre product followed by the étale projection. The tail is therefore an étale presentation over \(C/IC\). At some such stage \(D_0\), the image of \(c\) is zero. Lift \(D_0\) to an étale \(C\)-algebra \(D\). Then \(c\in ID\), and \(D\to D/ID=D_0\to B_0\) is a later object of (BX.1). Thus \(c\) is zero in the left side of (BX.2).

For every ind-étale \(A\)-algebra \(T\) there is a natural bijection \[ \operatorname{Hom}_A(T,H_A(B_0)) =\operatorname{Hom}_{A/I}(T/IT,B_0). \tag{BX.3} \] A map on the right makes each étale stage of \(T\) an object of (BX.1), giving its lift. For uniqueness, a map from a finitely presented stage factors through some \(C\) in (BX.1). Its composite to \(B_0\) fixes that stage's object in the indexing category; its map into the colimit is consequently the specified one. Passing to the colimit of stages proves uniqueness for \(T\).

Set \(X=\operatorname{Spec}A\), \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I)\). On the affine ind-étale bases let \(u(V)=V\times_XZ\) and \[ v(\operatorname{Spec}B_0)=\operatorname{Spec}H_A(B_0). \] Equations (BX.2)–(BX.3) say that \(v\) is a fully faithful left adjoint to \(u\), and \(u v=1\). Every point of \(v(V)\) specializes into \(V\). Indeed, if \(b\in H_A(B_0)\) becomes invertible modulo \(I\), the localization at \(b\) is ind-étale over \(A\). Equation (BX.3) supplies a map from this localization back to \(H_A(B_0)\) whose composite with localization is the identity. Hence \(b\) was already a unit, so \(I H_A(B_0)\) lies in the Jacobson radical.

The functor \(v\) sends finite covers to covers. Their lifted maps are flat: maps between ind-étale algebras over \(A\) are ind-étale by the same finite-stage argument used above. Their images are stable under generalization, by flat going down. They cover the closed part \(V\), and every point of \(v(V)\) has a specialization there. They therefore cover \(v(V)\). Furthermore, any cover of \(v(V)\) pulls back to one of \(V\); applying \(v\) to that cover gives, by adjunction, a refinement of the original cover.

If \(V\) is weakly contractible, so is \(v(V)\). A finite affine covering of \(v(V)\), pulled back to \(V\), has a section from \(V\) to its disjoint union. Apply \(v\) and the preceding refinement maps. Since a left adjoint preserves finite disjoint unions, this gives a section of the original disjoint-union cover. Refinement by affine ind-étale objects, proved in the pro-étale lesson, tests all covers. Thus evaluation at \(v(V)\) is exact, just as evaluation at \(V\) is.

BX.2. The ordinary localization sequence on the pro-étale site

Let \(i:Z\hookrightarrow X\) be closed with quasi-compact open complement \(j:U\hookrightarrow X\). All closed immersions between the Noetherian schemes used here satisfy this condition. The formula for inverse image on the preceding affine bases is sheafification of \(V\mapsto F(v(V))\). This follows directly from (BX.3): the neighbourhood colimit defining inverse image has the specified initial geometric neighbourhood. At a weakly contractible \(V\), sheafification leaves that value unchanged: \[ (i^{-1}F)(V)=F(v(V)). \tag{BX.4} \] For detail, the presheaf is separated since \(v\) sends covers to covers. It preserves finite disjoint unions as products. A finite cover of \(V\) can be replaced by its disjoint union and then split, so its matching family is already a section. This proves (BX.4), including its compatibility with maps of sheaves.

Limits of sheaves are computed on sections. Evaluating on the weakly contractible basis in (BX.4) proves that \(i^{-1}\) commutes with all small limits. As an inverse-image functor it is also exact and preserves colimits. In particular \[ i^{-1}R_X=R_Z,\qquad i^{-1}E_X=E_Z. \tag{BX.5} \] For an open immersion the same facts follow from restriction to the slice site.

The functor \(i_*\) is exact. Suppose \(F\to G\) is an epimorphism on \(Z\) and \(g\in G(V_Z)\) for an affine ind-étale \(V\to X\). Lift \(g\) on a finite affine ind-étale cover \(W\to V_Z\). Its lift \(v_V(W)\to V\), together with a finite affine cover of \(V_U\), is a pro-étale cover of \(V\). On its first piece \(g\) lifts by construction; on its other pieces the closed fibre is empty. This proves the required local surjectivity. The quasi-compactness of \(V_U\), and hence the hypothesis on \(U\), is used here. Equation (BX.4) also proves the counit \(i^{-1}i_*\to1\) is an isomorphism.

Open extension by zero \(j_!\) is exact, by the local finite-sum description in BL.1. We check its closed restriction. If \(V\) is weakly contractible over \(Z\), the affine \(v(V)\) is weakly contractible and each of its points specializes into \(V\). A section of \(j_!F\) is locally a finite collection of sections on pieces mapping into \(U\). Split such a finite cover of \(v(V)\). The splitting partitions \(v(V)\) into clopen pieces; any piece supporting one of those sections must lie in \(U\). It is empty: a nonempty clopen piece contains the specializations of its points, including one in \(V\). Consequently \(j_!F(v(V))=0\), so \(i^{-1}j_!=0\).

The exact functors \(i^{-1}\) and \(j^{-1}\) are jointly conservative. To verify this for a sheaf, cover the closed fibre of any affine object by weakly contractible affines, lift them by \(v\), and add its open complement. Zero on both restrictions gives zero sections locally on this cover. Applied to kernels and cokernels, this detects isomorphisms. We already have \(j^{-1}i_*=0\), \(j^{-1}j_!=1\), and \(i^{-1}i_*=1\). Applying the two restrictions therefore proves the functorial exact sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow j_!j^{-1}F\longrightarrow F \longrightarrow i_*i^{-1}F\longrightarrow0. \tag{BX.6} \] This proves the sequence without assuming that ordinary geometric stalks form a conservative family for all pro-étale sheaves.

Everything just proved applies to modules over \(R_X\), using (BX.5), and to \(E_X\)-modules. Exactness gives the corresponding triangle on the unbounded derived categories. These categories have exact products by BK.1 and its ringed version in BW.1. Thus \(i^{-1}\), being exact and product-preserving, commutes with the product-cone formula for derived inverse limits. The exact right adjoint \(i_*\) also commutes with those limits. Applied to \(Rj_*K\), (BX.6) gives \[ j_!K\longrightarrow Rj_*K \longrightarrow i_*i^{-1}Rj_*K. \tag{BX.7} \] The other two functors commute with homotopy limits, since \(Rj_*\) is a right adjoint. Taking fibres proves the same assertion for \(j_!\). All these functors commute with the two-term coefficient cones. Therefore ordinary \(i^{-1},i_*,j^{-1},j_!\) preserve derived completeness whenever their inputs are complete.

Their first reductions are the corresponding finite-coefficient operations. For \(i_*\) and \(j_!\), compatibility with classical finite-coefficient sheaves follows either from the coefficient comparison of BK.2 or directly on affine ind-étale presentations: finite-presentation descent and the finite sheaf equalizer commute with the filtered limit of the presentation; extension by zero is then determined by (BX.6). Consequently these four ordinary functors preserve the bounded constructible categories in BW.3. Ordinary and completed restriction and extension by zero agree there.

For later use closed support has an explicit right adjoint even on the ambient derived category. Set \[ i^!Q=i^{-1}\operatorname{Fib} \bigl(Q\longrightarrow Rj_*j^{-1}Q\bigr). \tag{BX.8} \] The fibre restricts to zero on \(U\), so (BX.6) identifies it with \(i_*i^!Q\). Every map, in every degree, from \(i_*L\) to \(Rj_*j^{-1}Q\) is zero by open adjunction. Hence the fibre triangle and the full faithfulness of \(i_*\) give \(i_*\dashv i^!\). Both (BX.7) and (BX.8) use their actual adjunction maps.

BX.3. Ordinary tensor and inverse image

For \(P\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\), ordinary restriction to a stratum now equals its completed restriction. BO therefore supplies a pro-étale local finite perfect \(O\)-complex on each connected stratum. As an \(R\)-complex this is the corresponding finite free complex with those same constant matrices. In particular its ordinary tensor with a complete complex is complete: locally it is made from finitely many shifts, sums and cones of that complex. Completeness is local in the pro-étale topology, because slice restriction preserves products, coefficient cones and the completion unit.

Here are the support formulas used to assemble the strata. For an arbitrary \(R_X\)-complex \(Q\), \[ \begin{aligned} (j_!L)\otimes_{R_X}^{L}Q &\simeq j_!\bigl(L\otimes_{R_U}^{L}j^{-1}Q\bigr),\\ (i_*L)\otimes_{R_X}^{L}Q &\simeq i_*\bigl(L\otimes_{R_Z}^{L}i^{-1}Q\bigr). \end{aligned} \tag{BX.9} \] These are the projection maps defined by adjunction. The first is the finite-sum extension-by-zero formula on the K-flat cell resolutions. For the second use the unit to the closed-support image. Applying \(i^{-1}\) makes this map the tensor identity, since (BX.5) makes restriction exact and monoidal. Applying \(j^{-1}\) makes both sides zero. Joint conservativity proves it is an isomorphism. Thus no flatness assertion about a closed-support module is being assumed to prove the formula.

Choose an open stratum where \(P\) has its local finite-perfect description and use (BX.6) for \(P\). Formula (BX.9) treats its open term. Induction on the finite closed-stratum filtration treats its closed term. BX.2 makes both ordinary extensions preserve completeness. We obtain \[ P\otimes_{R_X}^{L}Q \ \xrightarrow{\sim}\ P\widehat\otimes_{R_X}Q \qquad(P,Q\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_X). \tag{BX.10} \] Its first reduction is the constructible finite-coefficient tensor, so the ordinary tensor is constructible as well. Any finite stratification can be refined to the filtration used here: remove a dense open part of its finitely many generic strata, and repeat on the closed complement. Noetherian induction terminates; in the present finite-dimensional schemes the remaining dimension decreases after collecting all generic pieces.

The same argument identifies ordinary geometric inverse image. For \(f:X\to Y\) use the actual ringed inverse image \[ Lf_R^*P=R_X\otimes_{f^{-1}R_Y}^{L}f^{-1}P. \tag{BX.11} \] It takes a local finite perfect complex to the same finite complex over \(R_X\), after pulling back its trivializing cover. It commutes with extension by zero and with closed-support image in a cartesian square. For the closed formula, the pulled-back complex is zero on the complementary open, and its closed restriction is the claimed inverse image by associativity of scalar extension. Equation (BX.6) identifies the complex with that closed image. The open formula follows in the same way, or from the first cell formula in (BX.9). Devissage on strata now proves that (BX.11) is complete and constructible for \(P\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_Y\). Its completion map is therefore an isomorphism, so it is the transported inverse image of BW.5. The coefficient map \(f^{-1}R_Y\to R_X\) remains part of the formula for general \(f\).

BX.4. Bounded-below continuity

We need continuity in the target of derived Hom, including positive degrees. We give the site argument, so an unrestricted compactness assumption is unnecessary.

On the pro-étale site of a quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme, evaluation at a quasi-compact quasi-separated object commutes with filtered colimits of sheaves. Indeed that site has a basis of quasi-compact objects, finite fibre products can be covered by finitely many basis objects, and coverings of a basis object have finite covering refinements. The sheaf equalizer for any such finite cover uses finite products and equalizers. Filtered colimits of modules commute with these finite limits. Thus the sectionwise filtered colimit is already a sheaf on the basis.

The derived statement is \[ \varinjlim_\alpha R\Gamma(V,Q_\alpha) \ \xrightarrow{\sim}\ R\Gamma\bigl(V,\varinjlim_\alpha Q_\alpha\bigr) \quad\text{if every }Q_\alpha\in D^{\ge b}, \tag{BX.12} \] for one common \(b\). Here and below filtered colimits are derived colimits, computed termwise on complexes because filtered colimits of sheaves are exact. To prove (BX.12), cover \(V\) by finitely many weakly contractible affine objects. Cover the successive matching objects in the same way. They are quasi-compact quasi-separated: at each finite stage only finite products, fibre products and finite covers of the preceding objects occur. This constructs a hypercover with a finite disjoint union of weakly contractible affines in every degree.

Its augmented alternating-face free-module complex resolves the free module represented by \(V\). The exactness can be checked locally in each degree: choose a local vertex and lift the finitely many cones on the faces of a finite chain successively along the matching covers. The alternating boundary formula for these cones is \(\partial h+h\partial=1\), with augmentation in degree zero. Thus a cycle becomes a boundary on a covering, which is exactly sheaf exactness. Each term of this resolution is a finite sum of modules represented freely by weakly contractible affines. Such a module is projective, since Hom from it is exact section evaluation, and that Hom commutes with filtered colimits by the preceding paragraph.

Use this bounded-above projective resolution to compute derived Hom into \(Q_\alpha\). Replace each target by its good truncation in degrees at least \(b\). In total degree \(n\), only resolution degrees \(0,\ldots,n-b\) occur. The resulting diagonal is finite. Filtered colimits therefore commute with every term on the diagonal and with its cohomology. This proves (BX.12). The proof works for any of the sheaves of rings under discussion, using free modules over that sheaf, and on every quasi-compact slice.

It follows that \(Rg_*\) commutes with uniformly bounded-below filtered colimits for every quasi-compact quasi-separated geometric map under consideration, with its indicated coefficient map. Indeed its value as derived sections on an affine target object is \(R\Gamma\) of the quasi-compact quasi-separated base change on the source. Such evaluations test the comparison. For an open \(j\), (BX.8) and exact restriction consequently give the same continuity for \(i^!\). This functor preserves a common lower bound: \(Rj_*\) is left t-exact, and the fibre of a map between objects in \(D^{\ge b}\) lies in \(D^{\ge b}\).

Now fix \(P\in\widehat{\mathcal C}_X\). We claim \[ \varinjlim_\alpha R\operatorname{Hom}_{R_X}(P,Q_\alpha) \ \xrightarrow{\sim}\ R\operatorname{Hom}_{R_X} \bigl(P,\varinjlim_\alpha Q_\alpha\bigr) \qquad(Q_\alpha\in D^{\ge b}). \tag{BX.13} \] There is also the analogous internal-Hom comparison on every slice. On a stratum where \(P\) is locally finite perfect, internal Hom is computed by a finite dual complex and tensor. It preserves these colimits locally, hence as sheaves. Its targets have a common lower bound: use the common finite amplitude from BO, or take the maximum over a finite quasi-compact trivializing cover.

For the closed term of a stratification use the derived adjunction \[ R\mathcal Hom_X(i_*L,Q) =i_*R\mathcal Hom_Z(L,i^!Q). \tag{BX.14} \] For the open term use \(Rj_*R\mathcal Hom_U(L,j^{-1}Q)\). These identities hold internally because the adjunctions just proved hold on every slice; the formula for \(i^!\) restricts to that slice by its fibre formula. The functors \(i_*\) and \(i^{-1}\) preserve filtered colimits, either by (BX.4) and finite-cover section evaluation or by the same evaluation proof on the closed fibre. The other functors have the bounded-below continuity just established. Inducting on the finite strata with the contravariant Hom triangle proves the internal comparison and a uniform lower bound for its targets. Finally apply (BX.12) to obtain (BX.13). This argument retains a fixed lower bound throughout. It makes no assertion about arbitrary families unbounded below.

BX.5. Localization of every higher morphism

Take the multiplication-by-\(\pi\) sequence of a bounded constructible \(R_X\)-complex \(Q\). Its colimit is \(Q[1/\pi]\). Equation (BX.13), with no dependence of its lower bound on the transition index, gives for every integer \(m\) \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{D_R}(P,Q[m])[1/\pi] \ \xrightarrow{\sim}\ \operatorname{Hom}_{D_R}(P,Q[1/\pi][m]). \tag{BX.15} \] Localization is flat and left adjoint to restriction of \(E_X\)-modules. Its derived scalar adjunction identifies the right side with \(\operatorname{Hom}_{D(E_X)}(P[1/\pi],Q[1/\pi][m])\). The resulting map is precisely rationalization of a numerator followed by its scalar denominator. Thus (BW.18) is fully faithful, including all higher morphisms and their compositions. Applied on slices, the same proof gives the specified comparison \[ R\mathcal Hom_{R_X}(P,Q)[1/\pi] \simeq R\mathcal Hom_{E_X}(P[1/\pi],Q[1/\pi]). \tag{BX.16} \] It is compatible with evaluation, because both its adjunction and the filtered-colimit map are induced by evaluation.

The image has bounded constructible cohomology. BQ and BP express the cohomology of \(P\) on finitely many strata by finite \(O\)-modules. Localizing those modules gives finite-dimensional \(E\)-spaces, and localization is exact. This also shows that (BW.18) is t-exact.

BX.6. Constructible integral models

We first establish lattices étale locally for a lisse \(E_X\)-sheaf \(L\), without a hypothesis that \(L\) comes from a global profinite representation. On an affine pro-étale object \(V\), sections of \(R_X\) are continuous functions from the profinite component space of \(V\) to \(O\): this is the inverse limit of the finite locally constant \(O_n\)-valued functions. Sections of \(E_X\) are the corresponding continuous \(E\)-valued functions. Their denominators are bounded by compactness, so this follows by localizing the first description and the finite-cover colimit calculation in BX.4.

On a trivialization \(L=E_X^r\), the sheaf of integral lattices in \(L\) is the constant discrete sheaf with value \[ \operatorname{GL}_r(E)/\operatorname{GL}_r(O). \tag{BX.17} \] A proposed lattice, trivialized together with \(L\), is described by a continuous invertible matrix. Its coset is locally constant because \(\operatorname{GL}_r(O)\) is open; conversely each coset supplies a lattice. This proves the assertion as sheaves, allowing different cosets on different clopen pieces. The classical-descent proof in the pro-étale lesson, Lemma 7.1 then makes the lattice sheaf classical. It is locally inhabited on the pro-étale site, so its corresponding étale sheaf is locally inhabited: the fully faithful exact inverse image reflects the image subobject of its map to the terminal sheaf. Hence a lattice exists on an étale cover. This proof uses completeness, the finite residue quotients and the open subgroup in (BX.17); it works for the stated DVR \(O\), including equal characteristic.

There is a finite stratification on which that cover can be replaced by finite étale covers carrying lattices. Here are the algebraic details. A reduced irreducible affine stratum has an integral coordinate ring \(A\). Choose an affine piece of the étale cover meeting its generic point. Its coordinate algebra \(B\) is finitely presented and its generic fibre is a nonzero finite étale algebra over \(\operatorname{Frac}A\). Each of finitely many algebra generators satisfies a monic equation over that field. Clear all coefficient denominators. The equation evaluated in \(B\) is zero after passage to the generic fibre, so invert also the finitely many elements of \(A\) that kill these errors. On the resulting nonempty open, \(B\) is generated by finitely many integral elements and is therefore finite over \(A\). It remains étale; its positive generic rank is constant after taking a connected open part, so it is surjective there. Do this for the finitely many generic components and continue on the smaller closed complement. Finite dimension gives termination. Nonreduced strata cause no problem: reduction induces an equivalence of the pro-étale topoi, since (BX.6) for a nilpotent closed immersion has empty open complement and \(i^{-1}i_*=1\). We may perform the construction on the reduced strata.

Let \(W\to S\) be one of the resulting finite étale surjections, of constant degree \(d\), with a lattice on \(W\). The scheme \(T\) of orderings of its \(d\) geometric fibre points is a finite étale surjection: it is the clopen locus in \(W^d_S\) where all coordinates are distinct. Étale local splitting of \(W\), proved in N.1, identifies \(T\) with the permutations of \(d\) points. Thus \(T\to S\) is a torsor under the finite group \(G=\mathfrak S_d\). Pull the lattice to \(T\) through its first projection and call it \(N\subset L|_T\). Inside that same sheaf form \[ N'=\sum_{g\in G}gN. \tag{BX.18} \] This is again a lisse \(R_T\)-lattice. Locally trivialize \(L\) and the finitely many lattices. By (BX.17) refine into clopen pieces on which their relative lattice positions are fixed. On each piece their sum is the extension of a sum of finitely many \(O\)-lattices in \(E^r\). That sum is a finite torsion-free \(O\)-module of rank \(r\), hence free, and spans \(E^r\). Equation (BX.18) is invariant under \(G\). Its descent maps satisfy the cocycle condition as restrictions of those of \(L|_T\). Sheaf descent along the finite étale torsor therefore gives a lattice on \(S\). This argument uses a finite group of deck transformations, not a profinite classification on an arbitrary singular scheme.

A lisse integral lattice lies in the heart of \(\widehat{\mathcal C}_S\). Completeness is local on the trivializing pro-étale cover. Its first quotient is locally constant and finite over \(\kappa\); it is classical by the same descent lemma. Equivalently BP identifies its strict quotient system. BX.2 shows that its extension by zero from a locally closed stratum is still a constructible complete sheaf.

Every constructible \(E_X\)-sheaf \(F\) has a constructible integral model. Refine its stratification by the one just constructed. The exact sequence (BX.6), repeatedly applied, filters \(F\) by extensions of lisse stratum sheaves extended by zero, each with an integral model. Suppose two successive pieces have models \(N'\) and \(N''\). Equation (BX.15) in degree one identifies their extension class with \[ e=u/\pi^a,\qquad u\in\operatorname{Ext}^1_{R_X}(N'',N'). \tag{BX.19} \] The degree-one roof-to-extension construction in BT.2 supplies the sheaf extension with class \(u\): its normalization is \(\epsilon_1=1\), so the pushout represents the given degree-one derived morphism. BT.3 identifies this extension with the corresponding heart extension. Its middle sheaf belongs to the constructible complete heart by BQ's extension closure. After rationalization, rescale the identification of the first end term by \(\pi^{-a}\). The resulting extension class is \(e\), so the rationalized middle term is the desired extension. Induction constructs a model for \(F\). The result is a constructible model; no global lisse lattice has been asserted.

BX.7. Equivalence and the geometric operations

The essential image of the fully faithful functor (BW.18) is closed under all cones of morphisms between its objects. By (BX.15) each such morphism is a fraction of an integral one. Its cone is isomorphic to the localization of that integral cone, by rescaling the source. It is closed under shifts as well. BX.6 places every constructible \(E_X\)-sheaf in the image. The finite cohomological truncation tower of any bounded complex with constructible cohomology therefore places that complex in the image. We have proved the t-exact equivalence \[ \widehat{\mathcal C}_X[1/\pi] \ \xrightarrow[\ P\mapsto P[1/\pi]\ ]{\ \sim\ }\ D_{\mathrm{cons}}(X_{\mathrm{pro\acute et}},E_X). \tag{BX.20} \] This also proves that the indicated full subcategory on the right is triangulated and closed under standard truncations: it is the essential image of a triangulated functor and of its t-exact bounded truncations. Its heart is the category of constructible \(E_X\)-sheaves and is the rationalized strict heart of BW.7.

For clarity the operation comparisons use actual ambient functors. By (BX.10), ordinary derived tensor over \(R_X\), then localization, gives ordinary derived tensor over \(E_X\). Equation (BX.16) identifies the internal Homs with their evaluation. Ordinary ringed inverse image in (BX.11) already equals completed inverse image on the integral constructible category. Associativity of extension of scalars consequently gives \[ (Lf_R^*P)[1/\pi] \simeq E_X\otimes_{f^{-1}E_Y}^{L}f^{-1}(P[1/\pi]). \tag{BX.21} \] For ordinary derived image apply (BX.12) to the multiplication tower on every quasi-compact target slice: \[ (Rf_{R,*}P)[1/\pi] \simeq Rf_{E,*}(P[1/\pi]). \tag{BX.22} \] The map is the natural scalar-localization comparison. Coefficient restriction preserves the resolutions used to calculate these images, as in BW.2; alternatively the sectionwise calculation in BX.4 proves the same map. BV's constructibility result and (BX.20) show that its right side is constructible at the geometric scope of BV.

Ordinary \(j_!\) is already complete by BX.2 and commutes with localization by its exact finite-sum description. For a compactification \(f=pj\), equations (BX.22) and this open comparison identify the localized proper-support functor with \(Rp_*j_!\) on actual rational sheaf complexes. The refinement maps are induced by the same adjunction maps before and after localization. Thus the compactification independence proved in BM carries over with those maps.

Finally transport BV's \(f_c^!\) through (BX.20). This identifies its Hom adjunction with the actual proper-support functor just identified, for every pair of constructible rational complexes and in every degree. It is therefore that functor's exceptional right adjoint on the constructible categories. For a closed immersion it also agrees with the ambient right adjoint (BX.8), since that formula commutes with the same localization comparisons. No right adjoint on every unbounded nonconstructible complex is needed for this statement.

All tensor adjunctions, operation adjunctions and comparisons used above are their scalar-extension, restriction or support maps. Their mates consequently identify the projection, base-change and composition maps with those of BW.7. In particular the localized dualizing object is the exceptional image of the rational unit, (BX.16) identifies its duality functor with ambient internal Hom, and its double-evaluation map is BV's isomorphism under (BX.20). This proves the rational comparison with its six operations and duality at the established constructible scope.

The free comparison source is Bhatt–Scholze, version 2, §§2.2, 6.1 and 6.8. The neighbourhood calculation, finite-diagonal continuity, finite-group lattice descent and extension-class lifting above supply the proofs used here. Equivalence (BX.20) concerns the full constructible subcategory of the ambient derived category. Equivalence with the bounded derived category of its heart is a further assertion. BY proves it for curves over finite or algebraically closed fields. The higher-dimensional projection and effacement arguments are treated in BZ–CB.

Appendix BY. Constructible effacement and realization on curves

Let \(k\) be algebraically closed or finite, and let \(X\) be separated and of finite type over \(k\). Retain the complete discrete valuation ring \(O\), its finite residue field \(\kappa\), and its fraction field \(E\); the residue characteristic is invertible in \(k\). We prove realization in dimension at most one, including singular schemes, integral torsion and rational coefficients. The reduction in general dimension uses the precise projection assertion (BY.26). Appendix CB supplies its geometric argument from BZ–CA; the realization deduction retains the stated coefficient and foundational hypotheses of these appendices.

We use the equivalent actual completed-ring category of BW, with unit \(\mathbf1_X=R_X\), and write \(\mathcal H_X\) for its constructible heart. Thus \[ H^q(X,F)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(\mathbf1_X,F[q]) \] is ordinary derived cohomology of the corresponding \(R_X\)-module. BW's adjunction identifies this with the preceding complete-coefficient calculation. Inverse image on these hearts is exact by BQ and BX.3. The stratum support sequence is BX.2, constructibility of ordinary direct image is BV, and finite direct image is exact: proper comparison identifies its geometric restrictions with finite sums on zero-dimensional fibres. BU and finite-coefficient detection then give t-exactness. These assertions include nilpotent thickenings.

BY.1. Moving a monomorphism through an adjunction

Here is an elementary construction we shall use several times. Suppose \(L : \mathcal A\rightleftarrows\mathcal B : R\) is an adjunction of abelian categories and \(L\) is exact. Given \(B\in\mathcal B\) and a monomorphism \(u:RB\to A\), form the pushout \[ \begin{array}{ccc} LRB&\xrightarrow{Lu}&LA\\ \epsilon_B\downarrow&&\downarrow t\\ B&\xrightarrow{v}&B'. \end{array} \tag{BY.1} \] The map \(v\) is monic, because it is the pushout of the monomorphism \(Lu\). Under adjunction \(t\) corresponds to \(w:A\to RB'\), and naturality and the triangle identity give \[ w u=Rv. \tag{BY.2} \] For example, the adjoint of \(tLu=v\epsilon_B\) is respectively \(wu\) and \(Rv\). Thus any class killed after applying a functor to \(u\) is also killed after applying that functor to \(Rv\). The construction takes place inside the constructible hearts whenever both functors preserve them. No injective object of a constructible heart is required.

Call \(P\in\mathcal H_X\) effaceable as a source if, for every \(G\in\mathcal H_X\), \(q>0\), and \(\xi\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(P,G[q])\), there is a heart monomorphism \(G\to G'\) killing \(\xi\). This is a condition on individual classes. Finite lists of classes can be killed by successively applying the condition to their images and composing the resulting monomorphisms.

For an open immersion \(j:U\to X\), derived adjunction gives \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(j_!P,G[q]) =\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_U}(P,j^*G[q]). \tag{BY.3} \] If \(P\) is effaceable as a source on \(U\), kill the right-hand class by a monomorphism \(j^*G\to A\). Apply (BY.1) to \(j_!\dashv j^*\). Equation (BY.2) proves that \(j_!P\) is effaceable as a source on \(X\). Exactness of \(j_!\) and constructibility of the pushout follow from BX.2 and BQ.

We shall also use (BY.1) for \(f^*\dashv f_*\) when \(f\) is finite. In that case both heart functors are exact and \[ H^q(X,F)=H^q(Y,f_*F). \tag{BY.4} \] Consequently an embedding of \(f_*F\) on \(Y\) killing a specified cohomology class lifts to an embedding of \(F\) on \(X\) killing that class.

BY.2. The obstruction in degree one and gluing over opens

For an open \(U\subset X\), put \(P[U]=j_!j^*P\). There is a useful way to extend maps out of \(P[U]\) after enlarging their target. For \(G\in\mathcal H_X\), set \[ Q=j_*j^*G\oplus i_*i^*G,\qquad i:X\setminus U\to X. \tag{BY.5} \] Here \(j_*\) means the degree-zero ordinary image. BV and BQ make \(Q\) a constructible heart object. The two adjunction units give a monomorphism \(G\to Q\): over \(U\) its first component is the identity, and on the complement its second component is the identity. Exact restriction and the joint conservativity of BX.2 detect the kernel.

Moreover \[ \operatorname{Hom}(P[U],i_*i^*G)=0,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}(P[U],j_*j^*G) =\operatorname{Hom}(P,j_*j^*G). \tag{BY.6} \] The first identity uses \(i^*P[U]=0\); the second uses \(j^*P[U]=j^*P\) and the ordinary adjunction. In particular every map \(P[U]\to G\) extends to a map \(P\to Q\) after the monomorphism \(G\to Q\).

We record the exact-sequence arguments involved. If \(0\to A\to B\to C\to0\) has \(A,C\) effaceable as sources, then so is \(B\). Given a class from \(B\), first kill its restriction from \(A\). Exactness lifts the resulting class to one from \(C\), which can then be killed. If \(A,B\) are effaceable as sources, the same long exact sequence proves the assertion for \(C\) in degrees \(q>1\): first kill the image from \(B\), then the lifting class from \(A\) in degree \(q-1\). In degree one the remaining obstruction is a map \(A\to G\) modulo maps extending to \(B\). Thus the same conclusion for \(C\) holds if those obstructions can be killed by enlarging \(G\). Finite sums, direct summands and finite extensions preserve source effaceability by these arguments.

Taking \(A=P[U]\), \(B=P\), equations (BY.5)–(BY.6) handle precisely this degree-one obstruction. Thus \(P/P[U]\) is effaceable as a source whenever \(P\) and \(P[U]\) are. For opens \(V,W\), the exact sequence \[ 0\to P[V\cap W]\xrightarrow{(1,-1)} P[V]\oplus P[W]\xrightarrow{(1,1)} P[V\cup W]\to0 \tag{BY.7} \] is checked after restriction to the four parts of the open cover and its complement. A map from \(P[V\cap W]\) extends after (BY.5), with \(U=V\cap W\), to \(P\), hence to \(P[V]\). This supplies its degree-one obstruction condition. Source effaceability of the first three open terms therefore implies that of the union.

It follows that cohomological effacement on affine open subsets implies it on every separated \(X\). Indeed \(\mathbf1_U\) being effaceable as a source is precisely cohomological effacement on \(U\). Transfer by (BY.3) gives \(\mathbf1_X[U]\). Induct over a finite affine cover, using (BY.7). Intersections of affine opens in a separated scheme are affine: the intersection is the inverse image of the closed diagonal in the affine product of the two opens over \(k\), hence is a closed subscheme of that product. At the induction step \(V\cap W\) is covered by the intersections of \(W\) with the previous affine opens. This proves the induction with the same finite-cover bound.

BY.3. A diagonal kernel with zero ordinary image

For the affine-line projection \(\pi:T=S\times\mathbf A^1\to S\), the actual adjunction unit is an isomorphism \[ K\xrightarrow{\sim}R\pi_*\pi^*K,\qquad K\in\mathscr C_S. \tag{BY.8} \] Here is a deduction from the established trace, valid also for singular \(S\). BI.2 identifies \(R\pi_!\mathbf1_T\) with \(\mathbf1_S(-1)[-2]\), with its specified trace. BN's projection formula and BV.15 consequently identify \[ R\pi_!\pi^!A =R\pi_!\bigl(\pi^*A(1)[2]\bigr) \xrightarrow{\epsilon}A \] with an isomorphism, for every \(A\in\mathscr C_S\). BV.20–BV.21 identify its Verdier dual with the unit in (BY.8), taking \(A=\mathbb D_SK\). These are the specified counit and unit, because those exchange maps transpose evaluation. Biduality proves (BY.8), not merely an unspecified isomorphism of its endpoints. The section of a projection therefore inverts this unit by the adjunction triangle identity.

Suppose now that \(S=\mathbf A^{m-1}_k\), that \(Y\subset T=\mathbf A^m_k\) is closed, finite and surjective over \(S\), and that \(F\in\mathcal H_T\) vanishes on \(Y\) and is lisse on its complement. Suppose in addition that the ordinary fibre-comparison maps \[ s^*R\pi_*F\xrightarrow{\sim}R\Gamma(T_s,F|_{T_s}) \tag{BY.9} \] are isomorphisms at geometric points of \(S\), as complete complexes on the point. This is the extra hypothesis in this construction.

Then \(R\pi_*F\) is concentrated in degree one. To check the upper bound on a geometric fibre, use Torsion sheaves on curves, Theorem 1.1 and Section 10: an affine curve has torsion cohomological dimension at most one. Its curve, normalization and finite-cover prerequisites are supplied by P–AG, AK and AL. The derived first reduction of a heart object has cohomology in degrees \(-1,0\). Finite-coefficient comparison and its two truncation triangles therefore give the upper bound one for the first reduction of its derived sections. These sections are bounded and have finite \(O\)-module cohomology by BV and BU. If their largest nonzero degree were \(a>1\), the coefficient cone would give \[ H^a/\pi H^a=H^a(K\otimes_O^L\kappa)=0. \] Finite-module Nakayama contradicts its nonvanishing. This proves the adic upper bound without replacing derived reduction by an underived quotient.

Degree zero is zero as well. For each ordinary quotient of \(F|_{T_s}\), a section on the connected open \(\mathbf A^1_{\bar s}\setminus Y_s\) has open and closed zero locus. A nonzero section would thus be nonzero everywhere on that open, whereas extension by zero requires its support to avoid a neighbourhood of every point of the nonempty \(Y_s\). This is impossible. Sections of the adic sheaf are the inverse limit of those quotient sections by BP and BX.2, so they too vanish. Negative cohomology is zero for a sheaf. Finally inverse image to a geometric point is t-exact on these constructible categories, and those restrictions detect zero by first reduction and classical geometric stalks. Thus (BY.9) gives the asserted degree-one concentration on \(S\).

Write \(p_1,p_2:T\times_ST\to T\) for the projections and \(\Delta:T\to T\times_ST\) for the diagonal. Define the heart object \(B\) by \[ 0\to B\to p_1^*F\to\Delta_*F\to0. \tag{BY.10} \] The last map is restriction to the diagonal. It is an epimorphism by the support sequence, since \(\Delta^*p_1^*F=F\). Smooth base change gives \[ Rp_{2,*}p_1^*F\simeq\pi^*R\pi_*F. \tag{BY.11} \] For complete coefficients this is the reduction-compatible finite-coefficient smooth comparison of AS and BV.1; completeness detects its cone. The right side is concentrated in degree one. Applying \(Rp_{2,*}\) to (BY.10) consequently gives \[ \begin{gathered} 0\to F\xrightarrow{\delta}C\to\pi^*H^1(R\pi_*F)\to0,\\ C=H^1(Rp_{2,*}B),\qquad Rp_{2,*}B=C[-1]. \end{gathered} \tag{BY.12} \] All terms are constructible by BV and BQ. If \(\Pi=\pi p_1=\pi p_2\), then \[ R\pi_*C= \operatorname{Cone}\bigl(R\Pi_*p_1^*F\to R\Pi_*\Delta_*F\bigr)=0. \tag{BY.13} \] For the last equality, \(p_1\) is an affine-line projection. Under the unit (BY.8), the map \(F\to Rp_{1,*}p_1^*F\to Rp_{1,*}\Delta_*F=F\) is the identity because \(p_1\Delta=1\). Thus the second arrow is an isomorphism, and applying \(R\pi_*\) proves (BY.13). This verifies the actual arrow in the cone.

BY.4. Effacing cohomology on the affine line and on curves

For \(S=\operatorname{Spec}k\), hypothesis (BY.9) requires no higher-dimensional projection choice. Over algebraically closed \(k\) it is the identity at the chosen geometric point. Over a finite field, passage to its algebraic closure is the affine inverse limit of finite étale extensions. AS proves the finite-coefficient comparison for that inverse limit; the coefficient cone and completeness give the complete comparison. These chosen geometric points detect the required bounds.

Take any \(F\in\mathcal H_{\mathbf A^1_k}\). Choose a finite closed \(Y\) containing its nonlisse locus and the rational point zero. Put \(A=j_!j^*F\), and embed \(A\) into \(C\) by (BY.12). The pushout along \(A\to F\) gives a monomorphism \(F\to H\) and an exact sequence \[ 0\to C\to H\to D\to0,\qquad D=i_*i^*F. \tag{BY.14} \] Finite-image exactness and (BY.13) imply \[ R\pi_*H\simeq R\pi_*D=M[0],\qquad M=\pi_*H\in\mathcal H_k. \tag{BY.15} \] The counit \(e:\pi^*M\to H\) becomes an isomorphism after \(R\pi_*\). Indeed the composite of the unit \(M\to R\pi_*\pi^*M\) with \(R\pi_*e\) is the identity of \(R\pi_*H=M\), and the unit is (BY.8).

Over an algebraically closed field every \(M\) already has zero higher cohomology. Over \(\mathbf F_q\), BU identifies a heart object with a finite \(O\)-module \(M\) and an invertible arithmetic-Frobenius operator \(T\), and computes its cohomology by \([M\xrightarrow{T-1}M]\). On \(J=M\oplus M\) use the automorphism \[ T_J(x,y)=(Tx+y,y). \tag{BY.16} \] It defines a continuous \(\widehat{\mathbf Z}\)-action: on every finite quotient \(J/\pi^nJ\) its powers factor through a finite cyclic group, and these actions are compatible. The inclusion \(M\to J,\ x\mapsto(x,0)\), respects Frobenius and is monic. Since \[ (T_J-1)(0,y)=(y,0), \] it kills the induced map in \(H^1\); higher cohomology vanishes by BU. The argument includes torsion \(M\).

Use this embedding \(u:M\to J\), or the identity \(J=M\) in the algebraically closed case, and push out \(e:\pi^*M\to H\) along the monomorphism \(\pi^*u:\pi^*M\to\pi^*J\). This yields a monomorphism \(H\to G\). In the derived category the pushout is the cone of the monomorphism \((e,-\pi^*u):\pi^*M\to H\oplus\pi^*J\). Applying \(R\pi_*\), (BY.8) and (BY.15) identify this cone with the cone of \[ M\xrightarrow{(1,-u)}M\oplus J, \] which is \(J\). Under this identification the map \(R\pi_*H\to R\pi_*G\) is \(u:M\to J\). Thus \(F\to H\to G\) kills every positive cohomology group. Over algebraically closed \(k\), \(G\) itself has zero positive cohomology. Over finite \(k\), only the induced maps are asserted to vanish.

This proves cohomological effacement on every affine curve. First consider an integral affine curve \(X\). Polynomial normalization in Y.5 and AG.1 gives a finite morphism \(f:X\to\mathbf A^1_k\). Apply the affine-line result to \(f_*F\) and then (BY.1)–(BY.4). For a general reduced affine curve, its finite normalization \(\nu:\widetilde X\to X\), proved in AG, is a finite union of integral affine curves and points. The unit \(F\to\nu_*\nu^*F\) is monic: on a geometric fibre it is the diagonal into a nonempty finite sum of copies of the stalk. Kill the image of a prescribed class on each component of \(\widetilde X\), and push the resulting embedding down by the exact \(\nu_*\). The composite embedding of \(F\) kills the original class. Points are covered by BU and (BY.16); nilpotents are removed by BX.2. Finally BY.2 proves cohomological effacement on every separated curve and on every open subset of it.

BY.5. Elementary sources and a separating finite projection

We need the following geometric fact with its separability condition: for an integral affine scheme of dimension \(d\) over a perfect field there are algebraically independent functions \(t_1,\ldots,t_d\) over whose polynomial ring its coordinate ring is finite, and whose function-field extension is separable.

In characteristic zero Y.5 gives the finite polynomial normalization and every finite field extension in characteristic zero is separable. Here is the extra argument in characteristic \(p>0\). For a finitely generated field \(K/k\) of transcendence degree \(d\), take any transcendence basis \(z\). Frobenius identifies the finite degrees \([K:k(z)]=[K^p:k(z)^p]\). Since \(k\) is perfect, \([k(z):k(z)^p]=p^d\), by the monomial basis with exponents from \(0\) to \(p-1\). Computing \([K:k(z)^p]\) in two ways gives \[ [K:K^p]=p^d. \tag{BY.17} \] Adjoin successively elements outside the field already generated over \(K^p\). Each adjunction has degree \(p\), so after \(d\) steps the corresponding monomials form a basis of \(K\) over \(K^p\). Differentiation in these variables, with \(K^p\) constant, is well defined on that basis and obeys the product rule; the relations \(b_i^p\in K^p\) have zero derivative. The universal differential module therefore has basis \(db_i\). In particular \(\dim_K\Omega_{K/k}=d\).

Let \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\) generate the given domain, ordered so that \(dx_1,\ldots,dx_d\) are independent; the differentials of algebra generators span. If \(N>d\), choose a nonzero polynomial relation among them. Choose a sufficiently large power \(P\) of \(p\), larger than every exponent in that relation, and replace \[ x_i\ \text{by}\ y_i=x_i-x_N^{P^i}\quad(1\leq i<N). \tag{BY.18} \] After substitution, the terms involving only \(x_N\) have distinct exponents \(a_N+\sum_{i<N}a_iP^i\). The unique largest one has a nonzero scalar coefficient. Thus the relation is, after scaling, monic in \(x_N\) over \(k[y_1,\ldots,y_{N-1}]\). The original algebra is finite over this smaller algebra. Meanwhile \(dy_i=dx_i\), so the first \(d\) differentials stay independent. Repeating gives a finite polynomial normalization \(k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\), with the \(dt_i\) independent. Algebraic independence also follows from integrality and equality of transcendence degree.

The finite extension \(K/k(t)\) is separable because its relative differential module is zero. To recall the finite-field criterion, separable algebraic generators have invertible polynomial derivative and contribute no relative differentials. After adjoining the maximal separable subextension, a remaining nontrivial purely inseparable finite extension \(L/M\) has \(L\ne L^pM\): otherwise iteration would give \(L=L^{p^r}M=M\) for sufficiently large \(r\). A monomial basis over \(L^pM\), as above, supplies a nonzero relative differential. Hence an inseparable finite extension cannot have zero relative differentials. This proves the criterion and the required separability.

Such a finite projection becomes finite étale over a nonempty principal open \(W\subset\mathbf A^d\). Indeed choose a primitive element of its separable function field, make it integral by clearing denominators, and then invert a nonzero polynomial so that it generates the whole finite algebra. Invert also its nonzero polynomial discriminant. The resulting monic polynomial \(g(T)\) has invertible derivative at its root.
