Here is the lifting calculation: over a square-zero ideal \(I\), a lift \(t\) of a root is corrected uniquely to \(t-g(t)/g'(t)\). Taylor expansion has no higher correction terms since \(I^2=0\), and the unit \(g'(t)\) gives uniqueness. Iterating along the powers of a nilpotent ideal gives formal étaleness; finite presentation gives an étale algebra. The primitive-element proof over the infinite field \(k(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\), for \(d>0\), is Z.3. In dimension zero perfectness already gives a finite separable, hence finite étale, map to the point.

We use this projection to extend a lisse sheaf from a stratum as a summand. For \(P\in\mathcal H_X\), choose an affine open \(U'\) meeting a generic point of its support closure such that \(Z=U'\cap\overline{\operatorname{supp}P}\) is integral, closed in \(U'\), and \(P|_Z\) is lisse, while \(P\) is zero off \(Z\) in \(U'\). Such an open exists by removing the other components, the boundary of a locally constant stratum and then taking a principal neighbourhood of that generic point. Reducing \(Z\) does not change its coefficient category.

Choose the separating finite projection of \(Z\) just proved. Its coordinate functions lift along the surjection of affine coordinate rings, giving \(h':U'\to\mathbf A^d\). Restrict to \(U=h'^{-1}(W)\) and rename \(Z\cap U\) as \(Z\), so \(f=h'|_Z:Z\to W\) is finite étale. For \(G=P|_Z\), let \[ L=h^*f_*G,\qquad V=U\setminus Z,\qquad h=h'|_U. \tag{BY.19} \] Finite étale pushforward and inverse image make \(L\) lisse on \(U\). The diagonal is an open and closed component of \(Z\times_W Z\). Finite base change therefore exhibits \(G\) as a direct summand of \(f^*f_*G=i^*L\). Pushing by \(i:Z\to U\) gives \[ P|_U=i_*G\ \text{as a direct summand of}\ i_*i^*L=L/L[V]. \tag{BY.20} \] The last equality is the exact support sequence, not a claim that \(L\) itself extends \(G\).

Extend (BY.20) by zero to \(X\). The quotient \(P/P[U]\) has support closure a proper closed subset of the old support closure, missing the selected generic point. Noetherian induction yields a finite filtration of \(P\) whose successive quotients are summands of sheaves \[ j_!\bigl(L/L[V]\bigr),\qquad V\subset U,\quad j:U\to X. \tag{BY.21} \] For a finite-dimensional scheme termination can also be seen by ordering support dimension and the number of components of largest dimension. If \(P\) has torsion-free stalks on its strata, the same is true of its support quotients, and all the lisse \(L\) in this construction are finite free: their stalks are finite sums of stalks of \(P\), and a finite torsion-free module over a discrete valuation ring is free. This construction works over finite fields as well; (BY.18) did not require an infinite field.

BY.6. From cohomological effacement to every higher extension

Suppose cohomological effacement is known on every open subset of \(X\). For an open \(U\subset X\) and a lisse finite free object \(L\) on \(U\), we have \[ R\mathcal Hom(L,G)=L^\vee\otimes G,\qquad \operatorname{Hom}(L,G[q])=H^q(U,L^\vee\otimes G). \tag{BY.22} \] Locally this is the finite-free matrix calculation of BO and BW, so it is an identity of derived internal Homs, not an assertion about arbitrary constructible \(L\). Both \(L\otimes-\) and \(L^\vee\otimes-\) are exact on the heart and are adjoint. Kill the right-hand class in (BY.22) and apply (BY.1) to this adjunction. It follows that \(L\) is effaceable as a source.

Apply the same argument on \(V\), use (BY.3) to extend by zero to \(U\), and then use (BY.5)–(BY.6) for the quotient \(L/L[V]\). Another application of (BY.3) proves source effaceability of (BY.21). Finite extensions and summands, together with BY.5, prove it for every constructible heart object with torsion-free stratum stalks.

For such a source \(P\), all maps \[ \operatorname{Ext}^r_{\mathcal H_X}(P,G) \longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathscr C_X}(P,G[r]) \tag{BY.23} \] are isomorphisms. Here is the target version of the induction in BT.5. Degrees zero and one are BT.4. For a class in degree \(r>1\), choose a monomorphism \(G\to G'\) killing it, with cokernel \(Q\). The triangle lifts the class to a morphism \(P\to Q[r-1]\). Realize that morphism by induction and splice its heart extension with \(0\to G\to G'\to Q\to0\). This proves surjectivity. For injectivity, write a heart \(r\)-extension as the splice of its first short exact sequence \(0\to G\to B\to Q\to0\) and an \((r-1)\)-extension from \(P\) to \(Q\). If its ambient class is zero, the latter class comes from \(\operatorname{Hom}(P,B[r-1])\). Inductive surjectivity lifts this class to the heart, and inductive injectivity identifies its image with the given \((r-1)\)-extension. The heart connecting map kills it, proving injectivity.

These torsion-free objects generate both categories needed for realization. BP gives a uniform torsion exponent for the torsion subobject of a constructible heart object, with torsion-free quotient. A torsion object has a finite support filtration with terms \(j_!M\), where \(M\) is lisse with finite underlying stalk on a locally closed stratum. N's finite-monodromy construction provides a finite étale cover \(p:T\to Z\) trivializing \(M\). Choose a surjection \(O^a\to M|_T\). The composite \[ j_!p_*\mathbf1_T^{\,a}\longrightarrow j_!p_*p^*M\xrightarrow{\mathrm{sum}}j_!M \tag{BY.24} \] is an epimorphism. On each geometric fibre the last map adds the nonempty finite family of entries; it is onto even when the cover degree is divisible by the residue characteristic. The source is torsion-free, and its heart kernel is torsion-free as a subobject. Thus \(j_!M\) is the cone of a map between two torsion-free heart objects. Support filtrations, the torsion exact sequence and finite truncation triangles prove the generation assertion.

First use the target truncation triangles to extend (BY.23) to every bounded heart complex, keeping a torsion-free source. Then use the source generation just proved and long exact Hom sequences to obtain full faithfulness on all of \(D^b(\mathcal H_X)\). Every bounded constructible ambient complex is realized by induction on its cohomology interval: lift the connecting map by full faithfulness and take its cone, exactly as in BT.3. We have proved that cohomological effacement on all opens implies \[ D^b(\mathcal H_X)\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathscr C_X. \tag{BY.25} \] BY.4 supplies its hypothesis for every \(X\) of dimension at most one. This establishes the asserted integral realization theorem on all separated finite-type curves over finite or algebraically closed fields.

The rational realization theorem follows with its actual functor. By BX.6 every rational heart object has an integral heart model, and BX.5 expresses every positive derived morphism between such models as \(\pi^{-a}\) times an integral derived morphism. Integral realization and BT.5 give a heart epimorphism killing that integral morphism. Its exact rationalization is an epimorphism killing the original rational morphism. The proof of the criterion in BT.5 applies verbatim to the full rational heart and its exact realization functor. Hence (BY.25) holds with the rational heart and the category in (BX.20) as well.

BY.7. The geometric assertion and realization in higher dimension

The following geometric assertion, proved in Appendix CB, runs the preceding proof in every dimension. For \(m\geq2\):

For every bounded constructible \(\kappa\)-complex \(K\) on \(\mathbf A^m_k\), after an automorphism of affine space, there is a closed subset \(Y\), finite and surjective over \(\mathbf A^{m-1}_k\), such that the cohomology sheaves of \(K\) are lisse off \(Y\) and the open compactification \(a:\mathbf A^m_k\to\mathbf A^{m-1}_k\times\mathbf P^1_k\) satisfies \[ s^*Ra_*K\xrightarrow{\sim}Ra_{s,*}s^*K \tag{BY.26} \] at geometric fibres of \(\mathbf A^{m-1}_k\). Over finite \(k\), a finite extension of \(k\) may be made first.

Apply this assertion to the first derived reduction of an integral heart object \(F\). BO and BP then make \(F\) lisse off the same \(Y\). Every functor in the comparison for \(F\) commutes with that reduction, using the two-term free \(O\)-resolution of \(\kappa\), and its cone is bounded constructible and complete. Vanishing after first reduction forces vanishing by BK.4. Thus one coordinate change works for the integral object itself; choosing unrelated changes at every coefficient level would not prove this.

Replacing \(F\) by \(j_!j^*F\), for \(j:\mathbf A^m\setminus Y\to\mathbf A^m\), preserves (BY.26). Its quotient is supported on \(Y\), whose closure in the compactification stays away from infinity because \(Y\) is finite over the base. Proper comparison handles that quotient, and its triangle gives the claim. Proper comparison for \(\mathbf A^{m-1}\times\mathbf P^1\) then turns (BY.26) into (BY.9).

With this geometric input, the induction on affine dimension proceeds as follows. Construct \(C,H,D\) as in (BY.12)–(BY.14). Since \(Y\to S\) is finite, \(R\pi_*H=M[0]\) for a constructible heart object \(M\) on \(S=\mathbf A^{m-1}\). By induction choose \(M\to J\) killing positive cohomology. One embedding can kill all of it: those groups are finite \(O\)-modules, vanish outside finitely many degrees by BV and BU, and finitely many module generators can be killed successively. The counit and pushout calculation following (BY.15) then give \(F\to G\) killing all positive cohomology on \(\mathbf A^m\).

If the coordinate choice required a finite field extension, descend this conclusion without dividing by its degree. For \(q:X_{k'}\to X\), the unit \(F\to q_*q^*F\) is monic on geometric fibres. Compose it with the finite exact image of an embedding of \(q^*F\) killing the pulled-back class. Its cohomology map factors through the killed class on \(X_{k'}\), so the composite kills the original class. No trace splitting is needed.

For an arbitrary affine \(X\), choose a closed embedding \(i:X\to\mathbf A^N\). Apply the established affine-space effacement to \(i_*F\to G\). Exact \(i^*\) gives an embedding \(F\to i^*G\), and the natural diagram \[ \begin{array}{ccc} H^q(\mathbf A^N,i_*F)&\longrightarrow&H^q(\mathbf A^N,G)\\ \Vert&&\downarrow\\ H^q(X,F)&\longrightarrow&H^q(X,i^*G) \end{array} \tag{BY.27} \] proves effacement on \(X\). BY.2 handles arbitrary separated \(X\), and BY.5–BY.6 then give full integral and rational realization. Appendix CB proves (BY.26), so this argument gives the higher-dimensional deduction with the same coefficient and foundational inputs as BY.1–BY.6.

The freely accessible comparison texts are Nori, Constructible Sheaves, §§2–3, arXiv version 1 and Barrett, The derived category of the abelian category of constructible sheaves, §§2–3, arXiv version 1. The proof here uses the established étale constructibility and duality arguments, the explicit target pushouts, and the separating projection (BY.18). It does not import a topological constructibility theorem from Nori's Proposition 3.4.

For \(m\geq2\), Barrett's geometric argument for (BY.26) uses a dimension bound for étale microsupport and a transversality comparison at infinity. BZ proves the Radon inversion triangle and projective incidence dimension estimate. CA proves that the resulting cone controls transverse tests, and proves the canonical exceptional inverse-image comparison for transverse maps. CB proves the quadratic coordinate change at infinity, the characteristic-two descent of the actual comparison map, and the finite-field choice. The realization deduction retains the recursive prerequisites of BY.1–BY.6; it does not supply the separate nearby-cycle, weight or other later lesson theorems.

Appendix BZ. Projective incidence and the dimension of non-acyclic directions

Let \(k\) be a finite or algebraically closed field, and let \(\kappa\) be a finite coefficient field of characteristic \(\ell\ne\operatorname{char}k\). All complexes in this appendix are bounded and constructible unless another description is given. We prove the projective incidence dimension estimate needed to construct a cotangent bound for BY.26. We also prove the Radon inversion triangle, including its coefficient maps. The subsequent passage from that bound to noncharacteristic exceptional inverse image is a separate assertion.

BZ.1. Detecting failure of universal local acyclicity

For a finite-type map \(f:X\to Z\), a geometric point \(z\) of \(Z\), and a geometric point \(t\) of the strict localization \(Z_{(z)}\), put \[ X_z\xrightarrow{i}X\times_ZZ_{(z)} \xleftarrow{u}X_t,\qquad \Phi_f(K)_{z,t} =\operatorname{Cone}\bigl(K|_{X_z}\longrightarrow i^*Ru_*(K|_{X_t})\bigr). \tag{BZ.1} \] The morphism is the adjunction unit followed by restriction. AT.1–AT.4 identify its stalk at \(x\) with the restriction map from \(K_x\) to cohomology on the selected local geometric fibre. Thus the vanishing of (BZ.1) for all \(z,t\) is precisely local acyclicity. Universal local acyclicity requires the same vanishing after every change of base.

Let \(E_f(K)\) be the closure in \(X\) of the union of the images of the supports of (BZ.1), allowing every change of base \(Z'\to Z\) before forming the pair \(z,t\). Here the support means the union of the nonzero cohomology stalks; the nearby-cycle complex need not be constructible. This definition gives the smallest closed subset outside which \(f\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(K\). Indeed vanishing of the restricted cone is equivalent to vanishing at all of its geometric stalks. A closed set contains the support images if and only if its complement has that property after every base change.

The construction is local for the étale topology of source and base. For an étale neighbourhood, strict localizations at compatible geometric points agree, and therefore the local fibre and the unit in (BZ.1) agree. Taking closures commutes with restriction to an open set. These observations also prove \[ E_{f|_V}(K|_V)=E_f(K)\cap V \tag{BZ.2} \] for an open \(V\subset X\), and the corresponding inverse-image equality for étale changes of source or base. This argument uses the selected lift, as in AT.4; it does not identify an entire base-changed strict localization with one of its factors.

If \(f\) is smooth and \(K\) has locally constant cohomology on \(X\setminus D\), then \[ E_f(K)\subset D. \tag{BZ.3} \] For one locally constant sheaf this is AT.2–AT.3, or Smooth base change and local acyclicity, Lemma 9.2. For a bounded complex use its finitely many truncation triangles: (BZ.1) is exact in the coefficient complex, and two zero cones give the third. Local constancy and smoothness persist under every base change. No acyclicity of a whole smooth affine fibre is asserted.

BZ.2. Proper transport and finite detection

Suppose \(r:X\to Y\) is proper, \(g:Y\to Z\), and \(f=gr\). Then \[ E_g(Rr_*K)\subset r(E_f(K)). \tag{BZ.4} \] If \(r|_{E_f(K)}\) is finite, equality holds.

Here is the comparison that proves both assertions. Use the strict-local diagram of BZ.1 for \(f\) and \(g\). Proper base change identifies restriction of \(Rr_*K\) to either geometric fibre with proper image of the corresponding restriction of \(K\). On the strict-local total spaces, derived composition and the equality of the two maps from \(X_t\) to the total space over \(Y\) identify the ordinary direct images. A final proper base change along \(Y_z\) therefore gives \[ \Phi_g(Rr_*K)_{z,t} \simeq Rr_{z,*}\Phi_f(K)_{z,t}. \tag{BZ.5} \] Naturality of the adjunction units gives this isomorphism on the cones themselves. The proper comparison applies to these bounded-below torsion complexes by BE.7–BE.8; constructibility of the nearby cycles is unnecessary.

The support of a proper direct image is contained in the image of the support. Consequently each support image on the left of (BZ.5) lies in the proper image of the corresponding support image on the right. Apply this after every \(Z'\to Z\) and take closures. Proper maps are closed, so (BZ.4) follows.

For the reverse inclusion under the finiteness hypothesis, give \(E_f(K)\) its reduced closed scheme structure. The cone in (BZ.5) is supported on its pullback to \(X_z\), since a point of nonzero cohomology would otherwise contribute to the defining support union outside \(E_f(K)\). The closed-support equivalence and finite direct-image formula of AL.1 and BE give, for every geometric \(y\in Y_z\), \[ \bigl(Rr_{z,*}\Phi_f(K)_{z,t}\bigr)_y \simeq \bigoplus_{x\in E_f(K)\times_Y y} \bigl(\Phi_f(K)_{z,t}\bigr)_x. \tag{BZ.6} \] The sum is finite. It vanishes exactly when all its summands vanish, in each cohomological degree. Thus the support in (BZ.5) is exactly the image of the other support. This reasoning remains valid after every base change. Taking the union and then its closure proves equality in (BZ.4), because for a proper map \(r\) and any subset \(A\), continuity and closedness give \(r(\overline A)=\overline{r(A)}\). In particular, under this hypothesis, \[ \dim E_g(Rr_*K)=\dim E_f(K), \tag{BZ.7} \] with empty sets omitted. Finiteness, rather than an Euler characteristic or an alternating sum, prevents cancellation in this argument.

BZ.3. The projective-space calculation with its maps

For a projective bundle \(a:\mathbf P(V)\to S\) of relative dimension \(d\), the powers of the Kummer class \(c=c_1(\mathcal O(1))\) give \[ \bigoplus_{q=0}^{d}\kappa_S(-q)[-2q] \xrightarrow{(1,c,\ldots,c^d)}Ra_*\kappa_{\mathbf P(V)} \quad\text{as an isomorphism.} \tag{BZ.8} \] We spell out the normalization. The finite-coefficient versions of BG, BH and BJ give proper support, projection and the smooth trace. Iterating the affine-line calculation BI.2 gives \[ R\Gamma_c(\mathbf A^d_{\bar k},\kappa) =\kappa(-d)[-2d] \tag{BZ.9} \] with the product trace; BJ.3–BJ.6 prove its independence of coordinates and its compatibility with smooth-pair Gysin maps.

The closed hyperplane \(\mathbf P^{d-1}\) and its affine complement, together with (BZ.9), prove by induction that geometric \(\mathbf P^d\) has one copy of \(\kappa(-q)\) in each degree \(2q\), \(0\le q\le d\), and no other cohomology. Explicitly, the localization triangle with \(j_!\kappa\) has a term concentrated in degree \(2d\), while the hyperplane has degrees at most \(2d-2\). Its long exact sequence is therefore an isomorphism to the hyperplane in smaller degrees and an isomorphism from compact affine cohomology in degree \(2d\).

The class \(c\) restricts to the hyperplane class. Its powers are the generators in degrees below \(2d\) by induction. The smooth-pair Gysin counit for a hyperplane sends \(1\) to \(c\): on a local coordinate chart this is the Kummer boundary calculation in BJ.6, and its line-bundle transition functions give \(\mathcal O(1)\). The projection formula then sends the hyperplane's \(c^{d-1}\) to \(c^d\). The iterated trace sends that class to \(1\), by compatibility of the Gysin counit and the smooth trace. Hence \(c^d\) is the normalized top generator too. The case \(d=0\) is the identity.

Over any finite-type \(S\), the same global Kummer powers define the map (BZ.8). Proper base change identifies its geometric stalks with the just-proved isomorphisms. Stalks detect an isomorphism, proving (BZ.8), also when \(S\) is singular. This proves the splitting by actual classes; it does not merely list the ranks of the direct images.

Write \(P=\mathbf P^n_k\), let \(P^\vee\) parametrize its hyperplanes, and let \[ Q=\{(x,H):x\in H\}\subset P\times P^\vee, \qquad p:Q\to P,\quad p^\vee:Q\to P^\vee. \] For \(n\ge1\) define \[ \mathcal R F=Rp^\vee_*p^*F[n-1], \qquad \mathcal R^\vee G=Rp_*p^{\vee *}G[n-1]. \tag{BZ.10} \] Proper constructibility from M and BV makes these bounded constructible complexes. They are not ordinary unshifted direct images.

Consider \[ W=\{(x,H,y):x,y\in H\} \xrightarrow{b}P\times P. \] The fibre is \(\mathbf P^{n-2}\) when \(x\ne y\), and \(\mathbf P^{n-1}\) when \(x=y\). For \(n=1\) the off-diagonal fibre is empty. Pull back the hyperplane class from \(P^\vee\). Its powers through \(n-2\) define a map \[ B:=\bigoplus_{q=0}^{n-2}\kappa_{P\times P}(-q)[-2q] \longrightarrow Rb_*\kappa_W. \] The sum is zero for \(n=1\). By (BZ.8) and proper base change its cone is supported on the diagonal \(\delta:P\to P\times P\). Restriction of the cone to that diagonal is \(\kappa_P(-(n-1))[-2(n-1)]\): over the diagonal \(b\) is the projective bundle of hyperplanes through a point, and (BZ.8) identifies the displayed map with precisely the first \(n-1\) summands. The exact closed-support equivalence identifies the whole cone with its closed direct image. We have therefore proved the distinguished triangle \[ B\longrightarrow Rb_*\kappa_W \longrightarrow\delta_*\kappa_P(-(n-1))[-2(n-1)] \longrightarrow B[1]. \tag{BZ.11} \]

Tensor (BZ.11) with the inverse image of \(F\) from the first factor, and take proper image to the second factor. The projection formula and proper base change identify the middle transform, shifted by \(2n-2\), with \(\mathcal R^\vee\mathcal R F\). The diagonal term is \(F(-(n-1))\). The first term is \[ L_F= \bigoplus_{q=0}^{n-2} a_P^*R\Gamma(P,F)(-q)[\,2n-2-2q\,], \tag{BZ.12} \] where \(a_P:P\to\operatorname{Spec}k\). Thus \[ L_F\longrightarrow\mathcal R^\vee\mathcal R F \longrightarrow F(-(n-1))\longrightarrow L_F[1]. \tag{BZ.13} \] Over a finite field, \(R\Gamma(P,F)\) in (BZ.12) denotes the derived direct image to the étale topos of \(\operatorname{Spec}k\), retaining its Galois action. It is not the complex obtained by subsequently taking Galois invariants. Consequently \(L_F\) has locally constant cohomology over either allowed base field. Interchanging \(P\) and \(P^\vee\) proves the other inversion triangle. The proof uses no perverse-sheaf decomposition, semisimplicity or characteristic-cycle formula.

BZ.4. The incidence dimension estimate in families

Let \(S\) be an integral finite-type \(k\)-scheme, \(V\) a vector bundle of rank \(n+1\), \(P=\mathbf P(V)\), and \(P^\vee=\mathbf P(V^\vee)\). Denote the relative incidence projections by \(p:Q\to P\) and \(p^\vee:Q\to P^\vee\). For every \(G\in D_c^b(P,\kappa)\), there is a dense open \(S^\circ\subset S\) such that \[ \dim\bigl(E_{p^\vee}(p^*G)|_{S^\circ}\bigr) \le \dim S+n-1=\dim P-1. \tag{BZ.14} \] The dimension is absolute, not relative to a fibre of \(P^\vee\).

Choose a proper closed \(D\subset P\) outside which all cohomology sheaves of \(G\) are locally constant. Such a \(D\) exists by constructibility at the generic point and the finite cohomological interval. Smoothness of \(p^\vee\) and (BZ.3) give \[ E_{p^\vee}(p^*G)\subset p^{-1}(D). \tag{BZ.15} \] For \(n=0\) the incidence scheme is empty. For \(n=1\) it is isomorphic to both projective bundles, so (BZ.15) proves the bound. Proceed by induction on \(n\).

Take a relative line \(T\subset P\) whose generic point is outside \(D\), and begin with \(T^\circ=T\setminus D\). A hyperplane not containing \(T\) meets it at one point. Let \(P^\vee_{(T^\circ)}\) be the open set of hyperplanes whose intersection point \(t\) lies in \(T^\circ\), and let \(Q_{(T^\circ)}\) be its inverse image in \(Q\). Over \(T^\circ\), let \(\bar P\) parametrize the lines \(L\subset P_s\) through \(t\); it is a projective bundle of relative dimension \(n-1\). Let \(\widetilde P\) parametrize \((t,x,L)\) with \(x,t\in L\), with maps \[ q:\widetilde P\to P,\qquad r_T:\widetilde P\to\bar P. \] The latter is a projective-line bundle. Let \(\bar Q\) parametrize \((t,L,H)\) with \(L\subset H\) and \(H\cap T=\{t\}\). Let \(\widetilde Q\) additionally parametrize \(x\in L\). Its maps fit into \[ \begin{matrix} \widetilde P&\xleftarrow{\widetilde p}&\widetilde Q &\xrightarrow{\widetilde q}&Q_{(T^\circ)}\\ r_T\downarrow&&\downarrow r&&\downarrow p^\vee\\ \bar P&\xleftarrow{\bar p}&\bar Q &\xrightarrow{\bar p^\vee}&P^\vee_{(T^\circ)} . \end{matrix} \tag{BZ.16} \] The left square is cartesian, \(r\) is a projective-line bundle, and \(p\widetilde q=q\widetilde p\). Write this common map as \(\pi\).

For clarity, these assertions can be checked in vector spaces. For a line \(kt\subset V_s\), lines \(L\) through \(t\) are one-dimensional subspaces of \(V_s/kt\). A hyperplane \(H\) through \(t\) is a hyperplane in this quotient; excluding those containing \(T_s\) is an open condition in its dual projective space. Hence the bottom row is an open restriction of the incidence correspondence of \(\bar P/T^\circ\). For fixed \((t,L,H)\), the possible \(x\)'s form \(L\simeq\mathbf P^1\). The maps \(\widetilde Q\to P^\vee_{(T^\circ)}\) and \(Q_{(T^\circ)}\to P^\vee_{(T^\circ)}\) are smooth: the first has fibres the projective-line bundle over the \(\mathbf P^{n-2}\) of lines through \(t\) in \(H\), and both descriptions are relative flag bundles on coordinate charts.

Off \(x=t\), \(\widetilde q\) is an isomorphism, since \(x\) and \(t\) determine the unique line \(L\). On \(x=t\) the point lies outside \(D\). By smoothness and (BZ.3), both non-acyclicity loci avoid that exceptional locus. Étale locality and (BZ.2) consequently identify \[ E_{p^\vee\widetilde q}(\pi^*G) \simeq E_{p^\vee}(p^*G)\cap Q_{(T^\circ)}. \tag{BZ.17} \] Moreover \(\pi^{-1}(D)\to\bar Q\) is finite. It is proper as a closed subscheme of the projective-line bundle \(r\). No geometric fibre is the whole line, because its point \(x=t\) is outside \(D\). A proper closed subset of a projective line has finitely many points, so the map is quasi-finite and hence finite by AU.6/AW. The same is true for the closed subset on the left of (BZ.17).

Set \(\bar G=Rr_{T,*}q^*G\). Proper base change in the left square of (BZ.16) gives \(Rr_*\pi^*G=\bar p^*\bar G\). Applying BZ.2, including its equality case, now yields \[ \begin{aligned} \dim\bigl(E_{p^\vee}(p^*G)\cap Q_{(T^\circ)}\bigr) &=\dim E_{p^\vee\widetilde q}(\pi^*G)\\ &=\dim E_{\bar p^\vee}(\bar p^*\bar G). \end{aligned} \tag{BZ.18} \] The induction hypothesis applies to the projective bundle \(\bar P/T^\circ\). Shrinking \(T^\circ\) to a dense open gives a bound \(\dim T^\circ+(n-1)-1=\dim S+n-1\) on the last line. We have proved (BZ.14) on \(Q_{(T^\circ)}\) for each such line \(T\).

We finish the covering argument. After an étale neighbourhood of the generic point of \(S\), and then shrinking \(S\), choose a projective coordinate frame \(x_0,\ldots,x_n\) outside \(D\). Indeed the choices form a nonempty open of the space of frames over the function field; over its separable closure this open has a point. Its finitely many coordinates lie in a finite separable extension, which spreads to an étale neighbourhood. A basis stays a basis after shrinking, and avoiding \(D\) is open. An estimate over this neighbourhood descends to its open image by the étale equality of BZ.1 and invariance of dimension under an étale map.

Each line \(T_{ij}\) joining \(x_i\) and \(x_j\) is good. Apply (BZ.18) to its dense open \(T_{ij}^\circ\). Shrink \(S\) so that every complement \(T_{ij}\setminus T_{ij}^\circ\) is finite over \(S\): it is a proper closed subset of a projective-line bundle with finite generic fibre; removing the closed locus of positive-dimensional fibres makes it proper and quasi-finite. In this particular bundle that locus is exactly the closed set where all coefficients of a finite collection of homogeneous defining equations vanish, so no fibre-dimension theorem is needed for this step.

There are only finitely many hyperplanes in any geometric fibre outside the union of the \(P^\vee_{(T_{ij}^\circ)}\). To see this, write a hyperplane as \(\sum a_iX_i=0\) and choose an index with \(a_i\ne0\). For each \(j\ne i\), the line \(T_{ij}\) is not contained in the hyperplane, and its intersection point determines \(a_j/a_i\). Every such intersection must belong to the specified finite complement. These finitely many choices determine the hyperplane, and there are only \(n+1\) choices for \(i\). The residual closed subset of \(P^\vee\) is therefore proper and quasi-finite over \(S\), hence finite.

The inverse image of this residual subset in \(Q\) is a projective bundle of relative dimension \(n-1\) over a finite \(S\)-scheme; its dimension is at most \(\dim S+n-1\). On the other finitely many open sets the same bound was proved in (BZ.18). Their union with that residual inverse image covers \(Q\), proving (BZ.14).

BZ.5. A cotangent candidate and the next comparison

Over \(S=\operatorname{Spec}k\), (BZ.14) requires no shrinking. Thus for every \(G\) on \(\mathbf P^n\), \[ \dim E_{p^\vee}(p^*G)\le n-1. \tag{BZ.19} \] Apply the version with \(P\) and \(P^\vee\) interchanged to \(G=\mathcal RF\). The incidence variety identifies with \(\mathbf P(T^*P)\): a pair \((x,H)\) gives the conormal line of \(H\) at \(x\), and a nonzero covector up to scale determines that hyperplane uniquely. This is an isomorphism on the usual affine coordinate charts. Form the cone over the closed subset \(E_p(p^{\vee *}\mathcal RF)\subset Q\) under this identification, and adjoin the zero section. It is a closed conical subset \(C_F\subset T^*P\) with \[ \dim C_F\le n. \tag{BZ.20} \] The cone over a nonempty projective subset has dimension one larger, as is seen by trivializing the tautological line on its projective charts; adjoining the zero section adds a subset of dimension \(n\). This proves the bound also when the incidence subset is empty.

For \(F\) on affine space, extend it by zero to projective space and restrict this candidate cone back to the affine open. The same dimension bound holds. CA.1–CA.4 prove that every transverse test pair is universally locally acyclic, and CA.5–CA.6 prove the canonical exceptional inverse-image comparison for transverse maps. These comparisons turn the candidate into a microsupport bound. Appendix CB supplies the quadratic coordinate construction at infinity needed in (BY.26). Higher-dimensional realization uses that construction together with the coefficient comparisons and foundational hypotheses of BY–CA.

The freely accessible source for the incidence construction and its dimension induction is Beilinson, Constructible sheaves are holonomic, version 7, §§1.6 and 3. The arguments above supply the projective cohomology, kernel triangle, finite-support detection and covering steps used here.

Appendix CA. Transverse tests and exceptional inverse image

We keep the finite field of coefficients \(\kappa\) and the base-field assumptions of BZ. The aim is to prove that the cone constructed there controls transverse tests, and to prove the exceptional inverse-image comparison those tests imply. We first supply the local-acyclicity composition argument used in passing through the incidence correspondence. All local fibres retain the selected geometric specialization.

CA.1. A local comparison criterion

We need a criterion for a qcqs map \(r:V\to S\) and a bounded-below torsion complex \(K\). In its applications \(S\) and \(V\) are strict localizations or affine-transition limits of finite-type schemes, and \(K\) is pulled back from a bounded constructible complex. Cohomological continuity is therefore the one proved in AS.1 and BA.5.

For a geometric specialization \(t\to S_{(s)}\), let \(Z\) be the reduced closure of its underlying point in \(S_{(s)}\). Let \(N\) be the integral closure of \(Z\) in an algebraic closure of its function field. The selected map to \(s\) is understood. The following condition implies that \(Rr_*K\) commutes with finite, quasi-finite, and affine inverse limits of quasi-finite changes of base: \[ R\Gamma(V\times_SN,K)\longrightarrow R\Gamma(V_s,K) \quad\text{is an isomorphism for every such }N. \tag{CA.1} \] For the statement on strict-local bases, the right side uses the closed geometric fibre of \(N\); its residue field is purely inseparable over the selected residue field at \(s\), which does not change that fibre's étale topos. Condition (CA.1) is imposed after étale localization of \(S\).

We give the algebra and descent proof. The ring of \(N\) is a filtered union of finite integral algebras over the local domain of \(Z\): adjoining finitely many integral elements is module finite. Each such algebra is a domain. A finite algebra over a henselian local ring is a product of local rings, by the idempotent lifting of AX.1–AX.3; a domain has only one factor. The union is consequently local, with purely inseparable residue extension of the separably closed residue field. In addition, every localization of the integral closure has algebraically closed fraction field and is integrally closed. Every monic polynomial splits into linear factors there: its roots in that fraction field are integral and therefore belong to the ring. This proves that the residue field is algebraically closed. A simple residue root of a monic polynomial lifts to one of its roots, and the factorization gives the usual simple-root uniqueness. Thus these localizations are strictly henselian.

Finite maps have exact direct image and proper base change by AX.5 and BE. The same statements for coefficients pulled back along an affine inverse limit of finite maps follow from AS.1/BA.5. A surjective map \(N\to Z\) of this form gives cohomological descent for its augmented Čech nerve. Here this can be proved without a general descent theorem. After taking a geometric stalk, the nerve is the nerve of a nonempty profinite set mapping to a point. Its cochains are locally constant functions with values in the stalk module. Choose a point in that profinite set. Inserting it as the first entry gives the contracting homotopy for the augmented alternating complex. The insertion preserves local constancy. Direct image is exact in the vertical direction, so this stalk calculation proves exactness of the augmented complex of sheaves.

To apply it to the comparison, let \(D(S',s')\) be the cone of \[ R\Gamma(V\times_SS',K)\longrightarrow R\Gamma(V_{s'},K) \tag{CA.2} \] when \(S'\) is strictly local and is an inverse limit of quasi-finite schemes over an étale neighbourhood in \(S\). These cones have a common lower bound: if \(K\in D^{\ge a}\), then they are in \(D^{\ge a-1}\). We prove simultaneous vanishing of their cohomology by induction on degree.

The reductions used in this induction have finite models. Zariski Main factorization AW replaces a quasi-finite neighbourhood by an open in a finite scheme. At its selected strict-local point this is a local factor of that finite scheme; the open has become the whole local factor. Nilpotents may be discarded by étale invariance. A reduced Noetherian finite model is covered by the finite disjoint union of its integral components. The same Čech contraction, now for a finite closed surjection, reduces the degree induction to integral strict-local finite models. Passing to the affine inverse limit is legitimate degree by degree by AS.1. Thus no normalization is assumed finite.

For such an integral model \(S'\), take its integral closure \(N\) in an algebraic closure of its generic field. This is also the integral closure of the corresponding reduced image in the strictly localized original base: the two rings differ by an integral extension, and integrality is transitive. Its comparison cone is zero by (CA.1). Resolve \(S'\) by the Čech nerve \(N_\bullet/S'\). The column-zero comparison cone is zero. If all cones in (CA.2) have vanishing cohomology through degree \(q\), the cones of the positive Čech columns have that same vanishing. To check this for a column that is not local, take its geometric points over the selected closed point; the relevant comparison is stalkwise, and sections on their profinite fibre are exact by the preceding locally constant-function calculation. In the resulting first-quadrant horizontal totalization, a positive column contributes only above degree \(q+1\). Hence \(D(S',s')\) vanishes through degree \(q+1\). Starting below the common lower bound proves all degrees. Only finitely many columns contribute in any fixed degree.

We have proved (CA.2) for all the indicated local bases. Taking stalks gives finite base change for \(Rr_*K\). Open and étale localization commute with ordinary direct image by their slice adjunctions. Zariski Main factorization then gives quasi-finite base change, and the finite-data cohomology continuity gives the affine-limit assertion. This proves the criterion.

CA.2. Locally acyclic maps composed with smooth maps

Local acyclicity is preserved by quasi-finite changes of base in the present setting. For a finite change, localize the original base strictly at the image \(s\), and select a local factor \(B\) of the finite base. Its residue extension is purely inseparable. For a selected point \(x\) upstairs, the finite scheme \(V_{(x)}\times_{S_{(s)}}B\) has one geometric closed point, since its closed fibre is local with a purely inseparable residue extension. It is the selected strict localization upstairs. Its fibre at a geometric point \(t'\) of \(B\) is precisely the original local fibre at the composite geometric point \(t'\to S_{(s)}\). The two restriction maps agree. Thus the original local-acyclicity isomorphism proves the new one. Open and étale changes are immediate from the same local-fibre description. AW factorization and AS continuity give the quasi-finite and affine-limit cases.

Suppose \(r:V\to S\) is locally acyclic relative to \(K\), and fix \(x\mapsto s\). Write \(r_x:V_{(x)}\to S_{(s)}\). We claim \[ Rr_{x,*}(K|_{V_{(x)}})\simeq\underline{K_x}, \tag{CA.3} \] and that this direct image commutes with every ind-quasi-finite base change. The underline denotes the constant complex on the strictly local base, with its actual evaluation map.

To apply CA.1, first consider a normalization \(N\) for a specialization \(t\to S_{(s)}\). Local acyclicity persists over \(N\) by the preceding paragraph. Its fraction field is algebraically closed, and each \(N_{(z)}\) has that same geometric generic point. The adjunction map from \(K|_{V_{(x)}\times N}\) to the ordinary image of its geometric generic restriction is therefore an isomorphism at every geometric point, by local acyclicity. Hence \[ R\Gamma(V_{(x)}\times_SN,K) \xrightarrow{\sim}R\Gamma(V_{(x)}\times_St,K) \xleftarrow{\sim}K_x. \tag{CA.4} \] The right arrow is the original local-acyclicity map. The closed fibre in (CA.4) is a closed subscheme of the strictly local \(V_{(x)}\), so its cohomology is \(K_x\), by AT.1. Naturality of restriction shows that the map from the first term to this closed-fibre cohomology is inverse to the same identification with \(K_x\). This proves (CA.1).

For completeness, the criterion must also be checked at a geometric point \(z\) of \(S_{(s)}\) other than its closed point. The construction (CA.4) defines a cospecialization between any two geometric fibres over a specialization: invert generic restriction over the corresponding normalization and then restrict to the closed fibre. These maps compose. To verify this, normalize the closure of the most generic point in its algebraic closure, select the prime corresponding to the intermediate geometric specialization, and use the localization at that prime and the quotient by it. The quotient is again an absolutely integrally closed domain: every monic polynomial lifts to the original ring and its linear factorization descends. Thus the quotient and the localization supply the two intermediate normalization diagrams, up to the purely inseparable and geometric-field identifications already proved in AS. Restriction through the localization and then its residue field agrees with restriction through the quotient and then its fraction field. Pasting the adjunction units, and inverting the generic-restriction units, proves the composition identity. Every fibre over \(S_{(s)}\) has a specialization to its closed point. Its cospecialization to that closed fibre is the inverse of \(K_x\to R\Gamma(V_{(x)}\times_St,K)\), hence is an isomorphism by local acyclicity at \(x\). Transitivity forces every intermediate cospecialization to be an isomorphism as well. Applying (CA.4) at \(z\) now proves (CA.1) there. Thus the criterion applies on the whole strict-local base.

It follows that the geometric stalks of \(Rr_{x,*}K\) are the cohomology of these geometric fibres: a geometric residue point is an affine inverse limit of quasi-finite neighbourhoods. The evaluation \(\underline{K_x}\to Rr_{x,*}K\) is obtained from the evaluation of sections on \(V_{(x)}\), whose derived sections are \(K_x\). On every geometric fibre it is exactly the local-acyclicity isomorphism at \(x\). This proves (CA.3) as a morphism of complexes.

We specify the two limit reductions used in composing maps. First let \(L'/L\) be an extension of separably closed fields, let \(Z/L\) be qcqs, and let \(A\in D^+(Z_{\mathrm{\acute et}})\) have torsion cohomology of orders invertible in \(L\). The canonical pullback gives \[ R\Gamma(Z,A)\xrightarrow{\sim} R\Gamma(Z_{L'},A|_{Z_{L'}}). \tag{CA.4a} \] To prove this, first suppose both fields are algebraically closed. They are then perfect. Every finitely generated \(L\)-subalgebra \(B\subset L'\) is a domain. The separating-normalization argument of M.1 supplies a nonzero \(b\in B\) for which \(B_b\) is smooth over \(L\); this localization is still a subalgebra of \(L'\). Given two such smooth subalgebras, form the subalgebra generated by their finite generating lists and localize it once more in this way. It contains both. Every element of \(L'\) belongs to one of them. Thus \(L'\) is the filtered union of smooth finitely generated \(L\)-subalgebras, and \(\operatorname{Spec}L'\to\operatorname{Spec}L\) is an affine inverse limit of smooth morphisms.

Apply AS.7 to this change of base and the qcqs structural morphism \(Z\to\operatorname{Spec}L\). The étale topoi of the algebraically closed fields have exact sections by AB.1–AB.2, so the resulting ordinary direct-image comparison is exactly (CA.4a). This argument applies to the given bounded-below complex: AS.7 uses its common lower cohomological bound, rather than an unbounded totalization. No finite-type or properness assumption on \(Z\) has been introduced.

For merely separably closed fields, choose compatible algebraic closures \(\overline L\subset\overline {L'}\). Each vertical extension is purely inseparable: a finite separable subextension of a separably closed field is trivial, and the separable/purely-inseparable decomposition in AH.1 applies to every algebraic element. BE.4 identifies the two vertical cohomology pullbacks with isomorphisms, for the actual pulled-back complex. The algebraically closed case gives the isomorphism between the two upper fields. The square of pullback maps commutes, so its remaining edge is (CA.4a). Its construction is compatible with restrictions and successive field extensions because the AS.7 and BE.4 maps have those compatibilities. This is the cohomology-invariance statement of Stacks, Lemma 59.90.2(1), with its deduction from the earlier comparisons given here.

Second, suppose \(\eta=\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to\operatorname{Spec}B\) has image \(\mathfrak p\), and \(\Omega\) is algebraic over \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)=\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak p)\). Then \(\eta\to\operatorname{Spec}B\) is an affine inverse limit of quasi-finite morphisms. Indeed choose finitely many elements \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_a\) of \(\Omega\). Their monic algebraic equations have coefficients in \(\operatorname{Frac}(B/\mathfrak p)\). Invert a single nonzero \(u\in B/\mathfrak p\) containing all their denominators. The subalgebra \[ (B/\mathfrak p)_u[\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_a]\subset\Omega \] is finite over \((B/\mathfrak p)_u\), by the bounded-power argument of K.1. Its spectrum is therefore quasi-finite over \(\operatorname{Spec}B\): the composite is a finite morphism, followed by a principal open immersion and a closed immersion. These subalgebras form a directed system, since any two finite lists and their denominators fit in a third. Their union is \(\Omega\), as every element is algebraic. All transitions are affine, which proves the asserted inverse-limit presentation without requiring \(\Omega\) to be a finite extension.

Now let \(V\xrightarrow{r}S\xrightarrow{g}T\), where \(g\) is smooth and \(r\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(K\). Fix \(x\mapsto s\mapsto t\) and a geometric specialization \(\eta\to T_{(t)}\). It suffices to take the geometric field of \(\eta\) algebraic over the residue field of its image. To see this, pass to an algebraic closure of that geometric field using BE.4, take the algebraic closure of the image's residue field inside it, and apply (CA.4a) to the local fibres after this inclusion of algebraically closed fields. These local fibres are qcqs, since they are base changes of morphisms between the affine strict localizations. The comparison retains the chosen map to \(T_{(t)}\). The inverse-limit presentation just proved, followed by base change, makes \(S_{(s)}\times_{T_{(t)}}\eta\to S_{(s)}\) ind-quasi-finite. Apply the base-change part of (CA.3): \[ R\Gamma(V_{(x)}\times_{T_{(t)}}\eta,K) \simeq R\Gamma(S_{(s)}\times_{T_{(t)}}\eta,\underline{K_x}) \simeq K_x. \tag{CA.5} \] The last map is AT's smooth local acyclicity, applied to the finitely many cohomology vector spaces of the perfect complex \(K_x\). All maps are restriction maps. After any base change \(T'\to T\), the map \(g\) stays smooth and \(r\) stays locally acyclic. Thus \(gr\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(K\).

We also use smooth change of source. If \(e:V'\to V\) is smooth and \(r\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(K\), then \(re\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(e^*K\). In the strict-local nearby-cycle diagram BZ.1, smooth base change AS identifies the pullback of \(Ru_*K\) with the corresponding image upstairs. Its unit is the pulled-back unit. The defect cone upstairs is consequently the smooth pullback of the cone downstairs. It vanishes, before and after every base change.

CA.3. Universal local acyclicity over a field

We prove the generic statement used for the product projection. For \(r:V\to S\) separated of finite type over \(k\), \(S\) integral, and \(K\) bounded constructible, some dense open \(S^\circ\) makes \(r\) universally locally acyclic relative to \(K\).

Induct on the dimension \(d\) of the generic fibre. The empty generic fibre disappears after shrinking for a proper source. The question is local on the source, so one may cover by finitely many affines, take a projective closure of each over an affine base, and extend its coefficient complex by zero. The generic closure has the same dimension. It is therefore enough, at each induction stage, to handle \(r\) proper.

If \(d=0\), properness makes \(r\) finite after shrinking: its positive-dimensional fibre locus may be removed, or equivalently apply the generic quasi-finite locus and proper closedness of its complement. The finite-coefficient proper constructibility proved in Proposition 3.2 lets us shrink again so that every cohomology sheaf of \(Rr_*K\) is locally constant. BZ.2, applied with \(g=\mathrm{id}_S\), says that \(E_r(K)\) is empty: it is finite over \(S\), and its proper image equals the empty defect locus of the locally constant complex \(Rr_*K\). This proves the base case.

For \(d>0\), cover the proper \(V\) by affine opens \(V_\alpha\), and present each as a closed subscheme of \(\mathbf A^{N_\alpha}_S\). For every coordinate \(z_i\), consider \[ u_i:V_\alpha\longrightarrow\mathbf A^1_S, \qquad r|_{V_\alpha}=\operatorname{pr}_S u_i. \] The generic fibre of \(u_i\) over the integral base \(\mathbf A^1_S\) has dimension at most \(d-1\). A component on which \(z_i\) is algebraic over \(k(S)\) misses that generic point; on any remaining component adjoining the transcendental coordinate decreases the function-field transcendence degree by one. The induction hypothesis therefore gives a dense open \(U_i\subset\mathbf A^1_S\) over which \(u_i\) is universally locally acyclic. CA.2 makes \(r\) universally locally acyclic on \(u_i^{-1}U_i\).

After shrinking \(S\), the closed complement \(D_i=\mathbf A^1_S\setminus U_i\) is finite over \(S\). Its generic ideal contains a nonzero polynomial; clearing denominators and inverting its leading coefficient supplies a monic polynomial in its ideal, proving finiteness directly. Hence \[ E_r(K)\cap V_\alpha \subset T_\alpha:= V_\alpha\cap\prod_iD_i, \tag{CA.6} \] which is finite over \(S\). The map \(T_\alpha\to V\) has closed image: its graph is closed since \(V/S\) is separated, and projection from the product with the proper \(S\)-scheme \(T_\alpha\) is proper. Its image is still quasi-finite over \(S\). A finite union of these closed images contains \(E_r(K)\), is proper with finite fibres over \(S\), and is finite by AU.6/AW.

Shrink \(S\) once more so that \(Rr_*K\) has locally constant cohomology, using Proposition 3.2 and the finite cohomological bound. BZ.2 again gives \[ r(E_r(K))=E_{\mathrm{id}_S}(Rr_*K)=\varnothing. \tag{CA.7} \] Thus \(E_r(K)=\varnothing\). This proves the induction, with universal acyclicity throughout, rather than only for the original fibres.

In particular, for \(S=\operatorname{Spec}k\) the dense open is all of \(S\). Every finite-type \(V/k\) is universally locally acyclic relative to every bounded constructible \(K\). After change of base this gives \[ V\times Y\longrightarrow Y \quad\text{universally locally acyclic relative to }\operatorname{pr}_V^*K. \tag{CA.8} \] The proper constructibility input to (CA.7) is the curve-and-proper-support proof of Proposition 3.2; it does not use the generic-local-acyclicity statement being proved here.

CA.4. The cone from incidence controls transverse tests

Let \(X\) be smooth and \(C\subset T^*X\) closed and conical, containing the zero section. A map \(h:U\to X\) of smooth schemes is \(C\)-transverse when \(\ker(dh)\) meets \(C\times_XU\) only in zero. In that case the image \(h^\circ C=dh(C\times_XU)\) is closed and conical. To prove closedness, work on an affine chart and write the map as a map of nonnegatively graded algebras. Modulo the positive-degree ideal of the target algebra, its source algebra has only the zero vertex set-theoretically. Its positive-degree generators are therefore nilpotent modulo that ideal, so the quotient is finite over degree zero. Lift finitely many homogeneous generators of this quotient. Induction on degree shows that their lifts generate the source as a module over the target. The restricted map of cones is finite and its image is closed.

A map \(f:U\to Y\) is \(h^\circ C\)-transverse when \((df)^{-1}(h^\circ C)\) contains no nonzero covector of \(Y\). Since \(h^\circ C\) contains zero, this condition makes \(df\) injective; the coordinate Jacobian criterion AE.1 makes \(f\) smooth. Both transversality conditions are open: the bad locus is the proper image of the projectivization of the corresponding closed cone of kernel vectors. We say that \(K\) is micro-supported on \(C\) if every such transverse pair \((h,f)\) has \(f\) locally acyclic relative to \(h^*K\). The proof below gives universal local acyclicity for its pairs.

Put \(P=\mathbf P^n\), \(G=\mathcal RF\), and let \(E=E_p(p^{\vee *}G)\subset Q\), as in BZ.5. Let \(C_F\) be its cone, with the zero section adjoined. We prove that \(F\) is micro-supported on \(C_F\).

For a transverse pair \(P\xleftarrow{h}U\xrightarrow{f}Y\), form \(Q_U=U\times_PQ\), with \(p_U:Q_U\to U\) and \(p^\vee_U:Q_U\to P^\vee\). Proper base change gives \[ h^*(\mathcal R^\vee G) =Rp_{U,*}p_U^{\vee *}G[n-1]. \tag{CA.9} \] We show that \(fp_U\) is universally locally acyclic relative to \(p_U^{\vee *}G\).

Away from \(E_U=U\times_PE\), the map \(p_U\) is universally locally acyclic for that complex by the definition of \(E\) and base change. The map \(f\) is smooth, so CA.2 proves the desired assertion there. At \((u,H)\in E_U\), the map \[ (p^\vee_U,fp_U):Q_U\longrightarrow P^\vee\times Y \tag{CA.10} \] is smooth. Here is the differential check. Let \(x=h(u)\), \(y=f(u)\), and let \(\lambda\subset T_x^*P\) be the conormal line of \(H\). The cotangent space of \(Q\) is the pushout of \(T_x^*P\) and \(T_H^*P^\vee\) over their common conormal line. This follows by differentiating the single incidence equation \(\langle x,H\rangle=0\); the two derivatives are nonzero and give that common line. Since \(p\) is smooth, base change to \(U\) identifies the cotangent space of \(Q_U\) with the pushout of \(T_u^*U\) and \(T_H^*P^\vee\) along \(\lambda\). Thus injectivity of the cotangent map in (CA.10) is exactly injectivity of \[ \lambda\oplus T_y^*Y\longrightarrow T_u^*U, \qquad(\xi,\eta)\longmapsto dh(\xi)+df(\eta). \tag{CA.11} \] The first transversality condition says \(dh\) is nonzero on \(\lambda\). The second says its image cannot meet \(df(T_y^*Y)\) nontrivially, and that \(df\) is injective. These are exactly the needed assertions. The Jacobian criterion makes (CA.10) smooth near \(E_U\).

The product projection \(P^\vee\times Y\to Y\), with the complex pulled back from \(G\), is universally locally acyclic by (CA.8). Smooth change of source in CA.2 applies to (CA.10). This proves the desired assertion near \(E_U\), and hence everywhere on \(Q_U\). Proper transport BZ.2 and (CA.9) imply universal local acyclicity of \(f\) relative to \(h^*\mathcal R^\vee G\).

In the inversion triangle (BZ.13), the other term \(L_F\) has locally constant cohomology. Its inverse image under \(h\) is locally constant; smoothness of \(f\) gives universal local acyclicity for that term by AT. The defect-cone triangle now gives the assertion for \(h^*F(-(n-1))\), and therefore for \(h^*F\). We have proved \[ F\text{ is micro-supported on }C_F,\qquad \dim C_F\le n. \tag{CA.12} \] Extension by zero to projective space and restriction prove the same existence and dimension bound for every bounded constructible complex on \(\mathbf A^n\).

Two consequences follow directly from the definition. If \(h\) is \(C\)-transverse and \(K\) is micro-supported on \(C\), then \(h^*K\) is micro-supported on \(h^\circ C\). Indeed a transverse test after \(h\) composes to a transverse test before \(h\): if the composite differential kills a covector of \(C\), transversality for the second map first forces its image to be zero, and transversality for \(h\) then forces the covector to be zero. The condition on the test function is preserved by the same image calculation. Also microsupport conditions are closed under triangles, finite sums, direct summands and invertible locally constant twists, since each corresponding defect cone has those properties.

CA.5. The Cartier comparison from a locally acyclic parameter

Let \(f:X\to\mathbf A^1\) be smooth, \(i:D=f^{-1}(0)\to X\), and \(j:X\setminus D\to X\). If \(f\) is locally acyclic relative to \(K\), then the canonical map \[ K\otimes Rj_*\kappa\longrightarrow Rj_*j^*K \tag{CA.13} \] is an isomorphism. We prove it on geometric stalks; outside \(D\) it is the identity.

At \(x\in D\), replace the base by its strict henselian trait at \(0\), with generic point \(\eta\) and geometric generic point \(\bar\eta\). Let \(I\) be its absolute Galois group. The stalk of the right side of (CA.13) is \[ R\Gamma(X_{(x)}\times\eta,K) \simeq R\Gamma\!\left(I, R\Gamma(X_{(x)}\times\bar\eta,K)\right). \tag{CA.14} \] The last comparison is ordinary Galois descent. One can construct it by the Čech resolutions of finite Galois extensions of \(\eta\). Their geometric nerves are finite sets with the same insertion contraction as CA.1. Taking the filtered system of finite extensions gives continuous group cochains. The totalization computes the displayed derived invariants; for bounded-below coefficients every total degree has the usual finite range of nonnegative Čech degrees. AS continuity identifies the geometric-fibre limit in this construction.

Local acyclicity gives the \(I\)-equivariant isomorphism \[ K_x\xrightarrow{\sim}R\Gamma(X_{(x)}\times\bar\eta,K). \tag{CA.15} \] The action on \(K_x\) is trivial: its evaluation map comes from sections on \(X_{(x)}\), on which \(I\) acts trivially. Smooth local acyclicity gives the same assertion for the constant coefficient \(\kappa\). A bounded finite-dimensional complex commutes with the group-cochain construction under tensor product. This is checked first for one finite-dimensional vector space, a finite direct sum of copies of \(\kappa\), and then by the finitely many truncation triangles of \(K_x\). Equations (CA.14)–(CA.15) therefore identify the stalk of (CA.13) with the isomorphism \[ K_x\otimes R\Gamma(I,\kappa)\xrightarrow{\sim}R\Gamma(I,K_x). \tag{CA.16} \] The maps are the actual cup/evaluation maps of the Čech resolutions. No claim about the dimension of inertia cohomology or a trivialization of \(K\) on the whole strict localization is needed.

Take the fibres of (CA.13) and of the identity map \(K\to K\), using the open–closed localization triangles. Closed projection and the exact closed-support equivalence give \[ i^*K\otimes i^!\kappa\xrightarrow{\sim}i^!K. \tag{CA.17} \] This is the usual coefficient map for exceptional inverse image: transpose the closed counit and compare the two localization triangles to identify it. BJ.6's smooth-pair orientation gives \(i^!\kappa=\kappa_D(-1)[-2]\). Thus (CA.17) is the canonical comparison with that twist and shift.

CA.6. Noncharacteristic exceptional inverse image

Suppose \(X,W\) are smooth separated finite-type \(k\)-schemes, \(K\) is micro-supported on a cone \(C\) containing zero, and \(h:W\to X\) is \(C\)-transverse. Then \[ h^*K\otimes h^!\kappa\xrightarrow{\sim}h^!K. \tag{CA.18} \] For \(\dim W=m\) and \(\dim X=n\), the orientation is \(h^!\kappa=\kappa_W(m-n)[2(m-n)]\).

First let \(h\) be a closed immersion of codimension \(c\). Near a chosen point of \(W\), choose functions \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\) cutting it out whose differentials extend to a basis of the cotangent space of \(X\). Such functions are obtained by lifting a basis of its conormal space; smoothness of \(W\) and the coordinate Jacobian criterion give a smooth map to \(\mathbf A^c\) with this zero fibre after shrinking. Every intermediate zero locus is smooth.

Transversality says that the span of \(df_1,\ldots,df_c\) meets \(C\) only in zero along \(W\). In particular the first parameter \(f_1\) is \(C\)-transverse there; openness lets us shrink so that it is transverse near the chosen point. Microsupport makes \(f_1\) locally acyclic relative to \(K\), and CA.5 proves the first Cartier comparison. After restriction to \(f_1=0\), CA.4 gives microsupport on the image cone. The remaining differential span still meets that image only in zero: lifting an intersection would put a covector of \(C\) in the original span. Repeat for \(f_2,\ldots,f_c\). The resulting composite is (CA.18). Compatibility follows by transposing the successive counits; their composite is the counit for the composed closed immersion. BJ.6 supplies the product orientation \((-c)[-2c]\).

For general \(h\), factor it as its closed graph \(W\to W\times X\), followed by the smooth projection to \(X\). The pullback of \(C\) under that projection is transverse to the graph exactly when \(h\) is \(C\)-transverse: a covector in the graph's conormal annihilates its tangent precisely when \(dh\) kills the corresponding covector of \(X\). Smooth pullback gives microsupport for the pulled-back complex by CA.4. The closed-graph case and the smooth exceptional orientation of BJ/BV prove (CA.18), with shift \(2(m-n)\) and twist \(m-n\). The coefficient comparisons compose because their adjoint counits compose; this identifies the resulting map with the canonical one for \(h\).

Thus the cone bound in BZ is a microsupport bound with the canonical exceptional comparison for transverse fibres. Appendix CB applies these results to a quadratic coordinate change at infinity, including characteristic two and finite-field choices.

For local acyclicity and transversality, see Illusie's appendix to Deligne's Théorèmes de finitude, §§1.1 and 2.2–2.7, in the author-hosted SGA \(4\frac12\), Beilinson, version 7, §§1.2–1.3 and 3.3–3.5, and Saito, version 4, §7.4. CA.5 gives the needed exceptional comparison directly through the trait and its canonical evaluation map; it does not assume a characteristic-cycle pullback formula.

Appendix CB. A quadratic projection with constant boundary comparison

We prove (BY.26) over the finite or algebraically closed ground fields of BY–CA. Put \(m=n+1\geq2\), write \(T=\mathbf A^n\times\mathbf A^1\), and let \[ j:T\longrightarrow\overline T=\mathbf A^n\times\mathbf P^1, \qquad D=\overline T\setminus T. \tag{CB.1} \] For a bounded constructible \(\kappa\)-complex \(K\), choose a proper closed \(Y\subset T\) outside which its cohomology is locally constant. Such a set exists by the finite constructible partitions of those finitely many cohomology sheaves. We will find an automorphism \(g\) for which \(g^{-1}Y\) is finite over \(\mathbf A^n\) and \[ i_b^*Rj_*g^*K\longrightarrow Rj_{b,*}i_{b,T}^*g^*K \tag{CB.2} \] is an isomorphism for every geometric point \(b\) of the base. A finite extension of a finite ground field is allowed. Here \(i_b\) is the compactified fibre map and \(i_{b,T}\) its restriction to \(T\). The arrow is the base-change map obtained from the open adjunction unit.

CB.1. Choosing a boundary point and a direction

Use coordinates \((x_1,\ldots,x_n,s)\) on \(T\), and embed it in \(\mathbf P^{n+1}\) by \[ j'(x,s)=(1:x_1:\cdots:x_n:s). \] Write \(\overline Y\) for the projective closure of \(Y\). On the chart \(y_1\ne0\) consider the smooth affine space \(W\), with coordinates \((z,u_2,\ldots,u_n,v)\), and the finite map \[ \sigma:W\longrightarrow\{y_1\ne0\},\qquad (z,u_2,\ldots,u_n,v)\longmapsto (z^2:1:u_2:\cdots:u_n:v). \tag{CB.3} \] The divisor \(D'=\{z=0\}\) maps isomorphically to this chart of the hyperplane at infinity. Let \(H=\mathbb D_TK\). On the smooth open \(T\setminus Y\), this is the locally constant dual complex with twist \(m\) and shift \(2m\), by BJ and BV. In particular its cohomology is locally constant there.

Apply CA.4 to the bounded constructible complex \[ L=\sigma^*j'_!H \] on \(W\). We obtain a closed conical microsupport \(C\subset T^*W\), containing zero, of dimension at most \(n+1\). There is a dense open \(Q\subset D'\) such that every geometric fibre \(C_q\) has dimension at most one. Here is an algebraic proof of this uniform bound.

Write \(D'=\operatorname{Spec}A\), where \(A\) is a polynomial ring in \(n\) variables over \(k\), and put \(F=\operatorname{Frac}A\). The closed subset \(C|_{D'}\) is affine and has finitely many irreducible components. Remove the closures of the images of the components which do not dominate \(D'\). For a remaining reduced component \(Z=\operatorname{Spec}B\), dominance makes \(A\to B\) injective. The transcendence-degree calculation in M.1 gives \[ r=\operatorname{trdeg}_{F}\operatorname{Frac}B =\dim Z-n\leq1. \] Apply the monic-elimination argument of K.1 over the field \(F\). It gives algebraically independent \(t_1,\ldots,t_r\in B\otimes_A F\) such that \(B\otimes_A F\) is finite over \(F[t_1,\ldots,t_r]\). That argument uses only polynomial relations and division by a nonzero field element, so it applies in every characteristic.

Choose finitely many \(A\)-algebra generators \(b_1,\ldots,b_s\) of \(B\). Each \(t_i\) belongs to \(B_f\) after inverting one nonzero \(f\in A\). Enlarge \(f\) by the finitely many denominators in the coefficients of monic equations for the \(b_j\) over \(F[t_1,\ldots,t_r]\). Their equations then have coefficients in \(A_f[t_1,\ldots,t_r]\). The inclusion of this polynomial algebra into \(B_f\) is injective, since the \(t_i\) are independent over \(F\). The bounded powers of the \(b_j\) in their monic equations generate \(B_f\) as a module over it, by K.1. Thus \[ A_f[t_1,\ldots,t_r]\longrightarrow B_f \quad\text{is finite.} \] After tensoring with any geometric residue field \(\Omega\) at a point of \(\operatorname{Spec}A_f\), the resulting algebra is finite over \(\Omega[t_1,\ldots,t_r]\). For each prime of this fibre algebra, its domain quotient is integral over a quotient of the polynomial algebra. The fraction-field extension is algebraic, so its transcendence degree is at most \(r\), again by K.1. Consequently every irreducible component of that geometric fibre has dimension at most \(r\leq1\); an empty fibre contributes nothing. Taking the product of the finitely many choices of \(f\), and the preceding open complement of the nondominating images, gives the required dense open \(Q\). No flatness, equidimensionality or minimality of the microsupport is needed.

Shrink \(Q\) to avoid \(\sigma^{-1}\overline Y\). This still leaves a dense open. A component of \(\overline Y\) is the closure of a component meeting \(T\), so it cannot be the hyperplane at infinity. Its intersection with that hyperplane has smaller dimension, by the dimension calculation in M.1/Y. Thus \(\overline Y\) does not contain the whole chart \(D'\).

A closed conical subset of a vector space of dimension at most one is zero together with finitely many lines, after algebraic closure. To see this, projectivize its nonzero part; the projectivization is zero-dimensional and of finite type, hence is a finite set. Its inverse image is precisely those lines. Consequently, over each \(q\in Q\), there is a nonempty open set of tangent vectors of the form \[ (1,w)\in k\oplus k^n,\qquad w\ne0, \tag{CB.4} \] which are not annihilated by any nonzero covector in \(C_q\). Each of the finitely many lines excludes a proper affine hyperplane in \(w\)-space: a nonzero functional \(\alpha\,dz+\beta\,du\) cannot vanish identically on all \((1,w)\). The condition on \((q,w)\) is open, because its failure is the image of a closed incidence subset of the projective cone \(\mathbf P(C|_Q)\). Projection is proper.

The linear transformations of \(T\) fixing \(x_1\) include \[ a(x_1,y)=(x_1,Ay+b x_1), \qquad y=(x_2,\ldots,x_n,s),\quad A\in\mathrm{GL}_n. \tag{CB.5} \] Their lifts to \(W\) are \(\widetilde a(z,u)=(z,Au+b)\), and \(\sigma\widetilde a=a\sigma\). Starting at the origin of \(D'\) with tangent vector \(\tau=(1,0,\ldots,0,1)\), these lifts reach every pair in (CB.4): choose \(b=q\) and an invertible \(A\) carrying the last basis vector to \(w\). Such an \(A\) exists by extending each nonzero vector to a basis. We can therefore choose \(a\) so that \[ a(c)\notin\overline Y,\qquad C^a_0\cap\tau^\perp=\{0\}, \quad c=(0:1:0:\cdots:0),\quad C^a=\widetilde a^\circ C. \tag{CB.6} \] The complex \(\sigma^*j'_!a^*H=\widetilde a^*L\) is micro-supported on \(C^a\), by CA.4.

Over an infinite ground field the required open in the affine parameters of (CB.5), with \(\det A\ne0\), has a rational point: a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish on every point of affine space over an infinite field. The latter assertion follows by induction on the number of variables and the one-variable root bound. Over a finite field the same argument works after a finite extension whose cardinality is greater than the degrees of a nonzero polynomial defining a principal open inside the required open. Inductively choose each coordinate outside its finite forbidden root set. Thus all the coordinate choices occur over one finite extension, not over an unspecified infinite algebraic extension.

CB.2. The quadratic map and finite bad locus

Set \[ h(x_1,\ldots,x_n,s)=(x_1+s^2,x_2,\ldots,x_n,s), \qquad g=ah. \tag{CB.7} \] The inverse of \(h\) subtracts \(s^2\), so this is an automorphism in every characteristic. It extends to \[ \overline h:\overline T\longrightarrow\mathbf P^{n+1}, \qquad (x,(s:t))\longmapsto (t^2:t^2x_1+s^2:t^2x_2:\cdots:t^2x_n:st). \tag{CB.8} \] These coordinates have no common zero: \(t\ne0\) makes the first nonzero, while \(t=0\) makes the second nonzero. The whole \(D\) goes to \(c\).

By (CB.6), the closed subset \(\overline h^{-1}a^{-1}\overline Y\) misses \(D\) and equals \(g^{-1}Y\) on \(T\). It is proper over \(\mathbf A^n\). Its geometric fibres are proper closed subsets of \(\mathbf P^1\) missing infinity, hence are finite. Properness and AU.6/AW make \[ g^{-1}Y\longrightarrow\mathbf A^n \tag{CB.9} \] finite. This proves finiteness scheme-theoretically after giving the closed subset its reduced structure; no assumption that its projection is flat is used.

CB.3. Boundary transversality when \(2\) is invertible

Near \(D\), write the projective coordinate as \((1:t)\). Adjoin a variable \(v\) with \[ v^2=1+t^2x_1,\qquad v=1\text{ along }D. \] Restrict to \(v\ne0\) and \(v+1\ne0\). This is an étale neighbourhood \(e:V\to\overline T\), since \(2v\) is invertible, and its inverse image of \(D\) is exactly the selected copy \(v=1\). There is a lift of \(\overline h e\) through \(\sigma\): \[ \kappa:V\longrightarrow W,\qquad (x,t,v)\longmapsto \left(t/v,\ t^2x_2/v^2,\ldots,t^2x_n/v^2,\ t/v^2\right). \tag{CB.10} \] Substitution in (CB.3) verifies this equality of morphisms. Along the selected copy of \(D\), the equation for \(v\) gives \(dv=0\). Hence \(\kappa(D)=0\), all tangent vectors to \(D\) map to zero, and \[ d\kappa(\partial_t)=\tau. \tag{CB.11} \] By (CB.6), \(\kappa\) is \(C^a\)-transverse along \(D\), and therefore on an open neighbourhood of it by CA.4. Open-extension base change identifies \[ \kappa^*\sigma^*j'_!a^*H=e^*j_!g^*H. \tag{CB.12} \] Indeed both sides are the indicated pullback on \(t\ne0\) and have zero geometric stalks on \(t=0\); the open-extension adjunction gives the canonical identification.

CA.4 now gives microsupport on \(\kappa^\circ C^a\). At any point of \(D\), (CB.11) puts this cone inside the line generated by \(dt\), together with zero. The conormal space of a fibre of \(V\to\mathbf A^n\) is spanned by \(dx_1,\ldots,dx_n\), and meets that line only in zero. Thus the fibre immersion is transverse at the boundary. CA.6 applies there. This only requires containment in the conormal line; no equality of singular supports or characteristic-cycle pullback theorem is being assumed.

CB.4. Characteristic two and purely inseparable base change

In characteristic two an equation \(v^2=1+t^2x_1\) would not define an étale neighbourhood. Instead let \(q:\mathbf A^n\to\mathbf A^n\) square \(x_1\) and leave the other coordinates fixed, and let \(\overline q=q\times\mathrm{id}_{\mathbf P^1}\). These maps are finite universal homeomorphisms: on affine charts, and after any base change, their algebra has the form \(A[z]/(z^2-a)\), finite free with basis \(1,z\). Over an algebraically closed geometric field the polynomial is \((z-\sqrt a)^2\), so every geometric fibre is nonempty with one point. This proves surjectivity and universal injectivity as well as integrality. The composite \(\overline h\,\overline q\), on \(1+t x_1\ne0\), lifts through \(\sigma\) by \[ \chi(x,t)= \left( \frac{t}{1+t x_1}, \frac{t^2x_2}{1+t^2x_1^2},\ldots, \frac{t^2x_n}{1+t^2x_1^2}, \frac{t}{1+t^2x_1^2} \right). \tag{CB.13} \] The equality \((1+t x_1)^2=1+t^2x_1^2\) proves the lift. Direct differentiation at \(t=0\) gives \(\chi(D)=0\), zero differential on \(TD\), and \(d\chi(\partial_t)=\tau\). Consequently (CB.6), CA.4 and CA.6 give the same transverse fibre comparison for \[ \chi^*\sigma^*j'_!a^*H =\overline q^*j_!g^*H \tag{CB.14} \] near \(D\).

We will descend the desired ordinary base-change statement through \(\overline q\). The arbitrary-base equivalence (BE.7a), proved in BE.4, applies to \(\overline q\), its open restriction and each of their base changes. Their inverse-image functors are exact equivalences, with exact direct-image inverses. For a cartesian open-immersion square this proves the actual comparison \[ \overline q^*Rj_*M \xrightarrow{\sim}Rj_*q_T^*M. \tag{CB.15} \] For example, apply the conservative exact inverse \(\overline q_*\); composition of direct images identifies the result with \(Rj_*M\), and the adjunction units identify the resulting arrow with the identity. This also proves compatibility with restriction to any geometric fibre. Furthermore proper duality and \(q_T^!=q_T^*\), the two adjoints to the exact equivalence \(q_{T,*}\), give \(\mathbb D(q_T^*M)=q_T^*\mathbb D M\). Thus (CB.14) is precisely the dual coefficient complex required for (CB.2) after the base change \(q\). A cone vanishing after \(\overline q^*\) vanishes before it. This proves descent without asserting that singular support itself is unchanged by a radicial morphism.

CB.5. Duality identifies the actual fibre-comparison map

Work first after extending the ground field so that a chosen geometric base point is rational. The cone used above remains a microsupport after that extension. Here is why this holds for our particular cone. In CA.4 it is constructed by extension to projective space, the Radon transform and the closed universal non-acyclicity locus \(E\). Open extension and the proper Radon transform commute with extension of fields. Outside the pullback of \(E\), universal local acyclicity still holds by its definition. Thus the newly constructed defect locus, and then its cone, are contained in the pulled-back old ones. CA.4 applied over the algebraically closed extension proves microsupport on the smaller cone, hence also on the larger one. This argument applies to an algebraic closure of the residue field of any base point, including a nonclosed one. It does not replace that point by a closed point of the original base.

Write \(M=g^*K\), or \(q_T^*g^*K\) in CB.4. On the open complement of the corresponding finite bad locus in \(\overline T\), the restriction of \(M\) to \(T\) is locally constant. Near the boundary, CB.3 or CB.4 makes the compactified fibre immersion \(i_b\) transverse to a microsupport of \(j_!\mathbb D M\). Its codimension is \(n\). CA.6 and BJ's orientation give the canonical identifications \[ \begin{aligned} i_b^!j_!\mathbb D M &\simeq i_b^*j_!\mathbb D M(-n)[-2n]\\ &\simeq j_{b,!}\bigl(i_{b,T}^*\mathbb D M(-n)[-2n]\bigr)\\ &\simeq j_{b,!}\mathbb D_b(i_{b,T}^*M). \end{aligned} \tag{CB.16} \] The last equality uses local constancy on this punctured neighbourhood and the smooth orientations: the ambient dimension is \(n+1\) and the fibre dimension is one. Both duals include their actual twists and shifts. It is not an assertion that this equality holds through the arbitrary singularities on \(Y\).

Dualizing (CB.16), using biduality and the open and closed exchange maps in BJ/BV, gives \[ i_b^*Rj_*M\simeq Rj_{b,*}i_{b,T}^*M \tag{CB.17} \] near the boundary. This is the map in (CB.2), not merely an isomorphism between its source and target. To check the map, transpose the coefficient comparison in the first line of (CB.16); CA.6 identifies it by the closed counit. The second line is the open-extension pullback comparison, and its adjoint is the open unit. Their pasted adjoint is therefore the restriction of \(M\to Rj_*M\), which defines (CB.2). This is also the unit/counit description of the dual exchange maps used here.

On \(T\), (CB.2) is the identity and requires no transversality assumption, including at \(Y\). In odd characteristic the boundary check descends from the étale neighbourhood \(V\), since quasi-isomorphisms are detected on geometric stalks. In characteristic two it descends by (CB.15). This proves (CB.2) everywhere, for every geometric base point.

Finally enlarge the finite closed bad locus by the section \(s=0\). Its projection is now finite and surjective, and the locally constant complement has only become smaller. The comparison (CB.2) concerns \(K\) itself and is unchanged by this enlargement. Thus all parts of (BY.26) hold. The first-reduction, finite-extension descent and target-effacement arguments of BY.7 give the stated integral and rational realization in every dimension over the ground fields used there. This deduction retains the coefficient-comparison and recursive foundational hypotheses of those arguments; it does not assert the unrelated nearby-cycle or weight theorems.

The free primary comparison is Barrett, The derived category of the abelian category of constructible sheaves, version 1, Theorem 2.1 and Lemma 3.1. The argument above only uses the microsupport bound and the canonical comparison proved in CA. Characteristic two is handled by descending (CB.2) through the base universal homeomorphism, with the maps explicitly identified in (CB.13)–(CB.15).
